events.title: Śveta-Vārāha Kalpa begins
events.description: In Purāṇic cosmology a kalpa is one day in the life of Brahmā, the creator: 4.32 billion human years, followed by a night of equal length when the worlds dissolve. The present one is called the kalpa of the White Boar, after Viṣṇu's rescue of the Earth at its start. Each kalpa is divided into fourteen periods ruled by a Manu; we are in the seventh. These are sacred measures of time in the Purāṇas, not historical or scientific claims.
events.eraDesc: The Purāṇas measure time in vast cycles: four yugas make a mahāyuga of 4.32 million years, and a thousand of those make one day of Brahmā.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Varāha Avatāra lifts Bhūdevī
events.description: In the Purāṇas the demon Hiraṇyākṣa drags the Earth to the bottom of the cosmic ocean. Viṣṇu takes the form of a boar, Varāha, dives, kills the demon after a long fight, and lifts the Earth goddess Bhūdevī on his tusks. The present cosmic day is named after this boar. The great Gupta relief at Udayagiri shows the scene, perhaps as an image of the king rescuing the land. Traditional narrative, not dated history.
events.eraDesc: The Purāṇas measure time in vast cycles: four yugas make a mahāyuga of 4.32 million years, and a thousand of those make one day of Brahmā.

events.title: Svāyambhuva Manu, the first Manu
events.description: In Purāṇic cosmology time is divided into fourteen Manvantaras, each ruled by a Manu who fathers humanity for that age. The first is that of Svāyambhuva ("self-born") Manu, said to have sprung from Brahmā. With his wife Śatarūpā he had sons Priyavrata and Uttānapāda and daughters including Devahūti, Ākūti and Prasūti, from whom the Purāṇas trace sages, gods and royal lines. The date given is a Purāṇic calculation in divine years, not a historical estimate. The Manu works as a genealogical anchor, linking the cosmic story to the dynasties that follow.

events.title: Dhruva's tapas and the Pole Star
events.description: Dhruva, a five-year-old prince, was pushed off his father's lap by his stepmother and told he had no right to sit there. He went to the forest and meditated on Viṣṇu so fiercely that the god appeared and granted him a place from which he could never be moved: the Pole Star, which Indians still call Dhruva. The story is told to children as a lesson in resolve.
events.eraDesc: The Purāṇas measure time in vast cycles: four yugas make a mahāyuga of 4.32 million years, and a thousand of those make one day of Brahmā.

gitaQuote.transliteration: pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ | vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛk sāma yajur eva ca || gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt | prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||
gitaQuote.translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer and the grandsire. I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. events.title: Dakṣa-yajña and Satī's self-immolation
events.description: Satī, daughter of Dakṣa, married the ascetic Śiva against her father's wishes. When Dakṣa held a great sacrifice and invited every god but Śiva, she went uninvited, heard her husband insulted, and gave up her life in the fire. Śiva's rage destroyed the sacrifice. As he wandered carrying her body, Viṣṇu cut it apart, and the places where the pieces fell became the Śakti Pīṭhas, seats of the Goddess across the subcontinent.

events.title: Pṛthu milks the Earth
events.description: The Purāṇas and the Mahābhārata tell that the sages, angered by the tyrant Vena, churned his body and from it came Pṛthu, the first anointed king. The Earth, in the form of a cow, fled him because no one had been feeding her; Pṛthu pursued her with his bow until she agreed to yield. With Svāyambhuva Manu as the calf he milked grain from her, then levelled the ground for villages, farms and cities. The Earth took the name Pṛthvī after him. The story is a myth of the origin of settled agriculture and legitimate kingship.

events.title: Samudra Manthana: churning of the ocean
events.description: The gods, weakened by a curse, are told to churn the ocean of milk for amṛta, the nectar of immortality, and need the demons' help. They use Mount Mandara as the rod and the serpent Vāsuki as the rope, and Viṣṇu as a tortoise (Kūrma) holds the mountain up from below. Fourteen treasures rise, among them the goddess Lakṣmī, the moon, the physician Dhanvantari with the nectar, and first of all a deadly poison.

events.title: Śiva becomes Nīlakaṇṭha
events.description: The first thing to come out of the churned ocean was Hālāhala, a poison that threatened to destroy all the worlds. No one else could contain it, so Śiva drank it. Pārvatī pressed his throat so that it would not go down, and it stayed there, turning his neck blue. This is why he is called Nīlakaṇṭha, "blue-throated". The story presents him as the god who takes the world's poison on himself.

events.title: Mohinī and the origin of Kumbha
events.description: When the nectar finally appeared, the demons seized it. Viṣṇu took the form of Mohinī, an enchanting woman, and persuaded them to let her serve it, then gave it all to the gods. In the struggle over the pot (kumbha), tradition says, drops fell at four places on earth: Prayāga, Haridvāra, Ujjain and Nāsik. The Kumbha Melā is held at these four in rotation.

events.title: Vaivasvata Manvantara begins
events.description: Vaivasvata Manvantara is the seventh Manvantara, the one Hindu tradition says we are living in now. Its Manu is Śrāddhadeva, also called Vaivasvata or Satyavrata, son of the Sun-god Vivasvān. The Matsya Purāṇa and Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa tell that a fish warned him of the great flood and he saved life in a boat. In this age the seven sages are Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Gautama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni, and the four yugas have been cycling; Kali Yuga belongs to its twenty-eighth cycle. The figure given is a Purāṇic calculation, not a historical date.

events.title: Matsya Avatāra and the great flood
events.description: Manu, the first man of this age, finds a tiny fish in his washing water that asks for protection. It grows until only the sea can hold it, then warns him of a coming flood and tells him to build a boat. When the waters rise, Manu ties the boat to the fish's horn and is towed to a northern mountain. The oldest version is in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; the Purāṇas identify the fish as Viṣṇu's first avatāra, Matsya.

events.title: Ikṣvāku founds the Solar dynasty
events.description: The Purāṇas and the Rāmāyaṇa tell that Ikṣvāku, a son of Vaivasvata Manu, became the first king of Ayodhyā and founded the Sūryavaṃśa, the line descended from the Sun. Its later members include Māndhātā, Sagara, Bhagīratha who brought down the Gaṅgā, the truthful Hariścandra, Raghu, Daśaratha and Rāma. The name Ikṣvāku already appears in the Ṛgveda, but the long genealogy is known only from epic and Purāṇic lists, which scholars treat as later compilations. In the tradition, the dynasty is the standard for righteous kingship, and the Buddha's Śākya clan also claimed Ikṣvāku descent.

events.title: Purūravas founds the Lunar dynasty
events.description: Tradition names Purūravas as the founder of the Candravaṃśa, the Lunar dynasty. He was the son of Ilā and Budha, himself a son of the Moon, and ruled from Pratiṣṭhāna, near Prayāga. His romance with the celestial nymph Urvaśī is told as a dialogue in Ṛgveda 10.95, retold in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, and made into a drama by Kālidāsa. His descendants include Nahuṣa and Yayāti, whose sons Yadu and Pūru begin the Yādava and Paurava lines, and so lead to Kṛṣṇa and the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas. The dating is Purāṇic and symbolic, not historical.

events.title: Pan-Homo Divergence & Bipedal Biomechanics
events.description: Divergence of the hominin lineage from the chimpanzee (Pan) ancestor in the Late Miocene. Sahelanthropus tchadensis and Orrorin tugenensis display forward migration of the foramen magnum beneath the skull base, initiating the biomechanical transition to bipedal locomotion. Inverted-pendulum mechanics cut energetic cost of movement across opening African savannahs.

events.title: Australopithecus & Obligate Bipedal Anatomy

events.title: Narasiṃha Avatāra saves Prahlāda
events.description: The demon king Hiraṇyakaśipu had won a boon that he could be killed neither by man nor beast, by day or night, indoors or out, on earth or in the air, by any weapon. events.title: Hariścandra's ordeal of truth
events.description: King Hariścandra of Ayodhyā had never told a lie. To test him the sage Viśvāmitra asked for his whole kingdom as a gift, and then for a fee on top. To pay it the king sold his wife and son into service and himself to the keeper of a cremation ground at Kāśī. When his wife brought their dead son to be burned, he demanded the fee from her as duty required. The gods then intervened. Gandhi recalled that seeing a play about Hariścandra as a boy left a deep mark on him.

events.title: Homo Habilis & Oldowan Lithic Technology

events.title: Tretā Yuga begins
events.description: In the Purāṇic scheme the second age lasts 1,296,000 years, and virtue declines by a quarter from the Kṛta Yuga. People now act for reward, and sacrifice becomes the chief religious practice. Kingship, the four social orders and agriculture appear. The avatāras Vāmana, Paraśurāma and Rāma belong to this age, and the Rāmāyaṇa is its story. The dating is a traditional calculation, not a historical estimate.

events.title: Vāmana Avatāra and Mahābali
events.description: Bali, a generous demon king, had conquered the three worlds. Viṣṇu came to his sacrifice as Vāmana, a dwarf brāhmaṇa boy, and asked for as much land as he could cover in three steps. Bali agreed. The dwarf grew to cosmic size, covered earth with one step and heaven with the second, and Bali offered his own head for the third. He was sent to rule the underworld, with leave to visit his people once a year, which Kerala celebrates as Oṇam.

events.title: Bhagīratha brings down the Gaṅgā
events.description: Sixty thousand sons of King Sagara had been burned to ash by a sage's glance, and only the heavenly river Gaṅgā could free their souls. Their descendant Bhagīratha performed austerities for a thousand years. Gaṅgā agreed to descend, but her fall would have shattered the earth, so Śiva caught her in his matted hair and let her out in streams. She is called Bhāgīrathī after him, and a "Bhagīratha effort" is a proverb for heroic persistence.

events.title: Viśvāmitra becomes a Brahmarṣi
events.description: Viśvāmitra was a king who tried to seize the wish-granting cow of the sage Vasiṣṭha and was routed by its power. His story is the classic proof that the highest rank can be won by effort.

events.title: Paraśurāma Avatāra clears the earth
events.description: Paraśurāma, "Rāma with the axe", was a brāhmaṇa of the Bhṛgu clan who took up arms. When the thousand-armed king Kārtavīrya Arjuna stole his father's wish-giving cow, he killed him; the king's sons murdered his father in revenge, and Paraśurāma is said to have cleared the earth of tyrannical warriors twenty-one times. The west coast, from the Koṅkaṇa to Kerala, is by legend land he reclaimed from the sea by throwing his axe.

events.title: Homo Erectus & Controlled Mastery of Fire
events.description: Humanity harnesses exogenous thermodynamic energy. Homo erectus achieves controlled mastery of fire for cooking, warmth, and defense. Acheulean teardrop handaxes reflect geometric cognitive symmetry; populations expand across Afro-Eurasia.

events.title: Agastya crosses the Vindhyas

events.title: Birth of Śrī Rāma
events.description: Rāma is born at Ayodhyā to King Daśaratha and Queen Kausalyā on the ninth day of the bright half of Caitra, celebrated each spring as Rāma Navamī. events.title: Hanumān leaps to Laṅkā
events.description: Hanumān, son of the Wind, minister of the monkey king Sugrīva, leapt a hundred leagues across the sea to Laṅkā. He found Sītā held in a grove of aśoka trees, gave her Rāma's ring, and refused to carry her back because she wished Rāma himself to free her. He let himself be captured, and when the demons set his tail alight he burned the city with it. This book of the Rāmāyaṇa, the Sundara Kāṇḍa, is the one most often recited.

events.title: Rāma Setu is built
events.description: To reach Laṅkā, Rāma's army of monkeys and bears built a causeway across the sea from the tip of India, directed by the engineer Nala; the stones, tradition says, floated because Rāma's name was written on them. A chain of shoals between Rāmeśvaram and Sri Lanka is identified with it and called Rāma Setu. Before crossing, Rāma is said to have worshipped Śiva there, the origin of the Rāmeśvaram temple.

events.title: Fall of Rāvaṇa
events.description: After a long war in which Rāvaṇa's son and giant brother fell, Rāma met Rāvaṇa himself. Each time he cut off one of the ten heads another grew, until he used the weapon of Brahmā. Rāvaṇa was a great scholar and a devotee of Śiva undone by pride and desire. His defeat is celebrated at Daśaharā, when effigies of him are burned across north India.

events.title: Rāma's return and Rāma-rājya
events.description: Rāma returned to Ayodhyā after fourteen years, and the people lit rows of lamps to welcome him, the origin of Dīpāvalī in the north. His reign became the image of perfect government: no one died young, the rains came on time, and no one went hungry or was robbed. "Rāma-rājya" has meant just rule ever since, and Gandhi used the phrase for the India he hoped for.

events.title: Vālmīki composes the Rāmāyaṇa (tradition)
events.description: The sage Vālmīki, by legend a reformed robber, saw a hunter shoot one of a pair of mating cranes and cursed him in a spontaneous verse. Brahmā told him that this new metre, born of grief (śoka), would be called śloka, and that he should tell Rāma's story in it. The Rāmāyaṇa is therefore called the first poem. Sītā, sent away by Rāma, is said to have borne her twin sons in his hermitage.

events.title: Dvāpara Yuga begins
events.description: The third age lasts 864,000 years and dharma stands on two legs. Disease, desire and disaster grow, the single Veda has to be split into four, and temple worship is the fitting practice. It ends with Kṛṣṇa's life and the great war. The dice throw called dvāpara, "two", gives the age its name. The dating is a traditional Purāṇic calculation, not a historical estimate.

gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.

events.title: Bharata Dauṣyanti, the eponymous emperor
events.description: The Mahābhārata and Purāṇas say that Bharata was the son of King Duṣyanta and Śakuntalā, a hermitage-raised girl whose story Kālidāsa later dramatised. As a boy he was said to play with lion cubs. Grown up, he became a universal emperor, a cakravartin, and the Epic derives the name Bhārata, and so Bhāratavarṣa, from him. Vedic texts also remember a Bharata Dauṣyanti as a great sacrificer by the Gaṅgā and Yamunā. Jaina tradition derives the same name from a different Bharata, son of Ṛṣabha, so the etymology is traditional rather than settled.

events.title: Kuru and the field of Kurukṣetra
events.description: According to the Mahābhārata and the Purāṇas, King Kuru, ancestor of the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas, ploughed a field by the Sarasvatī with a golden plough, practising austerity there. Indra is said to have granted that anyone who died in the field would attain heaven, so it became Kurukṣetra, "Kuru's field". The Brāhmaṇas already call the region the gods' sacrificial ground, and in the first line of the Bhagavad Gītā it is the dharmakṣetra where the great war begins. The area is near modern Thanesar in Haryana, and it remains a major pilgrimage site, especially at eclipses.

events.title: Emergence of Homo Sapiens & Genomic Diversity
events.description: Anatomically modern humans emerge with a rounded globular braincase (1,350–1,500 cm³) and distinctive mental protuberance (chin), identified at Jebel Irhoud. Pan-African population structure and subsequent archaic admixture with Neanderthals (1–2%) and Denisovans (EPAS1 altitude gene) endow modern humans with high immunological and metabolic plasticity.

events.title: Bhimbetka rock shelters and their paintings
events.description: The Bhimbetka rock shelters in Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh, were identified by V. S. Wakankar in 1957. Hundreds of shelters in the Vindhya sandstone hold paintings of bison, deer, tigers, hunters, dancers, and later horse riders. They span the Mesolithic and later periods, with the oldest layers estimated at roughly ten thousand years or more, and some art continuing into historic times. This makes the site one of the longest records of human life in India. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. Dates for particular paintings are uncertain.

events.title: Mehrgarh: first farmers of the subcontinent
events.description: At Mehrgarh, at the foot of the Bolan Pass in Balochistan, people were growing barley and wheat and keeping humped cattle by about 7000 BCE, in mud-brick houses with storerooms. The site was lived in for over four thousand years and shows farming, pottery, copper-working and long-distance trade developing step by step on South Asian soil. It is the main evidence that the Indus civilization grew from local roots.
events.eraDesc: Farming villages appear from Balochistan to the Gaṅgā plain. Barley, wheat, rice, and zebu cattle are domesticated.
events.trustedSource: Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) & Epigraphia Indica Attested Records

events.title: Bhirrana's earliest levels
events.description: Bhirrana, in Fatehabad district of Haryana, lies on the dry bed of the Ghaggar-Hakra, which many scholars identify with the Vedic Sarasvatī. Excavations led by L. S. Rao uncovered a "Hakra Ware" phase beneath Early and Mature Harappan layers, and radiocarbon dates reported from it reach back toward the seventh millennium BCE. If those dates hold, it would be among the oldest known settlements of the plain. Other archaeologists regard the early dates as uncertain and suggest a later start, so the site's antiquity remains a matter of dispute.

events.title: Lahuradewa and early rice
events.description: Lahuradewa, a lake-side site in Sant Kabir Nagar district of Uttar Pradesh, has produced charred rice and a sequence of occupation from pre-agricultural to village life. Excavators reported dates around the seventh to sixth millennium BCE, suggesting early rice use in the middle Gaṅgā plain. Rice from sites like Koldihwa near Prayāgrāj has been discussed in the same context. Supporters see an indigenous eastern Neolithic, independent of the northwestern wheat-and-barley villages such as Mehrgarh. The early dating and the question of whether the rice was truly domesticated are still debated.

events.title: Proto-dentistry at Mehrgarh
events.description: Mehrgarh, on the Kachi plain in Balochistan, was excavated by Jean-François Jarrige and his team from 1974. A study published in Nature in 2006 described eleven drilled molar crowns from living individuals, dated to some seven to nine thousand years ago. Flint-tipped bow drills had apparently been used to remove decayed tissue. The authors called it the earliest evidence of dentistry in a Neolithic farming society, though older cases of dental work have since been reported elsewhere. The settlement also shows early wheat, barley and cattle, and it is the usual starting point for the story of the Indus tradition.

events.title: Cotton fibres at Mehrgarh and Mohenjo-daro
events.description: Cotton fibres preserved in the corrosion of a copper bead at Mehrgarh have been dated to the sixth millennium BCE and are often cited as among the earliest evidence of cotton use. Later, Mohenjo-daro yielded actual cotton cloth, dyed with madder. Indus cotton was an Old World species, probably Gossypium arboreum, spun and woven in the valley, and cotton cloth later appears in Mesopotamian and Greek accounts of Indian goods. The record makes textiles one of the oldest continuous Indian crafts, running from the Neolithic into historic times.

events.title: Kot Diji and Amri cultures
events.description: Kot Diji in Sindh, across the Indus from Mohenjo-daro, was excavated in the 1950s by F. A. Khan. It had a fortified citadel and wheel-made pottery with designs such as fish-scales, pipal leaves and bull motifs. Amri, also in Sindh, shows an earlier sequence leading into the same tradition. These Early Harappan or "Kot Diji" communities of roughly the fourth to the early third millennium BCE are seen as forerunners of the mature Indus cities, which grew from their town planning, crafts and symbols. Some Kot Diji sites show burning at the end of the phase.

events.title: Vyāsa born to Satyavatī and Parāśara
events.description: Vyāsa was born on an island in the Yamunā to the fisher-girl Satyavatī and the wandering sage Parāśara, and so is called Dvaipāyana, "island-born". Tradition makes him the arranger of the four Vedas and author of the Mahābhārata, the eighteen Purāṇas and the Brahma Sūtra, and also the biological father of the epic's kings. Gurus are honoured in his name on Guru Pūrṇimā.

events.title: Early Harappan (Ravi) phase at Harappa
events.description: Harappa, on the old bed of the Ravi in Punjab, Pakistan, was the first Indus city to be recognised, after Cunningham's visit in 1853 and Daya Ram Sahni's and Madho Sarup Vats' excavations in the 1920s. Later work by Meadow and Kenoyer found its earliest levels, the Ravi phase, with small farming and herding settlements from before 3000 BCE. Marks scratched on pottery from this phase are among the earliest signs that later developed into the Indus script, which has never been deciphered. The city grew into a major centre of the Mature period.

events.title: Bhīṣma's terrible vow
events.description: Prince Devavrata was heir to King Śāntanu of Hastināpura. When his father fell in love with the fisher-girl Satyavatī, her father demanded that her sons inherit. Devavrata gave up the throne, and to make sure no child of his would ever dispute it, vowed lifelong celibacy. The gods cried "Bhīṣma!", "terrible", and it became his name. That vow leads, three generations on, to the Mahābhārata war.

events.description: Kṛṣṇa was born at midnight in a prison cell in Mathurā. His uncle Kaṃsa, warned that his sister Devakī's eighth child would kill him, had murdered her first six. events.title: Kṛṣṇa's Vraja līlā
events.description: Raised by the cowherd chief Nanda and his wife Yaśodā, Kṛṣṇa passed his childhood in the villages and forests of Vraja. events.title: Kṛṣṇa slays Kaṃsa
events.description: Kaṃsa invited Kṛṣṇa and his brother Balarāma to a wrestling festival at Mathurā, meaning to have them killed. They defeated his wrestlers and his war elephant, and Kṛṣṇa dragged the king from his throne and killed him. He freed his parents and restored his grandfather Ugrasena as king. He never returned to live in Vṛndāvana, and the gopīs' grief at the parting is a great theme of devotional poetry.

events.title: Kṛṣṇa at Sāndīpani's āśrama
events.description: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa tells that after their initiation the young Kṛṣṇa and his elder brother Balarāma went to study with Sāndīpani at Avantī, the Ujjayinī of later times. In sixty-four days they are said to have mastered the Vedas, the sixty-four arts and the sciences of weapons and government. For his fee, the guru asked that his drowned son be restored, and Kṛṣṇa brought the boy back from Yama's realm. The poor Brahmin Sudāmā is remembered as a classmate in the same tradition. The episode is Purāṇic, not in the Mahābhārata, and its dating is traditional; a Sāndīpani Āśrama is still shown at Ujjain.

events.title: Founding of Dvārakā
events.description: Kaṃsa's father-in-law Jarāsandha, king of Magadha, attacked Mathurā seventeen times. To spare his people, Kṛṣṇa moved the whole Yādava clan to the western coast and built the fortified city of Dvārakā on land granted by the sea. The epic says the sea took it back after his death. Marine archaeologists have found stone structures and anchors off modern Dvārakā, though their date is debated.

events.title: Draupadī Svayaṃvara at Kāmpilya
events.description: King Drupada of Pāñcāla set a contest for his daughter's hand: to string a mighty bow and hit the eye of a revolving fish while looking only at its reflection. The kings failed. When they brought her home their mother, not looking up, told them to share what they had won, and Draupadī became the wife of all five Pāṇḍavas.

events.title: Indraprastha and the Rājasūya
events.description: The Mahābhārata's Sabhāparvan tells that Dhṛtarāṣṭra gave the Pāṇḍavas the wild Khāṇḍava tract, which Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna cleared by burning the forest, and the asura architect Maya built a famous hall there. Indraprastha on the Yamunā became their capital. Yudhiṣṭhira then performed the Rājasūya, the royal consecration of a sovereign, after Bhīma killed Jarāsandha of Magadha. At the rite Kṛṣṇa slew Śiśupāla, who had insulted him. The splendour provoked Duryodhana's envy and led to the dice game and exile. Excavations at Purānā Qilā in Delhi have been linked to the site by some, but the identification is not proven.

events.title: The dice game and Draupadī's humiliation
events.description: Invited to a game of dice, Yudhiṣṭhira played against the cheat Śakuni and lost his kingdom, his brothers, himself and finally Draupadī, the Pāṇḍavas' wife. She was dragged by the hair into the assembly, where she asked a question no elder could answer: can a man who has already lost himself stake his wife? When Duḥśāsana tried to strip her, her garment became endless. The Pāṇḍavas went into thirteen years of exile.

events.title: Arjuna obtains the Pāśupata
events.description: In the Vanaparvan of the Mahābhārata, Arjuna goes to the Himalayan hill of Indrakīla to win celestial weapons by austerity. Śiva appears as a Kirāta, a mountain hunter, and quarrels with him over a boar that both have shot. Arjuna's arrows have no effect, and even in wrestling he is overcome. Recognising the god, he worships him, and Śiva gives him the Pāśupatāstra, a weapon he is told never to use against lesser foes. The episode is the subject of Bhāravi's poem Kirātārjunīya and is a standard image of divine grace given to a persevering hero.

events.title: Kṛṣṇa's peace embassy fails
events.description: In the Udyogaparvan of the Mahābhārata, Kṛṣṇa goes to Hastināpura as envoy of the Pāṇḍavas to prevent the war. He first asks for their half of the kingdom, and then offers to settle for just five villages. Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Vidura and Dhṛtarāṣṭra support him, but Duryodhana replies that he will not give even as much land as the point of a needle can pierce. He tries to have Kṛṣṇa seized, and the envoy displays his cosmic form. Returning, Kṛṣṇa tells the Pāṇḍavas that war is inevitable. The dating is traditional.

events.title: Bhagavad Gītā spoken at Kurukṣetra
events.description: As the two armies face each other, the warrior Arjuna sees teachers and cousins on the other side and puts down his bow. His charioteer Kṛṣṇa answers in 700 verses.¶He teaches that the Self cannot be killed; that one must act according to duty without clinging to results (karma yoga); that knowledge and devotion lead to the same freedom; and finally reveals himself as God. Tradition places the scene in 3138 BCE. Scholars date the text's composition between about 400 BCE and 200 CE. It has become the best-known Hindu scripture in the world.

events.title: The Mahābhārata War
events.description: Eighteen days of battle at Kurukṣetra between two branches of the Kuru family, the five Pāṇḍavas and their hundred Kaurava cousins, after a rigged dice game, a thirteen-year exile and a failed peace mission by Kṛṣṇa. Nearly every warrior dies, and the victors inherit a kingdom of widows.¶Tradition dates the war to 3138 BCE, thirty-six years before Kali Yuga. Historians who accept a real conflict behind the epic usually place it around 1000–900 BCE, in the Painted Grey Ware period. The epic itself insists its subject is not victory but dharma: how to act rightly when every choice does harm.

events.title: Bhīṣma on the bed of arrows
events.description: Bhīṣma, commander of the Kauravas, fell on the tenth day pierced by so many arrows that his body did not touch the ground. Having the boon of choosing his time of death, he lay on this bed for fifty-eight days until the sun turned north. There he taught the victorious Yudhiṣṭhira the duties of a king, the ways of peace and the thousand names of Viṣṇu. These teachings fill two long books of the epic.

events.title: Yudhiṣṭhira's coronation and Aśvamedha
events.description: After the war, the Mahābhārata says, Yudhiṣṭhira was consecrated at Hastināpura but grieved at the slaughter of kin. Vyāsa advised him to perform the Aśvamedha, the horse sacrifice, to wash away the sin, and Bhīṣma instructed him in the duties of kings from his bed of arrows. A consecrated horse wandered for a year, followed by Arjuna, and was brought back to be sacrificed, with wealth fetched from an old hoard in the Himalaya. events.title: Sūta recites the epic at Naimiṣāraṇya

events.title: Rakhigarhi, India's largest Harappan site
events.description: Rakhigarhi, in Hisar district of Haryana, is made up of several mounds and is the largest known Harappan site in India, with an extent comparable to Mohenjo-daro. It lay on the plain between the Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī of the Vedic texts. Excavations since the 1960s, by Amarendra Nath and later Vasant Shinde, found occupation from an early phase through Mature Harappan times. In 2019 a study of ancient DNA from a skeleton there reported no steppe-pastoralist ancestry, a result used in debates over Indo-Aryan origins that remain unresolved.

events.title: Kalibangan's ploughed field
events.description: At Kalibangan, in Hanumangarh district of Rajasthan, B. B. Lal and B. K. Thapar's excavations in the 1960s uncovered beneath the Mature Harappan city a ploughed field of the Early Harappan period, with two sets of furrows crossing at right angles. This is widely cited as the earliest known ploughed field in the world. Scholars suggest the pattern was for growing two crops together. The name Kalibangan means "black bangles", from the many bangle fragments found, and the site lies on the dry bed of the Ghaggar.

events.title: Burzahom's pit-dwellers of the Kashmir valley
events.description: Burzahom, about 16 kilometres north-west of Srinagar, is the northernmost excavated Neolithic site in India. Four phases of occupation are placed between about 3000 and 1000 BCE, and the earliest levels are radiocarbon-dated to before 2357 BCE. The first settlers lived in circular and oval pits dug into the Karewa soil, and later people built houses at ground level over filled pits. Some floors were painted with red ochre.¶Human burials in oval pits include those with dogs and antlered deer, and the third phase is marked by standing menhirs. A trial dig by the Yale–Cambridge expedition in 1936 preceded the main excavations of 1960–71 under T. N. Khazanchi.

events.title: Mature Harappan urbanism begins
events.description: Around 2600 BCE the scattered regional cultures of the northwest merged into a single civilization with remarkable uniformity. From Shortughai on the Oxus to Lothal in Gujarat, bricks were made in the same 1:2:4 proportion, weights followed one system, and seals carried the same script. More than a thousand settlements are known, most of them along the Indus and the Ghaggar-Hakra. No palaces, royal tombs or signs of large-scale war have been found.

events.title: Mohenjo-daro and the Great Bath
events.description: Mohenjo-daro, on the Indus in Sindh, was a city of perhaps 40,000 people laid out on a grid, with baked-brick houses, private wells and covered drains, around 2500 BCE.¶On its raised western mound stands the Great Bath: a watertight brick tank twelve metres long, sealed with bitumen, with steps at both ends and small rooms around it. Nothing like a palace or royal tomb has been found, but this bath has. Many archaeologists read it as a place of ritual bathing, which would make purification by water one of the oldest continuous practices in India.

events.title: Harappa's citadel and the granary debate
events.description: By the Mature Harappan period, Harappa had grown into a walled city with a raised citadel mound, brick lanes, drains, and workshops. Mortimer Wheeler described a "granary" and nearby circular working platforms, though later scholars think the platforms were for pounding grain and doubt the granary identification. Cubical weights found there follow a regular system, showing standardised trade. The city's bricks were taken in the nineteenth century as ballast for the Lahore–Multan railway, which destroyed much of it before archaeologists arrived.

events.title: The "Paśupati" seal
events.description: A small soapstone seal from Mohenjo-daro shows a figure seated cross-legged on a low platform, wearing a horned headdress, with an elephant, tiger, rhinoceros and buffalo around him. The excavator John Marshall called it a "proto-Śiva", seeing the lord of animals (Paśupati) in a yoga posture. Others read a buffalo deity, a goddess or a shaman. Since the script cannot be read, the question stays open, but the seal is central to every discussion of Harappan religion.

events.title: Meluhha trades with Mesopotamia
events.description: Mesopotamian records of the Akkadian and Sumerian periods mention a land called Meluhha, which most scholars identify with the Indus region. Its name was given by the excavators who assumed an authority figure; no one knows who the person was or what office he held. events.title: Indus weights and the decimal ratio
events.description: Harappan merchants and officials used small cubes of chert as weights across the whole civilisation. The lower weights double each time, 1, 2, 4, 8 up to 64, and the higher ones follow a decimal-based progression, with values such as 160, 200, 320 and 640. The basic unit is about 0.87 grams. Weights of this kind turn up from Gujarat to the Punjab and beyond, which shows a single standard held over a very large area for several centuries. It is one of the clearest signs of organised trade and administration, although no text explains who enforced it.

events.title: Chanhu-daro bead factories
events.description: Chanhu-daro, a Harappan town in Sindh south of Mohenjo-daro, was excavated by N. G. Majumdar and Ernest Mackay in the 1930s. It was a craft centre, with workshops for bead-making, seal-cutting, and shell and metal work. Its craftsmen made long carnelian beads using drills of hard stone, and similar beads have been found in the royal graves of Ur in Mesopotamia. The site shows how specialised industry supported the Indus trade, and bead-making still continues in Gujarat today.

events.title: Svastika and pīpal on Indus seals
events.description: Some Indus seals and pottery carry the svastika, and others show a figure in the branches of a pipal tree. Because the svastika, the pipal and the bodhi-tree are central symbols in Hindu, Jaina and Buddhist traditions, many scholars see these motifs as early evidence of long-lasting symbolism. Others caution that without readable texts the meaning at Harappa cannot be known, and that similar signs appear in many ancient cultures. The motifs are best taken as a possible, not proven, link between the Indus cities and later Indian religion.

events.title: The 4.2-kiloyear aridification event
events.description: Around 2200 BCE a global dry spell, called the 4.2-kiloyear event, hit many early civilisations, and records from India show a weakening of the monsoon. The Harappan cities seem to have changed gradually over the next few centuries: large cities declined, trade and writing faded, and people dispersed toward the Gaṅgā plain, Gujarat and the south. Scholars such as Liviu Giosan have also argued that shifts in the rivers mattered. Climate is now seen as one factor among several, not a single cause of collapse.

events.title: Shortughai outpost on the Oxus
events.description: Shortughai, in northeastern Afghanistan near the Oxus, is a Harappan settlement found far from the Indus valley. Excavated by Henri-Paul Francfort in the 1970s, it had Harappan pottery, seals and weights. It lay close to the lapis lazuli mines of Badakhshan, and is understood as a trading colony set up to obtain the blue stone, which was prized in Mesopotamia and Egypt. It dates to roughly the end of the third millennium BCE and is evidence of the reach of the Indus traders.

events.title: Copper Hoard culture
events.description: The Copper Hoard culture is known from caches of copper objects found in the Gaṅgā–Yamunā doab and elsewhere: flat axes, harpoons, antenna-hilted swords and flat human-shaped figures called anthropomorphs. They are generally dated to the second millennium BCE, with the Saipai find in Uttar Pradesh among the famous ones. Their makers and purpose are not agreed; some link them to the Ochre Coloured Pottery settlements, and others to ritual or votive use. They show that metalworking continued in the doab after the Indus cities declined.

events.title: Surkotada horse-bone debate
events.description: Surkotada in Kutch, excavated by J. P. Joshi in the 1960s and 70s, was a small fortified Harappan settlement. The zoologist Sándor Bökönyi identified bones from it as those of a true horse, which would be relevant to the debate over whether Indus people knew the horse. Other specialists argue the bones could be those of wild ass or hemione, and the identification remains disputed. Because the horse is prominent in the Ṛgveda, the question has had a long place in the discussion of Indo-Aryan origins.

events.title: Sanauli chariot burials
events.description: At Sanauli, near Delhi, excavations in 2018 found burials of about 1900 BCE containing three wheeled vehicles with solid wheels decorated in copper, along with copper-covered coffins, shields, helmets and long swords. The excavators call the vehicles chariots and link them to a warrior class of Vedic type; others think they were carts drawn by bulls. The find has reopened debate about who lived in the upper Gaṅgā plain at that time.

events.title: The Sarasvatī dries
events.description: The Ghaggar-Hakra, which many scholars identify with the Vedic Sarasvatī, was a major river of the northwest with many Harappan sites along it. By about 1900 BCE it had shrunk to a seasonal stream, possibly because the Sutlej and Yamunā shifted away from it, though the timing and mechanism are debated; some argue it was already largely monsoon-fed. Later texts such as the Brāhmaṇas and the Mahābhārata speak of the Sarasvatī disappearing in the desert at Vinaśana. The identification with the Ghaggar-Hakra is widely accepted but not universal.

events.title: Late Harappan de-urbanisation
events.description: After about 1900 BCE the great cities emptied. Writing, seals and standard weights went out of use. The people did not vanish: the number of small villages rose sharply to the east, in Haryana and the upper Gaṅgā plain, and south in Gujarat. Weakened monsoons, the drying of the Sarasvatī and the collapse of trade with Mesopotamia are the leading explanations; no evidence of invasion has been found.

events.title: Cemetery H culture
events.description: Cemetery H was excavated at Harappa by M. S. Vats in the 1930s. Its burials in painted urns, with designs of peacocks, antelopes and star-like motifs, date to the Late Harappan period of about 1900–1300 BCE. Vats read the peacock as carrying the soul of the dead, and earlier scholars once linked the culture to the arrival of Indo-Aryans. Most archaeologists now see it as a local development after the decline of the city, showing continuity of settlement and a change in burial practice.

events.title: Ochre Coloured Pottery culture
events.description: The Ochre Coloured Pottery culture is known from sites in the upper Gaṅgā-Yamunā doab, such as Bisauli and Rajpur Parasu, discovered in the 1950s. The pottery was coated in an ochre wash that rubs off easily, perhaps because the sites were affected by floods. It is dated to the early second millennium BCE and overlaps with Late Harappan settlements in the same region. Some archaeologists connect it with the Copper Hoards, but this is unproven. The culture shows the movement of populations eastward after the decline of the Indus cities.

events.title: Daimabad bronzes of the Deccan
events.description: Daimabad, in Ahmednagar district of Maharashtra on the Pravarā river in the Godāvarī basin, is known for a hoard of four large bronzes found in 1958: a chariot with two oxen and a driver, an elephant, a rhinoceros and a buffalo. They are cast by the lost-wax method and weigh over sixty kilograms. Some scholars connect them to Late Harappan craftsmen who moved south, which would show the tradition reaching the Deccan around 1800 BCE; others date them to the later Jorwe culture at the site. Their origin remains discussed.

events.title: Jorwe and Malwa chalcolithic villages
events.description: The Malwa culture, centred in central India with sites such as Navdatoli on the Narmadā, and the Jorwe culture of Maharashtra, with Inamgaon on the Ghod, were Chalcolithic farming societies of the second millennium BCE. They grew wheat, barley, millets and pulses, kept cattle, and made painted pottery, Malwa ware being among the most elaborate of the age. Inamgaon had mud-brick houses and an embankment against floods. They are the main evidence for village life on the Deccan before the Iron Age.

events.title: Origins of the Indo-Aryan languages
events.description: How the Indo-Aryan languages, of which Vedic Sanskrit is the oldest, came to be spoken in India is the most disputed question in Indian prehistory. Most linguists and geneticists hold that speakers moved in from the northwest during the second millennium BCE. Others argue for an indigenous development continuous with the Harappan civilization. The older picture of a violent "Aryan invasion" destroying the Indus cities has been abandoned by nearly everyone.

events.title: Sapta Sindhu: the land of seven rivers
events.description: The poets of the Ṛgveda called their country the land of the seven rivers. The core is the Indus with the five rivers of the Punjab, the Vitastā, Asiknī, Paruṣṇī, Vipāś and Śutudrī, and the Sarasvatī to the east. The Persians pronounced the name Hapta Hindu, and from "Hindu" for the river and its people came the Greek "Indos" and the word India.

events.title: Gandhara Grave culture in Swat
events.description: The Gandhāra Grave culture, also called the Swat culture, is known from cemeteries in the Swat valley in northern Pakistan, where the river was called Suvāstu in the Ṛgveda. Burials with copper and bronze objects, and some with horse remains, date from roughly the middle of the second millennium to the early first millennium BCE. Because of the horses, some scholars link these graves to the arrival of Indo-Aryan speakers, while others emphasise local development and continuity. The sites are important to that debate, which is still open.

events.title: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā composed
events.description: The Ṛgveda is the oldest text of Hinduism and one of the oldest in any Indo-European language: 1,028 hymns in ten books, addressed mainly to Agni (fire), Indra (the storm-warrior) and Soma (the sacred drink). The poets were families of seers living between the rivers of the Punjab and the Sarasvatī.¶Scholars date its composition to roughly 1500–1200 BCE on linguistic grounds. Tradition holds something different: the Veda has no human author at all. It is eternal sound that the ṛṣis "saw", which is why it is called śruti, "what was heard". It was never meant to be written. Elaborate methods of recitation carried it, syllable for syllable, across three thousand years.

events.title: Family books of the Ṛgveda
events.description: The Ṛgveda is a collection of 1,028 hymns in ten books or maṇḍalas. Books 2 to 7, the "family books", are generally held to be the oldest core, each attributed to a seer family: Gṛtsamada (2), Viśvāmitra (3), Vāmadeva (4), Atri (5), Bharadvāja (6) and Vasiṣṭha (7). They were composed in the northwest, in the area called Sapta Sindhu, and are usually dated to about 1500–1200 BCE. The hymns were handed down orally with great exactness, and later families arranged them by deity and length.

events.title: Gāyatrī mantra revealed
events.description: A single verse of the Ṛgveda (3.62.10), seen by the sage Viśvāmitra, asks the divine Sun, Savitṛ, to awaken the mind: "May we meditate on the radiant glory of the divine Savitṛ; may he inspire our understanding."¶It became the most important mantra of Hindu life. A child receives it at the upanayana initiation, and it is repeated at dawn, noon and dusk in the sandhyā rite. Because Viśvāmitra was born a king and became a sage by his own effort, the verse also carries a message: insight is earned, not inherited.

events.title: Mitanni treaty names Vedic gods
events.description: A treaty of about 1380 BCE between the Hittite king and the king of Mitanni, in what is now Syria and Turkey, calls on the gods Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra and the Nāsatya twins as witnesses. Mitanni rulers also had names like "having an attacking chariot", and a horse-training manual from the region uses Indo-Aryan number words. It is the earliest securely dated mention of these gods, found in Anatolia, far from India.

events.title: Battle of the Ten Kings (Dāśarājña)
events.description: The Dāśarājña battle is the best known event of the Ṛgveda. Sudās, king of the Bharatas, whose priest was Vasiṣṭha, faced a coalition of ten peoples on the Paruṣṇī (the Rāvī), according to hymns such as ṚV 7.18, 7.33 and 7.83. Vasiṣṭha's prayers are said to have helped Sudās cross the river and the enemy was routed, with many drowned. Among the defeated were the Pūrus, whose lands later merged with the Bharatas into the Kuru people. Scholars treat it as a historical memory, not a precisely datable event.

events.title: Indra slays Vṛtra in Ṛgveda hymns
events.description: The central myth of the Ṛgveda tells how Indra, after drinking Soma, killed the serpent Vṛtra with his thunderbolt (vajra), made by Tvaṣṭṛ, and released the waters that Vṛtra had held back. The hymn ṚV 1.32 retells the deed, and many other hymns refer to it. It has been read as a myth of the monsoon, of the creation of order, and of the triumph of the rain-god. Similar dragon-slaying stories occur elsewhere in Indo-European traditions, and the Avestan word Verethragna is related to Vṛtrahan, "Vṛtra-slayer".

events.title: Agni and Soma liturgy
events.description: Agni, the sacred fire, is the first deity invoked in the Ṛgveda (1.1), and is called the priest and messenger who carries offerings to the gods. About 200 hymns are addressed to him. Soma is both a plant and a god, and its juice was pressed, filtered and offered; the whole of Maṇḍala 9, with over a hundred hymns, is devoted to Soma Pavamāna, "Soma being purified". The identity of the plant is unknown, and proposals include ephedra and others. Fire and Soma together are the basis of the later śrauta sacrifices.

events.title: Women seers of the Ṛgveda
events.description: The traditional index to the Ṛgveda names about two dozen women among its poets. Ghoṣā, afflicted with a skin disease, addresses the healing Aśvins; Lopāmudrā argues with her ascetic husband Agastya about the claims of love; Apālā and Viśvavārā offer the Soma and the fire themselves. Later law books restricted women's study of the Veda; these hymns show an earlier practice.

events.title: Divodāsa defeats Śambara
events.description: In several hymns, such as ṚV 4.26 and 6.26, the Bharata king Divodāsa Atithigva is helped by Indra in his war against Śambara, a hill chief, whose ninety-nine forts are broken. Scholars debate what the "forts" were, wooden stockades or fortified settlements of the older cultures of the region, and some have linked them to the Indus towns. The hymns are among the Ṛgveda's clearest memories of conflict with the earlier inhabitants.

events.title: Vāk Sūkta of Vāgāmbhṛṇī
events.description: In hymn 10.125 of the Ṛgveda the speaker is the goddess Speech herself, and the poet is a woman, Vāc, daughter of the sage Ambhṛṇa. "I move with the Rudras and the Vasus... I make whom I love mighty, a sage, a seer. I blow like the wind, holding all the worlds." It is among the earliest texts in which the Goddess declares herself supreme, and is recited in her worship as the Devī Sūkta.

events.title: Sarasvatī praised as greatest river
events.description: One hymn, ṚV 2.41.16, calls the Sarasvatī "best of mothers, best of rivers, best of goddesses", and the Nadī-stuti and ṚV 7.95 describe her as flowing pure from the mountains to the sea. Together they show that she was a great river for the Ṛgvedic poets. Many scholars link her with the Ghaggar-Hakra. In later Vedic texts, as the river diminished, she became associated with Vāc, speech, and then with learning and the arts, the role she has in Hindu worship today.

events.title: Bharadvāja lineage at the Bharata court
events.description: In the sixth maṇḍala of the Ṛgveda, the hymns are ascribed to Bharadvāja Bārhaspatya and his family, who were priests of the Bharata king Divodāsa. Later tradition remembers Divodāsa as an ancestor of Sudās, the victor of the Ten Kings' battle, so the Bharadvājas were linked to the same royal house. Their association with Divodāsa shows how priestly families and kings worked together, and later the Bharadvājas would be among the seven seers.

events.title: Vasiṣṭha–Viśvāmitra rivalry in the Ṛgveda
events.description: In Ṛgveda 3.33, Viśvāmitra, priest of the Bharata king Sudās, prays to the rivers Vipāś (Beas) and Śutudrī (Sutlej) to let the army cross. Later, in the family book of Vasiṣṭha, it is Vasiṣṭha who is Sudās's priest and who calls for his victory in the Ten Kings' battle, and the hymns speak harshly of rivals. The epics turn the rivalry into a long legend of Viśvāmitra, a Kṣatriya who becomes a Brahmarṣi, and Vasiṣṭha.

events.title: Puruṣa Sūkta and the cosmic Person
events.description: Ṛgveda 10.90 pictures the universe as the body of a cosmic Person with a thousand heads and eyes. The gods offer him in the first sacrifice, and from his parts come the sun, moon, sky, earth and the hymns themselves.¶One verse derives the four social orders from his mouth, arms, thighs and feet. It is the earliest mention of the four varṇas, and it has been read in opposite ways ever since: as a picture of society as one living body, and as a charter for hierarchy. The hymn is still chanted in almost every temple ritual.

events.title: Nāsadīya Sūkta, the Hymn of Creation
events.description: The "Hymn of Creation" (Ṛgveda 10.129) is seven verses long and unlike any other ancient creation story. Perhaps the overseer in the highest heaven knows, "or perhaps even he does not". This comfort with open questions set the tone for all later Indian philosophy.

events.title: Ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti
events.description: In a long riddle hymn (Ṛgveda 1.164) the poet Dīrghatamas says: "They call it Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni, and it is the heavenly bird Garutmān. The wise speak of what is one in many ways." The line is one of the most quoted in the Veda. It is the root of the Hindu view that different deities and different religions are names and paths for a single truth.

events.title: Hiraṇyagarbha and Viśvakarman hymns
events.description: Late hymns of the tenth maṇḍala turn from the gods of the sacrifice to the question of the one source of the world. ṚV 10.121 praises Hiraṇyagarbha, the "golden germ" that arose at the beginning as lord of all that lives, and ends each verse by asking which god to worship. ṚV 10.81 and 10.82 describe Viśvakarman, the all-maker, who has eyes and faces on every side. These are among the first texts to ask about a single creator, and they prepare the way for Upaniṣadic thought and for Prajāpati.

events.title: Rudra in the Ṛgveda
events.description: Rudra, "the howler", has only three whole hymns in the Ṛgveda. He is the dangerous archer of the wild whose arrows bring disease, and also the best of physicians, with cooling remedies. Worshippers ask him mainly to stay away. One verse to him, the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya, asks for release from death "like a cucumber from its stalk". In later religion he becomes Śiva, the auspicious.

events.title: Viṣṇu's three strides
events.description: The Ṛgveda, in hymn 1.154, praises Viṣṇu as the one who measured out the earthly realms and propped up the high abode, striding three times. His third step is said to be beyond the reach of mortals. Viṣṇu is a minor god in the Ṛgveda, a close companion of Indra, but this image of the three strides would later be developed into the story of Vāmana and Trivikrama in the Brāhmaṇas and Purāṇas, and became a central part of Vaiṣṇava tradition.

gitaQuote.verse: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत । अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥ परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् । धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur; Madhvācārya Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Nadī-stuti lists the rivers
events.description: Hymn 10.75 of the Ṛgveda names nineteen rivers in order from east to west, beginning with the Gaṅgā, Yamunā and Sarasvatī and ending with the western tributaries of the Indus. It is the earliest geographical list in Indian literature and shows the world the poets knew. The eastern rivers it names are mentioned only rarely elsewhere in the older books, a sign that the people were moving east.

events.title: Painted Grey Ware culture begins
events.description: From about 1200 BCE villages in the region between the Sutlej and the upper Gaṅgā used a fine grey pottery painted with black patterns, along with iron tools, horses and glass. The area matches the land of the Kurus and Pañcālas in the later Vedic texts, and the Painted Grey Ware levels at sites named in the Mahābhārata, such as Hastināpura, belong to this culture. Many archaeologists therefore connect it with the world the epic remembers, though the link is debated.

events.title: Iron working at Malhar and Raja Nala-ka-tila
events.description: Iron objects appear in the middle Gaṅgā plain at sites such as Malhar and Raja Nala-ka-Tila. Some excavators argue for iron smelting there as early as the later second millennium BCE, earlier than the usual dating in India of about 1000 BCE or after. These early dates are disputed, but the sites show iron use in the region before the great cities of the sixth century. Vedic texts later speak of śyāma ayas, "dark metal", and iron's effects on farming and warfare are often counted among the causes of eastern urbanisation.

events.title: Sāmaveda Saṃhitā, the Veda of chants
events.description: The Sāmaveda consists of about 1,875 verses, nearly all taken from the Ṛgveda, set to melodies for singing at the Soma sacrifice. The same words are stretched, repeated and filled out with extra syllables according to musical rules. Its chanting tradition preserves some of the oldest Indian musical practice on record. In the Gītā Kṛṣṇa says, "Among the Vedas I am the Sāmaveda." Indian tradition traces classical music to this chant.

events.title: Yajurveda Saṃhitās, the sacrificial formulas
events.description: The Yajurveda is the handbook of the priest who performs the physical acts of the sacrifice, giving the formula to be spoken at each step. It survives in two forms. The "Black" (Kṛṣṇa) Yajurveda mixes the formulas with prose explanation; the "White" (Śukla), ascribed to the sage Yājñavalkya, keeps them separate. Most brāhmaṇa families of south India belong to the Black Yajurveda and most of the north to the White.

events.title: Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa of Lagadha
events.description: The Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, ascribed to Lagadha, is the oldest Indian text on astronomy. Its purpose is practical: to fix the right days for sacrifices. It describes a five-year cycle that reconciles lunar months with the solar year, lists the twenty-seven star-groups through which the moon passes, and gives rules for the length of daylight. The position of the solstice it records suggests observations made around 1200 BCE.

events.title: Saptarṣi tradition of the seven seers
events.description: The seven seers, saptarṣis, are Atri, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Jamadagni, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra in the list of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, though lists vary in different texts and ages. They are honoured as founders of Vedic lineages and as the seers of Ṛgvedic hymns, and the seven stars of the Great Bear are named after them. They are a symbol of the transmission of sacred knowledge.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ | ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||
gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.
gitaQuote.source: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) Critical Edition; Rāmānuja Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Āprī hymns and family identity
events.description: The Āprī hymns are a set of ten Ṛgvedic hymns, each belonging to a different family of seers, for the animal sacrifice. They follow the same sequence of invocations, addressing the kindling sticks, Tanūnapāt, Narāśaṃsa, the ritual grass, the doors, Dawn and Night, the two divine priests, three goddesses, Tvaṣṭṛ and the lord of the forest, and have common elements with differences in wording. They show how families kept their own versions of the shared rite and used hymns as a mark of identity.

events.title: Black-and-Red Ware in the east
events.description: Black-and-Red Ware is a pottery type fired so that the inside and rim are black and the outside red. In eastern India it marks Neolithic and Chalcolithic farming communities, including Chirand on the Gaṅgā in Bihar and Pandu Rajar Dhibi in West Bengal. Dated roughly from 1500 to 700 BCE, these villages grew rice and kept cattle. They show a sizeable agrarian population in the east before and during the arrival of Brahmanical culture and the later Painted Grey Ware sites, and they are a basis for understanding that expansion.

events.title: Śatarudrīya (Śrī Rudram)
events.description: In the middle of the Yajurveda stands a long litany to Rudra, the fierce archer-god of storms and disease. It greets him in every form: as lord of thieves, of carpenters and potters, of dogs, of green leaves and dry. Near its end occur the words "namaḥ śivāya ca", the earliest source of the five-syllable mantra "namaḥ śivāya". Known as the Rudram, it is the most important Vedic text for worshippers of Śiva and is chanted daily in his temples.

gitaQuote.verse: पिताहमस्य जगतो माता धाता पितामहः । वेद्यं पवित्रमोंकार ऋक्साम यजुरेव च ॥ गतिर्भर्ता प्रभुः साक्षी निवासः शरणं सुहृत् । प्रभवः प्रलयः स्थानं निधानं बीजमव्ययम् ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ | vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛk sāma yajur eva ca || gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt | prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||
gitaQuote.translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer and the grandsire. I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the creation and dissolution, the foundation and the imperishable seed.

events.title: Atharvaveda Saṃhitā, the fourth Veda
events.description: The Atharvaveda, the fourth Veda, is different in character from the other three. Its 730 hymns include charms to cure fever and snakebite, to win love or a lawsuit, to secure a long life, and blessings for a new house or a king's consecration. Alongside them are some of the boldest speculative hymns in the Veda, on Time, Breath and the cosmic pillar. It is the main source for the everyday religion of ancient India.

events.title: Pṛthivī Sūkta, the Hymn to the Earth
events.description: The Hymn to the Earth, Atharvaveda 12.1, addresses the earth in sixty-three verses as a mother who bears people of many languages and customs as if in one house. The poet declares, "Earth is my mother, I am her son", and prays that what he digs from her may grow back quickly and that he may not wound her heart. It is often cited today as an ancient statement of ecological conscience.

events.title: Kuru kingdom, the first Vedic state
events.description: Around 1100 BCE the Kuru tribe, in the region of modern Delhi and Haryana, built what historians call the first state in India. Under kings named Parīkṣit and Janamejaya, the hymns were collected into the Vedas, the great public sacrifices were standardised, and a specialised priesthood took shape. The Kuru country was regarded as the home of correct speech and conduct. These are the kings the Mahābhārata remembers as the heirs of the Pāṇḍavas.

events.title: Śrauta ritual systematised
events.description: The Brāhmaṇas and Yajurveda texts set out the large public rituals called śrauta, performed with three sacred fires and a team of priests: the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ and Brahman. The Agniṣṭoma is the basic Soma sacrifice, the Vājapeya and Rājasūya are royal rites, and the Aśvamedha is the horse sacrifice of a conquering king. They took canonical form among the Kuru and Pāñcāla peoples. A few of these rites are still performed in Kerala and elsewhere, and they form the ritual background to the Upaniṣads.

events.title: Atharvan and Aṅgiras fire-priests
events.description: The Atharvaveda is also called Atharvāṅgirasa, after Atharvan and Aṅgiras, ancient families of priests. Atharvan is the name for fire-priests who performed rites of healing and welfare, and Aṅgiras for those associated with spells. The Bhṛgus are another ancient clan connected with the fire cult, and the Ṛgveda credits the Bhṛgus with helping bring fire to humankind. These families explain why the fourth Veda was linked to household and healing ritual, and why it was later accepted.

events.title: Megalithic cultures of the south
events.description: From about 1000 BCE, large stone burial monuments appear across the peninsula: stone circles, cists and dolmens, often with iron tools and black-and-red pottery. Brahmagiri in Karnataka, excavated by Mortimer Wheeler, and Hallur and Adichanallur are among the sites. They continue for more than a thousand years in places and show societies using iron and horses. The builders' language and beliefs are not recorded, and scholars debate their links to later Dravidian-speaking and Sangam-age societies.

events.title: Hastināpura flood layer
events.description: Excavations at Hastināpura in Meerut district, begun by B. B. Lal in the 1950s, found a Painted Grey Ware settlement that was damaged by heavy flooding. The Purāṇas tell that during the reign of the Kuru king Nicakṣu, a few generations after Janamejaya, the Gaṅgā swept Hastināpura away, and he moved the capital to Kauśāmbī. Lal connected the two, and some scholars accept the link as a memory of a real event. Others point out that the dating of Painted Grey Ware and its match with the Mahābhārata is uncertain.

events.title: Gaṅgā becomes the sacred axis
events.description: The Ṛgveda's river hymn (10.75) names the Gaṅgā first in its list of rivers, but she is a minor river there. As Vedic communities and their rites moved east into the Gaṅgā-Yamunā plain, the Gaṅgā took the central place in ritual life. The Mahābhārata calls it the best of tīrthas, and the Purāṇas tell the story of Bhagīratha bringing her down from heaven. Vārāṇasī, Prayāga and Haridvāra became the great pilgrimage places on her banks. Her prominence reflects a shift in the centre of Vedic culture over many centuries.

events.title: Agnicayana, the fire-altar of bricks
events.description: The Agnicayana is the most elaborate Vedic rite: over twelve days a great altar in the shape of a bird of prey is built from 10,800 bricks in five layers, each brick laid with a mantra. The texts say it reconstructs the body of the creator Prajāpati, who fell apart in creating the world. Nambūtiri brāhmaṇas of Kerala have preserved it, and their performance in 1975 was filmed and studied in detail.

events.title: Vedic oral transmission by pada, krama, ghana
events.description: The Vedas were handed down without writing by a system of cross-checking. A student learns each verse as continuous speech, then word by word, then in patterns that repeat the words in changing order: step-wise, braided, and the "dense" recitation that goes forward and back. An error in any one pattern shows up against the others. As a result the Ṛgveda is recited today with its wording and accents remarkably intact over about three thousand years, and UNESCO recognised Vedic chanting as intangible heritage in 2008.

events.title: Pāñcāla rises as a Vedic centre
events.description: Pāñcāla, in the Gaṅgā-Yamunā doab with its capital at Kāmpilya, became under the Kuru-Pāñcāla alliance one of the leading centres of late Vedic culture. In the Upaniṣads the Pāñcāla king Pravāhaṇa Jaivali is shown teaching the five-fire doctrine to the Brahmin Āruṇi, an unusual case of a king instructing priests. Their courts are a setting for learned debate, and in the epic Draupadī is a Pāñcāla princess.

events.title: Nakṣatra system of lunar mansions
events.description: The Atharvaveda (19.7) and the Taittirīya Saṃhitā and Brāhmaṇa list the nakṣatras, the 27 (or 28, with Abhijit) lunar mansions through which the moon moves in a month, beginning with Kṛttikā, the Pleiades. They were used to fix the times of rites. Later Indian lists begin with Aśvinī instead, and the nakṣatras remain the basis of the lunar calendar, of muhūrta selection and of Jyotiṣa, Indian astrology and astronomy.

events.title: Janamejaya Pārikṣita's Aśvamedha
events.description: The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (8.21) lists great kings consecrated with the Indra-style royal consecration, among them Janamejaya Pārikṣita, consecrated by the priest Tura Kāvaṣeya. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa also records his horse sacrifice. This Janamejaya is a Kuru king whose name also belongs to the Mahābhārata, where his snake sacrifice frames the epic, though the epic's genealogy and the Vedic evidence do not always agree. The texts show the Kurus at their height.

events.title: Varṇa and dharma in late Vedic thought
events.description: The Puruṣa Sūkta (ṚV 10.90), a late hymn of the Ṛgveda, names the four varṇas in a cosmic myth: the Brahmin from the mouth of the primal Puruṣa, the Rājanya from the arms, the Vaiśya from the thighs and the Śūdra from the feet. Later Vedic texts expand the four classes and their duties. Dharma, a word from the root dhṛ, "to hold", comes to name right order, a role ṛta held in the Ṛgveda. Scholars differ on how rigid the system was in this period.

events.title: Ṛta: cosmic order
events.description: Ṛta is the Ṛgvedic principle of the true order of the world, seen in the course of the sun, the seasons and the rivers, as well as in truthful speech and the rite. The gods Varuṇa and Mitra are its guardians. It is related to the Avestan aša and is the forerunner of later ideas: dharma for moral and social order, satya for truth, and karma as the working of cause and effect. The idea set the tone of Indian thinking on cosmic and moral law.

events.title: Śrī Sūkta, hymn to Lakṣmī
events.description: The Śrī Sūkta is a short hymn, not part of the standard Śākala text of the Ṛgveda but preserved as a khila, an appendix. It begins by calling on Jātavedas, the fire, to bring Śrī-Lakṣmī, golden and radiant, and asks for wealth, cattle and prosperity. It is one of the earliest praises of the goddess of fortune and is recited today in Lakṣmī worship, including at Dīpāvalī. Its date is later than the core of the Ṛgveda.

events.title: Khila hymns outside the Ṛgveda canon
events.description: The khilas are supplementary hymns attached to the Ṛgveda but outside the 1,028 hymns of the Śākala recension, and some come from the lost Bāṣkala school. They were collected and edited in modern times, notably by Scheftelowitz in 1906. Among them is the Śrī Sūkta, which is recited in Lakṣmī worship. Other khilas include prayers for blessing and protection. They show that the tradition was more varied than any one recension, and they are generally later than the core hymns.

events.title: Aditi and Uṣas, early goddesses of the Ṛgveda
events.description: Though most Ṛgvedic deities are male, the hymns also honour goddesses. Aditi, the "boundless", is the mother of the Ādityas and in one verse is identified with the sky, the air, mother, father and son. Uṣas, the Dawn, is addressed in about twenty hymns that are among the finest poetry of the Ṛgveda, as a young woman who drives away darkness. These figures are the earliest in the long history of the Goddess in India, which continues with Vāc and Śrī.

events.title: Aśvins, the divine physicians
events.description: The Aśvins, twin gods who ride a chariot at dawn, are the divine physicians in the Ṛgveda, to whom some fifty hymns are addressed. They are said to have made the aged sage Cyavana young again, rescued Bhujyu from the sea, and healed the blind and lame. Later tradition makes them the doctors of the gods and ancestors of Ayurveda, and the story of Cyavana's rejuvenation lives on in the Cyavanaprāśa tonic.

events.title: Yama and the ancestors
events.description: Ṛgveda 10.14 praises Yama as the first mortal who died and found the path for others, and as the king of the dead. He rules with the Pitṛs, the fathers, who are invited to the sacrifice, and two dogs guard his realm. Later he became Dharmarāja, judge of the dead, in the epics and Purāṇas. The hymns are among the earliest evidence of Indian belief in a world of the ancestors.

events.title: Wedding hymn of Sūryā
events.description: Ṛgveda 10.85 is the wedding hymn of Sūryā, the daughter of the Sun, who marries Soma with the Aśvins as groomsmen. Its verses are used in Hindu weddings even now, such as those where the groom takes the bride's hand and blessings of prosperity and a long life together are said. The saptapadī, the seven steps taken together, is prescribed in the Gṛhya Sūtras, which draw on this hymn. It is a basis for the Hindu marriage ritual.

events.title: Saṃjñāna: hymn of concord
events.description: The last hymn of the Ṛgveda, 10.191, ends the collection with a prayer for unity: "saṃ gacchadhvaṃ saṃ vadadhvaṃ", "go together, speak together, let your minds be in accord". It is often quoted as a Vedic ideal of harmony and common purpose. The hymn is also notable for where it stands: it closes the whole Ṛgveda, so the collection of hymns to many gods ends not with a ritual formula but with a call to cooperation, a note that later Indian thought on dharma and community often returns to.

events.title: Weapons and war-chariots in the Ṛgveda
events.description: Ṛgveda 6.75 is a hymn to the warrior's equipment: armour, bow, bowstring, quiver, arrows and chariot, and another hymn (6.47) is to the war-drum. They show how weapons were treated with ritual, and the importance of chariots in Vedic war. The word Dhanurveda, "science of the bow", is used later for treatises on warfare, which are attached to the Yajurveda as an upaveda. The hymns are older than these treatises.

events.title: Kurukṣetra as the gods' sacrificial ground
events.description: The Brāhmaṇas call Kurukṣetra the devayajana, the sacrificial ground of the gods, where the gods once performed a sacrifice, and later texts promise merit to those who live or die there. The region between the Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī was the centre of the Kuru realm and later of Brahmāvarta, where Manu's text says correct conduct is found. This ritual importance explains why the epic sets its war there.

events.title: Adichanallur urn burials
events.description: Adichanallur, on the Tāmraparṇī (Tamiraparaṇi) river in Thoothukudi district, was explored by Alexander Rea around 1899–1905. It is a large urn-burial field with bronze animal figures, iron tools, gold diadems and Black-and-Red pottery. Estimated dates run from about the first millennium BCE, and recent excavations have prompted new claims of greater antiquity. It is the main site for studying early Iron Age society in the far south, before the Sangam period.

events.title: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa of the Ṛgveda
events.description: The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa is the principal Brāhmaṇa of the Ṛgveda, ascribed in tradition to Mahidāsa Aitareya. It explains the Soma rites and also describes the royal consecration (the Aindra Mahābhiṣeka). Its seventh book contains the story of Śunaḥśepa, and the refrain "caraiveti", "keep moving", from the tale of Rohita, is a famous encouragement to wander and strive. Its date is placed in the early first millennium BCE, and it shows the Vedic liturgy in its developed form.

events.title: Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa of the Ṛgveda
events.description: The Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, also called the Śāṅkhāyana Brāhmaṇa, is the second Brāhmaṇa of the Ṛgveda and belongs to the Kauṣītaki school. Its thirty chapters deal with the ritual of the new and full moon, the Agnihotra and the Soma sacrifices, and give a different arrangement of Ṛgvedic rites from the Aitareya. One passage says that people go north to learn speech, a reminder of the prestige of the northwest. It is linked with the Kauṣītaki Āraṇyaka and Upaniṣad.

events.title: Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka
events.description: The Taittirīya school belongs to the Kṛṣṇa ("black") Yajurveda, in which mantras and explanatory prose are mixed together. Its Brāhmaṇa discusses the Soma, Agnihotra and horse sacrifices and gives lists of the lunar mansions. The Taittirīya Āraṇyaka continues in a more meditative vein and contains the Taittirīya Upaniṣad and the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad, with its hymn to Nārāyaṇa. This school is still followed by many Brahmins of southern India.

events.description: The Pañcaviṃśa (or Tāṇḍya) Brāhmaṇa and the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa belong to the Sāmaveda and explain the chants of the Udgātṛ priests. They describe the vrātyastoma, a rite by which outsiders (vrātyas) were admitted into Vedic society, and the Sarasvatī sattras, long sacrificial sessions held along the river. events.title: Vrātyas of the east
events.description: Book 15 of the Atharvaveda praises the Vrātya, a wandering figure who is described as a cosmic being, and the Brāhmaṇas describe the vrātyastoma, a rite that admitted vrātyas into Vedic society. Scholars debate who they were: itinerant bands of warriors or ascetics outside the Brahmanical fold, perhaps related to the eastern Magadha region and later to the śramaṇa movements. The texts show that Vedic culture absorbed groups from outside, and that the boundary of the Vedic community was negotiated.

events.title: Brahmodya riddle debates at royal rites
events.description: The brahmodya was a ritual contest of riddles about the sacrifice and the cosmos, in which priests challenged each other at royal rites such as the Aśvamedha. Ṛgveda 1.164, with its riddles of the year and the sun, is an early example. In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad the sage Yājñavalkya wins such a contest at the court of Janaka of Videha against Aśvala, Gārgī and others. The form shows how public debate led from ritual to metaphysical enquiry.

events.title: Kāśī, Kosala and Videha rise
events.description: Between the Gaṅgā-Yamunā doab and the Himalaya foothills, the eastern peoples of Kāśī, Kosala and Videha entered the Vedic world in the later Vedic period. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa knows Videha under King Janaka, and the Upaniṣads place much of their teaching in these courts. The Buddha and Mahāvīra later taught in the same region. The shift of leadership from the Kuru lands to the east shaped the philosophy and politics of the following centuries.

events.title: Rājasūya and royal consecration
events.description: The Brāhmaṇas describe the Rājasūya as a year-long series of rites that made a king. It includes his anointing with water, a symbolic chariot drive and mock cattle raid, a dice game, and a recitation of the Śunaḥśepa story. Subordinate officials called ratnins gave their homage. The ritual presents kingship as a sacred office. The Mahābhārata tells of a Rājasūya performed by Yudhiṣṭhira.

events.title: Sabhā and Samiti
events.description: The sabhā and samiti were assemblies of the Vedic people. The Atharvaveda (7.12) calls them the two daughters of Prajāpati, and prays for their favour. The samiti seems to have been a general assembly of the people at which the king was present, and the sabhā a smaller meeting-place of leading men, though their exact roles are debated. Such bodies limited a king's power in some measure, and similar assemblies appear in the later gaṇasaṅgha republics.

events.title: Pārśvanātha, 23rd Tīrthaṅkara
events.description: Jaina tradition holds that Pārśvanātha, the twenty-third Tīrthaṅkara, was born in Vārāṇasī, the son of King Aśvasena, and lived about 250 years before Mahāvīra. He taught the four restraints (cāturyāma) of non-violence, truthfulness, not stealing and non-possession, and Mahāvīra is said to have added celibacy as a fifth vow. Modern scholars, from Hermann Jacobi onward, generally accept that Pārśva was a real teacher, though the dates are traditional. His symbol is the serpent hood.
