events.title: Yājñavalkya and the Śukla Yajurveda
events.description: The tradition about Yājñavalkya says that he studied the Yajurveda with Vaiśampāyana and left after a quarrel in which his teacher demanded penance for a sin. Yājñavalkya vomited up the knowledge he had learned, and other students, as partridges (tittiri), picked it up, giving the Taittirīya school. He then worshipped the Sun, who taught him new Yajus mantras, the Śukla or "white" Yajurveda, called Vājasaneyi. In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad he is the great teacher at the court of Janaka of Videha, who debates with Gārgī and teaches Maitreyī.

events.title: Kauśāmbī's rampart and Vatsa capital
events.description: Kauśāmbī, on the Yamunā near Prayāgrāj, was the capital of the Vatsa kingdom, whose king Udayana is celebrated in later Sanskrit literature. G. R. Sharma's excavations uncovered a massive rampart faced with brick, which he dated early in the first millennium BCE; other archaeologists put it later, around the sixth century. The Purāṇas say the Kuru kings moved here after the Gaṅgā destroyed Hastināpura. The Buddha visited the city, and an Aśokan pillar stands there. It remained an important trading centre for centuries.

events.title: Ujjayinī rises on the Śiprā
events.description: Ujjayinī, on the Śiprā in Malwa, was the capital of the Avanti kingdom and one of the sixteen Mahājanapadas. Excavations show settlement with ramparts and ironwork from around the eighth century BCE. In Indian astronomy it served as the prime meridian, with longitudes counted from Laṅkā–Ujjayinī, and an observatory tradition continued there. It is a sacred city, home to the Mahākāla jyotirliṅga, and one of the four places of the Kumbha Mela. Later it was the capital of the Mālava rulers and the legendary Vikramāditya.

events.title: Early settlement at Rājghāṭ, Kāśī
events.description: Excavations at Rājghāṭ, on the Gaṅgā at Vārāṇasī, by Banaras Hindu University scholars in the 1960s found occupation from about the eighth century BCE, with later layers showing a prosperous city. Kāśī was already a famed centre of Brahmanical learning, a reputation continued by its scholars and by Banaras Hindu University, founded in 1916.

events.title: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa composed in Videha
events.description: The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, "of a hundred paths", is the longest of the prose works that explain the sacrifices, running to fourteen books. Composed in the eastern land of Videha around 800 BCE, it is a storehouse of early myth, including the flood of Manu and the love of Purūravas and Urvaśī, and of the first Indian reasoning about why rituals work. Its final section is the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.

events.title: Videgha Māthava carries Agni east
events.description: The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.4.1) tells of Videgha Māthava, who carried the sacred fire Agni Vaiśvānara in his mouth from the Sarasvatī eastward. The fire burnt the rivers, but did not cross the Sadānīrā (usually the Gaṇḍakī), and the Brahmins later crossed it. Beyond it lay the land of Videha. Scholars read the story as a memory of the eastward spread of Vedic culture and of the clearing and settling of the marshy east, though the details are legendary.

events.title: The Āraṇyakas: forest books
events.description: The Āraṇyakas, "forest books", were studied outside the village and are the link between the Brāhmaṇas and the Upaniṣads. They include the Aitareya, Kauṣītaki, Taittirīya and Bṛhad Āraṇyakas. They deal with dangerous or esoteric rites such as the Mahāvrata, and also reinterpret the ritual as meditation, so that offering the fire, for example, becomes an offering within the breath. Several Upaniṣads are embedded in them, and they mark the shift from external rite to inner knowledge.

events.title: Śulba Sūtra of Baudhāyana
events.description: The Śulba Sūtras are manuals for laying out sacrificial altars with pegs and cords (śulba). Baudhāyana's, the oldest, states that the diagonal of a rectangle produces as much area as its two sides together, the theorem later named after Pythagoras, and gives a value for the square root of two correct to five decimal places. Geometry in India grew out of the need to build altars of exact shape and area.

events.title: Karma and rebirth doctrine emerges
events.description: The idea that actions shape one's future births first appears clearly in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. A questioner asks Yājñavalkya what becomes of a person at death. He takes him aside, saying this is not to be discussed in public, and what they spoke of was action (karma): one becomes good by good action and bad by bad. Within a few centuries this teaching was the shared ground of Hindu, Buddhist and Jaina thought.

events.title: Āyurveda's roots in the Atharvaveda
events.description: The Atharvaveda includes many hymns for the cure of illness: against fever (takman), wasting disease (yakṣma), wounds and poisons, with the use of herbs, amulets and water. These mix practical remedy and charm, and they name physicians and surgeons. Later medical authors, such as Suśruta, connect Āyurveda with the Atharvaveda, and the tradition makes it an upaveda, a subsidiary Veda. The hymns are the earliest Indian medical source.

events.title: Śunaḥśepa legend in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa
events.description: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 7.13–18 tells the story of Śunaḥśepa. King Hariścandra, childless, vowed to Varuṇa to sacrifice his first son, and later postponed it. Śunaḥśepa, son of Ajīgarta, was sold by his father and tied to the post, but he prayed to the gods with hymns and was released, and Viśvāmitra adopted him as his eldest son. The tale is recited at the Rājasūya, and has been discussed as a possible memory of human sacrifice, which scholars debate.

events.title: Flood legend of Manu recorded
events.description: The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.8.1) tells that Manu, washing his hands, found a small fish in the water that asked for protection and promised to save him. Manu kept it in a jar, a pond and the Gaṅgā as it grew, and at last released it into the sea. It warned him of a flood, and he built a ship, which the fish towed to the northern mountain. Manu alone survived and began creation again. It is the earliest Indian flood narrative, later reworked in the Mahābhārata and the Matsya Purāṇa.

events.title: Purūravas–Urvaśī and Cyavana legends
events.description: The Brāhmaṇas retell Ṛgvedic dialogues as stories. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa narrates the love of Purūravas and Urvaśī, building on Ṛgveda 10.95, and the tale of the sage Cyavana, who was made young by the Aśvins and married Sukanyā. These show the Vedic hymns' brief sketches being turned into narrative, in the manner of the later epics and Purāṇas. They are among the first examples of the storytelling tradition called Itihāsa-Purāṇa.

events.title: Sarasvatī sattras along the sacred river
events.description: The Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa describes sattras, long sacrificial sessions, held along the Sarasvatī. Participants moved upstream, starting where the river disappears at Vinaśana, to Plakṣa Prāsravaṇa, where it rises. In later texts such as the Mahābhārata the same river is lined with tīrthas, and Balarāma goes on a pilgrimage along it. The sessions are an early form of tīrtha-yātrā, pilgrimage, and of the idea of sacred geography.

events.title: Janaka of Videha's philosophical court
events.description: King Janaka of Videha, in what is now north Bihar and Nepal, appears in the Upaniṣads as a ruler who cared more for knowledge than wealth. events.title: Northern Black Polished Ware
events.description: Northern Black Polished Ware is a fine, glossy black pottery that appears in the middle Gaṅgā plain around 700–500 BCE and lasts to about 200 BCE. Its distribution marks the second urbanisation: Kauśāmbī, Vārāṇasī, Śrāvastī, Rājagṛha and Pāṭaliputra. It is found with iron tools, punch-marked coins and brick buildings, which suggest elite trade. The ware helps archaeologists date the world of the Mahājanapadas, the Buddha and Mahāvīra, and the rise of Magadha.

events.title: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad and Yājñavalkya's teaching
events.description: The largest and probably oldest Upaniṣad, attached to the Śukla Yajurveda. Its hero is the sage Yājñavalkya, who debates the scholars at King Janaka's court and teaches his wife Maitreyī before leaving home.¶Here are found the statement "ahaṃ brahmāsmi" (I am Brahman), the method of "neti neti" (not this, not this) for pointing at what cannot be described, and the first clear teaching of karma: a person becomes good by good action and bad by bad action. Every later school of Vedānta had to interpret this text.

events.title: Gārgī questions Yājñavalkya
events.description: At a great debate hosted by King Janaka of Videha, the woman philosopher Gārgī Vācaknavī twice challenges Yājñavalkya. She asks what the world is woven upon, pressing layer by layer until he warns her that she is asking too much.¶She returns with two final questions, compares them to arrows, and draws from him the teaching of the imperishable (akṣara) on which space itself is woven. She then tells the assembly that no one will defeat him. The passage (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.6 and 3.8) shows women taking part in the highest philosophical debate of the age.

events.title: Yājñavalkya and Maitreyī on the Self
events.description: About to leave home for the life of a wanderer, the sage Yājñavalkya offers to divide his property between his two wives. Maitreyī asks whether all the wealth in the world would make her immortal. When he says no, she asks for what he knows instead. He teaches that a husband, a wife, children and wealth are dear not for their own sake but for the sake of the Self, and that the Self is what must be seen, heard and understood.

events.title: Chāndogya Upaniṣad and tat tvam asi
events.description: An Upaniṣad of the Sāmaveda, built from stories. A father, Uddālaka, teaches his proud son Śvetaketu with small experiments: salt dissolved in water cannot be seen but is tasted everywhere; a banyan seed split open shows nothing, yet a great tree comes from that nothing.¶Each lesson ends with the same line: "tat tvam asi", that subtle essence is what you are. The text also tells of Satyakāma, accepted as a student because he told the truth about not knowing his father's name. It is the single most quoted source in the Brahma Sūtra.

events.title: Satyakāma Jābāla admitted as student
events.description: A boy named Satyakāma wished to study the Veda and asked his mother his family name. She told him honestly that she had served in many houses in her youth and did not know who his father was. He repeated this to the teacher Gautama, who said that only a true brāhmaṇa would speak the truth so plainly, and accepted him. The story, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, is the classic text for the view that character, not birth, makes a brāhmaṇa.

events.title: Pañcāgni-vidyā of Pravāhaṇa Jaivali
events.description: In the Chāndogya and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣads, Āruṇi Gautama approaches the Pāñcāla king Pravāhaṇa Jaivali, who teaches him that the soul after death goes along one of two paths. Those with knowledge go by the path of the gods to Brahman; those with ritual merit go by the path of the fathers and return as rain, food and then new life. The "five fires" are the stages of this cycle, from heaven to woman. It is one of the earliest statements of rebirth in the Upaniṣads.

events.title: Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, "all this is Brahman"
events.description: Śāṇḍilya's teaching in Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14 begins with the statement "sarvaṃ khalv idaṃ brahma": all this is Brahman, and one should meditate in peace on it as that from which the world arises, dissolves and breathes. It goes on to describe the Self in the heart, smaller than a grain of rice or barley, and yet greater than the earth, sky and heavens. The passage is a key early text for the identity of the individual self and the universal Brahman, and was cited by later Vedāntins.

events.title: Om as sacred syllable
events.description: The syllable Om was the note with which the chanting priest began. The Upaniṣads made it an object of meditation: the Chāndogya opens by calling it the essence of all essences, the Kaṭha calls it the goal all the Vedas proclaim, and the Māṇḍūkya says it is all that was, is and will be. It became the most sacred sound in Hinduism, said before every mantra, and is shared with Buddhists, Jainas and Sikhs.

events.title: Prajāpati teaches Indra and Virocana
events.description: In Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7–12 the creator Prajāpati says that the Self is free from evil, and the god Indra and the Asura Virocana come as students for thirty-two years. Told that the Self is the person seen in the eye, and then in water, Virocana is satisfied that it is the body and goes away. Indra sees the flaw and returns three times, studying 101 years in all, until he learns the Self that is not tied to the body, dreams or deep sleep. The story contrasts a partial view with true insight.

events.title: Nārada and Sanatkumāra
events.description: Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7 tells how Nārada comes to Sanatkumāra and lists everything he has studied, including the Vedas, Itihāsa-Purāṇa, grammar, and arts, saying he knows only words and not the Self, and that those who know the Self cross beyond sorrow. Sanatkumāra leads him step by step, from name and speech through mind, will and breath, to the Infinite (bhūmā), in which one sees nothing else, and which is bliss. It is a classic statement that learning alone is not liberation.

events.title: Madhu-vidyā of Dadhyañc
events.description: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5 teaches that the earth is like honey to all beings and all beings like honey to the earth, and likewise water, fire, wind, the sun and the directions, and that the Self within each is the same immortal being. It is called the Madhu-vidyā and is credited to the sage Dadhyañc, who in the Ṛgveda taught the Aśvins. The honey image expresses the mutual dependence of everything in the world and its unity in Brahman.

events.title: Gotra and pravara lineages
events.description: A gotra is a patrilineal descent group traced to a founding sage, and Brahmin clans trace themselves to the seven ṛṣis and Agastya. Baudhāyana's Pravara section lists the names of ancestors to be recited at rites, called pravaras. The rule of gotra exogamy forbids marriage within the same gotra. The idea survives today in Hindu marriage customs and in family priests' recitation of lineage. How it began, and how widely it applied beyond Brahmins, is debated.

events.title: Pāṇini's predecessors among Sanskrit grammarians
events.description: Before Pāṇini, there was a long tradition of Sanskrit grammarians, ten of whom he cites by name, including Āpiśali, Śākaṭāyana, Gārgya and Śākalya. Yāska's Nirukta (1.12) reports that Śākaṭāyana held that all nouns derive from verbs, while Gārgya and some grammarians denied it. This debate over the origin of words is early evidence of a scientific study of language in India, and Pāṇini's grammar, written later, supplanted most of this earlier work.

events.title: "Itihāsa-Purāṇa" named as fifth Veda
events.description: Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.2 lists Itihāsa-Purāṇa, "the ancient tales", as the "fifth Veda" in a catalogue of what Nārada has studied. It refers to a body of lore of legends and cosmogony, not to the Purāṇas as they are known today. Later, the Mahābhārata and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa also claim the title of fifth Veda, which expresses their wish to be taught and heard like Vedic texts, including by those not able to study the Vedas.

events.title: End of the Bārhadratha dynasty of Magadha
events.description: The Purāṇas record the Bārhadratha dynasty as the earliest royal line of Magadha, ruling from Girivraja (Rājagṛha) and including Jarāsandha, Kṛṣṇa's great opponent in the epic. Their lists give over twenty kings. The last, Ripuñjaya, is said to have been murdered by his minister Sunika (Śunaka), who placed his own son Pradyota on the throne. The Purāṇas then place the Pradyotas, followed by the Śiśunāgas, a line that includes Bimbisāra, whereas Buddhist sources name Bimbisāra's family Haryaṅka. This is traditional Purāṇic history, not confirmed by inscriptions, and its dates are uncertain.

events.title: Taittirīya Upaniṣad and the five sheaths
events.description: The Taittirīya Upaniṣad describes a human being as five sheaths, one inside the other: the body made of food, the vital breath, the mind, the understanding, and innermost, bliss. It also contains the teacher's parting advice to students: speak the truth, practise dharma, do not neglect study, and treat your mother, father, teacher and guest as gods. That address is still read at university convocations in India.

events.title: Aitareya Upaniṣad and prajñānaṃ brahma
events.description: A short Upaniṣad of the Ṛgveda. It tells how the Self alone existed, created the worlds and their guardians, and entered the human body through the crown of the head. It ends by asking what this Self is, and answers that everything, gods, elements, creatures born from egg or womb, is guided by consciousness: "prajñānaṃ brahma", consciousness is Brahman, one of the four "great sayings".

events.title: Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad and Ajātaśatru's teaching
events.description: The Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad belongs to the Ṛgveda and has four chapters. It describes the soul's journey after death to the world of Brahmā, and it teaches that Indra is prāṇa, the breath of life and consciousness, who must be known as the self. In its last chapter the king Ajātaśatru of Kāśī instructs the proud Brahmin Bālāki, a story also told in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka. The text is notable for kings as teachers and for its early ideas of the breath as the principle of life.

events.title: Raikva and King Jānaśruti
events.description: In Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1–3 the generous king Jānaśruti hears two geese say that the poor cart-driver Raikva knows more than he does. He sends Raikva cows, a necklace and a mule cart, but is refused, and finally offers his daughter and a village, whereupon Raikva teaches him the saṃvarga-vidyā: how wind absorbs the other elements and breath absorbs the senses. The story shows the Upaniṣads' view that wisdom does not depend on wealth or rank.

events.title: Keeladi settlement near Madurai
events.description: Keeladi, on the Vaigai near Madurai, has been excavated since 2015. It is a brick-built settlement with drains, ring wells and workshops, and potsherds scratched with names in Tamil-Brāhmī script. Radiocarbon samples from the Tamil Nadu Department of Archaeology's excavations point to a beginning in the sixth century BCE, though the full chronology is still debated. If the early dates hold, city life and literacy in the Tamil country are as old as those of the Gaṅgā plain, and the world of the Sangam poems had a long history behind it.

events.title: Śulba Sūtras and Vedic geometry
events.description: The Śulba Sūtras, "rules of the cord", are manuals for building the altars of the Vedic sacrifice, and they are the earliest Indian mathematics. Baudhāyana's is the oldest, followed by those of Āpastamba and Kātyāyana. They state the rule that the diagonal of a rectangle gives the sum of the squares on its sides, give a close approximation to the square root of two, and describe ways of turning a circle into a square of nearly equal area. They show geometry developed for ritual needs.

events.title: Prātiśākhyas and Śikṣā
events.description: Each Vedic school had its own Prātiśākhya, a manual of phonetics that set out the rules of pronunciation and of sandhi, the changes of sounds at word junctions, for its text, with the accents, udātta, anudātta and svarita. The Śikṣā literature, the first of the Vedāṅgas, deals similarly with correct recitation. These works classify sounds by place and manner of articulation and show a developed phonetic science, which prepared the way for Pāṇini's grammar and which kept the Vedic text unchanged.

events.title: Śākalya's Padapāṭha
events.description: Śākalya is the traditional compiler of the Padapāṭha, in which the Ṛgveda is broken into its separate words, with compounds divided and sandhi undone. This word-by-word text sits beside the continuous Saṃhitā and shows an early analysis of the language. Pāṇini cites Śākalya as a grammarian. The Padapāṭha was a tool for preserving the sacred text, and later the Vedic text was memorised in several other patterns as well, such as the jaṭā and ghana.

events.title: Kalpa Sūtras take shape
events.description: The Kalpa Sūtras, the sūtra texts of the Kalpa Vedāṅga, set out the rules of ritual in compact aphorisms for each Vedic school. The Śrauta Sūtras describe the large public sacrifices, the Gṛhya Sūtras the domestic rites such as marriage, birth, initiation and funerals, and the Dharma Sūtras give the rules of conduct and law. Together with the Śulba Sūtras for altars, they form the basis of later Hindu rites and of Dharmaśāstra.

events.title: Āśvalāyana and Śāṅkhāyana Sūtras
events.description: The Āśvalāyana and Śāṅkhāyana Sūtras are the ritual manuals of Ṛgvedic schools, each in a Śrauta and a Gṛhya part. They describe the rites for the Vedic fires, the Soma sacrifice, and domestic ceremonies such as marriage and initiation. Āśvalāyana's Gṛhya Sūtra is still widely used by Ṛgvedic Brahmins, notably in Maharashtra and southern India. They preserve the Ṛgvedic ritual practice in detail.

events.title: The sixteen saṃskāras
events.description: The saṃskāras are rites that mark and sanctify each stage of a person's life. The household manuals describe them: rites before birth, naming, first solid food, first haircut, initiation into study with the sacred thread (upanayana), marriage, and finally cremation. Lists vary from twelve to forty; sixteen became standard. Marriage, with its seven steps around the fire, and the funeral rites are still performed by almost all Hindus.

events.title: Four āśramas articulated
events.description: The Dharma Sūtras describe four ways of life: the celibate student living with a teacher, the householder, the forest hermit, and the wandering renouncer. At first these were alternatives a young man might choose between. Later they were arranged as four successive stages of one life, so that the duty to raise a family and the urge to seek liberation could both be honoured, each in its season.

events.title: Gautama Dharma Sūtra
events.description: Among the oldest surviving treatises on dharma, in terse prose. Estimates of its date range from about 600 to 200 BCE, with recent scholarship favouring the later part of that range. It covers the student's duties, marriage, inheritance, the king's obligations, crime and penance. It names the sources of dharma as the Veda, tradition, and the conduct of those who know the Veda, and lists eight virtues of the soul, beginning with compassion to all creatures, which it holds to matter more than ritual observance alone.

events.title: Śākhās of the four Vedas
events.description: Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya, a grammatical work of the second century BCE, says that the Ṛgveda has 21 branches, the Yajurveda 101, the Sāmaveda 1,000 and the Atharvaveda 9: 1,131 śākhās or recensions in all. These were schools that each preserved their own version of the text and its pronunciation. Only about a dozen survive today, among them the Śākala Ṛgveda, the Taittirīya and Vājasaneyi Yajurveda, the Kauthuma and Jaiminīya Sāmaveda, and the Śaunaka and Paippalāda Atharvaveda. The figures show how much has been lost.

events.title: Ajātaśatru instructs Bālāki Gārgya
events.description: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (2.1) tells how the learned Brahmin Bālāki Gārgya offers to teach King Ajātaśatru of Kāśī about Brahman and names a series of beings, among them the sun, the moon, lightning, space, wind and fire, as Brahman. The king finds each answer inadequate. When Bālāki falls silent, Ajātaśatru takes him to a sleeping man and shows that the Self is what remains when the senses rest, the source from which breath and the worlds arise. The Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad has a parallel version. The tale is notable for a king teaching a Brahmin.

events.title: Taxila as a seat of learning
events.description: Takṣaśilā, near modern Islamabad, in Gandhāra, was a centre of learning in the early historic period. The Jātakas describe princes and young Brahmins travelling there from Kāśī, Magadha and elsewhere to study the Vedas, archery, medicine and the arts under individual famed teachers. Tradition connects Pāṇini, Cāṇakya and the physician Jīvaka with the area. It was not a university in the modern sense but a cluster of teachers. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.title: Kāśī as a seat of learning
events.description: Vārāṇasī (Kāśī) was known as a seat of Brāhmaṇical teaching by the time of the Buddha. The Buddha gave his first sermon at nearby Sārnāth in the Deer Park, and the Jātakas describe students from many kingdoms studying there. The Upaniṣads also place teachers such as Ajātaśatru in Kāśī. Scholarship continued in the city through the centuries, and Kāśī is still associated with Sanskrit learning today.

events.title: Jaiminīya and Kauthuma Sāma traditions
events.description: The Sāmaveda is the Veda of melodies, with verses taken largely from the Ṛgveda and set to chants for the Udgātṛ priests. Three schools survive: the Kauthuma, the Rāṇāyanīya and the Jaiminīya, with different chant traditions. The Jaiminīya tradition is preserved in Kerala and Tamil Nadu, while the Kauthuma is followed in Gujarat, Maharashtra and elsewhere. The chants are one of the oldest living musical traditions, and are often considered a source of Indian classical music.

events.title: Śrāddha and pitṛ rites
events.description: Śrāddha is the ritual of offering food to the ancestors. It includes piṇḍa, balls of rice offered to the father, grandfather and great-grandfather, and is described in the Gṛhya Sūtras and later Smṛtis. Gayā in Bihar, on the Phalgu river, became the chief place for these rites, and the Vāyu Purāṇa has a Gayā Māhātmya about it. Hindus still perform śrāddha, especially in the fortnight of Pitṛ Pakṣa. The rite expresses the bond between the living and the dead.

events.title: Three debts (ṛṇa-traya)
events.description: Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.10 says that a Brahmin is born with three debts: to the seers, to be paid by study (brahmacarya), to the gods, paid by sacrifice, and to the ancestors, paid by having offspring. The doctrine, called ṛṇa-traya, ties the householder's duties to the cosmic and social order. Later texts add a fourth debt to humans, and the idea of debts shaped views of marriage and the stages of life.

events.title: Puruṣārthas formulated
events.description: Indian thought recognises four legitimate goals of human life. Dharma is right conduct; artha is wealth and worldly success; kāma is pleasure and love. The oldest texts list these three. Mokṣa, freedom from the cycle of rebirth, was added as the fourth and highest. Each has its own literature, and the ideal is to pursue wealth and pleasure within the limits of dharma, not to reject them.

events.title: Sixteen Mahājanapadas
events.description: By about 600 BCE the tribal territories of north India had grown into sixteen "great states" named in Buddhist and Jaina texts, stretching from Gandhāra in the northwest to Aṅga in the east and Aśmaka on the Godāvarī.¶Some were monarchies, like Magadha and Kosala. Others, like the Vṛji confederacy, were republics run by assemblies of clans. Iron tools, rice surpluses, coins and walled cities appear together. Over the next three centuries Magadha swallowed the rest and became the base of the Maurya empire.

events.title: Vṛji (Vajji) confederacy
events.description: The Vṛji or Vajji confederacy, with the Licchavis the best known of its clans and Vaiśālī (Basarh in Bihar) its capital, was a gaṇasaṅgha, a government by assembly of clan chiefs, rather than a kingship. Buddhist texts praise the Vajjis for meeting often, and the Buddha is said to have said that so long as they did so they would not decline. Ajātaśatru of Magadha later conquered them. The Licchavis married into the Gupta family centuries later.

events.title: Kapila and the Sāṃkhya system
events.description: Sāṃkhya, "enumeration", may be the oldest Indian philosophical system; its founder Kapila is a figure of legend. It explains everything by two principles: countless conscious selves (puruṣa), which only witness, and one unconscious nature (prakṛti), made of three strands, which evolves into mind, senses and matter. Suffering ends when the self sees that it was never part of nature. Yoga and the Gītā build on it.

events.title: Cārvāka and Lokāyata materialism
events.description: The Cārvākas or Lokāyatas were India's materialists. They accepted only what the senses perceive: no soul apart from the body, no afterlife, no karma. Consciousness arises from the elements as the power to intoxicate arises from fermenting grain. The Vedas, they said, are the work of rogues. Their own books are lost; they survive in quotations by opponents, who took them seriously enough to answer for two thousand years.

events.title: Ājīvika order of Makkhali Gosāla
events.description: Makkhali Gosāla, a contemporary and for a time companion of Mahāvīra, taught that everything is fixed by fate: no action, good or bad, changes the course a soul must run through 8.4 million great ages. His naked ascetics, the Ājīvikas, were for centuries a rival to Buddhists and Jainas. Aśoka's grandson gave them rock-cut caves. They died out in south India around the fourteenth century.

events.title: The six āstika darśanas as a set
events.description: The "six systems" (ṣaḍ-darśana) are Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta, which accept the authority of the Veda and are called āstika. Schools that reject it, among them the materialist Cārvāka and the Jaina and Bauddha traditions, are called nāstika. The date is only a rough marker, since the schools took shape over many centuries. The grouping into six was fixed later, in medieval doxographies, and these differ: Haribhadra's Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, for example, counts a different six that includes Bauddha and Jaina views.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ | ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||
gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.
gitaQuote.source: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) Critical Edition; Rāmānuja Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Birth of Vardhamāna Mahāvīra
events.description: Vardhamāna was born a prince of a warrior clan near Vaiśālī in Bihar. At thirty he left home, and after twelve years of extreme austerity attained omniscience and was called Mahāvīra, "great hero", and Jina, "victor". Jainas hold him the twenty-fourth and last ford-maker of this age, not a founder. He taught that every living thing has a soul and that non-violence is the highest duty.

events.title: Birth of Siddhārtha Gautama
events.description: Siddhārtha Gautama was born at Lumbinī, in the Nepal foothills, to a chief of the Śākya clan. The sights of old age, sickness and death drove him from home at twenty-nine. He taught a middle way between indulgence and self-torture, and denied the permanent Self of the Upaniṣads. Hindu tradition later counted him an avatāra of Viṣṇu. Dates for his life vary by about eighty years.

events.title: Prasenajit of Kosala
events.description: Prasenajit, called Pasenadi in Pali texts, ruled Kosala from Śrāvastī in the time of the Buddha and of Mahāvīra. He was a patron of the Buddha and heard his teaching, and his sister married King Bimbisāra of Magadha, bringing the village of Kāśī as dowry, according to Buddhist sources. Kosala held Kāśī and dominated the Śākya clan. Late in his life his son Viḍūḍabha rebelled and later attacked the Śākyas. Kosala was in time absorbed into Magadha.

events.title: Udayana of Vatsa
events.description: Udayana ruled Vatsa from Kauśāmbī, near present-day Prayāgrāj, around the Buddha's time. Tradition remembers him as an expert player of the vīṇā and a romantic hero, especially in his love story with Vāsavadattā, daughter of Pradyota of Avanti. This story is the subject of Sanskrit plays attributed to Bhāsa, such as the Svapnavāsavadattā, and of Harṣa's Ratnāvalī, as well as the Bṛhatkathā tradition. He also appears in Buddhist and Jaina texts, and Kauśāmbī was an important city of the age.

events.title: Pradyota of Avanti
events.description: Pradyota, known as Caṇḍa ("fierce") in Buddhist texts, ruled Avanti from Ujjayinī in the time of the Buddha. He was one of the main rivals of Magadha, Kosala and Vatsa in the age of the sixteen mahājanapadas. Tradition says that Bimbisāra sent him the physician Jīvaka when he fell ill, and that his daughter Vāsavadattā became the wife of Udayana. Ujjayinī grew into a great commercial and religious city, and Avanti was later conquered by Magadha.

events.title: Bimbisāra becomes king of Magadha
events.description: Bimbisāra became king of Magadha, in south Bihar, by one common reckoning about 544 BCE, though modern estimates run some decades later. He conquered Aṅga to the east, with its river port, and made marriage alliances with the royal houses of Kosala and Vaiśālī. Magadha's iron and rice-growing plains gave it wealth. Both the Buddha and Mahāvīra taught in his capital Rājagṛha, and Buddhist and Jaina texts each claim him as a patron. His son Ajātaśatru imprisoned him and took the throne.

events.title: The Buddha's awakening and first sermon
events.description: By the Buddhist tradition, Siddhārtha Gautama, a prince of the Śākya clan, attained awakening under the pipal tree at Bodh Gayā in Bihar after years of austerity and became the Buddha. He then went to the Deer Park at Sārnāth near Vārāṇasī and preached the Dharmacakra-pravartana, the "turning of the wheel of dharma", to five former companions, setting out the Four Noble Truths and the Middle Path. The traditional date is one of several; modern scholars place his life in the fifth century BCE. Buddhism arose in the same śramaṇa milieu as Jainism, and later Hindu texts, such as some Purāṇas, count the Buddha among Viṣṇu's avatāras.

events.title: Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa at Pāvā
events.description: Jaina tradition says that Mahāvīra, the twenty-fourth Tīrthaṅkara, attained liberation at Pāvā (Pāvāpurī, in Bihar), on the new-moon night that Hindus celebrate as Dīpāvalī. Jainas count the Vīra Nirvāṇa era from this event, and light lamps to mark the light of knowledge that left the world. The traditional year, 527 BCE, is the starting point of that era, though modern scholars generally place Mahāvīra's death some decades later, in the fifth century BCE. The Jala Mandir at Pāvāpurī marks the place.

gitaQuote.transliteration: pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ | vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛk sāma yajur eva ca || gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt | prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||
gitaQuote.translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer and the grandsire. I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the creation and dissolution, the foundation and the imperishable seed.
gitaQuote.chapter: Bhagavad Gītā 9.17–18 (Rāja Vidyā Rāja Guhya Yoga)

events.title: Achaemenid Persia annexes Gandhāra and Sindh
events.description: About 518 BCE the Persian king Darius I annexed the Indus valley. His inscriptions list Gandhāra and "Hindush" among the provinces of his empire, and Herodotus says it paid more tribute than any other, in gold dust. This is the first written appearance of the word that became "Hindu" and "India". Persian rule brought the Aramaic script, from which the northwestern Kharoṣṭhī script was made.

events.title: Kautsa's critique of Vedic mantras
events.description: The Nirukta of Yāska, the ancient treatise on Vedic word-meanings, records an early critic named Kautsa who argued that Vedic mantras have no meaning, because they are not sensible statements and their words are fixed. Yāska answers him, saying that the fault lies in the reader, not in the text, and it is part of his defence of studying the Veda for sense. The passage is a rare case of internal criticism of the Veda, and shows that debate on the status of mantras is very old.

events.title: Dīpāvalī, Holī and the festival year
events.description: Many of India's major festivals are fixed to the agricultural and lunar calendar. Gṛhya sūtras and Purāṇas connect rites to harvests, the solstices and particular lunar days, and the dates were set by the pañcāṅga. Dīpāvalī, the autumn festival of lamps, appears under names such as Dīpamālikā and Yakṣarātri in early sources, while Holī marks the spring full moon, and the Holākā rite is already known to ancient ritual and Mīmāṃsā texts. Stories of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Lakṣmī and Prahlāda were attached to these seasonal occasions over time.

events.title: Gopatha Brāhmaṇa
events.description: The Gopatha Brāhmaṇa is the only surviving Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda. It deals with the Atharvaveda's place among the Vedas, the role of the Brahman priest in the sacrifice, and the meaning of Om, and it draws on other Vedic texts. It is generally dated later than the Brāhmaṇas of the other Vedas, and it shows the effort of the Atharvan tradition to gain recognition as a fully Vedic school, since it was at first excluded from the "threefold knowledge".

events.title: Yāska's Nirukta
events.description: By about 500 BCE many words in the Vedic hymns were no longer understood. Yāska's Nirukta explains them by tracing each to a verbal root, working through an older list of difficult words. In doing so he discusses the parts of speech and whether all nouns come from verbs. It is the oldest surviving Indian work on the science of language, and one of the six "limbs" needed to study the Veda.

events.title: Brāhmī at Anuradhapura and Kodumanal
events.description: Pottery fragments with short Brāhmī inscriptions have been found at Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka and at Kodumanal in Tamil Nadu. Radiocarbon dating has led some scholars to place them in the fifth century BCE or earlier, before the edicts of Aśoka, which are the oldest securely dated Brāhmī. The origin of Brāhmī is disputed, between those who see it as derived from a Semitic script and those who see it as an indigenous creation. If the early dates hold, writing was in use in the south long before the Mauryan state.

events.title: Kaṭha Upaniṣad
events.description: A boy, Naciketas, is sent by his angry father to Yama, the god of death. Kept waiting three nights, he is offered three boons. For the third he asks what happens after death. Yama offers wealth, long life and pleasure instead; the boy refuses them all.¶Yama then teaches the deathless Self, "unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain". The text gives the famous image of the body as a chariot, the senses as horses, the mind as reins and the intellect as driver. Its ideas and even its wording reappear in the Bhagavad Gītā.

events.title: Īśā Upaniṣad
events.description: One of the shortest of the major Upaniṣads, eighteen verses forming the last chapter of the White Yajurveda. It opens, "All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is pervaded by the Lord; enjoy by renouncing; do not covet anyone's wealth." It insists that one should wish to live a hundred years doing one's work. Gandhi said that if all other scriptures were lost and only its first verse remained, Hinduism would survive.

events.title: Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra
events.description: The Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra belongs to the Black Yajurveda. It defines Āryāvarta, the land of the cultured, as lying east of where the Sarasvatī disappears, west of Kālakavana, and between the Pāriyātra mountains and the Himalaya. It also lists customs that differ between north and south, such as marriage to a maternal uncle's daughter in the south and trade in wool in the north, and allows each region to follow its own usage. It is one of the oldest law texts.

events.title: Bṛhaddevatā of Śaunaka
events.description: The Bṛhaddevatā, attributed to Śaunaka, is a Sanskrit work of about twelve hundred verses on the deities of the Ṛgveda. For each hymn or verse it says which deity is addressed, and it often retells the legend connected with it, quoting the story as it was known in tradition. It is useful as a source for early narrative traditions that lie behind the epics and Purāṇas, and for how Vedic hymns were understood in the centuries after their composition.

events.title: Anukramaṇīs of Śaunaka and Kātyāyana
events.description: An anukramaṇī is an index to a Vedic text. The Sarvānukramaṇī, attributed to Kātyāyana, lists for every hymn of the Ṛgveda its seer, deity, metre and opening words, and Śaunaka is credited with similar works. These indices acted as a check on the accuracy of the text and are used by scholars to identify authorship and metre. Together with the pāṭhas and prātiśākhyas, they helped keep the Vedic text unchanged for thousands of years.

events.title: Pañca-mahāyajña
events.description: The five great sacrifices, pañca-mahāyajña, are daily duties of the householder, mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and detailed in the Gṛhya and Dharma Sūtras. They are brahmayajña (study of the Veda), pitṛyajña (water or food for the ancestors), devayajña (offering in the fire to the gods), bhūtayajña (food for animals and beings), and manuṣyayajña (hospitality to guests). They express the idea that a person owes a debt to all.

events.title: Pāṇini composes the Aṣṭādhyāyī
events.description: Pāṇini, from Śalātura in Gandhāra, described the whole Sanskrit language in about 4,000 short rules arranged in eight chapters. The rules work like a program: start from roots and suffixes, apply operations in order, and correct words come out.¶He used abbreviations, meta-rules and recursion, and modern linguists and computer scientists have compared his formal method with their own. His grammar fixed Saṃskṛta, the perfected speech, so firmly that classical Sanskrit stayed essentially unchanged for two thousand years. He built on earlier work such as Yāska's Nirukta on the origin of Vedic words.

events.title: Suśruta Saṃhitā and early surgery
events.description: The compendium ascribed to Suśruta, a physician of the Kāśī school, is one of the oldest detailed treatises on surgery. Its core is traditionally placed in the middle of the first millennium BCE, but the text was revised and enlarged over centuries and reached its present form perhaps in the early centuries CE.¶It describes over 300 procedures and 120 instruments, the dissection of bodies soaked in water, and practice cuts on gourds and skins. Best known are couching for cataract and rebuilding a severed nose with a skin flap from the cheek or forehead. British surgeons saw the latter performed near Pune in the 1790s and reported it in London, which helped inspire modern plastic surgery.

events.title: Ātreya, Agniveśa and the Caraka tradition
events.description: Āyurvedic tradition holds that the sage Ātreya Punarvasu taught medicine to a circle of pupils, of whom Agniveśa composed the first systematic treatise, the Agniveśa Tantra. That work is now lost as such. It was later revised by Caraka, and the portions missing from it were completed by Dṛḍhabala, probably in the early centuries CE, giving the Caraka Saṃhitā we have. The tradition is placed in Takṣaśilā and the north-west, and its text is the chief classical source on internal medicine (kāyacikitsā).

events.title: Jīvaka, physician of Magadha
events.description: Jīvaka Komārabhacca was a physician at Rājagṛha who, according to the Buddhist Vinaya, studied medicine for seven years at Takṣaśilā. He is said to have served King Bimbisāra, cured him of a fistula, performed surgery on the head, treated the king of Avanti, and attended the Buddha. He gave the Buddha a mango grove in Rājagṛha. The stories are legendary in part, but he is remembered as the model of the healer and shows the link between Takṣaśilā and Magadha.

events.title: Punch-marked coins
events.description: Punch-marked coins are India's earliest coinage, appearing from about the sixth to fifth centuries BCE. They are pieces of silver, often bent bars, stamped with punches showing the sun, a six-armed wheel, hills, trees and animals, and they follow a weight standard called the kārṣāpaṇa, which Pāṇini mentions. They were issued by Mahājanapadas, later by the Mauryas, and show a money economy in the Gaṅgā plain and Gandhāra.

events.title: Śākya, Malla and Koliya clan republics
events.description: The Śākyas of Kapilavastu, the Koliyas of Rāmagrāma and Devadaha, and the Mallas of Kuśinagara and Pāvā were clan-based gaṇa-saṅghas, governed by assemblies of clan heads, in the Himalayan foothills and the plain below them. The Buddha was a Śākya, and Buddhist texts say that the Śākyas and Koliyas quarrelled over the water of the Rohiṇī river. The Śākyas acknowledged Kosala's overlordship, and the Mallas received a share of the Buddha's relics. Kosala and Magadha later absorbed these small republics.

events.title: Āyurveda's eight limbs
events.description: The classical medical tradition divides medicine into eight branches, listed in the Caraka and Suśruta texts. They are kāya (general medicine), bāla (paediatrics), graha (diseases ascribed to seizing spirits), ūrdhvāṅga (ear, nose, throat, eye and head), śalya (surgery), daṃṣṭrā (toxicology, so called for animal fangs), jarā (geriatrics and rejuvenation) and vṛṣa (aphrodisiacs and reproductive medicine). The scheme shaped the structure of later works such as Vāgbhaṭa's Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya. The date given here, about 500 BCE, is a rough placement for the system, since the existing texts took final form over centuries.

events.title: Śramaṇa teachers Ajita, Pūraṇa and Sañjaya
events.description: Early Buddhist texts, notably the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, name several śramaṇa teachers who rivalled the Buddha in Magadha. Ajita Keśakambalī taught a materialism that denied rebirth and the fruit of action. Pūraṇa Kassapa held that deeds bring neither merit nor demerit. Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta refused to commit himself on questions about the other world, a stance later called agnosticism. We know these teachers only through their opponents' reports. Ajita's view is an early ancestor of the Cārvāka tradition, and Sañjaya's pupils Sāriputta and Moggallāna later joined the Buddha.

events.title: Bharadvāja brings Āyurveda from Indra
events.description: The opening of the Caraka Saṃhitā tells that when disease troubled living beings, sages gathered in the Himalaya and chose Bharadvāja to go to Indra, the king of the gods, and bring back the science of life. Indra taught him Āyurveda, and Bharadvāja passed it on to the sages, among them Ātreya Punarvasu, who taught Agniveśa and others. This is the tradition's own account of its divine origin and not historical record. The Suśruta tradition gives a different line, tracing the science through Dhanvantari.

events.title: Tapas and yoga in the Upaniṣads
events.description: The Upaniṣads speak of tapas, austerity or inner heat, as the way to knowledge, as when Bhṛgu is told in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad to seek Brahman through tapas. Kaṭha 6.11 gives the first known definition of yoga, "the steady holding of the senses". The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (2.8–15) describes a firm posture, control of the breath and a quiet place for meditation, and the Maitrī Upaniṣad later teaches a six-limbed yoga. These passages are the roots of the classical yoga of Patañjali.

events.title: Ajātaśatru expands Magadha
events.description: Ajātaśatru, son of Bimbisāra, became king of Magadha at Rājagṛha, according to Buddhist and Jaina accounts after imprisoning his father. He fought Kosala, under King Prasenajit, over the city of Kāśī, and defeated the Vṛji confederacy of Vaiśālī, using, according to the sources, catapults and a chariot fitted with blades. His ministers fortified the village of Pāṭaligrāma on the Gaṅgā against the Vṛjis, and it later grew into Pāṭaliputra. His conquests made Magadha the strongest power in the north.

events.title: The Buddha's Mahāparinirvāṇa
events.description: According to tradition the Buddha died at Kuśinagara (modern Kushinagar, Uttar Pradesh) at about eighty, after eating a meal at the house of the smith Cunda, and his last words urged his monks to keep striving. Buddhist texts call this the Mahāparinirvāṇa. The date of 483 BCE follows one long chronology; Theravāda calendars count from 544 or 543 BCE, and many modern scholars favour a date nearer 400 BCE, so the question is still debated. His relics were divided among claimants and placed in stūpas, which became pilgrimage places.

events.title: Pāṭaliputra becomes capital
events.description: Udāyin (Udayabhadra), son of Ajātaśatru, moved the capital of Magadha from Rājagṛha to Pāṭaliputra, at the meeting of the Gaṅgā and the Śoṇa, close to the Gaṇḍaka. The site, a former village that Ajātaśatru had fortified, controlled river trade and communication. It became the capital of the Nandas and Mauryas and the greatest city of ancient India, described by Megasthenes as Palibothra. The modern city of Patna stands here, and traces of its wooden palisade have been found.

events.title: Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra
events.description: The Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra, a text of the Taittirīya school of the Black Yajurveda, is probably from the Deccan, perhaps the Andhra country. It is well preserved and is among the clearest of the early Dharma Sūtras. Scholars date it between about the fifth and third centuries BCE. It gives the authorities for dharma as the Vedas and the customs of the learned who know them, and sets out the duties of students, householders and ascetics, the rules for kings, and penances. It was commented on in later centuries and remained in use.

events.title: Śiśunāga dynasty takes Magadha
events.description: According to the Purāṇas, Śiśunāga, a minister, became king of Magadha and destroyed the power of the Pradyota kings of Avanti, so adding Avanti to Magadha. Buddhist sources order the dynasties differently, placing Śiśunāga after the Haryaṅka kings, and his son Kālāśoka is associated with the Second Buddhist Council at Vaiśālī. The dynasty was brief and was overthrown by the Nandas. The sources disagree on details, but all agree Magadha was by now the dominant kingdom.

events.title: Kena Upaniṣad
events.description: "By whom is the mind sent forth? By whom does the first breath move?" The answer is that which the eye cannot see but by which the eye sees. In a story, the gods win a victory and take the credit; Brahman appears as a strange being and none of them can burn or blow away a blade of grass before it. The goddess Umā tells Indra what it was.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.

events.title: Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad
events.description: The Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad distinguishes two kinds of knowledge: the lower, which includes the Vedas themselves and all the sciences, and the higher, by which the imperishable is known. It gives the image of two birds on one tree, one eating the fruit and the other simply watching. A phrase from it, "satyam eva jayate", "truth alone triumphs", is the national motto of India.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ | ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||
gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.
gitaQuote.source: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) Critical Edition; Rāmānuja Gītā Bhāṣya

events.trustedSource: Puranic Corpus & Surya Siddhanta Astronomical Tradition

events.title: Praśna Upaniṣad
events.description: The Praśna Upaniṣad of the Atharvaveda is built as six questions put to the sage Pippalāda by six seekers. The questions concern the origin of creatures, the powers that sustain the body, the greatness of prāṇa, the states of waking, dream and sleep, the meaning of meditation on Om, and the sixteen-part Person. Its answers are given in clear prose. Later Vedānta teachers such as Śaṅkara wrote commentaries on it, and it is counted among the principal Upaniṣads.

events.title: Gṛhya rites of Pāraskara and Gobhila
events.description: The Pāraskara Gṛhya Sūtra belongs to the White Yajurveda and the Gobhila Gṛhya Sūtra to the Sāmaveda. Both are household manuals that set out the domestic rites of a Brahmin family: marriage, the birth ceremonies, naming, the first haircut, initiation into study (upanayana) and the daily offerings in the home fire. Pāraskara's text was widely followed by priests of the Vājasaneyi tradition and had many later commentaries. Together with the manuals of other schools, they show how the rites later called saṃskāras were fixed in practice.

events.title: Mānava and Vaikhānasa Sūtras
events.description: The Mānava Śrauta and Gṛhya Sūtras belong to the Maitrāyaṇīya school of the Black Yajurveda and are not the Manusmṛti. The Vaikhānasa Sūtras, of a Taittirīya school, cover Śrauta, Gṛhya and Dharma. The Vaikhānasas later developed a separate system of Viṣṇu temple worship, set out in their Āgama texts, and Vaikhānasa priests still serve at temples such as Tirumala. The tradition connects Vedic domestic ritual with the later temple.

gitaQuote.verse: पिताहमस्य जगतो माता धाता पितामहः । वेद्यं पवित्रमोंकार ऋक्साम यजुरेव च ॥ गतिर्भर्ता प्रभुः साक्षी निवासः शरणं सुहृत् । प्रभवः प्रलयः स्थानं निधानं बीजमव्ययम् ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ | vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛk sāma yajur eva ca || gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt | prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||
gitaQuote.translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer and the grandsire. I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the creation and dissolution, the foundation and the imperishable seed.
gitaQuote.chapter: Bhagavad Gītā 9.17–18 (Rāja Vidyā Rāja Guhya Yoga)
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Bhāṣya

events.title: Mahābhārata's composition begins
events.description: The epic says of itself that it began as a poem called Jaya, "Victory", of 8,800 verses, grew to 24,000, and finally to 100,000, several times the length of the Iliad and Odyssey together. Scholars generally hold that it was built up by many hands over roughly eight centuries, absorbing law, philosophy, myth and geography. Its own boast is that what is found here may be found elsewhere, but what is not here is nowhere.
events.eraDesc: Sixteen great states, coinage and walled cities rise on the Gaṅgā plain.

gitaQuote.verse: अहमेवाक्षयः कालो धाताहं विश्वतोमुखः ॥ कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो लोकान्समाहर्तुमिह प्रवृत्तः ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: aham evākṣayaḥ kālo dhātāhaṁ viśvatomukhaḥ || kālo 'smi loka-kṣaya-kṛt pravṛddho lokān samāhartum iha pravṛttaḥ ||
gitaQuote.translation: I alone am inexhaustible, imperishable Time (Akṣaya Kāla), and I am the dispenser of destiny facing all directions... I am all-destroying Time, grown mighty to extinguish the worlds.
gitaQuote.source: Mahabharata (Bhishma Parva 35.32); Abhinavagupta Gītārtha-Saṁgraha

events.trustedSource: Puranic Corpus & Surya Siddhanta Astronomical Tradition

events.title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa's core composed
events.description: The Rāmāyaṇa has about 24,000 verses in seven books. Scholars regard books two to six, from the exile to the death of Rāvaṇa, as the original poem, composed in the eastern Gaṅgā plain around the fifth or fourth century BCE and showing Rāma as an ideal human prince. The first and last books, which present him fully as Viṣṇu and tell of Sītā's banishment, were added later.
events.eraDesc: Sixteen great states, coinage and walled cities rise on the Gaṅgā plain.

gitaQuote.verse: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत । अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥ परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् । धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur; Madhvācārya Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Second urbanisation
events.description: From about the sixth to the fourth centuries BCE the Gaṅgā plain saw its second urbanisation, the first being the Indus cities. Walled towns such as Kauśāmbī, Śrāvastī, Vārāṇasī and Rājagṛha grew, using iron tools and rice farming. Punch-marked coins and trade guilds (śreṇi) developed, and writing came back. The new wealth and mobility supported the rise of the Mahājanapadas and of religious movements such as Buddhism and Jainism.

events.title: Śālihotra on horses and Pālakāpya on elephants
events.description: Ancient Indian tradition ascribes early veterinary science to the sages Śālihotra, who is credited with the lore of horses (aśvāyurveda), and Pālakāpya, who is credited with the lore of elephants (hastyāyurveda). The treatises that survive under their names, such as the Hastyāyurveda, are in later redactions, and their authors' dates are not known. They describe the anatomy and diseases of the animals, their feeding and the treatment of wounds, and they reflect the great importance of cavalry and war elephants in Indian states.

gitaQuote.verse: ईश्वरः सर्वभूतानां हृद्देशेऽर्जुन तिष्ठति । भ्रामयन्सर्वभूतानि यन्त्रारूढानि मायया ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: īśvaraḥ sarva-bhūtānāṁ hṛd-deśe 'rjuna tiṣṭhati | bhrāmayan sarva-bhūtāni yantrārūḍhāni māyayā ||
gitaQuote.translation: The Supreme Lord abides in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all living creatures to spin as if mounted upon a cosmic machine (yantra) made of nature.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1 correlation

events.title: Pañcaśikha and Āsuri
events.description: The Mahābhārata's Mokṣadharma section names Kapila as the founder of Sāṃkhya, and lists Āsuri and then Pañcaśikha as his successors. This lineage also appears at the end of Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhya Kārikā. In the Mahābhārata, Pañcaśikha teaches the king Janaka of Mithilā a doctrine of the self that is distinct from the body and mind. These figures are known only through later reports, and their texts have not survived.

events.title: Early Vedānta teachers cited by Bādarāyaṇa
events.description: The Brahma Sūtra of Bādarāyaṇa cites several earlier teachers by name, including Bādari, Kāśakṛtsna and Auḍulomi, who held various views about the self and its relation to Brahman and about liberation. Their works are lost, and we know their views only through these references and later commentators. Their presence indicates that Vedānta was already an active tradition of debate, with different positions, before Bādarāyaṇa composed his systematic text.

events.title: Second Buddhist Council at Vaiśālī
events.description: Buddhist tradition says that, about a century after the Buddha's death, a council at Vaiśālī dealt with a dispute over monastic rules, including ten practices that stricter monks rejected. In the Theravāda account, this council is linked with the first major split in the saṅgha, into Sthaviras (the elders) and Mahāsāṅghikas (the great assembly). Modern scholars debate both the date and the sequence, and sources differ on whether the split came here or later. The schools that resulted shaped the later Buddhist world.

events.title: Pañcarātra and Sātvata traditions
events.description: The oldest organised worship of Viṣṇu centred on Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa and his kinsmen, heroes of the Vṛṣṇi clan. Its theology says the one God manifests in four forms, Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna and Aniruddha, and it taught devotion with image worship, open to all classes, as an alternative to animal sacrifice. A section of the Mahābhārata, the Nārāyaṇīya, is its early charter.

events.title: Vyāḍi's Saṅgraha
events.description: Vyāḍi, a grammarian said by tradition to be related to Pāṇini, composed the Saṅgraha, a work on grammar and the philosophy of language, which is lost. Patañjali knew it, and later authors say it had 100,000 verses, though this figure rests on late tradition. It is thought to have discussed the relation of words and meaning, themes taken up later by Bhartṛhari. It shows the depth of linguistic thought in ancient India.

events.title: Mahāpadma Nanda founds the Nanda empire
events.description: Mahāpadma Nanda, who according to the Purāṇas was the son of a Śūdra woman by the last Śiśunāga king, took power in Magadha and is called the destroyer of all Kṣatriyas (sarvakṣatrāntaka). The Nandas commanded a very large army and treasury, which impressed the Greeks, who called the last Nanda king Agrammes or Xandrames. Their empire reached from Magadha across the Gaṅgā plain and into the Deccan, and some sources associate the dynasty with Jainism. It was overthrown by Candragupta Maurya, according to tradition with the help of Cāṇakya.

events.title: Alexander invades the northwest
events.description: Alexander of Macedon crossed the Hindu Kush in 327 BCE after conquering Persia. The king of Taxila submitted and supplied troops; the hill tribes of Swat fought bitterly. His stay in India lasted under two years and no Indian source mentions him. Its importance is that Greek writers who came with him left the first outside descriptions of India, and that it fixes Indian dates.
events.eraDesc: Sixteen great states, coinage and walled cities rise on the Gaṅgā plain.
events.trustedSource: Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) & Epigraphia Indica Attested Records

events.title: Battle of the Hydaspes
events.description: In the summer of 326 BCE Alexander crossed the flooded Jhelum at night in a storm to attack Porus, king of the Pauravas. Porus fielded two hundred elephants and fought from his own until he was badly wounded. Asked how he wished to be treated, he answered, "Like a king." Alexander returned his kingdom and added to it. Greek writers describe him as exceptionally tall.
events.eraDesc: Sixteen great states, coinage and walled cities rise on the Gaṅgā plain.
events.trustedSource: Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) & Epigraphia Indica Attested Records

events.title: Alexander's army halts at the Beas
events.description: In 326 BCE, after defeating the king Porus (Puru) at the Hydaspes, Alexander the Great marched on to the Hyphasis (Beas). The Greek historians Arrian, Curtius and Diodorus say that his men, exhausted and learning of the powerful Nanda army beyond, refused to go farther. Alexander built altars at the river and turned back, going down the Indus. The Greek conquest of the northwest was brief, but it made the area known to the Mediterranean world and opened the way for the Mauryas.
events.eraDesc: Sixteen great states, coinage and walled cities rise on the Gaṅgā plain.
events.trustedSource: Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) & Epigraphia Indica Attested Records

events.title: Greeks meet the gymnosophists
events.description: Greek writers who accompanied Alexander, such as Onesicritus, wrote of the "gymnosophists", naked ascetics near Taxila, with whom they held philosophical discussions. One of them, Kalanos, joined Alexander and went with him to Persia, where he burned himself on a pyre in front of the army. It is unclear whether these ascetics were Brahmins, Jainas or others. The accounts are among the earliest outside descriptions of Indian renunciants and show how they impressed the Greeks.
events.eraDesc: Sixteen great states, coinage and walled cities rise on the Gaṅgā plain.
events.trustedSource: Muktikā Canon of 108 Upaniṣads & Prasthānatrayī Commentarial Tradition

events.title: Candragupta Maurya founds the empire
events.description: Candragupta, of obscure birth, overthrew the unpopular Nanda dynasty of Magadha about 322 BCE with the help of the brāhmaṇa strategist Cāṇakya, then took the northwest from Alexander's successors. His empire ran from Afghanistan to Bengal and south into the Deccan, the first to unite most of the subcontinent. A Greek ambassador described his capital Pāṭaliputra as fifteen kilometres long with 570 towers.
events.eraDesc: Candragupta and Aśoka unite most of the subcontinent for the first time.
events.trustedSource: Puranic Corpus & Surya Siddhanta Astronomical Tradition

events.title: Cāṇakya's vow against the Nandas
events.description: Tradition tells that Cāṇakya (also called Kauṭilya or Viṣṇugupta), a brāhmaṇa from Takṣaśilā, was insulted by the Nanda king Dhana Nanda at court in Pāṭaliputra. He is said to have vowed to leave his tuft of hair unbound until the dynasty was destroyed. Sources such as the Mudrārākṣasa and Buddhist and Jaina texts tell the story with differences. Helped by him, Candragupta Maurya overthrew the Nandas around 321 BCE. The Arthaśāstra is traditionally attributed to Cāṇakya, though scholars think it took shape over time.
events.eraDesc: Candragupta and Aśoka unite most of the subcontinent for the first time.

events.title: Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra
events.description: The Arthaśāstra is a manual for running a kingdom, in fifteen books: the training of a prince, the duties of some thirty departments, law, taxes, mines, spies, war and diplomacy. Its theory of foreign policy holds that a neighbour is a natural enemy and the neighbour's neighbour a natural friend. It is cool and practical about means, but states that the king's happiness lies in the happiness of his subjects. Its date is debated: some scholars see a Mauryan core, while others, such as Patrick Olivelle, place the text in the first centuries CE.

events.title: Candragupta and Seleucus conclude a treaty
events.description: After a war around 305 to 303 BCE between Candragupta Maurya and Seleucus Nicator, the successor of Alexander in the east, the two made peace. Greek and Roman writers such as Strabo report that Seleucus gave up territories west of the Indus, usually read as Arachosia, Gedrosia and the Paropamisadae, and in return received 500 war elephants. A marriage alliance may also have been agreed. The treaty set the Maurya frontier in the northwest, and the elephants helped Seleucus at the battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE.

events.title: Megasthenes at Pāṭaliputra
events.description: Megasthenes was sent by Seleucus as ambassador to Candragupta's court about 302 BCE and wrote a book, Indica, known through later quotations. He describes the wooden-walled capital, the king's bodyguard of women, a society of seven occupational classes, and the absence of slavery. He says the people of Mathurā worship "Herakles" and those of the hills "Dionysos", usually identified with Kṛṣṇa and Śiva.

events.title: Upavedas enumerated
events.description: Tradition names four upavedas, auxiliary sciences linked to the four Vedas: Āyurveda (medicine), Dhanurveda (archery and warfare), Gāndharvaveda (music and dance) and Sthāpatyaveda (architecture) or Arthaśāstra (statecraft). Sources differ on which is attached to which Veda; many link Āyurveda with the Ṛgveda or Atharvaveda, Dhanurveda with the Yajurveda, and Gāndharvaveda with the Sāmaveda. The list is found in later texts such as the Caraṇavyūha and the Purāṇas, and shows how practical arts were brought under Vedic authority.

events.title: Piṅgala's Chandaḥśāstra on Sanskrit metre
events.description: Piṅgala's treatise on Sanskrit metre, perhaps of the third century BCE, treats verse lines as sequences of light and heavy syllables. To list every possible pattern of a given length he used what are in effect binary numbers, and he gave rules for counting them that amount to fast exponentiation and, in the later commentary tradition, to the arrangement known in the West as Pascal's triangle (the meruprastāra). He also uses the word śūnya, "empty", as a marker in the calculation. The work shows combinatorial thinking applied to poetry.

events.title: Narmadā as the southern boundary
events.description: The Narmadā, also called Revā, flows west through central India between the Vindhya and Sātpura ranges. Many ancient texts treat the Vindhya and Narmadā as the dividing line between the north (Āryāvarta) and the Deccan (Dakṣiṇāpatha). She is worshipped as a goddess, and stones from her bed are revered as natural Śiva liṅgas. Her parikramā, a walk of about 2,600 kilometres along both banks, is among the longest pilgrimages and is traditionally done in about three years. The Revā Khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa celebrates her.

events.title: Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad
events.description: The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad is an early text to identify the absolute of the Upaniṣads with a personal God, whom it names Rudra and Śiva: the one Lord who rules all, hidden in every being like butter in milk. It uses terms that later belong to the Sāṃkhya and Yoga systems, describes the right place and posture for meditation, and in its final verse uses the word bhakti, devotion to God and to the teacher.

events.title: Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad
events.description: The Maitrāyaṇīya or Maitrī Upaniṣad belongs to the Maitrāyaṇīya school of the Black Yajurveda. It opens with King Bṛhadratha, who gives up his kingdom out of despair and approaches a sage for instruction. It teaches a six-limbed yoga, including breath control, withdrawal of the senses, meditation and concentration, and reflects on time as a form of Brahman. Scholars regard it as a late principal Upaniṣad, showing influence of Sāṃkhya and Yoga ideas.

events.title: Vasiṣṭha Dharma Sūtra
events.description: The Vasiṣṭha Dharma Sūtra is a Dharma Sūtra attached to the Ṛgveda, and is generally considered later than those of Āpastamba and Baudhāyana. It contains passages in verse and quotes earlier authorities, including Manu, and shows how Dharma Sūtras were turning toward the verse smṛtis such as the Manusmṛti. Its topics include sources of dharma, inheritance, penances and the position of women.

events.title: Jaimini's Mīmāṃsā Sūtra
events.description: The Mīmāṃsā Sūtra, dated to about 300-200 BCE, begins, "Now, the inquiry into dharma," and defines dharma as what the Veda enjoins. To know what that is, Jaimini worked out rules for interpreting any text: how to tell a command from a description, a main rite from a subsidiary, a literal sense from a figurative. Later Indian courts used these rules to construe legal texts. The school holds the Veda to be eternal and authorless.

events.title: Early Bhāgavata worship of Vāsudeva
events.description: The grammarian Pāṇini (4.3.98) includes a rule on followers of Vāsudeva and Arjuna, which shows that Vāsudeva was already a god of devotion around the fourth century BCE. The Vṛṣṇi heroes, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, Sāmba and Aniruddha, were worshipped at Mathurā. This is the early Bhāgavata or Vaiṣṇava cult, which later merged with the worship of Nārāyaṇa and Viṣṇu. The Heliodorus pillar of c. 113 BCE at Vidiśā also shows a Greek devotee of Vāsudeva.

events.title: Sangam age begins in Tamiḻakam
events.description: Tamil tradition tells of three academies (Sangams) of poets at Madurai under the Pāṇḍya kings. What survives is a body of 2,381 poems by 473 poets, some of them women, composed between about the third century BCE and the third century CE. They divide into poems of the "interior", love, set in five landscapes each with its mood, and the "exterior", war, kings and generosity. They are largely secular, precise and distinct from Sanskrit literature.

events.title: Tolkāppiyam
events.description: The oldest surviving work in Tamil is a grammar in three parts: on sounds, on words, and on subject matter, the last a poetics that classifies the situations of love and war by landscape. Its author is called a pupil of Agastya. It shows knowledge of Sanskrit grammar but describes a language and a literary culture standing on their own. Its date is placed anywhere between the third century BCE and the fifth CE.

events.title: Murugaṉ, lord of the hills
events.description: Murugaṉ, also called Cēyōṉ ("the red one"), is in Sangam poetry the god of the hills (kuṟiñci landscape) and of youth and war, and his spear (vēl) is central. He is honoured with dancing by a priest called the vēlaṉ. In later centuries he was identified with Skanda-Kārttikeya, the son of Śiva worshipped in the north, and the combined figure is worshipped in the six abodes of Tamil Nadu. How the two figures merged is debated.

events.title: Mānava Dharma tradition
events.description: Early authors, such as Baudhāyana, quote verses ascribed to Manu, which suggest that a Mānava Dharma tradition existed before the Manusmṛti as we have it. Patrick Olivelle argues that the Mānava Dharmaśāstra was composed between the second century BCE and the second century CE, and probably had a lost Mānava Dharma Sūtra of the school behind it. Such texts were a stage in the shift from Dharma Sūtras to the metrical Dharmaśāstras.

events.title: Bādarāyaṇa's Brahma Sūtra
events.description: The Upaniṣads do not speak with one voice. Bādarāyaṇa's aphorisms, about 555 in number and dated between about 400 BCE and 200 CE, set out to show that they teach one doctrine: Brahman is that from which the world arises, in which it rests and into which it returns. The sūtras are so brief, often two or three words, that they cannot be read without a commentary. Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, Madhva and others each wrote one, and so founded their schools.

events.title: Bhagavad Gītā takes textual form
events.description: The Bhagavad Gītā, 700 verses in eighteen chapters, is part of the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata. In it Kṛṣṇa instructs Arjuna on the field of Kurukṣetra, in a crisis over fighting his kin, on duty, action without attachment, knowledge and devotion. Tradition places it at the time of the war, but scholars date its composition to between about 400 BCE and 200 CE, and some argue that it was revised. It has since been commented on by Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, Madhva and many others.

events.title: Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra begins to form
events.description: The Nāṭyaśāstra, in thirty-six chapters, covers every aspect of theatre: building the playhouse, the opening rituals, gesture, costume, speech, music, plot types. Its central idea is rasa, the "taste" a spectator relishes, of which there are eight: love, laughter, sorrow, anger, heroism, fear, disgust and wonder. It says Brahmā created drama as a fifth Veda open to all classes. Indian classical dance traditions draw on it.

gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.

events.title: Vātsyāyana's predecessors on kāma
events.description: The Kāmasūtra of Vātsyāyana says that it condenses the work of earlier authorities. It names Bābhravya of Pāñcāla, who compiled a large treatise on kāma in seven parts, and later authors who wrote on single parts, including Dattaka on courtesans, Cārāyaṇa on general matters, Suvarṇanābha on sexual union, Ghoṭakamukha on marriage, Gonardīya on the wife, Gonikāputra on others' wives and Kucumāra on secret arts. These works are lost and are known only from Vātsyāyana. They show that erotics was already a systematic science when it was condensed.

events.title: Jaina schism begins
events.description: Jaina tradition says that during a twelve-year famine in Magadha Bhadrabāhu led a group of monks south to Karnataka, while those who stayed in the north, under Sthūlabhadra, began to wear white cloth. This is how the two main sects came about, Digambara ("sky-clad") and Śvetāmbara ("white-clad"). Historians see the divide as a slower process, finalised in the first centuries CE, and the migration story as recorded in later sources.

events.title: Pāṭaliputra council and the Jaina Āgamas
events.description: Śvetāmbara tradition says that after a twelve-year famine the Jaina monks met in a council at Pāṭaliputra, about 300 BCE, under Sthūlabhadra, to collect the scriptures, and compiled the eleven Aṅgas. The twelfth Aṅga, the Dṛṣṭivāda, was already lost. The canon was fixed in writing much later, at the council of Valabhī in the fifth century CE. The Digambaras hold that the original canon was lost. Among the texts the Uttarādhyayana, thirty-six chapters of verse on monastic discipline, is regarded as one of the oldest.

events.title: Śvetadvīpa and Nārāyaṇīya
events.description: The Nārāyaṇīya section of the Mahābhārata (12.321–339) tells how Nārada visits Śvetadvīpa, the "white island", where he sees white men worshipping Nārāyaṇa with exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti), and learns of the four forms, called vyūhas, of the deity. It is an early text of the Pāñcarātra tradition and of Vaiṣṇava theology, with ideas close to the Gītā. Scholars debate where Śvetadvīpa was and the date of this part of the epic.

events.title: Sanatsujātīya and Anugītā
events.description: The Sanatsujātīya (Udyogaparvan 41–46) is a dialogue in which the sage Sanatsujāta consoles Dhṛtarāṣṭra by teaching about death, immortality and Brahman. The Anugītā (Aśvamedhikaparvan) records Kṛṣṇa's further teaching to Arjuna after the war. Both are philosophical sections of the Mahābhārata, and later Vedāntins commented on them; Śaṅkara is traditionally credited with a commentary on the Sanatsujātīya, which is one reason the text carries weight in Advaita circles.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
