gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. events.title: Vidura-nīti and Yakṣa-praśna
events.description: The Vidura-nīti (Udyogaparvan 33–40) is Vidura's night-time counsel to Dhṛtarāṣṭra on ethics and government, describing the qualities of a wise man and warning against anger and greed. The Yakṣa-praśna (Vanaparvan) has a Yakṣa, who is Dharma in disguise, questioning Yudhiṣṭhira at a lake; asked what is the greatest wonder, he answers that every day beings go to the house of Yama and the rest live as if immortal. These are among the epic's best known wisdom passages.

events.title: Tīrthayātrā Parva
events.description: In the forest book of the Mahābhārata the sage Pulastya describes to Bhīṣma hundreds of holy places, and the Pāṇḍavas then tour them, moving clockwise around India. The text says that pilgrimage gives the poor what kings gain from costly sacrifices. It is an early map of India as a single sacred land, and the model for later pilgrimage guides and the Purāṇic tīrtha-māhātmyas that praise individual sites.

events.title: Mauryan administration
events.description: Sources for Mauryan government include the Greek envoy Megasthenes, whose lost work survives in quotations, and the Arthaśāstra, a Sanskrit treatise on statecraft attributed to Kauṭilya. Megasthenes describes a city administration of boards, each with several members, that handled matters such as crafts, foreigners and trade. The Arthaśāstra describes salaried officials, spies and tight state oversight of the economy. Pliny, citing Megasthenes, gives the army as 600,000 infantry along with cavalry and elephants. The Arthaśāstra's date is debated, so the two sources are not always read as a single picture.

events.title: Mokṣadharma Parva
events.description: The Mokṣadharma is the large section on liberation in the Śānti Parva of the Mahābhārata, in which Bhīṣma instructs Yudhiṣṭhira. It collects teaching from several traditions, including early forms of Sāṃkhya and Yoga and Pāñcarātra teaching in the Nārāyaṇīya portion. It also includes dialogues such as those between Janaka and Sulabhā. It was compiled over centuries, and scholars use it to trace the development of philosophy before the classical systems.

events.title: Nāstika defined
events.description: The term nāstika originally referred, in Pāṇini's grammar, to someone who denies an afterlife. It later came to mean a person or school rejecting the authority of the Veda. Manu 2.11 uses the phrase nāstiko veda-nindakaḥ, "a nāstika is one who reviles the Veda". The schools classed as nāstika include the materialist Cārvāka, the Jainas, the Buddhists and the Ājīvikas, although these traditions had their own sophisticated philosophy and ethics.

events.title: Tridoṣa and pañca-mahābhūta theory
events.description: Classical Āyurveda explains health through the three doṣas, vāta, pitta and kapha, which are broadly understood as principles of movement, transformation and cohesion, and through the five great elements of earth, water, fire, air and space (pañca-mahābhūta). Health is a balance of the doṣas; illness arises from their imbalance, and diet, drugs and regimen aim to restore it. The framework draws on wider Indian natural philosophy, especially Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika, and is set out in the Caraka and Suśruta compilations, which scholars date to the last centuries BCE and early centuries CE.

events.title: Candragupta's renunciation
events.description: Jaina tradition says that Candragupta Maurya in his old age gave up the throne to his son Bindusāra, became a Jaina monk, and followed the teacher Bhadrabāhu to the south during a famine. He is said to have died by sallekhanā, ritual fasting, at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa in Karnataka, where a hill is called Candragiri and a temple bears his name. The inscriptions that tell this are later, and historians are divided over whether the story is accurate.

events.title: Bindusāra succeeds Candragupta
events.description: Bindusāra, son of Candragupta and father of Aśoka, ruled c. 297–273 BCE. The Greeks called him Amitrochates, from Sanskrit amitraghāta, "slayer of enemies". The Greek writer Athenaeus reports that he asked Antiochus I for sweet wine, dried figs and a philosopher; Antiochus sent the first two but said philosophers were not for sale. Buddhist sources say he patronised the Ājīvikas, and later accounts credit him with extending the empire south, though evidence is limited.

events.title: Aśoka becomes emperor
events.description: Aśoka, grandson of Candragupta, was consecrated about 268 BCE after a contested succession. Buddhist legend paints his early years as cruel. He ruled one of the largest empires India saw before the British, and is the first Indian king whose own words survive, cut on rocks and pillars. He had been largely forgotten in India for about two thousand years when James Prinsep deciphered his inscriptions in 1837.

events.title: Kaliṅga War
events.description: Around 261 BCE the Maurya emperor Aśoka conquered Kaliṅga, on the coast of modern Odisha. His own inscription (Rock Edict 13) gives the cost: a hundred thousand killed, a hundred and fifty thousand deported, and many more dead of other causes.¶The same edict says the suffering filled him with remorse. He gave up conquest by arms for "conquest by dhamma": moral persuasion, welfare works, respect for all sects, and gentleness to animals. It is a rare case of an ancient ruler publicly regretting a victorious war.

events.title: Aśoka's edicts
events.description: Aśoka had some thirty-three inscriptions carved across his empire, in local dialects and, in the northwest, in Greek and Aramaic. They are personal in tone. He tells his subjects that he has planted shade trees and dug wells, set up hospitals for people and animals, cut the palace's meat consumption, and appointed officers of dhamma. He asks that all sects honour one another, since to praise one's own by blaming another harms one's own.

events.title: Barābar caves gifted to the Ājīvikas
events.description: The Barābar hills in Bihar hold the oldest surviving rock-cut caves in India, hewn out of granite with a smooth, mirror-like polish typical of Mauryan work. Aśoka dedicated some to the Ājīvikas, the ascetic sect founded by Makkhali Gosāla, in the twelfth year of his reign, and his grandson Daśaratha gave others at nearby Nāgārjunī. They show state support for different sects. The caves later inspired the Marabar caves in E. M. Forster's A Passage to India.

events.title: Lion Capital of Sārnāth
events.description: Aśoka set up a polished sandstone pillar at Sārnāth, where the Buddha first taught. Its capital has four lions seated back to back on a drum carved with an elephant, bull, horse and lion separated by wheels, over an inverted lotus. A large wheel once stood on top. Independent India adopted the lions as its state emblem and placed the wheel at the centre of its flag.

events.title: Brāhmī script in Aśoka's edicts
events.description: Brāhmī appears across India in Aśoka's inscriptions, already fully developed: each sign is a consonant with the vowel "a", modified by strokes for other vowels, and the letters are arranged by place of articulation as the phoneticians had analysed them. Whether it was invented in India or adapted from a Semitic model is disputed. Devanāgarī, Tamil, Tibetan, Thai and Javanese are all its descendants.

events.title: Kātyāyana's Vārttikas
events.description: Kātyāyana, writing in the fourth or third century BCE, made vārttikas, short critical notes, on a large number of the roughly four thousand rules of Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, pointing out omissions and corrections. His work was later taken up by Patañjali in the Mahābhāṣya, who discusses and sometimes defends Pāṇini against it. Together, Pāṇini, Kātyāyana and Patañjali form the "three sages" of Sanskrit grammar, who fixed the standard language.

events.title: Third Buddhist Council and missions
events.description: Buddhist chronicles of Sri Lanka say that the emperor Aśoka held the Third Buddhist Council at Pāṭaliputra under the monk Moggaliputta Tissa and sent missionaries to various lands, among them his son Mahinda (Mahendra) to Laṅkā, where he converted King Devānaṃpiya Tissa. Aśoka's own edicts mention envoys to Greek kings and to Tāmraparṇī, but do not mention the council, so some scholars doubt it. Buddhism became the main religion of Sri Lanka.

events.title: Brāhmaṇas and śramaṇas in Mauryan sources
events.description: Aśoka's edicts repeatedly pair brāhmaṇas and śramaṇas, as groups to whom gifts and respect are due. Megasthenes, as quoted by Strabo, likewise divides India's philosophers into Brachmanes and Sarmanes. The grammarian Patañjali, commenting on Pāṇini, cites the compound śramaṇa-brāhmaṇam as an example of two groups in permanent opposition. Together these sources show that by the Mauryan age Indians themselves saw the Vedic Brahmins and the wandering ascetic movements, among them Buddhists, Jainas and Ājīvikas, as two distinct streams of religious life that argued and coexisted.

events.title: Lomas Ṛṣi cave façade
events.description: The Lomas Ṛṣi cave in the Barābar hills, near Gayā in Bihar, is one of the rock-cut caves made for Ājīvika ascetics in the Mauryan period, probably under Aśoka or his grandson Daśaratha, though the Mauryan date rests on style. Its entrance is carved to copy a wooden hut with curved bamboo and thatch, in an arch with a frieze of elephants approaching stūpas. The polished interior is typical of Mauryan craft. The arch form became a model for later caitya halls of Buddhist and other cave temples.

events.title: Tamil kingdoms named by Aśoka
events.description: Aśoka's Rock Edict 2 mentions the Coḍas, Pāṇḍyas, Satiyaputas and Keralaputas as neighbours, as far as Tāmbapaṇṇi, in whose lands he provided medical care for humans and animals. The edict shows that these southern kingdoms were not part of the Mauryan empire but friendly, independent states. It is one of the earliest records of the names Cōḻa, Pāṇḍya and Cēra. The identity of the Satiyaputas is unclear.

events.title: Death of Aśoka
events.description: Aśoka died in about 232 BCE after ruling for about thirty-seven years, during which he had turned from conquest, at the Kaliṅga war, to the policy of dhamma recorded in his edicts. His successors, among them Daśaratha and Samprati, held the empire for only a few decades. The last Maurya, Bṛhadratha, was killed by his general Puṣyamitra around 185 BCE. Provinces drifted away and the Bactrian Greeks, Śuṅgas and Sātavāhanas appeared.

events.title: Daśaratha and Samprati succeed Aśoka
events.description: After Aśoka's death around 232 BCE the Maurya empire lost its unity. The Purāṇas and later texts name his grandsons Daśaratha and Samprati as successors, and tradition suggests that they ruled different regions, with Daśaratha in the east and Samprati from Ujjayinī in the west, though sources conflict. Daśaratha's inscriptions at the Nāgārjunī caves record gifts to the Ājīvikas. Jaina tradition remembers Samprati as a great patron of Jainism, comparable to Aśoka for Buddhism, who is said to have built many temples.

events.title: Sātavāhana dynasty founded
events.description: Simuka (Śrīmukha), according to the Purāṇas, founded the Sātavāhana or Āndhra dynasty in the Deccan after the decline of the Mauryas. A Sātavāhana inscription at Nāneghāṭ lists him among the family's ancestors. They ruled from Pratiṣṭhāna (Paithan) and later Amarāvatī, and controlled trade between the Gaṅgā plain, the west coast and the Tamil country. The date of the dynasty's rise is debated: Purāṇic regnal lists point to about 230 BCE, while some scholars place it as late as the first century BCE.

events.title: Arikamedu and early Indian Ocean trade
events.description: Arikamedu, on the coast near Puducherry, was identified by Mortimer Wheeler in the 1940s with Poduke, a port mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea. Excavations found Roman amphorae, glass and bead-making, showing a major trade centre linking the Tamil country with the Mediterranean. Later work by Vimala Begley placed the first occupation around the second century BCE, possibly a little earlier, and Roman trade peaked in the first two centuries CE. Exports included beads, cotton cloth and spices. The exact chronology is still discussed.

events.title: Godāvarī, the Dakṣiṇa Gaṅgā
events.description: The Godāvarī rises at Tryambakeśvara near Nāsik, a jyotirliṅga site, and flows across the Deccan to the Bay of Bengal. Tradition calls her Gautamī, after the sage Gautama who is said to have brought her down, and Dakṣiṇa Gaṅgā, the Gaṅgā of the south. The Rāmāyaṇa places Rāma's forest dwelling at Pañcavaṭī on her bank. Pratiṣṭhāna, modern Paithan, on her banks was an early capital of the Sātavāhanas. The Kumbha Mela is held at Nāsik on her banks every twelve years.

gitaQuote.verse: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत । अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥ परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् । धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥

gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.

events.title: Kāverī in Sangam poetry
events.description: Sangam poems of the early centuries CE praise the Kāverī, called Ponni ("golden") or Kāviri, as the nourisher of the Cōḻa country. The Paṭṭiṉappālai describes the port city of Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam at her mouth and praises King Karikāla, and later works like the Cilappatikāram sing of her. Her floods made the delta one of the most fertile regions of India. The river came to be regarded as sacred, as "Dakṣiṇa Gaṅgā", and its festivals, such as Āṭi Perukku, continue.

events.title: Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad
events.description: The Māṇḍūkya is the shortest major Upaniṣad, only twelve sentences. It analyses the syllable Om as three sounds, a, u and m, matching three states of experience: waking, dreaming and deep sleep. Beyond them is a "fourth", turīya, which in the Advaita reading is not a state but the awareness present in all three, and which is the Self. Gauḍapāda's verses on this text are the earliest surviving systematic work of Advaita.

events.title: Akṣapāda Gautama's Nyāya Sūtra
events.description: The Nyāya Sūtra is the founding text of Indian logic. It recognises four means of knowing: perception, inference, comparison and reliable testimony. It sets out a five-step form of argument, "the hill has fire, because it has smoke, like a kitchen", and catalogues the tricks and fallacies of debate. Its aim is practical: right knowledge removes false belief, and with it desire and suffering.

events.title: Tamil-Brāhmī cave inscriptions
events.description: Short inscriptions in Tamil-Brāhmī, the Brāhmī script adapted to Tamil, are found in natural caves in Tamil Nadu, such as Māṅkuḷam near Madurai, from about the third to first centuries BCE. They record gifts made to Jaina monks, and the Māṅkuḷam record names a Pāṇḍya, Neḍuñceḻiyaṉ. They are among the earliest known writing of Tamil and show that Jainism and the Pāṇḍya court were already established in the south.

events.title: Cedi dynasty of Kaliṅga
events.description: After the Mauryan decline, Kaliṅga, conquered by Aśoka in about 261 BCE, regained independence under the Cedi or Mahāmeghavāhana dynasty. Its most famous king, Khāravela, left the Hāthigumphā inscription at Udayagiri near Bhubaneswar, a Jaina record of his reign which mentions a Nanda king taking a Jina image from Kaliṅga. The dynasty patronised Jainism, and the caves of Udayagiri and Khaṇḍagiri near Bhubaneswar, cut for Jaina monks in this period, still survive. Kaliṅga's revival shows how regional kingdoms rose after the empire weakened.

events.title: Yaudheya, Mālava and Ārjunāyana republics
events.description: In north-west India several tribal republics, or gaṇas, issued their own coinage from around the second century BCE. The Yaudheyas of Punjab and Haryana, the Mālavas of Rajasthan and Mālwā, and the Ārjunāyanas around Mathurā and Āgrā struck coins bearing their tribal names. The Yaudheya coins show Kārttikeya. These republics continued for some centuries until Samudragupta's Prayāga inscription lists them among frontier peoples who paid tribute in the fourth century CE.

events.title: Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra and the White Yajurveda
events.description: The Śukla or White Yajurveda, the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, survives in two recensions, the Mādhyandina, followed mainly in north India, Gujarat and Maharashtra, and the Kāṇva, found chiefly in the Deccan and the east. Its ritual manual is the Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, which sets out the Vedic sacrifices in line with the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, and the Pāraskara Gṛhya Sūtra covers its household rites. The Īśā Upaniṣad forms its final chapter. These texts connect the White Yajurveda's mantras to the sacrificial practice of its schools.

events.title: Puṣyamitra Śuṅga ends the Mauryas
events.description: About 185 BCE the last Maurya emperor was killed at a military parade by his own commander-in-chief, Puṣyamitra, a brāhmaṇa, who founded the Śuṅga dynasty. He is recorded as performing the horse sacrifice twice, which is often read as a return to Vedic royal ritual after the Mauryas' patronage of Buddhism. Later Buddhist texts call him a persecutor; the great stūpas at Sāñcī and Bhārhut were nevertheless enlarged under his dynasty.

events.title: Puṣyamitra's Aśvamedhas
events.description: The Ayodhyā inscription of Dhanadeva, a Sanskrit record, states that Puṣyamitra Śuṅga performed two horse sacrifices. Patañjali also speaks of priests performing sacrifices for Puṣyamitra. After the Mauryas, who favoured Buddhism and Jainism, this is often seen as a revival of Vedic royal ritual. Some Buddhist texts accuse Puṣyamitra of persecuting monks, but archaeology shows continued Buddhist building under the Śuṅgas, and scholars are cautious about the claims.

events.title: Indo-Greek rule begins in northwest India
events.description: Demetrius I of Bactria crossed the Hindu Kush around 180 BCE and began Greek rule in northwestern India. The Indo-Greek or Yavana kings governed Gandhāra and the Punjab for about two centuries, issuing bilingual coins in Greek and Kharoṣṭhī. Patañjali mentions a Yavana attack on Sāketa, and the Yuga Purāṇa speaks of Yavanas reaching Pāṭaliputra. The meeting of Greek and Indian culture led to Gandhāran art.

events.title: Agathocles' coins show Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma
events.description: Six silver coins found at Ai-Khanoum on the Oxus were struck by the Indo-Greek king Agathocles about 180 BCE. One side shows a figure holding a plough and club, the other a figure holding a wheel and conch: Balarāma and Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa, with the king's name given in Greek and Brāhmī. They are among the oldest securely dated images of any Hindu deity, and show Kṛṣṇa worship important enough for a Greek king to put on his money.

events.title: Kuṇinda kingdom
events.description: The Kuṇindas, called Kulindas in the Mahābhārata, held the Himalayan hills between the Yamunā and the Sutlej from about the second century BCE. Their ruler Amoghabhūti issued silver coins bearing a deer and the goddess Lakṣmī, with legends in both Brāhmī and Kharoṣṭhī scripts. The coins bear Buddhist and Śaiva-linked symbols as well, showing how mixed the religious life of the hills was. They are among the few records of this small kingdom.

events.title: Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya
events.description: The "Great Commentary", about 150 BCE, examines Pāṇini's grammar rule by rule in the form of a lively debate between an objector and a teacher. It is counted the model of Sanskrit prose. Its examples preserve scraps of daily life and history: a Greek siege of Sāketa, plays about the killing of Kaṃsa, Puṣyamitra's sacrifice. Whether this Patañjali also wrote the Yoga Sūtra is an old question.

events.title: Menander (Milinda)
events.description: Menander (Milinda), the best known Indo-Greek king, ruled from Śākala (Sialkot) in the second century BCE. The Pali Milindapañha records his dialogues with the Buddhist monk Nāgasena, on topics such as the self, which Nāgasena explains with the analogy of a chariot, and rebirth. Plutarch says that cities competed for his ashes after he died. His coins have both Greek and Kharoṣṭhī legends, and the dialogue shows Greek interest in Indian thought.

events.title: Ghosuṇḍī inscription
events.description: The Ghosuṇḍī (or Nagarī) inscription, from near Chittorgarh in Rajasthan, is an early Sanskrit record, which says that a stone enclosure was built for the worship of Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva by a devotee who had performed an Aśvamedha. It refers to a Nārāyaṇa shrine. It is one of the earliest inscriptions showing the Bhāgavata cult, and also shows Sanskrit being used in inscriptions.

events.title: Khāravela and the Hāthigumphā inscription
events.description: A long inscription in a cave near Bhubaneśvara records, year by year, the reign of Khāravela, king of Kaliṅga in the second or first century BCE: the walls he repaired, the canal he extended, his campaigns as far as Magadha, and his recovery of a Jina image carried off by the Nandas centuries before. He was a Jaina, yet describes himself as honouring every sect and repairing the temples of all gods.

gitaQuote.transliteration: pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ | vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛk sāma yajur eva ca || gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt | prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||
gitaQuote.translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer and the grandsire. I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the creation and dissolution, the foundation and the imperishable seed.

events.title: Dīdārgañj and Besnagar yakṣī sculptures
events.description: Two famous sandstone figures date from around the Mauryan and Śuṅga periods. The Dīdārgañj Cāmara-bearer, found near Patna in 1917, is a tall female figure holding a fly-whisk, with a mirror-like polish; its date, Mauryan or later, is debated. The Besnagar Yakṣī comes from near Vidiśā. They are early examples of Indian monumental sculpture, and the yakṣī, a nature spirit, became part of the visual language of Hindu, Buddhist and Jaina art.

events.title: Heliodorus pillar at Vidiśā
events.description: Around 113 BCE a Greek named Heliodorus, ambassador of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas of Taxila, set up a stone pillar at Vidiśā in central India. Its Brāhmī inscription calls it a Garuḍa-standard of Vāsudeva, "god of gods", and calls Heliodorus a Bhāgavata, a devotee of that god.¶It is one of the earliest datable monuments of Kṛṣṇa-Vāsudeva worship, and shows that a foreigner could become a Vaiṣṇava over two thousand years ago. A second inscription on the pillar names three steps to heaven: self-control, generosity and vigilance. The pillar still stands.

events.title: Jaina classification of numbers and infinity
events.description: Jaina texts such as the Sthānāṅga and the Anuyogadvāra Sūtra classify numbers as enumerable (saṃkhyāta), innumerable (asaṃkhyāta) and infinite (ananta), with several levels in each category. Their authors were concerned with huge numbers in cosmology and the measurement of time, and they distinguished kinds of infinity. They are among the earliest thinkers anywhere to treat infinity as a mathematical concept with degrees. The texts took their present form over several centuries, and the canon was fixed only in the fifth century CE.

events.title: Bhāsa's plays
events.description: Thirteen Sanskrit plays, found in 1912 in manuscripts from Kerala by T. Ganapati Śāstrī, are attributed to Bhāsa, among them Svapnavāsavadattam, Pratijñāyaugandharāyaṇa, Cārudatta, Karṇabhāra and Ūrubhaṅga. Some draw on the epics. events.title: Manusmṛti (Mānava Dharmaśāstra)

events.title: Paripāṭal hymns to Tirumāl and Cevvēḷ
events.description: The Paripāṭal is one of the Eight Anthologies, a collection of poems in praise of gods set to music. The surviving poems, about two dozen of an original seventy, honour Tirumāl (Viṣṇu) at Tirumāliruñcōlai, Cevvēḷ (Murugaṉ) at Tirupparaṅkuṉṟam near Madurai, and the river Vaiyai. They are among the earliest Tamil devotional poems and a forerunner of the later bhakti hymns of the Āḻvārs and Nāyaṉmārs.

events.title: Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣika Sūtras and atomism
events.description: The Vaiśeṣika school traces its teaching to the sūtras of Kaṇāda, whose date is uncertain, with estimates from the last centuries BCE to the early centuries CE. The text names six categories (padārthas): substance, quality, action, universal, particularity and inherence; later authors added non-existence. It holds that the physical world is built from indivisible atoms (paramāṇu) of earth, water, fire and air. The relation of inherence (samavāya) binds qualities to substances, and universals explain why individual things fall into classes. Praśastapāda later systematised these ideas.

events.title: Śaka rule in northwest India
events.description: The Śakas, called Scythians by the Greeks, were Central Asian nomads who migrated into Bactria and then India around the first century BCE. Maues and then Azes I established Śaka power in Gandhāra and Punjab, and Śaka satraps ruled Mathurā and later western India, as the Western Kṣatrapas of Ujjayinī. The Śaka era, begun in 78 CE, is the basis of the Indian national calendar, though its origin is uncertain. Tradition holds that Vikramāditya drove out the Śakas.

events.title: Śuṅgas give way to Kāṇvas

The four Kāṇva kings were Brahmins who ruled Magadha for about forty-five years. They were overthrown by the Sātavāhanas, according to the Purāṇas. They were a minor power, and the Magadhan empire's centre moved away.

events.title: Vikrama Saṃvat epoch
events.description: The Vikrama era begins in 57 BCE. Tradition says it marks the victory of King Vikramāditya of Ujjain over the Śaka invaders; legend gathered round him as the ideal wise and generous king, with nine gems of learning at his court. Historians find the era first used by the Mālava people and attached to his name later. It is the everyday calendar of north and west India and the official one of Nepal.

events.title: Nāneghāṭ inscription of Nāganikā
events.description: The Nāneghāṭ inscription, in a cave pass near Junnar in Maharashtra, was made by the Sātavāhana queen Nāyanikā (Nāganikā), widow of Śātakarṇi I, who ruled for her young sons. It lists the Vedic sacrifices she performed, including the Aśvamedha, with the large gifts she gave to priests. The record begins with invocations to Dharma, Indra, Saṅkarṣaṇa-Vāsudeva, the Moon, the Sun and the guardians of the directions, showing royal support for Vedic and Bhāgavata worship.

events.title: Tirukkuṟaḷ of Tiruvaḷḷuvar
events.description: The Kuṟaḷ is 1,330 two-line verses in Tamil, arranged in 133 chapters of ten, on three subjects: virtue, public life and love. It names no king or place and is largely free of sectarian detail, which is why Hindus, Jainas, Buddhists and Christians have all claimed its author, Tiruvaḷḷuvar, said to have been a weaver. Tradition dates him to 31 BCE, but scholars place the text anywhere from the first to the fifth century CE. It teaches gratitude, hospitality, plain speech and the avoidance of harm, and has been translated into over forty languages.

events.title: Caraka Saṃhitā redacted
events.description: The Caraka Saṃhitā is the foundation text of Āyurveda's internal medicine, a teaching by the sage Ātreya revised by Caraka around the first century CE. It discusses diagnosis, some five hundred plant drugs, the growth of the embryo, and an oath in which the student promises to put the patient's good before his own.

events.title: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali
events.description: In 195 brief aphorisms Patañjali defines yoga as "the stilling of the movements of the mind". When the mind is still, the seer rests in its own nature.¶He lays out eight limbs: ethical restraints, observances, posture, breath control, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation and absorption (samādhi). Posture gets only three sūtras; the book is about meditation. Its philosophy is that of Sāṃkhya with the addition of Īśvara, a special Self untouched by suffering. Dated somewhere between 200 BCE and 400 CE, it became the classical text of yoga.

events.title: Mora Well inscription of the five Vṛṣṇi heroes

events.title: Kujula Kadphises founds Kuṣāṇa power

events.title: St Thomas tradition in Kerala
events.description: Christian tradition among the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala holds that the apostle Thomas landed at Muziris in 52 CE, founded seven churches and was later martyred near Chennai. Jews, Christians and later Muslims all settled in the trading ports of the Malabar coast, adding to India's religious variety.

events.title: Śaka era begins
events.description: The Śaka era counts from 78 CE. It is usually linked to the accession of a Scythian or Kuṣāṇa king; the name means "era of the Śakas". Astronomers adopted it for their calculations, which spread it across India and to Southeast Asia, where Cambodian and Javanese inscriptions are dated by it. In 1957 it became the basis of India's national civil calendar.

events.title: Vima Kadphises, the "Māheśvara"
events.description: Vima Kadphises, a Kuṣāṇa ruler of the late first or early second century CE, minted gold coins in the Roman style. Many show Śiva, with the bull Nandī, and bear the Kharoṣṭhī title "Maheśvara", a worshipper of Śiva. They are among the earliest clearly identifiable depictions of Śiva, and show that Śaiva devotion was accepted by foreign rulers in the northwest, just as Buddhism was under his successors.

events.title: Karikāla Cōḻa and the Grand Anicut
events.description: Karikāla Cōḻa, an early Cōḻa king, is celebrated in Sangam poems as the victor at Veṇṇi over the Cēra, Pāṇḍya and their allies, and the Paṭṭiṉappālai praises him. Later tradition credits him with the Kallaṇai, the Grand Anicut, an earth and stone dam on the Kāverī near Tiruchirappalli that irrigates the delta. The attribution is from later sources, and the dam has been rebuilt many times, but it is one of the oldest working water-diversion structures in the world.

events.title: Jābāla and Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads
events.description: The Jābāla and Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads deal with renunciation. The Jābāla Upaniṣad says that one may renounce on the very day one feels detached from the world, whatever stage of life one is in, rather than having to pass through all the stages in order. The group of Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads, mostly later, describe the rules and types of renunciants. They are minor Upaniṣads, probably composed in the early centuries CE or later, and they show the tension between the householder's ideal and that of the renunciant.

events.title: Nahapāna the Kṣaharāta
events.description: Nahapāna was a ruler of the Kṣaharāta branch of the Western Kṣatrapas, controlling Gujarat, Konkan and parts of Mahārāṣṭra. His dating is disputed, with proposals from the first to the early second century CE. His son-in-law Uṣavadāta (Ṛṣabhadatta) left inscriptions at Nāsik and Karle recording gifts to brāhmaṇas and Buddhist monks, including feeding brāhmaṇas, and donations at pilgrimage sites such as Prabhāsa and Puṣkara. Many of Nahapāna's coins were later overstruck by the Sātavāhana Gautamīputra Sātakarṇi.

events.title: Triveṇī Saṅgama at Prayāga
events.description: At Prayāga the brown Gaṅgā meets the darker Yamunā, and tradition adds a third, invisible river, the Sarasvatī, flowing underground. The meeting of the three is the Triveṇī Saṅgama. The Mahābhārata praises Prayāga, later called Tīrtharāja, the king of holy places, and says bathing here in the month of Māgha equals the fruit of great sacrifices. Pilgrims are rowed out to the line where the two colours join.

events.title: Mathurā school of sculpture
events.description: In the first three centuries CE the sculptors of Mathurā, working in spotted red sandstone, gave the gods the forms by which they are still known. Viṣṇu with four arms holding mace and wheel, Śiva with his liṅga and bull, Durgā killing the buffalo, the Sun in northern boots, Lakṣmī on her lotus: all appear here among the earliest stone images, beside the earliest Indian-style Buddhas and Jinas.

events.title: Gandhāra school of Buddhist art
events.description: In the Kuṣāṇa-era northwest, workshops around Taxila and the Peshawar valley carved Buddha and bodhisattva images in grey schist and stucco, combining Indian iconography with Hellenistic and Roman features such as wavy hair, heavy drapery and classical proportions. Mathurā was producing Buddha images in red sandstone at about the same time, and scholars still debate which centre came first. Gandhāran art travelled along the Silk Road into Central Asia and China, shaping how the Buddha was pictured across much of Asia.

events.title: Lakulīśa organises the Pāśupatas
events.description: Lakulīśa, "the lord with the club", is traditionally placed in Gujarat around the second century CE. Pāśupata tradition holds that Śiva entered a corpse in a cremation ground and was born as him, and that he taught four disciples. He is remembered as the teacher who organised the Pāśupata order, the earliest known Śaiva ascetic movement, whose members lived in cremation grounds, smeared themselves with ash and deliberately courted contempt to destroy pride. He is carved on temples across India, seated and holding a club.

events.title: Aśvaghoṣa's Buddhacarita
events.description: The Buddhacarita, "Acts of the Buddha," retells the Buddha's life from birth to awakening in polished Sanskrit kāvya verse. Its author Aśvaghoṣa, said to have been a brāhmaṇa from Sāketa who converted to Buddhism, is linked by tradition with the Kuṣāṇa king Kaniṣka. Only the first part survives in Sanskrit; the whole poem is preserved in Tibetan and Chinese. He also wrote the Saundarananda. His work shows courtly Sanskrit poetry already fully formed, with clear debts to the Rāmāyaṇa's style, and it stands among the earliest surviving mahākāvyas.

events.title: Śabara's Mīmāṃsā Bhāṣya
events.description: Jaimini's Mīmāṃsā Sūtras deal with how Vedic injunctions are to be interpreted and why ritual action (dharma) is known only through the Veda. Śabara wrote the oldest surviving full commentary on them, explaining each sūtra, framing objections and answers, and defending the view that Vedic words are authoritative and the Veda authorless (apauruṣeya). His date is uncertain, with estimates from the 1st to the 5th century CE. Later thinkers, above all Kumārila Bhaṭṭa and Prabhākara, built their rival schools as sub-commentaries on his text.

events.title: Early Tamil kingdoms and Yavana trade
events.description: The Tamil epic Cilappatikāram, composed centuries later, is set in the early historic Tamil country, when the Cōḻa port Puhār, the Pāṇḍya capital Madurai and the Cēra capital Vañci were enriched by trade with the Roman world. Early Tamil poetry mentions Yavana (Greek and Roman) traders who brought gold and took away pepper. The epic follows Kōvalaṉ and his wife Kaṇṇaki: he is wrongly executed by the Pāṇḍya king for allegedly stealing her anklet, and she proves his innocence and burns Madurai. It is literature, not chronicle, but its backdrop reflects real early-historic Tamil society.

events.title: Indian traders at Berenike and Socotra
events.description: Excavations at Berenike, a Roman-era port on Egypt's Red Sea coast, have yielded Indian pepper, teak, pottery and potsherds inscribed in Tamil-Brāhmī. On the island of Socotra, the Hoq cave holds hundreds of visitors' inscriptions and drawings, many in Brāhmī script, left by Indian sailors and merchants of roughly the first to fourth centuries. Together with the Greek Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, these finds show regular monsoon-driven commerce between India, Arabia and Egypt, and a lively Indian presence at the crossroads of ocean trade.

events.title: Funan, early Indianised kingdom of the Mekong
events.description: Chinese envoys of the third century describe a kingdom in the Mekong delta they called Funan. Its founding legend tells of an Indian brāhmaṇa, Kauṇḍinya, who arrived by ship, married the local serpent-princess Somā and became king. Archaeology at its port, Óc Eo, has found Indian seals, jewellery and images of Viṣṇu. It is one of the earliest of the Sanskrit-using kingdoms of Southeast Asia.

events.title: Nāga and Yakṣa shrines
events.description: Early India had widespread cults of yakṣas, nature and wealth spirits, and nāgas, serpent deities. Large yakṣa images, such as the one from Parkham near Mathurā, and nāga images and shrines around Mathurā show the importance of these cults. Purāṇic Hinduism absorbed them rather than replacing them: Kubera and Maṇibhadra became lords of wealth, the serpent Śeṣa became Viṣṇu's couch, and Balarāma was linked with nāga imagery. Worship of nāgas continues today in festivals such as Nāgapañcamī.

gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||

events.title: Ekamukha-liṅgas of Mathurā
events.description: The liṅga, Śiva's aniconic emblem, was often carved with a human face, producing the ekamukha ("one-faced") liṅga. Examples from Mathurā in the Kuṣāṇa and Gupta periods show Śiva's face emerging from the shaft, sometimes with a topknot and third eye. Later forms added four faces (caturmukha) and, in time, five. These images combine abstract and figural worship and became a standard form of Śaiva icon across northern India, which later temple traditions continued.

events.title: Kuṣāṇa royal shrine at Māṭ
events.description: At Māṭ, near Mathurā, excavations in the early twentieth century uncovered a Kuṣāṇa royal sanctuary of the kind called a devakula, a "house of gods". It held portrait statues of Kuṣāṇa kings, among them a large seated statue of Vima Kadphises identified by its inscription, in which the king is styled devaputra, "son of god". The shrine shows how Kuṣāṇa rulers combined Iranian and Indian ideas of divine kingship, and its sculptures in Mathurā red sandstone are important evidence for royal cult and portraiture.

events.title: Dharmaśāstra on women's property
events.description: The Dharmaśāstra texts developed a concept of strīdhana, a woman's own property such as gifts at marriage, which she controlled. Manu lists several kinds of strīdhana. Yājñavalkya's code, from the early centuries CE, extended women's rights by placing the widow among the heirs of a man without sons. Later commentators such as the authors of the Mitākṣarā and Dāyabhāga interpreted these provisions differently, and they shaped property law in different regions up to modern times.

events.title: Gaja-Lakṣmī on early coins and seals
events.description: Gaja-Lakṣmī, the goddess of fortune seated on a lotus while elephants pour water over her, appears on coins, seals and sculpture from about the last centuries BCE onward, and on lamps and doorways in later times. It is one of the most widely found images of an auspicious goddess in India, used by Hindus, Buddhists and Jainas. The elephants' lustration (abhiṣeka) stands for kingly consecration and abundance, and it is placed at thresholds to bring good fortune.

events.title: Digambara teacher Kundakunda
events.description: Kundakunda is a revered Digambara Jaina teacher, usually placed around the first century CE, though the dating is debated. Tradition connects him with southern India. His Samayasāra, Pravacanasāra and Pañcāstikāya are among the most respected Jaina works. They describe the soul in two ways: from the vyavahāra standpoint, as bound to karma, and from the niścaya standpoint, as in its pure nature, a distinction that has parallels with Advaitic and Buddhist two-truth theories, and that influenced later Digambara thinkers.

events.title: Luni-solar calendar with intercalary months
events.description: The traditional Indian calendar follows the moon's phases for months, but the solar year for seasons. To keep the two aligned, an extra month, adhika-māsa, is inserted roughly every three years; this practice goes back to the Vedic Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa. In the early centuries CE the pañcāṅga, the almanac with five limbs (tithi, vāra, nakṣatra, yoga and karaṇa), became standard. It still guides the dates of festivals, weddings and rites, and regional calendars differ only in details such as month-naming and year-starting.

events.title: Gautamīputra Sātakarṇi
events.description: Gautamīputra Sātakarṇi, greatest of the Sātavāhana kings of the Deccan, ruled in the early second century CE. An inscription at Nāsik in the name of his mother, Gautamī Balaśrī, says he destroyed the Śakas, Greeks and Parthians, that his horses drank the water of three oceans, and that he stopped the mixing of the four classes. That he is known by his mother's name is typical of the dynasty.

events.title: Kaniṣka the Great
events.description: Kaniṣka, the greatest Kuṣāṇa emperor, ruled from about 127 CE over a realm stretching from the Oxus to the middle Gaṅgā, with capitals at Peshawar and Mathurā. His gold coins show an extraordinary range of deities: Śiva with his bull, the Buddha, Iranian fire and sun gods, Greek Helios. Buddhist tradition claims him as a patron. A headless statue of him in boots and long coat survives at Mathurā.

events.description: Vāsiṣṭhīputra Pulumāvi was a Sātavāhana king in the second century CE, son of Gautamīputra Sātakarṇi, whose capital was Pratiṣṭhāna (Paiṭhaṇ). events.title: Rudradāman's Junāgaḍh inscription
events.description: On a rock at Junāgaḍh in Gujarat, beside edicts of Aśoka, the Śaka ruler Rudradāman had an inscription cut about 150 CE recording that he repaired a storm-breached dam at his own cost, without extra taxes. It is the first long inscription in polished classical Sanskrit; earlier ones used the everyday Prakrits. A king of foreign descent thus pioneered the use of Sanskrit for public royal statements.

events.title: Nāgārjuna and Madhyamaka
events.description: Nāgārjuna, traditionally linked with Andhra, founded the Madhyamaka, or "Middle Way," school of Mahāyāna Buddhism. His Mūlamadhyamakakārikā argues that nothing has intrinsic nature (svabhāva), so that all things are empty (śūnya) and exist only in dependence on conditions. His Vigrahavyāvartanī attacks the Nyāya claim that valid means of knowledge can establish reality. Nyāya authors, including later portions of the Nyāya Sūtra and Vātsyāyana, answered him, which made Madhyamaka a main interlocutor for Hindu logicians for centuries.

events.title: Yavanajātaka and Greek astrology
events.description: The Yavanajātaka, "Greek horoscopy," is a Sanskrit text on astrology. It says that Yavaneśvara, a Greek or Greek-speaking scholar, translated a Greek work into Sanskrit prose in 149/150 CE, in the time of the Western Kṣatrapa Rudradāman at Ujjayinī, and that Sphujidhvaja turned it into verse in 269/270. It introduced to India the zodiac signs, horoscopic charts and planetary doctrines of Hellenistic astrology, which Indian astronomers reworked into the Jyotiṣa tradition.

events.title: Caṣṭana and the Kārdamakas of Ujjain
events.description: Caṣṭana was the founder of the Kārdamaka line of Western Kṣatrapas, a Śaka ruling house of Ujjayinī. The Greek geographer Ptolemy mentions a ruler called Tiastenes at Ozene, which is usually taken to be Caṣṭana and Ujjayinī. His grandson Rudradāman I is known from the Junāgaḍh inscription of about 150 CE, the first long Sanskrit inscription in refined kāvya style. The dynasty ruled Mālwā and Gujarat for generations, until the Guptas ended it around 400.

events.title: Yajña Śrī Sātakarṇi
events.description: Yajña Śrī Sātakarṇi ruled the Sātavāhana kingdom in the late second century CE and is regarded as the last important king of the line. He recovered the Koṅkaṇa and parts of Aparānta from the Western Kṣatrapas, and his coins, which show a ship, were found along the Coromandel and Andhra coasts. After his death the Sātavāhana state weakened and broke apart into smaller successor states.

events.title: Vārṣagaṇya's Ṣaṣṭitantra
events.description: Vārṣagaṇya was an early Sāṃkhya teacher whose own works are lost. The Ṣaṣṭitantra, "the system of sixty topics", is ascribed to him in some sources, though others connect it with Kapila or Pañcaśikha. He is known from references in later works, including Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra, which quotes him, and Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhyakārikā mentions the Ṣaṣṭitantra. Scholars date him roughly to the early centuries CE, though the dates are uncertain. He is a significant link in the development of Sāṃkhya before the surviving classical texts.

events.title: Viṣṇu Smṛti and Nārada Smṛti
events.description: Two Dharmaśāstra works of the early centuries CE. The Viṣṇu Smṛti is a Vaiṣṇava-leaning law book in prose and verse that mixes rules of conduct with devotional teaching. The Nārada Smṛti is different: it leaves out most ritual and penance and concentrates on vyavahāra, the practice of courts, setting out eighteen titles of law such as debt, deposits, inheritance and partnership, along with rules for evidence, witnesses and ordeals. Later digest-writers and commentators drew heavily on Nārada for questions of procedure.

events.title: Bhagavad Gītā emerges as scripture
events.description: The Gītā is a 700-verse dialogue in the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata, in which Kṛṣṇa instructs Arjuna on the field of Kurukṣetra about duty, action without attachment (karma yoga), knowledge and devotion. Scholars place its composition between about the 2nd century BCE and the 2nd century CE, drawing on Upaniṣadic, Sāṃkhya and Yoga ideas and on Bhāgavata devotion. Though embedded in the epic, it came to be treated as a scripture in its own right. The earliest surviving commentary is Śaṅkara's, of the 8th century, after which it became one of the most commented texts in Indian philosophy.

events.title: The five marks of a Purāṇa
events.description: Indian tradition defines a Purāṇa by five marks (pañcalakṣaṇa): sarga (primary creation), pratisarga (re-creation after dissolution), vaṃśa (genealogies of gods and sages), manvantara (the ages of the Manus) and vaṃśānucarita (histories of royal dynasties). Scholars believe the oldest layer of this material, transmitted by bards called sūtas, was taking written form in the early centuries CE. The Purāṇas later grew far beyond these five topics, absorbing pilgrimage lore, ritual manuals and sectarian theology.

events.title: Kaṇṇaki worship and the Pattini cult
events.description: According to the Cilappatikāram, the Cēra king Ceṅkuṭṭuvaṉ established a temple for Kaṇṇaki, the wronged wife who burned Madurai, as the chaste goddess Pattini ("the faithful wife"). Tradition says he brought a stone from the Himalaya and bathed it in the Gaṅgā; the Laṅkān king Gajabāhu is said to have attended and carried the cult to Laṅkā. Pattini worship survives in Sri Lanka, among Sinhalese Buddhists and Tamil Hindus, and in Kerala as part of Bhagavatī worship. The historical detail of the legend is uncertain.

events.title: Saptamātṛkā worship
events.description: The Saptamātṛkās, seven mother goddesses, are Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Aindrī and Cāmuṇḍā. Each is the śakti of a major male deity. Panels at Mathurā from Kuṣāṇa times show a row of mothers, and Gupta-era sculpture often places them with Śiva, Skanda and Gaṇeśa. Their story in the Purāṇas, especially in the Devī Māhātmya, shows them aiding the Goddess in battle against demons. The cult spread widely and appears in temples across the subcontinent.

events.title: Skanda-Kārttikeya cult at its height
events.description: Skanda, also called Kārttikeya and Kumāra, the young god of war and son of Śiva, was among the most popular deities of north India in the early centuries CE. The warrior republic of the Yaudheyas put him on their coins with six heads and a spear; Gupta emperors were named for him. His worship later faded in the north but remained central in the Tamil south as Murugaṉ.

events.title: Sūrya worship and the Maga priests
events.description: Sun worship in northwestern India drew on Vedic Sūrya and on Iranian influences. The Bhaviṣya Purāṇa tells that Kṛṣṇa's son Sāmba brought Maga priests, Śākadvīpī brāhmaṇas, from Śākadvīpa to serve the Sun at Mūlasthāna, modern Multan, where he had been cured of leprosy. Sculptures show Sūrya in northern dress with boots and a belt, a feature often linked to Iranian models. The Multan temple later impressed Xuanzang in the 7th century and remained a major Sūrya shrine until the medieval period.

events.title: Bakhshālī manuscript mathematics
events.description: Found in 1881 in the village of Bakhshālī, now in Pakistan, this birch-bark manuscript contains arithmetic and algebraic problems on fractions, progressions, equations and square roots. It uses a dot as a placeholder for zero, a very early form of the symbol. In 2017 radiocarbon dating of three of its folios gave different results, ranging from about the 3rd–4th century to the 9th–10th, and scholars still debate whether the leaves belong to one text and what its date is. The manuscript is in the Bodleian Library, Oxford.

events.title: Vātsyāyana's Kāmasūtra
events.description: The Kāmasūtra treats kāma, pleasure, as one of the three aims of worldly life and a proper subject of study. Only one of its seven books concerns sexual technique. The rest describe the daily life of a cultivated townsman, the sixty-four arts, courtship, marriage, the conduct of wives and of courtesans. Its author says he wrote it in chastity and meditation, and that pleasure must never override dharma.

events.title: Śūdraka's Mṛcchakaṭika
events.description: "The Little Clay Cart" is a Sanskrit play in ten acts, attributed to a king or poet named Śūdraka, though his identity and date are uncertain. It tells of the generous but impoverished brāhmaṇa merchant Cārudatta and the courtesan Vasantasenā, who fall in love in Ujjayinī. A political subplot involves the overthrow of the tyrant Pālaka by the herdsman Āryaka. Unlike most Sanskrit drama, it centres on ordinary townspeople, including thieves, judges and servants, and offers a vivid picture of urban life.

events.title: Tamil epics Cilappatikāram and Maṇimēkalai
events.description: The Cilappatikāram, "The Tale of the Anklet," is ascribed to Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ, said to be a Cēra prince turned ascetic. events.title: Champa's Vo Canh inscription
events.description: The Vo Canh inscription, found near Nha Trang in central Vietnam, is a stone stele in Sanskrit and the earliest known Sanskrit inscription in Southeast Asia. It was set up in the kingdom later called Champa, and is usually dated between the 2nd and 4th centuries. It is fragmentary; it appears to record a donation connected with a king of a Śrī Māra lineage. Scholars differ on its precise date and religious character. It shows that Sanskrit was used for royal and religious purposes in Southeast Asia very early.

events.title: Vaikhānasa Sūtras and temple priesthood

events.title: Kriyā Yoga in Patañjali
events.description: In the Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali, kriyā yoga is the yoga of action, defined at the start of the second chapter (2.1) as three practices: tapas, or austerity, svādhyāya, or study and recitation, and īśvara-praṇidhāna, or devotion to the Lord. It is offered as a preparatory path to reduce afflictions and lead to samādhi. The date of the Yoga Sūtra is disputed, and scholars place it between about the second century BCE and the fourth century CE.

events.title: Indianised Pyu and Mon city-states
events.description: In the first millennium CE, city-states of the Pyu in the Irrawaddy valley of Myanmar and of the Mon in the Chao Phraya basin of Thailand took up Indian scripts, Sanskrit and Pāli, and religious ideas. Śrī Kṣetra, a Pyu centre, and Dvāravatī, a Mon-associated culture, have yielded images of Viṣṇu alongside the Buddha, as well as Indian-style inscriptions. These communities show how Indian religion spread by sea trade and court adoption, rather than conquest, and they laid the base for later kingdoms in mainland Southeast Asia.

events.title: Vāsudeva I, a Kuṣāṇa with a Vaiṣṇava name
events.description: Vāsudeva I, who reigned in the later 2nd and early 3rd century, is the last great Kuṣāṇa king. events.title: Fall of the Sātavāhanas
events.description: The Sātavāhanas ruled much of the Deccan for centuries from Pratiṣṭhāna (Paithan) and later from Andhra, and are remembered as patrons of Prakrit literature such as the Gāthāsaptaśatī, of Vedic sacrifice and of Buddhist monuments. By about 225 CE central authority collapsed. Their domain split among successors including the Ikṣvākus of the Kṛṣṇā valley, the Ābhīras in the northwestern Deccan, and the Vākāṭakas further north and east. These regional kingdoms shaped the political map of the Deccan for the next two centuries.

events.title: Ikṣvākus of Vijayapurī
events.description: The Ikṣvākus ruled the Kṛṣṇā valley from Vijayapurī at Nāgārjunakoṇḍa in the third century CE. Their first king Vāsiṣṭhīputra Cāṃtamūla performed Vedic sacrifices, including the Aśvamedha and Vājapeya, as inscriptions record. Women of the royal family, however, were notable donors to Buddhist monasteries at the site, so the valley shows royal Vedic ritual and large Buddhist foundations side by side. Much of the site was moved to a nearby hill when a dam was built.

events.title: Śrī Gupta
events.description: Śrī Gupta is the earliest ancestor named in Gupta records. He bears only the modest title mahārāja, and his son and successor Ghaṭotkaca has the same. Where they ruled is unclear: Magadha and eastern Uttar Pradesh are both proposed. Nothing certain is known of his reign beyond his name, but later Gupta kings counted their line from him, and the dynasty's era, founded by Candragupta I, was reckoned from 319–320 CE. He is the starting point of a dynasty that would unify much of northern India.

events.title: Amarāvatī and Nāgārjunakoṇḍa
events.description: In the Kṛṣṇā valley, the Ikṣvāku kings (3rd century) mixed Vedic and Buddhist patronage. King Vāsiṣṭhīputra Cāntamūla performed the Aśvamedha and Vājapeya sacrifices, while royal women endowed monasteries and stūpas. At Nāgārjunakoṇḍa the excavations found Buddhist vihāras beside brick temples for Kārttikeya (Mahāsena), Aṣṭabhujasvāmin (an eight-armed Viṣṇu) and other deities. The older Amarāvatī stūpa, famous for its carved limestone reliefs, is also in the Kṛṣṇā valley. The Nāgārjunakoṇḍa valley was submerged by a dam in the 1960s and its monuments were relocated.

events.title: Bhāraśiva Nāgas
events.description: The Bhāraśiva Nāgas ruled parts of central India and the Gaṅgā valley in the third century CE, after the Kuṣāṇas. A later inscription says they were anointed with Gaṅgā water won by their valour, carried Śiva's liṅga on their shoulders, and performed ten horse sacrifices. Tradition connects those sacrifices with the Daśāśvamedha ghāṭ at Vārāṇasī, "the ghāṭ of ten horse-sacrifices".

events.title: Vāyu and Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas
events.description: These two Purāṇas share a large body of text and are often treated as sister works, perhaps once a single compilation. They are counted among the oldest Purāṇas. Their historical sections give lists of kings, Paurava, Ikṣvāku, Magadhan and later dynasties, written as prophecy in the future tense. The lists run through the Śiśunāgas, Nandas, Mauryas, Śuṅgas and Āndhras and end with the early Guptas, which suggests that this material was fixed around the mid-4th century CE.

events.title: Harivaṃśa completed
events.description: The Harivaṃśa, "Lineage of Hari", is an appendix of about 16,000 verses to the Mahābhārata. The epic shows Kṛṣṇa only as an adult prince and counsellor; this work adds his birth, his childhood among the cowherds, the lifting of Mount Govardhana, the dance with the cowherd girls and the killing of Kaṃsa. It is the oldest full account of the boy Kṛṣṇa of later devotion.

events.title: Vākāṭaka dynasty founded
events.description: The Vākāṭakas, a brāhmaṇa dynasty of the Viṣṇuvṛddha gotra, ruled Vidarbha and neighbouring regions of the Deccan. events.title: Ābhīra king Īśvarasena and the Kalacuri era
events.description: The Ābhīras were a pastoral people who became rulers in western and central India in the third century. An inscription at Nāsik records the Ābhīra king Īśvarasena. Many scholars connect the origin of the Kalacuri-Cedi era, which started in 248 or 249 CE, with Ābhīra rule. Later dynasties of the region, such as the Traikūṭakas and the Kalacuris, used this era in their records for centuries.

events.title: Pravarasena I Vākāṭaka
events.description: Pravarasena I, the second ruler of the Vākāṭaka dynasty of Vidarbha, took the title samrāṭ, which later records say none of his successors used. Inscriptions credit him with performing four Aśvamedha sacrifices and other grand Vedic rites. His rule extended across a large part of central India, and his descendants intermarried with the Guptas. The Vākāṭakas were brāhmaṇas and stood out as Vedic patrons, but later members also supported Buddhist monasteries.

events.title: Pallavas emerge at Kāñcī
events.description: The early Pallavas ruled from Kāñcīpuram and are known from copper-plate charters, first in Prakrit and later in Sanskrit. Śivaskandavarman, for example, is recorded as having performed Vedic rites including the Aśvamedha and Vājapeya. The dynasty's origins are debated: some scholars link it to a northern Pahlava group, others see a local Tamil or Telugu-region family rising as Sātavāhana power faded. The Pallavas later became the great temple-builders of the Tamil country.

events.title: Tiruvaḷḷuvar and the Tirukkuṟaḷ
events.description: The Tirukkuṟaḷ, attributed to Tiruvaḷḷuvar, has 1,330 couplets in three parts on aram (virtue), poruḷ (wealth and governance) and inpam (love). Its teaching is general and ethical, and Jaina, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist and secular readers have all claimed it. Its opening verse praises the "primal" Lord. Its date is disputed, with estimates ranging from the early centuries CE to about the 6th century. It is among the most widely translated works of Tamil literature.

events.title: Kaḷabhra interregnum
events.description: The Kaḷabhras are known mainly from later Pāṇḍya and Pallava inscriptions, which describe them as intruders who overthrew earlier kings and cancelled the land grants of brāhmaṇas and temples. Traditional history treats their rule, roughly the 3rd to 6th centuries, as a dark age for Tamil kingdoms, and later sources associate them with Jaina and Buddhist patronage. Some modern historians think the evidence is thin and one-sided, and that the period was also one of literary activity. Little direct evidence of the Kaḷabhras themselves survives.

events.title: Nāgas of Padmāvatī and Mathurā
events.description: After the Kuṣāṇas, several Nāga dynasties ruled in central India, with seats at Padmāvatī (modern Pawāyā near Gwalior) and Mathurā. The Purāṇas speak of nine Nāga kings. Samudragupta's Prayāga pillar inscription lists Gaṇapatināga and Nāgasena, among others, as kings whom he defeated or uprooted in Āryāvarta. The Nāgas were Śaiva, and their coins and sculpture are important to the early art of the Gupta age.

events.title: Harihara and Ardhanārīśvara icons
events.description: By the Kuṣāṇa and Gupta periods, sculptors in Mathurā and elsewhere were carving composite images. Harihara joins Hari (Viṣṇu) and Hara (Śiva) in a single body, with each half carrying its own emblems, while Ardhanārīśvara combines Śiva with his consort Pārvatī, the right half male and the left half female. The images express a theological view of unity between deities and between the male and female principles, and they became common in temples across India.

events.title: Early vṛttikāras on the two Mīmāṃsās
events.description: The vṛttikāras, "commentators", are early scholars whose works on the Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta sūtras are lost but known from quotations. Upavarṣa is cited as an authority on both Mīmāṃsā and the Brahma Sūtras, and Bodhāyana is named as the author of a vṛtti on the Brahma Sūtras that later Vaiṣṇava thinkers, notably Rāmānuja, invoked. Their dates are uncertain, but they precede Śabara and Śaṅkara. These names show that there was a long tradition of commentary on both Mīmāṃsās before Śabara, Kumārila and Śaṅkara.

events.title: Candragupta I and the Gupta era
events.description: In 319–320 CE Candragupta, ruler of a small kingdom in the Gaṅgā plain, took the title "great king of kings" and began a new era. His rise owed much to his marriage to Kumāradevī, a princess of the old Licchavi clan; gold coins show the couple together with her name beside his. Their son Samudragupta proudly called himself "son of the daughter of the Licchavis".

events.title: Yājñavalkya Smṛti
events.description: This law book of about a thousand verses is shorter, better organised and more practical than Manu. Its date is debated, with proposals from the first to the fifth century CE and recent scholarship favouring the fourth or fifth. Its three parts deal with conduct, legal procedure and penance. It gives rules on documents, evidence, partnerships and deposits, and recognises a widow's right to inherit. Through its commentary the Mitākṣarā, written by Vijñāneśvara around 1100, it governed Hindu family law over most of India, outside Bengal, until 1956.

events.title: Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhya Kārikā
events.description: Īśvarakṛṣṇa compressed the old Sāṃkhya teaching into seventy-two verses around the fourth century CE. The world unfolds from unconscious nature for the sake of the conscious self, as milk flows for the calf. Nature is compared to a dancer who, once seen by the spectator, withdraws. Liberation is the knowledge "I am not, nothing is mine, there is no I". It was translated into Chinese in the sixth century.

events.title: Western Gaṅgas and Kadambas arise
events.description: In the 4th century two dynasties emerged in Karnataka. The Kadamba tradition says Mayūraśarman, a brāhmaṇa from Talagunda, went to the Pallava capital Kāñcī to study the Vedas, was insulted there, and took up the sword; the Pallavas eventually recognised him as an independent ruler at Banavāsi. The Western Gaṅgas established themselves at Talakāḍ. Both families patronised Sanskrit and Brahmanical temples, and their rule laid the foundation for later Karnataka kingdoms.

events.title: Samudragupta's conquests
events.description: A pillar at Prayāga carries a long Sanskrit eulogy of Samudragupta, about 350 CE, by his minister Hariṣeṇa. It lists nine kings of the north whom he "violently exterminated", twelve of the south whom he captured and released as tributaries, and frontier peoples who paid homage. It also praises him as a poet and musician; his coins show him playing the lyre. Historians call him the Indian Napoleon.

events.title: Samudragupta's Aśvamedha
events.description: Samudragupta's gold coins show a horse before a sacrificial post and carry a legend proclaiming him as restorer of the Aśvamedha. This ancient royal rite, in which a horse was let loose for a year and kings it passed through had to submit, had not been widely performed for centuries. Another coin type shows him playing the vīṇā, and the Allahabad pillar inscription composed by Hariṣeṇa praises him as a poet and musician. His reign symbolises the Gupta court's blend of Vedic ritual, military conquest and refined arts.

events.title: Viṣṇu Purāṇa
events.description: The Viṣṇu Purāṇa, of about the fourth century CE, is among the oldest and best-ordered of the Purāṇas, covering in six books all five classic topics: creation, re-creation, genealogies, the ages of Manu and royal dynasties. It tells the stories of Dhruva and Prahlāda and gives an early life of Kṛṣṇa. Rāmānuja relied on it more than on any other Purāṇa as scriptural support for his theology.

events.title: Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa
events.description: The Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa is generally counted among the oldest Purāṇas. It is framed as the sage Mārkaṇḍeya's answers to questions put by wise birds, and it covers cosmology, the story of Hariścandra, the Madālasā episode and the nature of yoga. In its later form it includes the Devī Māhātmya, chapters 81 to 93. Its date is debated, but the older portions are usually placed in the 3rd to 5th centuries. It is a main source for the early Śākta tradition.

events.title: Matsya Purāṇa
events.description: The Matsya Purāṇa opens with Viṣṇu's fish incarnation warning Manu of the great flood. It is considered one of the older Purāṇas and preserves valuable early material: lists of dynasties, including the Āndhras, chapters on image-making and temple architecture (vāstu), and rules for vows and gifts. Scholars use its architecture chapters to understand early Hindu temple design. Like other Purāṇas it was revised over several centuries, so its sections date from different periods.

events.title: Varmans of Kāmarūpa
events.description: Puṣyavarman founded the first historical dynasty of Kāmarūpa, in present Assam, around the fourth century. The Varmans claimed descent from Naraka, the legendary king born of Viṣṇu and the Earth in the Purāṇas, and from his son Bhagadatta of the Mahābhārata. Samudragupta's Prayāga inscription includes Kāmarūpa among the frontier states paying tribute. The dynasty's greatest king was Bhāskaravarman, in the seventh century, who was a friend of Harṣa.

events.title: Śālaṅkāyanas and Viṣṇukuṇḍins of Veṅgī
events.description: The Śālaṅkāyanas ruled the Veṅgī country, between the Godāvarī and Kṛṣṇā, in the fourth and fifth centuries. Their records show devotion to Citraratha-svāmin, a form of the sun god, and they are known from copper-plate grants. The Viṣṇukuṇḍins followed in the Āndhra region and honoured Śrīparvata-svāmin, generally understood as Śiva at Śrīśailam. Both dynasties made grants to brāhmaṇas and paved the way for later Eastern Cālukya rule in Veṅgī.

events.title: Māṭharas and early Kaliṅga kings
events.description: After the Mauryan period, coastal Odisha and northern Andhra were divided among several small dynasties. The Māṭharas ruled Kaliṅga from Siṃhapura in the fourth and fifth centuries, and Piṣṭapura (modern Piṭhāpuram) was another centre. Samudragupta's Prayāga inscription names Svāmidatta of Piṣṭapura among the southern kings he overcame. The area remained a meeting point of Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist and Jaina communities.

events.title: Vindhyavāsin defeats Buddhamitra at Ayodhyā
events.description: According to the Buddhist biography of Vasubandhu by Paramārtha, a Sāṃkhya teacher named Vindhyavāsin defeated Vasubandhu's teacher Buddhamitra in a debate at Ayodhyā. Vasubandhu is said to have later refuted him in writing. Some scholars identify this Vindhyavāsin with the Sāṃkhya author Īśvarakṛṣṇa or with another thinker, but the story comes from Buddhist tradition and its details are uncertain.

events.title: Candragupta II Vikramāditya
events.description: Candragupta II, who took the title Vikramāditya, ruled about 375–415 CE. By defeating the Śaka rulers of western India he gained Gujarat and its seaports, and Ujjain became in effect a second capital. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian found his realm peaceful and lightly governed. Tradition places Kālidāsa and eight other "jewels" at his court; legends of King Vikramāditya probably draw on him.

events.title: Rāmagupta and Dhruvadevī episode
events.description: The lost Sanskrit play Devīcandraguptam, by Viśākhadatta, survives only in quotations. It tells how the Gupta king Rāmagupta, besieged by a Śaka ruler, agreed to hand over his queen Dhruvadevī. His younger brother Candragupta went to the Śaka camp disguised as the queen and killed the king. Candragupta later married Dhruvadevī, according to the story. The episode is known only from later sources, but Rāmagupta is also attested by coins and inscriptions, so historians take the tradition seriously while debating its details.

events.title: Gupta gold coinage
events.description: The Gupta emperors issued fine gold coins, called dīnāras, which depict kings in different roles: shooting a bow, killing a lion, playing the vīṇā. The reverse often shows a goddess, frequently Lakṣmī seated on a lotus or Gaṅgā on her makara, with a legend. Samudragupta and Candragupta II were among the issuers. Because the coins carry royal names, titles and symbols, and some later issues carry dates, historians use them as sources for Gupta politics, art and the ideal of kingship.

events.title: Mahāśivarātri and Ekādaśī vratas
events.description: Purāṇic and Dharmaśāstra literature of the early centuries CE prescribes vratas, vows of fasting and worship, such as Ekādaśī, the eleventh lunar day, observed for Viṣṇu, and Mahāśivarātri, the night of vigil in honour of Śiva in the dark fortnight of Māgha or Phālguna. These texts present such vows as open to people of every varṇa and to women, unlike the Vedic sacrifices, which needed priests and wealth. Vratas became a main form of Hindu devotion, and both are still widely kept.

events.title: Vātsyāyana's Nyāya Bhāṣya
events.description: The Nyāya Sūtra, attributed to Gautama (Akṣapāda), lays out sixteen categories of debate and knowledge. Vātsyāyana wrote its earliest surviving commentary. He explains each sūtra, discusses the valid means of knowledge such as perception and inference, and argues that the self is distinct from body and senses, citing memory and recognition as evidence that one knowing subject unifies experiences across time. This argument answers Buddhist no-self doctrines. His date is debated, usually between the 4th and 5th century CE.

events.title: Gaṇeśa's earliest images
events.description: Gaṇeśa is absent from the Vedas and from the older parts of the epics. His earliest securely identified images, showing an elephant-headed, pot-bellied figure, appear in the fourth and fifth centuries CE, in northern India including Mathurā. In the Gupta and post-Gupta period he is shown with one tusk and a bowl of sweets; the mouse as his mount comes later still. He was at first Vighneśvara, the lord of obstacles, to be appeased; he became the one who removes them, worshipped before any undertaking.

events.title: Kālidāsa, classical Sanskrit poet
events.description: The most celebrated poet of classical Sanskrit, usually placed at the court of Candragupta II around 400 CE, though his dates are uncertain. Tradition says he was an unlettered man blessed by the goddess Kālī.¶His play Abhijñānaśākuntalam, about a king who forgets the woman he loves, astonished Europe when it was translated into English in 1789. The Meghadūta has a banished spirit ask a cloud to carry a message to his wife, describing India from above. The Raghuvaṃśa tells of Rāma's dynasty and the Kumārasambhava of the marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī.

events.title: Amarakośa of Amarasiṃha
events.description: The Amarakośa of Amarasiṃha, perhaps of the fifth or sixth century, is a thesaurus of about ten thousand Sanskrit words grouped by subject (heaven, earth, town, plants, animals, people), in verse so that it can be memorised. For many centuries Indian children learning Sanskrit began by committing it to memory, often before they could understand it. Tradition makes Amarasiṃha one of the nine jewels of Vikramāditya's court, and the work was also rendered into Tibetan and has been widely commented upon.

events.title: Sūrya Siddhānta
events.description: The Sūrya Siddhānta, presented as taught by the Sun, is the best known of the Indian astronomical treatises; its core is of the fourth or fifth century, revised later. It gives methods for computing the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets, the times of eclipses and the length of the year, using sines instead of the Greek chords. Traditional almanacs in much of India are still calculated from it.

events.title: Viṣṇuśarman's Pañcatantra
events.description: A king despairs of his three dull sons, and the old brāhmaṇa Viṣṇuśarman promises to teach them statecraft in six months, by stories. The result is five books of animal fables nested inside one another, on losing friends, winning friends, war and peace, losing what one has, and acting rashly. Translated into Persian in the sixth century and thence into Arabic, it reached Europe as the Fables of Bidpai; some two hundred versions exist.

events.title: Bhartṛhari's Vākyapadīya
events.description: Bhartṛhari, in the fifth century, turned grammar into philosophy. His Vākyapadīya, "On Sentence and Word", opens by saying that Brahman is the Word, without beginning or end, from which the world unfolds. Meaning, he argued, is grasped whole, in a flash, from the sentence, not built up from separate words; that flash he called sphoṭa. His ideas shaped Indian poetics and Kashmir Śaivism.

gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. events.title: Bhartṛhari's Śatakatraya
events.description: The Śatakatraya, "three centuries," consists of the Nītiśataka on worldly wisdom and conduct, the Śṛṅgāraśataka on love, and the Vairāgyaśataka on renunciation, each of about a hundred verses. Tradition identifies the poet with a king of Ujjayinī who abandoned his throne, and sometimes with the grammarian Bhartṛhari, author of the Vākyapadīya, though scholars generally treat these as distinct. The verses are among the best-known Sanskrit subhāṣitas, short polished poems quoted ever since for their wit and moral reflection.

events.title: Daśāvatāra concept standardised
events.description: The idea that Viṣṇu descends to restore dharma has early roots, but the fixed list of ten avatāras took shape gradually. Purāṇic lists are usually given as Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha and Kalki, though some texts vary, for instance by listing Balarāma. Gupta-period sculpture, such as the Varāha at Udayagiri and the panels of the Deogarh temple, shows several of these forms. The system gave Vaiṣṇavism a flexible framework that could absorb local deities and heroes.

events.title: Trimūrti doctrine
events.description: From the Gupta period texts and images present three gods as aspects of one power: Brahmā creates the universe, Viṣṇu maintains it and Śiva dissolves it. Kālidāsa's verses address the one who divides himself into three. In practice Brahmā has almost no temples, and Vaiṣṇavas and Śaivas each regard their own deity as the source of all three functions; the Goddess makes a fourth claim.

events.title: Smārta pañcāyatana roots
events.description: The word Smārta refers to those who follow smṛti, the remembered tradition. Smārta household worship centres on five deities: Viṣṇu, Śiva, Devī, Sūrya and Gaṇeśa, with one chosen as the family's main deity (iṣṭadevatā) while the others are also honoured. This system grew out of Purāṇic religion in the Gupta and post-Gupta centuries, when these cults were widely established and often shown side by side. Later tradition credits Śaṅkara with systematising the practice, which was also reflected in temple layout.

gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.

events.title: Temple worship and mūrti-pūjā become central
events.description: In the centuries around the Gupta age the centre of Hindu religious life shifted from the Vedic fire sacrifice, which needs no building or image, to the worship of a deity present in a consecrated image housed in a temple. The god is woken, bathed, dressed, fed and put to rest like an honoured king. A rite called "establishing the breath" turns the carved stone into a living presence.

events.title: Gaṅgā and Yamunā at temple doors
events.description: In Gupta-period temples, the doorframes often show the river goddesses Gaṅgā and Yamunā at the base of the two sides. Gaṅgā stands on a makara (a crocodile-like creature) and Yamunā on a tortoise (kūrma), usually holding vessels or being attended. The figures symbolise purity and auspiciousness at the threshold, as a worshipper who enters is cleansed. The motif spread across northern India and, with variations, to other regions, remaining a feature of temple doorways.

events.title: Pūrṇavarman of Tārumānagara
events.description: Tārumānagara was an early Hindu kingdom in west Java, near modern Bogor. Its king Pūrṇavarman left Sanskrit inscriptions on rocks, written in a script derived from southern Indian Pallava forms. Some inscriptions carry footprints and compare the king's footprints to those of Viṣṇu; the Tugu inscription records canal-building. They are among the earliest evidence of Indian religion and Sanskrit in Indonesia, indicating Vaiṣṇava ideas of kingship.

events.title: Mūlavarman's yūpa inscriptions
events.description: Seven stone posts found at Kutai in eastern Borneo bear Sanskrit verses in a south Indian script of about 400 CE. They record that King Mūlavarman gave thousands of cattle and gold to brāhmaṇas "who came here", and set up the posts used for tying sacrificial animals. His grandfather's name is local, his father's and his own are Sanskrit. They are the oldest inscriptions of Indonesia.

events.title: Traikūṭakas of the Koṅkaṇa
events.description: The Traikūṭakas ruled northern Koṅkaṇa and southern Gujarat in the fifth century, and their records use the Kalacuri-Cedi era. Their first known king Dahrasena is said in an inscription to have performed an Aśvamedha sacrifice. They called themselves Parama-vaiṣṇava, devotees of Viṣṇu. Their coins have been found in the Thāṇe and Nāsik region, and they were later overshadowed by the Cālukyas.

events.title: Brahmanandin and Dramiḍācārya
events.description: Brahmanandin, also known as Ṭaṅka, and Dramiḍācārya were Vedāntins who commented on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad before Śaṅkara. Their works are lost, but both are quoted by later teachers, including Śaṅkara and Rāmānuja, who each treated them as authorities supporting their own interpretation. Their existence indicates that a continuous commentarial tradition on the Upaniṣads existed before the great Vedānta schools.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
