events.title: Iron Pillar of Meharaulī
events.description: In the Qutb complex at Delhi stands an iron column over seven metres tall and about six tonnes in weight, forged around 400 CE. Its Sanskrit verse inscription praises a king named Candra, usually identified with the Gupta ruler Candragupta II, who is said to have defeated a coalition in Vaṅga (Bengal), crossed the seven mouths of the Indus and conquered the Vāhlikas, and who was a devotee of Viṣṇu. The pillar was a Viṣṇu standard originally set up elsewhere, perhaps at Udayagiri, and was moved to Delhi centuries later. It has resisted rusting for about sixteen centuries, largely through a protective film formed by its high phosphorus content.

events.title: Ratha-yātrā festivals
events.description: The Chinese pilgrim Faxian, travelling in the early fifth century, described a procession of image-carrying chariots at Pāṭaliputra, though his account refers to a Buddhist festival. Such car processions, in which a deity's image is drawn through the town, became central to Hindu temple life. The best known is the Jagannātha Ratha-yātrā at Purī, but towns like Śrīraṅgam, Madurai and Tiruvārūr hold their own. The festival lets devotees see the deity outside the sanctum and brings the whole town into the ritual.

events.title: Bhadravarman's Śiva temple at Mỹ Sơn
events.description: Mỹ Sơn, in central Vietnam, became the principal religious centre of the Cham kingdom of Champa. Cham inscriptions credit King Bhadravarman with founding a sanctuary of Śiva as Bhadreśvara, a name that joins his own to the god's. Later kings rebuilt the temple after it was destroyed by fire. Over the following centuries many brick temples were added to the valley, dedicated to Śiva and other deities, and the complex is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.title: Udayagiri caves
events.description: At Udayagiri near Vidiśā in central India twenty caves were cut into a sandstone ridge about 401 CE, two with inscriptions of Candragupta II's reign. The masterpiece is a four-metre relief of Viṣṇu as the boar, lifting the Earth goddess on his tusk while rows of sages and gods look on. The site also has early images of Durgā, Gaṇeśa and Viṣṇu asleep on the serpent.

events.title: Faxian in India
events.description: The Chinese monk Faxian walked to India across the Central Asian deserts and travelled in the Gupta realm in the early fifth century, collecting Buddhist texts; his journey is usually dated about 399–412. His short account describes a prosperous country where people could travel without passes, taxes were light, and capital punishment was not used. He notes free hospitals in Pāṭaliputra. He returned home by sea by way of Sri Lanka.

events.title: Prabhāvatīguptā, Gupta princess and Vākāṭaka regent
events.description: Prabhāvatīguptā, daughter of the Gupta king Candragupta II, married the Vākāṭaka king Rudrasena II. After his early death she acted as regent for her young sons for about two decades. Her copper-plate grants, issued in her sons' names, trace the Gupta ancestry and show her devotion to Rāma, referred to as Rāmagirisvāmin, the lord of Rāmagiri (Rāmṭek). The alliance linked the two most important dynasties of the age, and her charters are a rare record of a woman governing in her own right.

events.title: Kumāragupta I
events.description: Kumāragupta I succeeded Candragupta II and ruled for about forty years, a period of relative peace and prosperity for the Gupta realm. His inscriptions and coins, many bearing the title Mahendrāditya, show peacocks and the god Kārttikeya (Skanda), whose cult he evidently favoured. He also performed the Aśvamedha, according to some coins. Later tradition connects him with the foundation of Nālandā's monastery. Toward the end of his reign the empire began to feel pressure from the Hūṇas in the northwest.

events.title: Temple 17 at Sāñcī and Tigawa
events.description: Hindu temple architecture in stone begins with small, simple shrines of the early Gupta period. Temple 17 at Sāñcī and the Kaṅkālī Devī temple at Tigawa have a square sanctum with a flat roof and a pillared porch, with no tower. Earlier temples were presumably of wood, brick and thatch, and have not survived. These modest stone structures set the basic plan, a dark inner garbhagṛha for the image fronted by a porch, from which later temple forms developed.

events.title: Gupta temple inscriptions at Bilsad and Gadhwa
events.description: Inscriptions at Bilsad, in Uttar Pradesh, record the building of a gateway of a Kārttikeya (Svāmin Mahāsena) temple in 415 in the reign of Kumāragupta I. Gadhwa, near Prayāgrāj, has Gupta-period inscriptions and sculptural fragments from Viṣṇu and Śiva shrines. These records are valuable evidence that Gupta kings and officials supported temple construction in the 5th century, and they allow historians to follow the development of the early structural temple.

events.title: Nālandā Mahāvihāra founded
events.description: Nālandā, in Bihar, grew from the fifth century under Gupta patronage into the largest centre of learning in Asia. Excavation has uncovered eleven monasteries and six brick temples in a row; the Chinese visitor Xuanzang speaks of ten thousand residents and a gatekeeper who examined applicants. Buddhist doctrine was the core, but the Vedas, logic, grammar and medicine were taught too. It lasted until about 1200.

events.title: Mandasor silk-weavers' Sun temple
events.description: A stone inscription from Mandasor, ancient Daśapura, dated 436 CE, records that a guild of silk weavers who had migrated from Lāṭa in Gujarat built a temple of the Sun, and that the guild later restored it. It is written in elaborate kāvya style by Vatsabhaṭṭi, with descriptions of the city, the seasons and the weavers' prosperity. The inscription is valued as evidence for the role of merchant and artisan guilds in patronising temples, and for the spread of Sūrya worship in western India.

events.title: Kadamba Kākutsthavarman
events.description: Kākutsthavarman, a king of the Kadamba dynasty of Banavāsi in the 5th century, brought it to its height. The pillar inscription at Talagunda, composed under his son Śāntivarman, records the dynasty's brāhmaṇa origin, telling of Mayūraśarman, and mentions the tank and Śiva temple at the site. It is a Sanskrit prose-and-verse record composed by the poet Kubja. Kākutsthavarman is also said to have made marriage alliances with the Guptas, according to the inscriptions.

events.title: Rāmṭek temples
events.description: Rāmṭek, a hill near Nagpur, was under Vākāṭaka rule an important Vaiṣṇava centre. Its early temples, among them shrines of Narasiṃha, Varāha and Trivikrama, are associated with the Vākāṭaka court and its Gupta-linked queens. The hill is called Rāmagiri, and many identify it with the Rāmagiri where the exiled yakṣa of Kālidāsa's Meghadūta stays. It remains a pilgrimage site tied to Rāma's exile, and its early shrines are among the oldest Hindu temples of the Deccan.

events.title: Kāmandaka's Nītisāra
events.description: The Nītisāra, also called the Kāmandakīya, is a verse summary of the political teaching of Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra. The author says he writes it for the benefit of kings, honouring Kauṭilya (Viṣṇugupta) as his source. It covers the king's training, the elements of the state, the seven limbs of government, diplomacy and war. Its more accessible form made it popular, and it was used and quoted by later writers on polity, including in Java and Bali.

events.title: Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana Smṛtis
events.description: The Bṛhaspati Smṛti and Kātyāyana Smṛti, known mostly from quotations in later digests, are advanced legal works of the Gupta age. Bṛhaspati separates civil and criminal law more clearly than earlier texts and gives detailed rules on procedure and on loans and contracts. Kātyāyana is especially cited on the property of women (strīdhana), listing what a woman may hold as her own. They show Dharmaśāstra moving from general moral guidance toward the technical rules of a legal system.

events.title: Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās
events.description: The Pāñcarātra tradition is a Vaiṣṇava system that holds Viṣṇu as supreme and teaches a doctrine of divine emanations (vyūhas): Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna and Aniruddha. Its manuals, the Saṃhitās, deal with temple building, image installation, daily worship and initiation (dīkṣā). Three early ones, the Sāttvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya, are called the "three gems." Pāñcarātra ritual shaped worship in many Viṣṇu temples and influenced the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition.

events.title: Śaiva Āgamas
events.description: Beside the Vedas grew a second body of texts held to be revealed by Śiva, the Āgamas or Tantras. The twenty-eight Āgamas of the Śaiva Siddhānta each have four parts: doctrine, yoga, ritual and conduct. They lay down how a temple is planned, how an image is made and brought to life, the daily cycle of worship, and the initiations open to members of different classes. The earliest Śaiva scriptures date from about the fifth century, but the corpus was compiled over many centuries. Temple worship in south India follows them today.

events.title: Liṅga worship and the Liṅgodbhava myth
events.description: The Purāṇas tell that Brahmā and Viṣṇu quarrelled over which was supreme, and Śiva appeared between them as an infinite pillar of fire (liṅga). Brahmā flew upward as a swan and Viṣṇu dug downward as a boar to find its ends; Viṣṇu admitted defeat, while Brahmā falsely claimed success and was cursed. The story presents Śiva as beyond both. Tamil tradition ties the myth to Aruṇācala (Tiruvaṇṇāmalai), and Liṅgodbhava images appear on the back wall of Śiva temples, especially in the south.

events.title: Halmidi inscription
events.description: The Halmidi inscription, found in a village in Karnataka's Hassan district, is the oldest known inscription in the Kannada language, usually dated to about 450 CE. It is a royal grant in the time of the Kadamba king Kākutsthavarman, written in the Kannada language rather than in Sanskrit. The record begins with an invocation. It shows that Kannada was being used for official purposes at this period, long before the flowering of medieval Kannada literature.

events.title: Bāgh caves and Vākāṭaka painting
events.description: The Bāgh caves, in the Narmadā valley of Madhya Pradesh, are a group of nine Buddhist rock-cut monasteries, and their murals date approximately to the 5th and 6th centuries, close in time and style to those of Ajaṇṭā. The region was ruled by the Vākāṭakas and neighbouring dynasties. Only fragments of the paintings survive, showing figures of royal and divine scenes. They show that a painting tradition similar to Ajaṇṭā's was practised across central India.

events.title: Candramati's Daśapadārthaśāstra
events.description: Candramati was a Vaiśeṣika philosopher who wrote the Daśapadārthaśāstra, the "treatise on ten categories", which extended the classic six categories of the school with additional ones. His work is lost in Sanskrit and survives only in a Chinese translation made by the pilgrim Xuanzang in 648. It is important because it preserves a stage of Vaiśeṣika thought earlier than the commentaries of Praśastapāda, and the dating to about 450 is approximate.

events.title: Skandagupta repels the Hūṇas
events.description: Around 455 CE the Hūṇas, a people from Central Asia, broke into northwest India. The young Gupta emperor Skandagupta met them; his pillar inscription at Bhitarī says that when he joined battle with the Hūṇas the earth shook. He held them off for a generation. The effort drained the treasury, and the late Gupta coinage shows debasement. His inscriptions at Bhitarī and Junāgaḍh are the main sources for his reign, and the Hūṇa threat returned under his successors.

events.title: Lokavibhāga and early decimal place-value
events.description: The Lokavibhāga, "Division of the Universe," is a Jaina work on cosmology. A colophon dates its completion to the year Śaka 380, equivalent to 458 CE. It is cited by historians of mathematics because its numbers are written using decimal place-value with a word for zero, and so it is one of the earliest dated Indian texts to use such a system. The place-value system later spread through the Islamic world to Europe, where it became known as Hindu-Arabic numerals.

events.title: Jaina councils at Valabhī
events.description: According to Śvetāmbara tradition, a council at Valabhī in Gujarat, led by Devarddhi Gaṇi Kṣamāśramaṇa, committed the Jaina canon to writing after centuries of oral transmission. The date is given as 980 or 993 years after Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa, which corresponds to 453 or 466 CE. The Śvetāmbara Āgamas as we have them are largely based on this redaction, though the Digambara tradition does not accept this canon.

events.title: Mānadeva's Cāṅgu Nārāyaṇa pillar
events.description: At the temple of Cāṅgu Nārāyaṇa in the Kathmandu valley stands a pillar bearing an inscription of the Licchavi king Mānadeva, dated to 464 CE. It is the oldest dated inscription found in Nepal. It records the king's deeds, including his devotion to Viṣṇu and his mother's act of sati after his father's death, as the text is usually read. The inscription shows Vaiṣṇava worship established in the valley by the fifth century.

events.title: Death of Skandagupta
events.description: Skandagupta, who reigned from about 455, is remembered for turning back a Hūṇa invasion, as recorded on the Bhitarī pillar, and for repairing the Sudarśana lake in Saurashtra, as recorded at Junāgaḍh. These wars strained the imperial treasury, and the late Gupta coinage shows debasement. After his death in about 467 the succession was disputed among relatives, and provincial governors and feudatories increasingly acted on their own. The empire's decline over the following decades began from this point.
events.eraDesc: Often called the classical golden age: Kālidāsa writes, Āryabhaṭa computes, and stone temples flourish.

events.title: Hariṣeṇa Vākāṭaka
events.description: Hariṣeṇa ruled the Vatsagulma branch of the Vākāṭakas in the late fifth century and was one of the dynasty's last powerful kings. An inscription in Ajaṇṭā Cave 16 credits his minister Varāhadeva with the excavation, and other caves belong to the same period. Although the Vākāṭakas were Vedic brāhmaṇas, they and their ministers supported the Buddhist monasteries of Ajaṇṭā. After his reign the dynasty faded, and its lands passed to powers such as the Kalacuris and the Cālukyas.

events.title: Ajaṇṭā's Vākāṭaka phase
events.description: Though Ajaṇṭā is a Buddhist site, its richest phase was financed by courtiers of the Brahmanical Vākāṭakas. Inscriptions show that officials and feudatories of King Hariṣeṇa (r. c. 475–500) sponsored some of the finest caves: Cave 16 was dedicated by his minister Varāhadeva, and Cave 17, whose paintings illustrate Jātaka stories, by a feudatory prince. Cave 1, with its famous bodhisattva figures, is dated by some scholars to the same era. The paintings are the main surviving example of ancient Indian mural art.

events.title: Maitrakas of Valabhī
events.description: The Maitraka dynasty was founded by Bhaṭārka, a general who had served the Guptas and made himself independent in Saurashtra. Valabhī became its capital. The Maitrakas styled themselves devotees of Śiva (paramamāheśvara) but also gave generously to Buddhist monasteries and Jaina communities. Xuanzang, who visited, and Yijing, who wrote of it, describe Valabhī as a centre of learning comparable to Nālandā, and a Jaina council is traditionally held to have met there. The dynasty ruled until the 8th century.

events.title: Birth of Āryabhaṭa
events.description: In the Āryabhaṭīya, Āryabhaṭa says that when sixty times sixty years and three quarters of a yuga of the Kali Yuga had passed, he was twenty-three years old, a statement that gives 499 CE for the text and 476 for his birth. Later writers place him at Kusumapura, near Pāṭaliputra. His short work includes trigonometric sine tables, a close value of π, rules for eclipses and the proposal that the Earth rotates daily on its axis.

events.title: Dignāga and Buddhist logic
events.description: Dignāga, a Buddhist scholar associated with the Kāñcī region and Nālandā, wrote the Pramāṇasamuccaya, a treatise on valid knowledge. He argued that there are only two means of knowing, perception and inference, and developed a theory of how words convey meaning by excluding other things (apoha). His work reshaped debate in India: Nyāya authors such as Uddyotakara replied to him, and the Buddhist school of Dharmakīrti developed his ideas, so the dispute continued across several centuries.

events.title: Budhagupta's Eraṇ pillar
events.description: At Eraṇ in Madhya Pradesh, a tall stone column topped by a Garuḍa figure was set up in 484–485 CE, in the reign of Budhagupta, by the brothers Mātṛviṣṇu and Dhanyaviṣṇu. It is dedicated to Janārdana, a name of Viṣṇu. The inscription names the Gupta king and the local ruler and shows the spread of Vaiṣṇava worship in central India. Such Garuḍa pillars (garuḍadhvaja) stand before Viṣṇu's temples as flag-staves, continuing the tradition seen earlier at Besnagar.

events.title: Āryabhaṭīya
events.description: Written in 499 CE by Āryabhaṭa at the age of twenty-three, in just 121 verses. It uses a place-value number system, gives π as 3.1416 and calls that value "approximate", tabulates sines, and solves equations of the kind now called linear Diophantine.¶In astronomy it states that the stars appear to move because the Earth rotates, like a man in a boat who sees the banks moving backward, and it explains eclipses by the shadows of the Earth and Moon. India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named after him.

events.title: Kāśyapa Saṃhitā on children's medicine
events.description: The Kāśyapa Saṃhitā, also called the Vṛddhajīvakīya Tantra, is the main surviving Āyurvedic work on kaumārabhṛtya, the care of infants and children, with sections on pregnancy and childbirth. Tradition ascribes it to the sage Kāśyapa, as taught to Vṛddha Jīvaka and later revised. The Nepalese manuscript on which the modern edition rests is incomplete. Scholars generally place its present form well after the Caraka and Suśruta works, around the middle of the first millennium CE, although it may preserve older material.

events.title: Bower Manuscript
events.description: The Bower Manuscript, bought in 1890 by Lieutenant Hamilton Bower near Kucha in Xinjiang, is a set of birch-bark leaves in Gupta-period Brāhmī script, dated to about the fifth or sixth century CE. It contains medical formulas, charms and a section on omens. Its most important part is the Nāvanītaka, a compendium of recipes and treatments, which shows Indian medicine travelling along the Silk Road into Central Asia. It is among the oldest surviving Sanskrit manuscripts of medicine and helped scholars date the transmission of Āyurvedic recipes.

events.title: Devī Māhātmya (Durgā Saptaśatī)
events.description: The Devī Māhātmya, "Greatness of the Goddess," has thirteen chapters and about 700 verses, and sits within the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa. It narrates three episodes: the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, of Mahiṣāsura, and of Śumbha, Niśumbha and Raktabīja. In them the Goddess, as Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Sarasvatī, or as Caṇḍikā, is the supreme power behind gods and the universe. Scholars date it to about the 5th–6th century. Recited as the Caṇḍī Pāṭha, it remains central to Navarātri worship.

events.title: Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār, Śaiva poet-saint
events.description: Punitavati, a merchant's wife of the port of Kāraikkāl, served a mango to a Śaiva devotee and miraculously produced another for her husband, who fled from her in awe. She asked Śiva to take away her beauty and became a gaunt ghost-like figure who, by tradition, walked to his mountain on her hands. Her poems, of about the sixth century, describing his dance in the cremation ground, are among the earliest Tamil hymns to Śiva.

events.title: Daśāvatāra temple, Deogarh
events.description: The temple at Deogarh in central India, of about 500 CE, is one of the first in stone planned with a tower over the sanctum, though the tower has long since fallen; it marks the beginning of the north Indian temple form. Three large panels on its walls are among the finest Gupta sculptures: Viṣṇu asleep on the serpent Ananta, Viṣṇu rescuing the king of elephants from a crocodile, and the twin sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa in meditation.

events.title: Bhitargaon brick temple
events.description: The Bhitargaon temple in Uttar Pradesh is one of the oldest surviving brick temples in India. It stands on a square plinth and has a tall pyramidal superstructure and a pointed arched niche, and it was decorated with terracotta panels showing deities, including Gaṇeśa and Durgā. Built in the Gupta period, it demonstrates a move from flat-roofed shrines to a towering śikhara that would become the defining feature of northern Indian temples, though its upper part has been heavily restored.

events.title: Nachna and Bhumara Śiva temples
events.description: Two Gupta-era shrines in central India show Śaiva worship in the late 5th and 6th centuries. At Bhumara, in Madhya Pradesh, a small stone temple is dedicated to Śiva and has an ekamukha-liṅga, with fine carvings of river goddesses and other figures on its doorway. The Pārvatī temple at Nachna has a two-storey design and carved images that include Gaṇeśa. Together they show how the Guptas' stone shrine tradition spread to the Bundelkhand region.

events.title: Toramāṇa's Hūṇa invasion
events.description: The Hūṇas, in the form usually called Alchon Huns, entered India from the northwest in the late 5th century. Toramāṇa established himself in the Punjab and then pushed into Malwa. An inscription at Eraṇ, on a colossal Varāha (boar) image, is dated to the first year of his reign and records its dedication, showing that he held central India. The invasions weakened Gupta control and affected the political map of the north for decades.

events.title: Vyāsa's Yoga Bhāṣya
events.description: Patañjali's Yoga Sūtras define yoga as the stilling of the mind's fluctuations (citta-vṛtti-nirodha) and set out an eightfold path. The Yoga Bhāṣya, attributed to Vyāsa, is the oldest and most authoritative commentary, and some scholars hold that sūtras and commentary were produced close together. It explains Yoga's metaphysics in Sāṃkhya terms, with the distinction between puruṣa and prakṛti. Later writers such as Vācaspati Miśra and Vijñānabhikṣu wrote sub-commentaries on it.

events.title: Praśastapāda's Padārthadharmasaṅgraha
events.description: The Padārthadharmasaṅgraha, "Compendium of the Properties of Categories," is the classic exposition of Vaiśeṣika. Though often called a commentary on Kaṇāda's sūtras, it is more a free systematic digest. It expands the list of qualities to twenty-four, discusses the atomic theory, the nature of the self and knowledge, and includes an account of the creation and dissolution of the world, which brings in God. Later Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika philosophers took it as the standard reference for their ontology.

events.description: Uddyotakara, who describes himself as a Pāśupata teacher, wrote the Nyāyavārttika as a sub-commentary on Vātsyāyana's Nyāya Bhāṣya. He defends the Nyāya position against the attacks of the Buddhist logician Dignāga, who had criticised Nyāya's accounts of perception and inference. The work shows the lively exchange between Hindu and Buddhist philosophers, and was in turn commented upon by Vācaspati Miśra in the 9th century. His date is usually placed around the 6th century.

events.title: Viśākhadatta's Mudrārākṣasa
events.description: The Mudrārākṣasa, "Rākṣasa's Signet Ring," is a Sanskrit political drama of Cāṇakya's strategy to secure Candragupta Maurya's throne by winning over Rākṣasa, the former minister of the Nandas. A seal ring (mudrā) plays a key part in the plot. It has no love story and few female characters, unusual for the genre. The author's date is uncertain, with estimates ranging from the 4th to the 8th century. It preserves the Cāṇakya legend as told in the classical period.

events.title: Suśruta Saṃhitā's final redaction
events.description: The Suśruta Saṃhitā, the main Ayurvedic text on surgery, is attributed to Suśruta, a teacher associated with Kāśī, but reached its present form over several centuries. Tradition credits Nāgārjuna with revising it and adding the final section, the Uttaratantra. It describes surgical instruments and operations, including plastic reconstruction of the nose, cataract treatment, and the handling of wounds, along with rules for training surgeons. It remained a core medical authority and was translated into Arabic and Tibetan.

events.title: Niśvāsatattva Saṃhitā
events.description: The Niśvāsatattva Saṃhitā is the oldest known Śaiva tantric scripture, usually dated to about the 5th–6th century, though the only manuscript is a Nepalese palm-leaf copy of the 9th century. It belongs to the Mantramārga, the path of mantra in the Śaiva Siddhānta, and comprises several sections, including one on public religion and one on initiation and ritual. Its discovery has changed the understanding of when Śaiva tantra emerged, and it shows doctrines and rites that later Siddhānta works developed.

events.title: Aulikaras of Daśapura
events.description: The Aulikaras ruled from Daśapura (Mandasor) in western Malwa. They first appear as feudatories of the Guptas. Their inscriptions record Śiva and Viṣṇu temples and are composed in refined Sanskrit verse. Yaśodharman Viṣṇuvardhana, the best-known Aulikara king, set up victory pillars at Mandasor in about 532 claiming conquest of regions even the Guptas and Hūṇas had not held. The dynasty's inscriptions are among the finest surviving examples of Sanskrit kāvya on stone.

events.title: Caturaṅga, the Indian ancestor of chess
events.description: A game called caturaṅga, "four limbs", after the four divisions of an Indian army, elephants, chariots, cavalry and infantry, was played on a board of sixty-four squares in northern India by about the sixth century. It passed to Persia as chatrang, where "shāh māt", the king is helpless, gave "checkmate", and from there to the Arab world and Europe. The elephant became the bishop and the chariot the rook.

events.title: Elephanta's Great Cave begun
events.description: On an island in Mumbai harbour a temple to Śiva was cut into a basalt hill in about the mid-sixth century. Its pillared hall, about forty metres square, is lined with reliefs over five metres high: Śiva as dancer, as the androgyne, as bridegroom, as bearer of the Gaṅgā. At the back is a colossal bust with three faces, fierce, serene and gentle, often interpreted as Śiva in his aspects of destroyer, preserver and creator. The Portuguese later damaged some of the sculptures.

events.title: Jogeśvarī and Maṇḍapeśvar caves
events.description: On Sālsette island, today within Mumbai, rock-cut caves at Jogeśvarī and Maṇḍapeśvar (Mount Poinsur, Borivali) date to about the 6th–8th century and are Śaiva in character. Jogeśvarī is a large cave temple with a central shrine and long halls, and Maṇḍapeśvar has a sanctum and carvings of Śiva forms. Their style relates them to Elephanta nearby and the Deccan cave temples. The Pāśupata Śaiva ascetic movement is often linked to such shrines in western India.

events.title: Śarabhapurīyas and Pāṇḍuvaṃśīs
events.description: In Dakṣiṇa Kosala, now Chhattisgarh, the Śarabhapurīyas ruled in the fifth and sixth centuries and were Vaiṣṇava in their copper-plate grants. The Pāṇḍuvaṃśīs, who were largely Śaiva, then ruled and moved the capital to Śrīpura (Sirpur) on the Mahānadī. Sirpur contains a brick Lakṣmaṇa temple of Viṣṇu from this period, and also Buddhist and Jaina remains. It is one of the best examples of early brick architecture in central India.

events.title: Pāśupata Sūtra with Kauṇḍinya's Bhāṣya
events.description: The Pāśupata Sūtra is the basic text of the Pāśupata Śaivas and is attributed to Lakulīśa. It is explained in a commentary by Kauṇḍinya, the Pañcārthabhāṣya. It teaches five topics, namely kārya (the effect, or the soul and world), kāraṇa (the cause, or Śiva as Paśupati), yoga (union), vidhi (the prescribed practice) and duḥkhānta (the end of suffering). Pāśupata practice involved ascetic discipline, and the movement was strong in Gujarat.

events.title: Tāla-māna iconometry
events.description: Tāla-māna is the system of proportions by which Indian sculptors and painters shape images of gods. The unit is the tāla, taken from the face or the hand, and the whole figure is measured as a set number of such units, with different figures such as a god, a demon or a child given their own measurements. Rules are set out in the Bṛhat Saṃhitā of Varāhamihira and in Āgama and śilpa texts. They ensured that images followed consistent forms across regions and centuries.

events.title: The Buddha as Viṣṇu's avatāra
events.description: By about the Gupta age the Purāṇas listed the Buddha as one of the ten avatāras of Viṣṇu, as in the Matsya, Agni and Garuḍa Purāṇas and in the Bhāgavata. Accounts of why he took birth differ: some say to turn away the demons or the unworthy from the Vedic path, others that he taught compassion and ended animal sacrifice, as in Jayadeva's later Gītagovinda. Scholars have read this as a Brahmanical absorption of a rival tradition; Buddhists generally reject the identification.

events.title: Sārnāth and Mathurā Gupta style
events.description: Sārnāth and Mathurā were the two major centres of sculpture in the Gupta age. At Sārnāth, the seated Buddha with downcast eyes, a transparent robe and a carved halo set a style of calm; Mathurā produced Buddhas, Jinas and Hindu images in sandstone. Craftsmen of the period also made images of Viṣṇu and Śiva, as at Udayagiri. Later Indian sculpture, in Buddhist, Hindu and Jaina contexts, often referred back to this model, and its influence reached Southeast Asia.

events.title: Navarātri and the autumn Durgā festival
events.description: Navarātri, the "nine nights" of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, honours the goddess Durgā. The Devī Māhātmya, a text of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa composed around this period, is recited over the nine nights and tells how the Goddess slays the buffalo demon Mahiṣāsura. The tenth day, Vijayadaśamī or Dasarā, is a day of victory, when kings traditionally worshipped their weapons before campaigns. The festival takes regional forms, from Bengal's Durgā Pūjā to Rāmlīlā in the north and doll displays in the south.

events.title: Liṅgaparvata and the Śaiva sanctuary of Vat Phou
events.description: At Vat Phou, in Champasak province in southern Laos, a mountain with a natural liṅga-shaped peak was taken to be the home of Śiva, and the river below was likened to the Gaṅgā. The inscription K.365 from nearby names Devānīka, who is said to have established a tīrtha in the area. The first structure on the mountain is placed about the late fifth century, with a brick building of the seventh and megalithic remains that may be older.¶Khmer builders later laid out a long axis from a causeway up to the shrine. The site is a clear example in Southeast Asia of a landscape planned around Śaiva sacred geography. UNESCO inscribed it in 2001.

events.title: Dah Parvatiya doorframe and Assam's earliest temple art
events.description: Dah Parvatiya, a village just west of Tezpur in Assam, has the ruins of a temple whose stone doorframe, found in excavation, is called the finest and oldest sculpture in Assam. The Archaeological Survey of India dug the site in 1924, and again in 1989–90. The carvings are dated to the fifth or sixth century and show the influence of Gupta art.¶The door-posts have figures of the river goddesses Gaṅgā and Yamunā, and flying geese. The style is close to that of the Gupta temples of the central Gaṅgā plain, which shows the spread of Brahmanical temple building to Kāmarūpa in the period before Bhāskaravarman. It is the earliest well-preserved example of temple art in the region.

events.title: Varāhamihira's Pañcasiddhāntikā
events.description: Varāhamihira, astronomer and astrologer at Ujjayinī, composed the Pañcasiddhāntikā, a summary of five earlier astronomical treatises: the Paitāmaha, Vāsiṣṭha, Romaka, Pauliśa and Sūrya Siddhāntas. Some of these show Greek and Alexandrian influence. His text dates itself to about 505 CE and is an important record of astronomical knowledge before it was superseded by later works. Its value is that it preserves doctrines from earlier siddhāntas that are otherwise lost.

events.title: Eraṇ inscription records earliest dated satī
events.description: A pillar at Eraṇ dated 510 CE records that Goparāja, a general serving the Gupta king Bhānugupta, died in battle and that his wife burned herself on his funeral pyre. It is the earliest dated inscription recording satī, the immolation of a widow. The practice was never universal, and later Dharmaśāstra authors disagreed about it, some praising and some condemning it. Historians use the Eraṇ record as an early indication of how the custom was remembered and honoured in some warrior circles.

events.title: Mihirakula and the Hūṇa kingdom
events.description: Mihirakula, son of Toramāṇa, ruled the Hūṇa kingdom from Śākala (Sialkot). Buddhist travellers such as Xuanzang, and the Kashmiri chronicle Rājataraṅgiṇī, depict him as extremely cruel and as hostile to Buddhism. A Gwalior inscription, however, shows him as a patron of a Sun temple. Hūṇa power was broken in the 530s by a coalition that included Yaśodharman of Malwa and the Gupta king Narasiṃhagupta Bālāditya. The sources are partisan, so historians treat the lurid details with caution.

events.title: Yaśodharman defeats Mihirakula
events.description: The Hūṇa king Mihirakula ruled northwest India from about 515 with a cruelty remembered in Kashmir's chronicle centuries later. Around 528 Yaśodharman, a king of Mālwā, defeated him. Two victory pillars at Mandasor claim that Mihirakula, who had bowed to none but Śiva, touched Yaśodharman's feet with his head. Hūṇa power in India never recovered, though the Gupta empire was already breaking up.

events.title: Mahābhārata described as 100,000 verses
events.description: A copper-plate inscription of the Mahārāja Śarvanātha, dated to 532–533 CE, refers to the Mahābhārata as a śata-sāhasrī saṃhitā, a collection of a hundred thousand verses. Tradition holds that the epic grew from a shorter Jaya into Bhārata and then the Mahābhārata, and the text itself claims this size. The BORI critical edition, based on comparison of manuscripts, is considerably shorter, since many verses prove to be regional additions. The inscription is firm early evidence that the epic had reached its enormous, recognisable form.

events.title: Pulakeśin I founds Bādāmi Cālukyas
events.description: Pulakeśin I fortified the hill-fort of Vātāpi (Bādāmi) in Karnataka around 543, according to an inscription there, and is said to have performed an Aśvamedha sacrifice, a claim to imperial status. He founded the Cālukya dynasty that would dominate the Deccan for two centuries. His successors expanded the kingdom and left some of the oldest and finest stone temples in the south, at Bādāmi, Aihoḷe and Paṭṭadakal.

events.title: Bhāravi's Kirātārjunīya
events.description: Bhāravi's Kirātārjunīya is a mahākāvya in eighteen cantos on an episode from the Mahābhārata, in which Arjuna practises austerities to obtain a weapon from Śiva, who appears disguised as a Kirāta (mountain hunter) and fights him before revealing himself. The poem is known for its dense, intricate language. The poet is named in a 634 CE inscription at Aihoḷe, so he lived before then; he is usually placed in the 6th century. It became a model for later court epics, including Māgha's.

events.title: Bṛhat Saṃhitā
events.description: Varāhamihira of Ujjain, in the sixth century, wrote an encyclopaedia in 106 chapters of everything a court astrologer should know. Beside planetary omens it covers rainfall and clouds, finding underground water, earthquakes, the testing of gems, the proportions of temples and images, perfumes, and the signs of horses and elephants. It is a main source for the science and daily life of the Gupta age.

events.title: Bṛhajjātaka
events.description: The Bṛhajjātaka is Varāhamihira's major treatise on horoscopy, the casting and interpretation of birth charts. It sets out the zodiac signs, planets, houses and rules for predicting life events, and it draws on both Indian and Greek astrological sources. He also wrote the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, a wide-ranging work on omens, architecture and weather, and a shorter treatise, the Laghujātaka. The Bṛhajjātaka became a standard text for Indian astrologers and has been widely commented upon.

events.title: End of the imperial Guptas
events.description: By the middle of the 6th century the Gupta line was reduced to a small domain in eastern India. Viṣṇugupta is the last emperor named in records. The north was divided among successor powers: the Maukharis at Kanauj, the Later Guptas, who were a separate dynasty in Magadha, the Maitrakas in Gujarat and others. This fragmentation set the stage for Harṣa's attempt to reunite the north a half-century later.

events.title: Gauḍapāda's Māṇḍūkya Kārikā
events.description: Gauḍapāda, by tradition the teacher of Śaṅkara's teacher, wrote 215 verses on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad around the sixth century. They are the first systematic statement of Advaita. Reasoning from dream and waking, he argues that nothing is ever really born: there is no creation, no bondage, no seeker and no liberation, only the unborn Self. His terms show close engagement with Buddhist thought.

gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.

events.title: Subandhu, Daṇḍin and Sanskrit prose romance
events.description: Subandhu's Vāsavadattā is an early Sanskrit prose romance, known for long compounds and elaborate wordplay (śleṣa). Daṇḍin, who is associated with the Pallava court at Kāñcī and is usually placed in the 7th century, wrote the prose Daśakumāracarita, "Tale of the Ten Princes," a picaresque story with lively characters, and the Kāvyādarśa, a manual of poetics that defines the qualities of good poetry. Together these works defined the ornate classical prose and the theory of kāvya.

events.title: Bādāmi cave temples
events.description: Four temples cut into a red sandstone cliff above a lake at Bādāmi, capital of the early Cālukyas, date from the later sixth century; one is dated 578. They hold some of the finest early sculpture of the Deccan: an eighteen-armed dancing Śiva showing the poses of dance, Viṣṇu seated on the serpent, the boar and the three strides. Traces of one of the oldest surviving Hindu wall paintings remain on a ceiling.

events.title: Maukharis of Kanauj
events.description: The Maukhari dynasty ruled in the Gaṅgā plain in the sixth century. Īśānavarman's Haraha inscription, dated 554, claims victory over the Āndhras, the Śūlikas and the Gauḍas. Under the Maukharis, Kānyakubja (Kanauj) became a major political centre, a role it kept for centuries. They fought the later Guptas and the Hūṇas. Graha-varman Maukhari married Rājyaśrī, sister of Harṣa, and after his death Harṣa took Kanauj.

events.title: Kalacuris of Māhiṣmatī
events.description: The Kalacuris of the sixth century ruled from Māhiṣmatī on the Narmadā, and their territory ran from Mālwā to Mahārāṣṭra. The kings Kṛṣṇarāja, Śaṅkaragaṇa and Buddharāja are known from inscriptions and coins, and their records show devotion to Śiva as Paśupati, a sign of the Pāśupata movement. Buddharāja was defeated by the Cālukya Maṅgaleśa, and the Kalacuri power declined thereafter.

events.title: Rāvaṇa Phaḍi, Aihoḷe
events.description: The Rāvaṇa Phaḍi is a rock-cut Śaiva cave at Aihoḷe in Karnataka, dating to about the mid-6th century under the early Cālukyas. Its sanctum holds a liṅga, and its walls carry notable relief sculpture, including a dancing Śiva with ten arms, and the group of Seven Mothers, Saptamātṛkās, with Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya. The Naṭarāja figure here is among the early examples of what became a famous subject in Indian art, and it shows the Cālukya experiments that preceded their temples at Paṭṭadakal.

events.title: Chenla
events.description: Chenla is the Chinese name for an early Khmer polity of the sixth to eighth centuries. Its king Īśānavarman, who ruled in the early seventh century, built a capital called Īśānapura at what is now Sambor Prei Kuk in Cambodia. The site has brick temples dedicated to Śiva, and to Harihara, the combined form of Hari (Viṣṇu) and Hara (Śiva). Sanskrit inscriptions praise the gods and record royal gifts. This was a formative stage in the Khmer tradition of temple-building that later produced Angkor.

events.title: Siṃhaviṣṇu revives the Pallavas
events.description: Siṃhaviṣṇu, who ruled from about 575, restored Pallava power after the Kaḷabhra period. Later Pallava records say he conquered the Kaḷabhras and defeated the Cōḻas, Pāṇḍyas, Cēras and the king of Siṃhala (Laṅkā) and extended his domain to the Kāverī. Tradition links the poet Bhāravi with his court. Siṃhaviṣṇu began the line of Pallava rulers whose successors, Mahendravarman I and Narasiṃhavarman I, would build rock-cut and structural temples.

events.title: Maṅgaleśa's Vaiṣṇava cave
events.description: Cave 3 at Bādāmi in Karnataka is a Vaiṣṇava cave temple with large relief sculptures of Viṣṇu, including as Narasiṃha and Varāha. An inscription in Sanskrit records that Maṅgaleśa, the Cālukya king, dedicated it in 578, in the twelfth year of his brother Kīrtivarman's reign, which makes it the earliest firmly dated Cālukya monument. The date marks the point at which the Cālukyas were building and sponsoring Hindu temples in the region.

gitaQuote.verse: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत । अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥ परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् । धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.

events.title: Prabhākaravardhana of Thāneśvara
events.description: Prabhākaravardhana ruled Thāneśvara around 580 to 605 and made the Puṣyabhūti dynasty a power in northern India. His son Harṣa's biographer Bāṇa, in the Harṣacarita, calls him "a lion to the Hūṇa deer" and describes him as a devotee of the Sun. He married Yaśomatī and had two sons, Rājyavardhana and Harṣa, and a daughter, Rājyaśrī. His family later controlled much of the north.

events.title: Kaḍuṅgōṉ restores the Pāṇḍyas
events.description: Kaḍuṅgōṉ, who ruled around 590, is credited in the later Vēḷvikuṭi copper plates with defeating the Kaḷabhras and restoring the Pāṇḍya kingdom, with its capital at Madurai. His reign opens the second Pāṇḍya line, which ruled during the age of the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava saints and fought the Pallavas for the Tamil country. The sources are later inscriptions, so details are known mostly through the dynasty's own accounts.

events.title: Muṇḍeśvarī temple
events.description: The Muṇḍeśvarī temple stands on a hill in the Kaimur range in Bihar. It is an octagonal stone shrine with doorways on four sides. An inscription found there, dated in year 30 of a king Udayasena in an unnamed era, has been read as 108 CE, 636 CE or, on palaeography, about 570–590 CE; the existing structure is generally placed in the 6th–7th century or later. The temple is dedicated to Śiva and the goddess, and is often described as one of the oldest still in use for worship in India.

events.title: Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa and the Citrasūtra
events.description: The Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa, probably composed in Kashmir or the northwest in about the sixth or seventh century, covers a wide range of subjects, including cosmology, genealogy, ritual and law. Its third part includes the Citrasūtra, the oldest surviving treatise on painting in India, along with passages on sculpture, dance, music and iconography. It is a key source for early Indian art theory and shows how closely image-making and ritual were connected in Purāṇic culture.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.

events.title: Skanda Purāṇa (early recension)
events.description: The earliest Skanda Purāṇa was a shorter Śaiva work, with strong Pāśupata influence and a focus on Śiva, the Goddess and Śiva's family. A Nepalese manuscript dated 810 CE preserves it. Modern editors have reconstructed it, showing that it differs greatly from the printed Skanda Purāṇa, a huge collection of regional khaṇḍas and māhātmyas assembled over centuries. The early version is an important witness to the emergence of Śaivism within Purāṇic literature, and is generally dated to about the sixth or seventh century.

events.title: First three Āḻvārs
events.description: Three wandering devotees of Viṣṇu, Poykai, Pūtam and Pēy, took shelter from a storm one night in a tiny porch at Tirukkōvalūr: room, they said, for one to lie, two to sit, three to stand. They felt a fourth pressing in among them. Each lit a lamp in a hundred Tamil verses to see who it was. These are the first hymns of the Āḻvārs, of about the sixth or seventh century.

events.title: Mahendravarman I Pallava
events.description: Mahendravarman I, Pallava king at Kāñcī from about 600, was a painter, musician and the author of a Sanskrit farce mocking drunken ascetics of several sects. He began cutting shrines into granite hillsides and boasted in an inscription of making a temple without brick, timber, metal or mortar. Tamil tradition says the saint Appar turned him from Jainism to the worship of Śiva.

events.title: Appar (Tirunāvukkarasar)
events.description: Appar, "father", was born to a farming family, became a Jaina monk of distinction, and returned to Śiva after his sister's prayers cured him of a painful illness. Tradition says the Pallava king had him thrown into a lime kiln and the sea without effect. He spent a long life walking from temple to temple with a hoe to clear weeds from their courtyards, singing. Some three thousand of his verses survive in the Tēvāram.

events.title: Guhilas of Mewar
events.description: The Guhilas were the ruling house of Mewar, tracing their descent from a founder called Guhadatta or Guhila. Early centres included Nāgdā, close to the shrine of Ekaliṅgajī, the form of Śiva venerated as the true lord of the kingdom, with the Guhila rulers serving as his dīwān. Bāppā Rāwal, who lived in the eighth century, is the best known of the early kings. Their descendants, the Sisodias, ruled Mewar until the twentieth century.

events.title: The Īśvara Gītā and later Gītās
events.description: Following the Bhagavad Gītā, several later texts adopted the form of a Gītā, a dialogue of teaching in verse. The Īśvara Gītā, part of the Kūrma Purāṇa, is a Śaiva work in which Śiva teaches the sages. The Gaṇeśa Gītā belongs to the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, and the Devī Gītā to the Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa. The Avadhūta Gītā is a nondual poem attributed to Dattātreya. These works date to different periods, and they apply the Gītā's approach to different deities.

gitaQuote.verse: अहमेवाक्षयः कालो धाताहं विश्वतोमुखः ॥ कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो लोकान्समाहर्तुमिह प्रवृत्तः ॥

gitaQuote.translation: I alone am inexhaustible, imperishable Time (Akṣaya Kāla), and I am the dispenser of destiny facing all directions... I am all-destroying Time, grown mighty to extinguish the worlds.
gitaQuote.source: Mahabharata (Bhishma Parva 35.32); Abhinavagupta Gītārtha-Saṁgraha

events.title: Maṇḍagappaṭṭu cave temple of Mahendravarman
events.description: At Maṇḍagappaṭṭu in Tamil Nadu, the Pallava king Mahendravarman I had a cave shrine cut that is regarded as among the first of its kind in the Tamil country. A Sanskrit inscription says he built it for Brahmā, Īśvara (Śiva) and Viṣṇu, "without brick, timber, metal or mortar," and the claim is taken to mean that this was a new method of building in stone. It is early in a Pallava tradition that led to the monuments at Mahābalipuram.

events.title: Sittannavāsal paintings
events.description: Sittannavāsal, near Pudukkoṭṭai in Tamil Nadu, has a rock-cut Jaina cave temple, the Arivar Koil, whose wall and ceiling paintings are among the few early murals surviving in South India. They are commonly dated to the 7th century, in the time of the Pallava king Mahendravarman I, though some scholars favour a Pāṇḍya date in the 9th century. The murals show a lotus pond with flowers, birds and fish, and dancers, and are linked stylistically to the Ajaṇṭā tradition. The site also has natural caves with Jaina inscriptions and stone beds used by monks.

events.title: Six Gāṇapatya sub-sects
events.description: The Gāṇapatya are worshippers of Gaṇeśa as the supreme deity. Ānandagiri's Śaṅkaravijaya, a late biography of Śaṅkara, lists six Gāṇapatya sub-sects, named after forms of Gaṇapati: Mahā, Haridrā, Ucchiṣṭa, Navanīta, Svarṇa and Santāna. The list is traditional rather than a precise historical record, but it shows how varied the cult was. The Gāṇapatya were strong in Maharashtra, where Gaṇeśa devotion remains strong today.

gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.

events.title: Bhartṛprapañca and pre-Śaṅkara Vedānta
events.description: Bhartṛprapañca was a Vedānta teacher who lived before Śaṅkara and whose works are lost. He is known through Śaṅkara's commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad and Sureśvara's gloss on it, which criticise his view. He taught a form of bhedābheda, "difference and non-difference", in which the world is both identical with and different from Brahman. His case shows that Vedānta had a range of interpretations before Śaṅkara's non-dualism became dominant.

events.title: Aṃśuvarman of Nepal
events.description: Aṃśuvarman was a Licchavi-period ruler of Nepal who held power as regent and then king in the early seventh century. His inscriptions are in Sanskrit, and he was known for patronage of learning. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who recorded information about Nepal from others, describes a king of this name as a scholar who wrote a treatise on grammar. His reign is an important point in Nepal's early history, and links with Tibet and India grew in his time.

events.title: Harṣavardhana becomes king
events.description: Harṣa came to the throne of Thanesar at sixteen in 606 after his brother's murder, joined it with Kanauj, and in six years of campaigning became overlord of north India. He was a dramatist, with three Sanskrit plays to his name, and kept a brilliant court. He honoured Śiva, the Sun and the Buddha. Two detailed portraits of him survive, by his court poet Bāṇa and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang.

events.title: Śaśāṅka of Gauḍa
events.description: Śaśāṅka ruled Gauḍa (Bengal) from Karṇasuvarṇa, in the early 7th century. His coins show Śiva with the bull Nandī, and he is regarded as a Śaiva. Bāṇa's Harṣacarita, written at the court of Harṣa, tells that he treacherously killed Harṣa's brother Rājyavardhana, and Xuanzang says he persecuted Buddhists, cutting down the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gayā. These sources are hostile, so historians treat these claims with caution. He was an important political rival to Harṣa and Bhāskaravarman.

events.title: Pulakeśin II becomes Cālukya king
events.description: Pulakeśin II of the Cālukyas ruled the Deccan from Bādāmi from 610 to 642. He stopped Harṣa's advance at the Narmadā, exchanged ambassadors with the king of Persia, and took the Andhra coast. A poem by Ravikīrti on a temple wall at Aihoḷe, dated 634, records his victories; it is also the earliest inscription to mention Kālidāsa by name. He died when the Pallavas sacked his capital.

events.title: Īśānavarman's Īśānapura at Sambor Prei Kuk
events.description: Sambor Prei Kuk, in central Cambodia, is the archaeological site of Īśānapura, the capital of the pre-Angkorian kingdom the Chinese called Chenla. Īśānavarman I, who reigned from about 616 to 637, is regarded as its probable founder. The northern and southern temple groups date to the seventh century and are Śaiva; Prasat Sambor was dedicated to Gambhīreśvara, a form of Śiva.¶The brick sanctuaries, with their octagonal towers and carved lintels, are the best-preserved monuments of the period before the Khmer empire of Angkor and show how Indian Śaiva temple forms were adapted in mainland Southeast Asia. UNESCO inscribed the zone as a World Heritage Site in 2017.

events.title: Pulakeśin II halts Harṣa at the Narmadā
events.description: Harṣa of Kanauj ruled most of northern India, but when he moved south, the Cālukya king Pulakeśin II stopped him at the Narmadā river around 618. The Aihoḷe inscription of 634, written by the poet Ravikīrti, celebrates this. Xuanzang also mentions it. The Narmadā became the southern limit of Harṣa's realm, and Pulakeśin took the title Parameśvara. The two rulers represent northern and southern powers of the early 7th century.

events.title: Bāṇabhaṭṭa's Harṣacarita and Kādambarī
events.description: Bāṇa was court poet to Harṣa. His Harṣacarita is a prose biography of the king, among the earliest in Sanskrit, and an important source for the history of the period, though written as courtly praise. His Kādambarī is a long romance of reincarnated lovers, a parrot narrator and a love story across lives. It was unfinished at his death and was completed by his son. It is regarded as the high point of Sanskrit prose and gave its name to the word for "novel" in several Indian languages.

events.title: Khair Khaneh temple and its sun-god image
events.description: At Khair Khaneh, in a pass between the Kabul valley and Kohistan, Joseph Hackin excavated a temple in the 1930s. It is dated to 608–630, in the time of the Turk Shāhis. Among the finds was a whitish-grey marble image of a solar deity in a tunic and boots, now in the Kabul Museum and assigned to the seventh or eighth century.¶Scholars have identified the figure as Sūrya, though some read it as Mithra, and the dress shows the influence of Central Asia on Hindu iconography. Khair Khaneh is one of the sites that show that the royal houses of the Kabul valley before the Hindu Shāhis supported the worship of Hindu deities.

events.title: Eastern Cālukyas of Veṅgī
events.description: Kubja Viṣṇuvardhana, a brother of the Cālukya emperor Pulakeśin II, was placed in charge of the Veṅgī region of the eastern Deccan around 624. He became the founder of a line that lasted for about four and a half centuries. The Eastern Cālukyas supported Sanskrit and Telugu literature, and Nannaya's Telugu Mahābhārata was composed in their court. The line eventually merged with the Cōḻas through marriage and succession.

events.title: Śailodbhavas of Koṅgoda
events.description: The Śailodbhavas were Śaiva rulers of Koṅgoda, in the coastal part of Odisha, from the sixth to the eighth century. They controlled the territory between Chilika and Gañjām. Their records mention Śaśāṅka as overlord in the early seventh century. The earliest surviving Bhubaneśvara temples, including the Paraśurāmeśvara, are generally dated to their time and show the start of the Odishan temple style.

events.title: Karkoṭa dynasty of Kashmir
events.description: According to Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī, Durlabhavardhana founded the Karkoṭa dynasty in Kashmir in about 625. Under his descendants, especially Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa in the 8th century, Kashmir expanded its power and prestige. The Karkoṭas built Sun and Viṣṇu temples such as the Mārtāṇḍa temple, and fostered links with Central Asia and Tibet. Kashmir became a centre of Sanskrit learning, of Śaiva philosophy and of Buddhist scholarship during their rule.

events.title: Brahmagupta's Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta
events.description: Brahmagupta of Bhinmāl in Rajasthan completed his treatise on astronomy in 628, aged thirty. Two of its chapters are on mathematics, and they contain the first known rules for arithmetic with zero and with negative numbers, called "debts" as against "fortunes": a debt minus zero is a debt; the product of two debts is a fortune. Translated into Arabic at Baghdad about 770, the work carried Indian numerals west.

events.title: Bhāskara I's commentary on Āryabhaṭa
events.description: Bhāskara I wrote a commentary on Āryabhaṭa's work in 629 and also the Mahābhāskarīya. His works write numbers using decimal place-value notation and a circle for zero, in one of the earliest dated cases. He gives a rational approximation to the sine function, a formula that does not need a table, and explains and defends Āryabhaṭa's ideas. His writing helped spread Āryabhaṭa's school across western and southern India.

events.title: Xuanzang's pilgrimage to India
events.description: The Chinese monk Xuanzang left China secretly in 629, crossed the Gobi and the mountains of Central Asia, and spent some fifteen years in India. He studied at Nālandā for years and visited almost every region. His detailed record of distances, cities, customs and the state of each religion is so exact that nineteenth-century archaeologists used it to locate lost sites. He returned with 657 texts.

events.title: Narasiṃhavarman I Māmalla
events.description: Narasiṃhavarman I, called Māmalla ("great wrestler"), ruled the Pallava kingdom in the mid-7th century. He defeated Pulakeśin II and was known as a military leader. Māmallapuram (Mahābalipuram), named for him, has rock-cut shrines and monolithic temples, the Pañca Rathas, that are traditionally attributed to his reign, though their exact attribution is debated. The site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a key centre of early Drāviḍa art.

events.title: Nīlamata Purāṇa
events.description: The Nīlamata Purāṇa is a Sanskrit text of Kashmir, usually dated between the sixth and eighth centuries. It tells of the valley's origin from a lake, the Nāga Nīla, and gives rules for rites and festivals through the year, along with descriptions of local tīrthas and nāga shrines. It is the main source for early Kashmiri religion and is used by the historian Kalhaṇa. It records customs, such as water pilgrimages and the worship of springs, that shaped later Kashmiri Hindu practice.

events.title: Ravikīrti's Aihoḷe praśasti inscription
events.description: The Aihoḷe inscription of 634, composed by the poet Ravikīrti for the Cālukya king Pulakeśin II, records the king's conquests, including his defeat of Harṣa of Kanauj. It is notable for giving a date in two eras, the Śaka year 556 and a count of 3,735 years since the Bhārata war, which places that war in the late fourth millennium BCE by traditional reckoning. Ravikīrti also compares himself with the poets Kālidāsa and Bhāravi, which is a useful marker in the dating of Sanskrit literature.

events.title: Arab naval raids on the Konkan coast
events.description: According to Arabic sources such as al-Balādhurī, in the caliphate of ʿUmar, Arab governors in Oman and Bahrain sent naval expeditions against Thāne on the Konkan coast, Bharuch in Gujarat and Debal in Sindh, in about 636. They were small raids rather than conquests and are not well documented from the Indian side. They show that Arab seafarers knew the western coast of India and set the stage for later land campaigns in Sindh.

events.title: Tiruñāṉacampantar
events.description: Sambandar, a brāhmaṇa child of Sīrkāḻi, is said to have been fed milk by the Goddess at three and begun to sing at once. Travelling with a low-caste lute-player, he composed hymns at over two hundred temples before his death at sixteen. At Madurai he cured the Pāṇḍya king of a fever and defeated the Jaina monks in contests of miracles. His 4,000 verses open the Tamil Śaiva canon.

events.title: Pallavas sack Vātāpi
events.description: In about 642, Narasiṃhavarman I of Kāñcī invaded the Cālukya kingdom and captured Vātāpi, where Pulakeśin II was killed. The Pallavas recorded the victory in inscriptions. Tamil tradition says that the general Parañjōti, who became the Śaiva saint Śiruttoṇṭar, brought back a Gaṇapati image from Vātāpi, which is the origin of the "Vātāpi Gaṇapati" worshipped in Tamil Nadu. The war reversed the earlier Cālukya triumph and began a long rivalry.

events.title: Harṣa's Prayāga assembly
events.description: The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang attended a great assembly in 643 at Prayāga, the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā. He says that Harṣa gave away his accumulated wealth to Brahmins, Buddhists, the poor and others, for several days, as he had done every five years. Some scholars see in this a forerunner of the Kumbha Mela, though textual evidence for the Kumbha gatherings in their present form comes later. The account is valuable as an eyewitness description of religious life under Harṣa.

events.title: Yuktidīpikā
events.description: The Yuktidīpikā is the most detailed surviving commentary on Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhya Kārikā, by an unknown author, and is generally dated to the sixth or seventh century. It discusses the arguments for Sāṃkhya doctrines and replies to rival schools, including Buddhists and Vaiśeṣikas. It also preserves quotations and views of earlier Sāṃkhya teachers like Vārṣagaṇya that are known nowhere else, so it is a key source for the history of the school.

events.title: Kūrma Purāṇa and the Īśvara Gītā
events.description: The Kūrma Purāṇa, in which Viṣṇu as a tortoise narrates to sages, took shape over several centuries from about the middle of the first millennium CE. It contains strong Pāśupata Śaiva material, including the Īśvara Gītā, a Śaiva counterpart to the Bhagavad Gītā, and the Vyāsa Gītā. Its tīrtha sections praise sacred places such as Vārāṇasī and Prayāga. Like other Purāṇas it was revised for centuries, so its parts differ in date, and scholars disagree on when its earliest layer was composed.

events.title: Vāgbhaṭa's Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya
events.description: Vāgbhaṭa, probably of Sindh in the early seventh century, condensed the teachings of Caraka and Suśruta into a single well-ordered work in verse, the Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya, "Heart of the Eight Branches" of medicine. Being easy to memorise, it became the most widely used textbook of Āyurveda, especially in Kerala, and was translated into Tibetan, Arabic and Persian.

events.title: Māmallapuram rock-cut monuments
events.description: At Māmallapuram, the Pallava port south of Chennai, granite boulders and outcrops were carved in the seventh century into temples and sculptures. Five free-standing shrines, each cut from a single rock, imitate wooden buildings of different types. A cliff face thirty metres long shows gods, sages, elephants and a cat doing penance around a cleft down which water once ran: the descent of the Gaṅgā, or Arjuna's penance.

events.title: Kumārila Bhaṭṭa
events.description: Kumārila, in the seventh century, was the most formidable defender of the Vedic tradition against Buddhism. He argued that knowledge is valid in itself unless shown to be false, that the Veda, having no author, can contain no author's errors, and that the external world is real. Legend says he studied under Buddhists in disguise to learn their arguments, and died on a slow fire in penance for deceiving his teachers.

events.title: Prabhākara Miśra
events.description: Prabhākara Miśra, called Guru, founded one of the two main schools of Pūrva Mīmāṃsā, the Prābhākara school, through his commentary the Bṛhatī on Śabara's Bhāṣya. Its distinctive teachings include the view that words convey meaning only in relation to action (anvitābhidhāna) and that all knowledge is valid in itself. It competed with the school of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, and the two views were debated for centuries. Prabhākara's date is roughly the 7th century.

events.title: Dharmakīrti and the Pramāṇavārttika
events.description: Dharmakīrti, a Buddhist scholar linked to Nālandā, wrote the Pramāṇavārttika, which builds on Dignāga's theory of knowledge. He analysed perception, inference and the nature of universals, and argued that only particulars are real. His work was highly influential in Indian and Tibetan Buddhism, and later Hindu thinkers of the Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā schools, such as Vācaspati Miśra, answered his arguments in detail. The debates show a shared logical vocabulary even when the philosophical conclusions differed.

events.title: Maṇḍana Miśra
events.description: Maṇḍana Miśra, of the seventh or early eighth century, wrote on ritual theory, the philosophy of language and Advaita. His Brahmasiddhi is an independent statement of non-dualism that differs from Śaṅkara's on several points, holding for example that ritual action can aid knowledge. He also wrote the Vidhiviveka, on Vedic injunction. Hagiography makes him Śaṅkara's defeated opponent and later disciple Sureśvara; many scholars doubt the identification.

events.title: Lakṣmaṇa temple, Sirpur
events.description: The Lakṣmaṇa temple at Sirpur in Chhattisgarh is a brick temple dedicated to Viṣṇu, built in the 7th century by Vāsaṭā, mother of the Pāṇḍuvaṃśī king Mahāśivagupta Bālārjuna. It stands out for its detailed brickwork, decorated doorway and moulded bricks, and is among the best-preserved early brick temples in India. Sirpur was the capital of Dakṣiṇa Kosala and had Buddhist and Hindu shrines in close proximity.

events.title: Aihoḷe temples of the early Cālukyas
events.description: Aihoḷe in northern Karnataka has about a hundred temples, built mostly in the 6th–8th centuries. Under the early Cālukyas, builders experimented here with different forms: flat roofs, apsidal plans and the beginnings of tower styles, drawing on northern and southern traditions. The Durgā temple has an apsidal shape and a surrounding pillared corridor. The site is called a "cradle of temple architecture" because of this variety. Its Meguti Jaina temple holds the 634 inscription of Ravikīrti.

events.title: Bhāskaravarman of Kāmarūpa
events.description: Bhāskaravarman, king of Kāmarūpa (Assam) in the early 7th century, was a Śaiva and a ruler of the Varman dynasty. He allied with Harṣa against Śaśāṅka and later welcomed the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang in 643, giving a detailed account of the kingdom. His Nidhanpur copper-plate inscription records land grants to Brahmins. He represents Kāmarūpa's growing role in political and religious life of eastern India.

events.title: Māgha's Śiśupālavadha

It became one of the most admired court epics in Sanskrit.

events.title: Kāśikā Vṛtti
events.description: The Kāśikā Vṛtti is a running commentary on Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, attributed to two authors, Jayāditya and Vāmana, and written in the 7th century. events.title: Chāhamānas of Śākambharī
events.description: The Chāhamānas, or Cauhāns, were a Rajput dynasty whose early centre was Śākambharī, near Sāmbhar lake in Rajasthan. events.title: Tirumala Veṅkaṭeśvara in early sources

It later grew into one of the richest pilgrimage sites in the world.

events.title: Ālampur Navabrahmā temples
events.description: Ālampur, on the Tuṅgabhadrā in Telangana, has a group of nine Śiva temples, the Navabrahmā temples, built under the Bādāmi Cālukyas in the 7th and 8th centuries. They are in the Nāgara style, with curved towers, though built in the south, and show the exchange between northern and southern forms. The name refers to Brahmā, the lord of creation. The site later suffered damage but was restored, and the temples are still a place of worship.

events.title: Katas Raj, Śiva's tears and the Yakṣa Praśna
events.description: Katas Raj, in the Salt Range of the Punjab in Pakistan, is a group of temples around a sacred pool. Hindus hold that the pond formed from the tears of Śiva at the death of Satī. Tradition also says that the Pāṇḍavas spent part of their exile here and that the Yakṣa Praśna, the riddle contest of the Mahābhārata, took place on its banks.¶The oldest temple, in the Satghara group, is dated to the late sixth century. Most of the others were built by the Śāhi dynasties between the mid-seventh and the tenth century and resemble Kashmiri temple architecture. The site was a major tīrtha of the northwest and is evidence of Hindu sacred geography in what is now Pakistan.

events.title: Vikramāditya I restores the Cālukyas
events.description: Vikramāditya I, who became king around 655, restored Cālukya power after the Pallava king Narasiṃhavarman I had captured the capital Vātāpi in 642 and set up a victory pillar. He recovered the territory and fought back against the Pallavas, eventually entering Kāñcī around 670. The Cālukyas remained the major power of the Deccan until the eighth century. The wars between the two kingdoms also helped spread the architecture of Bādāmi and Pallava Mahābalipuram.

events.title: Indian numerals travel west
events.description: By the seventh century, Indian positional numerals had reached the Near East. In 662 the Syriac bishop Severus Sebokht, writing in Qenneshre, praised the Hindus' method of calculation with nine signs, saying it surpassed Greek science. Around 825 the Baghdad mathematician al-Khwārizmī wrote a treatise on Indian arithmetic, which survives only in Latin translations. Through it the decimal place-value system, including zero, passed to the Arabic-speaking world and later to Europe, where it displaced Roman numerals in commercial and scientific calculation.

events.title: Mahākūṭa temple group near Bādāmi
events.description: Mahākūṭa, near Bādāmi in Karnataka, is a group of early Cālukya temples around a spring-fed pond, built in the 7th century. They are mostly dedicated to Śiva, such as the Mahākūṭeśvara and Mallikārjuna temples. The pool, fed by a natural spring, and the old shrines show how temples developed around sacred water. The site is related to those at Paṭṭadakal and Aihoḷe, where the Cālukyas tried out different architectural styles.

events.title: Sundarar and the Tiruttoṇṭattokai
events.description: Sundarar, called Cuntarar, was one of the three principal Tēvāram poets, along with Appar and Campantar. In his Tiruttoṇṭattokai, "Sacred Collection of Servants," he praises the sixty-three Nāyaṉārs, Śaiva devotees from all walks of life. The list is the basis of the later Periya Purāṇam by Cēkkiḻār (12th century), which tells each saint's story. Tradition calls Sundarar Śiva's friend. His hymns are sung in Tamil Śaiva temples.

events.title: Śaka 605 zero inscription at Sambor
events.description: An inscription found at Sambor (Trapeang Prei) in Cambodia is dated to Śaka 605, equal to 683 CE. It records a date with a dot as a zero, in the number 605, and is one of the earliest known inscriptions to show a zero in a numeral. It is evidence that Indian numerals and Sanskrit-based dating spread to Southeast Asia. Some earlier Indian examples may exist, but dated inscriptions of the 7th century are rare.

events.title: Ahirbudhnya and Lakṣmī Tantras
events.description: The Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā and the Lakṣmī Tantra are important texts of the Pāñcarātra tradition of Viṣṇu worship. The Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā teaches about Sudarśana, Viṣṇu's discus, as a divine power, and about the creation of the world. The Lakṣmī Tantra presents Lakṣmī as Viṣṇu's śakti, or active power, and is narrated by her to Indra. Their dates are uncertain: the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā is usually placed in the middle of the first millennium CE or somewhat later, and the Lakṣmī Tantra around the 9th or 10th century, though both may contain older material.

events.title: Parāśara's Horā tradition
events.description: The Bṛhat Parāśara Horāśāstra, a major text of Indian astrology, is presented as the teaching of the sage Parāśara to his disciple Maitreya. It covers planets, signs, houses, divisions of the chart and the daśā system of planetary periods. The attribution to Parāśara reflects an old tradition, but the extant text is considerably later. Its date is uncertain, though it is generally placed no earlier than the early medieval period, and it may incorporate older material. Many practitioners of Jyotiṣa still treat it as their foundational manual.

events.title: Tirumūlar's Tirumantiram
events.description: The Tirumantiram is a Tamil work of three thousand verses on yoga, the body's energy centres, mantra, ritual and the philosophy of Śiva, attributed to the yogin Tirumūlar. Its most famous lines say that the ignorant think love and God are two, while those who know see that love itself is God; and "one humanity, one God". It is the tenth book of the Tamil Śaiva canon. Scholars date it variously from about the fifth to the ninth century.

events.title: Rājasiṃha Pallava builds the Kailāsanātha
events.description: Narasiṃhavarman II, called Rājasiṃha, ruled the Pallavas around the end of the 7th and early 8th century. He built the Kailāsanātha (Rājasiṃheśvara) temple at Kāñcī and the Shore Temple at Māmallapuram, both made of cut stone blocks rather than carved from rock. These are among the earliest major structural temples in the Drāviḍa (southern) style, with the stepped tower (vimāna) that later Cōḻa builders developed on a larger scale.

events.title: The Āḻvārs and the Divya Prabandham
events.description: The twelve Āḻvārs were Tamil Vaiṣṇava poet-saints, whose hymns were later collected as the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham, about 4,000 verses, by Nāthamuni in the 10th century. Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār was among the most prolific, and Tirumaḻicai Āḻvār also composed. Their songs praise Viṣṇu as he is present in the 108 divya deśas, the temples they visited and sung. Scholars date the Āḻvārs from about the 6th to the 9th century.

events.title: Tamil bhakti of the Nāyaṉārs and Āḻvārs
events.description: The Śaiva Nāyaṉārs and Vaiṣṇava Āḻvārs composed devotional hymns in Tamil, and sang them in temples. These shifted emphasis from Vedic ritual and Sanskrit to personal devotion expressed in the regional language. The Tēvāram and Divya Prabandham were later regarded as a "Tamil Veda," and the temple became the centre of religious and social life. This movement influenced later bhakti traditions across India, including in Karnataka and Maharashtra.

events.title: Hindu and Buddhist Tantra develop together
events.description: Between about the 7th and 10th centuries, Buddhist Vajrayāna and Hindu Śaiva and Śākta tantra developed in the same regions, especially eastern India, and shared many features: goddesses and fierce deities, sacred sites called pīṭhas, mantras, maṇḍalas and yogic practices. Which tradition influenced the other is debated, though some scholars argue that Śaiva sources came first and Buddhist tantras borrowed from them. Both traditions spread to Nepal, Tibet and Southeast Asia.

events.title: Śrīvijaya maritime power rises at Palembang
events.description: Śrīvijaya was a maritime power centred at Palembang on Sumatra, with control over the Straits of Malacca and the trade between India and China. Its earliest inscription dates to 683. It was a major centre of Buddhist learning, visited by the Chinese monk Yijing, and used Sanskrit and Indian-derived scripts. Hindu elements also appear in its culture. Its influence spread Sanskritic culture, religion and art around Southeast Asia, and it remained powerful until the 11th century, when the Cōḻas attacked it.

events.title: Pāṇḍya revival under Arikesari Māravarman
events.description: Arikesari Māravarman was a Pāṇḍya king of Madurai in the seventh century, a time when the Pāṇḍyas were regaining power after the Kalabhra period. Śaiva tradition, in the Periya Purāṇam, says that the saint Tirujñānasambandar converted him from Jainism to Śaivism, after which he came to be called Neṭumāṟan. The tradition's account of conflict with the Jains is not independently confirmed. The Pāṇḍyas then expanded, and their influence in Kerala grew.

events.title: Paṭṭadakal temples of the Cālukyas
events.description: Paṭṭadakal in Karnataka, a royal consecration site of the Cālukyas, has several 8th-century temples in the northern Nāgara style, such as the Galagaṇātha, beside the southern Dravida Virūpākṣa and Saṅgameśvara temples. The Pāpanātha temple mixes both styles. This blend, which UNESCO recognised with World Heritage listing in 1987, shows the dynasty's experimenting and its links with both north and south. The site is a major reference in the history of Indian architecture.

events.title: Māsrūr rock-cut temples
events.description: At Māsrūr in Himachal Pradesh there is a group of about fifteen monolithic temples carved from a ridge of sandstone, in the Nāgara style, usually dated to the 8th century. The central temple has a Śiva shrine and sculptures of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā. The temples face the Dhauladhar range. The complex is unusual because rock-cut temples of this style are rare in North India, and was damaged by an earthquake in 1905.

events.title: Kaḻugumalai Veṭṭuvāṉ Kōyil
events.description: The Veṭṭuvāṉ Kōyil at Kaḻugumalai, in the south of Tamil Nadu, is a Pāṇḍya temple of about the eighth century, cut out of a single rock outcrop from the top down. It is unfinished, and the work was left incomplete. The monolithic technique recalls the later and much grander Kailāsa temple at Ellora. The same hill has Jaina reliefs, so Kaḻugumalai shows Hindu and Jaina art side by side in the early medieval south.

events.title: Oṇam in Tamil and Kerala sources
events.description: Oṇam, now Kerala's harvest festival connected with the return of King Mahābali, is attested early. The Tamil Saṅgam-era poem Maturaikkāñci mentions Tiruvōṇam being celebrated at Madurai, and medieval Kerala temple records mention endowments for Ōṇam observance. Tradition links the festival to Viṣṇu's Vāmana avatāra, who sent the generous Asura king Bali to the underworld but allowed him to visit his people once a year. These records show the festival's long history as a temple and community occasion.

events.title: Śāradā Pīṭha, Kashmir's seat of learning
events.description: Śāradā Pīṭha was a temple and centre of learning dedicated to Sarasvatī in the Kiṣangaṅgā valley, in what is now Pakistan-administered Kashmir. Scholars from across India travelled there, and tradition holds that those who founded great schools had to be tested in its southern door. The Kashmiri script called Śāradā takes its name from the place and was used for many manuscripts. Pilgrims long visited the site, and its ruins survive in the Nīlam valley.
