events.title: Ravigupta's Siddhasāra and Indian medical compendia
events.description: After the great Saṃhitās, Indian physicians produced shorter compendia. One of them is the Siddhasāra of Ravigupta, a compendium on medicine in verse, which was translated into Tibetan and became part of the Tibetan medical tradition. Others reached Central Asia, where fragments of Sanskrit medical manuscripts have been found. These works show how Āyurveda travelled with Buddhism and trade, and formed a base of Tibetan medicine.

events.title: Gardez Gaṇeśa consecrated by Khiṅgāla
events.description: The Gardez Gaṇeśa is a marble image of Gaṇeśa, about 61 by 36 centimetres, found at Gardez in Afghanistan and now kept in the Dargah Pir Ratan Nath temple in Kabul. A pedestal inscription in Siddhamātṛkā script records that the image was consecrated by 'Śrī Ṣāhi Khiṅgāla', king of Oḍḍiyāna. D. C. Sircar dated the inscription to the seventh century.¶The identity of Khiṅgāla is uncertain. He may be the Turk Shāhi ruler Khinkhil whom Arab sources report submitting to al-Mahdī around 775–785, while older scholarship argued for the fifth century. More recent work, based on style, favours the Turk Shāhi period. The statue is among the earliest evidence of Hindu worship under the rulers of the Kabul region.

events.title: Meruvarman's Lakṣaṇā Devī temple at Bharmour
events.description: The Lakṣaṇā Devī temple at Bharmour, in the Chamba region of Himachal Pradesh, is dedicated to Durgā as Mahiṣāsuramardinī. It is dated to the late seventh or early eighth century and was commissioned by Meruvarman, who made Bharmour (Brahmapura) the capital of Chamba; his reign is generally taken to begin about 680.¶A late-Gupta-style inscription on the pedestal of the brass image names Meruvarman and three ancestors and credits the craftsman Gugga. The wooden entrance, façade and ceiling carry Gupta-style carving with Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava motifs, including Viṣṇu on Garuḍa. The temple is one of the oldest surviving wooden-style shrines in the western Himalaya.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Muhammad bin Qāsim conquers Sindh
events.description: In 711–712 an Arab army sent by the governor of Iraq and led by the seventeen-year-old Muhammad bin Qāsim invaded Sindh by land and sea. King Dāhir, a brāhmaṇa, was killed in battle near his capital; his queen and the women of the fort burned themselves. The Arabs took the Indus valley up to Multan. Hindus and Buddhists were given the status of protected subjects on payment of the poll tax.

events.title: Multan's Sun temple spared for revenue
events.description: Arab forces under Muḥammad ibn Qāsim took Multan in 713. According to the Persian Chachnāma and Arabic chroniclers, they found large offerings in the Sun temple at Multan and chose to keep the temple intact, as pilgrims continued to bring wealth to the city. The temple's income became a source of revenue for the conquerors. The report is one of the earlier recorded instances of a temple preserved for practical reasons after conquest.

events.title: Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa, conqueror-king of Kashmir
events.description: Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa, king of Kashmir from about 724 to 760, is described in the chronicle Rājataraṅgiṇī as a world-conqueror who defeated the king of Kanauj and campaigned into Central Asia; Chinese records confirm his embassies. He built the great Sun temple of Mārtaṇḍa, whose colonnaded ruins still stand on a plateau above the valley, and a new capital with huge Viṣṇu and Buddha images.

events.title: Yaśovarman of Kanauj
events.description: Yaśovarman ruled Kānyakubja (Kanauj) in the early 8th century and was a significant northern power, sending an embassy to China. His court is associated with the dramatist Bhavabhūti and the poet Vākpatirāja, whose Prakrit poem Gauḍavaho celebrates his victory over the king of Gauḍa. He was defeated by Lalitāditya of Kashmir, according to Kalhaṇa, and his death ended a short revival of Kanauj's power.

events.title: Mārtaṇḍa Sun temple
events.description: The Mārtaṇḍa temple, near Anantnāg in Kashmir, was built to the sun god Sūrya, traditionally by Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa of the Kārkoṭa dynasty in the 8th century, according to Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī. A central shrine stands in a large courtyard surrounded by a colonnaded peristyle of small cells. Its style blends Kashmiri features with influences from Gandhāra and Gupta architecture. It lies in ruins today, which tradition and some historians ascribe to the later destruction of the temple, while others point to earthquakes.

events.title: Narasiṃhavarman II builds the Shore Temple
events.description: The Shore Temple at Māmallapuram was built by the Pallava king Narasiṃhavarman II, called Rājasiṃha, who reigned about 700 to 728. It is built of granite blocks and has two Śiva shrines, with a small shrine of the reclining Viṣṇu between them. It is one of the earliest large structural temples of South India, built of cut stone and not carved from rock as the earlier monuments at the site were.¶With Rājasiṃha's Kailāsanātha at Kāñcī, it marks the Pallava move from rock-cut to free-standing stone temples. It is part of the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, a UNESCO site since 1984. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami struck the temple but caused only limited damage, and it briefly uncovered older structures along the shore.

events.title: Nāgabhaṭa I founds the Imperial Pratihāras
events.description: Nāgabhaṭa I ruled in the early eighth century from Avanti (Ujjayinī) and the Rajasthan region. The later Gwalior inscription of Bhoja states that he stopped the advance of Arab forces coming from Sindh, around 738. The dynasty's claim to descent from Lakṣmaṇa, who guarded Rāma's door, explains the name Pratihāra, meaning doorkeeper. His successors built a large empire centred on Kanauj.

events.title: Bhavabhūti's Uttararāmacarita
events.description: Bhavabhūti's Uttararāmacarita, "Later Acts of Rāma," is a play in seven acts that dramatises the end of Rāma's story after his return to Ayodhyā, including the exile of Sītā and their reunion. Unlike Vālmīki's epic, it ends in reconciliation. It is admired for its portrayal of grief, tenderness and the psychological conflict between Rāma's duty as king and his love as husband, and Sanskrit critics see it as a high point of karuṇa rasa, the sentiment of pathos.

events.title: Nandivarman II Pallavamalla chosen king
events.description: Paramesvaravarman II of the Pallavas died without a son, and the ministers, scholars and the ghaṭikā assembly of Kāñcīpuram chose a boy of twelve from a collateral branch as king. He became Nandivarman II Pallavamalla and reigned for many decades. He faced an invasion by the Cālukya Vikramāditya II, who entered Kāñcī. Nandivarman built the Vaikuṇṭha Perumāḷ temple there, and the Vaiṣṇava saint Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār belongs to his period.

events.title: Sañjaya's Canggal inscription
events.description: The Canggal inscription, from the Gunung Wukir hill in central Java and dated 732 CE, is in Sanskrit. It records that the king Sañjaya set up a Śiva liṅga on the hill, and praises Java as an island rich in grain and gold. The inscription also invokes Śiva, Brahmā and Viṣṇu. It is regarded as marking the early Mataram kingdom as a Śaiva realm, and shows the spread of Sanskrit and Śaiva religion into Java.

events.title: Bappā Rāval and Mewar
events.description: Bappā Rāval, of the eighth century, is the founding hero of Mewar. Legend says he was a herd-boy who served a Śaiva hermit in the forest near Nāgdā and received from him the kingdom. He took the fortress of Chittor and built the temple of Ekaliṅga, a four-faced form of Śiva. Ever since, the god has been held to be Mewar's real king and the Mahārāṇā only his minister.

events.title: Delhi founded as Ḍhillikā
events.description: Local tradition and later bardic chronicles say that Delhi was first established in 736 by the Tomara king Anaṅgapāla I, under the name Ḍhillikā. Historians treat the early date with caution, as the Tomara records are later. The Tomaras are better attested in the eleventh century, and Anaṅgapāla II is credited with building the fort of Lāl Koṭ around 1052. The Cauhāns took the city from the Tomaras, and it later became the centre of the Sultanate.

events.title: Battle of Rājasthān against the Arabs
events.description: After taking Sindh, Arab governors raided deep into Rajasthan and Gujarat in the 720s and 730s. They were beaten back by several Indian rulers: Nāgabhaṭa I of the Pratihāras, who "crushed the army of the powerful barbarian king", the Cālukya governor of southern Gujarat, whose grant of 739 describes the fight, and by tradition Bappā Rāval of Mewar. Arab power stayed confined to Sindh for three centuries.

events.title: Vikramāditya II and Virūpākṣa temple
events.description: After Vikramāditya II of the Cālukyas defeated the Pallava ruler of Kāñcī in about 740, his queen Lokamahādevī built the Virūpākṣa temple at Paṭṭadakal to commemorate the victory. The design draws on the Kailāsanātha at Kāñcī, and Pallava sculptors are said to have worked on it. It is one of the largest early temples of Karnataka and part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It later inspired the Kailāsa temple at Ellora.

events.title: Pāla dynasty founded
events.description: After a century the Bengali sources call "the law of fishes", where the big eat the small, the chiefs of Bengal about 750 chose one of themselves, Gopāla, as king. His dynasty ruled Bengal and Bihar for four hundred years. The Pālas were Buddhists and revived Nālandā and founded Vikramaśīlā, yet their ministers were brāhmaṇas and their grants endowed Śiva and Viṣṇu temples.

events.title: Ellora's Hindu caves
events.description: At Ellora in Maharashtra, caves of Hindu, Buddhist and Jaina traditions stand side by side. The Hindu caves include the Rāmeśvara cave, the Daśāvatāra cave and the Dhūmar Leṇa, and have large panels of Śiva and Viṣṇu. Famous scenes include Rāvaṇa shaking Mount Kailāsa (Rāvaṇānugraha) and Śiva's marriage to Pārvatī (Kalyāṇasundara). The nearby Kailāsa temple, carved from a single rock under the Rāṣṭrakūṭas, is the greatest of these works.

events.title: Vaikuṇṭha Perumāḷ temple
events.description: The Vaikuṇṭha Perumāḷ temple at Kāñcī was built by the Pallava king Nandivarman II Pallavamalla in the mid-8th century. It is a Viṣṇu temple with a processional corridor around its sanctum, and its inner walls carry a series of sculpted panels that depict the history of the Pallava dynasty, including the scene of Nandivarman's own selection as king. It is therefore a rare case of a temple that doubles as a visual chronicle of a royal house.

events.title: Āṇḍāḷ's Tiruppāvai
events.description: According to tradition, Āṇḍāḷ was found as a baby in a basil garden by the temple priest and poet Periyāḻvār. As a girl she secretly wore the garlands meant for the deity; when her father found out, the god is said to have declared that he preferred them so. She refused any human husband. Her thirty-verse Tiruppāvai, in which girls wake one another before dawn to go and worship Kṛṣṇa, is sung in Vaiṣṇava homes and temples throughout the month of Mārgaḻi.

events.title: Periyāḻvār and Kulaśekhara
events.description: Periyāḻvār (Viṣṇucitta) was a Tamil Vaiṣṇava saint of Śrīvilliputtūr, known for hymns in which he takes on the voice of Yaśodā, singing lullabies and describing the childhood pranks of the infant Kṛṣṇa. He was also the foster father of Āṇḍāḷ. Kulaśekhara, a Cēra king, wrote the Tamil Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi and the Sanskrit devotional poem Mukundamālā. Both are numbered among the twelve Āḻvārs and show that royal and humble devotees shared the same movement.

events.title: Agni and Garuḍa Purāṇas
events.description: The Agni Purāṇa, presented as Agni's teaching to the sage Vasiṣṭha, is a Purāṇic encyclopedia that covers worship and temple building along with poetics, grammar, medicine, warfare, and statecraft. The Garuḍa Purāṇa, framed as Viṣṇu's teaching to Garuḍa, includes sections on gemmology, medicine and astrology, and a part on death and the afterlife, the Preta Khaṇḍa, which is recited at funeral rites. Both works show the Purāṇas serving as general reference books.

events.title: Liṅga and Kūrma Purāṇas
events.description: The Liṅga Purāṇa is a Śaiva text that explains the meaning of the liṅga, tells the Liṅgodbhava myth, and describes Śiva's forms and the rites of his worship. The Kūrma Purāṇa is told by Viṣṇu in the form of a tortoise, but its second part is strongly Śaiva and includes the Īśvara Gītā, a teaching of Śiva on knowledge and yoga, and shows the influence of the Pāśupata tradition. Both works are examples of how Śaiva ideas entered the Purāṇic corpus.

events.title: Paśupatinātha in Licchavi Nepal
events.description: The Paśupatinātha temple on the Bāgmatī river in Kathmandu is a major Śaiva shrine. Licchavi-period inscriptions, such as that of Jayadeva II dated 733, praise Paśupati as the guardian lord of the valley, and the kings are said to rule under his protection. The site is thus attested as a central religious centre in the 8th century, though the existing buildings are much later. It has been a pilgrimage site for Hindus from across the subcontinent.

events.title: Bhauma-karas of Toṣalī
events.description: The Bhauma-kara dynasty ruled much of Odisha from Toṣalī in the eighth to tenth centuries. Its early kings supported Buddhism, and the monasteries of Ratnagiri, Udayagiri and Lalitagiri flourished, while later rulers favoured Śiva and Viṣṇu. Unusually, several women ruled in their own right, including Tribhuvana Mahādevī. Their copper-plate grants record these queens as sovereigns, a rare case in early Indian history.

events.title: Śālikanātha's Prakaraṇapañcikā
events.description: Śālikanātha Miśra was a leading thinker of the Prābhākara school of Pūrva Mīmāṃsā, which follows Prabhākara. His Prakaraṇapañcikā, "the five-chapter treatise", is a concise manual of the school's doctrines, setting out its theory of knowledge and its view of Vedic injunction. It is regarded as the standard introduction to the Prābhākara system. He also wrote a commentary on Prabhākara's work, the Ṛjuvimalā.

events.title: Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā commentators Umbeka and Pārthasārathi
events.description: Umbeka and Pārthasārathi Miśra were commentators of the Bhāṭṭa school of Mīmāṃsā, which follows Kumārila Bhaṭṭa. Umbeka wrote a commentary on Kumārila's Ślokavārttika. Pārthasārathi Miśra, who is generally placed a few centuries later, wrote the Śāstradīpikā, which became the school's standard textbook. Mithilā was a centre of the Bhāṭṭa tradition. These works kept Kumārila's arguments for the authority of the Veda in use.

events.title: Śaṅkarācārya Temple on Gopādri hill
events.description: The hill known as Gopādri, above Śrīnagar, carries an old Śiva temple, called Jyeṣṭheśvara, now also known as the Śaṅkarācārya temple. Kalhaṇa's chronicle and later tradition attribute early building to Gopāditya and later work to other rulers, and the present stone structure rests on a high octagonal base. Tradition also says Śaṅkara visited the hill. Its history in the 8th century is uncertain, and the temple has been rebuilt more than once.

events.title: Haribhadra Sūri's Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya
events.description: Haribhadra Sūri was a Jaina monk and scholar, traditionally associated with Chittor in Rajasthan, who wrote on logic, doctrine and yoga. His Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya summarises six philosophical systems, which in his account include Bauddha, Nyāya, Sāṅkhya, Jaina, Vaiśeṣika and Jaiminīya, with notable fairness and without polemic. He also wrote the Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya, comparing Jaina stages with the yoga of Patañjali and others. His work is an early model of presenting rival schools in their own terms.

events.title: Pañcatantra becomes Kalīla wa Dimna
events.description: The Pañcatantra, the Sanskrit collection of animal fables, was translated into Middle Persian (Pahlavi) around 570 by the physician Burzoy for the Sasanian king Khusrow I. In about 750, Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ rendered it into Arabic from the Pahlavi as Kalīla wa Dimna, named after two jackal characters. From Arabic it passed into Syriac, Greek, Hebrew and Latin, and then into European languages, so Indian fables reached storytellers across Eurasia.

events.title: Rāṣṭrakūṭas overthrow the Cālukyas
events.description: Dantidurga, a Rāṣṭrakūṭa feudatory of the Cālukyas, defeated Kīrtivarman II in about 753 and took control of the Deccan. His inscriptions say he performed a ritual called Hiraṇyagarbha at Ujjayinī. The dynasty ruled from Mānyakheṭa (Malkhed) for around two centuries, fought for Kanauj with the Pālas and Pratihāras, and built the Kailāsa temple at Ellora. They also patronised Jaina and Kannada literature.

events.title: Kailāsa temple, Ellora
events.description: The Kailāsa at Ellora is not built but carved. Around 760 CE, under the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Kṛṣṇa I, workers cut three trenches into a basalt hillside and then sculpted the isolated block from the top down into a complete temple: gateway, Nandī pavilion, pillared hall and a tower thirty metres high.¶An estimated 200,000 tonnes of rock were removed, with no scaffolding and no room for error. An old inscription has its own architect marvel, "How was it that I made this?" It represents Mount Kailāsa, the home of Śiva.

events.title: Dharmapāla and the tripartite struggle
events.description: Dharmapāla of the Pāla dynasty (r. c. 770–810) ruled Bengal and Bihar and was a patron of Buddhism, founding the Vikramaśīla monastery. He fought the Gurjara-Pratihāras of western India and the Rāṣṭrakūṭas of the Deccan for control of Kanauj, the symbol of supremacy over the Gaṅgā plain. This three-way contest, known as the tripartite struggle, continued for about two centuries and exhausted all three powers, while Kanauj changed hands several times.

gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.

events.title: The Sindhind reaches Baghdad
events.description: Arabic sources, notably the later writer al-Qifṭī, report that around 770 a traveller from India brought to the court of the Abbasid caliph al-Manṣūr in Baghdad a text on astronomy and mathematics, which the court astronomer Muḥammad al-Fazārī translated into Arabic as the Sindhind. It is usually linked with an Indian siddhānta, perhaps Brahmagupta's work. This translation helped Arabic astronomers learn Indian methods, including sine tables and planetary computation, and fed into the later tradition of Arabic zījes.

events.title: Naresar and Baṭeśvar temple groups
events.description: Near Morenā in Madhya Pradesh, the Pratihāra period left clusters of small sandstone temples. Naresar and Baṭeśvar hold hundreds of them, mostly Śiva and Viṣṇu shrines, built over the 8th to 10th centuries in the Nāgara style. Many collapsed in earlier centuries and lay in ruins. From 2005 the Archaeological Survey of India began reassembling the Baṭeśvar group, rebuilding the temples from scattered stones, which gave back a landscape once thought lost.

events.title: Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār and the Periya Tirumoḻi
events.description: Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār, born Kaliyan at Tirukkuraiyalūr near Sīrkāḻi, was a Vaiṣṇava poet-saint, also called Parakāla and Tirumaṅgai Maṉṉaṉ. Tradition dates him to a remote age, but modern scholars place him between the seventh and ninth centuries, and a date about 776 is often given. He is generally thought a contemporary of the Pallava king Nandivarman II (731–796), whom his hymns refer to.¶His six works total about 1,361 verses and the Periya Tirumoḻi, with 1,084 hymns, is the largest. The tradition holds that he visited 88 of the 108 Divya Deśams, and his hymns praise over forty forms of Viṣṇu, from Badrinath in the north to Tirukkurungudi in the south.

events.title: Pāṇḍya rock-cut cave at Tirupparaṅkuṉṟam
events.description: Tirupparaṅkuṉṟam, near Madurai, has a rock-cut cave temple at the foot of a hill, and its earliest layer is dated to the early Pāṇḍya period of the eighth century. The reliefs include Śiva as Naṭarāja and Ardhanārīśvara, a ten-armed Gaṇeśa, and Subrahmaṇya with his peacock; Kālī and Nandi also appear. A long inscription on the east wall of the maṇḍapa is attributed to the later king Māravarman Sundara Pāṇḍya (1216–1239).¶The cave is next to the Murugan temple, one of the six sacred abodes of Murugan, which grew at the northern foot of the hill between the seventh and fifteenth centuries. The cave belongs to the group of early Pāṇḍya rock-cut shrines and shows the layered use of a single sacred hill over some five hundred years.

events.title: Kalasan and the Śailendras
events.description: The Kalasan temple, dated to 778, was built in central Java for the Buddhist goddess Tārā, and the Śailendra dynasty was associated with the great Buddhist monument Borobudur. The same region, however, saw Hindu temples constructed, including the Śiva complex of Prambanan in the ninth century. Hindu and Buddhist monuments stood side by side in Java, patronised by related ruling families, and scholars debate how far the two communities were rivals or partners in the kingdom's religious life.

events.title: Dieng plateau temples
events.description: The Dieng plateau in central Java has small stone temples that are among the earliest on the island, dated to about the late eighth and ninth centuries. They are Hindu shrines, devoted to Śiva, and are known by names from the Mahābhārata, such as Arjuna, Bhīma, Puntadewa and Sembadra, although these names were given in later times and do not reflect the original dedications. The plateau was a sacred highland, and its temples demonstrate how Indian temple forms were adapted in Java.

gitaQuote.verse: अहमेवाक्षयः कालो धाताहं विश्वतोमुखः ॥ कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो लोकान्समाहर्तुमिह प्रवृत्तः ॥

gitaQuote.translation: I alone am inexhaustible, imperishable Time (Akṣaya Kāla), and I am the dispenser of destiny facing all directions... I am all-destroying Time, grown mighty to extinguish the worlds.
gitaQuote.source: Mahabharata (Bhishma Parva 35.32); Abhinavagupta Gītārtha-Saṁgraha

events.title: Dhruva Dhārāvarṣa campaigns in the north
events.description: Dhruva was a Rāṣṭrakūṭa king of the Deccan who ruled in the later eighth century. In the contest for control of Kanauj, which involved the Pratihāras of the west and the Pālas of the east, he defeated both Vatsarāja and Dharmapāla and carried his army to the Gaṅgā–Yamunā doab. Later Rāṣṭrakūṭa records show the rivers Gaṅgā and Yamunā as their emblems after this. The raid showed that a Deccan power could intervene in the north, and it began a long rivalry.

events.title: Vatsarāja and Nāgabhaṭa II
events.description: The Gurjara-Pratihāras rose in western India and Rajasthan. Vatsarāja fought for Kanauj but was defeated by the Rāṣṭrakūṭas, while his son Nāgabhaṭa II captured Kanauj in about 816. Earlier, Nāgabhaṭa I is credited in Pratihāra records with halting Arab forces advancing from Sindh. Because of this, the Pratihāras are often seen as having defended the north from Arab expansion for some time. Under later rulers, such as Mihira Bhoja, they became the leading power of northern India.

events.title: Śāntarakṣita's Tattvasaṅgraha
events.description: Śāntarakṣita was a Buddhist philosopher at Nālandā who later went to Tibet and helped found Samyé monastery. His Tattvasaṅgraha, a long verse treatise with a commentary by his student Kamalaśīla, surveys and criticises the doctrines of many schools, including Sāṅkhya, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā and Jaina views. Because it states the opponents' arguments in detail, including Hindu philosophers whose works are now lost or only partly preserved, it is a major source for the history of Indian philosophy.

events.title: Satyavarman restores Po Nagar at Kauthara
events.description: At Po Nagar, near Nha Trang in Vietnam, the Cham temple honoured Yan Po Nagar, the goddess identified in the inscriptions with Bhagavatī. Stele inscriptions record that raiders, perhaps from Java, carried off the temple's jewels and broke the liṅga, and that King Satyavarman of Kauthara restored it. They date to 781 and 784.¶The surviving brick towers were built later, between about the tenth and thirteenth centuries, and the main tower is about 25 metres high. The temple is an example of Cham devotion to Śiva and the goddess in the Indianised kingdoms of coastal Vietnam. Vietnamese settlers took over the temple in the seventeenth century, and it is still a place of worship.

events.title: Birth of Ādi Śaṅkarācārya
events.description: Śaṅkara was born at Kālaḍi in Kerala to a Nambūtiri brāhmaṇa couple. The traditional dates are 788–820 CE; many modern scholars prefer about 700–750, and some monastic lineages claim dates centuries earlier.¶The accounts of his life come from hagiographies written long after. They say he lost his father early, mastered the Vedas as a child, and at eight persuaded his mother to let him renounce the world. In a life of only thirty-two years he is credited with reviving Vedic religion by argument alone, walking the length of India to do it.

events.title: Govinda III Rāṣṭrakūṭa
events.description: Govinda III (r. 793–814) was one of the strongest Rāṣṭrakūṭa rulers. He defeated the Pratihāra Nāgabhaṭa II and the Pāla Dharmapāla and led campaigns across the north. Inscriptions claim that his horses drank the icy waters of the Himalaya, a poetic way of recording that his armies had reached the mountains. He also campaigned in the south against the Pallavas and others. His reign marks the high point of Rāṣṭrakūṭa power.

events.title: Śaṅkara takes saṃnyāsa and finds Govindapāda
events.description: Śaṅkara, the Advaita teacher, is placed by most scholars in the 8th century; the traditional dates used here differ. Hagiographies such as the Śaṅkaradigvijaya say that he was born at Kālaṭi in Kerala and, as a child, obtained his mother's permission to renounce the world. He then travelled north to the Narmadā, near Oṃkāreśvara, and became the disciple of Govinda Bhagavatpāda, who was in turn a pupil of Gauḍapāda, author of the Māṇḍūkya Kārikā. This account is traditional rather than documented.

events.title: Śilpa texts: Mānasāra and Mayamata
events.description: The Mānasāra and Mayamata are Sanskrit śilpa-śāstras, treatises on architecture and image-making, associated with the south. They deal with town planning, building temples and houses, proportions of images and the rules of sculpture. The Mayamata is traditionally linked to Maya, the divine architect, and the Mānasāra to a sage called Mānasāra. Both were compiled over centuries, and scholars place them roughly between the 6th and 12th centuries. They are used in the study of South Indian temple building and in traditional practice.

events.title: Kāmākhyā temple on Nīlācala hill
events.description: On a hill above the Brahmaputra at Guwahati stands the temple of Kāmākhyā, where the Goddess is worshipped not as an image but as a cleft in the rock kept moist by a spring. Tradition says Satī's womb fell here, and it is counted among the foremost seats of the Goddess and a major centre of Tantric practice. The oldest remains are usually placed in the 8th–9th centuries, and the present temple was rebuilt in 1565 under the Koch king Naranarayana. Each June the temple closes for three days during the Ambubācī festival, when the Goddess is held to menstruate, and a great fair follows.

events.title: Pramāṇa debates in Kashmir
events.description: Kashmir was a major centre of Indian logic and epistemology in the later first millennium. Buddhist thinkers such as Dharmottara, who commented on Dharmakīrti's work, and Śaṅkaranandana worked there, alongside Hindu logicians such as Jayanta Bhaṭṭa, author of the Nyāyamañjarī. They debated the nature of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), perception and inference. The exchange sharpened arguments on both sides.

events.title: Bhāskara's Bhedābheda Vedānta
events.description: Bhāskara wrote a commentary on the Brahma Sūtras in about the eighth or ninth century. He teaches bhedābheda, that Brahman is both different and non-different from the world and souls. He criticised Śaṅkara's doctrine of māyā, charging that it resembled Buddhist thought, and held that the world is a real transformation of Brahman. He also rejected the idea that renunciation alone leads to liberation, arguing for combining ritual action with knowledge.

events.title: First Pāṇḍya empire expands in the far south
events.description: The Pāṇḍyas of Madurai rose again in the later part of the eighth century, and the first Pāṇḍya empire expanded across the far south. Śrīmāra Śrīvallabha (c. 815–862) is remembered for invading Sri Lanka, and Varaguṇa II also ruled in this period. The Śaiva saint Māṇikkavācakar, author of the Tiruvācakam, is traditionally linked to a Pāṇḍya king, and some scholars connect him with Varaguṇa, though his dates are uncertain. The empire fell to Cōḻa expansion in the tenth century.

events.title: Śaṅkara's Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya
events.description: Śaṅkara's commentary on the Brahma Sūtra is the central text of Advaita Vedānta. It opens by observing that we constantly confuse the self with what is not the self, saying "I am thin" or "I am blind". That confusion is ignorance, and it has no beginning. The Upaniṣads remove it, as light removes the snake imagined in a rope. Brahman alone is real; the world is appearance; the individual is none other than Brahman.

events.title: Teli-kā-Mandir, Gwalior
events.description: The Teli-kā-Mandir stands in Gwalior fort and was built in the Pratihāra period, around the 8th–9th century. It is unusual in combining a northern curvilinear-style entrance with a tall rectangular roof in the form of a barrel or wagon vault, a form usually found in southern gateways. Its dedication, to Viṣṇu, Śiva or a goddess, is debated. It is one of the larger early temples of the region, with fine carvings of river goddesses and Garuḍa on its doorway.

events.title: Osian temples of the Pratihāra period
events.description: Osian, in the Thar desert near Jodhpur, has a group of temples built under the Pratihāras between the 8th and 10th centuries. They include shrines to Harihara (the combined form of Viṣṇu and Śiva), to Sūrya and to the goddess Saciyā Mātā, as well as a Jaina temple to Mahāvīra. The site is one of the earliest in Rajasthan with a sequence of temples in the northern Nāgara style and is important for studying the early evolution of that style. Osian was also a trading town.

events.title: Jageśvara and Baijnāth temple groups
events.description: In the Kumaon Himalaya, the Katyūrī dynasty, which ruled from places such as Baijnāth (ancient Kārttikeyapura), is associated with clusters of stone temples at Jageśvara and Baijnāth. events.title: Paraśurāmeśvara and Vaitāl Deul
events.description: Bhubaneśvara, in Odisha, has hundreds of temples from the 7th century on. The Paraśurāmeśvara temple (7th century) is among the earliest and best preserved, with a curved tower and finely carved walls. The Vaitāl Deul (8th century) has a wagon-vault roof, an arrangement more often seen in the south, and enshrines the goddess Cāmuṇḍā (Caṇḍī), whose imagery of a skeletal figure with jackals and corpses reflects tantric traditions. Both show the early Kaliṅga style.

events.title: Matsyendranātha and the Kaula tradition
events.description: Matsyendra, "lord of the fish", is the first human teacher of the Nātha yogīs and one of the eighty-four Siddhas honoured by Hindus and Buddhists alike. Legend says he overheard Śiva teaching yoga to Pārvatī while inside the belly of a fish. He is linked with Assam and Bengal around the ninth or tenth century and with the Kaula stream of Tantra. In Nepal he is worshipped as the rain-giving Macchendranāth.

events.title: Mālinīvijayottara Tantra of Kashmiri Trika
events.description: The Mālinīvijayottara Tantra is considered the chief scripture of Kashmiri Trika Śaivism. Trika, "the triad," refers to a system of three powers and goddesses, Parā, Parāparā and Aparā, as well as the triple division of Śiva, śakti and the individual soul. Abhinavagupta relies heavily on this text in his Tantrāloka. It combines teaching about ritual, yoga and non-dual philosophy, and presents Śiva as supreme reality.

events.title: The Krama tradition of twelve Kālīs
events.description: The Krama, or "sequence," tradition is a Kashmiri Śākta-Śaiva system in which the goddess is worshipped in a series of twelve Kālīs, representing stages through which consciousness creates, sustains and dissolves experience, ending in a transcendent state. It is traditionally connected with Oḍḍiyāna (the Swat valley) and developed in Kashmir, where the teachers Jñānanetra and Śivānanda are named. Abhinavagupta, who also studied Krama, incorporated its ideas.

events.title: Kāpālikas and Kālāmukhas
events.description: The Kāpālikas were Śaiva ascetics who carried a skull-bowl, smeared themselves with ash and lived in cremation grounds, imitating Śiva's penance for beheading Brahmā. They are mostly known from hostile or satirical portrayals in Sanskrit plays and from Buddhist and Brahmanical critics, so their actual practice is uncertain. The Kālāmukhas, a Śaiva order in Karnataka, ran temples and monasteries and taught philosophy. Both belong to the Atimārga, a stage of ascetic Śaivism before the Mantramārga.

events.title: Śrīvidyā and the Lalitā Sahasranāma
events.description: Śrīvidyā is the tradition that worships the Goddess as Lalitā Tripurasundarī, "the beautiful one of the three cities", through a fifteen-syllable mantra and the Śrīcakra, a diagram of nine interlocking triangles. events.title: Mādhavakara's Nidāna
events.description: Mādhavakara's Rugviniścaya, known as the Mādhava Nidāna, deals with diagnosis. It is a systematic work that lists diseases, their causes, early signs, symptoms and course, and drew on the Caraka and Suśruta Saṃhitās. It became a standard Āyurvedic textbook for diagnosis and was translated into Arabic. The author is usually placed in the 7th–8th century, and he is traditionally associated with Bengal.

events.title: Śilāhāras of the Koṅkaṇa
events.description: The Śilāhāras were a family of feudatories who ruled the Koṅkaṇa coast from the later Rāṣṭrakūṭa age onward. Historians distinguish three branches, in the northern Koṅkaṇa around Ṭhāṇe, in the south Koṅkaṇa and Goa, and in the Kolhāpur region. They were Śaiva and patronised temples and Sanskrit and Marathi writing. The Ambarnāth Śiva temple near Kalyāṇ, completed in 1060, is their best-known surviving monument, with fine sculpture in the Bhūmija style.

events.title: Toṭakācārya and Hastāmalaka
events.description: Tradition counts Toṭaka and Hastāmalaka among Śaṅkara's chief disciples. The Toṭakāṣṭaka is a set of eight verses in praise of the guru that is attributed to Toṭaka. The Hastāmalakīya, attributed to Hastāmalaka, is a brief poem that likens knowledge of the self to a fruit held in the palm. According to the monastic tradition, Toṭaka led the Jyotirmaṭh and Hastāmalaka the seat at Dvārakā, but scholars question the attributions.

events.title: Pāśupata temples at Pāvāgaḍh and Ekaliṅgajī
events.description: The Pāśupatas were a Śaiva ascetic order traced to Lakulīśa, and they flourished in Gujarat and Rajasthan in the early medieval period. A Lakulīśa temple stands at Pāvāgaḍh, while Ekaliṅgajī near Udaipur became the family temple of the Mewar kings, who are the "Dīwān" (steward) of the deity. An inscription at Ekaliṅgajī dated 971 gives the line of Pāśupata teachers at the site. These records document the order's influence on temples.

gitaQuote.verse: पिताहमस्य जगतो माता धाता पितामहः । वेद्यं पवित्रमोंकार ऋक्साम यजुरेव च ॥ गतिर्भर्ता प्रभुः साक्षी निवासः शरणं सुहृत् । प्रभवः प्रलयः स्थानं निधानं बीजमव्ययम् ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ | vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛk sāma yajur eva ca || gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt | prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||
gitaQuote.translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer and the grandsire. I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the creation and dissolution, the foundation and the imperishable seed.

events.title: Jayarāśi and the Tattvopaplavasiṃha
events.description: The Tattvopaplavasiṃha, "The Lion that Overturns All Principles", by Jayarāśi Bhaṭṭa, is a work of radical scepticism that attacks the means of knowledge, such as perception and inference, accepted by the other schools. It is the only surviving text generally linked to the Lokāyata or Cārvāka tradition, which is otherwise known mainly through its opponents' reports. It is usually dated to about the eighth or ninth century. Scholars debate whether Jayarāśi was a pure sceptic or a materialist, but the text shows the range of debate in India.

events.title: Caraka and Suśruta in Arabic
events.description: The Barmakids were a powerful family of viziers under the early Abbasid caliphs. Their ancestors, according to tradition, had been hereditary heads of the Nava Vihāra, a Buddhist monastery at Balkh. Around 800 they sponsored the translation of Indian medical works, including the texts of Caraka and Suśruta, into Arabic, and brought Indian physicians to Baghdad. The Barmakids fell from favour in 803, but the translations contributed to Arabic medicine.

events.title: Gedong Songo temples on Mount Ungaran
events.description: The Gedong Songo group lies on a hillside of about 1,270 metres near Mount Ungaran in Central Java. The scholars Williams and Dumarcay and others date the temples to roughly 780–830, in the time of the early Mataram kingdom; the wider range is the eighth to ninth century. The temples are Hindu, dedicated to Śiva and Pārvatī, and Temple III has a Nandi shrine paired with it.¶Five temple groups, with nine temples in all, survive, though the count is higher if the groups lower on the slope are included. Dutch scholars rediscovered the site in the nineteenth century. Placed high on a mountain, they recall the Indian idea of the hill as the home of Śiva.

events.title: Unakoti's rock-cut Śiva reliefs
events.description: Unakoti, or Subrai Khung, near Kailāśahar in Tripura, is a Śaiva site of rock carvings in the forest. The central relief, called Unakoṭīśvara Kāla Bhairava, is a head of Śiva about 30 feet high, including a 10-foot headdress. On the grounds of style the reliefs are placed in the seventh to ninth century, before the rule of the Māṇikya kings.¶Local tradition says that Śiva halted here with 99,99,999 gods on the way to Kāśī and, when none rose before dawn, turned them to stone. Another account says a sculptor, Kallu Gurjar, was told to carve a crore of figures in one night and fell one short, which gave the place its name. The legends are not evidence of dating, but they show how the site is remembered.

events.title: Encounter with the caṇḍāla at Kāśī
events.description: According to tradition, as Śaṅkara went to bathe in the Gaṅgā at Kāśī, he met a caṇḍāla, an outcaste, with four dogs, and asked him to move aside. The man replied by asking whether Śaṅkara meant the body or the self, since the self in both is the same. Śaṅkara realised the man was Śiva himself and composed five verses, the Manīṣā Pañcakam, declaring that anyone who knows the non-dual truth, whether of high or low birth, is his guru. The story is hagiographical.

events.title: Jayavarman II founds the Khmer Empire
events.description: In 802, on Mount Kulen north of the great lake of Cambodia, a king named Jayavarman had himself consecrated universal monarch by a brāhmaṇa in a rite that declared the country free of Javanese overlordship. A later inscription describes the ceremony and the royal Śiva-liṅga it established. The Khmer kingdom he founded lasted over six centuries and built Angkor.

events.title: Śaṅkara meets Kumārila at Prayāga
events.description: The hagiographies tell that Śaṅkara came to Prayāga seeking Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, the great Mīmāṃsā philosopher, and found him dying on a fire of husks as penance. Kumārila said he could not debate but directed Śaṅkara to Maṇḍana Miśra, his follower, at Māhiṣmatī. Historians note that Kumārila is generally dated earlier than Śaṅkara or as an older contemporary, so the meeting is regarded as legend, though the story reflects the real rivalry between Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta.

events.title: Śaṅkara–Maṇḍana Miśra debate
events.description: The most famous debate in Hindu tradition. Maṇḍana Miśra was the leading Mīmāṃsaka of his day, holding that the Veda's purpose is ritual action. Śaṅkara held that its purpose is knowledge of Brahman, which ends all action. They agreed that the loser would adopt the winner's way of life.¶Maṇḍana's wife, the scholar Ubhaya Bhāratī, was accepted by both as judge. After many days she declared her husband defeated; he became a monk, identified by tradition with Śaṅkara's disciple Sureśvara. The story comes from the Śaṅkara-digvijaya hagiographies of the 14th century and later, not from contemporary record, but it preserves a real philosophical divide.

events.title: Ubhaya Bhāratī challenges Śaṅkara
events.description: In the biographies, Śaṅkara debated Maṇḍana Miśra at Māhiṣmatī, and Maṇḍana's wife Ubhaya Bhāratī served as judge. When Maṇḍana was defeated and agreed to become a monk, she took up the debate herself and asked questions on kāmaśāstra, the science of love, about which a celibate monk knew nothing. Śaṅkara asked for time and, tradition says, entered the body of a dead king named Amaruka to gain experience, returning to answer her. The story is legend, but it features one of the notable women in Indian philosophical debate.

events.title: Four Āmnāya Maṭhas founded
events.description: Tradition credits Śaṅkara with founding four monasteries at the corners of India: Śṛṅgeri in the south, Dvārakā in the west, Purī in the east and Jyotirmaṭha in the north. Each was given one Veda, one "great saying" of the Upaniṣads, and one of his chief disciples as its first head.¶Their heads are still called Śaṅkarācārya. The idea of a pan-Indian network of monks, modelled partly on Buddhist monasteries, gave Advaita an institution that outlived kingdoms. Historians note that firm records for the maṭhas begin several centuries after Śaṅkara.

events.title: Devapāla of the Pāla dynasty
events.description: Devapāla was the second great Pāla king of Bengal and Bihar and ruled in the first half of the ninth century. Pāla inscriptions credit him with victories reaching from Assam and Odisha to the north-western frontier, though these claims are partly conventional praise. He supported the Buddhist monasteries at Nālandā and Vikramaśilā, and a Śailendra king of Suvarṇadvīpa asked him for land for a monastery at Nālandā. The Pāla court also gave grants to brāhmaṇas.

events.title: Daśanāmī order organised
events.description: The largest order of Hindu monks traces itself to Śaṅkara. Its members bear one of ten names after their own, such as Sarasvatī, Bhāratī, Tīrtha, Purī or Giri, and each name is attached to one of the four great monasteries. They carry a staff, wear ochre and take vows of poverty and celibacy. The order includes scholars and also the armed Nāgā regiments seen at the Kumbha.

events.title: Amoghavarṣa I rules the Rāṣṭrakūṭa empire
events.description: Amoghavarṣa I ruled the Rāṣṭrakūṭa empire from Mānyakheṭa for over sixty years, from 814. He is remembered as a patron of scholars and as a Jaina by inclination, with the monk Jinasena as a teacher, though his realm supported many faiths. The Kavirājamārga, the earliest surviving work on Kannada poetics, is associated with his court and is attributed to him or to Śrīvijaya. Mathematician Mahāvīra also worked under him. His reign was long, though marked by revolts.

events.title: Ṣaṇmata and pañcāyatana worship
events.description: Smārta tradition holds that Śaṅkara reconciled six rival cults, those of Śiva, Viṣṇu, the Goddess, the Sun, Gaṇeśa and Skanda, by teaching that each deity is a form of the one Brahman, so that a person may worship a chosen one without denying the others. In the household rite derived from this, five small symbols are worshipped together with the favourite placed in the centre.

events.title: Śaṅkara ascends the Sarvajña Pīṭha
events.description: The Śāradā temple in Kashmir is said in tradition to have had four doors, of which the southern was closed because no scholar from the south had ever been accepted there. Śaṅkara is reported to have debated the learned men of the other three directions and, having defeated them, opened the southern door and ascended the Sarvajña Pīṭha, the seat of the all-knowing. The story expresses Kashmir's reputation as a centre of learning. The Śāradā Pīṭha site now lies in Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

events.title: Hymns and prakaraṇas attributed to Śaṅkara
events.description: Many short devotional hymns and independent teaching texts are traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara, such as the Bhaja Govindam, Saundaryalaharī, Vivekacūḍāmaṇi and Ātmabodha. Modern scholarship doubts that most were composed by the author of the commentaries on the Brahma Sūtra, Upaniṣads and Gītā. Of the independent works, only the Upadeśasāhasrī, a work of teaching in verse and prose, is generally accepted as his. Even so, the attributed works have shaped Advaita devotion and teaching.

gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.

events.title: Śaṅkara's mahāsamādhi at Kedāranātha
events.description: Most accounts say that Śaṅkara, aged thirty-two, walked into the Himalaya behind the temple of Kedāranātha and was not seen again. The monastery at Kāñcī holds instead that he ended his days at Kāñcī. In either case his life as tradition tells it was a long journey on foot across India, including the four corners of the land, lasting about sixteen years after his studies. A memorial stands at Kedāranātha.

events.title: Sureśvara's Naiṣkarmyasiddhi and Vārttikas
events.description: Sureśvara was a disciple of Śaṅkara, and in tradition is identified with Maṇḍana Miśra after his conversion, though scholars differ on this. He wrote the Naiṣkarmyasiddhi, a work on how knowledge, not action, leads to liberation, and long verse sub-commentaries (vārttikas) on Śaṅkara's commentaries on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Taittirīya Upaniṣads. He is traditionally the first head of the Śṛṅgeri Maṭha.

events.title: Padmapāda's Pañcapādikā
events.description: Padmapāda, another disciple of Śaṅkara, wrote the Pañcapādikā, a commentary on the first five sections of Śaṅkara's commentary on the Brahma Sūtra. Only part survives. Prakāśātman later wrote the Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa on it, and from this the Vivaraṇa school of Advaita takes its name. This school has its own view on how ignorance and the self are related. Tradition places Padmapāda at Purī, as the first head of the Govardhana Maṭha.

events.title: Vasugupta's Śiva Sūtra
events.description: According to Kashmiri tradition, Śiva told the sage Vasugupta in a dream, in the ninth century, that a teaching lay inscribed on a rock on Mahādeva mountain. He found seventy-seven aphorisms, the Śiva Sūtra. The first says "consciousness is the Self". They teach that the bound soul and Śiva are the same awareness, contracted or expanded. Later Kashmiri non-dual Śaiva thinkers, including Kṣemarāja, who wrote a commentary on the text, treat them as foundational.

events.title: Kollam era begins
events.description: The Kollam era (Kollavarṣam) is the calendar traditionally used in Kerala, with its year beginning in the month of Ciṅṅam (August–September). It is reckoned from 825 CE. Its origin is debated: some link it to the founding or re-founding of the port of Kollam (Quilon), others to a reform of the calendar or an astronomical event. The Malayalam calendar is still used for festivals and agricultural events in Kerala.

events.title: Candellas of Khajurāho begin
events.description: The Candellas arose in Bundelkhand, with Nannuka credited as their founder in the early ninth century, when they were feudatories of the Pratihāras. They claimed descent from the moon (candra) through a legendary origin story, and their territory was called Jejākabhukti. From the mid-tenth century to the eleventh they built the Khajurāho temples, including the Lakṣmaṇa temple, the Viśvanātha and the Kandāriyā Mahādeva. These are now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

events.title: Mihira Bhoja of Kanauj
events.description: Mihira Bhoja ruled from Kanauj for nearly fifty years, from 836, over an empire that stretched from the Punjab border to Bengal and south to the Narmadā. He was a devotee of Viṣṇu and took the title Ādi Varāha, "the primal boar", shown on his coins. The Arab traveller Sulaimān wrote that no Indian king had finer cavalry, that he was the greatest enemy of the Arabs, and that his lands were safe from robbers.

gitaQuote.verse: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत । अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥ परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् । धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.

events.title: Vācaspati Miśra and the Bhāmatī
events.description: Vācaspati Miśra of Mithilā, in the ninth or tenth century, wrote authoritative commentaries on five different philosophical systems, Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Mīmāṃsā and Advaita, expounding each faithfully on its own terms. His Advaita work is named Bhāmatī after his wife; the story says he was so absorbed in writing that he forgot her for years, and gave the book her name in amends. It founded one of Advaita's two sub-schools.

events.title: Hindu Śāhis of Kabul
events.description: The Hindu Śāhis ruled Kabul and Gandhāra from the ninth century. According to al-Bīrūnī, the Turk Śāhi king Lagaturmān was removed by his brāhmaṇa minister Kallar, who founded a new line. Later kings, such as Jayapāla and Anandapāla, fought the Ghaznavid ruler Sabuktigin and then Mahmūd in the late tenth and early eleventh centuries. The dynasty was the principal barrier on the north-west frontier for about two centuries and was ended after 1021.

events.title: Tarisāppaḷḷi copper plates
events.description: The Tarisāppaḷḷi plates, issued in 849 by the Cēra ruler Sthāṇu Ravi at Kollam, grant land and trading privileges to a Christian church and to a merchant guild connected with the Syrian Christian merchant Īśodātā Vīrai. The witnesses signed in Middle Persian, Judeo-Persian and Arabic scripts, which shows the presence of Zoroastrian, Jewish and Muslim traders at the port. The grant is a key document for the history of Kerala's religious plurality.

events.title: Nammāḻvār's Tiruvāymoḻi
events.description: Nammāḻvār, "our own Āḻvār", was born in a farming caste at Tirukkurukūr in the far south. Legend says he sat silent in the hollow of a tamarind tree for sixteen years. His Tiruvāymoḻi, "sacred speech", has 1,102 verses linked so that the last word of each begins the next. Often he speaks as a girl longing for an absent lover. Śrīvaiṣṇavas rank it with the Veda.

events.title: Vijayālaya founds the imperial Cōḻas
events.description: The Cōḻas had long existed as a small power, but Vijayālaya is regarded as the founder of the line that became an empire. He captured Tañjāvūr from the Muttaraiyar chiefs, around 850, and made it his base, according to the later Cōḻa records. He is credited with a temple to Niśumbhasūdanī (a form of Durgā) there. His descendants, Āditya I and Parāntaka I, and later Rājarāja and Rājendra, took the dynasty to dominance in South India.

events.title: The Spanda Kārikā on divine pulsation
events.description: The Spanda Kārikā is a short Kashmiri Śaiva text of about fifty verses that teaches the doctrine of spanda, the divine "pulsation" or vibration of consciousness through which Śiva manifests all things. It is attributed to Vasugupta, who also received the Śiva Sūtras, or to his pupil Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa, who wrote the commentary. The Spanda teaching holds that liberation is recognising this creative energy in everyday awareness. It influenced later Pratyabhijñā and Trika writers.

events.title: Circular yoginī temples of central India and Odisha
events.description: Between the ninth and twelfth centuries a number of circular, roofless shrines were built in central India and Odisha, their inner walls lined with niches holding images of sixty-four yoginīs, powerful female spirits, some with animal heads. At the centre stood Śiva as Bhairava. The rites performed there belonged to esoteric Tantra and are little known. The one at Mitāolī is said to have inspired the plan of India's old Parliament building.

events.title: Jayanta Bhaṭṭa's Nyāyamañjarī
events.description: Jayanta Bhaṭṭa, a Kashmiri scholar of the late 9th century, wrote the Nyāyamañjarī, a long work that takes up the Nyāya Sūtra's topics and defends them against Buddhist, Mīmāṃsā and other opponents, in clear, witty prose. He also wrote a play, the Āgamaḍambara, "The Pomp of the Scriptures," in which representatives of different religious sects argue and are satirised. It is a notable mix of philosophy and comedy that depicts the religious diversity of Kashmir.

events.title: Ānandavardhana's Dhvanyāloka
events.description: Ānandavardhana of Kashmir, in the ninth century, argued in his Dhvanyāloka, "Light on Suggestion", that the soul of poetry is neither ornament nor plot but what is suggested without being stated. A poem's literal meaning is like a lamp; the suggested emotion is what it illuminates. The theory, completed by Abhinavagupta, became the foundation of Indian literary criticism.

events.title: Mahāvīra's Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha
events.description: Mahāvīra was a Jaina mathematician who worked under the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Amoghavarṣa. His Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha ("Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics") is considered the first Indian text devoted entirely to mathematics, separate from astronomy. It covers arithmetic operations, fractions, the rule of three, problems in algebra and geometry, and methods for working out permutations and combinations, and it gives rules for the ellipse. It was used in south India and later translated into Telugu.

events.title: Prambanan Śiva temple complex built
events.description: Prambanan, in central Java, was built around 850. Its three main towers are dedicated to Śiva, forty-seven metres high, Viṣṇu and Brahmā, each facing a smaller shrine for the god's mount, surrounded originally by over two hundred minor shrines. The balustrades carry the Rāmāyaṇa in relief, panel by panel. Ruined by earthquakes, it has been reconstructed and the Rāmāyaṇa is danced before it on moonlit nights.

events.title: Māṇikkavācakar's Tiruvācakam
events.description: Māṇikkavācakar, "he whose words are rubies", is traditionally said to have been minister to a Pāṇḍya king, and most scholars place him in the ninth century. According to later hagiography, sent with the treasury to buy horses, he met a teacher under a tree, recognised him as Śiva, and spent the money on a temple. His Tiruvācakam is the most personal of the Tamil hymnals, full of self-reproach and melting joy. A saying holds that one unmoved by it will be moved by nothing.

events.title: Cēramāṉ Perumāḷ and Kerala's temples
events.description: The Cēra Perumāḷs ruled Kerala from Mahodayapuram, near Kodungallur, from about the 9th to the early 12th century. Their inscriptions record grants to temples and to the Nambūtiri brāhmaṇas, who held large landed estates and ran temple councils and local assemblies. This partnership of crown, temple and Brahmin landholders shaped Kerala's society for centuries. The Perumāḷ kings were also known for their toleration of Jews, Christians and Muslims, who traded on the coast.

events.title: Paramāras of Mālwā
events.description: The Paramāras ruled Mālwā from Dhārā and later Ujjayinī. Upendra, who is also called Kṛṣṇarāja, is named as the first ruler, in the ninth century, when they were feudatories of the Rāṣṭrakūṭas. A later legend, preserved in Padmagupta's Navasāhasāṅkacarita, says the line arose from a sacrificial fire-pit of the sage Vasiṣṭha on Mount Ābū, and this made the Paramāras one of the Agnikula clans. Their most famous king, Bhoja, ruled in the eleventh century.

events.title: Kalacuris of Tripurī
events.description: Kokalla I founded the Kalacuri kingdom of Ḍāhala, also called Cedi, in the later ninth century, with its capital at Tripurī near Jabalpur. The dynasty grew powerful in the eleventh century, especially under Gāṅgeyadeva, who took the title Vikramāditya, and his son Karṇa. Karṇa built the Karṇameru temple of Śiva at Kāśī, and the Kalacuris held a large part of central India until the twelfth century.

events.title: Sarvajñātman's Saṃkṣepaśārīraka
events.description: Sarvajñātman, an Advaita teacher of about the ninth or tenth century, wrote the Saṃkṣepaśārīraka, a work in verse that summarises the teaching of Śaṅkara's commentary on the Brahma Sūtras. He is known for the view that ignorance (avidyā) has Brahman as both its locus and its object. Later Advaitins discussed this view at length. The work was influential in the history of Advaita.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Uddhava Gītā and Bhramara Gītā in the Bhāgavata
events.description: The eleventh book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa contains Kṛṣṇa's final teaching to his friend Uddhava, known as the Uddhava Gītā, which covers devotion, knowledge and the soul. The Bhramara Gītā, in book ten, is the song in which a gopī addresses a bee that has come from Kṛṣṇa, expressing her sorrow of separation. The Bhāgavata is usually placed in South India in about the ninth or tenth century, and the Bhramara Gītā inspired many later poems, including Sūrdās's.

events.title: Vijayālaya Cōḻīśvaram, Nārttāmalai
events.description: Nārttāmalai, in Pudukkoṭṭai, has an early Cōḻa temple known as the Vijayālaya Cōḻīśvaram, built by the Muttaraiyar chiefs, who were vassals of the early Cōḻas, around the mid-9th century. It has a circular sanctum within a square outer shell, a rare plan, and is regarded as a precursor of the great Cōḻa temples. The site is among the oldest stone temples of the period and has other Jaina and Śaiva monuments.

events.title: Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra
events.description: The Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra is a short Sanskrit text of the Trika tradition of Kashmir, presented as a dialogue between Bhairava and the goddess. It teaches 112 dhāraṇās, or methods of focusing awareness, which use the breath, the senses, emotions, space and everyday experiences as doors to realisation. It is probably from about the eighth century or after, and is often cited in modern teachings on meditation, with commentaries by Kṣemarāja and others.

events.title: Kaṭārmal Sun temple and Katyūrī shrines
events.description: The Sun temple at Kaṭārmal, near Almora in Uttarakhand, is a Sūrya temple with a main shrine surrounded by many small ones. It is traditionally credited to the Katyūrī king Kaṭārmalla and commonly dated to the ninth century, within the Katyūrī period that runs from the seventh to the eleventh centuries. Its carved wooden doors were moved to a museum. Other temples in Kumaon, such as those at Jāgeśvar, show the building activity of the Katyūrī and later Cand rulers in the hills.

events.title: Chand Baori and the Harṣat Mātā temple at Abhaneri
events.description: At Abhaneri in Rajasthan, the Chand Baori is a stepwell of about 3,500 steps and a depth of some 30 metres, built in the eighth to ninth century on the evidence of style, by comparison with the temples at Paranagar and Maṇḍor. It is named for a Rājā Chanda of the Nikumbha line, but no inscription confirms this.¶Beside it is the Harṣat Mātā temple, of the seventh to eighth century, whose sculptures are now scattered and which was damaged, according to local tradition, by Mahmūd of Ghazni. Stepwells were part of the Hindu sacred landscape, with water as a public and ritual resource, and the Chand Baori is among the deepest and most elaborate of them.

events.title: Pandrethan, a Śiva temple in a pool
events.description: The Pandrethan temple at Srinagar is a small Śiva temple standing on a high platform in the middle of a tank fed by a spring near the Jhelum. Scholars generally date the present structure to the eighth or ninth century, though Debala Mitra argued for the tenth century or earlier. No builder is named for it.¶Colonial-era visitors identified it with the Meruvardhanasvāmin temple mentioned in Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī, but that temple was dedicated to Viṣṇu and built in the tenth century by the minister Meruvardhana in the Utpala dynasty, so scholars reject the link. Pandrethan is one of the best-preserved Kashmiri temples of the pre-Islamic period.

events.title: Avantivarman of Kashmir
events.description: Avantivarman (r. 855–883) founded the Utpala dynasty of Kashmir. He built two temples at Avantipura, the Avantisvāmin for Viṣṇu and the Avantīśvara for Śiva. His minister, the engineer Suyya, according to Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī, redirected the Vitastā (Jhelum) river and drained flooded land, greatly reducing famine and raising agricultural output. His reign is considered a time of order and prosperity before the later dynastic conflicts.

events.title: Nolambas, Bāṇas and Vaidumbas
events.description: These three families ruled at the borders between the larger powers of the Pallavas, Cōḻas and Rāṣṭrakūṭas. The Nolambas held the Nolambavāḍi region of southern Karnataka and the adjoining part of Andhra, the Bāṇas the Kolar area, and the Vaidumbas parts of Rāyalaseema. They commonly served stronger overlords and fought for gain on the frontier. Hemāvatī, the Nolamba centre, is notable for its temples and sculpture from the ninth and tenth centuries.

events.title: Śaṅkaranārāyaṇa's Laghubhāskarīya commentary
events.description: Śaṅkaranārāyaṇa, a Kerala astronomer, wrote a commentary on the Laghubhāskarīya in 869 at Mahodayapuram, the capital of the Cēra king Sthāṇu Ravi near present Kodungallur. His work is a key witness to astronomical practice in early medieval Kerala, where precise observation and calculation were prized for calendars and rituals. The region's astronomical tradition later reached its height in the Kerala school of Mādhava of Saṅgamagrāma in the fourteenth century, which developed infinite series for trigonometric functions.

events.title: Indrapura and Đồng Dương in Champa
events.description: Indrapura, near modern Đà Nẵng, was a Cham capital in the late 9th century. King Indravarman II founded a major Buddhist monastery at Đồng Dương in 875, dedicated to Lakṣmīndra Lokeśvara, while Śaiva worship continued at Mỹ Sơn and elsewhere. The Cham rulers used Sanskrit in inscriptions and followed the Indian court culture. The mix of Hindu and Buddhist traditions at the same court is typical of early Southeast Asian kingdoms.

events.title: Bhoganandīśvara temple at Nandi Hills
events.description: At the foot of Nandi Hills in Karnataka stands the Bhoganandīśvara temple, with early parts dated to the 9th century under the Bāṇa and Gaṅga rulers, and with later additions by the Cōḻas, Hoysaḷas and Vijayanagara kings. The temple has twin shrines to Śiva and its consort, and a hall with sculpted pillars. Its long record of building shows the continuous patronage of different dynasties over many centuries, and it remains in worship.

events.title: Gwalior zero inscription
events.description: In a small temple to Viṣṇu on the road up to Gwalior fort, an inscription dated 876 records a gift of land "270 hastas long" and a daily supply of "50" garlands. Both numbers are written with a small circle for zero in the modern decimal way. It is the oldest clearly dated zero in an Indian inscription on stone, though the system itself is some centuries older.

events.title: Nepal Saṃvat begins
events.description: The Nepal Saṃvat is a lunar calendar era of the Kathmandu valley, starting in 879 CE. According to tradition, it began when the merchant Śaṅkhadhar Sākhwa paid off the debts of all the people of the valley, a story found in local chronicles. The era was in official use for centuries and is still used by the Newar community. Tradition places its start in the reign of Rāghavadeva.

events.title: Battle of Tirupuṟampiyam
events.description: Around 880 the Pallava king Aparājita, with his Gaṅga ally Pṛthivīpati I and with help from the young Cōḻa ruler Āditya I, fought the Pāṇḍya king Varaguṇavarman at Tirupuṟampiyam near Kumbakoṇam. The Pāṇḍyas were defeated and their long dominance over the Tamil country ended. The real winner was Āditya I, who later overthrew Aparājita himself and annexed the Pallava lands, which is how the Cōḻas, long obscure, became rulers of the Kāveri basin and beyond.

events.title: Indravarman I completes the Bakong
events.description: The Bakong, at Hariharālaya near modern Roluos, was made the state temple of the Khmer king Indravarman I, whose reign is usually dated 877 to 889. The usual completion date is 881. It is a stepped pyramid of sandstone, an early temple-mountain, whose summit sanctuary held a Śiva liṅga.¶The Bakong is the first great Angkorian monument in stone and set the pattern of a royal liṅga on an artificial mountain that later kings followed. Its builder's capital, Hariharālaya, takes its name from Harihara, the combined form of Viṣṇu and Śiva.

events.title: Śaṅkaravarman's Paṭṭan temples
events.description: Śaṅkaravarman of the Utpala dynasty reigned in Kashmir from about 883 to 902. He founded the town of Śaṅkarapura, now Paṭṭan, near Srinagar, and it contains two Śiva temples, Śaṅkaragaurīśvara and Sugandheśvara, which survive in a damaged state. They are good examples of the stone architecture of Kashmir of that age, with triangular pediments and pillars. Kalhaṇa's chronicle is critical of the king's heavy taxation, but his building work is still visible.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥

gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.

events.title: Mahendrapāla I of Kanauj
events.description: Mahendrapāla I ruled the Gurjara-Pratihāra empire from Kānyakubja (Kanauj), from about 885. Inscriptions show his control reaching east into Magadha and parts of Bengal, at the expense of the Pālas, and west into Saurāṣṭra. The poet Rājaśekhara, who called himself his guru, wrote his plays and works under his patronage. The empire was at its height at the end of the ninth century.

events.title: Yaśovarman founds Yaśodharapura and Phnom Bakheng
events.description: Yaśovarman I, who ruled from 889, moved the Khmer court from Hariharālaya to a new capital, Yaśodharapura, the first city of Angkor. Its centre was Phnom Bakheng, a temple-mountain on a hill. The Sdok Kak Thom inscription, composed in 1052, says the king set up a liṅga on 'Śrī Yaśodharagiri'; scholars take this to mean the consecration of the temple, which was dedicated to Śiva.¶Phnom Bakheng fixed the site of Angkor as the royal centre for centuries, and the later temples in the area were built around it. The shrine was Hindu at first and was later converted to Buddhist use after Hinduism declined in the region. The temple is usually dated to the end of the ninth century.

events.title: Bhāgavata Purāṇa takes its final form
events.description: The Bhāgavata tells the stories of Viṣṇu's avatāras in 18,000 verses of unusually polished Sanskrit. Its tenth book, the life of Kṛṣṇa among the cowherds of Vṛndāvana, became the emotional centre of Hindu devotion.¶It teaches that loving devotion is higher than ritual, yoga or even liberation, and that the cowherd women who loved Kṛṣṇa without thought of self are the model devotees. Tradition ascribes it to Vyāsa; scholars place its final form in south India around the 9th–10th century. Caitanya, Vallabha and many others built their theologies on it.

events.title: Kubjikā and Paścimāmnāya tantras
events.description: The Kubjikāmata Tantra belongs to the Kubjikā tradition, centred on the goddess Kubjikā and called the Paścimāmnāya or "Western Transmission" of Kaula Śaivism. It is an early text to describe a system of six cakras and kuṇḍalinī, the energy at the base of the spine, which later spread widely in Indian yoga. The tradition was strong in the Himalaya and Nepal. Modern scholarship has stressed its significance for the history of yoga and Tantra.

events.title: Āditya I Cōḻa ends Pallava rule
events.description: Around the turn of the tenth century, Āditya I of the Cōḻas defeated the Pallava king Aparājita, who had earlier been his ally, and absorbed Toṇḍaimaṇḍalam. This ended the Pallava dynasty's independent rule, which had lasted for centuries. Later Cōḻa records say that Āditya built Śiva temples on both banks of the Kāverī. His son Parāntaka I and his successors went on to build a large empire.

events.title: Somānanda's Śivadṛṣṭi
events.description: Somānanda, a Kashmiri philosopher, wrote the Śivadṛṣṭi, usually regarded as the first systematic philosophical treatise of the Pratyabhijñā ("Recognition") school. The text argues that Śiva is the single reality, that consciousness is free and creative, and it critiques rival schools such as Buddhist and Mīmāṃsā views. The school's name refers to liberation through recognising one's own nature as Śiva. His pupil Utpaladeva developed the system in the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā, and Abhinavagupta later gave it its final form.

events.title: Nāthamuni recovers the Divya Prabandham
events.description: The hymns of the Āḻvārs had almost been forgotten when Nāthamuni, a tenth-century brāhmaṇa of the Kāverī delta, heard visitors sing ten verses and went in search of the rest. Tradition says he recovered all four thousand by meditating at Nammāḻvār's birthplace. He set them to music and had them sung in the temple at Śrīraṅgam beside the Sanskrit Veda. He is the first teacher of the Śrīvaiṣṇava line.

events.title: Rājaśekhara's Kāvyamīmāṃsā
events.description: Rājaśekhara was a Sanskrit poet who lived at the Pratihāra court of Kanauj, under Mahendrapāla I and his successor. His Kāvyamīmāṃsā is a manual of poetics for the aspiring poet, covering the training of poets, the qualities of poetry, and even the poet's daily routine. It survives only in part. He also wrote the Prakrit play Karpūramañjarī, and the Sanskrit plays Bālarāmāyaṇa and Viddhaśālabhañjikā. His works offer a vivid picture of court literary life.

events.title: Somavaṃśī dynasty of Kosala and Utkala
events.description: The Somavaṃśīs, or Lunar dynasty, ruled Kosala and Utkala between the ninth and eleventh centuries. Yayāti I (Mahāśivagupta) is credited with uniting the western Kosala territory with the coastal region of Utkala. The temple chronicle Mādalā Pāñji says that a king called Yayāti Keśarī rebuilt the Jagannātha shrine at Purī, but historians treat this tradition with caution, since the details of the early shrine are poorly known. The dynasty built many temples in Bhubaneśvara.

events.title: Nārada and Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtras
events.description: The Nārada Bhakti Sūtra and the Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra are two collections of short aphorisms on devotion. Both treat bhakti as an independent path to liberation, and not only a preparation for knowledge. Nārada's text describes it as supreme love directed toward God. They are dated roughly between the tenth and twelfth centuries, and they gave later bhakti movements a theoretical vocabulary.

events.title: Tiruvicaippā and Tiruppallāṇḍu of the Tirumuṟai
events.description: The ninth book of the Tirumuṟai, the Tamil Śaiva canon, contains the Tiruvicaippā, hymns by several poets, and the Tiruppallāṇḍu by Cēntanār, a short blessing on the Lord of Cidambaram. The canon was arranged by Nambiyāṇḍār Nambi around the time of Rājarāja I, in about the early eleventh century. These hymns are sung daily in the temple of Naṭarāja at Cidambaram.

events.title: Nāgeśvara temple, Kumbakoṇam
events.description: The Nāgeśvara temple at Kumbakoṇam was built under early Cōḻa rulers, in the late 9th and early 10th centuries, and is known for its delicate stone sculptures on the walls. Among them are figures of Śiva forms and goddesses, and an arrangement of the temple that lets sunlight fall on the liṅga on certain days in the Tamil month of Cittirai. The temple is one of the finest examples of early Cōḻa art, before the great temples of Tañjāvūr and Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram.

events.title: Ambikā Mātā, Jagat
events.description: The Ambikā Mātā temple at Jagat, in the Mewar region of Rajasthan, was built in the 10th century, with an inscription recording work in 961. It is a Devī temple known for its dense sculptures of dancers, musicians and divine couples, and is sometimes called the "Khajurāho of Mewar" because of the similarity to the carvings at Khajurāho. The temple shows the artistry of the Mewar region and is still in worship.

events.title: Pālas of Kāmarūpa
events.description: From about the tenth century, a line of rulers called the Pālas governed Kāmarūpa from Durjayā, a capital near present Guwahati. Brahmapāla founded the line, and the copper-plate grants of later kings such as Ratnapāla record land gifts to brāhmaṇas and praise the river Lauhitya, the Brahmaputra. The plates are in Sanskrit and give royal genealogies, making them key evidence for the region's history. The dynasty's rule marked a period when Brahmanical culture and temple building grew in the Assam valley.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Sanskrit stotra literature of the early medieval age
events.description: Sanskrit devotional hymns, or stotras, flourished across the early medieval period. Mayūra's Sūryaśataka, a hundred verses to the Sun, was composed in the seventh century. The Śivamahimnaḥ stotra, ascribed to Puṣpadanta, praises Śiva's greatness, and Mūka's Pañcaśatī, five hundred verses to Kāmākṣī of Kāñcī, became a devotional classic, though the dates of both authors are uncertain. The Ādityahṛdaya, a hymn to the Sun that the sage Agastya teaches Rāma in the Yuddhakāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa, is also recited daily by many. Together such works made stotra recitation part of everyday practice.

events.title: Vaikhānasa and Pāñcarātra Āgamas in temples
events.description: Two Vaiṣṇava ritual traditions govern temple worship. The Vaikhānasa Āgama, which is linked to the sage Vikhanas, is followed at Tirumala and many other Viṣṇu temples in Andhra and Tamil Nadu. The Pāñcarātra Āgama is followed in others, including Śrīraṅgam. They differ in how images are consecrated and worshipped and in the training of priests, and the choice of rite often marks a temple's identity. Both traditions are old, though the texts that survive are mostly medieval.

events.title: Old Javanese Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata
events.description: The Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa is an Old Javanese poem that retells the story of Rāma, closely following the Sanskrit Bhaṭṭikāvya, a poetic work of the seventh century. It is usually dated to about the ninth century. About a century later, around 990, parvans of the Mahābhārata began to be rendered into Old Javanese prose at the court of King Dharmavaṃśa. These works made the Indian epics part of Javanese literature, and their stories live on in Balinese and Javanese shadow-puppet and dance performance.
