events.title: Sāmba Purāṇa and the Saura sect
events.description: The Sāmba Purāṇa, an Upapurāṇa composed and revised over several centuries, tells how Kṛṣṇa's son Sāmba was cured of leprosy by worshipping Sūrya, and how he brought Maga priests from Śākadvīpa (probably Iran) to serve the sun-god. The Saura sect, devoted to Sūrya as supreme, flourished from late antiquity to the medieval period. Great sun-temples were built at Mārtaṇḍa in Kashmir, Modherā in Gujarat and Koṇārka in Odisha. After the thirteenth century the sect declined, and Sūrya's worship became mostly part of Smārta and Vaiṣṇava practice, as in the daily Sandhyā prayers and the Sūryanamaskāra.

events.title: Parāntaka I Cōḻa
events.description: Parāntaka I (r. 907–955) expanded the Cōḻa kingdom by conquering the Pāṇḍya capital Madurai, taking the title "Maduraikoṇḍa," and campaigning in Laṅkā. He gave generously to the temple at Cidambaram, which is said to have been given a gilded roof. Inscriptions at Uttaramērūr dated to 919 and 921 describe how village assemblies were chosen: eligible members were selected by drawing lots, under rules about age, property and learning. These records are an important source on local administration.

events.title: Indra III sacks Kanauj
events.description: Indra III, the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king, led an army north around 916, crossed the Yamunā and sacked Kanauj, the capital of the Pratihāra Mahīpāla. Later Rāṣṭrakūṭa records celebrate the campaign, and Arab travellers such as al-Masʿūdī describe both empires around the same period. The raid caused lasting damage to Pratihāra authority, and several feudatories became independent in the following decades. The Rāṣṭrakūṭas did not occupy the north permanently.

events.title: Uttaramērūr inscription on self-government
events.description: On the wall of a temple at Uttaramērūr, a brāhmaṇa village near Kāñcī, inscriptions of about 920 set out how its assembly chose committees for gardens, tanks, gold and justice. Names of eligible men from each of thirty wards were written on palm-leaf tickets, put in a pot, and drawn by a child. Candidates needed property, learning and a clean record; those who had failed to submit accounts were barred, with their relatives.

events.title: Candellas rise in Jejākabhukti
events.description: The Candellas, a Rājpūt dynasty of Bundelkhand (Jejākabhukti), began as feudatories of the Pratihāras. Under Harṣa and especially Yaśovarman (c. 925–950) they became independent and powerful. Yaśovarman built the Lakṣmaṇa temple at Khajurāho, which was consecrated in about 954. Later Candella kings added other temples at Khajurāho, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and defended the fortress of Kāliñjara against Ghaznavid attacks in the early 11th century.

events.title: Utpaladeva's Īśvara-pratyabhijñā-kārikā
events.description: Utpaladeva, in the early tenth century, gave Kashmir Śaivism its philosophical method. His verses on "the recognition of the Lord" argue step by step, against Buddhist opponents, that memory, knowledge and action are possible only if there is one enduring conscious subject, and that this subject is Śiva. Liberation is not acquiring something new but recognising what one already is, as a woman recognises a long-described lover standing before her.

events.title: Jayavarman IV builds Koh Ker, city of liṅgas
events.description: Jayavarman IV took the Khmer royal seat to Koh Ker, in the northern plains, and ruled from there from 928; his successor Harṣavarman II held it until 944. Inscriptions call the place Lingapura, 'city of liṅgas', or Chok Gargyar. The Prang, a seven-tiered pyramid about 36 metres high, was probably his state temple, and a Sanskrit inscription at Prasat Thom records the consecration of a Śiva liṅga named Tribhuvaneśvara.¶For some sixteen years a provincial site was the empire's capital, and the sculpture and scale of the monuments are unlike those at Angkor. Power returned to the Angkor region after 944. UNESCO inscribed Koh Ker in 2023.

events.title: Mūlarāja founds the Caulukyas (Solaṅkīs)
events.description: Mūlarāja, who took power in Gujarat around 940, founded the Caulukya (Solaṅkī) dynasty and made Aṇahilapāṭaka (modern Patan) the capital. His family patronised Śaiva temples, including Somanātha, and later also Jaina leaders and scholars. Under Bhīma I, Jayasiṃha Siddharāja and Kumārapāla, Gujarat became a wealthy and influential kingdom, and the Solaṅkī period produced notable temples such as those at Modherā and Mount Ābū.

events.title: Battle of Takkōlam
events.description: In about 949 the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Kṛṣṇa III met the Cōḻa army of Parāntaka I at Takkōlam in the northern Tamil country. The Cōḻa crown prince Rājāditya led his forces and was killed there. Kannada inscriptions credit the Gaṅga feudatory Būtuga II with the deed and say Rājāditya was struck while seated on his elephant. Kṛṣṇa III's records claim that he then advanced as far as Rāmeśvaram. The Rāṣṭrakūṭas held parts of the Tamil north for a time, but Cōḻa power recovered under Rājarāja I, while the Rāṣṭrakūṭas themselves declined within a generation.

gitaQuote.translation: I alone am inexhaustible, imperishable Time (Akṣaya Kāla), and I am the dispenser of destiny facing all directions... I am all-destroying Time, grown mighty to extinguish the worlds.
gitaQuote.source: Mahabharata (Bhishma Parva 35.32); Abhinavagupta Gītārtha-Saṁgraha

events.title: Lakṣmaṇa temple, Khajurāho
events.description: The Lakṣmaṇa temple was built by the Candella king Yaśovarman and consecrated in 954 under his son Dhaṅga. It is the earliest of the great temples at Khajurāho and the best preserved. It stands on a high platform with four corner shrines, its towers rising in steps like a mountain range. The famous erotic groups occupy a small part of walls crowded with gods, dancers, warriors and daily life.

events.title: Mukteśvara temple at Bhubaneśvara
events.description: The Mukteśvara temple at Bhubaneśvara, built in about the 10th century, is a small Śiva temple. It is famous for its richly carved decoration and for its ornamental arched gateway (toraṇa), which is unusual in Odisha. It is often described as a "gem of Odishan architecture." The temple represents a mature stage of the Kaliṅga style, with a curved tower (deul) and a separate hall, and influenced later buildings including the great Liṅgarāja temple.

events.title: Yāmunācārya (Āḷavandār) of Śrīraṅgam
events.description: Yāmuna, grandson of Nāthamuni, is said to have won half a kingdom as a boy by defeating the court scholar in debate, and to have given it up later for the service of Raṅganātha. He wrote the first philosophical works of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas, defending the authority of the Pāñcarātra scriptures and the reality of a personal God. He died just before the young Rāmānuja, summoned as his successor, could reach him.

events.title: Abhinavagupta, Kashmir’s philosopher of Trika
events.description: The most versatile mind of medieval India, working in Kashmir around 975–1025. In the Tantrāloka he brought the many Śaiva tantric traditions into one system: the universe is the free self-expression of a single consciousness, Śiva, and liberation is recognising that one's own awareness is that.¶He was equally a philosopher of art. His commentary on the Nāṭyaśāstra explains rasa, aesthetic relish, as a taste of the same blissful self-awareness, which is why art can be a spiritual experience. Legend says he walked into a cave with 1,200 disciples and was not seen again.

events.title: Kashmiri theologians of Śaiva Siddhānta
events.description: The Śaiva Siddhānta, a dualist Śaiva tradition, teaches the distinction between God (pati), souls (paśu) and the bonds that limit them (pāśa). Sadyojyotis, a Kashmiri theologian of about the late seventh or eighth century, set out its philosophy in works such as the Nareśvaraparīkṣā. Later teachers including Rāmakaṇṭha and Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇakaṇṭha developed it in the tenth century. Over time the school's centre moved to the south, where it merged with Tamil Śaiva devotion and became the dominant philosophy of Tamil Śaivism.

gitaQuote.verse: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत । अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥ परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् । धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.

events.title: Somadeva Sūri's Yaśastilaka and Nītivākyāmṛta
events.description: Somadeva Sūri was a Digambara Jaina monk who wrote the Yaśastilakacampū, a long prose and verse work completed in 959, at the court of a Rāṣṭrakūṭa feudatory. He also wrote the Nītivākyāmṛta, a manual on statecraft in Sanskrit prose aphorisms that draws on the Arthaśāstra tradition. These show a Jaina writer taking part in the wider Sanskrit discussion on kingship and conduct.

events.title: Kachchhapaghātas of Gwalior
events.description: The Kachchhapaghātas were a Rajput line, ancestors in part of the Kachhwāhas, who ruled at Gwalior, Narwar and Dubkund from the tenth century. They were feudatories of the Candellas and Pratihāras. The Sās-Bahū temples at Gwalior fort, dated by inscription to 1093, are their major legacy. The name Sās-Bahū is a popular corruption of Sahasrabāhu, "thousand-armed", a name of Viṣṇu to whom the larger temple is dedicated.

events.title: Vimuktātman's Iṣṭasiddhi
events.description: Vimuktātman was an Advaita Vedāntin whose date is uncertain but who is usually placed around the tenth century or somewhat later. His Iṣṭasiddhi is a major work of the school, and discusses the status of māyā or ignorance. It analyses what it means for the world to be anirvacanīya, neither real nor unreal, and examines different definitions of that term. It answered objections from other schools and was cited by later Advaitins.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ | ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||
gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.

events.title: Sās-Bahū temples at Nāgdā
events.description: At Nāgdā, near Udaipur, stand twin Viṣṇu temples now known as the Sās-Bahū temples, a name which comes from the Sanskrit Sahasrabāhu, "thousand-armed," an epithet of Viṣṇu. They were built in the 10th century when the town was a capital of the Guhila rulers of Mewar. The larger one has a finely carved porch with scenes from the Rāmāyaṇa. The temples were damaged by later conflicts but have been preserved by the Archaeological Survey of India.

events.title: Sixty-four Yoginī temples of Bherāghāṭ and Mitāolī
events.description: The yoginī temples are open circular enclosures with shrines for sixty-four yoginīs, goddesses connected with Tantric worship. The one at Bherāghāṭ near Jabalpur was built by the Kalacuri dynasty in the tenth century. The temple at Mitāolī in Morena, Madhya Pradesh, is attributed to the Kacchapaghāta king Devapāla and is generally dated to the eleventh century, although an inscription of Vikrama 1383 (1323 CE) is also known there. It has often been suggested as a model for the old Parliament House in Delhi, but this is only a theory. These temples show royal support for Tantric traditions, and each yoginī has her own image.

events.title: Āryabhaṭa II and Śrīpati, siddhāntic astronomers
events.description: Āryabhaṭa II, perhaps of the tenth century, wrote the Mahāsiddhānta, a thorough treatise on planetary theory and arithmetic. Śrīpati, who worked in the eleventh century, composed the Siddhāntaśekhara and also works on astrology and calendrical rules. Both carried forward the tradition of mathematical astronomy begun by Āryabhaṭa I and Brahmagupta, refining computation and explaining eclipses. Their books were widely studied and commented upon in later centuries and show the continuity of Sanskrit scientific writing outside the courts of the far south.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha's Nareśvaraparīkṣā commentary
events.description: Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha was a Kashmiri teacher of Śaiva Siddhānta, a dualist Śaiva school. His commentary on the Nareśvaraparīkṣā, a text by Sadyojyotis, argues for a permanent, conscious self, against the Buddhist view that there is only a stream of momentary states. The debate is typical of the philosophical argument between Śaiva and Buddhist thinkers in Kashmir. His writing is a major source for Śaiva Siddhānta thought in this period.

events.title: Baroli temples on the Chambal
events.description: The Baroli temple complex lies near the Chambal river in Chittorgarh district, Rajasthan. It is attributed to the Gurjara-Pratihāra period and dated to the tenth to eleventh century. Eight major temples stand within a walled enclosure and a ninth lies about a kilometre away. The Ghāṭeśvara Mahādeva temple, the largest, is a Śiva shrine of the early tenth century that houses five liṅgas and takes its name from a pot-shaped liṅga.¶The group shows the Pratihāra temple style in the Mālwā and Hāḍautī region, with a tall curved tower and a profusion of sculpture. It is an important source for the art of Śaiva shrines in northern India before the Candella temples.

I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the creation and dissolution, the foundation and the imperishable seed.

events.title: Harṣanātha temple completed on Harṣagiri
events.description: The Harṣanātha temple stands on the hill of Harṣagiri, near Sikar in Rajasthan, where Śiva is worshipped as Harṣa. It was completed in 956 and was commissioned by a Pāśupata teacher, Allaṭa, also called Bhāvarakta. An inscription of 973 gives an account of the temple and credits Bhāvarakta together with the Chāhamāna king Vigraharāja.¶The inscription is a record of the connection between Pāśupata ascetics and the Chāhamāna rulers of the Śākambharī region, who supported the temple. It places an ascetic order at the centre of royal patronage in early medieval Rajasthan, and the temple is one of the few Pāśupata foundations of the period whose date is firmly known.

events.title: Dhaṅga makes the Candellas independent
events.description: Dhaṅga ruled the Candella kingdom from about 950 to 1002 and made it an independent power by casting off Pratihāra overlordship. He took imperial titles and extended his control over a wide region of central India. At Khajurāho he built or completed the Viśvanātha temple, whose inscription is dated 1002, and the Pārśvanātha Jaina temple belongs to his time. He supported the Hindu Śāhi king Jayapāla against the Ghaznavids.

events.title: Rājendravarman consecrates Pre Rup
events.description: Pre Rup was built as the state temple of the Khmer king Rājendravarman II and consecrated in 961, or early 962. It is a temple-mountain of brick, laterite and sandstone, dedicated to Śiva, standing south of the East Mebon, which the same king had built in 953.¶Its name means 'turn the body', and local tradition says that cremations were held here, but scholars take the stone trough in the courtyard to have been the base of a Nandi statue and not a cremation site. Pre Rup shows the tenth-century Khmer style between the early temple-mountains and the later Angkorian temples, and it records Śaiva royal patronage in the years after the capital returned from Koh Ker.

events.title: Kacchavāhas settle in Dhundhār
events.description: The Kacchavāhas, later the Kachhwāhas of Amber and Jaipur, claim descent from Kuśa, son of Rāma. In tradition, their chief Dulha Rāy established the line in the Dhundhār region of Rajasthan and made Dausā his base. The date of about 966 is traditional, and some modern accounts place him much later, even in the early twelfth century. Amber, with the temple of Ambikeśvara, later became their capital, and in 1727 Sawai Jai Singh II founded Jaipur. Under Akbar they became close allies of the Mughals and rose to prominent positions.

events.title: Banteay Srei temple founded near Angkor
events.description: Banteay Srei, built in 967 near Angkor, is a small Śiva temple of pink sandstone, remarkable for its deep and precise carving. Its inscription says it was founded by Yajñavarāha, a brāhmaṇa teacher of King Jayavarman V, not by a king himself. Its pediments show scenes from the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata, including Rāvaṇa shaking Mount Kailāsa. The temple is an example of the high quality of Khmer art and shows how learned brāhmaṇas could found major monuments.

gitaQuote.verse: अहमेवाक्षयः कालो धाताहं विश्वतोमुखः ॥ कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो लोकान्समाहर्तुमिह प्रवृत्तः ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: aham evākṣayaḥ kālo dhātāhaṁ viśvatomukhaḥ || kālo 'smi loka-kṣaya-kṛt pravṛddho lokān samāhartum iha pravṛttaḥ ||
gitaQuote.translation: I alone am inexhaustible, imperishable Time (Akṣaya Kāla), and I am the dispenser of destiny facing all directions... I am all-destroying Time, grown mighty to extinguish the worlds.
gitaQuote.source: Mahabharata (Bhishma Parva 35.32); Abhinavagupta Gītārtha-Saṁgraha

events.title: Sembiyaṉ Mahādevī, Cōḻa queen and temple patron
events.description: Sembiyaṉ Mahādevī was the widow of the Cōḻa king Gaṇḍarāditya and the mother of Uttama Cōḻa. She lived through the reigns of several kings and became one of the great patrons of early Cōḻa temple building. Inscriptions record her gifts of land and ornaments, and her rebuilding of older brick shrines in stone, among them temples at Kōnēripuram and other places. She is also credited with the commissioning of bronze images, and the sculptural tradition of Cōḻa bronzes, including the Naṭarāja form, owes much to this patronage.

events.title: Western Cālukyas of Kalyāṇī
events.description: In 973, Tailapa II, a Cālukya feudatory, defeated the last Rāṣṭrakūṭa ruler, Karka II, and established the Western Cālukya dynasty. Its capital was Kalyāṇī in Karnataka. Over the following two centuries the Cālukyas fought the Cōḻas and Paramāras, and supported Kannada and Sanskrit literature and a distinctive temple style in the Tuṅgabhadrā region. Their greatest king was Vikramāditya VI, whose long reign is remembered for peace, scholarship and temple building.

events.title: Lāṭa Cālukyas and Mūlarāja of Gujarat
events.description: Two powers shared Gujarat in the later tenth century. Bārappa, a general of the Western Cālukya Taila II, founded a Cālukya line in Lāṭa, in southern Gujarat, around 973. Mūlarāja of the Caulukya (Solaṅkī) line, who ruled from Aṇahilapāṭaka, fought with Bārappa. Tradition credits Mūlarāja with beginning the Rudra Mahālaya at Siddhapur and with bringing Audīcya brāhmaṇas from the north to settle there. Later Caulukya kings completed the temple, which was damaged in later centuries.

events.title: Paramāra Muñja rules Mālwā
events.description: Muñja (Vākpati II), who ruled Mālwā from Dhārā in the late 10th century, was a warrior and a poet. He fought the Cālukya king Tailapa II repeatedly, and, according to later accounts, was captured and executed by him after an invasion. His court was a centre of learning that included Dhanañjaya, author of the Daśarūpaka on dramaturgy, and the poet Halāyudha. His nephew Bhoja later made the Paramāras famous.

events.title: Śambhunātha and Abhinavagupta’s Kaula initiation
events.description: Śambhunātha, from the Jālandhara pīṭha in the Punjab hills, was the teacher from whom Abhinavagupta received the Kaula rites, according to Abhinavagupta's own writings. The Kaula tradition, a current of Tantra, brought a transgressive and embodied emphasis to the Trika system of Kashmir. Abhinavagupta describes the Kaula rites in chapter 29 of his Tantrāloka. Śambhunātha's role is a reminder that Kashmiri Śaivism drew on teachers from many regions.

events.title: Sabuktigīn attacks the Hindu Śāhis
events.description: The Hindu Śāhis ruled the Kabul valley and Gandhāra, with a capital at Udabhāṇḍapura (Waihind). According to Persian chroniclers such as al-ʿUtbī, the Ghaznavid ruler Sabuktigīn began raiding their territory after 977, and their king Jayapāla fought him and was eventually defeated. The Śāhis were the first Indian dynasty to face the Ghaznavids and held the northwestern frontier for decades. Jayapāla's son Ānandapāla continued the struggle, and the dynasty ended in the early 11th century.

events.title: Diddā of Kashmir
events.description: Diddā, who belonged to the Lohara family and was married to King Kṣemagupta, ruled Kashmir after his death in 958, first as regent for her young son and then grandsons, and then as sovereign until 1003. The historian Kalhaṇa, in his Rājataraṅgiṇī, describes her as ruthless but also capable, and records that she defeated rebels and invading forces. She named her nephew Saṅgrāmarāja as heir, and he began the Lohara dynasty.

events.title: Gommaṭeśvara at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa
events.description: At Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa in Karnataka a statue of the Jaina saint Bāhubali, seventeen metres high, was carved from a single granite peak about 981 for Cāmuṇḍarāya, minister of the Gaṅga king. He stands naked in meditation so long that creepers have grown up his legs. It is among the largest free-standing monoliths in the world. Every twelve years it is anointed from scaffolding with milk, saffron and sandal.

events.title: Rājarāja I Cōḻa
events.description: Rājarāja I came to the Cōḻa throne in 985 and in thirty years made a regional kingdom into an empire: Kerala, the Pāṇḍya country, northern Sri Lanka and the Maldives. He built a navy, had all the land of his realm surveyed and assessed, and began his inscriptions with a standard account of his deeds, a new practice. He was a devout Śaiva who also endowed Viṣṇu temples and a Buddhist monastery.

events.title: Śrīdhara's Nyāyakandalī
events.description: Śrīdhara wrote the Nyāyakandalī, a commentary on Praśastapāda's Padārthadharmasaṅgraha, the main early Vaiśeṣika text. He completed it in Śaka 913, or 991 CE, at Bhūriśreṣṭhi, a village in southwestern Bengal, under a local king. The work is one of the best explanations of Vaiśeṣika and Nyāya thought, defends the realist view, and shows that Bengal was a centre of philosophical learning before the rise of Navadvīpa.

events.title: Mahīpāla I restores the Pālas
events.description: Mahīpāla I took the Pāla throne around 995 after a period of weakness, during which the empire had lost control of much of northern and eastern Bengal. He recovered these territories and restored Pāla power in Bihar. A Sārnāth inscription of 1026 records that he had two Buddhist shrines repaired, and the Pāla court also supported Hindu shrines. He also faced the invasion of the Cōḻa king Rājendra I, whose armies marched through Bengal around 1021 to 1023.

events.title: Udayana's Nyāyakusumāñjali
events.description: Udayana of Mithilā, around 1000, wrote the classic set of rational arguments for the existence of God, the "Handful of Flowers of Logic": the world is an effect and needs a maker; atoms need a first mover; the Veda needs an author. In another work he attacked the Buddhist denial of the self. A story has him scold the image of Jagannātha at Purī for keeping its doors shut to the one who had proved its existence.

events.title: Abhinavagupta’s Pratyabhijñā commentaries
events.description: Abhinavagupta, the great Kashmiri philosopher, wrote the Īśvara-pratyabhijñā-vimarśinī as a commentary on the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā of Utpaladeva, as well as a longer one, the Vivṛtivimarśinī. The Pratyabhijñā ("recognition") philosophy holds that liberation is the recognition that one's own consciousness is Śiva. His commentaries give the doctrine its classical form. He is also known for his Tantrāloka and for his work on aesthetic theory.

events.title: Nambi Āṇḍār Nambi compiles the Tirumuṟai
events.description: Tamil tradition says that in Rājarāja's time the hymns of the three great Śaiva poets were known only in fragments. The young priest Nambi learned from Gaṇeśa that the manuscripts lay sealed in a room at Cidambaram. When opened, most had been eaten by white ants, and what remained, about 8,000 verses, he is said to have arranged in seven books. These, with later additions, form the twelve-book Tirumuṟai. This is a pious tradition, and scholars see the canon as taking shape over a longer period.

events.title: Prakāśātman's Vivaraṇa
events.description: Prakāśātman wrote the Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa, a commentary on Padmapāda's Pañcapādikā, which itself comments on Śaṅkara's Brahma Sūtra commentary. It gave rise to the Vivaraṇa school of Advaita, which holds that the individual soul is a reflection of Brahman in ignorance. This differs from the Bhāmatī school, which follows Vācaspati Miśra and takes a different view of how the soul is limited. The two lines of interpretation shaped later Advaita debate.

events.title: Bhoja's Tattvaprakāśa
events.description: The Tattvaprakāśa is a short Sanskrit treatise attributed to the Paramāra king Bhoja of Dhārā, a ruler famed as a patron and author. It sets out the doctrine of Śaiva Siddhānta, the dualist school in which Śiva, the souls and the bondage binding them are all real. Its central subject is the thirty-six tattvas, the categories of existence running from earthly elements up through the powers of māyā to Śiva himself. A later commentary by Śrīkumāra helped the text circulate, and it remains an early, compact statement of the school's cosmology.

events.title: Tantrasāra and Paramārthasāra of Abhinavagupta
events.description: Abhinavagupta, the Kashmiri polymath who systematised non-dual Trika Śaivism, wrote vast works such as the Tantrāloka, but also shorter ones for readers who needed an entry point. The Tantrasāra condenses the Tantrāloka's doctrine and ritual in prose, while the Paramārthasāra, a verse work adapted from an earlier text, presents the path to recognising one's identity with Śiva. Alongside his commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā, the Gītārthasaṅgraha, these texts show how he read both scripture and Tantra through a single non-dual lens.

events.title: Tyāgarāja temple at Tiruvārūr
events.description: The Tyāgarāja temple at Tiruvārūr was an important Cōḻa-period Śaiva centre, praised in the Tēvāram hymns and favoured with royal endowments. The deity is a form of Śiva shown in the Somāskanda manner with Umā and Skanda. Its car festival, with a very large chariot, is said to be the biggest of its kind in Tamil Nadu. Tiruvārūr is also the birthplace of the composers Tyāgarāja, Śyāmā Śāstri and Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar, the three masters of Karnatak music, who lived many centuries later.

events.title: Kārttikai lamps in Cōḻa temple life
events.description: Inscriptions of the Cōḻa period record gifts to Tamil temples for lamps, oil and offerings, including support for the Kārttikai Dīpam, the festival of lights celebrated when the moon is in the Kṛttikā nakṣatra. The great lamp lit on the hill at Tiruvaṇṇāmalai is still famous today, and the festival itself is much older, since early Tamil poetry already refers to it. Royal and temple endowments of lamps, oil and feeding made such seasonal observances a regular part of Cōḻa temple life.

events.title: Kaumāra tradition of Skanda worship
events.description: The Kaumāra tradition worships Skanda, also called Kārttikeya, Murugan and Subrahmaṇya, as the supreme god. It is strongest in Tamil lands, where Murugan is a central deity. The festival of Skanda Ṣaṣṭhī, celebrated at Tiruchendur and other temples, re-enacts the slaying of the demon Sūrapadma. Murugan devotion is very old in Tamil culture, and it appears in early Tamil poetry and in the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai.

events.title: Cōḻa bronze sculpture
events.description: Cōḻa metalworkers cast images by the lost-wax technique, producing bronzes for temple processions, such as the dancing Śiva Naṭarāja, the half-male half-female Ardhanārīśvara and Pārvatī. The great Rājarājeśvaram (Bṛhadīśvara) temple at Tañjāvūr, consecrated in 1010, was a major centre of patronage, and royal women such as Sembiyan Mahādevī donated many images. The bronzes are admired for their grace, balance and fluid modelling and are now in museums around the world.

events.title: Battle of Peshawar
events.description: On 27 November 1001 Mahmūd of Ghazni defeated Jayapāla, the Hindu Śāhi king whose realm guarded the passes into India, near Peshawar. Jayapāla and fifteen of his family were taken prisoner. Ransomed, and holding that a king three times defeated was unfit to rule, he abdicated in favour of his son and mounted a funeral pyre. His descendants fought on for another twenty-five years.

events.title: Lohara dynasty of Kashmir
events.description: Saṅgrāmarāja, nephew of Queen Diddā, succeeded her in 1003 and began the Lohara dynasty of Kashmir. In Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī and Muslim chronicles, Mahmūd of Ghazni twice attempted to take the Lohara fortress, in 1015 and 1021, and in both cases failed and withdrew. Saṅgrāmarāja also sent troops to help the Hindu Śāhis. Kashmir remained under Hindu kings for another three centuries.

events.title: Battle of Chach
events.description: Around 1008, according to Persian chroniclers, a confederacy of Indian rulers led by the Śāhi king Ānandapāla faced Mahmūd of Ghazni near Chach (Hund) and Waihind, and was defeated. Mahmūd then went to Nagarkoṭ (Kāṅgṛā), and the sources say that he took the treasure of its famous temple, linked with the goddess Vajreśvarī, in about 1009. The accounts are mostly from Ghaznavid court historians, who emphasise the plunder, and Indian sources on the event are scarce.

events.title: Bṛhadīśvara temple consecrated
events.description: Rājarāja I completed his great temple to Śiva at Tañjāvūr in 1010. Its tower rises 66 metres, then the tallest in India, and is capped by a granite block weighing about 80 tonnes, raised, according to tradition, up a ramp several kilometres long.¶The walls carry inscriptions listing every gift: gold, jewels, bronze images, lamps, villages, and the names and house addresses of 400 dancers and scores of musicians assigned to the temple. It was a statement of imperial power and also a working institution that employed hundreds. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and still in worship.

events.title: Bhoja Paramāra
events.description: Bhoja ruled Mālwā from Dhārā for some forty-five years in the eleventh century and is India's proverbial scholar-king. Eighty-four works are ascribed to him, on poetics, grammar, medicine, yoga, astronomy and architecture; his treatise on building includes a chapter on machines. He founded a Sanskrit college, built a vast lake, and began the temple at Bhojpur. "Where is King Bhoja and where is Gaṅgū the oilman" is still a Hindi proverb.

events.title: Rājendra I Cōḻa
events.description: Rājendra I, son of Rājarāja I, became co-ruler in 1012 and was king from 1014 to 1044. He completed the Cōḻa conquest of Laṅkā, taking the island's king prisoner, and led an army to the Gaṅgā, from which he took water to his new capital. His navy attacked the Śrīvijaya kingdom across the Bay of Bengal in 1025, one of the few overseas expeditions in Indian history. He took the title Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻa.

events.title: Thanesar's Cakrasvāmin temple destroyed
events.description: In 1014, according to the chronicler al-ʿUtbī, Mahmūd of Ghazni attacked Thanesar (Sthāṇvīśvara) and took away its image of Cakrasvāmin, a form of Viṣṇu, to Ghazni. The sources say it was set up in public in Ghazni, where it was humiliated. Thanesar was a major tīrtha near Kurukṣetra. The account is from the conquerors' side, and this episode is one in a series of Ghaznavid raids on northern Indian temples that held large treasuries.

events.title: Birth of Rāmānujācārya
events.description: Rāmānuja was born at Śrīperumbudūr near Chennai; the traditional dates, 1017–1137, give him a life of 120 years, and scholars generally place him about 1077–1157.¶He became head of the great Viṣṇu temple at Śrīraṅgam and the chief teacher of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas. Against Śaṅkara he argued that the world and individual souls are real, and that God is a person with infinite good qualities whom one reaches by loving devotion and surrender. He joined the Sanskrit Upaniṣads with the Tamil hymns of the Āḻvārs, and opened devotion to people excluded by caste.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥

gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.

events.title: Mahmūd sacks Mathurā and Kanauj
events.description: In the winter of 1018 Mahmūd of Ghazni crossed the Yamunā and fell on Mathurā. His own secretary records the sultan's amazement at the main temple, which he reckoned would take two hundred years to build, and five gold images with eyes of rubies. He ordered every temple burned. He went on to take Kanauj, the imperial city, and returned with booty reckoned at three million dirhams and fifty-three thousand captives.

events.title: Vidyādhara Candella confronts Mahmūd
events.description: When Mahmūd of Ghazni advanced to Kanauj in 1018–1019, its Pratihāra ruler Rājyapāla fled without resistance. The Candella king Vidyādhara is said to have regarded this as a betrayal and to have had Rājyapāla attacked and killed; the Dubkund inscription credits the Kachchhapaghāta chief Arjuna with the deed. Mahmūd's later campaigns against Vidyādhara, which reached Kāliñjara in 1022, ended without a clear conquest according to Persian sources, and the Candellas kept their kingdom. The episode shows how Indian kingdoms dealt with the invasions in different ways.

events.title: Airlangga rebuilds the Javanese kingdom
events.description: Airlangga rebuilt the East Javanese kingdom from about 1019, after an attack in 1016 destroyed the court of his father-in-law Dharmawangsa. He reigned until about 1042, when he divided the realm between two sons and withdrew from rule; he died about 1049. Later art portrays him as Viṣṇu riding Garuḍa, as in the Belahan statue. Under his patronage the poet Mpu Kanwa composed the Arjunawiwāha, an Old Javanese poem on Arjuna's penance and winning of weapons from Śiva, often read as an allegory of the king's own career.

events.title: Trilocanapāla, last Śāhi
events.description: Trilocanapāla was the last important ruler of the Hindu Śāhi dynasty. Defeated by Mahmūd of Ghazni and driven from the Punjab, he sought help from the Candellas and Kashmir. He was killed, probably by his own troops, in 1021 or thereabouts. Al-Bīrūnī, writing soon after, speaks well of the Śāhi rulers, calling them noble in character. The end of the line left the Ghaznavids in control of the north-west and the Punjab plains.

events.title: Rājendra's Gaṅgā expedition
events.description: Rājendra Cōḻa sent an army in about 1023 some 1,600 kilometres north through Odisha to Bengal, where it defeated the Pāla king. Its purpose was religious and symbolic: it brought back water of the Gaṅgā in golden pots, carried on the heads of defeated kings according to his inscription. He poured it into a great reservoir at his new capital, named "the city of the Cōḻa who took the Gaṅgā".

events.title: Kṣemarāja's Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam
events.description: Kṣemarāja was a disciple of Abhinavagupta. His Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam, "The Heart of Recognition," sums up the Pratyabhijñā philosophy in twenty short sūtras with a commentary. It presents the idea that universal consciousness (citi) freely manifests the world through its power, and that a person can recognise this in their own experience. Because it is brief and clear, it is often used as an introduction to Kashmiri Śaiva thought.

events.title: Cōḻa naval raid on Śrīvijaya
events.description: About 1025 a Cōḻa fleet crossed the Bay of Bengal and attacked the maritime empire of Śrīvijaya, which controlled the straits between India and China. Rājendra's inscription lists the ports taken, among them Palembang in Sumatra and Kedah in Malaya, and the capture of the king with his jewelled war-gate. No Indian state had mounted an overseas expedition on this scale; its motive was probably control of trade.

events.title: Somanātha sacked by Mahmūd of Ghazni
events.description: In January 1026 Mahmūd of Ghazni attacked Prabhāsa Paṭṭana in Saurashtra, site of the Somanātha temple, one of the twelve jyotirliṅgas. Persian chroniclers say that the temple was plundered, its liṅga broken and its treasure taken away. Sanskrit and Jaina sources say that the Caulukya king Bhīma I rebuilt it, and Somanātha was rebuilt and damaged again in later centuries. Historians use the event to study memory as well as history: its Persian and Indian narratives are quite different in emphasis.

events.title: Modhera Sun temple
events.description: The Sun temple at Modhera in Gujarat was built in 1026–27 under the Solaṅkī king Bhīma I, at about the time of Mahmūd's raid on Somanātha. It is aligned so that at the equinoxes the rising sun shone through the hall onto the image. In front lies a rectangular stepped tank whose sides are lined with 108 miniature shrines. events.title: Kandāriyā Mahādeva temple
events.description: The Kandāriyā Mahādeva, built about 1030 by the Candella king Vidyādhara, is the largest and most perfect temple at Khajurāho. Its main tower, thirty-one metres high, is surrounded by eighty-four smaller replicas of itself that climb toward the summit like foothills. Nearly nine hundred figures, most about a metre high, cover the walls inside and out. It is dedicated to Śiva as lord of the mountain cave.

events.title: Al-Bīrūnī's Kitāb al-Hind
events.description: Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī, a scientist from Central Asia, was brought to Ghazni by Mahmūd and spent years in the conquered Punjab. He learned Sanskrit, read the Gītā, Patañjali and the astronomical texts with pandits, and rendered a text of Patañjali's Yoga and a Sāṃkhya work into Arabic. About 1030 he wrote the Kitāb al-Hind, a survey of Indian thought and science remarkable for its fairness. He says frankly that Mahmūd's raids ruined the country's prosperity and scattered Hindu learning to places his hand could not reach.

events.title: Vimala Vasahī, Mount Ābū
events.description: The Vimala Vasahī is a Jaina temple on Mount Ābū in Rajasthan, built in 1031 by Vimala Śāh, a minister of the Solaṅkī (Caulukya) king Bhīma I. Dedicated to Ādinātha, the first Tīrthaṅkara, it is built wholly of white marble, with intricate carving on its ceilings and pillars. It is one of the Dilwāṛā temples, and it is the best known of the group for its craftsmanship, and still visited by pilgrims and tourists.

events.title: Battle of Bahraich (tradition)
events.description: According to a legend preserved in the Persian Mirāt-i-Masʿūdī (17th century), Ghāzī Sālār Masʿūd, said to be a nephew of Mahmūd of Ghazni, was killed in battle at Bahraich in 1033 by a local Hindu king named Suheldev (Suhaldev). His tomb at Bahraich became a major shrine visited by Muslims and Hindus alike. Historians doubt the details because the earliest sources are much later, and Suheldev has been celebrated in modern times as a local hero.

events.title: Bhojeśvara temple at Bhojpur
events.description: The Bhojeśvara temple at Bhojpur near Bhopal is traditionally attributed to the Paramāra king Bhoja and dates to the eleventh century. It was never completed. It holds a single large Śiva liṅga, about eighteen feet high, on a massive platform. The surrounding rocks and the site have lines and plans engraved, which are thought to be builders' working drawings, and a ramp used for lifting stones can be seen. The site shows how large Indian temples were planned and built.

events.title: Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram temple
events.description: After his northern campaign, Rājendra I founded a new capital, Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram, "the city of the Cōḻa who took the Gaṅgā," and built a great Śiva temple there in the 1030s. It has a tall curved-sided vimāna and elaborate sculptures, and is considered a counterpart to Rājarāja's Tañjāvūr temple. Together with the temples at Tañjāvūr and Dārāsuram, it is part of the UNESCO site "Great Living Chola Temples."

events.title: Karṇa Kalacuri
events.description: Karṇa, son of Gāṅgeyadeva, ruled the Kalacuri kingdom of Tripurī from around 1041 and was known as Lakṣmī-Karṇa. His inscriptions claim wide conquests, and he fought campaigns against neighbours including the Candellas and the Paramāras, sometimes allying with Bhīma I of Gujarat. He built the Karṇameru temple of Śiva at Kāśī. His successors could not hold the kingdom together.

events.title: Hindu confederacy retakes Hansi and Nagarkoṭ
events.description: The Persian historian Firishta, writing centuries later, says that in 1043 a number of Hindu rulers, led by the king of Delhi, drove Ghaznavid garrisons out of Hansi, Thānesar and Nagarkoṭ in the Himalayan foothills. The image of the goddess at Nagarkoṭ (Kāṅgṛā) was said to have been restored, and the confederates then besieged Lahore. The Ghaznavid ruler was able to hold the city. Since Firishta's account is late, historians treat the details with caution.

events.title: Besakih, Bali's mother temple
events.description: Besakih is the largest and most sacred temple complex of Bali, on the slopes of Mount Agung, the island's highest volcano. It is made up of many shrines on rising terraces, and the oldest are thought to go back to the period around the eleventh century, with centuries of additions after. It serves as a place where communities of the whole island make offerings. The complex reflects the Balinese form of Hinduism, which developed from Śaiva and Buddhist traditions of Java.

events.title: Rāmānuja and the open mantra
events.description: According to Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition, Rāmānuja went to Tirukkōṣṭiyūr to learn the aṣṭākṣara mantra (Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya) from Gōṣṭhīpūrṇa (Tirukkōṣṭiyūr Nambi), who made him promise to keep it secret. Rāmānuja climbed onto the temple tower and proclaimed it aloud to everyone, saying he would accept punishment for the sake of others. Nambi, the story says, was moved and honoured him as Emperumānār. The story is a famed example of the tradition's openness to all castes.

events.title: Bhoramdeo, Barsūr and the temples of Dakṣiṇa Kosala
events.description: The region of Dakṣiṇa Kosala, now Chhattisgarh, has temples from the early medieval period. The Bhoramdeo temple, near Kawardhā, built by the Nāga dynasty, is called the "Khajurāho of Chhattisgarh" for its sculptures. At Barsūr in Bastar, the Chindaka Nāga rulers built temples in the 11th century. The region is less known than others, but these monuments show the spread of Nāgara-style temple architecture in the forests of central India.

events.title: Liṅgarāja temple
events.description: The Liṅgarāja, of the eleventh century, is the largest temple of Bhubaneśvara, with a tower fifty-five metres high whose curved outline defines the Odishan style. It has four halls in a row: for offerings, for dance, for assembly, and the sanctum. The liṅga here is worshipped as both Śiva and Viṣṇu, with basil leaves and bilva leaves together. Some 150 smaller shrines stand in its compound.

events.title: Īśānaśiva and Somaśambhu Śaiva ritual manuals
events.description: Two Śaiva ritual manuals are placed in the eleventh century. The Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati, attributed to Īśānaśiva, and the Somaśambhupaddhati, by Somaśambhu, who is associated with the Śaiva Siddhānta tradition, give step-by-step instructions on initiation (dīkṣā), daily worship and temple rites, along with domestic ceremonies. They were widely used and were later commented on, and they show how the Śaiva Siddhānta, a dualist school, organised practice in South and Central India.

events.title: Somadeva's Kathāsaritsāgara
events.description: The Kathāsaritsāgara, "Ocean of the Streams of Story," is a collection of tales in Sanskrit verse, of about 22,000 verses in eighteen books. Somadeva composed it in Kashmir for Queen Sūryamatī. It is based on Guṇāḍhya's lost Bṛhatkathā, written in Paiśācī, and contains fairy stories, animal fables, tales of magic and love and the frame story of Udayana and of Naravāhanadatta. It was an important source of story material across Indian and, later, world literature.

events.title: Devī Bhāgavata and Kālikā Purāṇas
events.description: Two Purāṇas of the early second millennium present the Goddess as the supreme reality. The Devī Bhāgavata, in twelve books, retells many Purāṇic stories with Devī at the centre, and includes the Devī Gītā, a philosophical teaching in the manner of the Bhagavad Gītā. The Kālikā Purāṇa, probably composed in Assam or Bengal, deals with Kālī and Śiva's consort in various forms, details rules for her worship, including animal sacrifice, and has much to say of the Kāmākhyā shrine near Guwahati. Both shaped the Śākta culture of eastern India.

events.title: Śāradātilaka and Prapañcasāra
events.description: These two Sanskrit manuals gather the rules of mantra worship into orderly systems. The Śāradātilaka, ascribed to Lakṣmaṇadeśika, sets out deity mantras, yantras, initiation and daily rites in full. The Prapañcasāra, traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara although scholars doubt this, begins with a cosmology and moves to mantra practice. Both were written in a tantric milieu but were adopted by orthodox Smārta households, who practised the worship of Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Śiva and the Devī through them. They helped bring tantric methods into mainstream temple and home ritual in both north and south India.

events.title: Yādavaprakāśa, Rāmānuja’s first teacher
events.description: Yādavaprakāśa of Kāñcīpuram was a teacher of Advaita leaning toward Bhedābheda, the view that the world is both different and not different from Brahman. Tradition makes him the first guru of Rāmānuja, who disagreed with his readings of the Upaniṣads and left his school. Later accounts say Yādavaprakāśa was won over and became Rāmānuja's disciple under the name Govinda Jīyar. He is credited with the Yatidharmasamuccaya, a manual on the duties of renunciants, and is a useful marker of the intellectual world in which Viśiṣṭādvaita emerged.

events.title: Bhoja’s Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra and mechanical devices
events.description: King Bhoja of the Paramāras of Dhārā was a patron and author. His Rājamṛgāṅka, a short work, is generally taken to be a treatise on astronomical calculation. The Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra, a large treatise on architecture and town planning attributed to him, devotes a chapter to yantras, mechanical devices, including fountains and moving figures and a flying wooden bird. It gives instructions rather than proof of working machines. Bhoja's court, with its scholars, made Dhārā a famous centre of learning in the eleventh century.

events.title: Civavākkiyar, the Tamil Siddha poet
events.description: Civavākkiyar was a Tamil Siddha poet whose verses are known for their bold language. He mocks caste divisions, ritual worship of images and empty rituals, and urges direct knowledge of the self. His date is uncertain, and various times have been proposed, and some verses may be by later poets. He belongs to the Siddha tradition of Tamil Nadu, in which yogis wrote in colloquial Tamil, and his songs are still known.

events.title: Surapāla's Vṛkṣāyurveda, a treatise on plants
events.description: The Vṛkṣāyurveda ascribed to Surapāla, from perhaps the eleventh century or somewhat later, is a Sanskrit treatise on plants. It covers the choosing and preparation of soil, planting of trees and gardens, seed treatment, grafting, watering, protection against pests and diseases, and ways to make trees flower and fruit out of season. It is one of the few surviving works on Indian horticulture and arboriculture and shows that the Āyurvedic idea of care for living bodies was extended to the plant world.

events.title: Preah Vihear, Śiva's mountain temple
events.description: Preah Vihear stands on a cliff of the Dângrêk range, some 525 metres above the Cambodian plain. It was built for Śiva, worshipped there as Śikhareśvara, 'lord of the peak', and as Bhadreśvara. Work began as early as the ninth century, and the surviving complex is mostly of the reigns of Sūryavarman I (1006–1050) and Sūryavarman II (1113–1150).¶A line of gateways and causeways climbs the ridge to a sanctuary at the cliff edge. The temple later became a Buddhist site. In 1962 the International Court of Justice ruled by nine votes to three that it lies in Cambodia, and it was inscribed by UNESCO in 2008, which revived the border dispute with Thailand.

events.title: Gunung Kawi rock-cut candis at Tampaksiring
events.description: Gunung Kawi, on both sides of the Pakerisan river at Tampaksiring in Bali, is a group of ten shrines cut into niches in a cliff, five on the east bank and five on the west. They are dated to the eleventh century and are thought to be funerary monuments of the Udayana dynasty, commonly connected with King Anak Wungsu and his queens. One theory ties the eastern group to King Udayana, his queen and their sons.¶An inscription on the north shrine of the eastern group reads 'haji lumah ing jalu', which is taken to mean the king made a temple here. The monuments belong to the period of Hindu-Buddhist Bali before the arrival of Javanese rule and are one of the finest examples of rock-cut shrines in Indonesia.

events.title: Battle of Koppam
events.description: The Battle of Koppam in 1054 was fought on the Tuṅgabhadrā between the Cōḻa king Rājādhirāja I and the Western Cālukya king Someśvara I. Rājādhirāja was killed on his elephant while leading the attack, but his brother Rājendra II took the crown on the field and turned the battle into a Cōḻa victory. The wars continued, and at Kūḍal-Saṅgamam in about 1062 the Cōḻas again defeated Someśvara. The conflict was about control of the Vengī region and the Deccan.

events.title: Brahmeśvara and Rājarāṇī temples
events.description: The Rājarāṇī temple at Bhubaneśvara was built in the 11th century and is known for its sculptures of graceful women and guardians of the directions, and it was never consecrated. The Brahmeśvara temple, built in the mid-11th century, is credited in its inscription to Kolāvatī Devī, the mother of the Somavaṁśī king Udyotakeśarī. Both are examples of the mature Kaliṅga style, with a tall curved tower, and they lead toward the later Liṅgarāja temple.

events.title: Kṣemendra's Daśāvatāracarita
events.description: Kṣemendra, a Kashmiri poet of the mid-11th century, was known for condensing long works into short poems. He composed epitomes of the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata (the Rāmāyaṇamañjarī and Bhāratamañjarī), the Bṛhatkathāmañjarī, and the Daśāvatāracarita, which recounts the ten incarnations of Viṣṇu. He also wrote satires, such as Samayamātṛkā about a courtesan's cunning, that poke fun at social types. His work reveals the lively literary life of Kashmir.

events.title: Ambarnāth Śiva temple
events.description: The Ambarnāth temple, near Mumbai in Thane district, was built by a Śilāhāra king and is dated by an inscription to Śaka 982, or 1060 CE. Its building is in the Bhūmija style, with a pillared hall and a carved tower, and its exterior has fine sculpture including images of Śiva and goddesses. The temple lies on the banks of a river, and it is one of the best preserved temples from the Śilāhāra dynasty in the Konkan.

events.title: Rāṇī-kī-Vāv stepwell at Pāṭaṇ
events.description: At Pāṭaṇ, the old capital of Gujarat, Queen Udayamatī built a stepwell in memory of her husband Bhīma I in the later eleventh century. It descends seven storeys, some twenty-seven metres, to the water, and its walls carry over five hundred large sculptures, chiefly the avatāras of Viṣṇu and celestial women. Silted up by a river flood, it was buried for seven centuries and excavated only in the 1980s.

events.title: Kṛṣṇa Miśra's Prabodhacandrodaya
events.description: This Sanskrit play is an allegory of the soul's liberation. Its characters are abstractions: Mind, Delusion, Passion, Wisdom, Faith and others. They fight a war in which Viveka (discrimination) and Vedānta overcome Kāma and Moha, and the Supreme Self at last recovers its awareness. Kṛṣṇa Miśra wrote it in the later eleventh century and, according to tradition, it was staged before King Kīrtivarman of the Candella dynasty, whose victory over the Kalacuri king Karṇa is celebrated in it. It also satirises Jaina, Buddhist and Cārvāka figures, and it was widely imitated by later allegorical dramas.

events.title: Kulottuṅga I unites Cōḻa and Eastern Cālukya lines
events.description: Kulottuṅga I, son of an Eastern Cālukya father and a Cōḻa mother, became Cōḻa king in 1070, bringing the two families together. Tamil inscriptions say that he abolished tolls, earning the title Śuṅgam Taviṛtta, "he who removed tolls." He sent a trade embassy to China in 1077. His long reign was relatively peaceful, but the Cōḻa empire lost control of Laṅkā and, later, of other regions.

events.title: Vikramāditya VI and the Cālukya-Vikrama era
events.description: Vikramāditya VI came to the Western Cālukya throne in 1076, and began a new era, the Cālukya-Vikrama era, to mark his reign. He ruled for fifty years from Kalyāṇī, and his court included the poet Bilhaṇa and the jurist Vijñāneśvara, author of the Mitākṣarā, the most widely used commentary on the Yājñavalkya Smṛti. His kingdom was prosperous and mostly peaceful, and it saw great activity in law, literature and temple building.

gitaQuote.verse: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत । अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥ परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् । धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur; Madhvācārya Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga
events.description: Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga of the Eastern Gaṅga dynasty came to the throne in 1078, and conquered Utkala, uniting Odisha's coastal regions under one power. Tradition and later inscriptions credit him with beginning the great Jagannātha temple at Purī, which was completed by his successors. The temple became Odisha's main religious centre, and Coḍagaṅga's rule marks the Gaṅgas' emergence as a major power in eastern India.

gitaQuote.verse: पिताहमस्य जगतो माता धाता पितामहः । वेद्यं पवित्रमोंकार ऋक्साम यजुरेव च ॥ गतिर्भर्ता प्रभुः साक्षी निवासः शरणं सुहृत् । प्रभवः प्रलयः स्थानं निधानं बीजमव्ययम् ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ | vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛk sāma yajur eva ca || gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt | prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||
gitaQuote.translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer and the grandsire. I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the creation and dissolution, the foundation and the imperishable seed.

events.title: Udayeśvara temple, Udaypur
events.description: The Udayeśvara temple at Udaypur, in Madhya Pradesh, was built by the Paramāra king Udayāditya, who ruled in the late 11th century, and an inscription dates its completion to about 1080. It is regarded as one of the finest temples in the Bhūmija style, a form of Nāgara architecture with a tower made of clustered miniature shrines. Its red sandstone walls are richly carved. It continues as a place of worship, and it is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.

events.title: Bilhaṇa and Vikramāṅkadevacarita
events.description: Bilhaṇa was a Kashmiri poet who left his homeland and settled at the Western Cālukya court of Vikramāditya VI at Kalyāṇī. His Vikramāṅkadevacarita is a poem on the life of his patron, with historical details about the dynasty. The Caurapañcāśikā, a set of fifty love verses attributed to him, tells of a poet awaiting execution who recalls his lover. Bilhaṇa's career shows the movement of scholars across India.

events.title: Gāhaḍavālas of Kāśī and Kanauj
events.description: The Gāhaḍavālas established themselves in the Gaṅgā plain around 1090 under Candradeva, with Kanauj and Kāśī as major centres. Candradeva's inscriptions say he protected tīrthas such as Kāśī and Ayodhyā and gave many gifts to Brahmins. They mention a tax called the turuṣka-daṇḍa, possibly levied to fund defence against Turkic attacks, though historians interpret it in different ways. The dynasty lasted until the Ghurid conquest at the end of the 12th century.

events.title: Siddharāja Jayasiṃha
events.description: Jayasiṃha Siddharāja, who ruled Gujarat from 1094, brought the Caulukya kingdom to its height. He conquered Mālwā and expanded the kingdom's boundaries. He is credited with the Rudra Mahālaya, a huge Śaiva temple at Siddhapur, now in ruins, and the Sahasraliṅga tank at Patan. He supported Śaiva and Jaina scholars, including the polymath Hemacandra. Later Gujarati tradition remembers him as a model king.

events.title: Sena dynasty of Bengal
events.description: The Senas were of Karṇāṭa origin, from southern India, and the dynasty's ancestors had settled in Rāḍha in Bengal. Vijayasena, who ruled for many decades from about 1097, overthrew the declining Pālas in much of Bengal. His successors Ballālasena and Lakṣmaṇasena were Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava patrons, and the poet Jayadeva, author of the Gītagovinda, was at Lakṣmaṇasena's court. Muhammad Bakhtiyār Khaljī overran the capital at Nadiyā around 1204, according to Muslim chroniclers.

events.title: Nānyadeva's Karṇāṭa dynasty of Mithilā
events.description: Nānyadeva, a ruler of Karṇāṭa origin, founded a dynasty in Mithilā about 1097, with its capital at Simraungaṛh, now on the Nepal border. His line ruled Tirhut until 1324, a time of notable Sanskrit learning in Mithilā. In that year, Ghiyās-ud-dīn Tughluq captured Simraungaṛh. Tradition says that the last king, Harisiṃhadeva, escaped to Nepal and took the goddess Taleju with him, who later became the tutelary deity of the Malla kings.

events.title: Rāmānuja at Melkoṭe
events.description: Tradition says a Cōḻa king, a zealous Śaiva, demanded that Rāmānuja sign a statement that none is greater than Śiva. A disciple went in his place and was blinded; Rāmānuja escaped to the Hoysaḷa kingdom in Karnataka. There he lived twelve years, won over the king, restored the Viṣṇu temple at Melkoṭe, and arranged that the outcaste community who had helped him could enter it on certain days each year.

events.title: Mitākṣarā of Vijñāneśvara
events.description: Vijñāneśvara, at the court of the Cālukya king Vikramāditya VI about 1100, wrote a commentary on the Yājñavalkya Smṛti that became a legal treatise in its own right. Its key doctrine is that a son acquires a share in ancestral property by birth, so that a father cannot dispose of it alone. British courts applied it as the governing law of Hindus across most of India outside Bengal and Assam, where the Dāyabhāga prevailed. It remained influential until the Hindu Succession Act of 1956.

events.title: Rāmānuja’s Śrī Bhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtra
events.description: Rāmānuja's commentary on the Brahma Sūtra is the foundation of Viśiṣṭādvaita, "non-dualism of the qualified". It opens with a long attack on Śaṅkara's doctrine that the world is illusion.¶His own view is that there is only one reality, Brahman, identified with Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa, but souls and matter are real and belong to him as a body belongs to its soul. Liberation is not merging into a featureless absolute; it is eternal loving service in God's presence. The work made devotional theism intellectually equal to Advaita.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Rāmānuja's Gītā Bhāṣya and Vedārthasaṅgraha
events.description: Rāmānuja, the philosopher of Viśiṣṭādvaita ("qualified non-dualism"), taught that the world and souls are real but are the body of Brahman, identified with Viṣṇu. His Vedārthasaṅgraha summarises Vedic teaching, and his Gītā Bhāṣya reads the Gītā as a teaching on devotion (bhakti), which he links with surrender (prapatti). The three Gadyas, short prose works attributed to him, express this surrender. His major work is the Śrī Bhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtra.

events.title: Kōyil Oḻugu and Rāmānuja’s temple reforms
events.description: The Kōyil Oḻugu is a chronicle of the Śrīraṅgam temple, compiled in later centuries, that credits Rāmānuja with reorganising the temple's administration and worship. Tradition says that he settled the roles of priests and servants, regulated daily rites according to the Pāñcarātra texts and set up festivals. Whatever the details, Śrīraṅgam became the chief centre of Śrīvaiṣṇavism and a model of the large Tamil temple that serves as a social, economic and religious institution.

events.title: Dāyabhāga of Jīmūtavāhana
events.description: The Dāyabhāga is a treatise on inheritance by Jīmūtavāhana, and became the main authority on inheritance in Bengal. Unlike the Mitākṣarā school followed elsewhere, which gave sons a right by birth in ancestral property, the Dāyabhāga held that a son's right arises only on the father's death. It also based inheritance on the capacity to offer religious oblations (piṇḍa). British colonial courts later applied it to Hindus in Bengal.

events.title: Aparārka and Lakṣmīdhara's Kṛtyakalpataru
events.description: Lakṣmīdhara, a minister of the Gāhaḍavāla king Govindacandra, compiled the Kṛtyakalpataru, a large digest (nibandha) in fourteen books gathering rules on rites, vows, gifts, pilgrimage and law from many texts. It was one of the first major works of this kind. Aparārka, a Śilāhāra king of the Konkan, wrote a well-known commentary on the Yājñavalkya Smṛti. Digests like these set the way later Dharmaśāstra was organised and used.

events.title: Hemacandra, Jaina polymath of Gujarat
events.description: Hemacandra, a Jaina monk at the Solaṅkī court of Gujarat in the twelfth century, was called "the omniscient of the Kali age". He wrote a complete grammar of Sanskrit and the Prakrits, dictionaries, a treatise on poetics, a universal history of the Jaina heroes, and a work on yoga. According to Jaina sources, King Kumārapāla forbade the killing of animals throughout Gujarat under his influence.

events.title: Gorakṣanātha and the Nātha Sampradāya
events.description: Gorakhnāth, disciple of Matsyendra, is the great organiser of the Nātha yogīs, placed around the eleventh or twelfth century. Legends about him are told from Punjab to Bengal and Nepal, where the Gorkhās take their name from him. His followers wear large earrings through split ears. The physical yoga of postures, breath retention and inner energy, haṭha yoga, is traced to him. His chief seat is at Gorakhpur.

events.title: Nava Nātha and the eighty-four Siddhas
events.description: The Nāthas are a yogic order that looks back to Matsyendranātha and Gorakṣanātha, and tradition counts nine Nāthas, set beside a list of eighty-four Siddhas, wonder-working adepts also remembered in Tibetan Buddhist tradition. Between about the tenth and thirteenth centuries these ascetic lineages, with their hatha-yoga practices and vernacular songs, spread from Bengal and Nepal across north India to Maharashtra. Their teachers often came from outside Brahmanical circles. Their influence reached later saints such as Jñāneśvara, whose own guru-line is traced to the Nāths, and the Sant poets of north India.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Amṛtasiddhi, earliest haṭha-yoga text
events.description: The Amṛtasiddhi is the earliest known text to teach the techniques later grouped as haṭha-yoga. It describes bodily mudrās, bandhas and the retention of bindu (semen, or the vital essence) as the means of conquering death and realising an immortal body. Its ideas draw on both Buddhist Vajrayāna and Śaiva sources, and its authorship is traditionally linked with the Siddha Virūpa. A Nepalese manuscript colophon gives the date 1160, which fixes the latest point by which the work existed. Later Nātha manuals, including the Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā, inherit many of its practices.

events.title: Cakrapāṇidatta's Āyurveda Dīpikā
events.description: Cakrapāṇidatta worked in Bengal under the Pāla kings and is among the most respected medieval writers on Āyurveda. His Āyurveda Dīpikā is a line-by-line commentary on the Caraka Saṃhitā that explains difficult terms and records variant readings, and he wrote another on the Suśruta Saṃhitā. His Cikitsāsaṅgraha, a practical manual of treatments, is also called the Cakradatta. Physicians in Bengal and elsewhere relied on his explanations, and his commentary is often the way later readers have understood the Caraka text.

events.title: Rasa-śāstra and Nāgārjuna's Rasaratnākara
events.description: Rasa-śāstra is the Indian tradition of alchemy and mineral medicine, in which mercury (rasa) is purified and combined with sulphur and metals to prepare medicines and, in the tantric imagination, a body free of decay. The Rasaratnākara is attributed to a Nāgārjuna, a name shared with the Buddhist philosopher, though the author is probably a later alchemist. The text gives methods for processing mercury and other minerals. From around this period such works, with Śaiva and Siddha associations, made metallic preparations a lasting part of Āyurvedic pharmacy.

events.title: Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha composed in Kashmir
events.description: The Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha is a vast poem, some 29,000 verses, in which the sage Vasiṣṭha instructs the despondent young Rāma through a succession of stories within stories. It teaches that the world is a long dream of consciousness, and that liberation comes through one's own effort and inquiry while living an active life. It is thought to have been composed in Kashmir, with scholars proposing dates between the tenth and twelfth centuries. It was translated into Persian for the Mughals.

gitaQuote.verse: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत । अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥ परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् । धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur; Madhvācārya Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Gaṇeśa and Mudgala Purāṇas
events.description: The Gaṇeśa Purāṇa and the Mudgala Purāṇa are the main texts of the Gāṇapatyas, devotees who see Gaṇeśa as the supreme Brahman and creator. They were composed between roughly the eleventh and fourteenth centuries, though the dating is uncertain. The Mudgala Purāṇa describes eight incarnations of Gaṇeśa, each defeating a demon who embodies a human fault such as pride or anger. The Gaṇeśa Gītā, inside the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, retells the Bhagavad Gītā with Gaṇeśa as speaker. Maharashtra became the centre of the Gāṇapatya tradition, with the eight Aṣṭavināyaka shrines near Pune.

events.title: Kūreśa and Parāśara Bhaṭṭa
events.description: Kūreśa was among Rāmānuja's closest disciples and served as his scribe when the Śrī Bhāṣya was composed. Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition says a Cōḻa ruler hostile to Vaiṣṇavas had him blinded, though the king's identity and the details are debated by historians. His son Parāśara Bhaṭṭa became a leading teacher at Śrīraṅgam and wrote a commentary on the Viṣṇu Sahasranāma, the thousand names of Viṣṇu, the Bhagavad-guṇa-darpaṇa, which treats each name as a statement of divine qualities. Together they helped consolidate Rāmānuja's movement after his time.

gitaQuote.translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer and the grandsire. I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the creation and dissolution, the foundation and the imperishable seed.

events.title: Tirukkurukaippirāṉ Piḷḷāṉ's Six Thousand
events.description: Tirukkurukaippirāṉ Piḷḷāṉ was a disciple of Rāmānuja who wrote the earliest commentary on the Tiruvāymoḻi, the great Tamil hymn cycle of the Āḻvār Nammāḻvār. It is called the Āṟāyirappaṭi, the "six thousand," after its length in units of thirty-two syllables. It is written in Maṇipravāḷa, a "gem and coral" blend of Tamil and Sanskrit that let it speak both to Tamil devotees and to scholars. Later commentaries on the same hymns, of larger size, built on its approach.

events.title: Madan Kāmdev and Sūryapahāṛ in Assam
events.description: In Assam, early medieval temple remains survive in several places. Sūryapahāṛ, in Goalpara, has rock-cut shrines and carvings related to Sūrya and Śiva, and Madan Kāmdev, in Kāmarūpa, is a ruined group of temples with fine sculpture, usually dated to the 10th to 12th centuries under the Pāla dynasty of Kāmarūpa. The sculpture links Assam to the broader traditions of eastern India, with local features. Many buildings fell in ruins after earthquakes.

events.title: Smārta tradition and pañcāyatana worship
events.description: The Smārta tradition consists of Brahmins who follow the smṛtis, the law books, and generally follow Advaita Vedānta as taught by Śaṅkara. They practise pañcāyatana pūjā, the worship of five deities, Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Śiva and Devī, with one chosen as the main focus. Communities such as Tamil Ayyars, Deśasthas of Maharashtra and Nambūtiris of Kerala often belong to it. Its inclusive approach to deities has made it a broad and orthodox stream within Hinduism.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ | ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||
gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.

events.title: Vidyākara's Subhāṣitaratnakośa
events.description: Vidyākara compiled this anthology of roughly 1,700 Sanskrit verses around 1100, apparently while living in a Buddhist monastery, Jagaddala, in Bengal. It gathers short poems by some two hundred authors, arranged by theme, such as the gods, love, the seasons and the nature of kings, and preserves many poets whose other work is lost. The Sanskrit court poetry it records is largely secular in tone, though devotional verses to Hindu and Buddhist deities stand side by side. The text survived in Tibet and Nepal and was edited in the twentieth century by D. D. Kosambi and V. V. Gokhale.

events.title: Mammaṭa's Kāvyaprakāśa
events.description: Mammaṭa, a Kashmiri scholar, wrote the Kāvyaprakāśa as a compact handbook on poetry in ten chapters. It defines what makes a poem, classifies its meanings and figures of speech, and defends the theory of suggestion (dhvani) put forward by Ānandavardhana and the rasa theory of Bharata and Abhinavagupta. Because it joins the major earlier schools into one orderly system, it became the standard textbook of Sanskrit poetics across India. Dozens of commentaries were written on it, and students of literature in traditional schools were still reading it well into modern times.

events.title: Śivāditya’s Saptapadārthī
events.description: Śivāditya wrote the Saptapadārthī, a short text that combined Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika into a single system. Vaiśeṣika had six categories: substance, quality, action, universal, particular and inherence. Śivāditya added absence (abhāva), as a seventh. It was an introductory manual that was widely used in teaching, and the combined school, called Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, then became the standard form in which the two systems were studied in the later centuries.

events.title: Phanom Rung, Śaiva sanctuary on a volcano rim
events.description: Phanom Rung stands on the rim of an extinct volcano in Buriram province, Thailand. It was built in several phases from the tenth to the thirteenth century as a Khmer Hindu temple, and its central sanctuary is credited to Sūryavarman II in the twelfth century. The main tower once housed a Śiva liṅga. Its lintels show Hindu stories, including a dancing Śiva and the reclining Viṣṇu Anantaśayin.¶The Viṣṇu lintel was stolen in the 1960s and bought by the Art Institute of Chicago in 1967. It was returned in 1988 and put back in its place that December, after the Thai Fine Arts Department restored the complex between 1971 and 1988. The site shows Khmer Śaiva temple-building far west of Angkor.

events.title: Viṣṇuvardhana expands the Hoysaḷa kingdom
events.description: Viṣṇuvardhana (Bittideva) made the Hoysaḷas an independent power in southern Karnataka. He captured Talakāḍ from the Cōḻas, according to inscriptions, in about 1116, and gained control of Gaṅgavāḍi. Tradition says that he was converted from Jainism to Vaiṣṇavism through Rāmānuja, who found refuge in his realm; whether or not this is true, he supported both Jaina and Vaiṣṇava institutions, and built or endowed the Cennakeśava temple at Belūr in 1117.

events.title: Arṇorāja and Ajayameru
events.description: Ajayarāja II founded Ajayameru, today's Ajmer, early in the twelfth century and made it the Cauhān capital. His son Arṇorāja, who ruled from about 1133 to 1150, fought the Turkic forces from the north-west and, according to inscriptions, defeated them, and then built the Ānā Sāgar lake at Ajmer. Arṇorāja was later defeated by Kumārapāla of Gujarat. The lake still lies at the heart of the city.

events.title: Mahādeva temple, Iṭagi
events.description: The Mahādeva temple at Iṭagi in Karnataka was built in 1112 by Mahādeva, a general of the Kalyāṇī Cālukya king Vikramāditya VI. An inscription calls it the "emperor among temples," devālayagaḷa cakravarti, in praise of its workmanship. It is a Dravida temple with a carved porch, richly decorated ceilings and pillars, and detailed carvings. It is an important example of the Later Cālukya style, which was a forerunner of Hoysaḷa art.

events.title: Sūryavarman II and Angkor Wat
events.description: Sūryavarman II of Cambodia built Angkor Wat in the first half of the twelfth century as a temple to Viṣṇu and probably as his own funerary monument. Its five towers represent the peaks of Mount Meru and its moat the ocean. The outer gallery carries nearly a kilometre of reliefs from the Rāmāyaṇa, the Mahābhārata and the churning of the ocean. It is the largest religious building in the world, and appears on Cambodia's flag.

events.title: Cennakeśava temple, Belūr
events.description: The temple of "handsome Keśava" at Belūr was begun in 1117 by the Hoysaḷa king Viṣṇuvardhana, by tradition to mark his victory over the Cōḻas, and took over a century to finish. Built of soft soapstone that hardens in air, it is carved like ivory. Forty-two bracket figures of dancers and musicians under the eaves are its glory; several are signed by their sculptors, which is rare in Indian art.

events.title: Hoysaḷeśvara temple, Haḷebīḍu
events.description: The Hoysaḷeśvara temple at Haḷebīḍu (ancient Dorasamudra), begun about 1121 under Viṣṇuvardhana's rule, is a twin-shrine temple dedicated to Śiva, with two linked sanctums, Hoysaḷeśvara and Śāntaleśvara. It is built of fine-grained soapstone and covered with elaborate friezes of elephants, horses, scenes from the Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata, and deities. The temple was never fully completed. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing for the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas.
