events.title: Jayasiṃha of Kashmir
events.description: Jayasiṃha ruled Kashmir from about 1128 to 1155 and was a patron of letters and a builder in the Jhelum valley. The historian Kalhaṇa completed his Rājataraṅgiṇī, a Sanskrit verse chronicle of Kashmir's kings, in his reign, around 1148. The poet Maṅkha wrote his Śrīkaṇṭhacarita, an epic on Śiva's destruction of Tripura, and the last canto lists scholars of the court. Jayasiṃha's reign was one of the last strong periods of Hindu rule before the Sultanate.

events.title: Someśvara III's Mānasollāsa
events.description: The Mānasollāsa, also called Abhilaṣitārthacintāmaṇi, is an encyclopaedia compiled in 1129 by the Cālukya king Someśvara III of Kalyāṇī. It covers statecraft, the duties of kings, medicine, horses and elephants, food and cooking, music, dance, painting, sports and games. It is a rare record of courtly life in the Deccan, describing recipes, entertainments and the arts as practised, and its sections on music and cuisine in particular are used by historians as a window into twelfth-century culture.

events.title: Nimbārka and the Dvaitādvaita school
events.description: Nimbārka founded the Dvaitādvaita school, which teaches that God, souls and the world are both different and non-different. His dates are debated, with proposals from the seventh to the thirteenth century. His short commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, the Vedānta-pārijāta-saurabha, states the doctrine in concise form, and his pupil Śrīnivāsa wrote a longer commentary, the Vedānta-kaustubha. The school is centred in Braj and is devoted to Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.

events.title: Birth of Basava (Basaveśvara)
events.description: Basava was born to a brāhmaṇa family at Bāgevāḍi in north Karnataka, in about 1131 according to most modern accounts, though some traditions give 1105. Legend says he tore off his sacred thread as a boy. He rose to be a minister and treasurer under the Kalacuri king Bijjala at Kalyāṇa. He taught devotion to Śiva alone, worn as a small liṅga on the body, the dignity of all honest work, and the equality of men and women of every caste. A vacana attributed to him says: "The rich will make temples for Śiva. What shall I, a poor man, do? My legs are pillars, my body the shrine."

events.title: Cēkkiḻār's Periya Purāṇam
events.description: Cēkkiḻār, chief minister of the Cōḻa king Kulottuṅga II in the twelfth century, wrote the "Great Purāṇa", the lives of the sixty-three Tamil Śaiva saints, in 4,253 verses. They include kings and brāhmaṇas but also a potter, a hunter, a fisherman, an untouchable farm labourer and three women. Each is shown reaching Śiva through extreme, sometimes shocking devotion. It is the twelfth and last book of the Tamil Śaiva canon.

events.title: Rāmānuja's passing at Śrīraṅgam
events.description: According to tradition, Rāmānuja lived for 120 years, from 1017 to 1137, and died at Śrīraṅgam. Many modern scholars place his life later, roughly 1077 to 1157. His body was entombed in a seated posture inside the temple precinct, and Śrīvaiṣṇavas believe that it remains preserved. The shrine in the temple's fifth enclosure, in which it is venerated, is visited by devotees.

events.title: Kumārapāla of Gujarat
events.description: Kumārapāla was a Caulukya king of Gujarat who ruled from 1143 to about 1172. The Jain scholar Hemacandra was his adviser, and Jaina sources describe him as an ardent follower who banned the slaughter of animals in his realm. He also rebuilt the Somanātha temple at Prabhāsa in stone, as an inscription of 1169 records. His reign is thus remembered both for Jaina influence and for continued royal patronage of Śaiva shrines.

events.title: Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī
events.description: Kalhaṇa, son of a Kashmiri minister, completed the Rājataraṅgiṇī, "River of Kings", in 1148–49. It is the outstanding work of historical writing in Sanskrit. He drew on earlier chronicles, inscriptions, land grants and coins, and says a historian should judge like a magistrate, free of love and hatred. His account becomes more detailed from the seventh century and is unsparing about his own times.

events.title: Vīraśaivas honour the Purātanas
events.description: The Vīraśaiva movement of Karnataka, led by Basavaṇṇa in the twelfth century, honoured earlier Śaiva saints as the Purātanas, the ancients. These included the sixty-three Tamil Nāyaṉārs, whose lives are told in Tamil texts such as Cēkkiḻār's Periya Purāṇam. The Kannada Vīraśaiva authors, therefore, saw themselves as heirs of a longer Śaiva devotional tradition that came from the Tamil country, and told their stories in Kannada.

events.title: Jagannātha temple at Purī
events.description: The present temple of Jagannātha was begun by the Eastern Gaṅga king Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga in the twelfth century; its tower is sixty-five metres high. The three deities are made of wood and replaced at intervals. Its kitchen feeds tens of thousands daily, and the food is shared without distinction of caste. Each summer the deities ride out on three immense chariots pulled by the crowd.

events.title: Śrīkaṇṭha's Śaiva Viśiṣṭādvaita
events.description: Śrīkaṇṭha wrote a commentary on the Brahma Sūtra that reads the text as teaching Śiva as the supreme Brahman, rather than Viṣṇu or an attribute-less absolute. In this reading the world and the souls are real parts or modes of Śiva, a position often called Śaiva Viśiṣṭādvaita, parallel to Rāmānuja's Vaiṣṇava system. His date and background are debated among scholars, with estimates running from the eleventh to the thirteenth century. The work was later taken up by Appayya Dīkṣita and by Vīraśaiva thinkers, who found in it a Vedāntic basis for their theology.

events.title: Kambaṉ’s Irāmāvatāram
events.description: Kambaṉ, placed by most scholars in the twelfth century, retold the Rāmāyaṇa in about ten thousand Tamil verses. He follows Vālmīki's story but makes Rāma fully divine, gives the demons tragic dignity, and sets the tale in a Tamil landscape of rivers and rice fields. Tamils regard the Irāmāvatāram as the summit of their literature, and he is called the emperor of poets.

events.title: Bhāskara II's Siddhānta Śiromaṇi
events.description: Bhāskarācārya completed his "Crown of Treatises" in 1150 at the age of thirty-six. Its first part, Līlāvatī, teaches arithmetic through charming puzzles addressed to a girl; the second, on algebra, gives a general method for solving equations of the form now called Pell's, six centuries before Europe. events.title: Śrīharṣa's Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya
events.description: Śrīharṣa, a poet and philosopher at the court of the Gāhaḍavāla kings at Kanauj, wrote this Advaita work to show that the definitions used by Nyāya logicians cannot survive rigorous questioning. events.title: Ballāla Sena and the Kulīna tradition
events.description: The Sena dynasty, Karṇāṭa in origin, ruled Bengal in the twelfth century and patronised Brahmanical learning. Ballāla Sena wrote the Dānasāgara on gifts and the Adbhutasāgara on omens. Later Bengali tradition credits him with ranking brāhmaṇas and kāyasthas into kulīna families, though historians doubt this. His son Lakṣmaṇa Sena's court at Nadia drew poets, among them Jayadeva, author of the Gītagovinda, and Dhoyī, who wrote the messenger-poem Pavanadūta. The Senas' Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva patronage shaped Bengal's religious culture until the Turkic conquest.

events.title: Ḍallaṇa's commentary on Suśruta
events.description: Ḍallaṇa, probably a physician in northern India of the twelfth century, wrote the Nibandhasaṅgraha, the fullest surviving commentary on the Suśruta Saṃhitā, India's classical text on surgery. He quotes earlier commentators whose own works are lost, discusses variant readings, and explains the procedures for incision, bone-setting, cataract surgery and plastic surgery of the nose. The Suśruta text circulated in several recensions, and Ḍallaṇa's work helped fix the version that later readers used. It is a principal source for understanding how surgery was taught in medieval India.

events.title: Airāvateśvara temple, Dārāsuram
events.description: Rājarāja II, who ruled from 1146 to 1173, built this temple of Śiva at Dārāsuram near Kumbakoṇam. Its mandapa is shaped like a stone chariot, with wheels and horses. The deity is named for Airāvata, Indra's elephant, who by tradition worshipped Śiva here to be cured of a curse. With the temples at Tañjāvūr and Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram, it is part of the UNESCO Great Living Cōḻa Temples.

events.title: Cōḻa enlargement of the Cidambaram temple

events.title: Vigraharāja IV Vīsaladeva
events.description: Vigraharāja IV was a Cauhān king of Ajmer, ruling from about 1150 to 1164. events.title: Siddharāma and Cennabasava
events.description: Siddharāma of Solāpur and Cennabasava, nephew of the reformer Basavaṇṇa at Kalyāṇa, were among the Śaraṇas, the saints of the Vīraśaiva movement who composed vacanas, short free-verse prose poems addressed to Śiva. Their lives are known mostly through later hagiographies. The Śūnyasampādane, compiled in later centuries, anthologises dialogues among the Śaraṇas on the nature of the liṅga and the path to union with Śiva. It is one of the main sources for the movement's teachings, though its editors reshaped older material.

events.title: Pañcācārya tradition
events.description: Vīraśaivas of the Pañcācārya tradition trace their religious authority to five ancestral teachers, said to have emerged from the liṅga of Śiva at five seats: Rambhāpurī, Ujjayinī, Kedāra, Śrīśaila and Kāśī. Each seat has a pīṭha, headed by a jagadguru. Within the community there is a long debate: some Lingāyat writers regard the movement as founded by Basavaṇṇa in the 12th century as a break from Vedic orthodoxy, while the Pañcācārya line stresses an older, Vedic-Āgamic origin. The five-seat framework remains central to Vīraśaiva institutional identity.

events.title: Rudra Mahālaya, Siddhapur

According to historians, it was damaged by Sultanate forces around 1300 and later, and parts were converted for use as a mosque, with a congregational mosque built in part from its materials. Pillars and gateways still stand and show its original scale.

events.title: Jaisalmer founded
events.description: Rāval Jaisal of the Bhāṭī clan, who were Yādava Rajputs, founded Jaisalmer in 1156 and moved his capital from Lodhruva to a new fort on Trikūṭa hill. The fort, built in golden sandstone, sits on an important caravan route across the Thar desert. It remains partly inhabited, and its Jaina and Hindu temples and merchants' mansions (havelīs) reflect the trade wealth the Bhāṭīs gained from caravans.

events.title: Aghoraśiva’s Kriyākramadyotikā
events.description: Aghoraśiva, a Śaiva Siddhānta ritual specialist at Cidambaram, wrote his manual of temple worship and initiation, the Kriyākramadyotikā, in 1158. It forms the ritual counterpart to the philosophical writings of the Meykaṇḍa school, which followed in the thirteenth century.

events.title: Anubhava Maṇṭapa at Kalyāṇa
events.description: At Kalyāṇa, capital of the Kalacuri king Bijjala, the minister Basava is remembered as the founder of a "hall of experience" where Vīraśaiva devotees, the śaraṇas, met to discuss spiritual life. Tradition says Allama Prabhu presided, and that members came from every caste and included women such as Akka Mahādevī, as well as Basava's nephew Cennabasava. They composed vacanas, short Kannada prose-poems addressed to Śiva that reject ritual hierarchy, birth-status and temple worship in favour of the personal liṅga worn on the body. Vacana literature became the founding scripture of Lingāyat tradition.

events.title: Akka Mahādevī
events.description: Mahādevī, a twelfth-century woman of Karnataka, considered herself married to Śiva, whom she called "lord white as jasmine". Pursued or briefly married by a local king, she left, discarding even her clothes, and walked covered only by her hair to the gathering of saints at Kalyāṇa, where she answered their testing questions. Her 430 short poems in Kannada are among the most intense love poetry addressed to God. She died young at Śrīśaila.

events.title: Kalacuri Bijjala's coup at Kalyāṇa
events.description: Bijjala II, a Kalacuri feudatory minister of the Western Cālukyas, took control of the throne at Kalyāṇa in about 1162. He kept Basava, later Basaveśvara, the founder of the Vīraśaiva movement, as a minister and treasurer. Under Bijjala's rule, Basava and the Śaraṇas developed the vacana literature in Kannada, which rejected caste hierarchy and ritual formalism. Bijjala died around 1167, and tradition links his death to conflict with the Śaraṇas, but accounts vary.

events.title: Rudradeva Kākatīya and the Thousand Pillar temple
events.description: In 1163 the Kākatīya king Rudradeva (Rudra I) consecrated a temple at Hanamkoṇḍa, his capital before Warangal. It is a triple shrine (trikūṭa), with three sanctums facing a large pillared hall. They are dedicated to Śiva as Rudreśvara, to Viṣṇu and to Sūrya. The building, in dark stone on a star-shaped platform, is known as the Thousand Pillar temple. events.title: Paramardi Candella
events.description: Paramardi, or Paramāla, was a Candella king of Bundelkhand who ruled in the later twelfth century. In 1182 he lost the city of Mahobā to the Cāhamāna king Pṛthvīrāja III, a defeat that is recalled in the Hindi folk epic of Ālhā and Ūdal, who fought for him. Kāliñjara, the great fort, fell to Qutb-ud-Dīn Aibak in 1203. After this the Candellas were reduced to a small regional power, though they had earlier built the temples at Khajurāho.

events.title: Upheaval at Kalyāṇa and the end of Bijjala
events.description: Later Vīraśaiva texts such as the thirteenth-century Basavapurāṇa tell that a marriage between a brāhmaṇa śaraṇa's daughter and the son of a cobbler-born śaraṇa shocked the Kalyāṇa court. King Bijjala is said to have ordered harsh punishment, and violence followed. The community scattered, and Basava withdrew to Kūḍalasaṅgama, where he died. Bijjala himself was killed soon after, according to tradition. Historians treat these accounts with caution, since the sources are devotional and written long afterwards, but the episode is remembered as the tragic end of a bold attempt to dissolve caste in religious life.

events.title: Ballāla II Hoysaḷa
events.description: Ballāla II, who came to the throne in 1173, led the Hoysaḷas from a subordinate position to full independence. He defeated the Sevuṇa (Yādava) king at Soratūr in 1190 and extended the kingdom over much of southern Karnataka. His reign of nearly half a century, to about 1220, was a time of peace and cultural growth. The Hoysaḷa temples at Belūr, Haḷebīḍu and Somanāthapura, famous for their dense sculpture on star-shaped plans, were built across the dynasty's rule, and hundreds of shrines are attributed to it.

events.title: Chams sack Angkor
events.description: In 1177 the Chams of Champa, in what is now Vietnam, attacked the Khmer empire by travelling up the Mekong and Tonlé Sap with a fleet and captured the capital, Yaśodharapura. The Khmer king was killed. A Khmer prince who became Jayavarman VII rallied his people, defeated the Chams, and was crowned in 1181. He then built a new capital at Angkor Thom, with the Bayon temple, and turned the empire towards Mahāyāna Buddhism, even as Hindu traditions continued at court.

events.title: Battle of Kāyadarā
events.description: In 1178 Muhammad of Ghor led his first major invasion of India across the desert toward Gujarat. The Solaṅkī king was a boy; his mother Nāyikīdevī, a princess from Goa, took command with her son on her lap, according to the chronicles. In a pass near Mount Abu her army routed the invaders so thoroughly that Ghor never attacked Gujarat again, and turned to the Punjab route instead.

events.title: Chand Bardāī and the Pṛthvīrāja Rāso tradition
events.description: The Pṛthvīrāja Rāso is a long heroic poem in an early form of Hindi, traditionally ascribed to Chand Bardāī, court poet and friend of Pṛthvīrāja Cāhamāna. It tells of the king's wars, his love for Saṃyuktā and his defeat by Muḥammad of Ghūr. Scholars date the surviving text much later than the king's reign, with additions through the sixteenth century or beyond, and its historical details are often wrong. But the epic became the foundation of Rajput memory, including the story that the Rajput clans arose from a fire-sacrifice on Mount Abu.

events.title: Kulottuṅga III and Tribhuvanam
events.description: Kulottuṅga III came to the Cōḻa throne in 1178 and ruled for forty years. He is often called the last great Cōḻa, because after him the empire fell under Pāṇḍya pressure and later collapsed. He built the Kampahareśvara temple at Tribhuvanam near Kumbakoṇam, a fine late Cōḻa work, with sculpted panels of epic and Purāṇic scenes. The temple's name is usually explained as Śiva who stills trembling or fear. Like other Cōḻa kings, he gave generous gifts to Cidambaram and Tañjāvūr.

events.title: Pṛthvīrāja Cāhamāna defeats the Candellas
events.description: In 1182 the Cāhamāna king Pṛthvīrāja III of Ajmer and Delhi attacked the Candella ruler Paramardideva at Mahobā in Bundelkhand and took heavy spoils. An inscription at Madanpur records his victory. In popular memory the war is dominated by two Bundelā heroes, the brothers Ālhā and Ūdal, who defended Mahobā. Their deeds are sung in the ballad cycle called the Ālhā-khaṇḍa, still performed in the Hindi heartland. The Candella kingdom was weakened by this conflict, and within two decades Mahobā and Kālañjar passed to the Turkic invaders.

events.title: Yādavas of Devagiri
events.description: The Yādavas, also called Seuṇas, were feudatories of the Cālukyas in the northern Deccan. Bhillama V declared independence in 1187 and founded the Yādava kingdom with its capital at Devagiri, now Daulatabad. Marathi flourished under their patronage, and Jñāneśvara wrote his Marathi commentary on the Gītā in 1290 in their realm. Hemādri, minister of the later kings, compiled the Caturvargacintāmaṇi. Alāʾ-ud-dīn Khaljī began the dynasty's decline in 1296.

events.title: Cālukya decline and rise of Deccan dynasties
events.description: By the late twelfth century the Cālukyas of Kalyāṇī, who had ruled the Deccan for two centuries, were losing control, partly after the Kalacuri usurpation. Their last ruler Someśvara IV held on until about 1190. Their feudatories rose in his place. The Hoysaḷa king Ballāla II took the southern Karnataka plateau, the Yādava Bhillama V founded an independent kingdom at Devagiri, and the Kākatīyas became masters of the Telugu country. These three dynasties would dominate the Deccan until the early fourteenth century and left magnificent temples at Belūru, Halebīdu, Devagiri and Warangal.

events.title: First Battle of Tarāin
events.description: In 1191 Muhammad of Ghor, having taken Lahore, seized a fort in the territory of Pṛthvīrāja III, the Cauhān king of Ajmer and Delhi. The armies met at Tarāin, north of Delhi. A Rajput cavalry charge broke the Ghurid wings; the sultan was wounded and carried from the field. Pṛthvīrāja retook the fort but did not pursue. Ballads made him the last great Hindu hero of Delhi.

events.title: Second Battle of Tarāin
events.description: Muhammad of Ghor returned in 1192 with a reorganised army. He attacked before dawn, then used waves of mounted archers to harass the Rajput host all day, feigning retreat, before striking with his heavy reserve at sunset. Pṛthvīrāja was captured and soon put to death. Delhi and Ajmer fell. Within a dozen years Turkic commanders had overrun the Gaṅgā plain as far as Bengal.

events.title: Quwwat-ul-Islām mosque built from temples
events.description: The first mosque built in Delhi after the Ghurid conquest, called Quwwat-ul-Islām, stands beside the Qutb Minār. An inscription over its east gate states that it was built with materials from twenty-seven demolished Hindu and Jaina temples. Its cloisters are made of reused temple pillars, their carved figures defaced, stacked one on another. The iron pillar of about the fourth century stands in its courtyard. The complex is one of the clearest surviving records of the change of rule at Delhi.

events.title: Bakhtiyār Khaljī raids Bihar's monasteries
events.description: Nālandā in Bihar had taught for seven centuries. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who studied there in the 630s, describes thousands of resident monks, a nine-storey library, and an entrance examination most applicants failed. Logic, grammar, medicine and Hindu philosophy were taught alongside Buddhist doctrine.¶Around 1200 the Turkic commander Bakhtiyār Khaljī raided the monastic universities of Bihar. The Persian chronicle Ṭabaqāt-i-Nāṣirī records the killing of shaven-headed "brāhmaṇas" in a fortified college and the discovery that it had been a place of study. With the monasteries gone, Buddhism faded in the land of its birth.

events.title: Ajmer's Sarasvatī college converted
events.description: The Aḍhāī-din-kā-Jhoṃpṛā in Ajmer is a mosque built in about 1192–99 by Qutb-ud-Dīn Aibak, after the Ghurid conquest of Ajmer, out of the remains of an older building. Inscriptions and later tradition identify the older structure as a Sanskrit college and temple of Sarasvatī founded under the Cāhamāna king Vigraharāja IV. Its screen of arches, added by Iltutmish in 1213, is a celebrated early example of Indo-Islamic architecture. The name suggests a legend that it was built in two and a half days.

events.title: Battle of Candāwar; Kāśī sacked
events.description: In 1194 Muhammad of Ghor defeated Jayacandra, the Gāhaḍavāla king of Kanauj and Vārāṇasī, at Candāwar on the Yamunā; the king was killed by an arrow while leading from his elephant. The Ghurid general Aibak then took Vārāṇasī. The contemporary Persian chronicle says nearly a thousand temples were destroyed there and mosques raised on their foundations, and that fourteen hundred camels carried away the treasure.

events.title: Gaṇapatideva Kākatīya
events.description: Gaṇapatideva ruled from Warangal from 1199 to about 1262 and brought most of the Telugu country under one government, including the coastal districts. He also issued an assurance to overseas traders at the port of Motupalli, giving protection and reduced duties, which encouraged maritime trade. Marco Polo, visiting the coast in the 1290s, later described Motupalli and its trade. His daughter Rudramadevī succeeded him as ruler.

events.title: Bilvamaṅgala's Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta
events.description: The Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta is a collection of Sanskrit verses on the child and youthful Kṛṣṇa, composed by Līlāśuka, who is identified with the poet-saint Bilvamaṅgala. Tradition places him in Kerala, though the text spread widely across India. The verses dwell on the boy's beauty, his flute and his play with the cowherd girls, in a tender and sensuous vein. The Bengal saint Caitanya is said to have prized the work greatly on his southern journey, bringing a copy north, and it became part of Gauḍīya devotional literature.

events.title: Śārṅgadeva's Saṅgīta Ratnākara
events.description: Śārṅgadeva served at the court of the Yādava kings of Devagiri and wrote the Saṅgīta Ratnākara, the most complete medieval Sanskrit treatise on music and dance. It treats the notes, scales, rāgas, rhythm, instruments and stagecraft in considerable technical detail. Because it was composed before the northern and southern musical styles fully separated, both the Hindustani and Carnatic traditions look to it as a shared source. Later commentators such as Kallinātha and Siṃhabhūpāla made it a standard reference.

events.title: Vopadeva and the Muktāphala
events.description: Vopadeva was a grammarian at the Yādava court of Devagiri, author of the Mugdhabodha, a concise Sanskrit grammar that became the standard text in Bengal, where it was used for centuries. He is also credited with the Muktāphala and the Harilīlā, works that summarise the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, and tradition links him with spreading the Bhāgavata's popularity. His minister Hemādri wrote a commentary on the Muktāphala. The connection reflects how the Bhāgavata was becoming central to Vaiṣṇava devotion in the Deccan.

events.title: Gondeśvara temple, Sinnar
events.description: The Gondeśvara temple at Sinnar near Nashik in Maharashtra was built by the Yādavas in the 12th century. It is a pañcāyatana temple, with a main shrine to Śiva and four smaller shrines at the corners of its platform. The structure has a mandapa with carved pillars and a tower in the Bhūmija style. It is regarded as the best of its type in the Deccan and is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.

events.title: Kacciyappa's Kanda Purāṇam
events.description: The Kanda Purāṇam, written by Kacciyappa Civācāriyar, is a Tamil retelling of the Skanda Purāṇa's Śaṅkara Saṃhitā, telling the birth of Murukan and his defeat of Sūrapadma. According to tradition, it was composed at the Kumarakoṭṭam temple in Kāñcīpuram. Its date is disputed, with proposals from the eleventh to the seventeenth century. It is a basic text for Tamil Murukan devotion and is recited at Skanda temples during the Ṣaṣṭhī festival.

events.title: Bakhtiyār Khaljī takes Nadia
events.description: Muḥammad Bakhtiyār Khaljī, a general who served Muḥammad of Ghūr, led a small cavalry force into Nadia around 1204, according to the Persian chronicler Minhāj-i-Sirāj. The aged Lakṣmaṇa Sena was reportedly at table and fled by a back door, though historians doubt the story's details. The Sena court withdrew to eastern Bengal, where his sons ruled from Vikramapura for another generation or two. Bakhtiyār then made Lakhnauti his capital, and Bengal began its long integration into the Delhi Sultanate and its successor states.

events.title: Bakhtiyār's Tibet expedition destroyed in Kāmarūpa
events.description: Bakhtiyār Khaljī, conqueror of Bihar and western Bengal, set out in 1205–06 through Assam to invade Tibet with ten thousand horsemen. The expedition failed in the mountains, and on its retreat the king of Kāmarūpa destroyed the bridge behind it and fell upon it. Only about a hundred men returned. A Sanskrit rock inscription near Guwahati, dated 1206, records that the Turks who came to Kāmarūpa were annihilated.

events.title: Delhi Sultanate established
events.description: After Muḥammad of Ghūr was assassinated in 1206, his Turkic slave general Qutb-ud-dīn Aibak made himself ruler of the Indian conquests, founding what became the Delhi Sultanate. The Sultanate, which lasted until 1526 under five successive dynasties, brought north India under Muslim rulers who used Persian for administration. Aibak began the Quwwat-ul-Islām mosque and the Qutb Minār at Delhi, using material from earlier temples. The Hindu states of the plains, from the Gāhaḍavālas to the Cāhamānas, had already lost power, and Rajput and other Hindu rulers of the periphery would remain independent or fought back in later centuries.

events.title: Iltutmish consolidates the Delhi Sultanate
events.description: Iltutmish, Aibak's slave and son-in-law, took the Delhi throne in 1211 and ruled until 1236. He defeated rival Turkic commanders, won the caliph's recognition in 1229, and made the Sultanate a lasting state. He also led campaigns against Hindu kingdoms. Persian chronicles record that in 1234–35 he raided Ujjain and Vidiśā and destroyed the Mahākāleśvara temple, one of the twelve jyotirliṅga shrines. The sanctum was later restored, and the present temple dates largely from the eighteenth century, after the Marāṭhās took Mālwā.

events.title: Rāmappa temple at Pālampeṭ
events.description: The Rāmappa temple at Pālampeṭ, in Telangana, was built in 1213 by Recarla Rudra, a general of the Kākatīya king Gaṇapati. It is a shrine to Śiva as Rāmalingeśvara, but it is known by the name of its sculptor, Rāmappa, which is unusual. Its sandstone walls and pillars are intricately carved, and the dancers and musicians that stand as brackets are famous. Tradition holds that its tower was built from porous bricks light enough to float. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 2021.

events.title: Māravarman Sundara Pāṇḍya I
events.description: Māravarman Sundara Pāṇḍya I became king of Madurai in 1216 and began what historians call the second Pāṇḍya empire. He attacked the Cōḻa country, defeated Kulottuṅga III, and burned Tañjāvūr and Uraiyūr, according to Pāṇḍya inscriptions. The Cōḻa Rājarāja III later regained his position with Hoysaḷa help, but he was in effect a subordinate. This began the steady Pāṇḍya rise to supremacy in the south.

events.title: Citsukha's Tattvapradīpikā
events.description: Citsukha was an Advaita Vedāntin who wrote the Tattvapradīpikā, also called the Citsukhī, a work of sharp logical argument. It follows Śrīharṣa's Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya in using dialectic to show that the categories of Nyāya, such as perception and causation, cannot be defined without contradiction, so that the empirical world cannot ultimately bear scrutiny. This style of attack on rival systems shaped later Advaita debate. Citsukha also wrote a commentary on Śrīharṣa's Khaṇḍana, and his Tattvapradīpikā itself drew many later commentaries.

events.title: Ahom kingdom founded
events.description: In 1228 Sukaphaa, a Tai prince from the Mong Mao region in the south of present-day Yunnan, led his followers across the Patkai hills into the Brahmaputra valley. His people, the Ahoms, merged with local communities and set up a kingdom that lasted about six hundred years, until the British annexation in 1826. At first they followed their own Tai religion and customs, but over the centuries the royal house took up Hindu worship and Assamese language, supporting Vaiṣṇava sattras and Śākta shrines. Their resistance to Mughal expansion became a great regional legend.

gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||

events.title: Lūṇa Vasahī at Dilwāṛā, Mount Abu
events.description: The Dilwāṛā temples on Mount Abu are Jaina shrines in white marble. The Lūṇa Vasahī was built in 1230 by the brothers Vastupāla and Tejapāla, ministers of the Vāghelā rulers of Gujarat, in honour of the tīrthaṅkara Neminātha. The older Vimala Vasahī, dedicated to Ādinātha, was built in 1031 by Vimala Śāh, a minister of the Solaṅkī king. The ceilings and pillars show some of the most delicate stone carving in India and attest to Jaina patronage in Gujarat.

events.title: Birth of Madhvācārya
events.description: Madhva, also known as Pūrṇaprajña and Ānandatīrtha, was born at Pājaka near Uḍupi in coastal Karnataka. Tradition gives his life as 1238 to 1317, though some scholars have proposed a date about four decades earlier. Devotees consider him an incarnation of Vāyu, the wind-god, in the line of Hanumān and Bhīma. He took saṃnyāsa as a boy and studied Advaita under Acyutaprekṣa, then broke from it to teach a theology of strict difference between God and the soul. He founded the Dvaita school and travelled widely as a debater.

events.title: Narasiṃhadeva I rules the Eastern Gaṅgas
events.description: Narasiṃhadeva I of the Eastern Gaṅga dynasty ruled Odisha from 1238 to about 1264. He campaigned against the Muslim rulers of Bengal, and both sides claimed victories in the 1240s, and Muslim chronicles record the encounters. After securing the frontier, he built the great Sun temple at Koṇārka on the Odisha coast, shaped as a chariot with twelve pairs of wheels. It remains one of the best-known temples in India.

events.title: Vīsaladeva founds the Vāghelā dynasty
events.description: The Vāghelās succeeded the Caulukyas in Gujarat in the thirteenth century. Vīsaladeva, who came to the throne in 1244, is counted as the first king of the line, after his father Vīradhavala and grandfather Lavaṇaprasāda had held real power as Caulukya chiefs. His ministers Vastupāla and Tejapāla, who were Jains, financed major building, including the Lūṇa Vasahī temple at Mount Ābū and temples on Girnār. They also supported Hindu temples, mosques and scholars. The dynasty ended with Karṇa Vāghelā, defeated by the Delhi Sultanate around 1299.

events.title: Maheśvarānanda's Mahārthamañjarī
events.description: Maheśvarānanda wrote the Mahārthamañjarī in Prakrit, with his own Sanskrit commentary, the Parimala, to teach the Krama school of Kashmiri Śaivism, which centres on the goddess Kālī and the cycle of her phases of consciousness. He is placed in the Cōḻa country, at Cidambaram, famous for its Naṭarāja temple, and is usually dated to about the thirteenth century. His work is evidence that Kashmiri Śaiva ideas travelled to the far south and mingled with local Śaiva traditions.

events.title: Jayaratha’s Tantrālokaviveka
events.description: Jayaratha, a Kashmiri scholar of about the thirteenth century, wrote the Tantrālokaviveka, a verse-by-verse commentary on Abhinavagupta's Tantrāloka, a vast and difficult encyclopaedia of Trika Śaivism. Without the commentary, much of the Tantrāloka would be hard to understand, and the commentary also preserves quotations from lost texts. Jayaratha is the main interpreter of Abhinavagupta for later readers, and his work is the usual key to the Tantrāloka.

events.title: Nampiḷḷai and the Īḍu
events.description: Nampiḷḷai was a leading teacher of the Śrīvaiṣṇava community at Śrīraṅgam in the thirteenth century. His lectures on the Tiruvāymoḻi, the great Tamil hymns of Nammāḻvār, were recorded by his pupil Vaḍakkut Tiruvīdhi Piḷḷai as the Īḍu, a commentary of 36,000 units. It is written in Maṇipravāḷam, a mixture of Tamil and Sanskrit, and presents the poem's devotional and theological meanings, and it has been a central text for the community.

events.title: Koṇārka Sun temple
events.description: King Narasiṃhadeva I of the Eastern Gaṅga dynasty built the Sun temple at Koṇārka on the Odisha coast in the mid-thirteenth century. It was designed as a colossal chariot for Sūrya, drawn by seven horses on twenty-four finely carved stone wheels that also work as sundials. Its walls are covered with sculpture, including celestial musicians and erotic scenes. The great tower over the sanctum fell long ago, and the hall (jagamohana) is what stands today. European sailors called it the Black Pagoda. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1984.

events.title: Meykaṇḍār's Śivajñānabodham
events.description: Meykaṇḍār, a thirteenth-century saint of Tiruvennainallur, composed the Śivajñānabodham in twelve short sūtras in Tamil. They set out the structure of Śaiva Siddhānta in three categories: pati, the Lord Śiva; paśu, the souls; and pāśa, the bonds of impurity, karma and illusion that hold them. Souls are freed by Śiva's grace and attain unity with him while remaining distinct. The text is a Tamil statement of ideas found in the Sanskrit Āgamas, and Meykaṇḍār's pupils founded the Santāna lineage that produced the fourteen Meykaṇḍa śāstras.

events.title: Cakradhara and the Mahānubhāva Pantha
events.description: Cakradhara Svāmī, a thirteenth-century teacher in Maharashtra, founded the Mahānubhāva sect. Followers honour five Kṛṣṇas, including Dattātreya and Cakradhara himself. They reject caste, Vedic ritual, image worship and animal sacrifice, admit women as ascetics and used a secret script for their writings. Their early prose in Marathi is among the oldest in the language. The Līḷācaritra, compiled around 1278 by Mhāimbhaṭ from his disciples' memories, is the first Marathi prose biography and a rare detailed account of daily life in the Yādava period.

events.title: Amalānanda's Kalpataru
events.description: Amalānanda wrote the Kalpataru, a sub-commentary on Vācaspati Miśra's Bhāmatī, itself a commentary on Śaṅkara's Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya. He worked under the Yādava dynasty of Devagiri in the Deccan, where he is said to have enjoyed royal patronage. The Kalpataru expands the Bhāmatī school of Advaita, which holds that individual ignorance, not a single universal one, is the root of the world's appearance. A later commentary on it, the Parimala by Appayya Dīkṣita, shows its standing in the tradition.

gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.

events.title: Nṛsiṃha and Rāma Tāpanīya Upaniṣads
events.description: The Nṛsiṃha Pūrva- and Uttara-Tāpanīya and the Rāma Pūrva- and Uttara-Tāpanīya Upaniṣads are late Upaniṣads attached to the Atharvaveda. Unlike the older Upaniṣads, they centre on a chosen deity, Viṣṇu in his man-lion form or Rāma. They give mantras, such as the Nṛsiṃha Anuṣṭubh and the Rāma ṣaḍakṣara, with directions for their use and explanations of their meaning. Their dates are uncertain, the Nṛsiṃha texts probably being earlier than the Rāma texts. Vaiṣṇava teachers of later centuries drew on them to give scriptural footing to sectarian worship.

events.title: Hemāḍpantī temple style of Maharashtra
events.description: Hemāḍpantī temples are a group of medieval Maharashtra shrines built of black basalt, without mortar, with stones cut to fit and often with interlocking joints. They are named after Hemādri, or Hemāḍpant, a minister of the Yādava kings of Devagiri in the thirteenth century, who was also a scholar and author of a large digest of religious observances, the Caturvargacintāmaṇi. The temples are attributed to him by tradition, though many may be earlier or later than his time, and the term refers to the style.

events.title: Aruḷnandi's Śivajñāna Siddhiyār
events.description: Aruḷnandi Śivācārya, a pupil of Meykaṇḍār, wrote this long Tamil verse work, traditionally dated 1253, to expand his teacher's twelve sūtras. It has two parts. The first examines and rejects rival schools, including Buddhism, Jainism, Advaita and Pāñcarātra, and the second sets out Śaiva Siddhānta doctrine on the three categories, the soul's bondage and release, and the path of worship. It is regarded as the standard exposition of the system and is still studied in Tamil Śaiva monasteries such as Tiruvāvaduturai.

events.title: Inscriptions attest Viṭṭhala temple at Paṇḍharpūr
events.description: The temple of Viṭṭhala at Paṇḍharpūr in Maharashtra is the centre of the Vārakarī tradition. Inscriptions record donations to it over time, including a Hoysaḷa record of 1237 and Yādava grants of 1273 to 1277, with donors from kings to ordinary people. These records are important evidence that the temple and cult existed before the age of the great Marathi saints. Pilgrims known as Vārakarīs walk to the temple on Āṣāḍhī and Kārttikī Ekādaśī days.

events.title: Jaṭāvarman Sundara Pāṇḍya
events.description: Jaṭāvarman Sundara Pāṇḍya ruled from 1251 and was the greatest king of the second Pāṇḍya empire. He defeated the Cōḻa Rājendra III, the Hoysaḷas and others, and extended his sway to Nellore in the north. Inscriptions record that he covered the sanctums of Śrīraṅgam and Cidambaram with gold. His power meant that the Cōḻas were reduced to a subordinate position, and the old Cōḻa royal tradition came to an end soon after.

events.title: Keśava temple, Somanāthapura
events.description: The Keśava temple at Somanāthapura, near Mysuru in Karnataka, was built in 1258 under the Hoysaḷa king Narasiṃha III by his general Somanātha. It has three shrines, on a star-shaped platform, each with a tower, and its walls are filled with carvings of gods and scenes from the epics, set in horizontal bands. It is among the last major temples of the Hoysaḷa dynasty, and is part of the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysaḷas, inscribed by UNESCO in 2023.

events.title: Madhva's Dvaita Vedānta
events.description: Madhva's thirty-seven works include commentaries on the Brahma Sūtra, the Gītā and the Upaniṣads, as well as the Anuvyākhyāna, a verse treatise on the Brahma Sūtra. His system, called Tattvavāda ("doctrine of the real"), teaches five eternal differences: between God and soul, God and matter, soul and soul, soul and matter, and one portion of matter and another. Viṣṇu alone is independent, and all else depends on him. Liberation comes through his grace, and Madhva held that souls have different natures. He opposed Advaita sharply, and later Dvaita scholars such as Jayatīrtha and Vyāsatīrtha developed his school's logic.

events.title: Rudramādevī of the Kākatīyas
events.description: Rudramādevī was the daughter of the Kākatīya king Gaṇapati, who had no son. He named her his successor and gave her the male name Rudradeva. She ruled at Warangal from about 1262 until about 1289, according to inscriptions. She put down rebellions and Yādava invasions, though some nobles questioned her rule as a woman. The Venetian traveller Marco Polo praised the kingdom's good government. Her grandson Pratāparudra succeeded her. She is among the few women to rule a major Indian kingdom in her own right.

events.title: Piḷḷai Lokācārya and the Śrīvacanabhūṣaṇam
events.description: Piḷḷai Lokācārya, a leading Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher at Śrīraṅgam, wrote the Śrīvacanabhūṣaṇam in Maṇipravāḷa, a blend of Tamil and Sanskrit, setting out the teaching on surrender (prapatti) in a series of aphorisms. It holds that the soul is saved by God's grace alone, without needing effort of its own, and he is regarded as the chief forerunner of the Teṉkalai school. Tradition says he saved the processional image of Raṅganātha during the 1323 attack on Śrīraṅgam and died while taking it south. The Śrīvacanabhūṣaṇam later received a famous commentary by Maṇavāḷa Māmuni.

events.title: Vedānta Deśika born
events.description: Veṅkaṭanātha, later called Vedānta Deśika, was born near Kāñcīpuram in 1268, according to tradition, and lived to be 101. He became the leading thinker of Śrīvaiṣṇavism after Rāmānuja and is counted among the founders of the Vaḍakalai school. He wrote in Sanskrit, Tamil and Maṇipravāḷa. His works include the Rahasyatrayasāra, the Pādukāsahasra, a thousand verses on Raṅganātha's sandals said to have been composed in a single night, and the Śatadūṣaṇī, a criticism of Advaita. He also wrote poetry, drama and hymns.

events.title: Hemādri's Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi
events.description: Hemādri served the Yādava kings of Devagiri as a minister under Mahādeva and Rāmacandra. His Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi, a vast encyclopaedia, collects rules on vows (vrata), gifts (dāna), pilgrimage (tīrtha), liberation (mokṣa) and rites for the dead. It gathers quotations from older Purāṇas and Dharmaśāstras, some preserved nowhere else, and became an authority for later digests such as the Nirṇayasindhu. Hemādri's name is also attached to a style of Maharashtra temple building, called Hemāḍpanthī, and to the Modī script, though scholars question the latter attribution.

events.title: Nāmadeva born
events.description: Nāmadeva was born into a tailor's family and became one of the principal poets of the Vārakarī tradition, devoted to Viṭṭhala (Viṭhobā) of Paṇḍharpūr. His Marathi abhaṅgas speak of everyday life as a path to God. Tradition makes him a contemporary of Jñāneśvara. He travelled widely, and spent his later years in Punjab, where he is remembered at Ghumān. About sixty of his hymns appear in the Sikh Ādi Granth, and he influenced the Sant poets of northern India, among them Kabīr, who wrote of Nāmadeva's example.

events.title: Jñāneśvara born
events.description: Jñāneśvara, also called Jñānadeva, was born at Āpegāon, near Paiṭhaṇ, and later lived at Āḷandī on the Indrāyaṇī river. His father Viṭṭhalapant had taken saṃnyāsa and then returned to household life, which, in the eyes of the Brahmin orthodoxy, made his children outcasts. Jñāneśvara and his brothers and sister, Nivṛttinātha, Sopāna and Muktābāī, grew up scorned, yet they became saints. In his teens he composed the Jñāneśvarī, a Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā, which made the Gītā available to ordinary people and gave the Marathi language its first great classic.

events.title: End of the Cōḻas
events.description: Rājendra III was the last known Cōḻa king, whose final inscriptions date to around 1279. After years of defeat by the Pāṇḍyas, particularly Jaṭāvarman Sundara Pāṇḍya and Māravarman Kulaśekhara I, and by the Hoysaḷas, his kingdom shrank, and he disappears from the record. The Pāṇḍyas then took control of the Kāverī delta. The Cōḻa legacy of temple building and bronze casting continued under their successors.

events.title: Maṟaijñāna Sambandar, Śaiva Siddhānta teacher
events.description: Maṟaijñāna Sambandar was the third of the four Santāna ācāryas, the teachers who handed down Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta. The line began with Meykaṇḍar, author of the Śivajñānabodham, and continued with Aruḷnandi Śivācārya. Maṟaijñāna Sambandar, who is associated with Cidambaram, taught Umāpati Śivācārya, who systematised the doctrine in several works. This chain of teachers shaped the Tamil Śaiva tradition, which is still alive in the Śaiva monasteries of Tamil Nadu.

events.title: Rām Khamhaeng and Sukhothai
events.description: Rām Khamhaeng was a ruler of Sukhothai, an early Thai kingdom, who reigned from about 1279 to 1298. A stone inscription ascribed to him, dated 1292, says he devised the Thai script in 1283, though scholars have debated its authenticity. Thai kingship drew on Brahmanical court ritual, with coronation and royal ceremonies conducted by brāhmaṇa priests whose lineages are linked to southern India. Such rites continue at the Bangkok court alongside Theravāda Buddhism, an example of how Hindu ritual survived within a Buddhist society.

events.title: Uḍupi Kṛṣṇa and the Aṣṭa Maṭhas
events.description: Tradition says Madhva installed the image of Kṛṣṇa at Uḍupi after recovering it from the clay of a shipwrecked vessel, which he had been asked to remove from the shore. He placed the temple in the care of eight monasteries, the Aṣṭa Maṭhas, each headed by one of his disciples. The monks took turns, by paryāya rotation, to conduct the worship. In the sixteenth century the turn was lengthened to two years. Uḍupi's kitchens, its festival chariots and its Dvaita scholarship made it a centre of Kṛṣṇa devotion in south India.

events.title: Jñāneśvara dictates the Jñāneśvarī
events.description: In 1290, at Nevāse on the Godāvarī, a teenage renunciant's son named Jñāneśvara dictated a commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā in Marathi verse, some 9,000 stanzas long. His family had been outcast by the brāhmaṇas of Āḷandī; he answered by giving the highest scripture to everyone in their own language.¶The poem is loved as much for its imagery as its philosophy. It closes with the Pasāyadāna, a prayer asking nothing for himself: may the wicked lose their crookedness, and may every being get what it longs for. He entered samādhi at twenty-one. The Vārakarī tradition calls him Māulī, "mother".

events.title: Vārakarī pilgrim tradition of Paṇḍharpūr
events.description: The Vārakarīs are Maharashtra's devotional community of "pilgrims", who walk each year to Paṇḍharpūr to see Viṭhobā, a form of Viṣṇu-Kṛṣṇa. They mainly gather on the Āṣāḍhī and Kārttikī ekādaśī days, in processions that carry saints' sandals in palanquins. The tradition accepted the poets Cokhāmeḷā, Gorā the potter, Sāvatā the gardener and the women Janābāī and Muktābāī, whatever their birth. Their simple practice of wearing the tulasī-bead garland and singing the Name rests on the abhaṅgas of the saints and shaped Marathi religious life.

events.title: Marco Polo in the Pāṇḍya country
events.description: The Venetian traveller Marco Polo passed through the south of India in the 1290s, in the realm he calls Ma'abar, which was ruled by the Pāṇḍyas. He describes the pearl fisheries in the Gulf of Mannar and the sorcerers who charmed away the sharks, the trade in horses from Persia and the Gulf, and the brāhmaṇas, whom he calls Abraiamin and says came from the region of "Lar". His account is among the best foreign descriptions of medieval South India.

events.title: Majapahit founded
events.description: After the Mongol expedition of 1293 on Java, the prince Raden Wijaya set up Majapahit in east Java and made himself king. Under Hayam Wuruk and his minister Gajah Mada in the fourteenth century it dominated much of the Indonesian archipelago. It was the last great Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of Java. The poem Nāgarakṛtāgama, composed in 1365 by Prapañca, describes a court where Śiva and the Buddha were honoured together in a syncretic religion, and records temple rites and royal pilgrimages.

events.title: Jñāneśvara's sañjīvana samādhi
events.description: At about twenty-one, according to tradition in 1296, Jñāneśvara entered a stone chamber at Āḷandī and sat in meditation as the entrance was closed, an act called sañjīvana samādhi, meaning that he remained alive in yogic absorption. Saints including Nāmadeva are said to have been present. His brothers and sister were reported to have died within a year. His samādhi shrine on the Indrāyaṇī is among Maharashtra's most visited, and each year the Vārakarī pilgrims carry his palanquin from Āḷandī to Paṇḍharpūr.

events.title: Alauddin Khaljī raids Devagiri
events.description: In 1296 Alauddin Khaljī, then governor of Kara, led a force of several thousand horsemen to Devagiri, the Yādava capital in the Deccan. It was the first Muslim attack on the peninsula's interior. The Yādava king Rāmacandra, caught off guard while his army was away, surrendered after a siege and paid a heavy ransom of gold, silver, pearls and elephants, as Persian chroniclers record. Alauddin then returned north, murdered his uncle Sultan Jalāl-ud-dīn, and took the Delhi throne. The wealth taken financed his later campaigns.

events.title: Delhi Sultanate conquers Gujarat, sacks Somanātha
events.description: In 1299 Alauddin's generals Ulugh Khān and Nuṣrat Khān conquered Gujarat, and the Vāghelā king Karṇa fled. Persian sources record that the army plundered Cambay and the Somanātha temple, and that the Śiva liṅga was carried off to Delhi. Somanātha, rebuilt many times, had been a symbol of Hindu resistance since Maḥmūd of Ghazna's raid of 1025–26. A Sanskrit poem, the Kānhaḍade Prabandha, composed in 1455, tells that the Cāhamāna chieftain Kānhaḍade of Jālor freed captives and recovered the idol, a tradition historians treat with caution.

events.title: Rāmānanda and the Rāmānandī Sampradāya
events.description: Rāmānanda taught at Kāśī in the fourteenth or fifteenth century; his dates, here c. 1300–1410, are disputed. He is regarded as the founder of the Rāmānandī Sampradāya, which worships Rāma as the supreme Lord and traces its descent from Rāmānuja's line. Tradition says his disciples included Kabīr, Ravidāsa, the barber Sena, the Jāṭ Dhannā and the king Pīpā, along with women, and he taught in the common tongue. A line ascribed to him says no one asks about caste: "jāti-pāti pūche nahi koī." The Rāmānandīs became the largest ascetic order of north India.

events.title: Muktikā canon of 108 Upaniṣads
events.description: The Muktikā Upaniṣad, a late text, presents itself as a dialogue between Rāma and Hanumān, in which Rāma lists 108 Upaniṣads as the route to liberation. Ten are named as the principal ones, those commented on by Śaṅkara, plus others. The list sorted the large and growing body of Upaniṣads, many of them sectarian, Yogic or Saṃnyāsa works, into a single canon by Veda affiliation. Scholars date the text to around the 14th century, with the final canon reaching its present form between about the 15th and 17th centuries.

events.title: Yoga Upaniṣads
events.description: The Yoga Upaniṣads are a group of about twenty late Upaniṣads that treat meditation and yogic practice. Among them are the Yogatattva, Dhyānabindu and Haṃsa Upaniṣads. They describe breath control, the subtle channels, the awakening of kuṇḍalinī and the sound of Oṁ, and mix methods of haṭha yoga with the non-dual teaching of Vedānta. They show yoga and Vedānta moving closer, so that the physical discipline of the haṭha manuals could be read as serving the Upaniṣadic goal of self-knowledge.

events.title: Sudarśana Sūri's Śrutaprakāśikā
events.description: Sudarśana Sūri, a Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher of Śrīraṅgam, wrote the Śrutaprakāśikā, a long sub-commentary on Rāmānuja's Śrī Bhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtras. It explains Rāmānuja's arguments for Viśiṣṭādvaita and answers the objections of rival schools, especially Advaita. Tradition says his manuscript was nearly lost in a time of upheaval, with his sons saved. The work became the standard guide for later Viśiṣṭādvaita scholars studying the Śrī Bhāṣya.

events.title: Narahari Tīrtha and Padmanābha Tīrtha
events.description: Narahari Tīrtha and Padmanābha Tīrtha were among the immediate disciples of Madhva, the founder of Dvaita Vedānta. Narahari Tīrtha served as a minister in Odisha under the Gaṅga king, and an inscription of his survives in the region, while Padmanābha Tīrtha succeeded Madhva as head and wrote commentaries. Together they helped carry Madhva's dualist philosophy beyond the Tuḷu coast, into Odisha and the Kannada plains, laying the basis for the Mādhva maṭhas.

events.title: Trivikrama Paṇḍita's Vāyustuti
events.description: Trivikrama Paṇḍita was an Advaita scholar of Kāsaragoḍ who, according to Mādhva tradition, debated Madhva for days and was converted to Dvaita. He composed the Vāyustuti, a hymn to Vāyu, the wind god whom Dvaita regards as Madhva's divine origin, and it is still recited by Mādhvas. His son Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya wrote the Madhvavijaya, the standard biography of Madhva, in Sanskrit verse. The details of these accounts come mainly from Mādhva sources.

events.title: Janābāī, Muktābāī and Soyarābāī
events.description: Janābāī, a servant in the household of the Vārakarī saint Nāmadeva, Muktābāī, the younger sister of Jñāneśvara, and Soyarābāī, wife of Cokhāmeḷā, are among the first women poets in Marathi. Their abhaṅgas, devotional verses in a simple metre, draw on daily life. Janābāī speaks of grinding grain and washing clothes, and says that Viṭṭhala himself comes to help her. Muktābāī's verses reflect her spiritual maturity and her bold exchange with Cāṅgadeva. Their poems give women's voices to a movement that had room for people of every rank.

events.title: Cokhāmeḷā, the Mahār saint of Paṇḍharpūr
events.description: Cokhāmeḷā was a Mahār saint of Maṅgaḷveḍhā, near Paṇḍharpūr, who composed abhaṅgas as a devotee of Viṭṭhala. Regarded as an untouchable in his time, he was not allowed into the main temple, and his verses speak of caste pain and of the divine presence regardless of birth. Tradition says he died when a wall collapsed while he was working on it at Maṅgaḷveḍhā, around 1338, and that his bones were brought to Paṇḍharpūr and buried at the foot of the temple steps, where his samādhi lies. His family, including his wife Soyarābāī, also wrote devotional verse.

events.title: Jagannātha's Navakalevara rite
events.description: At the Jagannātha temple in Purī, the wooden images of Jagannātha, Balabhadra, Subhadrā and the Sudarśana disc are replaced with new ones in a rite called Navakalevara, "new body." It falls in years with an extra lunar month of Āṣāḍha, usually every eight, twelve or nineteen years. Priests undertake a ceremonial search for special neem trees bearing the required marks, from which the new images are carved. The old images are buried in the temple compound at Koili Baikuṇṭha. Temple records such as the Mādaḷā Pāñji describe the ritual, though the early history of the practice is uncertain.

events.title: Śārṅgadhara Saṃhitā
events.description: The Śārṅgadhara Saṃhitā, attributed to Śārṅgadhara and usually placed in the thirteenth or fourteenth century, is a compact medical handbook that became a standard text in later Āyurveda. It is notable for describing nāḍī-parīkṣā, diagnosis by feeling the pulse at the wrist, which is not clearly present in the older Caraka and Suśruta works. It also discusses pharmaceutical preparation in detail, including decoctions, powders and mineral compounds, and so reflects how practice shifted toward formulary medicine.

events.title: Gītā commentaries across the schools
events.description: The Bhagavad Gītā attracted commentaries from all the major Vedānta schools: Śaṅkara (Advaita), Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita) and Madhva (Dvaita). Later authors added more. Jñāneśvara's Marathi Jñāneśvarī dates to about 1290, Śrīdhara Svāmī wrote the Subodhinī, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī the Gūḍhārthadīpikā, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa of the Gauḍīya school the Gītābhūṣaṇa. The variety shows how the Gītā was read afresh by each tradition, each school drawing out its own doctrine from the same eighteen chapters.

events.title: Śrīvaiṣṇava rahasya literature
events.description: The rahasya literature of the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition expounds the three "secrets," the mantras central to the community: the Tirumantra, Dvaya and Caramaśloka. Piḷḷai Lokācārya's Aṣṭādaśa Rahasyas, composed in Maṇipravāḷa, set out surrender (prapatti) as the path to Viṣṇu, and later teachers such as Maṇavāḷa Māmuni wrote on them. The Teṉkalai and Vaṭakalai branches disagree about the soul's role in surrender, and the rahasya works are central to that debate.

events.title: Ānandagiri's sub-commentaries on Śaṅkara
events.description: Ānandagiri, also called Ānandajñāna, wrote sub-commentaries called ṭīkās on nearly all of Śaṅkara's commentaries, including those on the Upaniṣads and the Bhagavad Gītā, and on the Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya. His glosses explain difficult passages in Śaṅkara's Sanskrit, making them accessible to later students. They are among the most used aids to reading Śaṅkara and are valued as a link to older interpretation. He is associated with Gujarat, although his dates are uncertain and are debated.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Rasaratnasamuccaya and Rasārṇava
events.description: Rasaśāstra is the Sanskrit tradition of alchemy and medicinal chemistry, centred on mercury (rasa) and the preparation of minerals and metals. The Rasārṇava, a tantric text of perhaps the twelfth century, and the Rasaratnasamuccaya, attributed to a Vāgbhaṭa and usually placed in the thirteenth or fourteenth century, are among its classics. They describe laboratory equipment, such as crucibles and distillation devices, and methods of purifying and processing mercury for use in medicine. The tradition influenced Āyurvedic pharmacy, which includes many mineral preparations.

events.title: Fall of Raṇathambhor
events.description: Hammīra Cāhamāna ruled the fortress of Raṇathambhor in Rajasthan, a surviving branch of the Cāhamāna line. When he gave refuge to Mongol rebels who had fled Alauddin, the Sultan besieged the fort in 1301. Hammīra died in the defence, and the women of the fort, according to the poet Nayacandra's Hammīra Mahākāvya, performed jauhar, mass self-immolation to avoid capture. The poet Amīr Khusrau, who accompanied the campaign, records the fall. Hammīra's stubborn pledge, hammīra-haṭha, became a byword in Rajasthani tradition for resolute honour.

events.title: First siege of Chittor
events.description: In 1303 Alauddin Khaljī besieged and took the great fort of Chittor from the Guhila ruler Rāval Ratnasiṃha. The contemporary poet Amīr Khusrau recounts the capture and a massacre of the defenders, but says nothing of a queen. The story of Queen Padminī, whose beauty tempted the Sultan and who died by jauhar with the women of the fort, is told in Malik Muḥammad Jāyasī's Awadhi poem Padmāvat of 1540, a Sufi allegory. Historians regard it as legend, though it has shaped Rajput memory ever since.

events.title: Mālwā and Dhārā fall
events.description: In 1305 Alauddin Khaljī sent his general ʿAin-ul-Mulk Multānī against Mālwā. The Paramāra king, Mahlak Deva, was defeated and killed, and Dhārā and the fort of Māṇḍū came under the Sultanate. The Paramāras, the dynasty of the famed king Bhoja, had ruled in Mālwā since the tenth century but had declined by then. The conquest brought the region into the Delhi Sultanate's orbit and later led to the independent sultanate of Mālwā.

events.title: Bhojaśālā at Dhār
events.description: The Bhojaśālā in Dhār is a hall which Hindus link with the Paramāra king Bhoja's temple of Sarasvatī and school; its pillars and walls carry engraved grammatical charts. After the conquest of Mālwā by the Delhi Sultanate it was converted into a mosque, the Kamāl Maulā, in the fourteenth century. A Vāgdevī (Sarasvatī) statue, associated with a 1034 date, was taken to England in the nineteenth century and is now in the British Museum. The status of the site is still contested.

gitaQuote.verse: पिताहमस्य जगतो माता धाता पितामहः । वेद्यं पवित्रमोंकार ऋक्साम यजुरेव च ॥ गतिर्भर्ता प्रभुः साक्षी निवासः शरणं सुहृत् । प्रभवः प्रलयः स्थानं निधानं बीजमव्ययम् ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ | vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛk sāma yajur eva ca || gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt | prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||
gitaQuote.translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer and the grandsire. I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the creation and dissolution, the foundation and the imperishable seed.
gitaQuote.chapter: Bhagavad Gītā 9.17–18 (Rāja Vidyā Rāja Guhya Yoga)
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Bhāṣya

events.title: Malik Kāfūr's southern raids
events.description: Malik Kāfūr, a favourite general of Alauddin Khaljī, led armies into the south from 1307. Warangal's Kākatīya king Pratāparudra paid tribute in 1310; Dvārasamudra, the Hoysaḷa capital, was taken, and Madurai was plundered around 1311 during a Pāṇḍya succession dispute. The Persian chroniclers record huge hauls of gold, jewels, elephants and horses, and later accounts speak of temples sacked at places such as Śrīraṅgam and Cidambaram. The raids exposed the wealth of the south and began the decline of its great dynasties.

events.title: Fall of Jālor to Alāʾ-ud-dīn Khaljī
events.description: Kānhaḍadeva, a Sonigarā Cauhān ruler of Jālor in southern Rajasthan, was besieged by Alāʾ-ud-dīn Khaljī's army and fell about 1311 along with his son Vīramadeva. The Kānhaḍade Prabandha, a long Old Gujarātī-Rājasthānī poem by Padmanābha composed in 1455, tells the story as a heroic tale, in which the defenders ride out to die and the women perform jauhar. As it was composed a century and a half later, historians use it with care alongside Persian chronicles and inscriptions.

events.title: Madhva's disappearance
events.description: Madhva, the founder of Dvaita Vedānta, was born near Uḍupi in coastal Karnataka. According to tradition, in 1317 he was teaching the Aitareya Upaniṣad at Uḍupi's Anantēśvara temple when he disappeared amid a shower of flowers, and he is believed to live on at Badarī in the Himalaya. Madhva's followers see this as a departure from the world rather than death. He had set up the Kṛṣṇa temple at Uḍupi and the eight monasteries of the Aṣṭa Maṭhas.

events.title: Lallā, the Kashmiri yoginī poet
events.description: Lallā, also called Lalleśvarī or Lal Ded, was a fourteenth-century Kashmiri yoginī who wandered as an ascetic. Her four-line vākhs, in the Kashmiri language rather than Sanskrit, speak of the Self, Śiva and the breath, with ideas from the Trika Śaiva philosophy of Kashmir. Tradition says that Nūr-ud-dīn (Nund Ṛṣi), founder of the Kashmiri Rishi order of Sufis, was nourished by her. She is honoured by both Hindus and Muslims in Kashmir, and her verses are among the earliest literature in the Kashmiri language.

events.title: Raṅganātha's image leaves Śrīraṅgam after 1323 raid
events.description: In 1323 a Delhi army under Ulugh Khān, the future Sultan Muḥammad bin Tughlaq, advanced from Warangal into Tamil lands and attacked Śrīraṅgam. Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition says that Piḷḷai Lokācārya took the processional image of Raṅganātha away, and that it wandered for forty-eight years through places such as Tirupati and Madurai before returning. Sudarśana Sūri, an important commentator, is said to have been killed, with his Śrutaprakāśikā manuscripts saved by Vedānta Deśika. The Guruparamparā literature preserves these accounts.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ | ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||
gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.
gitaQuote.source: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) Critical Edition; Rāmānuja Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Fall of the Kākatīyas
events.description: In 1323 the prince Ulugh Khān, sent by Ghiyāth-ud-dīn Tughlaq, besieged Warangal after an earlier failed attempt. Pratāparudra, the last important Kākatīya king, surrendered and was sent as a prisoner towards Delhi, dying on the road. The Svayambhū Śiva temple in the fort was destroyed. The Kākatīyas had ruled most of the Telugu country for nearly two centuries and built the temples of Rāmappa and Hanamkoṇḍa, and their fall left the region in the hands of Tughlaq governors and, soon, local rebels.

events.title: Harisiṃhadeva flees Mithilā
events.description: In 1324, returning from a campaign in Bengal, Ghiyās-ud-dīn Tughluq attacked Simraungaṛh, the capital of the Karṇāṭa dynasty of Mithilā, and destroyed it. Tradition says the ruler Harisiṃhadeva escaped to Nepal. Mithilā was taken under Tughluq control, and a brāhmaṇa family, the Oinvāras, later ruled it as local kings in the fourteenth century under the Sultanate, becoming patrons of Maithili and Sanskrit learning, including the poet Vidyāpati.

events.title: Muḥammad bin Tughlaq's reign and failed schemes
events.description: Muḥammad bin Tughlaq ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1325 to 1351, a learned and ambitious sultan whose schemes often failed. In 1327 he made Devagiri, renamed Daulatabad, a second capital and forced much of Delhi's population to move. His token currency in copper was forged in large numbers and had to be withdrawn. Rebellions broke out in Bengal, the Deccan and the south, and Vijayanagara was founded in 1336 in the wake of the revolts. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Baṭṭūṭa served as his judge and left an account of his court.

events.title: Gaṅgeśa's Tattvacintāmaṇi founds Navya-Nyāya
events.description: Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya of Mithilā wrote the Tattvacintāmaṇi, a book in four parts on perception, inference, analogy and testimony, which started the school of Navya-Nyāya, the "new logic". It refined the older Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika by creating a precise technical language, with terms for the qualifier, the thing qualified and the limiting condition (avacchedaka), to state exactly what a statement means. The method spread to Navadvīpa and was used in grammar, law and Mīmāṃsā as well as philosophy. Generations of pandits wrote commentaries on his text.

events.title: Reḍḍi kingdom of Koṇḍavīḍu
events.description: After the Delhi Sultanate overthrew the Kākatīyas, Prolaya Vema Reḍḍi emerged in the 1320s as a local ruler in coastal Āndhra and founded the Reḍḍi kingdom, which was centred first at Addanki and later Koṇḍavīḍu. He restored agrahāras, the land grants to brāhmaṇas, rebuilt temples, and provided stability after the upheavals of the invasions. Under his successors Telugu literature flourished, and Eṟṟāpragaḍa, the poet who completed the Telugu Mahābhārata, was associated with the court.

gitaQuote.translation: I alone am inexhaustible, imperishable Time (Akṣaya Kāla), and I am the dispenser of destiny facing all directions... I am all-destroying Time, grown mighty to extinguish the worlds.

events.title: Hammīra recovers Chittor
events.description: After Alauddin's conquest in 1303 Chittor passed into the hands of a Cāhamāna governor of Jālor. Hammīra, of the Sisodiyā branch of the Guhilas, rebuilt the family's fortunes in the Mewar hills, and around 1326 he recovered the fort and the kingdom. Rajput tradition remembers him as the restorer of Mewar, whose line, the Sisodiyās of Chittor and Udaipur, included Rāṇā Kumbha, Rāṇā Sāṅgā and Mahārāṇā Pratāpa. His state would remain the foremost Hindu power of Rajasthan for centuries.

events.title: Musunūri Nāyakas retake Warangal
events.description: After the Tughlaq conquest of Warangal in 1323, Telugu chiefs of the Musunūri family organised resistance. Prolaya Nāyaka rallied warriors from many Telugu clans and called on them to free the land from Turkic rule. His cousin Kāpaya Nāyaka drove out the Tughlaq governors and by about 1336 had retaken Warangal and the Kākatīya heartland. Inscriptions, among them the Vilasa grant, record this confederacy of Nāyaka chiefs. The Musunūris ruled for roughly a generation, until pressure from the Bahmanī sultans in the later fourteenth century, and are remembered as Telugu defenders who preserved Hindu rule in the region.

events.title: Madurai Sultanate breaks from Delhi
events.description: About 1335 Jalāl-ud-dīn Aḥsan Shāh, the Tughlaq governor of Ma'bar, declared his independence and made Madurai the seat of a separate sultanate. The Pāṇḍya court survived only in the south. The traveller Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, who visited around 1344, wrote of the devastation of the country under the sultans. The sultans, who ruled for about forty-three years, were opposed by the Hoysaḷas and then by Vijayanagara, whose armies ended the sultanate in the 1370s and restored Hindu temples in Madurai and Śrīraṅgam.

gitaQuote.transliteration: pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ | vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛk sāma yajur eva ca || gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt | prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||
gitaQuote.translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer and the grandsire. I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the creation and dissolution, the foundation and the imperishable seed.

events.title: Vijayanagara founded on the Tuṅgabhadrā
events.description: In 1336 two brothers, Harihara and Bukka of the Saṅgama family, founded a new capital on the south bank of the Tuṅgabhadrā, where the hills form a natural fortress. A generation earlier the armies of the Delhi Sultanate had destroyed every major southern kingdom.¶Tradition says the sage Vidyāraṇya of Śṛṅgeri inspired them. For over two centuries their empire held the peninsula south of the Kṛṣṇā, and under its protection temples were rebuilt, the Vedas received Sāyaṇa's commentary, and Telugu, Kannada, Tamil and Sanskrit letters flourished. Its ruins at Hampi cover twenty-six square kilometres.

events.title: Shāh Mīr takes Kashmir
events.description: Shāh Mīr, a Muslim adventurer from the Swāt region who had risen in the Kashmir court, took the throne in 1339 as Shams-ud-dīn and founded the Shāh Mīr dynasty, which lasted until 1561. The last Hindu ruler was the queen Koṭā Rāṇī, who had ruled after the death of her husband. Chronicles say she was pressed into marriage with him and later died, perhaps by suicide, though accounts differ. Kashmir became a Muslim-ruled sultanate.

events.title: Mādhava of Saṅgamagrāma
events.description: Mādhava of Saṅgamagrāma (Irinjalakuda) in Kerala, who lived about 1340–1425, founded the Kerala school of mathematics and astronomy. He found infinite series for the sine, cosine and arctangent functions, and one for π, results that Europeans would rediscover in the seventeenth century as the work of Gregory, Newton and Leibniz. He also improved methods for calculating planetary positions. Most of his writing is lost and known from later students such as Nīlakaṇṭha and Jyeṣṭhadeva. Whether his results reached Europe is a matter of continuing debate among historians.

events.title: Jayatīrtha's Nyāyasudhā on Madhva's Anuvyākhyāna
events.description: Jayatīrtha, a Dvaita teacher born near Malkheḍ in Karnataka and a pupil in Madhva's lineage, is known as Ṭīkācārya, "the master of commentary". His Nyāyasudhā is a long sub-commentary on Madhva's Anuvyākhyāna, a work that takes up the arguments of Advaita, Nyāya and other schools. He also wrote the Tattvaprakāśikā on Madhva's Brahma Sūtra commentary and shorter works on logic. By explaining Madhva's compact verse, he gave Dvaita an authoritative philosophical form that later thinkers, such as Vyāsatīrtha, built on.

gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.

events.title: Death of Ballāla III at Kaṇṇanūr
events.description: Ballāla III was the last great Hoysaḷa king, who ruled from about 1292 until his death around 1343 and spent his later years fighting the Sultanate of Madurai, a breakaway state of the Delhi Sultanate. He was killed near Kaṇṇanūr, close to Śrīraṅgam. Accounts differ on how, but the traveller Ibn Baṭṭūṭa reports his defeat and death. After his death, the Hoysaḷa lands were taken over by the new Vijayanagara kingdom.

events.title: Śṛṅgeri grant of the Saṅgama brothers
events.description: In 1346 the brothers Harihara I and Bukka I, founders of Vijayanagara, made a grant at Śṛṅgeri to the pontiff Bhāratī Tīrtha, head of the Śāradā Pīṭha believed to have been established by Śaṅkara. An inscription records their gifts and their celebration of victory. The monastery's link to the new kingdom was later embroidered in tradition, which gives a leading role to Bhāratī Tīrtha's pupil Vidyāraṇya. Whatever the truth of the legend, the grant shows the early royal link between Vijayanagara and Śṛṅgeri.

events.title: Bahmanī Sultanate founded at Gulbarga
events.description: In 1347 the rebel officer Hasan Gangū took the title Alāʾ-ud-dīn Bahman Shāh at Gulbarga and founded the Bahmanī Sultanate, the first independent Muslim state of the Deccan. Its capital later moved to Bidar. For about 150 years the Bahmanīs fought Vijayanagara for the fertile Raichur doab between the Kṛṣṇā and Tuṅgabhadrā rivers, with great loss on both sides. Late in the fifteenth century the kingdom split into five sultanates, including Bijapur, Golconda and Ahmadnagar, which finally defeated Vijayanagara in 1565.

events.title: Shams-ud-dīn Ilyās raids Kathmandu
events.description: In 1349 Shams-ud-dīn Ilyās Shāh, sultan of Bengal, raided the Kathmandu valley, and the sources report damage to temples, among them the Paśupatināth shrine, whose liṅga was reportedly broken. The invasion was short and the invader withdrew, but it is remembered as a major attack on the valley's sacred sites. Later Malla rulers rebuilt and endowed the shrine, which remains the most important Śaiva centre in Nepal.

events.title: Sāyaṇa's Vedārtha Prakāśa
events.description: Sāyaṇa, minister of Bukka I of Vijayanagara and brother of Mādhava, led a team of scholars in writing a full commentary on the four Vedic saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas, titled Vedārtha Prakāśa for the Ṛgveda. It explains each hymn's words, ritual use and meaning in the Mīmāṃsā tradition. The commentary remained the chief key to the Vedas for centuries, and was used by Friedrich Max Müller in his nineteenth-century Western edition of the Ṛgveda. Modern scholars sometimes disagree with his readings, but no other work has been so widely used.

events.title: Vidyāraṇya's Pañcadaśī, an Advaita manual
events.description: The Pañcadaśī, in fifteen chapters, is a popular Advaita Vedānta manual, traditionally ascribed to Vidyāraṇya, the Śṛṅgeri teacher linked to Vijayanagara's founding. Its three groups of five chapters treat discrimination (viveka), illumination (dīpa) and bliss (ānanda), using analogies to explain the self. Tradition credits the early chapters to Bhāratītīrtha, Vidyāraṇya's teacher. Vidyāraṇya is often identified with Mādhava, to whom the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha is also ascribed, and with Sāyaṇa's brother, but scholars debate whether these were one man.

events.title: The Mādhavīya Śaṅkara-digvijaya biography
events.description: The Mādhavīya Śaṅkara-digvijaya is a Sanskrit verse biography of Śaṅkara, ascribed by tradition to Mādhava, usually identified with Vidyāraṇya. It tells of his birth in Kerala, his taking of saṃnyāsa, his debate with Maṇḍana Miśra and Ubhayabhāratī, and his founding of four maṭhas. It is the most popular life of Śaṅkara but is full of miraculous incident, and many scholars think it was written long after Vidyāraṇya, perhaps centuries later. Other hagiographies, such as the Cidvilāsīya Śaṅkaravijaya, differ in details, so historians use it with caution.

events.title: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, a Vedāntic Rāma story
events.description: The Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa is a Sanskrit retelling of Vālmīki's story inside the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, framed as Śiva's teaching to Pārvatī. It presents Rāma as the Supreme Self (Paramātman) in human form and Sītā as his māyā, and fills the narrative with Advaita Vedānta teaching and devotion. Scholars place it around the fourteenth or fifteenth century. It was the chief scripture of the Rāmānandī sect and a main source for later vernacular versions, including Eḻuttacchan's Malayalam Rāmāyaṇa and, by many accounts, Tulasīdāsa's Rāmacaritamānasa.

events.title: Vaṭakalai–Teṉkalai divergence in Śrīvaiṣṇavism
events.description: In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries the Śrīvaiṣṇava community divided into the northern (Vaṭakalai) and southern (Teṉkalai) schools. The question was how much effort the soul contributes to its salvation. Vaṭakalais, who stress Sanskrit tradition, compare the soul to a young monkey that clings to its mother, so that some effort is required. Teṉkalais, who emphasise the Tamil hymns, compare it to a kitten carried by the mother cat, which does nothing. They differ also on other matters, including the role of Lakṣmī and the status of caste, and use distinct sectarian marks.
