events.title: Umāpati Śivācārya's Śaiva Siddhānta works
events.description: Umāpati Śivācārya of Cidambaram is the fourth and last of the Santāna ācāryas of Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta, after Meykaṇḍār, Aruḷnandi and Maraiñāna Sambandhar. In the early fourteenth century he wrote several of the texts that make up the fourteen Meykaṇḍa śāstras, notably the Śivaprakāśam and Tiruvaruṭpayaṉ, which restate the doctrine in careful Tamil verse. Together the fourteen texts form the classical statement of the system. Umāpati also wrote in Sanskrit and was a learned priest of the Naṭarāja temple.

events.title: Purāṇic māhātmyas map the sacred land
events.description: Many of the Purāṇas grew by absorbing regional praise-texts called māhātmyas, which describe a holy place, its legends and the merit of visiting it. The Skanda Purāṇa, the largest, contains many such sections, among them the Kāśī Khaṇḍa on Vārāṇasī, the Kedāra Khaṇḍa on the Himalayan shrines and the Sahyādri Khaṇḍa on western India. Together with the Śiva Purāṇa they form a literary map of sacred geography that guided pilgrims. The dates of these parts are uncertain and often layered, with composition running across many centuries.

events.title: Twelve jyotirliṅgas listed in the Śiva Purāṇa
events.description: The Śiva Purāṇa gives a list of twelve jyotirliṅgas, the "liṅgas of light", where Śiva is said to have appeared as a pillar of radiance: Somanātha, Mallikārjuna, Mahākāla, Oṃkāreśvara, Kedāra, Bhīmaśaṅkara, Viśveśvara, Tryambaka, Vaidyanātha, Nāgeśa, Rāmeśvara and Ghṛṣṇeśvara. The shrines span India, from Gujarat to Kedārnāth and Rāmeśvaram. The list took its familiar form in the late medieval period, and traditions differ on the sites of several shrines, with more than one temple claiming to be Vaidyanātha or Nāgeśa. The twelve remain among the most visited pilgrimage places.

events.title: Fifty-one Śakti Pīṭhas
events.description: According to the Purāṇic story, Śiva carried the body of his wife Satī after her death at Dakṣa's sacrifice, and Viṣṇu cut it apart so that parts fell to earth at different places, each becoming a Śakti Pīṭha. The tantric lists, such as the Pīṭhanirṇaya, usually name fifty-one, though other texts give 52, 64 or 108. They are spread across South Asia, from Hiṅglāj in Balochistan to Kāmākhyā in Assam, with others in Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. They became a main framework for Śākta pilgrimage and for ideas about the sacred geography of the Goddess.

events.title: Ayutthaya kingdom founded in Siam
events.description: The Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya was founded in 1350 by Ramathibodi I (U Thong), and was named after Ayodhyā, Rāma's city. Its kings used the name Rāma, and brāhmaṇa priests from Indian traditions performed coronation and state rites, which still survive in Thai court ritual. The Rāmāyaṇa, adapted as the Ramakien, became the national epic and was performed in dance and shadow theatre. The kingdom ruled until the Burmese sack of 1767, though its Hindu elements were practised alongside Theravāda Buddhism.

gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||

events.title: Vidyāraṇya's Vivaraṇaprameyasaṅgraha on Advaita
events.description: Bharatītīrtha and Vidyāraṇya were heads of the Śṛṅgeri Śāradā Pīṭha in the 14th century, when the Vijayanagara empire was founded in nearby country. Vidyāraṇya is traditionally linked with Harihara and Bukka, the first Vijayanagara kings, though this relationship is debated by historians. The Vivaraṇaprameyasaṅgraha is his work on the Vivaraṇa school of Advaita, supporting the line of Prakāśātman. Śṛṅgeri's close ties to the court gave Advaita scholarship stable support in the south.

events.title: Vidyāraṇya's Jīvanmuktiviveka on living liberation
events.description: The Jīvanmuktiviveka is a Sanskrit work attributed to Vidyāraṇya, the Śṛṅgeri teacher. It discusses jīvanmukti, liberation attained while the body is still alive, and sets out how a knower of Brahman lives and what kind of practice leads there. It also covers the rules of the renouncer, including the stages of saṃnyāsa and its different kinds, drawing on the Upaniṣads, the Gītā and Yoga Vāsiṣṭha. It argues that knowledge and a life of renunciation support each other.

gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.

events.title: Yoga Yājñavalkya, a Sanskrit yoga text
events.description: The Yoga Yājñavalkya is a Sanskrit text on yoga presented as a dialogue between the sage Yājñavalkya and the woman philosopher Gārgī. It teaches an eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga) path, including postures, breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the arousal of kuṇḍalinī. Its date is uncertain, and has been placed from the early centuries CE to the late medieval period. It is one of the sources for the later Hatha yoga traditions, and has been important in South Indian yoga teaching.

events.title: Āndhra Mahābhāratamu completed
events.description: The Telugu Mahābhārata was written by three poets across three centuries, called the Kavitraya. Nannaya, at the court of Rājarāja Narendra in the eleventh century, composed the first parvas and is honoured as the ādi-kavi of Telugu. Tikkana, in the thirteenth century, translated the last fifteen parvas. Errana, in the fourteenth century, finished the part that Nannaya left incomplete, in the Araṇya Parva. The result is a complete Telugu epic and a principal landmark of Telugu literature, still studied as a model of classical Telugu.

events.title: Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍita's Gaṇita Kaumudī
events.description: Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍita completed the Gaṇita Kaumudī, a Sanskrit mathematics text, in 1356. It covers arithmetic and algebra and gives some of the earliest general treatment of permutations and combinations, along with rules for constructing magic squares and for cyclic quadrilaterals. It contains a problem about a cow that bears a calf every year, whose calves in turn bear calves, which produces a sequence similar to that of Fibonacci. The work builds on Bhāskara II's Līlāvatī and shows how lively Indian mathematics remained in the fourteenth century.

events.title: Fīrūz Tughlaq at Purī and Jvālāmukhī
events.description: The Delhi sultan Fīrūz Shāh Tughlaq led expeditions to Odisha in 1360, when, according to his chronicle, he desecrated the Jagannātha temple at Purī, and to Nagarkot (Kāṅgṛā) the following year. At the Jvālāmukhī temple, he found a library of Sanskrit manuscripts and had some of them rendered into Persian, including a work on astrology. His court histories portray the campaigns as acts of faith, while the translation shows a real interest in Sanskrit learning. Fīrūz also imposed the jizya on brāhmaṇas.

events.title: Akṣobhya Tīrtha–Vidyāraṇya debate
events.description: Dvaita tradition records that Akṣobhya Tīrtha, a leader of the Madhva line, debated the Advaitin Vidyāraṇya at Muḷbāgal on the meaning of the Upaniṣadic text "tat tvam asi" ("that thou art"). Dvaitins read it as stating likeness and Advaitins as identity. Vedānta Deśika is said to have judged it. Historians cannot confirm the account, which comes from later sources, and each side's tradition tells it in its own favour, but it illustrates the rivalry between the two systems in the Vijayanagara period.

events.title: Nāgarakṛtāgama praises Majapahit under Hayam Wuruk
events.description: The Nāgarakṛtāgama, written in 1365 by the Buddhist poet Prapañca, is an Old Javanese poem praising King Hayam Wuruk of Majapahit. It describes the court, the capital's ceremonies, the king's tours, and the territory ruled by the empire, with the great minister Gajah Mada. It shows a Majapahit religion that mixed Śaiva and Buddhist practice. For historians, it is the best contemporary description of a Southeast Asian Hindu-Buddhist state.

events.title: Bukka I's Jaina–Vaiṣṇava accord
events.description: A famous inscription at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, the Jaina pilgrim centre in Karnataka, records that in 1368 the Vijayanagara king Bukka I settled a quarrel between the Jainas and the Śrīvaiṣṇavas. He is said to have joined their hands and declared that there was no difference between the two faiths. The record also says Vaiṣṇavas were to protect Jaina basadis and shrines. It is often cited as an example of religious accommodation in the Vijayanagara empire, though it is one dispute and a single royal decision.

events.title: Maṇavāḷa Māmuni revives Śrīvaiṣṇava teaching
events.description: Maṇavāḷa Māmuni, born in 1370 at Sikkil Kiḍāram, was the greatest teacher of the Teṉkalai school. He revived Śrīvaiṣṇava teaching in Śrīraṅgam after the troubled period of the invasions, wrote on the Tamil hymns of the Āḻvārs and the writings of Piḷḷai Lokācārya, and led a lively circle of disciples. Tradition says that he gave a year-long exposition of Nammāḻvār's Tiruvāymoḻi in the temple, which the deity Raṅganātha himself listened to, after which the god honoured him with a verse of praise.

events.title: Kumāra Kampaṇa conquers Madurai
events.description: About 1370, Kumāra Kampaṇa, son of Bukka I of Vijayanagara, marched south and defeated the Madurai Sultanate. His wife Gaṅgādevī recorded the campaign in a Sanskrit mahākāvya, the Madhurāvijayam (also called Vīrakampa-rāya-caritam), which describes the desolation of the temples under the sultans and the revival of worship. Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition says that in 1371 the image of Raṅganātha, which had been moved away in 1323, was brought back to Śrīraṅgam. The conquest made Vijayanagara the main power south of the Tuṅgabhadrā.

events.title: Harihara II rules Vijayanagara
events.description: Harihara II, a son of Bukka I, ruled Vijayanagara from 1377 to 1404 and took the imperial title Mahārājādhirāja Rājaparameśvara. During his reign the kingdom extended from the Arabian Sea in the west to the Bay of Bengal in the east, according to his inscriptions. The scholar Sāyaṇa, the great Vedic commentator, and his brother Mādhava (Vidyāraṇya) were associated with the early court. Vijayanagara became the leading power in the south.

events.title: Vidyāpati, poet of Mithilā
events.description: Vidyāpati was a poet of Mithilā, in present-day Bihar, who served the kings of the Oinvāra line, notably Śivasiṃha. He wrote in Sanskrit, Avahaṭṭha and Maithili. His Maithili songs of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, with their language of love and separation, influenced the later Vaiṣṇava poetry of Bengal and Assam, and Caitanya is said to have loved them. He also wrote songs to Śiva, called nacārīs, and Sanskrit works on dharma and statecraft, such as the Puruṣaparīkṣā. His verses remain part of Maithili cultural life.

events.title: Caṇḍīdāsa, poet of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa songs
events.description: Caṇḍīdāsa is a name attached to one or more medieval Bengali poets of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa love. The Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtana, found in a village in Bankura district in 1909, is a long narrative in song attributed to Baḍu Caṇḍīdāsa, and is among the oldest surviving works of Bengali literature. A separate body of padāvalī songs is ascribed to a poet of the same name. A line often quoted, "above all is the truth of man; nothing is higher", expresses a humanist note in Bengali devotion, and Caitanya is said to have savoured his songs.

events.title: Jayasthiti Malla organises Newar society
events.description: Jayasthiti Malla ruled the Kathmandu Valley from 1382 to 1395 and is credited by later tradition with ordering society and law. He is said to have organised the Newar population into hereditary castes and set out rules for ritual and conduct, using Dharmaśāstra authorities. The Malla kings considered themselves Hindu rulers and patrons of Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava temples, though they also supported Buddhist institutions, and the valley's art and temple building flourished under them.

events.title: Sikandar Butshikan in Kashmir
events.description: Sikandar Shāh Miri, who ruled Kashmir from 1389 to 1413, is known as Butshikan, "breaker of idols". The Sanskrit chronicler Jonarāja and the Persian histories record that during his reign many temples were demolished, including, according to tradition, the great Mārtaṇḍa Sun temple, and that brāhmaṇas were pressed to convert or leave the valley. Some historians argue that the damage to Mārtaṇḍa was only partial and that the persecution later eased under his son Alī Shāh, but the chronicles agree that many Paṇḍits fled in his reign.

events.title: Śarqī Sultanate founded at Jaunpur
events.description: Jaunpur, in eastern Uttar Pradesh, became the seat of the Śarqī sultans, whose kingdom began in 1394 when Malik Sarwar, a Tughlaq governor, made himself independent of Delhi. The Śarqīs patronised Persian learning and music, and built mosques such as the Aṭālā Masjid, completed in 1408, which, according to later accounts, reused material from the temple of Aṭālā Devī. Jaunpur became a noted centre of learning and architecture. The dynasty lasted until 1479, when the Lodīs of Delhi conquered it.

events.title: Rāṭhoṛs take Maṇḍor
events.description: Cūṇḍā, a Rāṭhoṛ chief, took Maṇḍor, north of present Jodhpur, from the Parihāras around 1395 to 1405. A tradition holds that he received it as a dowry. He is regarded as the first real ruler of the Rāṭhoṛ kingdom of Mārwāṛ. The Rāṭhoṛs later moved their capital to Jodhpur in 1459, when Jodhā founded it. They became one of the leading Rajput houses.

events.title: Timur sacks Delhi
events.description: The Central Asian conqueror Timur (Tamerlane) reached the Indus in 1398 and marched on Delhi, whose Sultan Maḥmūd Tughlaq fled after a defeat. Timur's own memoirs record that he put many prisoners to death before the battle, and Delhi was sacked in December 1398 with heavy killing and plunder. On the way back he fought Hindu defenders near Haridvāra on the Gaṅgā. The invasion ruined Delhi and ended the Tughlaq dynasty's real power. The Sayyid dynasty took the throne in 1414.

events.title: Kabīr, the weaver-saint of Vārāṇasī
events.description: A weaver of Vārāṇasī, raised in a family of Muslim julāhās and by tradition a disciple of the Vaiṣṇava teacher Rāmānanda. He could not write; his verses were sung and remembered.¶He mocked the pandit and the mullah alike, rejected caste, pilgrimage, image and fasting, and spoke of one formless God, whom he called Rāma, found only within. "If God is in the mosque, whose is the rest of the land?" His songs are sung by Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims; over two hundred of them are in the Guru Granth Sāhib. Tradition says both communities claimed his body and found only flowers.

events.title: Śrīpati Paṇḍita’s Śrīkara Bhāṣya
events.description: The Śrīkara Bhāṣya is a Vīraśaiva commentary on the Brahma Sūtras, ascribed to Śrīpati Paṇḍita, a scholar traditionally identified with the twelfth-century Śrīpati Paṇḍitārādhya. Scholars date the work much later, tentatively around 1400, and some doubt the traditional attribution. It teaches Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita, a qualified non-dualism in which Brahman is Śiva possessed of Śakti. The work gave Vīraśaivism a Vedāntic framework beside its poetic vacana tradition. It should not be confused with the Siddhāntaśekhara, a treatise on astronomy by the unrelated astronomer Śrīpati.

events.title: Śrīdhara Svāmī's Bhāvārthadīpikā
events.description: Śrīdhara Svāmī's Bhāvārthadīpikā is the most widely respected Sanskrit commentary on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa. Tradition describes him as an Advaitin of the Daśanāmī renunciant lineage, and he reads the text as a devotional work while keeping to non-dual philosophy, which made him acceptable to many Vaiṣṇava schools. Caitanya is said to have valued it, and Gauḍīya writers cite him often. He is also credited with the Subodhinī on the Bhagavad Gītā. He is often linked with Odisha, near Purī. His dates are uncertain, with estimates from the thirteenth to the fifteenth century.

events.title: Aruṇagirinātha's Tiruppugaḻ hymns to Murugaṉ
events.description: Aruṇagirinātha, a poet of Tiruvaṇṇāmalai, composed the Tiruppugaḻ ("holy praise") in praise of Murugaṉ, the Tamil war-god and son of Śiva. Over a thousand of his hymns survive, written in intricate rhythmic metres whose syllable patterns can be heard in the sung versions. Tradition says he was a dissolute man who tried to end his life and was saved by Murugaṉ, after which he turned to devotion. His hymns name the god's hill shrines, from Pālani to Tiruttaṇi and Swāmimalai, and they remain the common song of Murugaṉ worshippers in Tamil Nadu and abroad.

events.title: Haṭha Yoga texts multiply
events.description: From about the thirteenth century a body of Sanskrit manuals on haṭha-yoga appeared. They include the Dattātreyayogaśāstra, the Gorakṣaśataka, the Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā and the Śivasaṃhitā, which teach postures, breath control, seals (mudrās) and the raising of Kuṇḍalinī, often with Nātha and tantric background. Each text covers somewhat different techniques and philosophical views. They prepared the way for the Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā, which gathered them into one standard handbook. The dates of these works are debated, and their sequence is reconstructed by scholars from their quotations.

events.title: Dattātreya tradition and Śrīpāda Śrīvallabha
events.description: Dattātreya, the son of the sage Atri and Anasūyā, is a composite divinity said to embody Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva, and he is honoured as a wandering avadhūta teacher. The Datta Sampradāya of Maharashtra and Karnataka regards Śrīpāda Śrīvallabha, who lived about 1320–1350, as his first historical incarnation, and Nṛsiṃha Sarasvatī (1378–1459), who settled at Gāṇagāpūr on the Bhīmā river, as the second. The Gurucaritra, a Marathi work of the sixteenth century, tells of their lives and has become the community's chief scripture.

events.title: Sadānanda's Vedāntasāra, an Advaita primer
events.description: The Vedāntasāra, attributed to Sadānanda Yati, is a short Sanskrit manual that introduces Advaita Vedānta in plain terms. It covers the qualifications of a student, the nature of ignorance, the two powers of māyā, the layers of the self and the path from hearing the teachings to realisation. Because it is brief and clear, it became the most widely used primer of the school and is still taught to beginners. Its date is usually given as about the 15th century, though some place it later.

events.title: Pīpā, Dhannā and Sena
events.description: Pīpā, Dhannā and Sena are remembered as disciples of Rāmānanda, the teacher who opened Rāma devotion to people of all backgrounds. Pīpā was a Rajput king who gave up his throne, Dhannā a Jāṭ farmer, and Sena a barber. Their devotional hymns are in the Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sāhib, alongside those of Kabīr and Ravidās. They are part of the sant tradition of North India, in which devotion mattered more than birth or rank.

events.title: Śabarimala and the Ayyappaṉ tradition
events.description: The temple at Śabarimala in Kerala is a forest shrine to Ayyappaṉ, also called Dharma Śāstā, whose legend ties him to the Pandalam royal house. Pilgrims observe about forty-one days of austerity, wearing black or blue clothes and a rosary, and climb to the shrine. All pilgrims are called Ayyappa, regardless of caste. The shrine has drawn debate over the entry of women of menstruating age, which the Supreme Court addressed in 2018 and later reviewed.

events.title: Guruvāyūr temple rises to prominence
events.description: The Guruvāyūr temple in Kerala is dedicated to Kṛṣṇa as Guruvāyūrappaṉ, the child-form of Viṣṇu. Tradition says the image was installed by Bṛhaspati (Guru) and Vāyu, the wind god, giving the place its name. Historically, it rose to prominence by the 14th to 16th centuries under the patronage of the Zamorins of Kozhikode. It is associated with the poet Melpputtūr Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri's Nārāyaṇīyam, composed there in 1586, and with strict ritual, and is among the most visited temples in Kerala.

events.title: Kūṭiyāṭṭam, Kerala's Sanskrit theatre
events.description: Kūṭiyāṭṭam is Kerala's Sanskrit theatre, performed by Cākyār actors with Nambiār drummers in temple theatres (kūttambalam). Its performances unfold slowly, with actors elaborating verses and episodes over many nights. It is considered the oldest surviving form of Sanskrit drama in performance, and UNESCO recognised it in 2001 as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam, a Kṛṣṇa cycle, appeared in the seventeenth century in Kerala and is thought to have influenced Kathakaḷi, which developed from these temple arts.

events.title: Aṭālā Masjid and the Aṭālā Devī temple claim
events.description: The Aṭālā Masjid in Jaunpur was completed in 1408 under the Śarqī sultan Ibrāhīm Shāh. Tradition and some historians hold that it stands on the site of a temple of Aṭālā Devī and that its builders reused temple stones, though the extent of this is disputed. The mosque is a grand example of Jaunpur's distinctive architecture, with a large propylon at the entrance. Its history has been the subject of recent legal claims by Hindu petitioners. Śarqī Jaunpur was also a centre of learning.

events.title: Annamācārya born at Tāḷḷapāka
events.description: Annamācārya was born at Tāḷḷapāka in Andhra and became a devotee of Veṅkaṭeśvara, the god of Tirumala. Tradition credits him with 32,000 Telugu and Sanskrit saṅkīrtanas, songs praising the god, which his descendants inscribed on copper plates kept in the Tirumala temple. Several thousand plates were rediscovered there in the twentieth century and about fourteen thousand songs survive. His songs speak in ordinary language of devotion, ethics and everyday life, and they are widely sung. He is regarded as the first major composer of Telugu devotional songs.

events.title: Narasiṃha Mehtā born
events.description: Narasiṃha Mehtā, born at Talājā and associated with Junāgaḍh in Saurāṣṭra, is honoured as Gujarat's ādi-kavi, the first poet. A Nāgara brāhmaṇa, he composed Gujarati songs of Kṛṣṇa devotion, including the morning songs called prabhātiyā, and is said to have joined low-caste groups for worship in defiance of his community. His best-known verse, "Vaiṣṇava jana to", describes the true devotee as one who feels others' pain. Mahatma Gandhi made it a favourite prayer in the twentieth century.

events.title: Rudra Mahālaya converted into a mosque
events.description: The Rudra Mahālaya at Siddhapur in Gujarat was a great Śaiva temple complex, begun under the Caulukya (Solaṅkī) kings and said to have been completed by Jayasiṃha Siddharāja in the twelfth century. It was damaged during the Delhi Sultanate's raids, and Ahmad Shāh I, the sultan of Gujarat, converted part of it into a congregational mosque in the early fifteenth century. Only some pillars and a gateway survive from the original, and they give a sense of the temple's former scale.

events.title: Zain-ul-Ābidīn recalls the Paṇḍits
events.description: Zain-ul-Ābidīn, called Bud Shāh, "the great king", ruled Kashmir from 1420 to 1470 and reversed his father Sikandar's policy. He invited back Hindu scholars who had fled, repaired temples, banned cow slaughter and abolished the jizya. He promoted translations between Sanskrit and Persian, and his court history, Jonarāja's continuation of the Rājataraṅgiṇī, records the rule. He also encouraged crafts such as papermaking and carpet-weaving, and he is remembered as Kashmir's most tolerant sultan.

events.title: Niccolò de' Conti and ʿAbd al-Razzāq at Vijayanagara
events.description: Two foreign visitors recorded the city's splendour. The Venetian merchant Niccolò de' Conti came around 1420, and the Persian ambassador ʿAbd al-Razzāq, who was sent by the Timurid ruler Shāhrukh, visited in 1443. Both reached Vijayanagara in the reign of Devarāya II. ʿAbd al-Razzāq wrote that he had never seen or heard of a city like it. They describe its seven concentric walls, its great bazaars full of jewels and flowers, and the king's army. Their accounts are among the main foreign sources on Hampi.

events.title: Amarnāth cave pilgrimage
events.description: The Amarnāth cave, high in the Kashmir Himalaya, holds an ice formation worshipped as a Śiva liṅga. Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī and the Nīlamata Purāṇa mention Amareśvara and the pilgrimage to a sacred place of that name, and later chronicles record royal visits. The modern annual pilgrimage is traced to a revival in the mid-19th century, with a legend of a Muslim shepherd, Buta Malik, finding the cave, which differs from older traditions. The yātrā takes place in summer and draws large numbers of pilgrims.

events.title: Vīraśaiva literary revival under Devarāya II
events.description: In the fifteenth century, Vīraśaiva literature flourished under the Vijayanagara king Devarāya II. The saint Tōṇṭada Siddhaliṅga was a leader of the revival. At court, Lakkaṇṇa Daṇḍeśa, a minister, wrote the Śivatattvacintāmaṇi, and the poet Cāmarasa wrote the Prabhuliṅgalīle, a narrative of the saint Allama Prabhu. These works recovered and collected the vacanas, and made the Vīraśaiva tradition a lasting part of Kannada literature.

events.title: Śrīnātha and the Telugu Śaiva poets
events.description: Telugu literature has a strong Śaiva strand. Pālkuriki Somanātha, writing in the 13th century, composed the Basava Purāṇa, a Telugu retelling of the life of the Vīraśaiva reformer Basavaṇṇa. Śrīnātha, who flourished around 1400 to 1450 and enjoyed the patronage of Reddi kings, wrote the Kāśīkhaṇḍamu, based on the Sanskrit Skanda Purāṇa's section on Kāśī, and other works. Their poetry in Telugu extended the Purāṇic and Śaiva traditions into the language of Andhra.

events.title: Devarāya II rules Vijayanagara
events.description: Devarāya II ruled Vijayanagara from 1424 to 1446. He is called Gajabeṇṭekāra, "the elephant hunter", and was the greatest ruler of the Saṅgama dynasty. He reorganised the army and extended control over the Kondavidu area. The Persian ambassador ʿAbd al-Razzāq visited around 1443 and wrote of the city's splendour and size. Kannada, Telugu and Sanskrit literature were supported at his court.

events.title: Tantrasamuccaya, Kerala's temple ritual manual
events.description: The Tantrasamuccaya was composed in 1428 by Cēnnās Nārāyaṇan Nambūtirippāḍ, of a Tantri family of Kerala. It is a handbook of temple ritual, setting out the rules of consecration, daily worship, festivals and expiation, with reference to the Āgama tradition and Kerala practice. Later authors wrote commentaries, and it governs worship in a large number of Kerala temples today. The family that composed it still performs the role of tantri in some of the major shrines.

events.description: Kumāravyāsa, whose real name was Nārāyaṇappa, a poet of Gadag in Karnataka, wrote the Karṇāṭa Bhārata Kathāmañjarī in about 1430, popularly called the Gadugina Bhārata ("Bhārata of Gadag"). It tells the first ten parvas of the Mahābhārata in Kannada verse, with Kṛṣṇa, in the form of the Vīranārāyaṇa of Gadag, as the hero. It was composed in the simple Bhāmini ṣaṭpadi metre, and it became the version of the epic that Kannada villagers heard recited in public readings for generations.

events.title: Parameśvara's Dṛggaṇita of Kerala astronomy
events.description: Parameśvara of Vaṭaśśeri in Kerala, who lived roughly 1360–1455, is said to have made eclipse observations for some fifty-five years. He used them to revise the parameters of the planets in the Āryabhaṭa tradition, and in 1431 produced the Dṛggaṇita ("computation by observation"). The system gave Kerala astronomers more accurate calendars and eclipse predictions, and it was widely followed in the region. He is a principal figure of the Kerala school, whose later members include his pupil Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī.

events.title: Rāṇā Kumbha of Mewar
events.description: Rāṇā Kumbhakarṇa of Mewar ruled from 1433 to 1468 and strengthened the kingdom against the Sultans of Mālwā and Gujarat. He built or rebuilt many forts, traditionally thirty-two, the greatest being Kumbhalgaṛh with its long encircling wall. He was a learned patron and himself an author, who wrote a commentary on Jayadeva's Gītagovinda and a treatise on music. Sanskrit inscriptions praise him as a master of dance and drama. He was killed by his own son Udā.

events.title: Kapilendra founds the Gajapati dynasty
events.description: Kapilendra Deva came to the Odisha throne in 1435 and founded the Sūryavaṃśa Gajapati dynasty. He expanded his kingdom from the Gaṅgā in the north to the Kāverī in the south, fighting the Bahmanīs and Vijayanagara. He took the title of "Gajapati", lord of elephants, and in the tradition of the kings of Odisha ruled as the deputy of Jagannātha, whose temple at Purī the dynasty patronised. The empire declined after his death in 1467, and the Gajapati kingdom was ended by the Bengal and Golconda sultanates in the sixteenth century.

events.title: Rāṇā Kumbha defeats Maḥmūd Khaljī at Sāraṅgpur
events.description: In 1437 Rāṇā Kumbha of Mewar defeated Maḥmūd Khaljī, the Sultan of Mālwā, at Sāraṅgpur and took him prisoner, according to Rajput and some Persian sources. The Sultan was held for some months before being released. Kumbha is credited with raising the Vijaya Stambha, the nine-storey tower of victory at Chittor, built between about 1440 and 1448, which tradition links to the Mālwā victory. His reign was among the most successful of the Mewar kings.

events.title: Rāṇakpur Jaina temple begun
events.description: The Caumukha (four-faced) Jaina temple at Rāṇakpur in the Aravalli hills was begun in 1439. A Jaina merchant, Dhaṇa Śāh, built it on land given by the Mewar ruler Rāṇā Kumbha, to a design by the architect Depāka. It is dedicated to Ādinātha, the first Tīrthaṅkara, and is known for its 1,444 carved pillars, no two exactly alike, and its marble domes. The temple shows the patronage of Jaina merchants under Hindu Rajput rulers and remains an important pilgrimage place.

events.title: Vijaya Stambha at Chittor
events.description: Between about 1440 and 1448 Rāṇā Kumbha raised the Vijaya Stambha, or "tower of victory", inside Chittor fort. According to tradition it commemorated his defeat of the Sultan of Mālwā, Maḥmūd Khaljī. The tower is nine storeys high, about thirty-seven metres, and dedicated to Viṣṇu. It is covered with carvings of Hindu gods and goddesses, and its inscriptions name the architects. A staircase inside leads to an upper pavilion. It stands alongside the Kīrti Stambha of a Jaina merchant as a symbol of Chittor.

events.title: Śaṅkaradeva born in Assam
events.description: Śaṅkaradeva (1449–1568) was a saint, poet, dramatist and reformer of Assam. He taught Ekaśaraṇa Nāma-dharma, devotion to Kṛṣṇa alone through hearing and singing the divine name, and he wrote the Kīrtana-ghoṣā, songs, bargīts and plays called Aṅkīyā Nāṭ. His followers built monasteries called sattras and prayer halls known as nāmghars, which became centres of Assamese religion, art and dance. He accepted disciples from tribal and low-caste groups. His pupil Mādhavadeva carried on the work, and the tradition shapes Assamese cultural life.

events.title: Kathmandu's Kumārī tradition
events.description: The Kumārī is a young girl worshipped as a living embodiment of the goddess, identified in Kathmandu with Taleju, the Malla kings' tutelary deity. The origins of the tradition are obscure; accounts link it with the Malla kings, from legends about Trailokya Malla in the fifteenth century to the building of the present Kumārī Ghar in the eighteenth. The king receives her blessing, and she is chosen from the Śākya caste of Newar Buddhists. She appears in public in festivals such as Indra Jātrā, an example of the blending of Hindu and Buddhist Tantric practice in Newar culture.

events.title: Bhālaṇ and Gujarati ākhyāna poetry
events.description: Bhālaṇ, who wrote in the fifteenth century, is regarded as an early master of the Gujarati ākhyāna, a narrative poem retelling Purāṇic and literary tales for recitation. He rendered parts of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and Bāṇa's Sanskrit prose romance the Kādambarī into Gujarati. The form flourished in the following centuries, notably in the work of Premānanda Bhaṭṭa. Narasiṃha Mehtā, honoured as Gujarat's first major poet, belongs to the same century, though his fame rests on devotional songs. These poets built a vernacular literary culture on Sanskrit foundations.

events.title: Potana's Telugu Bhāgavatamu
events.description: Bammera Potana rendered the Bhāgavata Purāṇa in Telugu, in a work that Telugu speakers still recite and sing. He is said to have refused to dedicate his poem to a king, and to have offered it instead to Rāma, as a sign that poetry should serve God and not a patron. Born in Telangana, he is thought to have been a farmer as well as a poet. The Bhāgavatamu's tales of Kṛṣṇa, Prahlāda and Gajendra are loved for their musical language, and its verses are recited in Telugu homes.

events.title: Śaṅkara Miśra and Vardhamāna
events.description: After Gaṅgeśa founded Navya-Nyāya, Mithilā became a centre of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika learning. Vardhamāna, Gaṅgeśa's son, wrote a commentary on his father's Tattvacintāmaṇi, and Śaṅkara Miśra, in the fifteenth century, wrote the Upaskāra, an influential commentary on the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra. Pakṣadhara Miśra, another Mithilā scholar, is traditionally said to have taught Raghunātha Śiromaṇi, who carried the new logic to Navadvīpa in Bengal. This is how the school's learning moved from Mithilā to Bengal.

events.title: Kapilendra seizes the Godāvarī delta
events.description: On the east coast, the Gajapati kings of Odisha and the Reḍḍi kings of Andhra contested the fertile Godāvarī delta. Kapilendra, who founded the Sūryavaṃśa Gajapati line in 1435, took advantage of Reḍḍi weakness and of conflict between the Reḍḍi branches. By about 1450 he had absorbed Rājamahendravaram (Rajahmundry), then held by the Reḍḍis, and pushed his boundary south. The Gajapati realm came to stretch from the Gaṅgā to the Kṛṣṇā, and they were also patrons of the Jagannātha temple at Purī.

events.title: Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā
events.description: Svātmārāma wrote the Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā in the fifteenth century, drawing on earlier Nātha texts. In four chapters it describes a short list of postures (āsanas), breath control (prāṇāyāma), the seals and locks (mudrās and bandhas), and the inner sound (nāda) heard in meditation. It presents haṭha-yoga as a way of preparing the body for rāja-yoga, which is samādhi. It is the most influential premodern text of its kind, and many of the physical practices now taught worldwide as yoga trace back to it.

events.title: Ravidāsa, Sant poet of Kāśī
events.description: Ravidāsa, the poet-saint of Kāśī who came from a family of cobblers, is a major voice of the Sant tradition of north India. His verses, composed in a medieval Hindi of the region, sing of a formless God and reject caste distinctions. A well-known poem imagines Begampurā, a city "without sorrow" with no taxes or distinctions, and forty or so of his hymns appear in the Sikh Ādi Granth. Tradition names him a disciple of Rāmānanda and a companion of Kabīr. The Ravidāsiyā community, with many followers in Punjab, honours him as its guru.

events.title: Saraḷā Dāsa's Oḍiā Mahābhārata
events.description: Saraḷā Dāsa, a fifteenth-century poet of Odisha who lived in the time of Kapilendra, retold the Mahābhārata in the Odia language. It is among the earliest renderings of the epic in an eastern Indian vernacular and is regarded as the first major Odia Mahābhārata. He adds many local stories and folk episodes not in the Sanskrit original, and gives Jagannātha-Kṛṣṇa a prominent place. He is traditionally called the Vyāsa of Odisha, and is also credited with an Odia Rāmāyaṇa, the Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa. He was reportedly of humble birth and wrote in the vernacular, not in Sanskrit.

events.title: Kṛttivāsa's Bengali Rāmāyaṇa
events.description: Kṛttivāsa Ojhā retold the Rāmāyaṇa in Bengali payār verse, in the fifteenth century, as the Śrīrāma Pāñcālī, to be sung. It follows Vālmīki's outline but adds Bengali settings and a more devotional tone, and in later centuries copyists added many episodes. It became the most loved Rāmāyaṇa in Bengal and was among the first Bengali books printed, at Serampore in the early nineteenth century. It ranks with Kāśīrām Dās's Mahābhārata as a pillar of Bengali literature.

events.title: Cerusseri's Kṛṣṇagāthā in Malayalam
events.description: Cerusseri Namboothiri, a poet at the court of Udayavarma of Kolathunādu in northern Kerala, composed the Kṛṣṇagāthā in the fifteenth century. events.title: Zamorins of Kozhikode and the Māmāṅkam
events.description: The Zamorins, or Sāmūtiri, ruled Kozhikode (Calicut) and were among Kerala's most powerful kings. They controlled much of the Malabar pepper trade. Their right to preside at the Māmāṅkam, a great festival held every twelve years at Tirunāvāya on the Bhāratappuḷa river, was a matter of political prestige. According to the tradition, the festival was a place of intense rivalry, and champions called Cāver were sworn to attack the Zamorin. Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498.

events.title: Vaiṣṇo Devī cave shrine in the Trikūṭa hills
events.description: The Vaiṣṇo Devī shrine lies in a cave on Trikūṭa hill in Jammu and Kashmir, where the goddess is worshipped in the form of three natural stone piṇḍīs representing Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī. Legends tell of Vaiṣṇavī, a devotee of Rāma, and of the demon Bhairava. The shrine's history is hard to date, and the 15th century is a rough estimate. Over time it has become one of the major Śākta pilgrimages, drawing millions of visitors a year.

events.title: Rāṇā Kumbha's Kumbhalgaṛh
events.description: Kumbhalgaṛh, in the Aravalli hills of Mewar, was built by Rāṇā Kumbha and completed around 1458, with the architect Maṇḍan usually associated with its design. A massive wall about 36 kilometres long, wide enough for several riders, surrounds the fort, and it is often cited as one of the longest in the world. Tradition says that Mahārāṇā Pratāp was born there in 1540. It is part of the UNESCO listing for the hill forts of Rajasthan.

events.title: Rāo Jodhā founds Jodhpur
events.description: In 1459 Rāo Jodhā of the Rāṭhoṛ clan founded Jodhpur and began the fort of Mehrangaṛh on a steep sandstone rock. The Rāṭhoṛs had previously ruled from Maṇḍor, a short distance north. The city became the capital of Marwar, a major Rajput kingdom of the Thar region, and Mehrangaṛh, with its high ramparts, remained the residence of its rulers. Marwar's kings fought and served the Mughals, and the Rāṭhoṛ lineage produced figures such as Māldeo and Durgādās.

events.title: Vyāsatīrtha, Dvaita scholar at Vijayanagara
events.description: Vyāsatīrtha (also Vyāsarāja, 1460–1539), a Dvaita scholar, served as the spiritual guide of the Vijayanagara court under several kings, notably Kṛṣṇadevarāya. His works include the Nyāyāmṛta, a long attack on Advaita, the Tarkatāṇḍava and the Tātparya Candrikā. The Advaitin Madhusūdana Sarasvatī answered the Nyāyāmṛta with the Advaitasiddhi, and the exchange became a main thread of Vedāntic debate. Vyāsatīrtha also encouraged the Haridāsa singers Purandara Dāsa and Kanaka Dāsa, and kept a monastery at Hampi.

events.title: Śaṅkaradeva stages the Cihna-yātrā
events.description: Around 1468 Śaṅkaradeva staged a dramatic presentation called Cihna-yātrā, in which painted scenery depicted the seven Vaikuṇṭhas, the heavenly realms of Viṣṇu. It was performed before the people with music and dance, and it is regarded as the first example of Assamese drama. From this beginning came Aṅkīyā Nāṭ, one-act devotional plays, and the sattra tradition of music and dance later recognised as Sattriya, which is now one of the classical dance forms of India.

events.title: Guru Nānak born
events.description: Nānak was born at Talvaṇḍī (now Nankāṇā Sāhib in Pakistan) in a Hindu family and became the first Guru of the Sikhs. He travelled widely in his four udāsīs, settled at Kartārpur and taught devotion to one formless God, summed up in the opening Ik Oṅkār of his Japujī. His hymns share the vocabulary and ideas of the Sant poets such as Kabīr, though Sikhs hold his teaching to be a distinct revelation and the Sikh panth developed as a separate religion. He rejected caste distinctions and ritual practice as paths to the divine.

events.title: Jonarāja and Śrīvara continue the Rājataraṅgiṇī
events.description: After Kalhaṇa's chronicle ended in the twelfth century, other Kashmiri writers carried the history forward in Sanskrit. Jonarāja wrote about the later Hindu kings and the early Muslim sultans, and his pupil Śrīvara continued the account into the time of Sultan Zain-ul-Ābidīn and his successors. Together with later authors, they give a continuous account of the valley from Sultanate to Mughal times in the same literary form, making Kashmir exceptional among Indian regions for its historical writing.

events.title: Fall of Vijaya in Champa
events.description: In 1471 the Vietnamese emperor Lê Thánh Tông captured Vijaya, the capital of Champa, in central Vietnam, and took tens of thousands of prisoners, according to Vietnamese sources. Champa had been a Hindu kingdom for about a thousand years, with Śiva worship at temples such as Mỹ Sơn, and with Sanskrit inscriptions. It survived only as a small state in the south, which the Vietnamese absorbed in 1832. Some Cham people continue to practise a local form of Hinduism, while others became Muslim.

gitaQuote.transliteration: pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ | vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛk sāma yajur eva ca || gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt | prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||

I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. events.title: Mahmūd Begaḍā takes Dvārakā and Junāgaḍh
events.description: Maḥmūd Begaḍā, the sultan of Gujarat from 1458 to 1511, campaigned against two of the region's Hindu strongholds. He besieged Junāgaḍh, taking it about 1470 and ending the rule of the Cūḍāsamā kings of Girnār, whose ruler was Rā Māṇḍalika. In 1473 he took Dvārakā, where the temple was sacked according to Persian chronicles such as the Mirāt-i-Sikandarī. He annexed Saurashtra's coastal land to Gujarat, and the region's politics changed for generations.

events.title: Fall of Majapahit and Hindu migration to Bali
events.description: Majapahit declined in the later fifteenth century and, by tradition, fell around 1478 (some sources give later dates) as Islam spread through coastal Java and the sultanate of Demak grew. Some priests, nobles and artists moved to Bali, bringing their court culture and religion. There Hindu worship, in the form known as Āgama Hindu Dharma, with its mixture of Śaiva and Buddhist elements and local ritual, survived and flourished. Bali remains the main Hindu community of Indonesia.

events.title: Vallabhācārya born at Campāraṇya
events.description: Vallabha was born in 1479 at Campāraṇya, according to tradition, to a Telugu brāhmaṇa family, and later lived at Kāśī, Vṛndāvana and Adail near Prayāga. He founded the Śuddhādvaita ("pure non-dualism") school, which sees the world as real, and the Puṣṭi Mārga, the path of grace in which the devotee serves Kṛṣṇa as a child with loving household devotion. His works include the Aṇubhāṣya, an incomplete commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, the Subodhinī on the Bhāgavata and sixteen short texts, the Ṣoḍaśagrantha. His descendants, called Gosvāmīs, lead the community.

events.title: Kabīr's Bījak and the Kabīr Panth
events.description: The Bījak is the main scripture of the Kabīr Panth, the community following the weaver-saint Kabīr of Kāśī. It collects his sākhīs (couplets), ramainīs (longer verses) and śabdas (songs), composed in a mixed Hindi of the Bhojpuri region. The poems criticise caste, ritual and Hindu and Muslim orthodoxy alike, and urge direct knowledge of the one God. The Bījak was compiled by followers after his death, and the Guru Granth Sāhib and the Pañcavāṇī offer other, differing collections of his verses.

events.title: Śaṅkaradeva's first pilgrimage
events.description: Śaṅkaradeva, the Assamese saint and reformer, set out on a long pilgrimage to the sacred sites of India, including Purī, Vṛndāvana and Badarī, according to his biographies. These years, said to have lasted about twelve, exposed him to Bhāgavata devotion and shaped his Ekaśaraṇa Nāma Dharma, which teaches exclusive devotion to Kṛṣṇa through hearing and singing his name. Returning to Assam, he composed songs, plays and translations of the Bhāgavata that made Vaiṣṇava bhakti a mass movement in the Brahmaputra valley.

events.title: Purandara Dāsa born
events.description: Purandara Dāsa, born about 1484, was a wealthy merchant, perhaps from Purandaragaḍa, who gave up his wealth and became a devotee of Viṭṭhala and a disciple of Vyāsatīrtha. Tradition ascribes hundreds of thousands of songs to him, of which several hundred survive in Kannada. He also arranged the basic lessons for learning Carnatic music, such as the sarali and janṭa varisais and alaṅkāras, which are still taught. For this he is called the Pitāmaha of Carnatic music. His songs speak of ethics, devotion and worldly life, and are sung widely.

events.title: Guru Jambheśvara and the Biśnoīs
events.description: Jambheśvara, also called Jāmbhojī, founded the Biśnoī community in the Thar desert, said to be in 1485. Its twenty-nine rules, the name meaning "twenty-nine," prohibit felling green trees, killing animals and eating meat, along with ordinary ethical guidance. The community came to be known for protecting trees and blackbuck. A story, set in 1730 at Khejaṛli, tells that more than three hundred Biśnoīs died trying to stop the cutting of khejaṛī trees, an event often cited in the history of environmental activism in India.

events.title: Sāḷuva Narasiṃha's usurpation
events.description: By the 1480s the Saṅgama dynasty of Vijayanagara was weak under Virūpākṣa II, and rebellion and invasion threatened the kingdom. In 1485 the general Sāḷuva Narasiṃha, ruler of Candragiri, took the throne. He restored order and recovered lost territory, and the kingdom was saved from breaking up. He died in 1491, and a regency followed. In 1505 the Tuḷuva general Vīra Narasiṃha took power, and his half-brother Kṛṣṇadevarāya came to the throne in 1509 to lead the empire to its greatest extent.

events.title: Caitanya Mahāprabhu born
events.description: Viśvambhara Miśra was born at Navadvīpa in Bengal in 1486 during a lunar eclipse, while the town chanted the names of God. A brilliant young logician, he was transformed by a pilgrimage to Gayā at twenty-two and began leading ecstatic public singing of Kṛṣṇa's names through the streets.¶He took monastic vows as Kṛṣṇa Caitanya, settled at Purī, and sent his learned followers to recover Vṛndāvana. His followers regard him as Kṛṣṇa himself, come to taste Rādhā's love. He left only eight verses of his own; the theology of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism was written by his disciples.

events.title: Mān Singh Tomar of Gwalior
events.description: Mān Singh Tomar ruled Gwalior from 1486 to 1516. He built the Mān Mandir palace in the fort, with elegant blue-tiled decoration, and is known as a patron of music. The dhrupad style developed at his court, and a treatise on music was compiled under his patronage. Tradition associates him with his queen Mṛgayanī, for whom the Gūjarī Mahal was built. After his death Gwalior was taken by the Lodī sultan.

events.title: Rāo Bīkā founds Bikaner
events.description: Rāo Bīkā, a son of the Rāṭhoṛ ruler Jodhā, founded Bikaner in 1488 in the dry country north of Mārwāṛ. The ruling family took Karṇī Mātā, a Cāraṇ woman revered as an incarnation of Durgā, as their patron deity. Her temple at Deśnoke, near Bikaner, is well known for the many rats kept there and revered as her kin. The Bikaner house continued its association with the goddess up to the twentieth century.

events.title: Vallabha finds Śrīnāthajī
events.description: According to the Puṣṭi Mārga, the image of Kṛṣṇa lifting Mount Govardhana emerged from the hill as a miraculous self-manifest form, with the upraised arm appearing first. In 1493, by tradition, Vallabha was called to the hill and established the worship of this image, Śrī Govardhananātha, as Śrīnāthajī. It became the heart of the Puṣṭi Mārga. In 1672 the image was moved to Nāthdvārā in Rajasthan, where Mewar's ruler gave it shelter, and the temple there is still the movement's greatest centre.

events.title: Ḥusain Shāh's Bengal and the Gauḍīya Gosvāmīs
events.description: Alāʾ-ud-dīn Ḥusain Shāh ruled Bengal from 1493 to 1519 and had Hindu officials in his government. The brothers Rūpa and Sanātana served him as ministers, known by the Muslim names Dabīr Khās and Sākar Mallik. They later left the court to join Caitanya, and settled at Vṛndāvana to write the theology of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism. Ḥusain Shāh's reign is also remembered for early Bengali literary patronage.

events.title: Pratāparudra Gajapati of Odisha
events.description: Pratāparudra ruled Odisha as Gajapati from 1497 to 1540 and held a large territory along the eastern coast. He is known as a devotee of Caitanya, whom he met at Purī in the early sixteenth century, and he supported the Jagannātha cult. He fought Vijayanagara under Kṛṣṇadevarāya, who took several of his forts, and he also faced Bengal's sultans. After his death the Gajapati line collapsed.

events.title: Vasco da Gama reaches Kozhikode
events.description: In May 1498 the Portuguese captain Vasco da Gama anchored off Kozhikode (Calicut) on the Malabar coast, having sailed round Africa. He was received by the Zamorin, the Hindu ruler of the port, a centre of the pepper trade that Arab and other merchants had long dominated. The Zamorin allowed trade but negotiations failed, and da Gama left with spices. The route opened direct European access to Asian trade, and in the following years the Portuguese came back with armed fleets and entered into conflict with the Zamorin and Arab traders.

events.title: Mīrābāī born in Rajasthan
events.description: Mīrābāī was born in a Rāṭhoṛ family at Kuḍkī, near Meṛtā in Rajasthan, and was married into the royal house of Mewar. Tradition says she cared only for her god Giridhara Gopāla and, after her husband's death, defied her in-laws and left the palace to sing and dance in devotion to Kṛṣṇa. Her songs, in a blend of Rajasthani and Braj, speak of longing for the beloved Lord. Scholars find it hard to say which of the many verses attributed to her are by her, but they are among the most widely sung in India.

events.title: Gaṇapati Atharvaśīrṣa, the Gaṇeśa Upaniṣad
events.description: The Gaṇapati Atharvaśīrṣa, or Gaṇapati Upaniṣad, is a short text attached to the Atharvaveda tradition. Scholars generally regard it as late medieval, with estimates ranging from about the fourteenth to the seventeenth century. It declares Gaṇeśa to be identical with Brahman and with the Ātman and sums up the Gāṇapatya outlook. In Maharashtra many families recite it daily, and large groups recite it together during the Gaṇeśa festival, notably in Pune at the Dagaḍūśeṭh Halwai Gaṇapati temple.

events.title: Haridāsa movement of Karnataka
events.description: The Haridāsas, "servants of Hari", were Dvaita devotees of Karnataka who spread Viṣṇu devotion through simple Kannada songs. The movement began with Śrīpādarāja and was carried on by Vyāsatīrtha and by Purandara Dāsa, Kanaka Dāsa and many others, with each poet using a signature name (aṅkita) in his verses. Their songs, often addressed to Viṭṭhala, brought Madhva's doctrine to ordinary people and shaped Karnatak music. Brāhmaṇas and non-brāhmaṇas alike took part, and the tradition continued through later singers such as Vijaya Dāsa and Gopāla Dāsa.

events.title: Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī's Tantrasaṅgraha
events.description: Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī, of the Kerala school, completed the Tantrasaṅgraha in 1500. He revised the Āryabhaṭan model of planetary motion so that Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn travel around the Sun, which in turn circles the Earth. This resembles the system Tycho Brahe proposed later in Europe. He also corrected the way the planets' latitudes were calculated. He was a student of Dāmodara and himself taught Śaṅkara Vāriyar, and his work was part of a long line of Kerala astronomy.

events.title: Viṣṇusvāmī and the Rudra Sampradāya
events.description: Viṣṇusvāmī is an early Vaiṣṇava teacher, little known historically and with few surviving works, whom the Rudra Sampradāya names as its founder. Vallabha's Puṣṭi Mārga later claimed descent from this line, linking its new teaching to an older lineage in keeping with the Indian preference for traditions with an ancient pedigree. Scholars have difficulty documenting any direct connection. The claim shows how the sixteenth-century communities placed themselves within one of the four recognised Vaiṣṇava sampradāyas, as a source of authority.

events.title: Four Vaiṣṇava Sampradāyas
events.description: Vaiṣṇava tradition recognises four classical lineages, often listed from a verse attributed to the Padma Purāṇa. The Śrī Sampradāya follows Rāmānuja, the Brahma Sampradāya follows Madhva, the Rudra Sampradāya follows Viṣṇusvāmī and later Vallabha, and the Sanaka Sampradāya follows Nimbārka. Each teaches a different relation between God and the soul. Newer movements placed themselves in this scheme: the Rāmānandīs in the Śrī line and the Gauḍīyas in the Brahma line. Historians see the fourfold scheme as a later way of organising a large and diverse tradition.

events.title: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi's Dīdhiti
events.description: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi of Navadvīpa wrote the Dīdhiti, a brilliant, critical commentary on Gaṅgeśa's Tattvacintāmaṇi. He questioned many of the older Nyāya positions and put forward new ones, such as his ideas on the nature of qualities. Tradition says he studied in Mithilā before returning to Bengal. His work made Navadvīpa in Bengal the leading centre of Navya-Nyāya, taking over from Mithilā, and the school's later teaching was largely a series of commentaries on his Dīdhiti, which are still studied in traditional centres.

events.title: Raghunandana's Smṛtitattva digest for Bengal
events.description: Raghunandana Bhaṭṭācārya of Navadvīpa compiled the Smṛtitattva, a digest of twenty-eight sections (tattvas) covering the rules for rites, festivals, penances and law as found in the Smṛtis and Purāṇas. It became the standard guide to Hindu ritual life in Bengal, including the proper way to worship Durgā, and so it shaped the practice of Durgā Pūjā that is the region's greatest festival. Bengal's inheritance law followed the Dāyabhāga of Jīmūtavāhana, and Raghunandana's authority covered the rest of dharma. His work is a key source for Bengali Hindu custom.

events.title: Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa's Tantrasāra
events.description: Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa of Navadvīpa compiled the Tantrasāra, a large digest of tantric rites, mantras and deity worship, drawn from many scriptures. Bengali tradition credits him with introducing the now familiar image of Dakṣiṇā Kālī, the dark goddess standing over Śiva, and with beginning the worship of Kālī at the new-moon festival of Dīpāvalī. events.title: Sūrdāsa, Braj poet of the Sūrasāgara
events.description: Sūrdāsa, traditionally said to have been blind from birth, was a poet of the Braj region. He is counted among the Aṣṭachāpa, the eight poets of the Puṣṭi Mārga, and is remembered as a singer at Śrīnāthajī under Vallabha. His Sūrasāgara, the "ocean of Sūr", is a collection of songs on the life of Kṛṣṇa, especially his childhood and play with the cowherd girls, and the longing of the gopīs. Tradition says it had thousands of verses, and several thousand survive. Written in Braj Bhāṣā, it is a landmark of Hindi devotional poetry.

events.title: Svāmī Haridāsa of Vṛndāvana
events.description: Svāmī Haridāsa was a saint and musician of Vṛndāvana who lived in the sixteenth century and founded the Haridāsī (Sakhī) tradition of devotion to Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. According to tradition, the image of Bāṅke Bihārī was revealed through his worship at Nidhivan, and the famed singer Tānsen was his pupil. Haridāsa sang in the dhrupad style, a slow, grave form of Hindustani music that grew in temple settings of Braj and at the Mughal and Gwalior courts. Historians cannot confirm all of the details of his life.

events.title: Hita Harivaṃśa and the Rādhāvallabha Sampradāya
events.description: Hita Harivaṃśa (about 1502–1552) founded the Rādhāvallabha Sampradāya at Vṛndāvana. Its followers worship Rādhā as the supreme goddess, the beloved to whom Kṛṣṇa himself is devoted, rather than treating Kṛṣṇa as the central deity. Harivaṃśa composed the Sanskrit Rādhāsudhānidhi and the Braj Hita Caurāsī, a collection of eighty-four songs. The community's temple of Rādhāvallabha in Vṛndāvana is among the most visited there, and it continues a style of loving devotion centred on Rādhā.

events.title: Tuñcattu Eḻuttacchan, father of Malayalam literature
events.description: Tuñcattu Rāmānujan Eḻuttacchan, who worked in the sixteenth century, is called the father of Malayalam literature. He composed the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam Kiḷippāṭṭu, in which a parrot sings the Rāmāyaṇa, based on the Sanskrit Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, and a Mahābhāratam in the same style. His verse set a standard for Malayalam and helped fix its alphabet. The Rāmāyaṇam is still read aloud in Kerala homes during the month of Karkaṭakam. He was from a community of village teachers, not a high-caste scholar.

events.title: Kathak, Odissi and temple dance
events.description: The Nāṭyaśāstra, an early treatise on drama and dance, supplied a vocabulary of gesture, expression and rasa for later Indian classical dance. In temples, from Purī to Tañjāvūr, women dancers dedicated to the deity, called mahārīs in Odisha and devadāsīs in the south, performed as part of worship. These traditions fed the forms now called Odissi and Bharatanāṭyam, while Kathak grew in the north in temples and then courts. Colonial-era social campaigns later led to the decline of the dedicated dancers, and the arts were revived on the stage.

events.title: Siddha medicine of the Tamil country
events.description: Siddha medicine is a Tamil system of healing associated with the Siddhars, a group of ascetic sages and poets traditionally numbered eighteen, among them Agastyar, Bhogar and Tirumūlar. Texts under their names deal with alchemy, mercury and mineral preparations, herbal remedies, yoga, and diagnosis by pulse. The attributions are traditional, and the surviving works date from many periods, mostly medieval. Siddha medicine is practised today in Tamil Nadu and is recognised in India's AYUSH framework alongside Āyurveda.

events.title: Pañcasakhā of Odisha
events.description: The Pañcasakhā, or "five companions", were Odia poet-saints of about the sixteenth century: Balarāma Dāsa, Jagannātha Dāsa, Acyutānanda, Ananta and Yaśovanta. They lived around the time of Caitanya's stay at Purī and linked the god Jagannātha with a mix of jñāna (knowledge) and bhakti (devotion), sometimes identifying him with the formless void. Balarāma Dāsa wrote the Odia Rāmāyaṇa and Jagannātha Dāsa the Odia Bhāgavata, which is still recited in Odisha. Their works are written in the Odia language and shaped the religious culture of the region.

events.title: Dhanya Māṇikya builds Tripurā Sundarī temple
events.description: In 1501 Mahārāja Dhanya Māṇikya of Tripura built the main shrine of the Tripurā Sundarī temple on a hillock near Udaipur, in the Bengali ek-ratna style. Legend says the goddess appeared to him in a dream and told him to begin her worship on the hill, where a Viṣṇu temple already stood. After the dream recurred, he concluded that Viṣṇu and Śakti are forms of one Deity. The tortoise-backed hill gives the site the name Kūrma Pīṭha.¶Tradition counts the site among the fifty-one Śākta pīṭhas, the place where part of Satī's right foot fell. The temple became the central shrine of the Māṇikya kings, who ruled Tripura for centuries, and it shows the meeting of Vaiṣṇava royal tradition and Śākta worship in north-eastern India.

events.title: Rāṇā Sāṅgā of Mewar
events.description: Rāṇā Saṅgrām Siṃha, known as Sāṅgā, ruled Mewar from 1508 to 1528. He gathered the Rajput chiefs into a coalition and fought the sultans of Mālwā, Gujarat and Delhi, capturing Maḥmūd Khaljī of Mālwā in 1519. His body carried many wounds, and he is said to have lost an eye and an arm in battle. He became the leading Hindu power in north India in the early sixteenth century and the main rival to Bābur, who founded the Mughal empire in 1526.

events.title: Kanaka Dāsa, Kuruba poet-saint of Karnataka
events.description: Kanaka Dāsa, born about 1509 in the Kuruba shepherd community, began as a chieftain, then turned to devotion and became a disciple of Vyāsatīrtha. He composed Kannada songs and long poems, among them the Rāmadhānya Caritre, and wrote against caste prejudice. Legend says that when he was denied entry to the Kṛṣṇa temple at Uḍupi, he sang outside, and the image turned to face him, leaving the opening known as Kanakana Kiṇḍi, "Kanaka's window". Devotees still pray through that window.

events.title: Kṛṣṇadevarāya crowned at Vijayanagara
events.description: Kṛṣṇadevarāya ruled Vijayanagara from 1509 to 1529, its most brilliant period. He defeated the Deccan sultans and the Gajapati of Odisha, and Portuguese visitors described a capital larger than Rome with markets selling diamonds in the street.¶He was a scholar in his own right, author of the Telugu poem Āmuktamālyada on the Tamil saint Āṇḍāḷ, and patron of eight great poets. He gave lavishly to Tirupati, Śrīśaila, Kāñcī and Hampi's own temples. The towering temple gateways of south India largely date from his age.

events.title: Nityānanda and Advaita Ācārya
events.description: Nityānanda and Advaita Ācārya were close associates of Caitanya in Bengal. Nityānanda, often seen as a manifestation of Balarāma, travelled among the people teaching the chanting of the names of Kṛṣṇa, nāma-saṅkīrtana, and is credited with bringing many people of low social standing and outcastes into the movement. Advaita, an older Vaiṣṇava scholar of Śāntipur, was a leading figure before Caitanya's emergence. Together they turned a Navadvīpa circle into a popular movement across Bengal.

events.title: Haridāsa Ṭhākura, nāmācārya of Caitanya's circle
events.description: Haridāsa Ṭhākura was a Bengali devotee of Kṛṣṇa, said in the Gauḍīya biographies to have been born in a Muslim family. He became one of Caitanya's chief followers, known as the nāmācārya, the teacher of the Name, for his daily chanting of the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra, reported as three lakh, or 300,000, names. Accounts say he was punished by a local Muslim official for his devotion. He spent his last years at Purī, where Caitanya is said to have attended his passing.

events.title: Sarvabhauma Bhaṭṭācārya debates Caitanya at Purī
events.description: Sarvabhauma Bhaṭṭācārya was a famed Naiyāyika, a scholar of the Nyāya logic school, from Navadvīpa who became court pandit of King Pratāparudra of Odisha at Purī. Caitanya's biographers describe a long debate in which Caitanya challenged his Advaita reading of the Vedānta, after which the scholar became a devotee. The conversion story, told in the Caitanya Caritāmṛta, shows how the Gauḍīya movement presented itself as scholarly as well as emotional, and drew a Navya-Nyāya authority into its circle.

events.title: Vallabha at Kṛṣṇadevarāya's court
events.description: Puṣṭimārga tradition tells that, around 1509, Vallabha went to the court of Kṛṣṇadevarāya at Vijayanagara, where he took part in a debate with scholars of other schools, such as Śaṅkara's and Madhva's followers, and won. The king is said to have honoured him with a kanakābhiṣeka, a bath of gold coins. The story rests on the community's accounts, and independent records of it are limited, so it is best seen as part of Puṣṭi memory.

events.title: Caitanya takes saṃnyāsa
events.description: In 1510 Caitanya, a young scholar of Navadvīpa whose devotion to Kṛṣṇa had made him a leader of saṅkīrtana, took initiation as a renunciant near Katwa under Keśava Bhāratī. He soon settled at Purī in Odisha, where he engaged the scholar Sārvabhauma Bhaṭṭācārya in debate and won him over to devotion. From 1510 to 1512 he travelled in the south, meeting among others Rāmānanda Rāya on the Godāvarī. His life is recorded in the Caitanya Caritāmṛta. His followers formed the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition.

events.title: Portuguese take Goa
events.description: In 1510 the Portuguese governor Afonso de Albuquerque seized Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate, with help from local Hindu groups, and made it the capital of Portugal's Asian empire. Under Portuguese rule, temples in the islands of Goa were demolished in the 1540s and conversion was encouraged, and in 1560 the Inquisition was established there. Many Goan Hindus moved to neighbouring regions with their deities. Goa remained under Portugal until 1961.

events.title: Kṛṣṇadevarāya's gopuram at Virūpākṣa Temple
events.description: At Hampi, the capital of Vijayanagara, the Virūpākṣa temple is a much older shrine to Śiva. Its tall eastern gateway, or gopuram, is dated to about 1510 and is credited to Kṛṣṇadevarāya, who is also remembered for gifts to other temples at the site. The tower rises in tiers of brick and stucco above a stone base. In a dark chamber of the complex the tower's shadow falls inverted on a wall, a feature shown to visitors.

events.title: Keśava Kāśmīrī Bhaṭṭa
events.description: Keśava Kāśmīrī Bhaṭṭa was a scholar of the Nimbārka school who, in the early sixteenth century, is said to have travelled across India defeating opponents in debate. Gauḍīya texts such as the Caitanya-caritāmṛta tell that he met Caitanya's circle and was humbled, while Nimbārka sources give a different account of the encounter. The accounts therefore diverge, and the incident shows the rivalry and exchange between Vaiṣṇava schools.

events.title: Rāmānanda Rāya's dialogue with Caitanya
events.description: According to the Caitanya Caritāmṛta, around 1511 Caitanya met Rāmānanda Rāya, the governor of Rājamahendravaram under the Gajapati king, on the bank of the Godāvarī. The dialogue moves through the levels of religion, from duty through to devotion, then loving service, and ends with the love of Rādhā for Kṛṣṇa as the highest. It is an important source for Gauḍīya theology, though it was written down decades later by Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja, and the dating given here is approximate.

events.title: Kṛṣṇadevarāya's gifts to Tirumala
events.description: The Vijayanagara emperor Kṛṣṇadevarāya (r. 1509 to 1529) is recorded as visiting the Veṅkaṭeśvara temple at Tirumala seven times and made rich gifts of jewels and gold, which are noted in inscriptions. Copper statues of him and his two queens, Tirumaladevī and Cinnādevī, stand at the entrance of the temple. Vijayanagara patronage in this period grew the temple's wealth and its buildings, and the emperor's gifts, along with those of earlier rulers, are part of why the temple is so prosperous.

events.title: Viṭṭhala and Kṛṣṇa temples at Hampi
events.description: In 1513 Kṛṣṇadevarāya of Vijayanagara returned from his campaign in Odisha with the image of Bālakṛṣṇa taken from Udayagiri and had a temple built for it at Hampi. The nearby Viṭṭhala temple, begun about the same time and added to over the following decades, has pillars that ring when struck and a famous stone chariot, which in truth is a shrine for Garuḍa. Both are in the Vijayanagara site that UNESCO listed as a World Heritage Site in 1986. They represent the height of the Vijayanagara style.

events.title: Caitanya in Vṛndāvana
events.description: In 1515 Caitanya visited Vṛndāvana, which had by then been largely forgotten as the place of Kṛṣṇa's childhood. According to his biographies he went about the Braj region, seeking out the sacred spots of Kṛṣṇa's līlā. He later sent two of his followers, the brothers Rūpa and Sanātana, to live there and to write on the theology of devotion. They and other Gosvāmīs established temples and a body of literature. This revived Vṛndāvana as a main centre of Kṛṣṇa devotion.

events.title: Kṛṣṇadevarāya's Kaliṅga campaign
events.description: Between about 1513 and 1518 Kṛṣṇadevarāya of Vijayanagara led armies against the Gajapati kingdom of Odisha, whose rulers had taken territory in the Telugu country. He took the forts of Udayagiri and Koṇḍavīḍu, and then pressed on to the Kaliṅga region. A peace was made in 1518, under which the Gajapati king Pratāparudra kept his kingdom and gave his daughter in marriage to the victor. The campaign extended Vijayanagara's reach up the east coast.

events.title: Kṛṣṇadevarāya writes the Āmuktamālyada
events.description: The Āmuktamālyada, a Telugu epic poem, is ascribed to the Vijayanagara emperor Kṛṣṇadevarāya (r. 1509–1529) and is dated to his reign, probably around the 1510s. It tells the story of Āṇḍāḷ, the only woman among the Tamil Āḻvārs, and of her marriage to Raṅganātha at Śrīraṅgam. The famous description of her beauty runs for thirty verses from head to foot.¶The poem is a Telugu work on a Tamil saint, written by a king, and it shows the way Śrīvaiṣṇava devotion crossed the languages of the south in the age of Vijayanagara. Its fourth canto also contains advice on kingship and statecraft, so it is a devotional poem and a manual of governance together. It is regarded as one of the five great Telugu kāvyas.

events.title: Battle of Khātolī
events.description: In 1517 Rāṇā Sāṅgā of Mewar met the Delhi Sultan Ibrāhīm Lodī in battle near Khātolī, in Rajasthan, and defeated him. Rajput tradition says Sāṅgā was wounded in the fight, and that he lost an arm and was left with a limp from an arrow wound. The victory shifted the balance towards Mewar and weakened the Lodī sultanate, which fell to Bābur at Pānīpat in 1526. Sāṅgā became the most powerful Hindu ruler in north India.

events.title: Battle of Raichur
events.description: In 1520 Kṛṣṇadevarāya of Vijayanagara besieged the fortress of Raichur in the doab between the Kṛṣṇā and Tuṅgabhadrā rivers, held by the Bijapur Sultan Ismāʿīl Ādil Shāh. In a large battle, he defeated the Bijapur army and took the fort. The Portuguese traveller Domingo Paes, who was with the army, described the campaign, and Fernão Nuniz later recorded it in his chronicle. The victory marked the high point of Vijayanagara's military power. The Raichur doab had been fought over by Hindu and Muslim kingdoms for generations.

events.title: Six Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana
events.description: At Caitanya's direction, six scholars settled at Vṛndāvana and built the theology of the Gauḍīya tradition: Rūpa, Sanātana, Jīva, Raghunātha Dāsa, Raghunātha Bhaṭṭa and Gopāla Bhaṭṭa. Rūpa wrote the Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, which analyses the stages and flavours of devotion, and Jīva wrote the Ṣaṭsandarbha, a six-part philosophical treatise that presents the doctrine of acintya-bhedābheda, "inconceivable difference and non-difference". They also had temples built and recovered the holy sites of Braj. Their writing is the basis of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism.
events.eraDesc: Vijayanagara rises as a southern shield, and saint-poets like Jñāneśvara, Kabīr and Caitanya lead the Bhakti renaissance.

events.title: First Battle of Pānīpat
events.description: On 21 April 1526 Bābur, the Timurid ruler of Kabul, defeated the Delhi sultan Ibrāhīm Lodī at Pānīpat, north of Delhi. Bābur's army used field artillery and matchlock guns together with mounted archers and wagons, which the Lodī army, though much larger, could not match, and Ibrāhīm was killed. Bābur took Delhi and Agra and established the Mughal empire, which ruled much of India until 1857. His rule also began a new phase in the history of the Rajput states.

events.title: Battle of Khānwā
events.description: On 16 March 1527 Bābur met Rāṇā Sāṅgā of Mewar at Khānwā near Āgrā. Sāṅgā had assembled a large confederacy of Rajput chiefs and some Afghan allies, who aimed to turn Bābur out of India. Bābur called his campaign a holy war, and his artillery and disciplined tactics won the day. Sāṅgā was badly wounded and carried from the field, and died in 1528. The defeat ended Rajput hopes of taking Delhi and secured the Mughal conquest of north India.

events.title: Babri mosque built at Ayodhyā
events.description: In 1528–29 Mīr Bāqī, a commander of Bābur, built a mosque at Ayodhyā, which came to be known as the Babri Masjid. Many Hindus have held that the site was Rāma's birthplace, the Rāmajanmabhūmi, and that an earlier temple stood there; Muslim parties disputed this. In 2003 the Archaeological Survey of India reported remains of a large earlier structure beneath it. The mosque was demolished in 1992, and in 2019 the Supreme Court gave the land to the Hindu side for a temple. A new Rāma temple was consecrated in 2024.

events.title: Death of Kṛṣṇadevarāya
events.description: Kṛṣṇadevarāya died in 1529 after twenty years of rule in which Vijayanagara reached its greatest size and prosperity. His half-brother Acyuta Rāya succeeded him. The new reign saw growing quarrels between court factions, and the power of the minister Rāma Rāya of the Āravīḍu family increased. Kṛṣṇadevarāya was also a poet who wrote the Telugu Āmuktamālyada and who patronised eight great Telugu poets, called the Aṣṭadiggajas. After him the empire began a slow decline.

events.title: Lepākṣī Vīrabhadra temple
events.description: The Vīrabhadra temple at Lepākṣī in Andhra Pradesh was built in the 1530s under the Vijayanagara king Acyuta Rāya, by the brothers Vīraṇṇa and Virūpaṇṇa, who were his officers. It is famed for its painted ceilings, with scenes from the epics and Purāṇas, and for a large monolithic Nandī bull close by, about 200 metres from the temple. A pillar that appears to hang from the ceiling is a well-known curiosity. The paintings form one of the best-preserved examples of Vijayanagara art.

events.title: Acyuta Rāya and the Tiruveṅgaḷanātha temple
events.description: Acyuta Rāya, who ruled Vijayanagara from 1529 to 1542, succeeded his brother Kṛṣṇadevarāya. At Hampi he built the Tiruveṅgaḷanātha, or Acyutarāya, temple, dedicated in 1534, which has a long colonnaded bazaar street. It was among the last great temples raised in the city before the empire's decline. The building shows the mature Vijayanagara style, with tall gopuras and large pillared halls, and the planned market street shows the link between temple and trade.

events.title: Jyeṣṭhadeva's Yuktibhāṣā in Malayalam
events.description: The Yuktibhāṣā, written in Malayalam by Jyeṣṭhadeva around 1530, explains the mathematical discoveries of the Kerala school, including the infinite series of Mādhava, by giving full demonstrations. Unlike most Sanskrit works, which state rules, it sets out proofs and reasoning step by step. It covers the series for π and the sine and cosine, as well as planetary astronomy. It is sometimes called the first textbook of calculus, though the school's methods differed from the later European ones.

events.title: Vallabha's jalasamādhi at Kāśī
events.description: Vallabha, the founder of the Puṣṭimārga, wrote the Subodhinī, a commentary on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, and the Aṇubhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtra. His philosophy, called Śuddhādvaita, holds that the world is real and a manifestation of Kṛṣṇa. Tradition says that in 1531 he entered the Gaṅgā at Hanumān Ghāṭ in Kāśī and ascended, a jalasamādhi. His sons and followers developed the rich devotional culture of the Puṣṭimārga, especially at Nāthadvārā.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Tulasīdāsa, poet of the Rāmacaritamānasa, born
events.description: Tulasīdāsa, the poet of the Rāmacaritamānasa, is traditionally said to have been born in 1532, though other dates, from 1497 to 1511, are also given, at Rājāpur or at Soron. A Rāmānandī saint, he wrote in Awadhi, the speech of the people, and began his version of the Rāma story at Ayodhyā in 1574. His other works include the Vinaya Patrikā, Kavitāvalī and Dohāvalī. Hindu households throughout north India recite the Mānas, and he made Rāma devotion a common part of Hindi-speaking culture.

events.title: Rāo Māldeo of Mārwāṛ
events.description: Rāo Māldeo ruled Mārwāṛ from 1532 to 1562 and expanded the kingdom to its greatest extent. The Persian historian Firishta describes him as the most powerful ruler in Hindustan in his day. He met Sher Shāh Sūrī at Giri-Sumel in 1544 and lost, though tradition says Sher Shāh remarked afterwards that he had almost lost the empire for a handful of millet. Akbar's forces took Jodhpur in 1565, a few years after Māldeo's death.

events.title: Caitanya's disappearance at Purī
events.description: Caitanya died at Purī in 1533 at about forty-seven. His followers' accounts say that he vanished while in ecstasy at the Jagannātha temple, merging with the deity, or into the image of Ṭoṭā Gopīnātha. Other early sources, such as the Caitanyamaṅgala of Jayānanda, tell of an accident that led to his death, and the accounts differ. His movement continued through the Gosvāmīs and through leaders such as Nityānanda and Advaita, spreading across Bengal, Odisha and Vṛndāvana.

events.title: Second siege of Chittor
events.description: In 1535 Sultan Bahādur Shāh of Gujarat attacked Chittor, then ruled by the young Vikramājīt under the regency of his mother, Rāṇī Karṇāvatī. Her small army could not withstand him, and the fort fell. Karṇāvatī led the women in jauhar, while the men rode out to fight. Popular legend says she sent a rākhī to the Mughal emperor Humāyūn to ask for help, but historians doubt the story. The fort was recovered by Mewar not long afterwards.

events.title: Guru Nānak dies and Aṅgad succeeds
events.description: Guru Nānak died at Kartārpur in 1539 and was succeeded by Guru Aṅgad (Lahiṇā), the second Sikh Guru, who had been his disciple. Aṅgad settled at Khaḍūr and is credited with standardising the Gurmukhī script for writing the Gurus' hymns, and with strengthening the free community kitchen (laṅgar). The succession of ten Gurus continued until 1708, and the line gave the Sikh community its structure.
