events.title: Sher Shāh Sūr takes Delhi
events.description: Farīd Khān, an Afghan noble who took the title Sher Shāh, defeated the Mughal emperor Humāyūn at Chausā in 1539 and at Kannauj in 1540, and ruled northern India until his death in 1545. In a short reign he introduced a standard silver coin, the rūpiya, a systematic land survey, and the road later called the Grand Trunk Road from Bengal to the Indus. His tomb at Sasarām in Bihar is a fine piece of architecture. Akbar built on many of his administrative reforms.

events.title: Koch kingdom under Naranārāyaṇa
events.description: Naranārāyaṇa ruled the Koch kingdom of western Assam and northern Bengal from about 1540 to 1587, with his brother Cilārāy as the commander of his armies. Under them the Koch kingdom reached its greatest extent. The Kāmākhyā temple near Guwahati had fallen into ruin, and the Koch king rebuilt it in 1565, giving it much of its present form. He also patronised the Vaiṣṇava teacher Śaṅkaradeva, though the two were not always on easy terms.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ | ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||
gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.
gitaQuote.source: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) Critical Edition; Rāmānuja Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Rūpa Gosvāmī's Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu
events.description: Rūpa Gosvāmī, a leading follower of Caitanya, completed the Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, "the Nectar Ocean of the Rasa of Devotion", in 1541 at Vṛndāvana. Using the categories of Sanskrit poetics, in which an aesthetic rasa is evoked in the audience, he analysed bhakti as a rasa, describing its stages and the types of relationship, such as servant, friend, parent and lover, between devotee and Kṛṣṇa. The work became the central text of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theology and practice.

events.title: Rāma Rāya's regency at Vijayanagara
events.description: After Acyuta Rāya's death in 1542, Aḷiya Rāma Rāya of the Āravīḍu family, a son-in-law of Kṛṣṇadevarāya, became the effective ruler of Vijayanagara and kept Sadāśiva Rāya as a titular king. He took advantage of rivalries among the Deccan sultanates of Bījāpur, Golkoṇḍa and Aḥmadnagar, shifting sides among them. When the sultans united against him, he was defeated and killed at Tālīkoṭa in 1565, and the capital was sacked.

events.title: Jīva Gosvāmī and Rādhā-Dāmodara
events.description: Jīva Gosvāmī, nephew of Rūpa and Sanātana and the youngest of the Six Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana, was the main systematic theologian of the Gauḍīya school, writing the Ṣaṭsandarbha. He established the Rādhā-Dāmodara temple at Vṛndāvana, where he gathered and copied manuscripts of the school, forming a library. The collection preserved the works of the Gosvāmīs, and many of its materials were later carried to Bengal and Orissa, helping the tradition spread.

events.title: Francis Xavier among the Paravas
events.description: Francis Xavier reached Goa in 1542 and soon began work among the Paravas, a pearl-fishing community on the Fishery Coast of Tamil Nadu, many of whom had accepted baptism a few years earlier in return for Portuguese protection. Over the next two years he visited their coastal villages, baptising, appointing catechists and teaching prayers in Tamil translation. His mission began a long Jesuit presence in the Tamil country, which later included Roberto de Nobili at Madurai, who adopted the dress of a renunciant to present Christianity in Hindu terms.

events.title: Battle of Sammel
events.description: In 1544 Sher Shāh Sūr's army met the forces of Māldeo Rāṭhoṛ of Marwar at Sammel (Giri-Sumel). Māldeo, mistrusting his generals because of forged letters, withdrew, and his commanders Jaitā and Kūmpā fought on with a small force and fell. Sher Shāh won with great difficulty, and the chronicle of Abbās Sarwānī reports him saying that for a handful of millet he had almost lost the empire of Hindustan. Marwar was then occupied, though the Rāṭhoṛs recovered it after his death.

events.title: Dādū Dayāl born
events.description: Dādū Dayāl, born at Ahmedabad in 1544, was a Sant poet in the nirguṇa tradition, devoted to a formless God and critical of caste and ritual. He settled in Rajasthan, where he taught in Dausa and Naraina, and gave rise to the Dādū Panth. His followers, among them Rajjab and Sundaradāsa, collected his verses and those of other saints in anthologies, such as the Pañcavāṇī and Sarvāṅgī, which are among the earliest compilations of Sant poetry. His teachings are in the Rajasthani form of Hindi.

events.title: Mīrābāī at Dvārakā
events.description: In her later years Mīrābāī left Mewar and went to Vṛndāvana and then Dvārakā. Tradition says that when Mewar sent brāhmaṇas to bring her back, she asked for time to worship at the temple of Raṇachoḍjī (Kṛṣṇa), and then merged into the image, leaving only her sari. The accounts are devotional, and the dates, put around 1542–1547, are not certain. Her songs travelled across Gujarat and Rajasthan and were collected much later.

events.title: Appayya Dīkṣita, Advaitin and Śaiva scholar
events.description: Appayya Dīkṣita (1520–1593) was a South Indian scholar, said to have written 104 works. He taught Advaita but was a Śiva devotee, and he wrote the Śivārkamaṇidīpikā, a commentary on Śrīkaṇṭha's Śaiva Brahma Sūtra bhāṣya. His Parimala, a commentary on the Kalpataru, is a major Advaita work, and his Kuvalayānanda deals with figures of speech in poetry. He served the Nāyaka rulers of Vellore and Tamil Nadu. He argued that Śiva and Viṣṇu worship need not be in conflict, and is revered in the Śaiva and Smārta traditions.

events.title: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī and the Advaitasiddhi
events.description: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, a Bengali who went to Kāśī and became a leading Advaita scholar, wrote the Advaitasiddhi, a long reply to Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta, defending the unreality of the world against the Dvaita critique. His Gūḍhārthadīpikā on the Gītā and the Bhaktirasāyana join Advaita with devotion to Kṛṣṇa. Tradition also says he organised armed Nāgā saṃnyāsīs to protect Hindu ascetics from harassment, though the evidence is late. The Advaitasiddhi remains central in Vedānta study.

events.title: Vijñānabhikṣu and Avibhāgādvaita Vedānta
events.description: Vijñānabhikṣu, a sixteenth-century scholar who lived in Kāśī, wrote commentaries on the Sāṅkhya Sūtras, the Yoga Sūtras and the Brahma Sūtra. He tried to show that Sāṅkhya, Yoga and Vedānta share the same teaching, and put forward his own view, Avibhāgādvaita, "non-dualism without division", in which Brahman and the world are united as whole and part. He argued that Śaṅkara's doctrine of illusion differed from the Upaniṣads, and he reread Sāṅkhya as theistic. His works shaped later understanding of Yoga and Sāṅkhya.

events.title: Vādirāja Tīrtha of the Sodhe maṭha
events.description: Vādirāja Tīrtha, head of the Sodhe maṭha, is among the best known of the Dvaita saints of Uḍupi, and tradition gives him a very long life, roughly 1480–1600. He reorganised the paryāya system by which the eight monasteries take turns to serve Uḍupi's Kṛṣṇa, making each term two years. He wrote the Yuktimallikā, a Dvaita work, as well as devotional poems in Sanskrit and Kannada, and he promoted the worship of Hayagrīva. He is also remembered for his lively relations with Haridāsa singers.

events.title: Bhāvamiśra's Bhāvaprakāśa on materia medica
events.description: Bhāvamiśra, a physician of Kāśī in the sixteenth century, wrote the Bhāvaprakāśa, the last of the three smaller classics of Āyurveda that follow Caraka, Suśruta and Vāgbhaṭa. It is a compact, clearly arranged handbook of materia medica and therapy. It is notable for including diseases and drugs unknown to the older texts, such as the disease called phiraṅga-roga, understood as syphilis and named after Europeans, and imported remedies. Because of its clarity it became a standard manual for practising vaidyas.

events.title: Mahānavamī at Vijayanagara and Mysore Dasarā
events.description: The Mahānavamī festival at Vijayanagara, described by the Portuguese visitors Domingo Paes and Fernão Nuniz in the sixteenth century, was a state ritual. It included worship of the goddess, animal sacrifice, processions of troops and elephants, and performances at the royal platform. After Vijayanagara's fall the Wodeyars of Mysore adopted the ceremony as their Dasarā, centred on Cāmuṇḍeśvarī, their tutelary goddess, who is worshipped on Cāmuṇḍī Hill. The pageantry survives today.

events.title: Nṛsiṃhāśrama and Rāmatīrtha
events.description: Nṛsiṃhāśrama was a Daśanāmī Advaitin of the sixteenth century, associated with Kāśī, who wrote the Advaitadīpikā, the Tattvaviveka and the Bhedadhikkāra, defending non-dualism against Dvaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita critics. Rāmatīrtha, a contemporary teacher, wrote the Vidvanmanorañjanī on the Vedāntasāra. They belong to a period of intense debate between schools, when Advaitins answered the polemics of Vyāsatīrtha of the Mādhva tradition, and their writing prepared the ground for Madhusūdana Sarasvatī.

events.title: Vijayīndra Tīrtha of Kumbakoṇam
events.description: Vijayīndra Tīrtha was a Dvaita scholar and head of the Mādhva maṭha at Kumbakoṇam in the Cōḻa country, and a prolific author. He wrote many works defending Madhva's philosophy against rivals. In the lineage he is the teacher of Sudhīndra Tīrtha, whose pupil was Rāghavendra Tīrtha. Tradition remembers him as both a friend and a debating opponent of Appayya Dīkṣita, the Advaitin and Śaiva scholar, an example of how learned exchange across schools was possible in the 16th-century south.

events.title: Gurucaritra, scripture of the Datta tradition
events.description: The Gurucaritra is a Marathi work, traditionally attributed to Sarasvatī Gaṅgādhar, that tells the lives of Śrīpāda Śrīvallabha and Nṛsiṃha Sarasvatī, regarded as the first two incarnations of Dattātreya in the Kali age. Its dating is uncertain, and scholars usually place it in the 15th or 16th century. It describes the saints' miracles and teachings in Karnataka and Maharashtra, with stories of devotees, and it prescribes a weekly reading, the saptāha pārāyaṇa. It is the main scripture of the Datta tradition in Maharashtra.

events.title: Tānsen and dhrupad
events.description: Tānsen, born near Gwalior, is the most famous musician of the Mughal court, one of the "nine jewels" of Akbar. He is traditionally said to have trained under Swāmī Haridāsa, a devotional singer of Vṛndāvana, and to have served the Rājā of Rewa before Akbar called him to Āgrā. His dhrupad compositions, in Braj, are still sung, and many gharānās trace their lineage to him. Dhrupad, a severe and meditative form, was the main art music of north India until khyāl rose in the eighteenth century.

events.title: Śivāgrayogin and Sanskrit Siddhānta in the south
events.description: Śivāgrayogin, a Śaiva scholar of Tamil Nadu in about the sixteenth century, wrote Sanskrit works that include a commentary on the Śivajñānabodha, the basic text of Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta. His work helped bring the Tamil tradition into a Sanskrit setting and linked it to the wider scholarship of the Āgamas. It shows that Śaiva Siddhānta in the south was both a Tamil devotional tradition and a Sanskrit philosophical one.

events.title: Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa and the Braj parikramā
events.description: The Braj region around Mathurā is a sacred landscape of Kṛṣṇa's life, and pilgrims make a circuit called the 84-kos parikramā, about 250 kilometres around the area. The Vaiṣṇava scholar Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, in his Vrajabhaktivilāsa, traditionally dated to 1552, set out the sites of the circuit and the legends connected to them, and is credited with reviving many sacred spots. The text gave a defined route to the pilgrimage, which is still performed.

gitaQuote.verse: अहमेवाक्षयः कालो धाताहं विश्वतोमुखः ॥ कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो लोकान्समाहर्तुमिह प्रवृत्तः ॥

gitaQuote.translation: I alone am inexhaustible, imperishable Time (Akṣaya Kāla), and I am the dispenser of destiny facing all directions... I am all-destroying Time, grown mighty to extinguish the worlds.

events.title: Hemū Vikramāditya crowned at Delhi
events.description: Hemū (Hemachandra) rose from a trader of Rewari to a general under the Sūr rulers and fought, by tradition, twenty-two battles. After Humāyūn's death in 1556 he marched on Delhi, defeated the Mughal governor at Tughlaqābād and took the title Vikramāditya in October. A few weeks later at the Second Battle of Pānīpat (5 November 1556) he was wounded by an arrow and captured, and he was executed. The Mughal general Bairām Khān ensured that Akbar's rule held, and Hemū remains a symbol of Hindu resistance.

events.title: Akbar's reign begins
events.description: Akbar became emperor in 1556 at the age of thirteen, under the guidance of the regent Bairām Khān, and ruled for nearly fifty years. He gradually broadened Mughal rule by giving high office to Rajput nobles, and later abolished the tax on Hindu pilgrims in 1563 and the jizya in 1564. He sponsored translation of Sanskrit works into Persian, held discussions among scholars of different religions at the Ibādat Khāna and promoted a policy of sulh-i-kul, "peace with all". His reign made the Mughal state stable.

events.title: Printing press at Goa
events.description: The first printing press in India reached Goa in 1556 with Jesuits who were on their way to Ethiopia but stayed. The earliest known publication was a Portuguese text of theological conclusions. Garcia da Orta's treatise on Indian drugs was printed there in 1563. Later Goa presses produced works in Konkani and Marathi, such as Thomas Stephens's Christian Purāṇa in 1616, and Jesuit presses on the south coast produced early Tamil books. Printing later spread to Indian-language use across the country.

events.title: Udaipur founded by Udai Singh II
events.description: Udai Singh II of Mewar, father of Mahārāṇā Pratāp, started building a new capital by Lake Pichola in the Aravalli hills in 1559, in a more secure position than Chittor. Chittor was besieged by Akbar and fell in 1568, and after that Udaipur became the royal seat for centuries. The city grew around the City Palace and the lakes, and the Mewar kings, who regarded themselves as servants of Ekaliṅgajī, kept their court here until 1947.

events.title: Goa Inquisition established
events.description: In 1560 the Portuguese set up the Inquisition at Goa. Hindu rites and public festivals were banned in Portuguese territory, as were Hindu priests and the keeping of idols. Temples in Bardez and Salcete were demolished in the sixteenth century, and Hindus who refused conversion could leave. Many families carried their deities across the river into neighbouring territories, where temples such as Mangeśī and Śāntādurgā were rebuilt. The Inquisition continued until 1812.

gitaQuote.verse: पिताहमस्य जगतो माता धाता पितामहः । वेद्यं पवित्रमोंकार ऋक्साम यजुरेव च ॥ गतिर्भर्ता प्रभुः साक्षी निवासः शरणं सुहृत् । प्रभवः प्रलयः स्थानं निधानं बीजमव्ययम् ॥

I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the creation and dissolution, the foundation and the imperishable seed.

events.title: Mangeśa liṅga moved from Kuśasthalī to Priol
events.description: The liṅga of Mangeśa (Mangueshi), a form of Śiva, was first consecrated at Kuśasthalī, today Cortalim in Mormugão. During the Portuguese conquest of Goa, the temple's patrons secretly moved it to Priol in Ponda taluka. Temple records give the date as 1560, and Jesuit reports place it before 1 May 1560.¶The removal to Ponda, then outside Portuguese territory, is one example of Goan Hindu communities saving their deities in the sixteenth century. The present temple at Priol was built in the Maratha period, and the Peśvās granted the village of Mangeshi to the temple in 1739. Mangeśa is still the family deity of many Goan Hindu families.

events.title: Amber's alliance with Akbar
events.description: In 1562, Rājā Bhārmal (Bihārī Mal) of Amber gave a daughter in marriage to the emperor Akbar at Sāmbhar and joined the Mughal service. This was the first major Rajput marriage alliance with the Mughals. His successor Bhagvant Dās and his grandson Mān Singh rose to high rank as generals and governors under Akbar. The Kachhwāhas gained land and status, and the alliance became a model for other Rajput houses.

events.title: Rānī Durgāvatī falls
events.description: Rānī Durgāvatī, a Candella princess of Mahobā, married the Gond king Dalpat Shāh and ruled the kingdom of Gaṛhā-Maṇḍlā as regent for her young son Vīra Nārāyaṇ after Dalpat Shāh's death. In 1564 the Mughal general Āsaf Khān invaded her kingdom. She fought him in person near Narrai, and when wounded and facing defeat, she stabbed herself on 24 June 1564 rather than be taken. She is remembered in central India as a symbol of courage.

events.title: Viṭṭhalanātha and the Aṣṭachāpa
events.description: Viṭṭhalanātha, the son of Vallabha, led the Puṣṭi Mārga from Gokul after his father's death. He organised the temple service of Śrīnāthjī, called sevā, with elaborate daily rites, and invited eight poet-singers, the Aṣṭachāp, to compose songs for it. Among them were Sūrdās and Paramānanddās. Tradition states that he obtained from the Mughal emperor Akbar farmāns, or royal orders, protecting Gokul's cows and the community's rights, which helped the sect settle in Braj.

events.title: Rāv Candrasen of Mārwāṛ
events.description: Rāv Candrasen was the son of Māldeo Rāṭhoṛ of Mārwāṛ. After Akbar's forces took Jodhpur in 1565, he refused to submit and held out from Bhādrājūn, Sivāṇā and hill refuges until his death in 1581, fighting a guerrilla war. Some Rajasthani writers call him the forgotten Pratāp, because his resistance came before and is overshadowed by that of Mahārāṇā Pratāp of Mewar. His son and heirs eventually made terms, and Mārwāṛ became a Mughal ally.

events.title: Battle of Tālīkoṭa
events.description: In January 1565 the four Deccan sultanates, usually rivals, combined against Vijayanagara. The armies met north of the Kṛṣṇā. The aged regent Rāma Rāya was captured and beheaded in mid-battle, reportedly after two of his Muslim commanders changed sides, and his army broke.¶The victors reached the capital within days and spent months looting and burning it. The city was never reoccupied. The empire continued in reduced form from Penukoṇḍa until 1646, but the great shield of the south was gone, and its governors, the Nāyakas, became independent kings.

gitaQuote.verse: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत । अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥ परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् । धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur; Madhvācārya Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Āravīḍu dynasty at Penukoṇḍa
events.description: After the defeat of Vijayanagara at Tālikoṭa in 1565, Tirumala of the Āravīḍu family moved the royal court to Penukoṇḍa and then to Candragiri. His successors, notably Veṅkaṭa II, ruled a reduced kingdom in the south, still patronising temples and arts, with Vellore as another capital. They continued to claim the Vijayanagara title until about the middle of the seventeenth century, when the Nāyakas and the Golconda sultanate absorbed the remaining territories.

events.title: Nāyakas of Keḷadi, Señji and Mysore
events.description: After Vijayanagara's defeat at Tālīkoṭa in 1565, its provincial governors, called nāyakas, became independent rulers. The Nāyakas of Keḷadi (Ikkeri) held coastal and western Karnataka, those of Señji (Gingee) the northern Tamil country, and the Wodeyars rose in Mysore. Others held Madurai and Tañjāvūr. They kept up the temple building, festivals and Sanskrit and vernacular patronage of Vijayanagara, and they preserved its institutions in the south for another century.

events.title: Kāmākhyā temple rebuilt; Ambubācī festival
events.description: The Kāmākhyā temple on Nīlācala hill in Guwahati is a Śākta Pīṭha, where Satī's yoni is said to have fallen. Tradition holds that the older temple was damaged by invaders, and the present structure was built in 1565 under the Koch king Naranārāyaṇa, with later additions by the Ahom kings of Assam, who also patronised it. Each year, in the monsoon, the temple closes for three days during the Ambubācī festival, when the goddess is believed to menstruate; its reopening draws Tāntrikas, ascetics and pilgrims from across eastern India.

events.title: Third siege of Chittor
events.description: In 1568 Akbar besieged Chittor, whose ruler Udai Siṃh had withdrawn to the hills. The garrison was led by Jaimal and Pattā, and Jaimal was shot by Akbar himself with a musket, according to the court histories. The fort fell after a long siege. The Mughal records state that thousands were killed, among them many peasants who had taken refuge there, and the women of the fort performed jauhar for the third time. Udai Siṃh founded Udaipur and Mewar kept resisting under his son Pratāpa.

events.title: Kālāpahāṛ's invasion of Odisha
events.description: In 1568 Kālāpahāṛ, a general of the Bengal sultan Sulaimān Karrānī, invaded Odisha and defeated Mukunda Deva, the last independent Gajapati king, ending Odia rule. The Odia temple chronicle Māḍaḷā Pāñji records that he damaged the Jagannātha temple at Purī and the Koṇārka temple. The priests hid the sacred brahma, the substance inside Jagannātha's image, and later restored it. Odisha was then ruled by the Bengal sultanate and, after 1592, by the Mughals.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Nanddās and Kṛṣṇadās
events.description: Nanddās and Kṛṣṇadās were two members of the Aṣṭachāp, the eight poets of the Puṣṭi Mārga who sang for the worship of Kṛṣṇa in Braj. Nanddās is known for his Braj-bhāṣā verses, including the Rāsapañcādhyāyī, a poetic rendering of the Bhāgavata's five chapters on the rāsa dance, and Kṛṣṇadās Adhikārī managed the temple at Govardhan. Their songs are still sung in Puṣṭi Mārga temples and helped establish Braj-bhāṣā as a language of devotional poetry.
events.eraDesc: Tulasīdāsa, Tukārāma and the Vṛndāvana Gosvāmīs compose devotional classics; Śivājī establishes Svarājya.

events.title: Jīva Gosvāmī's Ṣaṭ Sandarbha
events.description: Jīva Gosvāmī, nephew of Rūpa and Sanātana Gosvāmī, was the great systematiser of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theology at Vṛndāvana. His Ṣaṭ Sandarbha, the "six essays," argues from the Bhāgavata Purāṇa as the chief authority and sets out the doctrine of acintya-bhedābheda, the "inconceivable difference and non-difference" between God and the souls. It gave Caitanya's devotional movement a philosophical structure in Sanskrit that could answer the older Vedānta schools. He also wrote a Bhāgavata commentary.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥

gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.
gitaQuote.source: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) Critical Edition; Rāmānuja Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Prakāśānanda and dṛṣṭi-sṛṣṭi-vāda
events.description: Prakāśānanda, a Vedāntin of the sixteenth century, is the best-known exponent of dṛṣṭi-sṛṣṭi-vāda, the doctrine that the world exists only in being perceived and that the individual self is the source of apparent creation. His Vedāntasiddhāntamuktāvalī argues the position at length. Most other Advaitins held that the world has a provisional reality independent of the viewer, so this was a more radical idealism within the tradition. Later Advaita writers often discussed and criticised it as one of several competing accounts of how the appearance of the world arises.

events.title: Mādhavadeva composes the Nāmaghoṣā
events.description: Mādhavadeva (1489 to 1596) was the chief disciple of Śaṅkaradeva, who founded the Ekaśaraṇa Nāma Dharma of Assam. His Nāmaghoṣā, a collection of devotional verses on the glory of the divine name, is traditionally dated to the 1560s and is still sung in Assamese namghars, the village prayer halls. He also wrote Borgīts, devotional songs, and plays. His work shaped Assamese devotion, which stresses congregational chanting, with prayer halls centred on the Bhāgavata scripture rather than on an image.

events.title: Mahārāṇā Pratāp enthroned
events.description: When Pratāp became ruler of Mewar in 1572, Chittor had already fallen and almost every other Rajput house had made terms with Akbar, many giving daughters in marriage and sons in service.¶Akbar sent four embassies. Pratāp received them courteously and refused each. Bardic tradition says he vowed to sleep on straw and eat from leaf plates until Chittor was regained. He never did regain it, but he died in 1597 unconquered, and for later generations he became the purest symbol of the refusal to bow.

events.title: Tulasīdāsa begins the Rāmcaritmānas
events.description: On Rāma Navamī of 1574, at Ayodhyā, Tulasīdāsa began retelling the Rāmāyaṇa in Avadhī, the spoken language of the region. Pandits of Vārāṇasī are said to have objected to scripture in a common tongue.¶The "Lake of the Deeds of Rāma" became the most widely known book in north India, recited in homes and acted in Rāmlīlā each autumn. It presents Rāma as the supreme God and devotion to his name as the easy path for the present age. Indentured labourers later carried it to Fiji, Mauritius and the Caribbean as their one book.

events.title: Orchā's Caturbhuja and Rāma Rājā temples
events.description: Orchā, on the Betwa river, was the capital of the Bundelā kings. According to local tradition, Queen Gaṇeśa Kuṅvarī brought an image of Rāma from Ayodhyā, and when it was set down in the palace it could not be moved. The palace was therefore made into the Rāma Rājā temple, where Rāma is honoured as the king of Orchā and receives a daily armed salute. The Caturbhuja temple was built nearby to house the image, and both belong to the work of several Bundelā reigns, including Bīr Singh Deo's in the early seventeenth century.

events.title: Battle of Haldīghāṭī
events.description: On 18 June 1576, in a narrow pass in the Arāvalī hills, Mahārāṇā Pratāp of Mewar met a Mughal army commanded by the Rajput Mān Singh of Amber. Pratāp's force of about three thousand included Bhīl archers and the Afghan commander Hakīm Khān Sūr; the Mughals had perhaps three times as many.¶After four hours Pratāp, wounded, was carried from the field by his horse Cetak, which died of its injuries. The Mughals held the ground but failed to capture him or end his resistance. He fought on from the hills for twenty years and recovered most of Mewar.

events.title: Bārā Bhūiyāṅs of Bengal
events.description: After the Mughal victory over the Afghan ruler Dāʾūd Karrānī in 1576, Bengal's landed chiefs, known as the Bārā Bhūiyāṅs, resisted Mughal control for several decades. The leader of the confederation was Īsā Khān, a Muslim chief, and Hindu zamīndārs such as Pratāpāditya of Jessore and Kedār Rāy of Vikrampur also fought the Mughals. Mughal commanders including Mān Singh subdued them gradually in the early seventeenth century.

events.title: Amritsar founded by Guru Rām Dās
events.description: In 1577 Guru Rām Dās, the fourth Sikh Guru, began excavating the pool known as Amṛt Sarovar on land in the Punjab, and the settlement that grew around it was called Amritsar. His successor Guru Arjan laid out the Harmandir Sāhib, the "Golden Temple", in the middle of the pool between 1588 and 1604, with a door on each side to show that all are welcome. It became the central shrine of the Sikh faith and the main place of pilgrimage for Sikhs.

events.title: Wodeyars of Mysore
events.description: Rāja Wodeyar became ruler of Mysore in 1578. In 1610 he captured Śrīraṅgapaṭṭaṇa from the Vijayanagara viceroy and made it his capital. He also began the Mysore Dasarā celebrations there in the manner of Vijayanagara's royal Navarātri. The Wodeyar dynasty traces its origin to 1399 and ruled, with an interval under Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan, until 1947. The Mysore Dasarā procession still honours the goddess Cāmuṇḍeśvarī.

events.title: Tulasīdāsa's Hanumān Cālīsā and Vinaya Patrikā
events.description: Tulasīdāsa, the Rāmānandī poet of Kāśī, is credited with the Hanumān Cālīsā, forty verses in Awadhi in praise of Hanumān, which is among the most commonly recited Hindu prayers today, and with the Vinaya Patrikā, a long petition in verse addressed to Rāma. Tradition also says he founded the Saṅkaṭa Mocana Hanumān temple at Vārāṇasī and encouraged the Rāmlīlā, the staged retelling of the Rāmāyaṇa performed each autumn in Kāśī and across north India.

events.title: Razmnāma: the Persian Mahābhārata
events.description: Akbar set up a translation bureau at Fatehpur Sīkrī, and under it Hindu pandits and Persian scholars translated the Mahābhārata into Persian between 1582 and 1586. It was called the Razmnāma, "Book of War". The Rāmāyaṇa and other Sanskrit works, including the Atharvaveda, were also translated, and Mughal artists produced richly illustrated copies. The emperor wanted his nobles to know the Hindu tradition. Later Persian translations carried Indian thought to Iran and Europe.

events.title: Pūntānam composes the Jñānappāna
events.description: Pūntānam Nampūtiri was a devotee of Guruvāyūr in Kerala and wrote the Jñānappāna, "the song of wisdom", in simple Malayalam. It teaches devotion, detachment and the transience of life in plain verses meant to be sung. According to a famous story he was a contemporary of Melpathūr Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri and was told that the god valued his sincere devotion above the other's learning. The Jñānappāna remains a popular devotional poem in Kerala.

events.title: Akbar and Viṭṭhalanātha's farmāns
events.description: Viṭṭhalanātha, son of Vallabhācārya and leader of the Puṣṭimārga, settled at Gokul near Mathurā. Between about 1577 and 1581, Akbar issued farmāns, or imperial orders, granting land and tax exemption to him and his community and forbidding the slaughter of cows in the area. The grants show the emperor's policy of patronising Hindu religious institutions and his relations with Vaiṣṇava leaders. They also provided economic support for the temples of Braj.

events.title: Battle of Dewair
events.description: After the defeat at Haldīghāṭī in 1576 Mahārāṇā Pratāpa Siṃha of Mewar lived in the hills and waged guerrilla war against the Mughals. In 1582, at Dewair (Diver), he attacked the Mughal outposts, and his forces, with his son Amar Siṃh, gained a notable victory. In the following years he recovered most of Mewar, except Chittor and a few places, and ruled until his death in 1597. The battle is remembered in Rajput tradition as the turning of the tide in his long struggle.

events.title: Viśvanātha temple rebuilt at Kāśī
events.description: The Viśvanātha (Viśveśvara) temple of Kāśī had been destroyed and rebuilt several times after the twelfth century. Around 1585 the scholar Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, with the support of Akbar's Hindu minister Rājā Ṭoḍar Mal, rebuilt it. It remained the foremost Śiva shrine in Vārāṇasī, one of the twelve jyotirliṅgas. In 1669 Aurangzeb ordered its demolition, and the Gyānvāpī mosque was built on part of the site. The present temple was built next to it in 1780 by Ahilyābāī Holkar.

events.title: Nābhādāsa composes the Bhaktamāla
events.description: Nābhādāsa, a Rāmānandī from Rajasthan, composed the Bhaktamāla, a "garland of devotees", in Braj Bhāṣā, in the late sixteenth century. In several hundred short verses, it gives brief accounts of Vaiṣṇava saints and poets from many regions, castes and periods. Priyādāsa wrote a long commentary in 1712 with many stories. The Bhaktamāla became the main source for the hagiography of the Bhakti movement, and later writers such as the compilers of Sant lives drew on it.

events.title: Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri's Nārāyaṇīyam
events.description: Melpathūr Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri, a Kerala scholar, composed the Nārāyaṇīyam in 1586 at the Guruvāyūr temple. In a hundred daśakas and 1,036 verses it summarises the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and praises Kṛṣṇa as Guruvāyūrappan. Tradition says he wrote it while suffering from rheumatism, which was cured at the end. The work is admired for its Sanskrit poetry and is still recited by devotees at Guruvāyūr, where it is a central text of worship.

events.title: Mahīdhara completes the Mantramahodadhi
events.description: Mahīdhara, a brāhmaṇa scholar of Kāśī, completed the Mantramahodadhi in 1588. It is a large digest of mantra-śāstra, arranged in chapters called taraṅgas, or waves. It gathers the mantras, rites, yantras and procedures for the worship of deities such as Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu and the Devī, drawing on earlier Tantric sources. Mahīdhara also wrote a well-known commentary on the Śukla Yajurveda, the Vedadīpa, and both works circulated widely in northern India.

events.title: Govindadeva temple, Vṛndāvana
events.description: In 1590 Rājā Mān Siṅgh of Amber, a Rajput general in Akbar's service, built the Govindadeva temple at Vṛndāvana, to house the image revealed to Rūpa Gosvāmī. Made of red sandstone, it originally rose to seven storeys, though the upper floors were later damaged, and the style shows both Rajput and Mughal influence. It was a main centre of Gauḍīya worship. The image was later moved to Jaipur, where it is worshipped in the royal temple.

events.title: Vṛndāvana's Madana-mohana, Gopīnātha and Jugal Kiśor temples
events.description: In the later sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, new temples rose in Vṛndāvana on the initiative of the Gauḍīya Gosvāmīs, with the help of Rajput and other nobles and under the Mughal emperor Akbar's tolerant policy. Among them are the Madana-mohana, Gopīnātha and Jugal Kiśor temples, built in red sandstone, along with the grand Govindadeva temple, built by Rājā Mān Siṅgh of Amer in 1590. Many of the images were later moved to Rajasthan, in the late seventeenth century, for safety.

events.title: Gauḍīya books carried to Bengal and Odisha
events.description: Rūpa, Sanātana and their circle at Vṛndāvana wrote the core books of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism. Under Jīva Gosvāmī's direction, Śrīnivāsa Ācārya, Narottama Dāsa and Śyāmānanda were sent east with manuscripts of these works around the 1590s. Tradition says the book cart was robbed in Bengal by the Bishnupur king Bīr Hāmbīr, who was then converted. Narottama's Kheturī festival gathered the Bengal Vaiṣṇavas, and Śyāmānanda built a following in Odisha.

events.title: Keśavdās's Rāmacandrikā and Rasikpriyā
events.description: Keśavdās was a Braj-bhāṣā poet at the court of Indrajīt Singh of Orchā, in Bundelkhand, and is counted as a founder of the Rīti style of Hindi court poetry. His Rasikpriyā of 1591 is a treatise on rasa and the types of heroes and heroines, illustrated with verses on Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā, and the Rāmacandrikā is an epic retelling of the Rāma story in a range of metres. Both are celebrated for ornate craft.

events.title: Mān Singh in Odisha
events.description: Mān Singh of Amber, a Mughal general, led a campaign in Odisha against the Afghans and brought it under Mughal rule in 1592. He is said to have restored Rāmacandradeva, the Khurdā rājā, as the servant and superintendent of Jagannātha's temple at Purī, confirming the Gajapati's ritual role. The Khurdā rulers continued to oversee the temple's rituals for centuries under various overlords.

events.title: Raghavendra Tīrtha born
events.description: Raghavendra Tīrtha was born in 1595 in Tamil Nadu, studied under Sudhīndra Tīrtha at Kumbakoṇam, and became head of a Dvaita monastery. He wrote commentaries on Jayatīrtha and Vyāsatīrtha, including the Parimaḷa on the Nyāyasudhā, and was a gifted scholar and teacher. In 1671 he entered a brindāvana (tomb) at Mantrālayam on the Tuṅgabhadrā while alive, according to his followers. His shrine there draws large numbers of pilgrims from Karnataka and Andhra, and he is among the most widely revered of Dvaita saints.

events.title: Death of Mahārāṇā Pratāp
events.description: Mahārāṇā Pratāp of Mewar died on 19 January 1597 at Cāvaṇḍ. He had refused to accept Akbar's overlordship and fought Mān Singh's imperial army at Haldīghāṭī in 1576. After that battle he kept up guerrilla warfare in the hills, and by the 1580s he had recovered much of Mewar, though not Chittor. He is remembered in Rajasthan as a symbol of resistance, and his horse Cetak and the legends around the battle are widely told.

events.title: Āʾīn-i-Akbarī on Hindu learning
events.description: The Āʾīn-i-Akbarī, compiled by Akbar's minister Abuʾl Faẓl in the 1590s, is a long administrative and descriptive work on the Mughal empire. Its third volume includes an account of Hindu learning, with sections on the six philosophical systems, on the Purāṇas, on the sciences, and on the customs and rites of the Hindus. Abuʾl Faẓl also oversaw the Persian translation of the Mahābhārata, the Razmnāma. The work reflects Akbar's interest in knowing the religions of his subjects.

events.title: Akbar's grant to Vṛndāvana temples
events.description: In 1598 Akbar issued a farmān giving land to temples in the Vṛndāvana area of Braj. The grants supported Gauḍīya and other Vaiṣṇava establishments, whose leaders had rebuilt the sacred landscape of Kṛṣṇa's childhood. Imperial grants helped the founding of large stone temples there, such as Govindadeva, built in 1590 with the help of Rājā Mān Siṅgh. The documents are valuable evidence of Mughal patronage and Braj's revival.

events.title: Saint Ekanātha of Paiṭhaṇ
events.description: Ekanātha (1533–1599) of Paiṭhaṇ was a Vārakarī saint and scholar who revived interest in Jñāneśvara's work by preparing a reliable text of the Jñāneśvarī. He also wrote the Ekanāthī Bhāgavata, a Marathi commentary on the eleventh book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, and the Bhāvārtha Rāmāyaṇa. He also composed bhāruḍs, popular songs. Tradition tells that he shared meals with people of the lowest castes and cared for them. He is believed to have died in the Godāvarī at Paiṭhaṇ.

events.title: Dāsopant and Vāmana Paṇḍita's Marathi Vedānta
events.description: Dāsopant, a Marathi poet of the sixteenth century, served in the administration of a Deccan sultanate and became a devotee of Dattātreya. His Gītārṇava is a massive commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā in Marathi verse, and the Dattātreya tradition of Āmbejogāī in Marathwada is linked to him. Vāmana Paṇḍita, a seventeenth-century Marathi poet and Vedāntin, put Sanskrit Vedānta and the Gītā into Marathi verse in works such as the Yathārthadīpikā. Together their writing helped make philosophy available in a regional language.

events.title: Malūkdās and Sundardās
events.description: Malūkdās of Kaṛā, near Prayāg, was a Sant poet who taught the Name of Rāma and service to the poor. Sundardās, a disciple of Dādū Dayāl, was a learned poet from Rajasthan. His Sundara Vilāsa and Jñānasamudra put the teaching of Dādū's panth in polished Hindi and Sanskrit-based form. He is regarded as the most scholarly of the Dādū Panth, a Sant tradition that stressed formless devotion. Both belonged to the broader north Indian Sant movement.

events.title: East India Company chartered
events.description: On 31 December 1600 Queen Elizabeth I granted a royal charter to the Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies, giving it a monopoly on English trade with Asia. The company's early voyages went to the spice islands, and in 1612 it set up a trading post at Surat in Gujarat. It acquired political power in India after the Battle of Plassey in 1757 and ruled large territories until the Crown took over in 1858.

events.title: Madurai Nāyakas and the Mīnākṣī temple
events.description: The Nāyakas of Madurai, who were governors of Vijayanagara, became independent rulers after 1565. Viśvanātha Nāyaka planned the city and the Mīnākṣī-Sundareśvara temple on a grand scale, and his successor Tirumala Nāyaka, who ruled from 1623 to 1659, added halls such as the Pudu Maṇḍapa and the Vasanta Maṇḍapa, as well as tall gopurams. The goddess Mīnākṣī, who is regarded as the sovereign of Madurai, is worshipped alongside Śiva as her consort. The complex shows the culmination of Nāyaka architecture, with its thousand-pillared hall.

events.title: Raghunātha Nāyaka and Govinda Dīkṣita of Tañjāvūr
events.description: The Nāyakas of Tañjāvūr, who ruled in the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, were great patrons of music, dance and Sanskrit. Raghunātha Nāyaka (r. 1600–1634) was himself a poet and a musician, and is credited with the Raghunātha vīṇā. His minister Govinda Dīkṣita founded Vedic schools and made repairs to temples and tanks in Kumbakoṇam, including the Mahāmaham tank, where a festival is held every twelve years. Their court produced scholars such as Govinda Dīkṣita's son Veṅkaṭamakhin, the author of an important text on music.

events.title: Akhāṛā system of militant ascetics
events.description: Akhāṛās are monastic orders of ascetics who train in both scripture and arms. The Śaiva Daśanāmī Nāgās, including the Jūnā, Nirañjanī and Mahānirvāṇī akhāṛās, trace themselves to Śaṅkara. Historians date their organisation as fighting bodies mainly to the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries, when armed ascetics also worked as traders and mercenaries. Tradition credits Madhusūdana Sarasvatī with arming them against persecution. The Rāmānandī Vairāgīs formed similar orders, called anīs, meaning armies. Their leaders still take the first processional bath at the Kumbha.

events.title: Bengal's Maṅgala-kāvyas
events.description: The maṅgala-kāvyas are Bengali narrative poems, composed from roughly the fifteenth to the eighteenth century, praising regional deities and promising welfare to those who honour them. Mukundarāma Cakravartī's Caṇḍīmaṅgala celebrates the goddess Caṇḍī through the tales of a hunter and a merchant. The Manasā-maṅgalas tell of the snake goddess and of Behulā and Lakhindar, and the Dharma-maṅgalas concern Dharma Ṭhākura. They bring local and folk deities into the wider Purāṇic world while preserving rural Bengal's own stories.

events.title: Rāmānandī Rasik tradition
events.description: The Rasik branch of the Rāmānandī sect worships Rāma and Sītā through the sentiment of conjugal love, mādhurya bhāva, rather than only as king and servant. Agradās, a disciple of Kṛṣṇadās Payahārī, is regarded as its founder, at Galtā near Jaipur, and Raivāsā in Śekhāvāṭī was another centre. His Dhyānamañjarī and other works describe visualisation of the divine couple in their groves. The tradition links Rāma devotion to the Kṛṣṇa-bhakti style of Braj.

events.title: Āpadeva and Laugākṣi Bhāskara
events.description: Āpadeva's Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa and Laugākṣi Bhāskara's Arthasaṅgraha are two compact Sanskrit manuals of Pūrva Mīmāṃsā, the school that studies Vedic ritual and how to interpret injunctions. They explain its rules of interpretation, the means of knowledge and the way ritual acts are understood. Both authors were Kāśī-based scholars of the 17th century, and the books became the standard primers for beginners, as the Vedāntasāra is for Advaita.

events.title: Khaṇḍadeva's Bhāṭṭadīpikā
events.description: Khaṇḍadeva Mīmāṃsaka, a scholar at Kāśī, wrote the Bhāṭṭadīpikā, a commentary on the Bhāṭṭa school of Mīmāṃsā, that of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa. He applied the precise concepts of Navya-Nyāya to Mīmāṃsā, giving rise to what is sometimes called Navya Mīmāṃsā. His work and his pupil's helped make Kāśī a centre where the old ritual exegesis and the new logic combined, and the text remains a reference for the school.

events.title: Setu–Gaṅgā pilgrimage between Rāmeśvaram and Kāśī
events.description: Hindu pilgrims have long combined visits to the Rāmeśvaram temple at the southern tip of India with Kāśī in the north. The tradition holds that one should bathe at Rāmeśvaram at the Setu, and bring sand from there to the Gaṅgā at Prayāga, and carry Gaṅgā water back to offer to the liṅga at Rāmeśvaram. The circuit joins the south and north in one yātrā. The practice is described in texts on pilgrimage and continues today.

events.title: Cār Dhām of Bhārata
events.description: The Cār Dhām, or four abodes, are Badarīnātha in the north, Dvārakā in the west, Purī in the east and Rāmeśvaram in the south. Hindu tradition attributes the arrangement to Śaṅkara, who is said to have founded maṭhas in the four directions, though the maṭhas he is credited with are at Jyotirmaṭha, Dvārakā, Purī and Śṛṅgeri. Historians note that the idea of a pan-Indian circuit developed over centuries, and the entry's date is a rough guide. A separate Himalayan Chota Cār Dhām circuit also exists.

events.title: The Sapta Purī, seven sacred cities
events.description: The Sapta Purī are the seven sacred cities that are held to grant mokṣa, liberation: Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā (Haridvāra), Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantikā (Ujjain) and Dvārakā. The list is found in the Garuḍa Purāṇa and other texts. The Purāṇas value a visit to them as meritorious, and the cities remain centres of pilgrimage. The idea expresses a sacred map of India that includes Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva places, and the date given is only a rough one.

events.title: Rāgamālā painting in Rajput courts
events.description: Rāgamālā paintings picture the musical modes of North India, the rāgas and their consort rāgiṇīs, as human figures with a mood, season and time of day. Many are shown as lovers, kings or ascetics, or as gods such as Kṛṣṇa. The genre flourished in Rajput courts, such as Mewar, Bundi and Kota, and in the Pahāṛī hills from about the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries. A set of verses describing each rāga guided the artist, so the pictures translate sound into image.

events.title: Viṣṇupur's terracotta temples
events.description: The Malla kings of Viṣṇupur in Bengal, devotees of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism from the sixteenth century, built a series of fine temples in brick and terracotta. The Rāsmañca, a pyramidal structure built in about 1600 under Vīr Hāmbīr, was used for the Rāsa festival, and the Śyāma Rāya temple dates to 1643. Their walls carry panels of scenes from the Rāmāyaṇa, the Mahābhārata and the life of Kṛṣṇa, and they are a high point of the Bengal terracotta tradition.

events.title: Gāgā Bhaṭṭa's family at Kāśī
events.description: The Bhaṭṭa family of Paiṭhaṇ, a Brahmin lineage, settled in Kāśī and over five generations, from Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa to Viśveśvara Bhaṭṭa, who is known as Gāgā Bhaṭṭa, held a leading position among Banaras paṇḍits. Their learning and standing gave them authority in questions of dharma. Gāgā Bhaṭṭa is most famous for officiating at the Vedic coronation of Śivājī in 1674, which gave the Maratha ruler a ritual status as Chatrapati. The family's work linked Kāśī and Maharashtra.

events.title: Kerala temple arts
events.description: Kerala's temple arts form a distinct tradition. Sopāna saṅgītam is a slow style of singing at the temple steps, associated with the Kṛṣṇa devotion of Jayadeva's Aṣṭapadī. Murals at Eṭṭumānūr and Mattāñceri, painted in natural colours with a strong line, depict Purāṇic scenes. The ritual of the temples, run by tantri families, is governed by manuals such as the Tantrasamuccaya, compiled in 1428. Together these keep alive music, painting and rite within the temple setting.

events.title: Ādi Granth installed
events.description: In 1604 Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh Guru, completed the Ādi Granth, the first collection of Sikh scripture, and installed it in the Harmandir Sāhib at Amritsar. It contains the hymns of the first five Gurus, as well as those of earlier saints from various traditions, including the Sants Kabīr, Nāmdev and Ravidās, the Sufi Farīd and the Sanskrit poet Jayadeva. Later Guru Gobind Siṅgh added the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahādur, and in 1708 the scripture was declared the eternal Guru, the Guru Granth Sāhib.

events.title: Bīr Singh Deo of Orchā
events.description: Bīr Singh Deo became ruler of Orchā in 1605 and was one of the major Bundelā kings. He earned Jahāngīr's favour, partly because he killed Akbar's adviser Abū'l Fazl in 1602 at Jahāngīr's request. He built the Jahāngīr Mahal at Orchā and the Datiā palace, which are among the best-known examples of Bundelā architecture. He also built many temples, including the Keśavadeva at Mathurā.

events.title: Guru Arjan martyred
events.description: Guru Arjan died in 1606 in custody at Lahore. The Mughal emperor Jahāngīr had ordered his arrest, and the Mughal memoirs say it was because he had blessed the rebel prince Khusrau. Sikh tradition remembers that he was tortured and refused to change his teaching, so it speaks of his martyrdom. His son Guru Hargobind, who became the sixth Guru, wore two swords, which stood for mīrī (worldly authority) and pīrī (spiritual authority). From then on the Sikh community also developed a military tradition.

events.title: Guru Hargobind and the Akāl Takht
events.description: Guru Hargobind became the sixth Sikh Guru in 1606, after his father Guru Arjan died in Mughal custody under Jahāngīr. He wore two swords, said to stand for spiritual authority and temporal power (pīrī and mīrī), and had the Akāl Takht raised facing the Harmandir Sāhib at Amritsar. It became the seat for the community's political and judicial decisions. The Guru later fought several engagements with Mughal forces and moved to the hills, and the Takht remains the highest Sikh temporal seat.

events.title: Saint Tukārāma born at Dehū
events.description: Tukārāma was born in 1608 at Dehū near Pune into a family of grain merchants. After his business failed and famine took family members, he turned to devotion for Viṭṭhala. His abhaṅgas, about four thousand five hundred of which are attributed to him, are simple, direct Marathi poems about God, the world and the self, and are often compared to a living Veda for the people. They are a central part of the Vārakarī repertoire. Tradition says he met Śivājī, though historians debate the details.

events.title: Samartha Rāmadāsa born
events.description: Rāmadāsa was born in 1608 at Jāmb in Maharashtra and became a devotee of Rāma and Hanumān. He wrote the Dāsabodha, a long book of moral and spiritual instruction in verse, and the Manāce Śloka, 205 verses addressed to the mind. He founded maṭhas and temples of Hanumān (Māruti) across Maharashtra and encouraged physical fitness and community organisation. Maharashtra tradition calls him Śivājī's guru, though historians disagree about the extent of their relationship.

events.title: Durgā Pūjā of the Sābarṇa Rāycaudhurīs
events.description: The Sābarṇa Rāy Caudhurī family of Baṛiśā, now part of Kolkata, claims to have begun its Durgā Pūjā in 1610. This is counted among the oldest family-sponsored Durgā worships in Bengal, held in the family's own compound. The great landed families, zamindars, sponsored such pūjās with display and feeding of crowds, and the later community pūjās, called sārvajanīn, grew out of this model. The Baṛiśā puja is still held each autumn and is often cited when Bengali Durgā Pūjā history is discussed.

events.title: Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa's Nirṇayasindhu
events.description: Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa belonged to a Marāṭhī brāhmaṇa family settled at Kāśī, and finished the Nirṇayasindhu in 1612. Its purpose is to settle disputed questions of ritual timing, such as which day an observance of a tithi falls on when lunar days overlap two civil days. It examines the various sources and weighs them. Dharmaśāstra authorities still use it to fix dates for festivals such as Dīpāvalī, Holī and Śivarātri, especially in western and central India.

events.title: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja's Caitanya Caritāmṛta
events.description: Written in Bengali with Sanskrit verses, the Caitanya Caritāmṛta tells the life of Caitanya in three parts and expounds Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theology. Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja composed it in old age at Vṛndāvana, usually dated to about 1615, at the request of the Vṛndāvana Gosvāmīs. He drew on earlier biographies such as Murāri Gupta's and Vṛndāvana Dāsa's. The work presents Caitanya as Kṛṣṇa combined with the mood of Rādhā and sets out the doctrine of inconceivable oneness and difference.

events.title: Mewar's treaty with Jahāngīr
events.description: After years of Mughal campaigns, Rāṇā Amar Siṃh of Mewar agreed to a treaty with Jahāngīr in 1615. He accepted Mughal overlordship, but was spared the humiliation of personal attendance at court, and his son Karaṇ went in his place. Chittor was returned to Mewar on condition that it not be fortified. No Rajput princess had to be sent in marriage. Mewar's terms were more favourable than those of other Rajput states, and the treaty ended decades of hostility between Mewar and the Mughals.

events.title: Veṅkaṭa II's death and the Battle of Toppūr
events.description: Veṅkaṭa II, who ruled the Vijayanagara empire from Candragiri from 1586 to 1614, was the last strong ruler of the Āravīḍu dynasty. He held off the Deccan sultanates and strengthened control over the Nāyakas in the south. After his death, a succession dispute led to a civil war, which culminated in the battle of Toppūr in 1616. This weakened the empire and let the Nāyakas become more independent.

events.title: Bīr Singh Bundelā and Mathurā's Keśava temple
events.description: Bīr Singh Deo Bundelā of Orchā, a favourite of the Mughal emperor Jahāngīr, built a great Keśavadeva temple at Mathurā around 1618. Its reported cost was thirty-three lakh rupees. Visitors of the time described it as a very tall structure of sandstone, among the most splendid in North India. Aurangzeb ordered it demolished in 1670. The site, revered as Kṛṣṇa's birthplace, stands beside the Shāhī ʿĪdgāh and remains disputed.

events.title: Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita's Siddhānta Kaumudī
events.description: Pāṇini's Sanskrit grammar, the Aṣṭādhyāyī, presents its rules in a compact order that is hard to follow. Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita, who taught at Kāśī, reordered the rules by topic in the Siddhānta Kaumudī, so that a student looking for how nouns or verbs are formed finds all the relevant sūtras together. He wrote his own commentary on it, the Prauḍhamanoramā, and a larger commentary on Pāṇini, the Śabdakaustubha. Abridged versions, such as Varadarāja's Laghu Kaumudī, became the standard school texts of Sanskrit grammar, and are still used.

events.title: Nīlakaṇṭha Caturdhara's Bhāratabhāvadīpa
events.description: Nīlakaṇṭha Caturdhara, a Maharashtrian scholar who settled at Kāśī in the seventeenth century, wrote the Bhāratabhāvadīpa, a commentary on the whole Mahābhārata. It explains difficult passages, often giving a philosophical Advaita reading, and records variant readings. It became the standard commentary in northern India, and modern editors, including those of the Poona critical edition, consulted its text and readings. Nīlakaṇṭha also wrote on the Bhagavad Gītā and other works.

events.title: Mitra Miśra's Vīramitrodaya
events.description: Mitra Miśra, a scholar from the Gwalior region, wrote the Vīramitrodaya for his patron Vīrasiṃha Deva, the Bundelā king of Orchā, who ruled in the early seventeenth century. It is a huge dharma digest, gathering earlier smṛti and Purāṇic authorities on topics such as saṃskāras, worship, royal duties, law and ritual law. The work is named in honour of the king, and later jurists cited it as a major authority on Hindu law.

events.title: Yogacintāmaṇi and later Haṭha yoga compendia
events.description: In the seventeenth century and after, Sanskrit compendia gathered earlier yoga texts. Śivānanda's Yogacintāmaṇi is a compilation drawing on the Haṭhapradīpikā and other works. Commentaries on the Haṭhapradīpikā explained the postures, breath control and cleansing methods of haṭha yoga. These books combined the eight-limbed yoga of Patañjali with the physical methods of haṭha yoga, a synthesis that shaped later understanding of yoga.

events.title: Portuguese destroy Koṇēśvaram temple at Trincomalee
events.description: The Koṇēśvaram temple, a Śaiva shrine on the Koṇēsar Malai headland at Trincomalee, was attacked on 14 April 1622, the Tamil New Year, by Portuguese forces under Constantino de Sá de Noronha. According to the sources, they entered during the festival and plundered it, and then toppled it into the sea; the last remaining structure was destroyed in 1624, and its stones were used for Fort Frederick.¶The temple is among the oldest and most famous Śaiva centres in Sri Lanka and is mentioned in the Vāyu Purāṇa. The surviving accounts largely come from the Portuguese side. Bronze images buried by devotees were recovered in 1950, and a restored shrine was reopened on 3 March 1963, about three and a half centuries after its destruction.

events.title: Dharmarāja's Vedānta Paribhāṣā
events.description: Dharmarājādhvarīndra's Vedānta Paribhāṣā is a compact Sanskrit manual of Advaita epistemology. It explains the means of valid knowledge, pramāṇas, including perception, inference and scripture, and shows how the mind takes the shape of an object. It does so in the technical vocabulary of Navya-Nyāya, the new logic, that was then the dominant style of philosophical argument. It became the standard textbook for studying Advaita's theory of knowledge, and is still printed with commentary.

events.title: Śivājī born at Śivnerī
events.description: Śivājī was born on 19 February 1630 in the hill fort of Śivnerī near Pune. His father Śahājī served the Deccan sultanates as a general and was usually away. He was raised by his mother Jījābāī, who brought him up on the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata, and by the administrator Dādojī Koṇḍadev on the family's estate.¶The Deccan of his childhood was fought over by Bijapur, Golkonda and the Mughals. Among the Māvaḷā hill farmers of the Sahyādris he found the companions who would become his first soldiers.

events.title: Tirumala Nāyaka's Pudu Maṇḍapam
events.description: Tirumala Nāyaka ruled Madurai from 1623 to 1659 and was a major builder. The Pudu Maṇḍapam, a long pillared hall facing the Mīnākṣī temple, was built under him for the Vasanta festival, and is known for its sculpted pillars. He also had the large Vaṇḍiyūr tank excavated, where the Teppam float festival is held each year, with images of Mīnākṣī and Sundareśvara taken on a decorated raft. He also built a palace, part of which survives.

events.title: Shāh Jahān orders new temples demolished
events.description: In 1632 Shāh Jahān's court histories record that the emperor ordered the demolition of Hindu temples that had been begun but not finished, in the first years of his reign. At Vārāṇasī alone, seventy-six temples under construction were destroyed, according to the Bādshāhnāma, and similar action was recorded in other provinces. Such orders applied to new construction and not to old temples, and show a more orthodox attitude than Akbar's. Policy varied between reigns and regions.

events.title: Viśvanātha Pañcānana's Bhāṣā-pariccheda
events.description: Viśvanātha Nyāyapañcānana of Navadvīpa wrote the Bhāṣāpariccheda, a verse primer of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika in the form of 168 kārikās. He added his own prose commentary, the Muktāvalī, which explains each verse. The work lists the categories and the means of valid knowledge in a form that could be memorised, and it became a standard introduction in Bengal and beyond. It is often paired with Annaṃbhaṭṭa's Tarkasaṅgraha as an entry to the system.

events.title: Śahājī Bhosale in Karnataka
events.description: Śahājī Bhosale, father of Śivājī, served the Sultanate of Bijapur as a general and was granted the Bangalore jāgīr, a revenue assignment that made him a regional lord in the Karnāṭak country far from his Maharashtra home. His court there patronised Sanskrit and regional poets and scholars, and the family's later Tañjāvūr branch descended from his son Ekojī. Śivājī spent part of his youth under his father's arrangements, and Śahājī's southern career gave the Bhosales both resources and a presence in Karnataka that mattered to Marāṭhā politics for generations.

events.title: Madras granted to the English
events.description: In 1639 Francis Day and Andrew Cogan of the English East India Company received permission from Dāmarla Veṅkaṭapati Nāyaka, a local governor serving the Vijayanagara ruler, to build a trading post on the Coromandel coast. The place was called Cennapaṭṭaṇam after the Nāyaka's father, and the English called it Madraspatnam. Fort St George was built there, and it grew into the city of Madras (Chennai) and the Company's first major territorial base in the south.

events.title: Kavīndrācārya Sarasvatī and the pilgrim tax
events.description: Kavīndrācārya Sarasvatī, a Kāśī saṃnyāsī and scholar, headed a delegation of pandits that, during Shāh Jahān's reign, persuaded the emperor to abolish the tax on Hindu pilgrims to Kāśī and Prayāga. The scholars of Kāśī honoured him with the title Sarvavidyānidhāna, and compiled the Kavīndracandrodaya, an anthology of verses in his praise. He built up a large library of Sanskrit manuscripts, and a list of its holdings survives. The episode shows how Hindu scholars negotiated with the Mughal court.

events.title: Kṣetrayya and the Telugu padam
events.description: Kṣetrayya, also called Kṣetrajña, was a Telugu poet who signed his songs with the name Muvva Gopāla. His padams are short lyrics, often in the voice of a woman longing for her lover or scolding him, with the lover understood as the deity. They are sensual and devotional at once and have long been staples of Kuchipuḍi and Bharatanāṭyam dance and of Carnatic concerts. Tradition links him to Golkonda and the Krishna river country in the seventeenth century, though details of his life are poorly documented.

events.title: Rāṇī Karṇāvatī of Garhwal
events.description: Karṇāvatī was the widow of the Garhwal king Mahīpati Śāh and acted as regent for her young son Pṛthvīpati Śāh in the 1630s. Tradition says that when a Mughal force sent under Shāh Jahān approached, she had the noses of captured soldiers cut off, hence the epithet "nose-cutting queen", and the invaders withdrew. Historians note that the details come from later accounts and are hard to verify, but the tale is a well-known part of Garhwal's heritage.

events.title: Śivājī's oath at Rāyareśvara
events.description: According to Marathi tradition, in 1645 the young Śivājī, then about fifteen, and a few Māvaḷā friends, including Tānājī Mālusare, took an oath at the Rāyareśvara temple in the Sahyādri hills to found Hindavī Svarājya, a kingdom of their own. The story comes from later chronicles, and some historians view it with caution. The hills were then divided among Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and the Mughals. Śivājī soon began taking forts, and within a generation he had established the Maratha state.

events.title: Śivājī captures Toraṇā fort
events.description: In 1646 Śivājī captured the fort of Toraṇā (Prachaṇḍagaḍ) near Pune from the Bijapur Sultanate, in his first major conquest. According to tradition, he found treasure there and used it to fortify a nearby hill, which he named Rājgaḍ, the "king's fort", and made it his first capital. He continued by taking over other forts in the region, often without pitched battles. This was the foundation of the Maratha kingdom.

events.title: Fall of the last Vijayanagara emperor
events.description: Śrīraṅga III was the last important ruler of the Āravīḍu line of Vijayanagara. In 1646 he lost Vellore to the armies of the Sultanates of Golkonda and Bijapur, along with other local rivals. This is often taken as the end of the empire, though he fled and lived on for some years, sheltered by Śivappa Nāyaka of Keḷadi. The old imperial structure then dissolved into the rival Nāyaka kingdoms, which kept the Vijayanagara cultural heritage alive.

events.title: Battle of Purandar (Belsar)
events.description: In 1648 a Bijapur force under Fateh Khān was sent against Śivājī and met his troops near Purandar and Belsar in the Pune hills, in one of his earliest open engagements. According to Maratha accounts the Marāṭhās prevailed, and Śivājī strengthened his hold on the fort of Purandar and the surrounding country. It showed that his light, mobile troops could stand against a regular Deccan Sultanate force, an early sign of the military style his kingdom would rely on.

events.title: Annaṃbhaṭṭa's Tarkasaṅgraha
events.description: The Tarkasaṅgraha, written by Annaṃbhaṭṭa, a Telugu scholar active at Kāśī, is a short Sanskrit primer of the combined Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika system. It lists seven categories (padārthas) and the four means of knowledge, then explains qualities, actions and inference in a clear, schematic way. The author also wrote a commentary, the Dīpikā. Used as the first text for new students of logic and metaphysics, it is still widely studied. It is usually dated to about the 17th century.

events.title: Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya's Navya-Nyāya commentaries
events.description: Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya, of Navadvīpa in Bengal, was a leading logician of the Navya-Nyāya school after Raghunātha Śiromaṇi. His commentaries on Gaṅgeśa's Tattvacintāmaṇi, known collectively as the Gādādharī, are famed for their difficulty and precision, and they dominated advanced study of the discipline for generations in Bengal. He worked on definitions of relations such as pervasion. Because Navadvīpa's logic then shaped the philosophical argument of other schools, his work had wide influence.

events.title: Brahmānanda Sarasvatī's Laghucandrikā
events.description: Brahmānanda Sarasvatī of Kāśī wrote the Laghucandrikā, a commentary on Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi. That work answered the Dvaita thinker Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta, which had criticised Advaita. The Laghucandrikā defends Madhusūdana against the Dvaita rejoinders, such as the Taraṅgiṇī of Rāmācārya, and explains the argument. This exchange is among the most intense of the Vedānta school debates and is still studied in traditional centres of learning.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥

gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.
gitaQuote.source: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) Critical Edition; Rāmānuja Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Rāmeśvaram's long pillared corridors
events.description: The Rāmanāthasvāmi temple at Rāmeśvaram, one of the twelve jyotirliṅgas and a Char Dhām site, is known for its huge corridors with rows of carved pillars. The Setupati chiefs of Rāmanāthapuram, who guarded the pilgrimage route, built these corridors over the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. The third corridor, with more than a thousand pillars, is one of the longest in India. By tradition Rāma worshipped Śiva here before crossing to Laṅkā. The temple remains a major pilgrimage place.

events.title: Bathing fairs at Haridvāra and the Kumbha
events.description: Haridvāra, where the Gaṅgā leaves the hills, has long drawn pilgrims for bathing fairs, and by the seventeenth century Indian and foreign writers describe crowds there on great bathing days. The Kumbha as a named, twelve-year festival is firmly documented only in later sources, and scholars debate how far back that precise form goes. The armed ākhāṛās of Nāgā saṃnyāsīs organised processions and bathing order, and disputes over precedence sometimes led to violence. The best known occurred in 1760, between Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava ascetics.

events.title: Tukārāma's departure from Dehū
events.description: Tukārāma died in 1650 at Dehū. Vārakarī tradition holds that he left the world in his body (sadeha), ascending to Vaikuṇṭha in a celestial vehicle sent by Viṣṇu, and the date is marked each year by a festival. Some modern scholars suggest that he died or disappeared in less miraculous circumstances, but the accounts do not agree. Whatever happened, his abhaṅgas remained, and his family kept up his devotional tradition at Dehū.

events.title: Jagannātha Paṇḍitarāja and the Rasagaṅgādhara
events.description: Jagannātha Paṇḍitarāja, a Telugu brāhmaṇa from Andhra, is often called the last great classical Sanskrit literary critic. He served at the courts of Shāh Jahān, who is said to have given him the title Paṇḍitarāja, and of Prince Dārā Shukoh. His Rasagaṅgādhara, an unfinished work on poetics, is a sharp, argumentative treatment of aesthetic theory. His Gaṅgālaharī is a hymn to the Gaṅgā in fifty-odd verses. Later legend says he was cast out for loving a Muslim woman and composed the hymn on the riverside steps at Kāśī.

events.title: Veṅkaṭamakhin's Caturdaṇḍī Prakāśikā
events.description: Veṅkaṭamakhin, a Tañjāvūr scholar and son of Govinda Dīkṣita, wrote the Caturdaṇḍī Prakāśikā around the mid-seventeenth century. It sets out a mathematical frame for Carnatic rāga classification. From the seven notes and their variants he derived a table of 72 parent scales, called meḷakartās, though in practice his text names only a smaller number as then in use. Later musicians completed the system with the familiar sequence of names, and it remains the basis for rāga organisation in South Indian music.

events.title: Prāṇanātha and the Praṇāmī sect
events.description: Prāṇanātha, born Mehrāj Ṭhākur in Jāmnagar in 1618, founded the Praṇāmī or Nijānanda tradition. His teaching reads the Bhāgavata Purāṇa alongside the Qurʾān and holds that the two point to one truth, centring on devotion to Kṛṣṇa. He travelled through Gujarat and Rajasthan and settled at Pannā in Bundelkhand, where the ruler Chatrasāl became his follower. Tradition says he blessed Chatrasāl's campaigns. Prāṇanātha died at Pannā in about 1694, and the Praṇāmī community still honours the town.

events.title: Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita's satirical Sanskrit poetry
events.description: Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita was a Sanskrit poet and grand-nephew of Appayya Dīkṣita, who served as minister to Tirumala Nāyaka of Madurai. He wrote the Śivalīlārṇava, the Gaṅgāvataraṇa and the Nalacarita, but is best known for biting satires such as the Kaliviḍambana, which mocks the follies of the age, including pretentious scholars and corrupt officials. His work shows that Sanskrit literature could be topical and witty as late as the 17th century.

events.title: Mājulī's Vaiṣṇava sattras of Assam
events.description: Sattras are Vaiṣṇava monastic institutions founded in the tradition of Śaṅkaradeva and his disciple Mādhavadeva. In the seventeenth century, the large river island of Mājulī in the Brahmaputra became home to many of them, including Āuniāṭī, established in 1653, Dakhinpāṭ and Garamūr. They preserve music, mask-making, dance and drama, and they serve as centres of learning. The island is one of the best-known centres of Assamese Vaiṣṇavism and is the main site where Sattriya arts are practised.

events.title: Śrīnivāsa's Yatīndramatadīpikā
events.description: The Yatīndramatadīpikā, written by Śrīnivāsa, is a short and clear presentation of Viśiṣṭādvaita, the qualified non-dualism of Rāmānuja (the "yatīndra" of the title). It sets out the categories of the system, such as matter, soul, God and attributes, in simple language. Because of its clarity, it is the standard introduction for students and has often been used in teaching in Śrīvaiṣṇava schools. It dates from about the seventeenth century.

gitaQuote.verse: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत । अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥ परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् । धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥

gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.

events.title: Raṅgarāmānuja's Upaniṣad commentaries
events.description: Rāmānuja wrote a commentary on the Brahma Sūtra and one on the Gītā, but he left no commentary on the principal Upaniṣads. Raṅgarāmānuja, a later Viśiṣṭādvaita scholar of South India, wrote commentaries on the main Upaniṣads from the system's viewpoint. This allowed the school to claim full interpretation of the three sources of Vedānta, the Upaniṣads, the Gītā and the Brahma Sūtra, in the same way as the other major Vedānta traditions.

events.title: Haṭharatnāvalī and the 84 āsanas
events.description: The Haṭharatnāvalī, a text of Hatha yoga composed by Śrīnivāsa in the seventeenth century in South India, lists eighty-four āsanas and describes them in some detail, a larger set than most earlier works such as the Haṭhapradīpikā. The Jogapradīpikā, written by Jayatarāma in 1737, also lists eighty-four postures, and later illustrated manuscripts show them. These texts form an important record of how posture practice developed before modern yoga.

events.title: Morayā Gosāvī, saint of Gaṇeśa devotion
events.description: Morayā Gosāvī is the chief saint of the Gāṇapatyas, who worship Gaṇeśa as the supreme being. His dates are uncertain, with proposals ranging from the fourteenth to the seventeenth century. He walked every month from Cincvaḍ, near Pune, to the shrine at Morgāv, until in old age, tradition says, the god came to him as a stone in the river. He entered a tomb alive at Cincvaḍ. The cry "Gaṇapati Bāppā Morayā" heard at every Gaṇeśa festival joins his name to the god's.

events.title: Jagdīś temple at Udaipur
events.description: The Jagdīś temple at Udaipur, dedicated to Viṣṇu as Jagannātha, was completed in 1651 by Mahārāṇā Jagat Siṅgh I of Mewar. It stands on a high platform reached by a steep flight of steps, with a tall śikhara and a pillared hall, and enshrines a black stone image of Viṣṇu. The same reign saw the Mewar court artist Sāhibdīn illustrate a Rāmāyaṇa manuscript in the early 1650s, a landmark of Mewar painting under royal patronage.

events.title: Dārā Shukoh and Bābā Lāl's dialogues
events.description: Prince Dārā Shukoh, eldest son of Shāh Jahān, sought a common ground between Islam and Hindu thought. He translated the Upaniṣads into Persian as Sirr-i-Akbar and wrote the Majmaʿ-ul-Baḥrayn, on the meeting of the two oceans. He held conversations with the Vairāgī sage Bābā Lāl Dās of Dhyānpur in Punjab, which were recorded in Persian, and he admired the mystic Sarmad of Delhi, who was himself executed for heresy in 1661. After losing the succession war to Aurangzeb, Dārā was executed in 1659.

events.title: Śivājī conquers Jāvḷī
events.description: In 1656 Śivājī took the stronghold of Jāvḷī in the Sahyādri from the Moré chiefs, who held it as vassals of Bijapur. This brought him control of the hills above the Konkan, and he built the fort of Pratāpgaḍ nearby to guard the area. The conquest increased his resources and his reputation, and it caused Bijapur to send an army against him. It led directly to the encounter with Afzal Khān in 1659.

events.title: Dārā Shukoh and the Upaniṣads
events.description: Dārā Shukoh, the eldest son of Shāh Jahān, studied Vedānta and Sufism and joined with Sanskrit pandits at Kāśī to translate about fifty Upaniṣads into Persian, completing the Sirr-i-Akbar ("the great secret") in 1657. His earlier Majmaʿ-ul-Baḥrain argued that Sufism and Vedānta express a common truth. A Persian version of the translation reached Europe, and the French scholar Anquetil-Duperron made a Latin version in 1801–02, which Schopenhauer read and praised as a comfort of his life.

events.title: Kalyāṇ and Bhivaṇḍī taken
events.description: In 1657 Śivājī's officers seized Kalyāṇ and the neighbouring town of Bhivaṇḍī from Bijapur, carrying his power from the Sahyādri hills down into the northern Koṅkaṇa coast. This gave him ports and creeks on the Arabian Sea. Recognising the value of sea access, he began building ships at the coastal yards, the first step towards the Marāṭhā navy that would later guard the coast against the Siddīs, the Portuguese and the English. Control of the Koṅkaṇa also brought customs revenue and a route to the sea for trade.

events.title: Jasvant Singh and the Battle of Dharmat
events.description: Jasvant Singh I of Mārwāṛ, who ruled from 1638 to 1678, served the Mughals as a senior commander. In 1658 he fought on Shāh Jahān's side against Aurangzeb at Dharmat and was defeated. He later served Aurangzeb and was posted to Afghanistan, where he died in 1678. His death led to a long struggle in Mārwāṛ when Aurangzeb tried to take control of the state, as the heir Ajīt Singh was an infant. The war lasted until 1707.

events.title: Aurangzeb seizes the throne
events.description: After Shāh Jahān fell ill in 1657, his four sons fought for the throne. Aurangzeb defeated his brother Dārā Shukoh at Sāmūgaṛh in 1658, imprisoned his father at Āgrā Fort, where Shāh Jahān remained until his death in 1666, and took the crown. In 1659 Dārā Shukoh was executed on a charge of heresy. Aurangzeb ruled until 1707 and extended the empire to its widest extent while pursuing a more orthodox policy that included reimposing the jizya in 1679.

events.title: Afzal Khān slain at Pratāpgaḍ
events.description: In November 1659 Śivājī met the Bijapur general Afzal Khān, who had been sent to subdue him, at Pratāpgaḍ. Marathi chronicles say Afzal Khān had earlier desecrated the temples of Tuljāpūr and Paṇḍharpūr, though historians weigh such claims carefully. At the meeting, each man was to come lightly armed. Śivājī, wearing mail under his clothes, killed Afzal Khān with the wāgh-nakh, or tiger claws, and a dagger, and his troops then routed the Bijapur army in the surrounding hills.
