events.title: Keḷadi Śivappa Nāyaka
events.description: Śivappa Nāyaka ruled Keḷadi, also called Ikkeri, in western Karnataka from about 1645 to 1660. He is remembered for the land revenue system called sistu, based on a survey of land and standard assessments. He sheltered Śrīraṅga III, the last Vijayanagara emperor, and fought Bījāpur's armies. The kingdom he strengthened also built or supported temples and became one of the strong successor states.

events.title: Bājī Prabhu at Pāvan Khiṇḍ
events.description: In 1660 Śivājī was besieged in the fort of Panhāḷā by a Bijapur army under Siddī Jauhar. He escaped at night in the rain and headed for Viśālgaḍ. Bājī Prabhu Deśpāṇḍe held the narrow pass of Ghoḍ Khiṇḍ with about three hundred Māvaḷā soldiers against the pursuers. Though badly wounded, he kept fighting until the cannon from Viśālgaḍ signalled that Śivājī had arrived safely, and then died. The pass is now called Pāvan Khiṇḍ, "holy pass", in his honour.

events.title: Kumāragurupara founds the Kāśī Maṭh
events.description: Kumāragurupara was a seventeenth-century Tamil poet-saint, born at Śrīvaikuṇṭham, who composed works such as the Kandar Kalivenpā. According to tradition he travelled to Kāśī and, with the favour of the Mughal ruler of the day, founded the Kumārasvāmī Maṭh at Vārāṇasī. His work links Tamil Śaiva devotion to the Sanskrit centre at Kāśī and shows the south's reach in the north.

events.title: Siege of Cākaṇ
events.description: The fort of Cākaṇ, north of Pune, was small, but its garrison under the commander Phiraṅgojī Narsāḷā held out against the Mughal governor Shāista Khān for around two months in 1660. Shāista Khān had occupied Pune and pushed against Śivājī's territories after the Bijapur–Mughal pressure of those years. The long resistance of a modest mud-and-stone fort impressed even the Mughal side, and Phiraṅgojī is remembered in Marāṭhā tradition as an example of loyal, stubborn defence that bought time for Śivājī.

events.title: Mīr Jumla's invasion of Assam
events.description: Mīr Jumla, the Mughal governor of Bengal, invaded Koch Bihar and then Assam in 1661–62. He took the Ahom capital Gaṛgāon in March 1662, but the rains, disease and shortage of supplies weakened his army, and he agreed to a treaty in 1663 and withdrew. He died on the return journey. The Ahoms recovered most of their lands and later took back Guwahati in 1667. The campaign showed the difficulty of fighting in the Brahmaputra valley.

events.title: Night raid on Shāista Khān
events.description: In 1660 the Mughal governor Shāista Khān, Aurangzeb's maternal uncle, occupied Pune with a large army and lodged in the Lāl Mahal, where Śivājī had spent his childhood. On the night of 5 April 1663 Śivājī entered the house with a few companions and attacked. Shāista Khān escaped with the loss of some fingers, and his son and several others were killed. The raid was a humiliating blow to Mughal prestige in the Deccan, and Shāista Khān was soon transferred to Bengal.

events.title: First sack of Surat
events.description: In January 1664 Śivājī led a raid on Surat, the Mughals' richest port on the Gujarat coast. His men plundered the houses of wealthy merchants for several days, while the English and Dutch factories successfully defended themselves. He carried off a huge amount of valuables, which paid for his forts and army. The raid showed the weakness of Mughal defences, and he attacked Surat again in 1670.

events.title: Sindhudurg sea-fort begun
events.description: In 1664 Śivājī began building Sindhudurg on a rocky island off Malvan in the Konkan, a sea-fort that was finished in about three years. It was part of his effort to build a navy to protect the coast against the Portuguese, the Sīdīs of Janjira and the English. His fleets could stop trade ships and gave the Marathas a sea presence. In modern memory Śivājī is sometimes called the father of the Indian Navy, a title used in India today.

events.title: Bernier and Tavernier describe Banaras
events.description: The French travellers François Bernier and Jean-Baptiste Tavernier visited Banaras in the 1660s. Bernier called it the general school of the Hindus and compared it with Athens, a description that gave rise to the phrase "Athens of India". Tavernier described the Bindu Mādhava temple on the Gaṅgā. Their accounts are among the best European descriptions of Kāśī before the changes of the later seventeenth century, with details about its teachers, pilgrims and buildings.

events.title: Treaty of Purandar
events.description: In 1665 the Mughal general Mirzā Rājā Jai Siṃh besieged the fort of Purandar, where Murārbājī Deśpāṇḍe was killed defending it. Śivājī agreed to the Treaty of Purandar in June, giving up twenty-three of his thirty-five forts and the land attached to them, and agreeing to serve Aurangzeb. His son Sambhājī, a child, was given a Mughal rank. The treaty was the lowest point in his career, but the terms led to his visit to Āgrā the following year.

events.title: Murārbājī Deśpāṇḍe at Purandar
events.description: In 1665 the Mughal general Mirzā Rājā Jai Siṃh besieged Purandar, with Dilerkhān leading the assault. Murārbājī Deśpāṇḍe, the fort's commander, led a sortie with a picked force of Māvaḷās against the besiegers and fell in the fighting. His death is remembered as a heroic stand. Soon afterwards Śivājī negotiated the Treaty of Purandar, giving up many forts to the Mughals, and Murārbājī's sacrifice became a lasting symbol of Marāṭhā valour.

events.title: Escape from Āgrā
events.description: In May 1666 Śivājī visited Aurangzeb's court at Āgrā with his young son Sambhājī, but was placed among minor nobles and left in anger. He was confined to a house under guard. In August, according to the usual account, he and his son escaped by being carried out in baskets, supposedly of sweets for distribution to the poor, and then travelled in disguise through Mathurā and Kāśī back to Maharashtra. Historians doubt some details, but the escape is certain.

events.title: Ahoms retake Guwahati
events.description: In 1667 the Ahom general Lāchit Boṛphukan led a force that drove the Mughals out of Guwahati, which had been held since the treaty of 1663. Aurangzeb sent a large army under the Rajput general Rām Siṃh to retake it. At the naval Battle of Saraighāṭ on the Brahmaputra in 1671, Lāchit, though ill, rallied the Ahom fleet and defeated the Mughals. He died soon afterwards. He is remembered in Assam as a hero, and 24 November is celebrated as Lachit Divas.

events.title: Aurangzeb's order against temples and schools
events.description: On 9 April 1669 the Mughal chronicle Maāsir-i-ʿĀlamgīrī records that Aurangzeb sent orders to provincial governors to demolish the schools and temples of the non-Muslims and to put down their teaching and practices. Historians disagree about its reach. Some read it as a general policy; others link it to reports that Brahmin teachers in Thatta, Multan and Banaras were drawing Muslim students. Soon afterwards the Viśvanātha temple at Kāśī was pulled down. Aurangzeb also confirmed grants to other temples, so scholars stress that his record is mixed and regionally varied.

events.title: Kāśī Viśvanātha demolished
events.description: In 1669 Aurangzeb issued a general order to demolish the temples and schools of the "infidels". That year the Viśvanātha temple at Vārāṇasī, the city's chief shrine, rebuilt less than a century earlier, was pulled down. The court chronicle Maʾāsir-i-ʿĀlamgīrī records the report of its destruction.¶The Gyānvāpī mosque was raised on its platform; one wall of the old temple was left standing and can still be seen. Tradition says the priest threw the liṅga into the adjoining well. Ahilyābāī Holkar built the present temple beside the site in 1780, and the dispute over the mosque continues in court.

events.title: Jāṭ revolt of Gokulā
events.description: Gokulā, a Jāṭ landholder of Tilpat, led the cultivators of the Mathurā region against Mughal officials in 1669. Agrarian grievances over revenue demands were central, though some sources also point to resentment at the new religious policy. The rebels killed the local faujdār, ʿAbd-un-Nabī, and Aurangzeb marched in person to put down the rising. Gokulā was captured and executed at Āgrā in January 1670. The Jāṭs rose again under Rājārām and later Churāman, and these revolts formed the base of the later Bharatpur kingdom.

gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||

events.title: Śrīnāthajī leaves Govardhana
events.description: Śrīnāthajī is the main image of the Puṣṭimārga, the devotional tradition founded by Vallabhācārya, and had been worshipped at Govardhana near Mathurā. As Mughal pressure grew in Braj, the Gosvāmī priests took the image away in 1669 and travelled through Rajasthan. Tradition says that near Siṇhaḍ in Mewar the cart wheels sank in the earth and would not move, which was taken as the deity's choice of home. Mahārāṇā Rāj Singh of Mewar gave protection, and the temple at Nāthdvārā was consecrated in 1672. It remains the sect's principal centre.

events.title: Śivājī's revenue and fort administration
events.description: Śivājī's administration tried to replace the claims of local hereditary lords with officials paid by the state. Aṇṇājī Datto carried out a land survey to fix assessment, which was aimed at regulating collection and reducing exactions on cultivators. To prevent any single commander from holding a fort and rebelling, each fort was placed under three officers, traditionally of different castes, who kept watch over one another. These measures are seen as giving the early Marāṭhā state a more centralised system than the hereditary arrangements of many neighbours.

events.title: Keśavadeva temple of Mathurā destroyed
events.description: The Keśavadeva temple at Mathurā had been raised about 1618 by Bīr Singh Deo Bundelā of Orchā and was among the grandest shrines of Braj, standing on ground that tradition reveres as Kṛṣṇa's birthplace. Mughal court records place its demolition in 1670, soon after the Jāṭ revolt around Mathurā was crushed. A mosque, the Shāhī ʿĪdgāh, was built on the site. The shrine to Kṛṣṇa's birth now stands beside it, and ownership of the land remains a matter of continuing litigation and public debate.

gitaQuote.verse: अहमेवाक्षयः कालो धाताहं विश्वतोमुखः ॥ कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो लोकान्समाहर्तुमिह प्रवृत्तः ॥

gitaQuote.translation: I alone am inexhaustible, imperishable Time (Akṣaya Kāla), and I am the dispenser of destiny facing all directions... I am all-destroying Time, grown mighty to extinguish the worlds.
gitaQuote.source: Mahabharata (Bhishma Parva 35.32); Abhinavagupta Gītārtha-Saṁgraha

events.title: Śivājī's forces retake Siṃhagaḍ
events.description: Kondhāṇā, a hill fort near Pune, had been handed to the Mughals under the Treaty of Purandar in 1665. In February 1670 Śivājī's commander Tānājī Mālusare led a night assault, scaling the cliff by tradition with ropes, and fought the garrison under Udaybhān Rāṭhoṛ. Tānājī was killed in the fighting, and his brother Sūryājī finished the capture. Śivājī is remembered as saying that the fort was won but the lion was gone, and the fort was renamed Siṃhagaḍ, the lion's fort.

events.title: Bindu Mādhava temple destroyed
events.description: Bindu Mādhava, a Viṣṇu temple on the Pañcagaṅgā ghāṭ in Vārāṇasī, was a major shrine described by European travellers. According to the Maāsir-i-ʿĀlamgīrī, Aurangzeb ordered the destruction of the temples of Banaras in 1669, and the Bindu Mādhava temple was then demolished and replaced by a mosque, called the Ālamgīr or Beṇī Mādhava mosque. The sources and local memory vary in the dates given, and the building's history has been much discussed.

events.title: Braj's deities travel west
events.description: During the later seventeenth century, when conditions in the Mathurā area were unsettled, the main images of Braj's temples were taken to safe places in Rajasthan. Govindadeva, Gopīnātha and Madana-mohana went to Jaipur and Karaulī, Dvārakādhīśa to Kāṅkrolī, and Mathureśa to Koṭā. Rajput rulers received them and built new temples, and the traditions of Braj worship were continued there. This brought Braj devotional culture to Rajasthan and connected Vaiṣṇava communities across regions.

events.title: Battle of Sarāighāṭ
events.description: In 1671 a Mughal army and fleet under Rājā Rām Siṃh of Amber advanced up the Brahmaputra to retake Guwahati from the Ahom kingdom. The Ahom general Lāchit Boṛphukan, too weak to meet Mughal cavalry on open ground, drew them into the narrow river at Sarāighāṭ.¶Lāchit was seriously ill. According to Assamese tradition, when his boats began to fall back he had himself carried aboard and rowed straight at the enemy, and the fleet rallied and routed the Mughals. The Buranjis, the Ahom chronicles, also tell that earlier he had his own maternal uncle executed for neglecting the defences, saying that his uncle was not greater than his country.
events.eraDesc: Tulasīdāsa, Tukārāma and the Vṛndāvana Gosvāmīs compose devotional classics; Śivājī establishes Svarājya.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Chatrasāl's revolt against the Mughals
events.description: Chatrasāl Bundelā, son of the chieftain Campat Rāy of Bundelkhand, began his rising against Mughal power around 1671 with a very small band of horsemen. Tradition holds that he met Śivājī in the Deccan and was advised to fight for a kingdom in his own land rather than serve in the south. Over the following decades he took forts and districts from Mughal officers, building a state centred on Pannā and the Bundelā hills. His long struggle later brought him into the story of Bājīrāv's rescue in 1729.

events.title: Rāṇī Cennammā of Keḷadi
events.description: Cennammā became the queen of Keḷadi in the 1670s, after the death of her husband Somaśekhara Nāyaka, and ruled until 1696. When Aurangzeb's armies pressed on the Marathas, she sheltered Rājārām, Śivājī's son, in about 1689 as he fled from Mughal forces and helped him reach Jinji. In return she was attacked by a Mughal force, and she made a settlement. She is remembered as a capable ruler.

events.title: Raghavendra Tīrtha enters the Mantrālaya brindāvana
events.description: According to tradition, the Madhva teacher Raghavendra Tīrtha, born about 1595, attained brindāvana in 1671 at Mantrālaya (Mantrālayam), a village on the bank of the Tuṅgabhadrā in the Adoni region. A brindāvana is the sealed tomb-shrine in which an ascetic is held to remain present in meditation. Modern sources give his life as roughly 1595 to 1671; the exact day is a matter of tradition.¶The Dvaita-Vedānta pontiff was a respected commentator on Madhva and Jayatīrtha, and he is remembered in Kannada and Telugu devotional culture as a healer and giver of boons. His brindāvana at Mantrālaya became one of the largest pilgrimage centres of the Madhva tradition, drawing devotees of every community, and the matha that bears his name continues to this day.
events.eraDesc: Tulasīdāsa, Tukārāma and the Vṛndāvana Gosvāmīs compose devotional classics; Śivājī establishes Svarājya.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ | ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||
gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.
gitaQuote.source: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) Critical Edition; Rāmānuja Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Satnāmī revolt at Nārnaul
events.description: The Satnāmīs of Nārnaul, in present Haryana, were a devotional sect of "the true name" drawn largely from cultivators, artisans and small traders, who followed a strict, simple code of conduct. In 1672 a quarrel with a Mughal soldier escalated into open revolt, and the rebels briefly overran Nārnaul and drove off local officials. Imperial troops from Delhi were then sent against them, and the movement was crushed with heavy losses. Persian chroniclers such as Khāfī Khān describe it, and modern historians usually read it as an agrarian as well as a religious rising.

events.title: Battle of Sālher
events.description: Sālher is a hill fort in the Baglān region, north-west of Nashik. In early 1672 a Mughal force under Ikhlās Khān and Bahlol Khān came to relieve its siege and met the Maratha armies of Moropant Pingle and Pratāprāv Gujar in the open. The Marathas, who had mostly won by raids, forts and ambushes, defeated the Mughals in set battle and captured large stores of horses, elephants and equipment. The victory raised Maratha prestige shortly before Śivājī's coronation in 1674.

events.title: Bhūṣaṇ composes the Śivarāj-bhūṣaṇ
events.description: Bhūṣaṇ was a Braj-bhāṣā court poet, traditionally the brother of the poets Cintāmaṇi and Matirām, who worked in the Rīti style of ornate Hindi poetry. His Śivarāj-bhūṣaṇ treats rhetoric by giving each figure of speech an illustration praising the Marāṭhā king Śivājī. He also wrote the Chatrasāl-daśaka, in praise of the Bundelā ruler Chatrasāl, and is said to have received honours from both kings. His verses celebrate heroic resistance to Mughal power in an ornate style.

events.title: Śivājī's coronation at Rāygaḍ
events.description: On 6 June 1674, at his mountain capital Rāygaḍ, Śivājī was consecrated Chatrapati, "lord of the umbrella", by the Vārāṇasī scholar Gāgā Bhaṭṭa with waters from the sacred rivers.¶The ceremony mattered because it was a claim. He was no longer a rebel chief or another king's officer, but a sovereign Hindu monarch, the first to be so crowned in centuries. He began a new era, issued his own coins, and commissioned a dictionary replacing Persian terms of government with Sanskrit ones. He called the project Hindavī Svarājya, self-rule of the people of this land.

events.title: Aṣṭa Pradhāna council
events.description: Śivājī governed through a council of eight ministers, each with a defined department: the Peśvā (prime minister), Amātya (finance), Saciva (records), Mantrī (intelligence and household), Senāpati (army), Sumanta (foreign affairs), Nyāyādhīśa (chief justice) and Paṇḍitarāv (religious affairs and charity). Offices were paid in cash, not in hereditary land, and all but the last two ministers were expected to lead troops. The titles deliberately replaced the Persian terms used by the sultanates.

events.title: Bhadrācala Rāmadāsu's Rāma kīrtanas
events.description: Kancherla Gopanna, later called Bhadrācala Rāmadāsu, served as tax officer at Bhadrācalam under the Golkonda sultan Abul Hasan Tana Shah. Tradition says that he spent revenue funds on rebuilding the Rāma temple there, was imprisoned at Golkonda for around twelve years, and sang pleading songs to Rāma in his cell. Popular legend holds that Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa then repaid the money in coin and the Sultan freed him. His Telugu kīrtanas and the Dāśarathī Śatakam are still sung widely.

gitaQuote.verse: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत । अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥ परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् । धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.

events.title: Guru Tegh Bahādur martyred
events.description: In 1675 a group of Kashmiri Paṇḍits, facing forced conversion under the Mughal governor, sought the help of the ninth Sikh Guru at Ānandpur. He told them to say they would convert if he did.¶Summoned to Delhi, he refused. His companions were tortured to death before his eyes: one sawn in two, one boiled, one burned. He was beheaded in Chāndnī Chowk on 11 November. Sikh tradition honours him as Hind-dī-cādar, "the shield of India", a man who died for the religious freedom of people of another faith.

events.title: Śivājī's Dakṣiṇa Digvijaya
events.description: In 1677 Śivājī marched south with a large army in his one long campaign far from home. He first signed an alliance with the Qutb Shāh of Golkonda, whose Hindu ministers Madanna and Akkanna supported him, and on the way worshipped at the Śiva temple of Śrīśaila. He then took the great fortress of Jiñjī and the fort of Vellore in the Tamil country. Jiñjī proved its worth twelve years later, when it sheltered the Maratha government through an eight-year siege.

events.title: Sambhājī's defection and return
events.description: Śivājī's eldest son Sambhājī quarrelled with his father and in 1678 went over to the Mughal commander Diler Khān, a shocking break for the young kingdom. Little came of the arrangement, since he was uneasy among the Mughals and escaped back to Panhāḷā in 1679, the year before Śivājī died. His return made him the heir, though disputes in the court followed Śivājī's death, and the episode left an impression of an impulsive prince who would later face the full Mughal assault.

events.title: Aurangzeb reimposes the jizya
events.description: The jizya was a tax on non-Muslims under Islamic law, which Akbar had abolished in 1564. In April 1679 Aurangzeb brought it back. When Hindus of Delhi crowded the road to the mosque to petition him, elephants were driven through them. A letter sent in Śivājī's name reminded the emperor that Akbar, Jahāngīr and Shāh Jahān had ruled without it, and that God is the Lord of all people, not of Muslims only.

events.title: Durgādās Rāṭhoṛ rescues the infant Ajīt Singh
events.description: Mahārājā Jasvant Singh of Mārwāṛ died in December 1678 with no surviving son; a posthumous son, Ajīt Singh, was born months later. Aurangzeb occupied Jodhpur and meant to raise the infant in his own household. Durgādās Rāṭhoṛ and a small band cut their way out of Delhi with the child in July 1679 and hid him in the Arāvalī hills. The Rāṭhoṛs then fought the Mughals for nearly thirty years, until Ajīt Singh entered Jodhpur in 1707.

events.title: Temples of Khaṇḍelā, Jodhpur and Udaipur razed
events.description: The Maāsir-i-ʿĀlamgīrī, the official chronicle of Aurangzeb's reign, records that in 1679 the emperor ordered the demolition of temples at Khaṇḍelā, and that temples in Jodhpur and Udaipur were also destroyed during the Rajput war that followed the death of Jaswant Singh and the succession dispute. The chronicle gives figures that run into the hundreds. Historians discuss the motives, which included politics and the conflict with Mārwāṛ and Mewar, as well as religious policy.

events.title: Rāj Singh of Mewar resists Aurangzeb
events.description: When Aurangzeb seized Mārwāṛ, Mahārāṇā Rāj Singh of Mewar took the Rāṭhoṛs' side; he had already sheltered the image of Śrīnāthajī from Mughal pressure and protested the jizya. The emperor invaded in 1680. The Rajputs withdrew into the hills and raided his supply lines. The Maāsir-i-ʿĀlamgīrī records the destruction of about 170 temples around Udaipur and 63 at Chittor. The war ended inconclusively in 1681, after Aurangzeb's own son Akbar rebelled and joined the Rajputs.

events.title: Death of Chatrapati Śivājī
events.description: Śivājī died at Rāygaḍ on 3 April 1680 after a short illness, aged fifty. He left a compact kingdom along the western hills and coast, with outposts in the Tamil country, some three hundred forts, a navy and a full treasury. He had forbidden his soldiers to harm women, mosques or holy books, a rule even hostile chroniclers such as Khāfī Khān acknowledged. Within months his heirs faced the entire Mughal army.

events.title: Paramānanda composes the Śivabhārata
events.description: The Śivabhārata is a Sanskrit epic about the life of Śivājī, written by the poet Paramānanda, also known as Kavīndra Paramānanda, who is said to have composed it at Śivājī's court. It describes his campaigns in the form of a mahākāvya, in the style of the older Sanskrit epics, and is used by historians as a near-contemporary account of the Marāṭhā ruler, though with the usual praise of a court poet. Its Sanskrit form shows how a new Hindu kingdom sought a classical literary voice.

events.title: Pahāṛī and Kiśangaṛh painting schools
events.description: Pahāṛī painting is the name for the schools of the Himalayan foothills, including Basohlī, Guler and Kāṅgṛā, which flourished from the seventeenth to the nineteenth centuries. Their artists painted episodes of the Gīta Govinda and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, and portraits and love scenes in fine line and bright colour. Nainsukh, born in Guler, worked at the court of Rājā Balwant Singh of Jasroṭā in the mid-eighteenth century and made intimate portraits of his patron. Kiśangaṛh in Rajasthan developed its own elongated style, famous for the Bani Thani figure.

events.title: Rāmadāsa and Hanumān worship in Maharashtra
events.description: In Maharashtra the saint Samartha Rāmadāsa (1608–1681) is said to have installed eleven Hanumān (Māruti) images in temples, linking devotion with strength, discipline and service, and gymnasiums were commonly attached to such shrines. His movement helped make Māruti a protector deity in the region. In north India, Hanumān devotion grew with Rāma-bhakti, and the Hanumān Cālīsā, a forty-verse hymn attributed to Tulsīdās, became among the most widely recited hymns to the deity. Hanumān came to be regarded as a protector and a model of devotion.

events.title: Sambhājī crowned as Chatrapati
events.description: After a brief succession struggle, Śivājī's elder son Sambhājī was crowned in January 1681. He was learned in Sanskrit and wrote the Budhabhūṣaṇa on statecraft. For nine years he fought on every side at once: the Mughals inland, the Siddīs of Janjirā on the coast, and the Portuguese at Goa. Aurangzeb, who had come south to finish him, captured no major Maratha stronghold during Sambhājī's reign.

events.title: Samartha Rāmadāsa's samādhi
events.description: Samartha Rāmadāsa died at the fort of Sajjangaḍ near Sātārā in 1681. He had walked across India for twelve years as a young man, and what he saw of its condition shaped his teaching: devotion to Rāma joined with strength, discipline and effort. He founded monasteries and hundreds of Hanumān shrines with gymnasiums. Tradition makes him Śivājī's guru; historians date their meeting late in the king's life. His Dāsabodha is a practical manual for living well.

events.title: Aurangzeb marches to the Deccan
events.description: In 1681 Aurangzeb left north India for the Deccan with the imperial court, treasury and an army of several hundred thousand. He meant to destroy the Marathas and the two remaining sultanates in a few seasons. He never returned. The campaign lasted twenty-six years, emptied the treasury, and left the north ungoverned. A moving city of tents thirty miles around followed him until his death there in 1707.

events.title: Sambhājī's Goa campaign
events.description: The Portuguese at Goa had helped the Mughals. In late 1683 Sambhājī invaded, defeated the Viceroy's army at Ponda and came within a river's width of the city of Goa. The Viceroy is said to have opened the tomb of St Francis Xavier and laid his staff of office in the saint's hands. A Mughal army entering the Koṅkaṇa forced Sambhājī to withdraw. The Marathas kept much of the surrounding territory.

events.title: Bijapur and Golkonda annexed
events.description: The two Shia sultanates of the Deccan had survived two centuries. Aurangzeb besieged Bijapur in 1685–86 and starved it out. Golkonda's fortress held for eight months in 1687 until a gate was opened by treachery; its Brahmin ministers Madanna and Akkanna had been murdered the year before. With both gone, the Mughal empire reached its greatest extent, and the Marathas stood alone.

events.title: Newtonian Principia: 3 Laws of Motion & Gravitation
events.description: Sir Isaac Newton publishes Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, unifying celestial astronomy and terrestrial mechanics through differential calculus, three laws of motion (F=ma), and the inverse-square law of universal gravitation. Establishes the classical 3D Euclidean deterministic universe.

events.title: Rāṇī Maṅgammāḷ of Madurai
events.description: Rāṇī Maṅgammāḷ, the widow of Cokkanātha Nāyaka of Madurai, governed the kingdom as regent for her grandson from about 1689 until 1704. She is remembered for building roads, avenue trees, choultries for travellers and temples, and for maintaining her state through negotiations with the Mughals and neighbouring powers. Tamil tradition praises her administration, and several public works carry her name.

gitaQuote.verse: पिताहमस्य जगतो माता धाता पितामहः । वेद्यं पवित्रमोंकार ऋक्साम यजुरेव च ॥ गतिर्भर्ता प्रभुः साक्षी निवासः शरणं सुहृत् । प्रभवः प्रलयः स्थानं निधानं बीजमव्ययम् ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ | vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛk sāma yajur eva ca || gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt | prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||
gitaQuote.translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer and the grandsire. I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. events.title: Kavi Kalaś, Sambhājī's counsellor
events.description: Kavi Kalaś was a poet and scholar from the Kanauj region who became a close adviser and minister to Sambhājī, who was himself a Sanskrit author. In 1689 the Mughals captured both men at Saṅgameśvar in the Koṅkaṇa. According to Marāṭhā chronicles and later accounts, they were taken to Aurangzeb's camp, tortured and executed. Kalaś is remembered in Maharashtra as a faithful companion who shared his king's fate, and he figures in later poetry and drama about Sambhājī's death.

events.title: Sambhājī captured and executed
events.description: Śivājī's son ruled for nine years while Aurangzeb himself came south with the whole Mughal army. In February 1689 Sambhājī was surprised and captured at Saṅgameśvar.¶Paraded in a fool's cap, he was offered his life if he surrendered his forts and accepted Islam. He refused and, by Maratha accounts, was tortured for weeks: blinded, his tongue cut out, and finally hacked to death on 11 March at Tulāpūr. Aurangzeb expected the Marathas to collapse. Instead the killing united them, and the war lasted another eighteen years.

events.title: Rājārām escapes to Jiñjī
events.description: After Sambhājī's execution in 1689, Rāygaḍ fell and his wife and young son Śāhū were captured. His brother Rājārām slipped out disguised as a pilgrim and travelled six hundred miles to the fortress of Jiñjī in the Tamil country. From there the Maratha government functioned for eight years while a Mughal army sat outside. Ministers left in Maharashtra, above all Rāmcandra Nīlakaṇṭh, kept the war alive at home.

events.title: Yesūbāī and Śāhū captured
events.description: When the Mughals took Rāygaḍ in 1689 after Sambhājī's execution, they captured his wife Yesubāī and their young son Śāhū, whom the Marāṭhās regarded as heir. Aurangzeb kept them in his camp as hostages. Śāhū was released in 1707, after Aurangzeb's death, and later became Chatrapati. Yesūbāī stayed with the Mughals for about thirty years and was freed only around 1719. Her long captivity gave the Mughal court leverage over Marāṭhā succession politics for two decades.

events.title: Santājī Ghorpaḍe and Dhanājī Jādhav
events.description: With no capital and no field army, the Marathas turned to fast cavalry warfare under two commanders. Santājī Ghorpaḍe and Dhanājī Jādhav struck Mughal columns, cut off convoys and vanished. Tradition tells that Santājī raided the emperor's own camp at night and cut the ropes of the royal tent. Mughal chroniclers such as Khāfī Khān record the terror he inspired, and a popular tale says that the Mughals' horses refused to drink for fear of seeing his reflection in the water.

events.title: Ekrām Khān's attack on Purī
events.description: In 1692, Ekrām Khān, the Mughal governor in Odisha, led an attack on Purī, where the Jagannātha temple was damaged in the campaign. The priests hid the images, according to tradition on islands in Chilika lake, and the temple was closed to worshippers for a period. It was reopened after Aurangzeb died in 1707. The episode is one of a series of upheavals that Purī experienced between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries, and the temple's records preserve the memory of the images' repeated rescue.

events.title: Kānhojī Āṅgre commands the Maratha navy
events.description: Kānhojī Āṅgre commanded the Maratha fleet from about 1698 to his death in 1729. From fortified harbours such as Vijayadurg and Kolābā his light, fast vessels took ships of any nation that sailed without his pass. English, Portuguese and Dutch expeditions against him, alone and together, all failed. The English called him a pirate, while in Maratha eyes he was an admiral enforcing his sovereign's claim over the coastal waters.

events.title: Fall of Jiñjī and Rājārām's return
events.description: After Sambhājī's death, his half-brother Rājārām fled south to the fortress of Jiñjī in Tamil country, where the Marāṭhā government held out under a long Mughal siege that lasted around eight years. The fort finally fell in 1698, and Rājārām escaped just before. He returned to Maharashtra and the Marāṭhā headquarters moved back to Sātārā. The long defence tied down Mughal armies far from the Deccan heartland, while Marāṭhā chiefs in the north grew strong through independent raiding.

events.title: Khālsā founded at Ānandpur
events.description: On Vaisākhī day 1699 at Ānandpur, Guru Gobind Singh asked a great gathering who would give his head. Five men of different castes came forward one by one. He initiated them with sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword, then asked them to initiate him. They became the Khālsā, "the pure", with the five symbols and the surname Singh. A community of devotees became an order of saint-soldiers sworn to resist tyranny.

events.title: Rāmabhadra Dīkṣita and the Tañjāvūr paṇḍits
events.description: Under the Marāṭhā ruler Śāhajī II of Tañjāvūr, scholars received land grants in the village of Śāhajirājapuram, today known as Tiruvisanallur, where he settled forty-six learned families. Rāmabhadra Dīkṣita, a poet and grammarian, belonged to this circle and wrote works such as the Jānakīparīṇaya, a play on Rāma's marriage. The court supported both Sanskrit scholarship and the arts, and the settlement shows how Marāṭhā rulers in the south sustained Vedic and śāstric learning.

events.title: Tārābāī leads the Marathas
events.description: Rājārām died in 1700. His widow Tārābāī, about twenty-five, placed their small son on the throne and ran the government and the war herself, moving from fort to fort. Under her the Marathas went on the offensive, raiding Mālwā and Gujarat while the emperor wasted years besieging hill forts they later bought back. The Mughal chronicler Khāfī Khān, no friend of hers, credits her with great powers of command.

events.title: Viśvanātha Cakravartī at Vṛndāvana
events.description: Viśvanātha Cakravartī, a Bengali who settled at Vṛndāvana around 1700, was the leading Gauḍīya teacher of his time. He wrote commentaries on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and the Gītā and many short works on the stages of devotion, in a warm and clear style. He settled a long dispute by arguing that the gopīs' love for Kṛṣṇa is that of lovers, not wives. Baladeva was his pupil.

gitaQuote.verse: अहमेवाक्षयः कालो धाताहं विश्वतोमुखः ॥ कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो लोकान्समाहर्तुमिह प्रवृत्तः ॥

gitaQuote.translation: I alone am inexhaustible, imperishable Time (Akṣaya Kāla), and I am the dispenser of destiny facing all directions... I am all-destroying Time, grown mighty to extinguish the worlds.
gitaQuote.source: Mahabharata (Bhishma Parva 35.32); Abhinavagupta Gītārtha-Saṁgraha

events.title: Sadāśiva Brahmendra, the silent avadhūta
events.description: Tradition says Sadāśiva Brahmendra was a learned and talkative student until his teacher asked whether he would ever learn to be quiet. He took a vow of silence and wandered naked along the Kāverī, taken by many for a madman. Stories tell of a hand cut off and restored without his noticing. His short Sanskrit songs on the Self, such as Sarvaṃ Brahmamayaṃ, are widely sung in Carnatic concerts, and his samādhi is at Nerūr near Karūr.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Tāyumāṉavar's Tamil hymns
events.description: Tāyumāṉavar served as a minister to the Nāyaka of Tiruchirappalli before renouncing the world. His 1,454 Tamil hymns speak of God in the language of a longing child and insist that the Vedānta of the Upaniṣads and the Śaiva Siddhānta of the Tamil south reach the same silence. His prayer that all beings may live in bliss is among the best-loved lines in Tamil.

events.title: Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa and Pāṇinian grammar
events.description: Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa, a Maharashtrian at Vārāṇasī, wrote some forty works and was among the last great Pāṇinian grammarians. His Paribhāṣenduśekhara explains the rules of interpretation that govern the grammar itself, and is still a standard text of the traditional course. He is said to have declined an invitation to Jai Singh's horse sacrifice because he had vowed never to leave Kāśī.

events.title: Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā composed in Bengal
events.description: The Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā, composed in Bengal around 1700, is a dialogue in which the sage Gheraṇḍa teaches "the yoga of the pot", treating the body as a vessel to be fired hard. It has seven stages: cleansing, posture, seals, withdrawal, breath, meditation and absorption. It describes thirty-two postures, more than any earlier text, which is why modern yoga teachers consult it.

events.title: Kāśī's paṇḍit assemblies on dharma
events.description: When a question of religious law could not be settled locally, such as a disputed adoption, a return from overseas, or a caste's ritual status, it was sent to Vārāṇasī. There the leading scholars of every region met in the Muktimaṇḍapa hall of the Viśvanātha temple and issued a signed ruling. Such rulings were accepted from Nepal to the far south, the nearest thing Hinduism had to a court of appeal.

events.title: Śāhjī II's Maratha court at Tañjāvūr
events.description: Śivājī's half-brother founded a Maratha kingdom at Tañjāvūr in 1674. Under Śāhjī II, around 1700, its court wrote in Marathi, Telugu, Sanskrit and Tamil at once, and the king himself composed operas. He settled forty-six scholars in a village named for him. His successors built up the Sarasvatī Mahal, a palace library that now holds some fifty thousand manuscripts and is one of the oldest libraries in Asia.

events.title: Upaniṣad Brahmayogin's Upaniṣad commentaries
events.description: Upaniṣad Brahmayogin, also called Rāmacandrendra, was a scholar-monk of Kāñcīpuram who is credited with writing commentaries on all 108 Upaniṣads listed in the Muktikā canon, including many late and sectarian ones. His commentary is notable because it covered texts that had rarely been commented on before, and it forms the main basis for the standard Adyar Library editions. He also is said to have written on the Rāmāyaṇa and the Vedānta. His approach reads all the Upaniṣads in an Advaitic sense.

events.title: Vāsudeva Dīkṣita's Bālamanoramā
events.description: Vāsudeva Dīkṣita of Tañjāvūr wrote the Bālamanoramā, a commentary on the Siddhāntakaumudī of Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita, which is a reorganised version of Pāṇini's grammar. events.title: Pichvāī paintings of Nāthdvārā
events.description: Pichvāī are large painted or printed cloth hangings that hang behind the image of Śrīnāthjī, a form of the child Kṛṣṇa, in the temple at Nāthdvārā in Rajasthan, the main seat of the Puṣṭi Mārga. Artists of the town made them for different seasons and festivals, such as the autumn festival of Śarad Pūrṇimā, showing scenes of Kṛṣṇa's life and nature. They developed in the 17th and 18th centuries and are still made, and are one of the best known arts of the Puṣṭi tradition.

events.title: Sāhibzādās martyred at Sirhind
events.description: In December 1704 the Guru's family was separated in the flight from Ānandpur. His two elder sons, eighteen and fourteen, died fighting at Camkaur. The younger two, Zorāwar Singh, nine, and Fateh Singh, six, were betrayed to the governor of Sirhind, who offered them their lives for conversion. They refused and were bricked into a wall alive. Their grandmother died on hearing it. India now marks 26 December as Vīr Bāl Divas.

events.title: Tranquebar mission prints Tamil
events.description: Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg, a German Lutheran sent by the Danish king, landed at Tranquebar on the Tamil coast in 1706. He learned Tamil well, set up a press, and printed a Tamil New Testament in 1715. To understand the people he corresponded with Hindu scholars and wrote a careful account of their gods and worship. His superiors in Europe refused to publish it, saying his task was to root out heathenism, not spread it.

events.title: Death of Aurangzeb
events.description: Aurangzeb died at Ahmadnagar on 3 March 1707, aged eighty-eight, having ruled for forty-nine years. Letters attributed to his last days are full of regret: "I came alone and I go as a stranger. I do not know who I am, nor what I have been doing." He asked for a plain grave paid for from caps he had sewn. Within fifty years the empire he had stretched to its limit was a name only.

events.title: Śāhū's release and the Battle of Kheḍ
events.description: Śāhū, Sambhājī's son, had grown up a prisoner in the Mughal camp. Released in 1707 in the hope of dividing the Marathas, he was challenged by his aunt Tārābāī. At Kheḍ her general Dhanājī Jādhav went over to him, and he was crowned at Sātārā in 1708. Tārābāī's line kept a separate throne at Kolhāpur. Śāhū ruled for forty-two years and left the work of government to his Peśvās.

events.title: Savāī Jai Singh and Ajīt Singh retake their capitals
events.description: After Aurangzeb died in 1707, the Mughal state was weakened by succession wars. In 1708 the Rajput rulers Savāī Jai Singh of Āmer and Ajīt Singh of Mārwāṛ, who had been kept out of their lands, re-took their capitals and expelled the Mughal garrisons, with help from Durgādās Rāṭhoṛ and others, and later the support of the Mewar ruler Amar Singh II. Their success confirmed the shift of authority to regional powers.

events.title: Guru Granth Sāhib declared Guru
events.description: Guru Gobind Singh, wounded by an assassin at Nāndeḍ on the Godāvarī in October 1708, declared that there would be no human Guru after him. Authority would rest in the scripture, the Granth, and in the community, the Panth. The book holds the hymns of six Gurus together with those of Hindu and Muslim saints such as Kabīr, Nāmdev, Ravidās and Farīd, arranged by musical mode.

events.title: Bandā Singh Bahādur takes Sirhind
events.description: Mādho Dās was a Vaiṣṇava ascetic living by the Godāvarī when Guru Gobind Singh met him in 1708 and sent him north as Bandā, "the servant". He raised an army of peasants in Punjab, took Sirhind in 1710 and executed the governor who had killed the Guru's sons. He struck coins and gave the land to those who tilled it. Captured in 1715, he was tortured to death in Delhi with several hundred followers.

events.title: Puruṣottama writes the Prasthānaratnākara
events.description: Puruṣottama (1668–1725) was a leading thinker of the Śuddhādvaita school, the "pure non-dualism" taught by Vallabhācārya and followed in the Puṣṭimārga devotional tradition. Working in Surat, he wrote the Prasthānaratnākara, a large commentary-based work that defends the school's reading of the Brahma Sūtra, Upaniṣads, Gītā and Bhāgavata against rival Vedāntins, particularly Advaita. His arguments made him the school's most important dialectician. His work gave the Puṣṭimārga a philosophical foundation alongside its devotion to Kṛṣṇa.

events.title: Bāḷājī Viśvanāth becomes Peśvā
events.description: Bāḷājī Viśvanāth Bhaṭ came from Śrīvardhan on the Koṅkaṇa coast and rose as a revenue official. In the civil war between Śāhū and Tārābāī he won over the admiral Kānhojī Āṅgre by negotiation when force had failed. Śāhū made him Peśvā in 1713. He rebuilt the kingdom's finances and its alliances with the great Maratha families, and his office passed to his son, then his grandson, making the Peśvās hereditary rulers in all but name.

events.title: Rudra Siṃha and Śiva Siṃha of Assam
events.description: The Ahom kings, who had arrived in Assam from the east in the thirteenth century, gradually adopted Hindu religious practice. Rudra Siṃha (1696 to 1714) and his son Śiva Siṃha (1714 to 1744) supported brāhmaṇas and the Śākta tradition, with Śiva Siṃha under the influence of a Bengali Śākta guru. The Śivadol, a tall Śiva temple, and the Devīdol and Viṣṇudol were built at Śivasāgar in about 1734, under Queen Ambikā. The Ahoms ruled until 1826.

events.title: Manipur adopts Vaiṣṇavism
events.description: Vaiṣṇava influence reached the Meitei kings of Manipur from the seventeenth century, beginning with the reign of Khāgemba. Under Garīb Nivāz, who ruled in the early eighteenth century, the Rāmānandī form of Vaiṣṇavism was adopted as the state religion in 1717 through the teacher Śāntidās Gosāi. Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism, associated with Caitanya, later became dominant under Bhāgyacandra in the later eighteenth century. The Meitei traditional religion continued alongside it, and Manipur remains a notable Vaiṣṇava region in the north-east.

events.title: Maratha sanads from Delhi
events.description: In 1719 Bāḷājī Viśvanāth led a Maratha army to Delhi in alliance with the Sayyid brothers, the king-makers of the court. He returned with three imperial grants: recognition of Śivājī's home territory as Maratha, and the right to collect a quarter (cauth) and a further tenth (sardeśmukhī) of the revenue of the six Mughal provinces of the Deccan. Śāhū's mother came home with him after thirty years as a captive.

events.title: Govindadeva enshrined at Jaipur
events.description: When Aurangzeb's temple demolitions began, the priests of Vṛndāvana took the image of Govindadeva west for safety, about 1670. After years of moving it came to the Kacchavāha kingdom, where Sawāī Jai Singh II housed it in his gardens and, after the founding of Jaipur, in the royal palace complex. Jai Singh declared Govinda the true king of Jaipur and ruled in his name. Other Vaiṣṇava orders there challenged whether the Bengali Gauḍīyas were a legitimate tradition at all, since they had no commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, a challenge later answered by Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.

events.title: Bājīrāv I becomes Peśvā
events.description: Bājīrāv was nineteen when King Śāhū made him Peśvā in 1720 over the heads of older men. He argued in council that the Mughal empire was a rotten tree: "strike at the trunk and the branches will fall of themselves."¶He is traditionally credited with some forty battles and no defeats. His method was speed: light cavalry carrying no baggage, living off the land, covering great distances in a day and appearing where no one expected. He took Mālwā and Bundelkhand, rode to the walls of Delhi in 1737, and made Pune the centre of Maratha power. He died of fever on campaign at thirty-nine.

events.title: Jāṭ kingdom of Bharatpur
events.description: The Jāṭ farmers south of Delhi had been in revolt since Aurangzeb's time. Badan Singh made them a state, and his son Sūraj Mal made it a kingdom stretching from Delhi to Āgrā, with the water-palaces of Ḍīg and the mud-walled fort of Bharatpur that later beat off a British siege. He was known as a shrewd and frugal ruler. In 1761 he sheltered and fed the Maratha survivors of Pānīpat.

events.title: Hyderabad and Awadh break away
events.description: As Mughal power weakened after Aurangzeb's death, provincial governors began to act independently. Nizām-ul-Mulk Āsaf Jāh founded the Hyderabad state in the Deccan in 1724 after defeating a rival Mughal governor, and Saʿādat Khān had made Awadh a hereditary governorship from 1722. Both kept nominal respect for the emperor in Delhi but ruled their territories independently. Hyderabad lasted until 1948 and Awadh until 1856.

events.title: Jagajīvan Dās and Satnāmīs of Awadh
events.description: In the eighteenth century a number of sects arose across north India following Kabīr's teaching of a formless God, the true Name, and the equality of castes. Jagajīvan Dās founded one group of Satnāmīs in Awadh, Caraṇdās another at Delhi, where his women disciples Sahajobāī and Dayābāī wrote poetry, and Garībdās one in Haryana. Most drew their following from farmers and artisans.

events.title: Jaipur founded by Jai Singh
events.description: Savāī Jai Singh II of Amber, a mathematician and astronomer, laid out a new capital in the plain in 1727. With the Bengali scholar Vidyādhara he planned it on a grid of nine squares, as the Vāstu texts prescribe, with wide straight streets, uniform shopfronts and the palace at the centre. It was one of the first planned cities of early modern India. The pink wash came later, for a royal visit in 1876.

events.title: Battle of Pālkheḍ
events.description: In 1727–28 the Nizām of Hyderabad invaded Maharashtra to set up a rival king. Bājīrāv did not meet him. He rode away north into the Nizām's own lands, plundering as he went, and drew the heavy Hyderabad army after him. Then he doubled back, cut it off from water at Pālkheḍ near Aurangābād, and forced a surrender without a pitched battle. Field Marshal Montgomery called it a masterpiece of strategic mobility.

events.title: Marathas win Mālwā at Amjherā
events.description: Mālwā, the plateau between the Deccan and the Gaṅgā plain, was the gateway to the north. In November 1728 Bājīrāv's younger brother Cimājī Āpā crossed the Narmadā and at Amjherā defeated and killed the Mughal governor Giridhar Bahādur. Maratha officers named Holkar, Śinde and Pavār were posted to collect revenue there. Their descendants became the rulers of Indore, Gwalior and Dhār.

events.title: Bājīrāv rescues Chatrasāl
events.description: Chatrasāl had freed Bundelkhand from the Mughals over fifty years. At nearly eighty he was besieged by the Mughal general Muhammad Khān Bangash and wrote to Bājīrāv, comparing himself to the elephant in the Purāṇa caught by a crocodile and calling on Viṣṇu. Bājīrāv arrived by forced marches in 1729 and trapped Bangash. Chatrasāl adopted him as a son and left him a third of his kingdom, including Jhānsī.

events.title: Bhāskararāya Makhin and Śrīvidyā
events.description: Bhāskararāya, born in Maharashtra and settled in the Tañjāvūr country, was the greatest scholar of Śrīvidyā, the worship of the Goddess as Lalitā Tripurasundarī through her mantra and the Śrīcakra diagram. His commentary on her thousand names explains each one through grammar, Vedānta and Tantra. He showed that tantric worship of the Goddess stands on the Veda, and made a tradition once kept secret respectable among the orthodox.

events.title: Śanivār Vāḍā begun
events.description: Bājīrāv moved the Peśvā's seat from Sāsvaḍ to the small town of Pune and laid the foundation of a palace on a Saturday, hence Śanivār Vāḍā, in 1730. It grew into a seven-storeyed fortified complex with fountains and halls, the centre of Maratha power for eighty-five years. A fire in 1828 destroyed everything but the stone walls and the great Delhi Gate, which still stand.

events.title: Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa's Govinda Bhāṣya
events.description: Challenged at Jaipur to show that the Gauḍīya school had a Vedāntic foundation, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa, an Odia scholar of that school, composed a commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, according to tradition in a matter of days and at the direction of Govinda himself. It sets out acintya-bhedābheda: the soul and the world are at once one with God and different from him, in a way that cannot be reasoned out. It gave Caitanya's school its place among the Vedāntas.

gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.

events.title: Khejarlī sacrifice of the Biśnoīs
events.description: The Biśnoīs of the Rajasthan desert follow twenty-nine rules given by their founder in 1485, among them never to cut a green tree. In 1730 the Mahārājā of Jodhpur sent men to fell khejṛī trees at Khejarlī for lime kilns. A woman, Amṛtā Devī, wrapped her arms around a trunk and was cut down with it; her three daughters followed, and then 359 others. The king stopped the felling and forbade it for ever.

events.title: Ghṛṣṇeśvara and Bhīmaśaṅkara restored
events.description: Two of the twelve jyotirliṅgas of Maharashtra were rebuilt by Maratha patrons. At Ghṛṣṇeśvara, beside the Ellora caves, the temple was rebuilt by Śivājī's grandfather Mālojī Bhosale and again in red stone by Ahilyābāī Holkar. At Bhīmaśaṅkara, in the forested hills where the Bhīmā rises, Nānā Phaḍnavīs built the present spire and hall. The Portuguese bell there was captured at Vasai in 1739.

events.title: Treaty of Vārṇā
events.description: Since 1707 two branches of Śivājī's family had each claimed the Maratha throne. After the Kolhāpur ruler was defeated in battle, the Treaty of Vārṇā in 1731 divided the inheritance: Śāhū at Sātārā kept the north and the leadership of the confederacy, and his cousin Sambhājī II kept the lands south of the Vārṇā river around Kolhāpur. Kolhāpur remained a separate state until 1949.

events.title: Malhārrāv Holkar and Rāṇojī Śinde in Mālwā
events.description: After the Marathas gained rights over Mālwā in the 1730s under the Peshwa Bājīrāv I, he assigned its administration to trusted commanders. Malhārrāv Holkar established the house of Indore, and Rāṇojī Śinde (Scindia) based his family at Ujjain and later Gwalior. Pilājī Gāikvāḍ took Baroda in Gujarat. These Maratha houses ruled their territories as nearly independent states, and survived into the British period.

events.title: Peshwa's campaign against Janjirā
events.description: Janjirā is an island fortress off the Koṅkaṇa coast held by the Siddīs, African-descended commanders who served the Deccan Sultanates and later the Mughals. Despite several Marāṭhā attempts, it resisted capture. In 1733 Peshwa Bājīrāv's campaign pressed the Siddīs hard and freed Rāygaḍ from their occupation. Janjirā itself stayed in Siddī hands, but the campaign cut their power on the mainland. The contest over the Koṅkaṇa coast shaped Marāṭhā naval and fort policy for much of the century.

events.title: Jantar Mantar observatories
events.description: Jai Singh found that the astronomical tables in use did not match the sky. Brass instruments were too small and wore loose, so he built giant ones of stone: at Delhi about 1724, then at Jaipur, Ujjain, Vārāṇasī and Mathurā. The sundial at Jaipur is twenty-seven metres high and tells time to two seconds. He had European and Islamic works translated into Sanskrit and issued new tables. The Jaipur observatory is a World Heritage Site.

events.title: Jai Singh II performs the Aśvamedha
events.description: The Aśvamedha, the horse sacrifice of the Vedas, proclaims a king's sovereignty and is so costly and complex that few ever performed it. Savāī Jai Singh revived it at Jaipur in 1734 with scholars brought from across India, along with the Vājapeya. It is regarded as one of the last major performances of the rite. The act told the Mughal court, whose officer he still formally was, how he saw his own position.

events.title: Bhosales of Nāgpur
events.description: Raghujī Bhosale I received authority from Chatrapati Shāhū in the 1730s over Berar and the lands to the east, and ruled from Nāgpur from about 1734. He led expeditions into Bengal and Odisha, and by the 1750s the Marathas had taken Odisha from the Nawab of Bengal. He also brought the Gond kingdom of Deogarh under his control. The Bhosales of Nāgpur remained a major Maratha power until 1853.

events.title: Sivasagar Sivadol completed under the Ahoms
events.description: The Sivadol at Sivasagar in Assam was completed in 1734 by Bar Rājā Ambikā, the queen of the Ahom king Swargadeo Siva Siṃha (r. 1714–1744). Rising about 104 feet, it is described as the tallest Śiva temple tower in India. It stands beside the Viṣṇudol and the Devīdol, a Durgā temple, and the tank beside them was dug between 1731 and 1738.¶The Ahoms, a Tai people who entered the Brahmaputra valley in the thirteenth century, took on Hindu forms of worship over time, and the royal patronage of the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava and Śākta temples at Sivasagar shows the result. The complex, one of the major monuments of Ahom Assam, also reflects the prominence of royal women, such as Ambikā, in the religious life of the kingdom.

events.title: Mahākāleśvara temple rebuilt
events.description: The Mahākāla temple at Ujjain was destroyed by Sultan Iltutmish in 1235 and its liṅga thrown into a pond. When the Marathas took Mālwā five centuries later, Rāmcandra Bābā Śeṇvī, minister of Rāṇojī Śinde, rebuilt it in 1734–36 and recovered the liṅga. He also revived the Siṃhastha, the Kumbha fair on the Śiprā. The Śindes kept Ujjain as their capital until 1810.

events.title: Bājīrāv at the gates of Delhi
events.description: In March 1737 the Mughal court believed Bājīrāv was hundreds of miles away. He covered the distance in about ten days with his cavalry and appeared outside Delhi. The emperor prepared to flee. Bājīrāv defeated the force sent out against him, stayed three days to make his point, and left. When the Nizām marched north to help the emperor, Bājīrāv surrounded him at Bhopal and made him cede Mālwā.

events.title: Treaty of Doraha Sarāī
events.description: In late 1737 the Peshwa Bājīrāv defeated the Nizām-ul-Mulk and Mughal forces near Bhopal. The settlement of January 1738 at Doraha Sarāī confirmed the result, with the Nizām agreeing that Mālwa and the lands between the Narmadā and Chambal would be handed to the Peśvā, together with a payment. This gave the Marāṭhās formal control of central India, shortly before Nādir Shāh invaded Delhi, and it signalled how far Mughal authority had declined.

events.title: Nādir Shāh sacks Delhi
events.description: Nādir Shāh of Persia defeated the Mughal army at Karnāl in February 1739 and entered Delhi. When a rumour of his death set off a riot, he ordered a massacre in which some twenty to thirty thousand townspeople died in a few hours. He left with the Peacock Throne, the Koh-i-Nūr diamond and treasure worth several years of the empire's revenue. Delhi's prestige never recovered, and the northwest lay open.

events.title: Vasai (Bassein) taken from the Portuguese
events.description: The Portuguese had held the coast north of Bombay since the 1530s, and under them Hindu temples had been pulled down and public worship forbidden. In 1737 the Marathas attacked. Cimājī Āpā besieged the fortress of Vasai for months in 1739, mining its walls, and it surrendered in May. The garrison was allowed to march out with honours. Local families who had fled returned and rebuilt their shrines.

events.title: Death of Bājīrāv and rise of Nānāsāheb
events.description: Bājīrāv died of a sudden fever on 28 April 1740 beside the Narmadā, aged thirty-nine, while on campaign. His son Bāḷājī, called Nānāsāheb, succeeded him at nineteen. He was an administrator more than a soldier. Under him Maratha armies reached Bengal, Odisha, Punjab and the Tamil country, and after King Śāhū died in 1749 the Peśvā became head of the state openly. Pune grew into a capital of a hundred thousand people.

events.title: Peśvā patronage of the Aṣṭavināyaka temples
events.description: Eight temples around Pune each hold a naturally formed image of Gaṇeśa: Morgāv, Siddhaṭek, Pālī, Mahāḍ, Theūr, Leṇyādri, Ojhar and Rāñjaṇgāv. The Peśvās, whose family deity was Gaṇeśa, rebuilt most of them in the eighteenth century and visited constantly; Mādhavrāv chose to die at Theūr. Visiting all eight in sequence, beginning and ending at Morgāv, is the most popular pilgrimage in Maharashtra.

events.title: Battle of Colachel
events.description: The Dutch East India Company controlled the pepper trade of Kerala. When the young king of Travancore, Mārtāṇḍa Varmā, began absorbing his neighbours, a Dutch force landed at Colachel in 1741. His army surrounded it, a shot blew up its powder store, and it surrendered on 10 August. It was among the first defeats of a European power by an Asian state. A captured officer, Eustachius De Lannoy, trained Travancore's army for the next thirty-six years.

events.title: Battle of Gaṅgvānā
events.description: At Gaṅgvānā in Rajasthan, in 1741 by the usual dating, a small body of Rāṭhoṛ cavalry under Bakht Singh of Nāgaur confronted a larger force of the Kachwāhā army of Jaipur backed by Mughal troops. It is told as a famous charge in which a thousand horsemen took on a much larger army and won, and it is celebrated in Rajasthani bardic memory, though details vary. The battle belongs to the long contest between Jaipur and Jodhpur over succession and territory in the eighteenth century.

events.title: Maratha raids on Bengal
events.description: From 1741 to 1751 Raghujī Bhosale of Nāgpur sent cavalry into Bengal every dry season to force payment of tribute. The raiders, called bargīs, burned and plundered so widely that a Bengali lullaby still warns children of them. The Nawāb finally ceded Odisha and an annual payment. In Odisha the Marathas restored the endowments of the Jagannātha temple at Purī and managed it for fifty years.

events.title: Sikh massacres of 1746 and 1762
events.description: With the Mughal governors and then the Afghans hunting them, the Sikhs lived for decades in jungle and desert. In 1746 some seven thousand were killed in a drive near Lahore, the "lesser holocaust". In February 1762 Ahmad Shāh Abdālī caught a column of families on the move and killed perhaps twenty thousand in a day, the "greater". Within months the survivors had retaken Amritsar. By 1765 they held Lahore.

events.title: Mārtāṇḍa Varmā's Tṛppaṭidānam
events.description: On 3 January 1750 Mārtāṇḍa Varmā came to the temple of Padmanābha at Tiruvanantapuram, laid his sword on the steps before the deity, and gave him the kingdom. He received it back as a trustee, with the title Padmanābhadāsa, "servant of Padmanābha". Every ruler of Travancore after him reigned as the deity's deputy. It made his conquests sacred and, in principle, bound the king to answer to God for his rule.

events.title: Parvatī hill temples, Pune
events.description: Parvatī is a hill on the southern edge of Pune. Nānāsāheb Peśvā built a temple to Śiva on its summit in 1749, with shrines to Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, Sūrya and the Goddess. From here he is said to have watched for news of Pānīpat, and here he died. Each year the Peśvās gave gifts to tens of thousands of learned brāhmaṇas who came from all over India to be examined, which made Pune a capital of Sanskrit studies.

events.title: Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha and Bhajana Sampradāya
events.description: In the Kāverī delta a movement grew up teaching that in the present age, singing the names of God in company is the whole of religion. Bodhendra, a head of the Kāñcī monastery, wrote in its defence; Śrīdhara Ayyāvāḷ and Sadguru Svāmī of Marudānallūr gave it a fixed order of service drawing on songs in Sanskrit, Marathi, Telugu and Tamil. Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha's opera on Kṛṣṇa's life supplied many of them.

events.title: Sāṅgolā agreement makes Peśvā supreme
events.description: After the Chatrapati Śāhū died in 1749, the question of who would rule was settled by an arrangement at Sāṅgolā in 1750. By this settlement the Peśvā, hereditary chief minister, became the effective head of the Marāṭhā confederacy, while the Chatrapati at Sātārā became a figurehead. The shift had been developing under Bājīrāv and Bālājī Bājīrāv, and the agreement made the Peśvā's position formal, with Pune as the real centre of power.

events.title: Rāmprasād Sen and Śākta songs of Bengal
events.description: Rāmprasād Sen, a clerk who wrote hymns in his employer's ledgers, created a new kind of Bengali devotional song addressed to Kālī. He scolds her like a neglected child, bargains, sulks, and surrenders. The fierce goddess of the cremation ground becomes Mā, a mother who must answer. His simple melody is still called by his name, and his songs prepared the ground for Rāmakṛṣṇa.

events.title: Marathas guard the Mughal throne
events.description: When the Afghan Ahmad Shāh Abdālī began invading from 1748, the Mughal emperor had no army able to stop him. By an agreement of 1752 the Marathas undertook to defend the empire against internal and foreign enemies, in return for the revenue of Punjab, Sindh and the Doab and the right to appoint governors. It made them the emperor's protectors, and it committed them to a war in the far north.

events.title: Bhāratcandra's Annadāmaṅgala completed
events.description: Bhāratcandra Rāy, court poet of the king of Kṛṣṇanagar, completed the Annadāmaṅgala in 1752. It praises the Goddess as Annapūrṇā, giver of food, and includes the love story of Vidyā and Sundar, told with a wit and polish new to Bengali. It closes the long tradition of maṅgala-kāvyas, narrative poems that told how a deity won worship on earth.

events.title: Śrīraṅgam besieged in Carnatic Wars
events.description: Śrīraṅgam, the great Viṣṇu temple on an island in the Kāverī, was caught up in the Carnatic Wars of the 1750s between the French and British East India companies and their Indian allies. In 1753 and 1754 armies fought around the temple, which served as a fortress, and the surrounding area was occupied by troops for a time. The episode shows that temples in this period were often treated as strategic places, and this temple's treasury and walls made it a point of military control.

events.title: Marāṭhā pressure on the Rajput states
events.description: The Marathas demanded tribute (chauth) from the Rajput states after the 1740s, and also intervened in their succession disputes, as in Jaipur after the death of Sawai Jai Singh in 1743. Rajputana's rulers resented the payments and the military pressure. In 1755 Jayappā Śinde was killed at Nāgaur by Rāṭhoṛ assassins. These tensions meant that Rajput rulers did not strongly support the Marathas at Pānīpat in 1761.

events.title: Tryambakeśvara temple rebuilt
events.description: Tryambakeśvara, where the Godāvarī rises near Nāsik, is one of the twelve jyotirliṅgas; its liṅga is a hollow holding three small ones for Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva. The earlier temple is reported to have been damaged under Aurangzeb. Nānāsāheb Peśvā began the present one of black basalt in 1755, and it was finished in 1786 at a recorded cost of 1.6 million rupees.

events.title: Ghāsīdās, founder of the Satnāmī movement
events.description: Ghāsīdās was born in 1756 into a Camār family in Chhattisgarh. After a period of solitude he began teaching that God is "satnām", the true name, without form; that images should not be worshipped; and that all people are equal. He forbade meat, alcohol and tobacco. A large part of the region's Dalit population followed him, and a university there bears his name.

events.title: Fall of Vijayadurg and Tuḷājī Āṅgre
events.description: The Āṅgre family were admirals commanding the Marāṭhā fleet along the Koṅkaṇa and harassing English, Portuguese and Dutch shipping. In 1756 the Peśvā allied with the English East India Company, whose squadron under Commodore William James attacked Vijayadurg, while Marāṭhā troops moved on land. Tuḷājī Āṅgre was captured and his fleet destroyed. Many historians regard this as a serious mistake, since it removed the main native naval force on the west coast and left the English with the sea to themselves.

events.title: Battle of Plassey
events.description: On 23 June 1757, in a mango grove at Plassey, Robert Clive with three thousand men faced the Nawāb of Bengal with fifty thousand. The outcome had been arranged beforehand: the Nawāb's commander Mīr Jaʿfar and the banker Jagat Seṭh had been bought, and most of the army never fought. The East India Company became king-maker in India's richest province, and its servants made fortunes.

events.title: Abdālī sacks Mathurā and Vṛndāvana
events.description: In early 1757 Abdālī sacked Delhi and sent his army to Mathurā with orders to spare nothing. It arrived during the Holī festival; for days pilgrims were killed and the Yamunā, wrote a Muslim eyewitness, ran red and then yellow. Vṛndāvana suffered the same. At Gokul several thousand Nāgā ascetics, naked and smeared with ash, fought the Afghans off. Cholera in his camp finally sent Abdālī home.

events.title: Durgā Pūjā becomes Bengal's great public festival
events.description: Autumn worship of Durgā was an old household rite of Bengal's landed families. After Plassey in 1757 the new rich of Calcutta, such as Rājā Nabakṛṣṇa Deb, made it a grand display to which Company officers were invited. In 1790 twelve friends at Guptipāṛā pooled money for a shared celebration, the first "bārovārī" pūjā. Public neighbourhood pūjās, open to all, grew from that.

events.title: Marathas at Attock
events.description: In 1758 a Maratha army under the Peśvā's brother Raghunāthrāv and Malhārrāv Holkar, with Sikh help, drove Abdālī's son out of Lahore and went on to take Attock on the Indus and, briefly, Peshawar. Maratha power now reached from the Tamil country to the Afghan frontier. The phrase "flags beyond Attock" became proverbial. The victory had cost more than it earned, and it brought Abdālī back.

events.title: Battle of Udgīr
events.description: In February 1760 at Udgīr the Peśvā's cousin Sadāśivrāv Bhāu destroyed the Nizām's army using a new corps of infantry and French-style artillery under Ibrāhīm Khān Gārdī. The Nizām surrendered territory and forts including Daulatābād. It was the height of Maratha power. Bhāu, now the hero of the hour, was given command of the army going north against Abdālī, with the same artillery.

events.title: Battle of the ākhāṛās at Haridvāra
events.description: The right to bathe first at the Kumbha was a matter of honour and of income, and the armed ascetic orders fought for it. At Haridvāra in 1760 Śaiva saṃnyāsīs and Vaiṣṇava vairāgīs fought a pitched battle; accounts speak of eighteen hundred or more dead. The Vaiṣṇava orders were kept from Haridvāra for years. The fixed order of procession used today was laid down under British administration to end such fights.

events.title: Third Battle of Pānīpat
events.description: On 14 January 1761 a Maratha army under Sadāśivrāv Bhāu, far from home and short of food after months of blockade, attacked the Afghan king Ahmad Shāh Abdālī and his Indian allies north of Delhi. French-trained artillery nearly won the morning; by afternoon the Maratha centre had broken.¶Estimates of the dead run to tens of thousands in the fighting and as many camp followers in the massacre after it. The Peśvā's son and cousin were among the dead, and the Peśvā himself died within months. Maratha power recovered within a decade, but some historians argue that the delay helped the East India Company establish itself in Bengal unchallenged.

events.title: Mādhavrāv I becomes Peśvā
events.description: The Peśvā died of grief months after Pānīpat, and his second son Mādhavrāv succeeded at sixteen. He faced an empty treasury, an invasion by the Nizām and a guardian uncle who wanted the office himself. In eleven years he settled all three, defeated Hyder Ali of Mysore, and sent armies north that recovered what had been lost. He was known for strict justice and for punishing his own officers.

events.title: Mahīpati completes the Bhaktavijaya
events.description: Mahīpati, a village accountant of Tāharābād, wrote the lives of the saints of Maharashtra and north India in Marathi verse; his Bhaktavijaya was completed in 1762. He collected written accounts and the stories told by pilgrims on the road to Paṇḍharpūr. Much of what is popularly told of Jñāneśvara, Nāmadeva, Cokhāmeḷā and Tukārāma comes through him, with miracle and fact told together.

events.title: Śyāmā Śāstrī born
events.description: Śyāmā Śāstrī, eldest of the three great Carnatic composers, was hereditary priest of the golden image of Kāmākṣī at Tañjāvūr, which his ancestors had carried south from Kāñcī for safety. His songs, of which only a limited number survive, are addressed to the Goddess as a child speaks to its mother. They are known for rhythmic subtlety. Unlike the other two he had few disciples, and his work was preserved largely by his family.

events.title: Battle of Rākṣasabhuvan
events.description: In 1763 the Nizām took advantage of the Maratha family quarrel to invade, and his troops burned Pune and desecrated its temples. Mādhavrāv, eighteen, caught his army crossing the Godāvarī at Rākṣasabhuvan on 10 August and destroyed the half that was still on the near bank. The Nizām gave up land worth eight million rupees a year. The battle established the young Peśvā's authority.

events.title: Sūraj Mal falls near Delhi
events.description: Sūraj Mal, the Jāṭ ruler of Bharatpur, built up a powerful state in the Mathurā-Āgrā region and supported the Marathas after Pānīpat. He was killed in December 1763 in a skirmish with the Rohilla troops of Najīb-ud-Daulah near Shāhdara, across the Yamunā from Delhi. His reign saw the building of forts and palaces at Bharatpur and Dīg. His son Javāhar Singh took up the struggle against Najīb.

events.title: Battle of Buxar
events.description: At Buxar on 22 October 1764 the Company's army under Hector Munro defeated the combined forces of the Mughal emperor, the Nawāb of Awadh and the deposed Nawāb of Bengal. Unlike Plassey it was a real battle. The next year the emperor granted the Company the dīvānī, the right to collect the revenues of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha. A trading company now legally ruled twenty million people.

events.title: Javāhar Singh's march on Delhi
events.description: In 1764, Javāhar Singh of Bharatpur marched on Delhi to avenge his father Sūraj Mal's death, and attacked the capital's surroundings. Jāṭ tradition says that he took the gates that Mughal forces had earlier carried from Chittor, from the Red Fort to Bharatpur, where they were set up in the Lohagaṛh fort. Historians treat the details of this tradition cautiously, but the gates are shown at Bharatpur.

events.title: Mādhavrāv's Karnāṭak campaigns
events.description: The Peśvā Mādhavrāv I led four expeditions into the Karnāṭak country between 1764 and 1772 against Hyder Ali, who had taken power in Mysore and was expanding northwards. Mādhavrāv forced Hyder to pay tribute and give up territory, and restored Marāṭhā influence in the south. This was part of his effort, after the disaster at Pāṇipat in 1761, to rebuild Marāṭhā strength. Ill with tuberculosis, he died young in 1772, and the later breakdown of Marāṭhā unity is often contrasted with his steady rule.

events.title: Moropant and Marathi paṇḍit poetry
events.description: Moropant of Bārāmatī retold the whole Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa in Marathi in the Sanskrit āryā metre; a saying has it that the well-turned āryā belongs to him alone. At the other end of society the śāhīrs, balladeers attached to the army, sang povāḍās, heroic ballads of battles such as Pānīpat and Siṃhagaḍ, and lāvaṇīs, songs of love and satire. Together they are the literature of the Peśvā age.

events.title: Hyder Ali invades Malabar
events.description: Hyder Ali of Mysore invaded Kerala in 1766; the Zamorin of Calicut set fire to his palace and died in it. Malabar tradition and later accounts record that under Hyder and then Tipu many temples were plundered and large numbers of Nāyars and brāhmaṇas were forcibly converted or fled south to Travancore, though historians debate the scale. In 1789 the priests of Guruvāyūr hid the main image underground and took the festival image to Ambalappuḻa until Tipu's defeat in 1792.

events.title: Ahilyābāī Holkar rules Indore
events.description: Widowed at twenty-nine, Ahilyābāī lost her father-in-law and her only son within the next dozen years. In 1767 she took charge of the Holkar state herself, moved the capital to Maheśvar on the Narmadā, and ruled for twenty-eight years.¶She heard petitions in open court every day and was known for refusing to seize the property of the heirless. Her private fortune went into building and repair at sacred places across India: the Viśvanātha temple at Kāśī, a shrine at Somanātha, ghāṭs, wells and rest-houses from the Himalaya to Rāmeśvaram. Contemporaries, Indian and British, wrote of her as a saint on the throne.
