events.title: Tyāgarāja born at Tiruvārūr
events.description: Tyāgarāja, born at Tiruvārūr in 1767, lived by collecting alms and singing to his household image of Rāma. He refused invitations and gifts from the king of Tañjāvūr, answering in a song that asks whether wealth or the nearness of Rāma gives happiness. He composed, tradition says, twenty-four thousand songs, of which about seven hundred survive, most in Telugu. An annual festival at his samādhi in Tiruvaiyāṟu draws thousands of musicians.

events.title: Pṛthvī Nārāyaṇ Shāh unifies Nepal
events.description: Pṛthvī Nārāyaṇ Shāh, king of the small hill state of Gorkhā, spent twenty-five years conquering the three rich Malla kingdoms of the Kathmandu valley, completing it in 1768–69. He described his country as a yam between two boulders, China and British India, and as the "true Hindustān", unpolluted by foreign rule. He expelled the Capuchin missionaries. His successors extended Nepal along the Himalaya.

events.title: Moāmarīā rebellion against the Ahoms
events.description: The Moāmarīā rebellion was a long uprising against the Ahom kings, led by followers of the Moāmarā sattra, a Vaiṣṇava order from the tradition of Aniruddhadeva. The Moāmarīās drew many peasants and low-ranking groups, who resented the burdens of the Ahom system and the privileges of higher groups. The rising, which began in 1769, captured the capital for a period and did great damage to Ahom authority. The kingdom weakened and by the early nineteenth century could not resist Burmese invasion.

events.title: Great Bengal famine of 1770
events.description: The rains failed in 1769. The Company, newly in control of Bengal's revenue, kept collecting the land tax and even raised it, and its servants traded in grain. About ten million people, a third of the population, died in 1770. Whole districts returned to jungle. The disaster brought the Company near bankruptcy, led Parliament to regulate it, and inspired the first novel of Indian nationalism a century later.

events.title: Saṃnyāsī and Fakir Rebellion
events.description: Armed bands of Hindu saṃnyāsīs and Muslim fakirs had long travelled through Bengal on pilgrimage, collecting dues from landholders. When the Company restricted them and the famine came, they turned to raiding its treasuries and factories, from 1763 to about 1800, sometimes defeating regular troops. Baṅkimcandra made their revolt the setting of his novel Ānandamaṭh in 1882, which gave India the song "Vande Mātaram".

events.title: Marāṭhā ghāṭs and temples at Vāī and Māhulī
events.description: Along the Kṛṣṇā river in Maharashtra, towns such as Vāī, near Sātārā, and Māhulī, now part of Sātārā, were given stone ghāṭs and temples by Marāṭhā sardārs and ministers, mainly in the 18th century. Vāī is sometimes known as Dakṣiṇa Kāśī, "the Kāśī of the south," because of its many temples on the riverbank, such as the Dholya Gaṇapati temple of 1762. The sites show how Marāṭhā patronage added to the sacred landscape of Maharashtra.

events.title: Shāh patronage of Paśupatinātha and Hanumān Ḍhokā
events.description: After Pṛthvī Nārāyaṇ Shāh unified Nepal in the 1760s, the Shāh kings made themselves protectors of its temples. Paśupatinātha, the Śiva temple at Kathmandu, and Hanumān Ḍhokā, the old royal palace named for a Hanumān image at its gate, were both important in the royal and religious life of the realm. Rulers repaired and endowed temples, and Śaiva worship was linked to the state's identity as a Hindu kingdom until recent times.

events.title: Raṇachoḍarāya temple built at Ḍākor
events.description: The present Raṇachoḍarāya temple at Ḍākor in Gujarat was begun in 1769–70, and the image was installed in it in 1770–71. Its builder was Gopāl Tāṃbvekar, a Deccan Brahmin from Pune and a devotee of Veṅkaṭeśa, to whom the Peśvā Mādhavrāv had granted Ḍākor. The image is a standing four-armed Viṣṇu who holds a small golden flute, and is worshipped as Kṛṣṇa.¶According to the Ḍākor-māhātmya, in 1151 the Rajput devotee Boḍāṇo took the deity from Dvārakā to Ḍākor, hiding it in the Gomatī tank from the pursuing priests. The legend ties the shrine to Dvārakā. The temple became one of Gujarat's major Vaiṣṇava pilgrimage centres, and an example of Maratha patronage of Vaiṣṇava shrines far from Maharashtra.

events.title: Mahādjī Śinde restores Shāh Ālam
events.description: The Mughal emperor Shāh Ālam II had lived for years as a pensioner of the British at Allahabad. In 1771 Mahādjī Śinde occupied Delhi, and in January 1772 the emperor returned to his capital under Maratha escort. Ten years after Pānīpat, the Marathas were again the power behind the throne. The British stopped the emperor's pension in reply.

events.title: Death of Mādhavrāv Peśvā
events.description: Mādhavrāv died of tuberculosis at the Gaṇeśa temple of Theūr on 18 November 1772, aged twenty-seven. His wife Ramābāī died on his pyre. The historian Grant Duff, a British officer who had fought the Marathas, wrote that the plains of Pānīpat were not more fatal to their empire than the early end of this excellent prince. No later Peśvā commanded the same obedience.

events.title: Nārāyaṇrāv Peśvā murdered
events.description: Mādhavrāv's brother Nārāyaṇrāv, eighteen, succeeded him. On 30 August 1773 the palace guards, demanding pay, broke into Śanivār Vāḍā and cut him down as he ran to his uncle Raghunāthrāv for protection. The uncle became Peśvā. The chief justice, Rām Śāstrī Prabhuṇe, investigated, found Raghunāthrāv responsible, and told him to his face that the penalty was death. Unable to enforce it, he resigned and left Pune.

events.title: Rāmśāstrī Prabhuṇe's judgment on Raghunāthrāv
events.description: Rāmśāstrī Prabhuṇe served the Peśvā as nyāyādhīśa, chief judge, and was regarded as upright and unafraid of power. After the murder of the Peśvā Nārāyaṇrāv in 1773, he heard the case and found Raghunāthrāv, the victim's uncle, responsible, and when the verdict was not carried out as he expected, he left Pune and lived in simple retirement. Later Maharashtrian writers made him a model of judicial integrity, and his name is attached to ideals of honest public service.

events.title: Bārbhāī council and Nānā Phaḍnavīs
events.description: Twelve ministers and generals, the Bārbhāī, joined to remove Raghunāthrāv, and when the murdered Peśvā's widow bore a son in 1774 they proclaimed the infant Peśvā. The ablest of them, Nānā Phaḍnavīs, the finance minister, ran the Maratha state for the next twenty-five years by correspondence, accounts and an unmatched network of informants. Europeans called him the Maratha Machiavelli.

events.title: Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar born
events.description: Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar spent years at Vārāṇasī as a young man and absorbed the slow northern dhrupad style. Back in the south he travelled from temple to temple composing a song in Sanskrit for each deity, with details of the shrine worked into the text. His sets on the nine planets and on the Goddess of Tiruvārūr are complete liturgies in music. He was an initiate of Śrīvidyā and a player of the vīṇā.

events.title: Treaty of Surat
events.description: In 1775 Raghunāthrāv, who had been dislodged from the Peśvā's office, made an agreement at Surat with the English East India Company of Bombay. He asked for troops to regain power and offered Salsette, Bassein and other places in return. The Calcutta Council later rejected the terms and made the Treaty of Purandar in 1776, but the Bombay government kept supporting him. The quarrel led to the First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82), the first of three wars that eventually ended Marāṭhā independence.

events.title: Halhed's Code and Hastings's policy
events.description: In 1772 Warren Hastings laid down that in matters of inheritance, marriage and religious usage Hindus would be judged by the śāstra and Muslims by the Qurʾān. Pandits were attached to each court to advise the British judges, and in 1776 a digest compiled by eleven pandits was translated through Persian by Nathaniel Halhed as A Code of Gentoo Laws. The system lasted until the law officers were abolished in 1864, by which time judges relied on printed translations and precedent. It began the separate religion-based personal laws that India still has.

events.title: Hastings and Rājā Cait Singh of Banaras
events.description: Cait Singh was the Rājā of Banaras, from a Bhūmihār family that had become a regional power in the eighteenth century. In 1778 Warren Hastings, the Governor-General, demanded extra payments from him for the Company's wars, and the dispute led to open conflict in 1781, when Cait Singh was forced to flee. His successor ruled as a more dependent ruler. Later Kāśī rājās patronised the Rāmlīlā at Rāmnagar.
events.eraDesc: From Śivājī’s coronation to the Peśvās, the Marathas become the paramount power across India.

events.title: Battle of Vaḍgāv
events.description: Raghunāthrāv fled to the British at Bombay and promised them territory for their help. In January 1779 a Company army marching on Pune was cut off in the hills, harried day and night by Mahādjī Śinde's cavalry, and forced to sign a surrender at Vaḍgāv. The war dragged on until the Treaty of Sālbāī in 1782, which returned almost everything to the Marathas and kept the peace for twenty years.
events.eraDesc: From Śivājī’s coronation to the Peśvās, the Marathas become the paramount power across India.

events.title: Kāśī Viśvanātha rebuilt by Ahilyābāī
events.description: A hundred and eleven years after Aurangzeb's demolition, Ahilyābāī Holkar built the present Viśvanātha temple in 1780 on a plot beside the mosque. It is small, a sanctum under a spire with a pillared hall, because the land available was small. In 1835 Mahārājā Rañjīt Singh of Punjab gave the gold that plates its spire and dome, which is why visitors call it the Golden Temple of Kāśī.

events.title: Tiruvāvaḍuturai, Dharmapuram and the Ādhīnams
events.description: The ādhīnams are Śaiva monasteries of the Kāverī delta in Tamil Nadu, among them Tiruvāvaḍuturai, Dharmapuram and Tiruppanandāḷ. They are led by heads called pandāra sannidhis and are traditionally associated with the Veḷḷāḷa community rather than brāhmaṇas. They maintain temples and teach Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta and the Tēvāram hymns. They gained importance in the centuries after the Cōḻas, and some of them continue to maintain schools and publish texts.

events.title: Sahajānanda Svāmī born
events.description: Ghanaśyām Pāṇḍe was born on 3 April 1781 at Chapaiyā, a village near Ayodhyā. Orphaned at eleven, he left home and walked barefoot for seven years as the boy-ascetic Nīlakaṇṭha, through the Himalaya to Nepal, across Bengal to the far south and up the west coast, some twelve thousand kilometres, practising yoga and questioning the teachers he met. He ended his journey in Gujarat in 1799.

events.title: Somanātha shrine rebuilt by Ahilyābāī
events.description: The medieval temple of Somanātha had been turned into a mosque under Aurangzeb and stood in ruins. In 1783 Ahilyābāī Holkar built a new temple a short distance away, with the sanctum set below ground level for safety, so that worship of the jyotirliṅga could continue. It is still in use and is known as Old Somanātha. The great temple on the original site was rebuilt in 1951.

events.title: Mahādjī Śinde, Vakīl-i-Mutlaq
events.description: Mahādjī Śinde had been left for dead at Pānīpat with a leg wound that lamed him for life. He built a European-style army of infantry and guns under the Savoyard officer De Boigne, and in 1784 the helpless Mughal emperor made him regent of the empire with command of its armies. He is said to have had the emperor issue a decree forbidding the killing of cows throughout the Mughal dominions. He died in 1794.

events.title: Asiatic Society founded
events.description: Sir William Jones, a judge newly arrived in Calcutta, founded the Asiatic Society in 1784 to study "whatever is performed by man or produced by nature" in Asia. He learned Sanskrit from pandits in order to read Hindu law in the original.¶In 1786 he told the Society that Sanskrit was "more perfect than the Greek, more copious than the Latin", and so like both that all three must come from a common source. The remark is often seen as a founding moment of comparative linguistics. The Society's translations brought Indian literature to Europe, and critics add that they also began the colonial habit of deciding what Hinduism "really" was from texts alone.

events.title: Maratha ghāṭs of Kāśī
events.description: Almost nothing on the riverfront of Vārāṇasī is older than the eighteenth century. The long line of stone steps and palaces was built by the Marathas after Mughal control slipped: Daśāśvamedha and Maṇikarṇikā by the Peśvās and Ahilyābāī, others by the Śindes, Bhosales and their ministers. They also rebuilt the Annapūrṇā, Kālabhairava and other temples and endowed feeding-houses. The Banaras that pilgrims see is largely their work.

events.title: Wilkins translates the Bhagavad Gītā
events.description: Charles Wilkins, a Company servant who had learned Sanskrit from pandits at Vārāṇasī, published the Bhagavad Gītā in English in London in 1785, with a preface by Warren Hastings saying it would outlast British rule in India. It was the first Sanskrit book translated directly into a European language. Within a few years it was in French and German, and it reached Blake, Emerson and Thoreau.

events.title: Viṣṇupada temple, Gayā
events.description: At Gayā in Bihar, Hindus offer rice-balls for the peace of their ancestors, a rite the epics already mention. Its centre is a footprint in rock, said to be Viṣṇu's, where he pressed the demon Gayā into the earth. Ahilyābāī Holkar built the present temple over it in 1787, an octagonal tower of grey granite thirty metres high, by craftsmen brought from Jaipur.

events.title: Jones translates Śakuntalā
events.description: William Jones translated Kālidāsa's play Abhijñānaśākuntalam in 1789, calling its author the Shakespeare of India. A German version followed in 1791, and Goethe wrote that if one wanted heaven and earth in a single name, he would say Śakuntalā; he borrowed its prologue for Faust. The play convinced educated Europe that India possessed a classical literature equal to Greece's.

events.title: Rāmasnehī and Rāmānandī centres
events.description: Hanumāngaṛhī, the fortress-temple of Hanumān at Ayodhyā, belongs to the Rāmānandī warrior-ascetics. Its present buildings were raised in the mid-eighteenth century on land and with support given by the Shia Nawābs of Awadh, in gratitude, the story goes, for a cure. In Rajasthan around the same time Rāmcaraṇ founded the Rāmasnehīs, "lovers of Rāma", who worship without images.

events.title: Nepal's expansion and the Gorkhā empire
events.description: Pṛthvī Nārāyaṇ Shāh of Gorkhā conquered the Kathmandu Valley in 1768, and his successors continued to expand. Gorkhā armies took Kumaon in 1790 and Garhwal in 1804, and pushed west to the Kāṅgṛā region, until they were stopped by Rañjīt Singh's Sikh forces. The Anglo-Nepalese war of 1814 to 1816 ended with the Treaty of Sugauli, by which Nepal gave up much of this territory, including Kumaon and Garhwal, and accepted something close to its present borders.

events.title: Maratha raid on Śṛṅgeri and Tipu's letters
events.description: In 1791 Maratha irregular horse on campaign against Tipu Sultan plundered the Śṛṅgeri monastery, killing some brāhmaṇas and displacing the image of the goddess Śāradā. The Jagadguru appealed to Tipu, who sent money and gifts for the reconsecration; about thirty of his letters to the monastery survive. In the same years his own letters record forced conversions and temple destruction in Malabar and Coorg. Both sets of documents are genuine, and his record is argued over still.

events.description: Jonathan Duncan, the Company's Resident at Vārāṇasī, founded a Sanskrit college there in 1791 to train experts in Hindu law for the courts and to win the goodwill of the learned. It taught the Vedas, grammar, logic, law, medicine and astronomy in the traditional way. It later became a centre for editing and printing Sanskrit texts, and is now Sampūrṇānanda Sanskrit University.

events.title: Jones's Institutes of Hindu Law
events.description: To administer justice to Hindus "by their own laws", the British needed to know what those laws were. Halhed's Gentoo Code of 1776 was compiled by eleven pandits. Jones translated the Manusmṛti in 1794. Historians argue that in practice this turned a flexible body of texts, commentary and local custom into fixed statute, gave Manu an authority he had never had, and hardened many rules on caste and women.

events.title: Rhinoplasty reported from Pune
events.description: In 1794 the Gentleman's Magazine in London published a report of a nose reconstruction performed in the Pune region. A man called Cowasjee, a bullock-cart driver with the British army, had his nose cut off as a punishment, and a Maratha potter-caste practitioner rebuilt it using a flap of skin from the forehead. The account attracted European surgeons, and it is cited as an influence on the development of modern plastic surgery. The technique is also described in the Suśruta Saṃhitā.

events.title: Death of Mahādjī Śinde
events.description: Mahādjī Śinde, ruler of Gwalior, died in February 1794 at Vānavḍī near Pune. He had become the most powerful Marāṭhā in the north, holding the Mughal emperor Shāh Ālam II under his protection at Delhi and training his army with European officers under Benoît de Boigne. He also strengthened the Peśvā's influence and had defeated English forces in the first war. His death left the Marāṭhā confederacy without a strong leader and was followed by rivalry among the chiefs.

events.title: Battle of Khardā
events.description: In March 1795 at Khardā every Maratha chief, Śinde, Holkar, Bhosale and Gāikvāḍ, joined the Peśvā's army against the Nizām of Hyderabad, the last time the confederacy acted together. The Nizām's army was defeated after a brief fight and he made peace, ceding territory and agreeing to pay a large indemnity. Seven months later the young Peśvā Mādhavrāv II died after falling, or throwing himself, from a balcony of Śanivār Vāḍā, and the unity ended with him.

events.title: Death of Ahilyābāī Holkar
events.description: Ahilyābāī Holkar governed the Mālwa territories from Indore and Maheśvar from 1767 until her death on 13 August 1795. Widowed young, she took power after her father-in-law Malhārrāv's death and was admired for fair justice and for rebuilding and endowing temples, ghāṭs and rest-houses across India, including at Kāśī, Gayā, Somnāth and Dvārakā. She is still remembered in Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh as a model of careful, dharmic rule, and British writers of her own century also praised her administration.

events.title: Bājīrāv II becomes Peśvā
events.description: Bājīrāv II, son of Raghunāthrāv, became Peśvā in 1796. Mahādjī Śinde had died in 1794 and Ahilyābāī in 1795; Nānā Phaḍnavīs followed in 1800, and with him, a British observer wrote, departed all the wisdom and moderation of the Maratha government. The new Peśvā trusted no one and was trusted by none. Śinde and Holkar went to war with each other over control of him.

events.title: Sikhs and Gosains clash at Haridvāra Kumbha
events.description: At the Haridvāra Kumbha of 1796 the Śaiva Gosains, who policed the fair and collected its taxes, quarrelled with Sikh groups, including Udāsīs and Nirmalas. Sources record that the Gosains first attacked an Udāsī camp; on the last day, 10 April, a Sikh force took revenge and killed about five hundred Gosains, with many more drowned in flight. Captain Thomas Hardwicke, a British officer present, estimated the crowd at two to two and a half million from the tax register and wrote one of the earliest foreign descriptions of the gathering.

events.title: Sakthan Thampuran begins Thrissur Pooram
events.description: Thrissur Pooram was begun by Sakthan Thampuran, Mahārāja of Cochin (r. 1790–1805), usually dated to 1796; some accounts give a year or two later. The traditional story says temples around Thrissur arrived late for the Āṟāṭṭupuḻa Pooram in heavy rain and were turned away from its procession. Offended, they appealed to the king, who answered by founding a festival at Thrissur in honour of Vaṭakkunnāthan (Śiva).¶The Pooram is now one of Kerala's great temple festivals. Its two main sides, Pāṟamekkāvu and Tiruvampāṭi, face each other in the Kuṭamāṟṟam, about thirty caparisoned elephants with golden headdresses and silk parasols, to the sound of temple percussion. It is a fine example of a ruler creating a new public ritual that united many separate temples around one centre.

events.title: Thai Rāmakian compiled under Rāma I
events.description: The Rāmakian is the Thai version of the Rāmāyaṇa, based on Indian sources and local tradition. King Rāma I of the Chakri dynasty, who founded Bangkok, had it compiled in about 1797 as part of his cultural revival after the fall of Ayutthaya. Its scenes are painted in long murals around the Wat Phra Kaew, the Temple of the Emerald Buddha in Bangkok, and are also performed in dance-drama. The text shows how Rāma's story became part of Thai royal culture.

events.title: Colebrooke translates the Digest of Hindu Law
events.description: Henry Thomas Colebrooke, a Company official who taught himself Sanskrit, translated a great digest of Hindu law compiled by the Bengali pandit Jagannātha Tarkapañcānana, published in 1798. He went on to write the first accurate accounts in a European language of the Vedas, the six philosophical systems, Sanskrit grammar and Indian algebra. Max Müller called him the founder of Sanskrit scholarship in Europe.

events.title: Mahārājā Rañjīt Singh rises
events.description: Rañjīt Singh, head of one of the twelve Sikh confederacies, took Lahore in 1799 at the age of eighteen and by 1801 was Mahārājā of Punjab. He built a kingdom from the Sutlej to the Khyber with a modern army, and employed Hindus, Muslims and Europeans at every level. He covered the Harmandir at Amritsar in gold, giving it the name Golden Temple, and gave gold to the temples of Kāśī and Jvālāmukhī as well.

events.title: Pūrṇaiyā becomes Dīvān of Mysore
events.description: Pūrṇaiyā, a brāhmaṇa financial officer, served Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan of Mysore, and after the fall of Tipu in 1799 became the chief minister, or dīvān, under the restored Wodeyar king Kṛṣṇarāja III, who was a child. He ran the state's finances and administration through the regency, and is credited with repairing and endowing temples and irrigation tanks that had suffered in the wars. He retired in 1811.

events.title: Fall of Śrīraṅgapaṭṭaṇa
events.description: The British with their allies stormed Tipu Sultan's island capital on 4 May 1799, and he was killed at the gate. The Company restored the old Hindu dynasty of Mysore, the Wodeyars, placing a five-year-old boy on the throne with the experienced minister Pūrṇaiyā as regent. The Dasarā festival with its royal procession was revived, and Mysore became one of the best-governed Indian states.

events.title: Vīrapāṇḍya Kaṭṭabommaṉ hanged
events.description: The Pāḷaiyakkārars were hereditary chiefs who held forts across the Tamil country. Kaṭṭabommaṉ of Pāñcālaṅkuṟicci refused to pay tribute to the Company or wait upon its collector. He was captured and hanged from a tamarind tree in October 1799. Two years later the Marudu brothers of Śivagaṅgai issued a proclamation calling on all castes to rise against the foreigners, and were hanged with their families.

events.title: Tañjāvūr painting and Serfoji II
events.description: Serfoji II, the Maratha ruler of Tañjāvūr from 1798 to 1832, was a scholar-king educated by the missionary C. F. Schwartz. He built up the Sarasvatī Mahal Library, which holds thousands of Sanskrit, Tamil and Marathi manuscripts and remains one of India's great manuscript collections. He supported the Tanjore Quartet, four brothers who helped organise the Bharatanāṭyam repertoire, and Tañjāvūr painting, with its gold-leaf and gem-set images of deities, flourished under Maratha patronage.

events.title: Baptist Serampore Mission founded
events.description: The Company restricted missionary activity in its territory, so the Baptist William Carey, with Joshua Marshman and William Ward, settled at Serampore, a Danish enclave near Calcutta, in 1799–1800. Their press cast type for Bengali, Devanāgarī and many other scripts and printed the Bible in dozens of languages, as well as early editions of Bengali and Sanskrit classics. Their tracts attacking Hinduism drew replies from Rāmmohan Roy and others, and are seen as an early stimulus to modern Hindu apologetics.

events.title: Swaminarayan saints Guṇātītānanda and Gopālānanda
events.description: Guṇātītānanda Svāmī and Gopālānanda Svāmī were among the foremost paramahaṃsas, or senior renunciants, among the disciples of Sahajānanda Svāmī, the founder of the Swaminarayan tradition. Guṇātītānanda, who lived from 1785 to 1867 and was a head of the Junāgaḍh temple, is revered by the BAPS branch as the divine "Akṣara," the eternal abode of God in the Swaminarayan theology, and as Sahajānanda's ideal devotee. Gopālānanda is known for his scholarship and for teaching Vedānta in the community.

events.title: Colin Mackenzie gathers South Indian manuscripts and inscriptions
events.description: From his survey of Mysore, which began in 1799, the Scottish engineer Colin Mackenzie, with the Telugu Brahmin interpreter Kavali Venkata Boriah and later Boriah's brother Lakshmaiah, collected thousands of manuscripts, inscriptions, coins and local histories in Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Sanskrit. Boriah died in 1803. After Mackenzie's death in 1821 the collection was bought by the Company for Rs 100,000.¶The 'Mackenzie Collection' preserves temple records, family histories and village accounts that would otherwise be lost, and today is split between the British Library, the British Museum and the Government Museum in Chennai. It also records a joint enterprise: it was done through the knowledge of Indian pandits and interpreters, whose names historians have only recently begun to restore.

events.title: Death of Nānā Phaḍnavīs
events.description: Nānā Phaḍnavīs was the chief administrator of the Peśvā's government for decades, managing finance and diplomacy after the death of Mādhavrāv I and during the minority of Mādhavrāv II. He held the Marāṭhā confederacy together in the face of English and Mysorean pressure. He died in March 1800, and the English historian James Grant Duff recorded that with him went the wisdom and moderation of the Marāṭhā government. Within two years the Peśvā Bājīrāv II had signed the Treaty of Bassein, accepting English protection.

events.title: Svāminārāyaṇa Sampradāya begins
events.description: In 1799 the young ascetic Nīlakaṇṭha Varṇī joined the Vaiṣṇava teacher Rāmānanda Svāmī in Gujarat, who initiated him as Sahajānanda and, before his own death, entrusted the community to him. In 1801 Sahajānanda gave his followers a new mantra, "Svāminārāyaṇa", by which he and the movement came to be known. He required strict vows: no meat, alcohol, theft or adultery. Sir John Malcolm, governor of Bombay, met him in 1830 and later credited his influence with calming a lawless region.

events.title: Siddhivināyaka temple completed at Prabhādevī
events.description: The Śrī Siddhivināyaka temple in Prabhādevī, Mumbai, was completed on 19 November 1801, according to its own records. Its builders are named as Laxman Vithu and Deubai Patil. The first shrine was a small hall with an image of Gaṇeśa as Siddhivināyaka, the Gaṇeśa who grants one's wishes. Its sanctum doors are carved with the Aṣṭavināyaka forms of Gaṇeśa, and a public trust regulated by a statute of 1980 runs it.¶What began as a modest neighbourhood shrine in the Marāṭhā-influenced island city grew with Mumbai itself into one of its most visited temples. It stands as an example of how Gaṇeśa worship, strong in Maharashtra under the Peśvās, entered the new colonial metropolis and was carried into its public life, long before Ṭiḷak's Gaṇeśotsava of 1893.

events.title: Anquetil-Duperron's Oupnek'hat
events.description: In 1801–02 the French scholar Abraham Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron published the Oupnek'hat, a Latin version of fifty Upaniṣads. He took it from a Persian translation made in 1657 for the Mughal prince Dārā Shikoh, who had gathered pandits in Delhi. The Latin text was the means by which the Upaniṣads came to many European thinkers. The philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer read it and wrote that it had been the solace of his life and would be of his death.

events.title: Treaty of Bassein
events.description: In October 1802 Yaśvantrāv Holkar defeated the armies of the Peśvā and Śinde outside Pune. Bājīrāv II fled to the British and on 31 December signed the Treaty of Bassein: a British force would be stationed in his territory at his cost, and his foreign relations would go through the Company. He was restored to Pune by British troops. The other Maratha chiefs saw it as the sale of their independence.

events.title: Second Anglo-Maratha War
events.description: Śinde and the Bhosale of Nāgpur went to war against the treaty in 1803. Arthur Wellesley, the future Duke of Wellington, beat them at Assaye in the Deccan, which he later called the bloodiest action he ever saw for its size. General Lake took Delhi and Āgrā in the north, and the blind Mughal emperor passed into British keeping. The Company also took Odisha, including Purī.

events.title: British manage Jagannātha temple, tax pilgrims
events.description: When the British took Odisha in 1803, they took over management of the Jagannātha temple at Purī from the Marathas, paid its expenses and collected a tax from every pilgrim, at a profit. Missionary societies and others in Britain denounced a Christian government for running an "idol's" temple, and the Purī chariot festival gave the English word "juggernaut", from Jagannātha, its sense of an overwhelming force. The Company withdrew from management by 1840 and handed the temple to the Rājā of Khurdā.

events.title: Lallūlāl, Sadal Miśra and Hindi prose
events.description: At Fort William College in Calcutta, founded in 1800, the British employed writers to prepare Hindi and Urdu prose. Lallūlāl, of a Gujarati family settled at Āgrā, composed the Premsāgar, completed in 1803 and printed in 1810, a retelling of the tenth canto of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa about Kṛṣṇa in Khaṛī Bolī, the dialect that became modern Hindi. Sadal Miśra worked alongside him. These books were among the first printed Hindi prose and helped shape a literary standard.

events.title: Yaśvantrāv Holkar's resistance
events.description: Yaśvantrāv Holkar had stayed out of the war of 1803. In 1804 he fought alone, destroyed a British column under Colonel Monson in a long retreat through Rajasthan, and besieged Delhi. He wrote to the other Indian rulers that the foreigners must be driven out together or not at all. None joined him. He made peace in 1805 on terms that left him his kingdom, and died in 1811.

events.title: Vellore Mutiny over dress regulations
events.description: In 1806 the Madras army ordered its Indian soldiers to shave their beards, remove caste marks and earrings, and wear a new round hat. Hindu and Muslim soldiers alike took it as a first step to forced conversion. On 10 July the garrison at Vellore rose and killed over a hundred British troops. The mutiny was put down the same day with several hundred sepoys killed. The order was withdrawn.

events.title: Schlegel's On the Language and Wisdom of the Indians
events.description: Friedrich Schlegel's book Über die Sprache und Weisheit der Indier (On the Language and Wisdom of the Indians), published in 1808, argued that Sanskrit was related to Greek, Latin and German and held a high philosophical culture. It was a founding text of German Indology and Romanticism's interest in India. Franz Bopp then published his work on Sanskrit's verbal system in 1816, which established the comparative grammar of the Indo-European languages.

events.title: Kālīghāṭ temple in Kolkata
events.description: Kālīghāṭ in Kolkata is one of the Śākta Pīṭhas, the places where parts of Satī's body are said to have fallen, and the goddess Kālī here is a central deity for the city, whose name is said to be derived from "Kālīkṣetra." The present temple was built in 1809 with the support of the Sabarna Roy Choudhury family, replacing earlier structures. In the 19th century the area produced Kālīghāṭ paintings, a style of bold, simple pictures sold to pilgrims.

events.title: Velu Tampi's Kuṇḍara proclamation
events.description: Velu Tampi rose from a village official to chief minister of Travancore. When the British Resident's demands became unbearable he took up arms, and in January 1809 issued a proclamation from Kuṇḍara warning the people that the foreigners would destroy the temples, the caste order and the customs of the land. The rising was crushed. He killed himself in a temple to avoid capture, and his body was hung on a gibbet.

events.title: First printed Rāmcaritmānas
events.description: The Rāmcaritmānas, Tulsīdās's sixteenth-century Awadhi retelling of the Rāma story, was first printed in 1810 at Calcutta, when the printing of Indian-language texts was just beginning. The British scholar Frederic Salmon Growse published an English translation in the 1870s. The Mānas became the best-known Hindi religious text, and printing helped extend its reach, so that it became a staple of recitation and public readings in north India.

events.title: Charter Act admits missionaries
events.description: When the Company's charter was renewed in 1813, evangelicals in Parliament led by William Wilberforce won two changes. Missionaries could now enter British India under licence, and the Company had to set aside a hundred thousand rupees a year for education and the encouragement of learning. The argument over whether that money should go to Sanskrit and Arabic learning or to English was settled for English in 1835, after Macaulay's Minute.

events.title: Rāmmohan Roy's Ātmīya Sabhā
events.description: Rāmmohan Roy, a Bengali brāhmaṇa who had served the Company and mastered Persian, Arabic, Sanskrit and English, settled in Calcutta in 1815 and gathered friends in the Ātmīya Sabhā, or "Friendly Society", to discuss religion. He translated several Upaniṣads into Bengali and English, arguing that they teach the worship of one formless God, and that image worship and widow-burning were later corruptions. The Sabhā was a forerunner of the Brāhmo Samāj, which he founded in 1828.

events.title: Māṇik Prabhu and the Sakalamata Sampradāya
events.description: Māṇik Prabhu, who lived from 1817 to 1865, was a saint of Humnābād in Karnataka, regarded as an incarnation of Dattātreya, and founder of the Māṇiknagar seat. His teaching, called Sakalamata Sampradāya, accepts all faiths as paths to the same goal, and the community has long hosted Hindus, Muslims and others at its festivals. It belongs to the Datta tradition, which also includes Vāsudevānanda Sarasvatī, known as Ṭembe Svāmī.

events.title: Third Anglo-Maratha War
events.description: In November 1817 Bājīrāv II, pushed by his general Bāpū Gokhale, finally attacked the British residency at Pune. He was beaten at Khaḍkī, then pursued for months across the Deccan. Bāpū Gokhale died covering his retreat at Aṣṭī. At the same time the British defeated the Bhosale at Nāgpur and Holkar at Mahidpur. Every Maratha state was reduced to a dependent ally.

events.title: Paika rebellion in Odisha
events.description: The Pāikas were the hereditary peasant militia of Odisha, who held rent-free land in return for service to the Rājā of Khurdā, guardian of the Jagannātha temple. The British took their lands. In 1817 their commander Bakśī Jagabandhu led them, with tribal Kondh allies, in a revolt that seized Khurdā and Purī for a time. It was put down within a year. Odisha honours it as an early war of independence.

events.title: Hindu College founded
events.description: In 1817 leading Hindu families of Calcutta, with the watchmaker David Hare, raised the money for a college to teach their sons English, European science and literature. Twenty students enrolled on the first day. Its pupils, among them the radical "Young Bengal" circle around the teacher Derozio, questioned everything their fathers believed. It became Presidency College and the nursery of the Bengal Renaissance.
events.eraDesc: From Śivājī’s coronation to the Peśvās, the Marathas become the paramount power across India.

events.title: End of the Peśvāī
events.description: Bājīrāv II surrendered on 3 June 1818. The office of Peśvā was abolished, his lands were annexed, and he was sent with a large pension to Biṭhūr on the Gaṅgā near Kānpur, where he lived another thirty-three years. A descendant of Śivājī was kept as a minor prince at Sātārā. The British refusal to continue the pension to Bājīrāv's adopted son, Nānā Sāheb, was one of the grievances behind 1857.

events.title: Battle of Bhīmā Koregāv
events.description: On 1 January 1818 a Company detachment of about eight hundred men, many of them Mahārs, held the village of Koregāv on the Bhīmā for a day against the far larger army of Peśvā Bājīrāv II, who then withdrew. The British put up a pillar naming their dead. Dr Ambedkar visited in 1927 and made it a symbol of Dalit courage against a regime that had treated Mahārs as untouchable; thousands gather there each New Year.

events.title: Rajput states sign treaties with the Company
events.description: In 1817–18 the British East India Company, after the defeat of the Marathas and Pindārīs, signed treaties of subsidiary alliance with the Rajput states. Udaipur and Jodhpur signed in January 1818 and Jaipur in April of that year. These gave the Company control of foreign policy and defence, and a claim to tribute, while the princes kept internal rule. Rajput rulers had been under pressure from Maratha raids, and many welcomed protection, which tied them to British paramountcy until 1947.

events.title: Sikh conquest of Kashmir
events.description: In 1819 an army of the Sikh ruler Rañjīt Singh took Śrīnagar and ended the period of Afghan Durrānī governors, whom Kashmiri sources often describe as oppressive. Paṇḍit Bīrbal Dhar, a Kashmiri Pandit who had fled to Lahore, had asked for Sikh help. Kashmir remained under Sikh governors until 1846, when the Treaty of Amritsar gave it to Gulāb Siṅgh of Jammu. Sources differ on how Sikh rule was experienced: some record heavy taxation and restrictions on Muslims, while Kashmiri Pandit accounts often note improved conditions for them.

events.title: Elphinstone and the Dakṣiṇā fund
events.description: The Peśvās had given an annual gift, the dakṣiṇā, to thousands of Sanskrit scholars. Mountstuart Elphinstone, the first British commissioner of the conquered Deccan, kept part of the fund and in 1821 used it to open a Sanskrit college at Pune so as not to alienate the learned. English classes were added, and it grew into Deccan College, later famous for linguistics and archaeology.

events.title: Svāminārāyaṇa temple, Ahmedabad
events.description: Sahajānanda Svāmī built six temples in his lifetime. The first, at Kālupur in Ahmedabad, stands on land granted by the British government and was consecrated on 24 February 1822, with images of Nara-Nārāyaṇa. Built of carved Burmese teak and painted in bright colours, it set the style of the movement's temples and became the seat of its northern diocese, one of the two seats later established by Sahajānanda.

events.title: A. W. Schlegel's Latin Bhagavad Gītā
events.description: August Wilhelm Schlegel, brother of Friedrich and the first professor of Sanskrit in Bonn, published a Latin translation of the Bhagavad Gītā in 1823. The philosopher and statesman Wilhelm von Humboldt studied it and in an essay on the Gītā called it the most beautiful, perhaps the only true philosophical song in any known language. The statement was widely quoted in Europe and gave the Gītā a place in the canon of world literature.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Sanskrit College, Calcutta
events.description: The Sanskrit College was established by the East India Company in Calcutta in the 1820s to teach Sanskrit learning to Indian students. Early on it admitted only brāhmaṇas. Īśvaracandra Vidyāsāgar, a Sanskrit scholar and social reformer, became its principal in 1851, reformed the curriculum to include some modern subjects and opened admission to non-brāhmaṇas. The college was a place where traditional learning met colonial education, and Vidyāsāgar's changes were a landmark in educational reform in Bengal.

events.title: Rāṇī Cennammā's revolt at Kittūr
events.description: Kittūr, in northern Karnataka, was a small state whose ruler Mallasarja died in 1816. After his son died in 1824, Rāṇī Cennammā adopted an heir, but the East India Company refused to recognise the adoption and tried to take over the state. In October 1824 her forces defeated a Company force near Kittūr and killed the Collector, John Thackeray. The British later captured her after a second campaign and imprisoned her at Bailhongal, where she died in 1829. She is remembered as an early rebel against Company rule.

events.title: Śikṣāpatrī and Vacanāmṛta
events.description: Two texts define the Svāminārāyaṇa tradition. The Śikṣāpatrī of 1826 is a letter of 212 Sanskrit verses setting out daily duties for monks and householders: non-violence, vegetarian diet, no intoxicants, honesty and devotion to Kṛṣṇa. The Vacanāmṛta records 273 of the founder's discourses in Gujarati, delivered between 1819 and 1829 and compiled by senior disciples; each is dated and notes the place and audience, an unusually exact record in an Indian religious text.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Treaty of Yandabo
events.description: In 1826 the Burmese government signed the Treaty of Yandabo with the British East India Company, ending the First Anglo-Burmese War. Burma gave up its claims to Assam, Manipur, Kachar and Jaintia, and ceded Arakan and Tenasserim. Assam had suffered severely during the Burmese occupation of the 1810s and 1820s. The treaty brought the Brahmaputra valley under British control, after which the region was linked to the Bengal Presidency and was soon developed for tea plantations.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Naraina Pillai founds Śrī Mariamman temple
events.description: In 1827, eight years after the East India Company founded its trading settlement at Singapore, Naraina Pillai, a clerk from Penang, built a simple wood-and-thatch shrine to the goddess Mariyammaṉ and installed her image. He had first been allotted land near Telok Ayer Street but was later granted the South Bridge Road site, which had fresh water for rites. The three-tiered gopuram dates from 1903 and the present six-tiered one from 1925.¶It is regarded as Singapore's oldest Hindu temple, founded by and for the South Indian, mainly Tamil, migrants who came with the port city's earliest growth. Mariyammaṉ, a Tamil village goddess associated with rain and with disease, was carried overseas with them. The temple was gazetted a National Monument on 6 July 1973.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Brāhmo Sabhā founded
events.description: In 1828 Rāmmohan Roy opened a meeting-house in Calcutta where people of any background could worship one formless God, with readings from the Upaniṣads and no images, priests or sacrifices.¶Roy knew Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic and English, and argued from the Upaniṣads themselves that monotheism was the original Hindu faith. The society, later called the Brāhmo Samāj, stayed small but shaped modern India out of all proportion to its size: it campaigned against widow-burning and child marriage and for women's education, and the Tagore family were among its leaders.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ | ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||
gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.
gitaQuote.source: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) Critical Edition; Rāmānuja Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Svāti Tirunāḷ, composer-king of Travancore
events.description: Svāti Tirunāḷ Rāma Varma was the Mahārājā of Travancore from 1829 to 1846. He was one of the great composers of Carnatic and Hindustani music, said to have composed in Sanskrit, Malayalam, Tamil, Hindi, Telugu and Kannada. Most of his songs are in praise of Padmanābha, the deity of the royal temple at Tiruvanantapuram, whose "servant" (dāsa) the kings of Travancore claimed to be. He supported musicians and scholars, and his court became an important centre of music.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

gitaQuote.verse: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत । अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥ परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् । धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥

events.title: Satī abolished in Bengal
events.description: In December 1829 the Governor-General, Lord Bentinck, made it a crime to burn or bury alive a Hindu widow. The practice had been rare in most of India but had risen sharply in Bengal, where over five hundred cases a year were recorded.¶Rāmmohan Roy had campaigned for a decade, arguing from the Dharmaśāstras that the texts recommend an austere widowhood and nowhere require death. The orthodox Dharma Sabhā petitioned London against the ban as interference in religion and lost. The episode set the pattern for a century: reform argued from scripture, resisted from scripture, and settled by law.

events.title: Tod publishes Annals and Antiquities of Rajast'han
events.description: James Tod, a Company officer, became Political Agent for the western Rajput states in 1818 and resigned in 1823. Drawing on bardic chronicles, genealogies, inscriptions and coins, he wrote the Annals and Antiquities of Rajast'han, which appeared in London in two volumes, the first in 1829 and the second in 1832. The first volume carries a plea to George IV to restore the Rajputs' former independence.¶The work shaped the popular and scholarly picture of the Rajput clans, their valour, sacrifice and loyalty to dharma, and it was used by later nationalist writers and poets. Historians have long cautioned that Tod mixed legend with fact, applied a European feudal model, and wrote as a Company agent. It is both a quarry of sources and a text to read critically.

events.title: Haibatbābā and the Vārakarī pilgrimage
events.description: The Vārakarī tradition did not end with Tukārāma. Bahiṇābāī, a brāhmaṇa woman who took Tukārāma as her guru against her husband's wishes, left an autobiography in verse. In the early nineteenth century Haibatbābā Ārphaḷkar, a nobleman in the service of the Śinde court at Gwalior, is credited with giving the annual pilgrimage its present form, in which the padukās (sandals) of Jñāneśvara from Āḷandī and of Tukārāma from Dehū are carried in palanquins in organised processions to Paṇḍharpūr. The details and dates of this reorganisation are known mainly from tradition and later Vārakarī accounts.

events.title: Death of Svāminārāyaṇa at Gaḍhaḍā
events.description: Sahajānanda Svāmī died at Gaḍhaḍā in Gujarat on 1 June 1830, aged forty-nine. He had left five hundred initiated ascetics and a following of several hundred thousand. To avoid a succession dispute he divided the movement into a northern seat at Ahmedabad and a southern one at Vaḍtāl, each under a nephew he had adopted, with the office to pass by heredity. Later branches, such as BAPS, formed over who truly carried his presence.

events.title: Mummaḍi Kṛṣṇarāja Wodeyar
events.description: Kṛṣṇarāja Wodeyar III ruled Mysore from 1799. After a revolt in the Nagar region, the British took over the administration of the state in 1831 and he lost real power, though he remained king until 1868. He turned to scholarship and the arts, patronising Sanskrit scholars and musicians. He is credited with the Śrītattvanidhi, a large Sanskrit encyclopaedic work on topics including iconography, ritual and yoga.

events.title: Death of Rāmmohan Roy at Bristol
events.description: In 1830 Rāmmohan Roy sailed to England as envoy of the Mughal emperor, who gave him the title Rājā, and to make sure the ban on satī was not overturned on appeal. He was received by the king, gave evidence to Parliament on Indian affairs, and was sought out by reformers. He died of meningitis at Bristol on 27 September 1833 and is buried there under an Indian-style canopy.

events.title: Ayyā Vaikuṇḍar and the Ayyāvaḻi movement
events.description: Ayyā Vaikuṇḍar was a teacher from southern Travancore, said to have been born in 1809 and to have died in 1851, who taught among the Nāḍār community, then low in the caste order. His followers, called Ayyāvaḻi, hold that he was an incarnation of Viṣṇu, and they have their own scripture, the Akilattirattu. He protested against caste oppression and temple restrictions. Followers date the start of his mission to 1833, and many Ayyāvaḻi now regard their faith as a religion distinct from Hinduism.

events.title: Indentured Hindus cross the seas
events.description: After the abolition of slavery, sugar planters across the British empire recruited labour in India under five-year contracts. From 1834 to 1920 over a million people, mostly from Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh, sailed to Mauritius, Guyana, Trinidad, Natal, Suriname and Fiji. They called the agreement "girmit". Many carried one book, the Rāmcaritmānas, and its story of exile and return became the centre of their religion.

events.title: Rañjīt Singh's gold for Kāśī and Jvālāmukhī
events.description: Mahārājā Rañjīt Siṅgh, the Sikh ruler of Punjab, supported Hindu temples as well as Sikh shrines. In 1835 he is said to have donated gold, about a tonne by some accounts, for the spires of the Kāśī Viśvanātha temple, which were rebuilt in the 1780s by Ahilyābāī Holkar, and which gave the temple its popular name, the "Golden Temple." He also gave gold to the Jvālāmukhī temple in Kāṅgṛā. The gifts are often cited as an example of Sikh patronage of Hindu holy places.

events.title: Macaulay's Minute on Indian education
events.description: Thomas Macaulay, law member of the Governor-General's council, wrote a minute in February 1835 on how the education grant should be spent. He declared that a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia, which he could not read. The aim, he wrote, was a class Indian in blood but English in taste and intellect. The government adopted his view, and English replaced Persian in the courts.

events.title: Zorāwar Singh's Himalayan campaigns
events.description: Zorāwar Singh Kahlūriā was a general serving Gulāb Singh of Jammu, who was a vassal of the Sikh empire. He conquered Ladakh in 1834 to 1835 and later took Baltistan. In 1841 he led an army into western Tibet and reached the area of Mānasarovar and Mount Kailāsa. He was killed in battle against Tibetan and Chinese forces in December 1841. His conquests laid the base for the later Dogra control of Jammu and Kashmir.

events.title: Calcutta Medical College founded; Āyurveda loses patronage
events.description: The Calcutta Medical College, founded in 1835, taught Western medicine and became part of the colonial state's health system, which gave it official support and recognition. Earlier, the government had briefly funded Sanskrit and Arabic medical teaching, but policy shifted. Indigenous medicine lost much of its state patronage and institutional prestige. Physicians such as Gaṅgādhar Rāy of Bengal kept Āyurveda alive through private teaching and practice, and by the late nineteenth century a movement to revive and modernise the tradition had begun.

events.title: Birth of Rāmakṛṣṇa at Kāmārpukur
events.description: Gadādhar Caṭṭopādhyāya was born on 18 February 1836 in Kāmārpukur, a village in Bengal, to a poor and devout brāhmaṇa family. He had little schooling and no taste for it. From childhood he fell into trances, once at the sight of white cranes against a dark cloud. At nineteen he joined his brother as a priest at the new Kālī temple of Dakṣiṇeśvara.

events.title: James Prinsep deciphers the Brāhmī script
events.description: The script of the oldest Indian inscriptions had been unreadable for over a thousand years. James Prinsep, an assay-master at the Calcutta mint, worked on it from coins and short donative texts, and in 1837 recognised the word for "gift" and from it the letters of Brāhmī. The pillar and rock edicts could then be read, and their author, "Beloved of the Gods", was identified as the emperor Aśoka.

events.title: Śiśunāḷa Śarīfa and Govinda Bhaṭṭa
events.description: Śiśunāḷa Śarīfa was a Kannada saint-poet of Śiśunāḷa, in northern Karnataka, born to a Muslim family. His guru was Govinda Bhaṭṭa, a brāhmaṇa saint who, in tradition, initiated him into the path of devotion and knowledge. Śarīfa composed Kannada verses in a simple style that draw on Vedānta and Sufi imagery. He is regarded as an example of Hindu-Muslim harmony in Karnataka's devotional culture, and a shrine at Śiśunāḷa draws followers of both religions.

events.title: T. S. Burt visits Khajurāho temples
events.description: In 1838 Captain T. S. Burt, a British engineer, visited the temples of Khajurāho in central India, where he was guided to the overgrown site by local people, and he described them in the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal. Alexander Cunningham later mapped and named the groups of temples in the 1850s and 1860s. They were built mostly between the late ninth and early eleventh centuries under the Candella dynasty.¶The report introduced Khajurāho to the world of European scholarship, though the temples had not been forgotten by the Hindus of the region, and some remain in worship. About twenty-five of the eighty-five temples recorded in the twelfth century survive. UNESCO listed the group in 1986.

events.title: Debendranāth Tagore founds Tattvabodhinī Sabhā
events.description: Debendranāth Tagore, heir to a great Calcutta fortune and father of Rabindranāth, turned to religion after his grandmother's death and a chance reading of a page of the Īśā Upaniṣad. events.title: Wilson's Viṣṇu Purāṇa and Burnouf's Bhāgavata
events.description: Horace Hayman Wilson, the first Boden Professor of Sanskrit at Oxford, published his translation of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa in 1840, with notes comparing the other Purāṇas, an early scholarly study of that literature. In Paris Eugène Burnouf began publishing the Bhāgavata Purāṇa with a French translation in 1840; the work appeared in several volumes into the 1840s. Europe now had access to texts of living Hindu devotion, not only the Veda and the law books.

events.title: Company withdraws from temple management
events.description: British officials had inherited the old rulers' role of managing temples, attending festivals and collecting the pilgrim tax. Missionary societies in Britain campaigned against a Christian government's "connection with idolatry". In 1838–40 London ordered it to stop. The tax was abolished and temples were handed to local trustees, often with no supervision at all, which led to mismanagement and to later laws.

events.title: British annexation of Sindh
events.description: Sindh was ruled by Baloch chiefs, the Tālpur Amīrs. In 1843 General Charles Napier provoked a war, defeated them at Miāni and annexed the province. He admitted privately that it was a piece of rascality, but a useful one. For Sindh's Hindu merchants, a minority who ran its trade, it opened the way to Bombay and the world, until Partition forced nearly all of them to leave.

events.title: Hāthīrāmjī mahants manage Tirumala temple
events.description: After the East India Company took control of the Tirumala temple's administration in the early 19th century, the management was handed to Sevādās, the head of the Hāthīrāmjī Maṭh, in 1843. The mahants of this monastery then ran the temple's affairs until 1933, when the Madras legislature passed an act creating the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthānams (TTD) committee. The TTD is today one of the largest temple administrations in the world, which shows a shift from monastic to state-appointed management.

events.title: First Anglo-Sikh War
events.description: After Rañjīt Singh died in 1839 the Punjab court dissolved in murders and the army became its own master. War with the British came in December 1845. events.title: Emerson and Thoreau read the Gītā
events.description: Charles Wilkins's English translation of the Bhagavad Gītā (1785) was read by American Transcendentalists. Ralph Waldo Emerson drew on it, as in his poem "Brahma". Henry David Thoreau, at Walden Pond, wrote that he bathed his intellect each morning in the stupendous and cosmogonal philosophy of the Gītā, compared with which, he said, modern literature seemed puny. The Gītā thus became a part of American thought.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Ḍogrā rule in Jammu and Kashmir
events.description: Gulāb Singh, a Ḍogrā Rajput of Jammu who had risen in Rañjīt Singh's service, became ruler of Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh in 1846, when the Treaty of Amritsar transferred Kashmir to him. His son Raṇbīr Singh completed the Raghunātha temple complex at Jammu, founded schools, and had a staff of scholars collect and copy Sanskrit manuscripts; the library holds some six thousand. The dynasty ruled until 1947–52.

gitaQuote.verse: पिताहमस्य जगतो माता धाता पितामहः । वेद्यं पवित्रमोंकार ऋक्साम यजुरेव च ॥ गतिर्भर्ता प्रभुः साक्षी निवासः शरणं सुहृत् । प्रभवः प्रलयः स्थानं निधानं बीजमव्ययम् ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ | vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛk sāma yajur eva ca || gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt | prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||
gitaQuote.translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer and the grandsire. I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the creation and dissolution, the foundation and the imperishable seed.
gitaQuote.chapter: Bhagavad Gītā 9.17–18 (Rāja Vidyā Rāja Guhya Yoga)
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Bhāṣya

events.title: Jyotirāo and Sāvitrībāī Phule's girls' school
events.description: Jyotirāo Phule, of the gardener caste, had been insulted at a brāhmaṇa friend's wedding and concluded that only education would end such humiliation. In 1848 he and his wife Sāvitrībāī, whom he had taught to read, opened a school for girls in Pune. She was its first teacher. Orthodox neighbours threw mud and dung at her on the way; she carried a spare sari. They went on to open schools for Dalit children.

events.title: British annexation of the Punjab
events.description: A second war in 1848–49 ended the Sikh kingdom. At Chillianwala the British suffered one of their worst losses in India; at Gujrat their artillery was decisive. On 29 March 1849 the ten-year-old Mahārājā Dalīp Singh signed away his kingdom and the Koh-i-Nūr diamond, which was sent to Queen Victoria. He was later taken to England and baptised.

events.title: Max Müller begins editing the Ṛgveda with Sāyaṇa
events.description: In 1849 Friedrich Max Müller published the first volume of the first printed edition of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā with the commentary of Sāyaṇa, the fourteenth-century Vijayanagara scholar. He had persuaded the East India Company to allow the project, and he worked from manuscripts he could consult in Europe. The six volumes were completed in 1874.¶Sāyaṇa's commentary preserves the exegetical tradition of the Veda in India, and printing it alongside the text gave Western scholars and Indian pandits a common reference. Müller's reading of the hymns and his chronology were later criticised, but the edition itself became a foundation of Vedic philology. His later Sacred Books of the East series (1879) built on it.

events.title: Upper Gaṅgā Canal and Haridvāra pilgrimage
events.description: When the British built the Upper Gaṅgā Canal in the 1840s, with James Thomason's government in charge, there was concern that it would divert the river's water and affect Hindu pilgrimage at Haridvāra. Haridvāra's priests and pilgrims protested, and the arrangements were made so that water continued to flow past Har-kī-Pauṛī, the main bathing ghāṭ. The issue arose again later, and in 1916 Madan Mohan Mālavīya negotiated an agreement that guaranteed an unobstructed flow of the Gaṅgā at the ghāṭ.

events.title: Caste Disabilities Removal Act
events.description: Under the śāstra as the courts applied it, a Hindu who changed religion or was put out of caste lost the right to inherit. The Act of 1850 removed that penalty across British India. It was presented as liberty of conscience. Hindu petitioners in Calcutta and Madras saw a law made to help missionaries by removing the main cost of conversion, and it added to the fears that fed the revolt of 1857.

gitaQuote.verse: ईश्वरः सर्वभूतानां हृद्देशेऽर्जुन तिष्ठति । भ्रामयन्सर्वभूतानि यन्त्रारूढानि मायया ॥

gitaQuote.translation: The Supreme Lord abides in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all living creatures to spin as if mounted upon a cosmic machine (yantra) made of nature.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1 correlation

events.title: Death of Bājīrāv II at Biṭhūr
events.description: The last Peśvā, Bājīrāv II, was defeated by the English in 1818 and pensioned off to Biṭhūr near Kānpur, where he lived until his death in January 1851. He had adopted a son, Nānā Sāheb Dhoṇḍū Panta, but the East India Company, applying its policy of lapse, refused to continue the pension for the heir. Nānā Sāheb's grievance was one reason he joined the 1857 rebellion and led its forces at Kānpur, which made the death of the last Peśvā a prelude to a larger upheaval.

events.title: First Ayodhyā clash recorded
events.description: The first recorded violence over the Ayodhyā site was in the 1850s, when ascetics of the Nirmohī order and local Muslims clashed. After the revolt the British administration put up a railing in 1859: Muslims were to pray inside the building and Hindus on the platform in the outer court, called Rāma Cabūtrā, where they also kept a small shrine. The arrangement held, uneasily, for ninety years.

events.title: Birth of Cattampi Svāmikaḷ, Kerala reformer
events.description: Cattampi Svāmikaḷ, who lived from 1853 to 1924, was a Kerala sage and reformer who challenged caste privilege through scholarship. In his Vedādhikāra-nirūpaṇam he argued from Vedic and Sanskrit sources that people of all communities had a right to study the Vedas, a claim that went against orthodox practice. He also wrote on the history of Kerala, and criticised the Nambūtiri claim to superiority. He was a contemporary and friend of Nārāyaṇa Guru, and the two are remembered as pillars of Kerala's religious reform.

events.title: Jaṅg Bahādur's Mulukī Ain legal code
events.description: In 1854 the Rāṇā prime minister Jaṅg Bahādur issued the Mulukī Ain, a national legal code that organised Nepali society under a single hierarchy. It drew on Hindu dharmaśāstra, classing all groups, including Newars and hill peoples, within a caste order with rules on purity, punishment and marriage. It remained in force in various forms until 1963. The code is often cited in discussions of caste and state in Nepal, and scholars describe it as an important step in the formation of a Hindu state.

events.title: Dakṣiṇeśvara Kālī temple consecrated
events.description: Rāṇī Rāsmaṇi, a wealthy Kaivarta widow of Calcutta, built the Bhavatāriṇī Kālī temple on the east bank of the Gaṅgā and had it consecrated in May 1855. Because of her caste, many orthodox brāhmaṇas at first hesitated to officiate or eat food offered there, and the problem was resolved by finding a willing priest. Rāmakumār Caṭṭopādhyāy took the first post, and in 1856 his younger brother Gadādhar, the future Rāmakṛṣṇa, joined as priest. The temple became the centre of Rāmakṛṣṇa's practice and teaching.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

gitaQuote.verse: अहमेवाक्षयः कालो धाताहं विश्वतोमुखः ॥ कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो लोकान्समाहर्तुमिह प्रवृत्तः ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: aham evākṣayaḥ kālo dhātāhaṁ viśvatomukhaḥ || kālo 'smi loka-kṣaya-kṛt pravṛddho lokān samāhartum iha pravṛttaḥ ||
gitaQuote.translation: I alone am inexhaustible, imperishable Time (Akṣaya Kāla), and I am the dispenser of destiny facing all directions... I am all-destroying Time, grown mighty to extinguish the worlds.
gitaQuote.source: Mahabharata (Bhishma Parva 35.32); Abhinavagupta Gītārtha-Saṁgraha

events.title: Santāl Hūl rebellion in the Rājmahal hills
events.description: The Santāls of the Rājmahal hills had cleared forest land only to fall into debt-bondage to moneylenders and under the heel of police and railway contractors. On 30 June 1855 two brothers, Sidhu and Kānhu Murmu, told ten thousand assembled Santāls that their god had ordered them to drive the oppressors out. They fought with bows against muskets for six months. Fifteen thousand or more were killed.

events.title: Akkalkoṭ Svāmī Samartha
events.description: Akkalkoṭ Svāmī Samartha is a 19th-century saint revered by his devotees as an incarnation of Dattātreya, said to be the later form of Narasiṃha Sarasvatī. His origins are uncertain, and accounts differ about his early life. He settled at Akkalkoṭ in Solāpur district in 1856 and stayed there until his passing in 1878. His followers stress surrender to the guru and service, and the Svāmī Samartha Maṭh at Akkalkoṭ is a major pilgrimage site in Maharashtra.

events.title: Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act
events.description: Īśvarcandra Vidyāsāgar, principal of Sanskrit College, searched the law books for a text to help Bengal's child widows, condemned to a lifetime of fasting and drudgery. He found one in the Parāśara Smṛti permitting a woman to remarry in five cases, including the husband's death. A petition against him gathered many times more signatures than his own. The Act passed on 26 July 1856, and he paid for many of the first weddings himself.

events.title: British annexation of Awadh
events.description: Lord Dalhousie held that when an Indian ruler under British protection died without a natural son, his state "lapsed" to the Company; adopted heirs, though valid in Hindu law, were not recognised. Sātārā, Jhānsī and Nāgpur were taken in this way between 1848 and 1854. In February 1856 Awadh was annexed outright on the ground of misgovernment. Most of the Bengal army's soldiers came from Awadh.

events.title: Uprising begins at Meerut
events.description: New Enfield rifle cartridges, rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat and needing to be bitten open, were the spark. On 9 May 1857 eighty-five troopers at Meerut who refused them were shackled and jailed. The next evening their comrades rose, freed them, killed their officers and rode through the night to Delhi.¶There they proclaimed the aged Mughal emperor as their leader. Within weeks revolt spread across the Gaṅgā plain, joined by dispossessed rulers and peasants. Hindus and Muslims fought side by side. It took the British more than a year to suppress it, with great brutality on both sides.

events.title: Maṅgal Pāṇḍe at Barrackpore
events.description: On 29 March 1857 at Barrackpore near Calcutta, Maṅgal Pāṇḍe, a brāhmaṇa soldier of the 34th Native Infantry, came onto the parade ground with a loaded musket, called on his comrades to rise, and wounded two British officers. Only one Indian came to the officers' aid. He was hanged on 8 April, and the regiment was disbanded. British soldiers afterwards called every rebel "Pandy".

events.title: Nānā Sāheb at Kānpur
events.description: Nānā Sāheb was the adopted son of the last Peśvā, living at Biṭhūr near Kānpur; the British had refused to continue his father's pension or title. In June 1857 he took command of the rebel troops at Kānpur. The British garrison surrendered on a promise of safe passage and was attacked at the river; captive women and children were later killed. British revenge was savage. He escaped to Nepal and was never found.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Rānī Lakṣmībāī falls at Gwalior
events.description: Lakṣmībāī's husband, the Rājā of Jhānsī, died in 1853. The British refused to recognise their adopted son and annexed the state. When the 1857 revolt reached Jhānsī she took command, and in March 1858 defended the fort against a British siege for two weeks.¶With the walls breached she escaped on horseback at night with her son tied to her back, joined Tātyā Ṭope, and seized the fortress of Gwalior. She was killed in a cavalry action on 18 June 1858, dressed as a soldier. The British commander called her the best and bravest of the rebel leaders.

events.title: Kuṃvar Singh of Jagdīśpur
events.description: Kuṃvar Singh, a Rajput landholder of Jagdīśpur in Bihar, was nearly eighty when he took command of the mutinous regiments at Dānāpur in July 1857. He led them on a year-long campaign across north India. In April 1858, wounded in the arm while crossing the Gaṅgā, he is said to have cut it off and offered it to the river. He retook his own fort and died there three days later.

events.title: Crown rule and the Queen's Proclamation
events.description: By an Act of August 1858 the East India Company was abolished and India passed under the British Crown. On 1 November the Queen's proclamation was read in every town. It promised that treaties with the princes would be kept, that no more territory would be annexed, that all subjects would be treated alike whatever their religion, and that officials would abstain from interfering with belief or worship.

events.title: Tātyā Ṭope executed
events.description: Tātyā Ṭope, a Maratha brāhmaṇa and Nānā Sāheb's general, was the ablest rebel commander. After Gwalior fell he kept an army moving through central India for nine months, crossing the Narmadā and covering some three thousand miles with British columns always behind him. Betrayed by an ally while asleep, he was hanged at Śivpurī on 18 April 1859, saying he had only obeyed his master.

events.title: Rādhāsoāmī movement begins at Āgrā
events.description: Śiv Dayāl Singh, a banker's son of Āgrā, began teaching publicly in 1861, on Basant Pañcamī, a path of inner sound and light under a living master. His following became the Rādhāsoāmī movement, strong in Āgrā and Punjab, which later divided into several lineages, including the Beās branch. Its teaching draws on the Sant tradition of Kabīr and Nānak, and many of its members regard it as a distinct path rather than a form of Hinduism.

events.title: Archaeological Survey of India
events.description: Alexander Cunningham, an army engineer who had spent his leave tracing the sites named by the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, persuaded the government in 1861 that India's monuments should be recorded. He was appointed Archaeological Surveyor and over twenty-five years toured the north, identifying Taxila, Nālandā, Śrāvastī and many others. He also collected the first seal from Harappa, without knowing what it was.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Lāhiṛī Mahāśaya receives Kriyā Yoga
events.description: Śyāmācaraṇ Lāhiṛī, a government accountant, was posted to Rānīkhet in the Himalaya in 1861. According to his tradition, he met there a guru, Mahāvatār Bābājī, who initiated him into Kriyā Yoga, a set of breathing and meditation techniques. He then taught householders at Vārāṇasī, claiming that yoga need not require renunciation. The account is known mainly from his disciples and from Paramahansa Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi, and Bābājī himself is not documented in independent records.

events.title: Birth of Vivekānanda in Calcutta
events.description: Narendranāth Datta was born in Calcutta on 12 January 1863, son of a successful lawyer. He was a strong, restless boy with a fine singing voice and a memory that kept whole books. At college he read Mill, Hume and Spencer, joined the Brāhmo Samāj, and went about asking religious men one question: had they seen God? India keeps his birthday as National Youth Day.

events.title: Tota Purī initiates Rāmakṛṣṇa
events.description: Rāmakṛṣṇa first practised Tantra under a wandering woman ascetic, the Bhairavī Brāhmaṇī, who declared him an incarnation. Then in 1864 came Totā Purī, a naked monk of the Advaita school who taught that the personal God is itself an appearance. Rāmakṛṣṇa could not get past the form of Kālī until, he said, he cut it in two with the sword of knowledge. He remained in the formless state for three days.

gitaQuote.verse: अहमेवाक्षयः कालो धाताहं विश्वतोमुखः ॥ कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो लोकान्समाहर्तुमिह प्रवृत्तः ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: aham evākṣayaḥ kālo dhātāhaṁ viśvatomukhaḥ || kālo 'smi loka-kṣaya-kṛt pravṛddho lokān samāhartum iha pravṛttaḥ ||
gitaQuote.translation: I alone am inexhaustible, imperishable Time (Akṣaya Kāla), and I am the dispenser of destiny facing all directions... I am all-destroying Time, grown mighty to extinguish the worlds.
gitaQuote.source: Mahabharata (Bhishma Parva 35.32); Abhinavagupta Gītārtha-Saṁgraha

events.title: Bāṅke Bihārī temple built at Vṛndāvana
events.description: The present Bāṅke Bihārī temple at Vṛndāvana is dated to around 1864 in the standard account, though some sources give 1862. Its image is a form of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in tribhaṅga, the 'three-bend' pose, which gives the name 'bent one'. Tradition connects the deity with Svāmī Haridāsa, who first worshipped it as Kuñja Bihārī at Nidhivana; it was moved to the new building in the nineteenth century after a dispute between the sādhu and gosvāmī followers of Haridāsa.¶The temple is known for its distinctive darśana, when the curtain in front of the deity is repeatedly drawn and opened, and for its crowds at Holī and other festivals. It is one of the most visited temples in Braj.

events.title: Carnot Thermodynamics & Maxwellian Electromagnetism
events.description: Carnot, Clausius, and Kelvin formalize the First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics (entropy dS >= dQ/T and heat engine limits), driving the Industrial Revolution. James Clerk Maxwell unifies electricity, magnetism, and optics into four partial differential field equations, revealing light as an electromagnetic wave traveling at speed c.

events.title: Brāhmo Samāj splits over Keśab Sen
events.description: Keśab Candra Sen, a magnetic speaker, wanted the Brāhmo Samāj to give up caste marks entirely and to preach across India. Debendranāth Tagore thought him too radical and too Christian in tone. In 1866 Keśab's younger followers left to form the Brāhmo Samāj of India. It won the Civil Marriage Act of 1872. It split again in 1878 when Keśab married his under-age daughter to a prince.

events.title: The Paṇḍit journal at Queen's College, Benares
events.description: Queen's College in Benares taught both Sanskrit śāstra and Western science, a combination promoted by its earlier principal James Ballantyne. In 1866 the Paṇḍit journal was being published there, printing Sanskrit texts and discussions. Scholars such as Bāpūdeva Śāstrī, an astronomer and mathematician of the college, took part in debates on how traditional learning related to European science. The institution became a place of meeting between the traditions of Kāśī's paṇḍits and colonial scholarship.

gitaQuote.verse: ईश्वरः सर्वभूतानां हृद्देशेऽर्जुन तिष्ठति । भ्रामयन्सर्वभूतानि यन्त्रारूढानि मायया ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: īśvaraḥ sarva-bhūtānāṁ hṛd-deśe 'rjuna tiṣṭhati | bhrāmayan sarva-bhūtāni yantrārūḍhāni māyayā ||
gitaQuote.translation: The Supreme Lord abides in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all living creatures to spin as if mounted upon a cosmic machine (yantra) made of nature.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1 correlation

events.title: Prārthanā Samāj founded in Bombay
events.description: The Prārthanā Samāj, "Prayer Society", was founded in Bombay in 1867 after a visit by Keśab Candra Sen. Its leaders were the judge M. G. Rānaḍe and the Sanskritist R. G. Bhāṇḍārkar. Unlike the Brāhmos it stayed within Hindu society, drew on the hymns of Tukārāma and Nāmadeva, and concentrated on practical reform: widow remarriage, women's education, orphanages and night schools.
