gitaQuote.verse: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत । अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥ परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् । धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur; Madhvācārya Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Hindu Melā founded in Calcutta
events.description: The Hindu Melā was an annual fair held in Calcutta from 1867, organised by Nabagopāl Mitra with the Tagore family's money. It showed Indian handicrafts, held wrestling and gymnastic contests, and opened with patriotic songs written for it. Its stated purpose was to make Indians rely on themselves. It ran for about fourteen years and is counted the first organised expression of national feeling in India.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Rāmaliṅga Vaḷḷalār and the Vaḍalūr kitchen
events.description: Rāmaliṅgam, called Vaḷḷalār, "the great giver", was a Tamil poet-mystic who taught compassion for all living things as the only worship, and rejected caste and ritual. In 1867 he opened a kitchen at Vaḍalūr to feed anyone hungry; its fire has reportedly not gone out since. His temple of 1872 enshrines a lamp behind seven coloured curtains. In January 1874 he entered a room, asked that it be locked, and was not seen again.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Bhāratendu Hariścandra and modern Hindi literature
events.description: Bhāratendu Hariścandra (1850–85) was a writer of Kāśī, born into a Vaiṣṇava merchant family, who is regarded as the father of modern Hindi literature. He wrote plays, poems and essays, edited journals, and used Khaṛī Bolī for prose, while writing devotional verse in Braj. His works dealt with social and religious subjects, including colonial poverty. His influence on both Hindi writing and Vaiṣṇava public culture was great, despite his early death.

events.title: Birth of Mohandās Gāndhī at Porbandar
events.description: Mohandās Karamcand Gāndhī was born on 2 October 1869 at Porbandar on the coast of Gujarat, where his father was chief minister of a small state. The family were Vaiṣṇava merchants; his mother kept long fasts, and Jaina monks visited the house. From her and from the region he took the ideas of non-violence, vows and fasting that he later turned into political method.

events.title: Dayānanda's Kāśī śāstrārtha
events.description: In November 1869 Dayānanda Sarasvatī went to Vārāṇasī, the citadel of orthodoxy, and challenged its pandits to show him where the Vedas sanction the worship of images. The Mahārājā of Kāśī presided, and a crowd of many thousands gathered.¶About thirty leading scholars faced him alone. The debate turned on whether later texts count as "Veda"; it ended in uproar when the pandits declared victory and left. Both sides claimed to have won. For Dayānanda it was the turning point: he stopped trying to persuade scholars and took his case to the public in Hindi.

events.title: Rājā Ravi Varmā's first commissions
events.description: Ravi Varmā, of a princely Kerala family, taught himself oil painting by watching a European portraitist. From the 1870s he painted scenes from the epics and Purāṇas with realistic bodies, Maharashtrian saris and theatrical lighting. In 1894 he set up a colour press near Bombay. His cheap prints of Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī hung in homes and shops across India, and much of the calendar imagery of the gods since descends from them.

events.title: Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura revives Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism
events.description: Kedārnāth Datta, known as Bhaktivinoda, was a Bengali deputy magistrate who also wrote prolifically on Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism, which had declined in the centuries after Caitanya. He published Caitanya's teachings in Bengali and English, organised the community, and promoted the congregational chanting of the holy names. In 1888 he identified a site at Māyāpur as Caitanya's birthplace, now an important pilgrimage centre. His son Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī carried his work forward, and ISKCON later grew from that line.

gitaQuote.verse: पिताहमस्य जगतो माता धाता पितामहः । वेद्यं पवित्रमोंकार ऋक्साम यजुरेव च ॥ गतिर्भर्ता प्रभुः साक्षी निवासः शरणं सुहृत् । प्रभवः प्रलयः स्थानं निधानं बीजमव्ययम् ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ | vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛk sāma yajur eva ca || gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt | prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||
gitaQuote.translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer and the grandsire. I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the creation and dissolution, the foundation and the imperishable seed.
gitaQuote.chapter: Bhagavad Gītā 9.17–18 (Rāja Vidyā Rāja Guhya Yoga)
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Bhāṣya

events.title: Birth of Aurobindo Ghose in Calcutta
events.description: Aravinda Ghoṣ was born in Calcutta on 15 August 1872. His father, an anglophile doctor, sent him to England at seven with orders that he learn nothing Indian. He won prizes for Greek and Latin at Cambridge, passed the civil service examination, and deliberately missed the riding test. He returned in 1893 knowing many European languages, including Greek and Latin, and no Bengali.

events.title: Monier-Williams publishes his Sanskrit–English Dictionary
events.description: Monier Monier-Williams, the second Boden Professor of Sanskrit at Oxford, brought out his Sanskrit–English Dictionary at the Clarendon Press in 1872. He had won the chair in 1860 against Max Müller after the death of Horace Hayman Wilson. It was built on the Petersburg Sanskrit Dictionary but arranged for English readers. A thoroughly revised edition, prepared with Ernst Leumann and Carl Cappeller, followed in 1899.¶The 1899 edition remains the standard reference for students of Sanskrit and of Hindu texts in English, and it is now searchable online. Its entries are a record of the language of Vedic, epic and classical literature, though scholars note that its glosses sometimes reflect the Orientalist outlook of its age.

events.title: Phule founds the Satyaśodhak Samāj
events.description: In 1873 Jyotirāo Phule founded the Satyaśodhak Samāj, "Society of Truth-Seekers", in Pune. Members pledged to worship one God without a priest as go-between and to treat all people as equals; they conducted weddings themselves in Marathi. His book Gulāmgirī, "Slavery", published that year, was dedicated to the Americans who had abolished it, and argued that caste was a system imposed by brāhmaṇas on the labouring majority.

events.title: Tukārām's Gāthā printed
events.description: Tukārām, the seventeenth-century Marāṭhī saint and poet of Dehu, composed thousands of abhaṅgas, devotional verses to Viṭṭhala of Paṇḍharpūr. For long they passed in oral and manuscript form in varying versions. The first major printed edition, known as the Indu Prakāś edition, was published in Mumbai between 1869 and 1873 and fixed the collection that is widely used. Printing helped to give his verses a standard text and reached readers in new numbers.

events.title: Ārya Samāj founded
events.description: Svāmī Dayānanda Sarasvatī, a Gujarati renunciant, founded the Ārya Samāj at Bombay on 10 April 1875. His message was "back to the Vedas": the four Vedas alone are revelation, they teach one formless God, and everything later, including image worship, the Purāṇas, caste by birth and child marriage, is corruption.¶His book Satyārtha Prakāśa argued this in Hindi. The Samāj took root in Punjab and the north, founded hundreds of schools and colleges, promoted widow remarriage, and introduced śuddhi, a rite to bring converts back into the Hindu fold.

events.title: Theosophical Society founded in New York
events.description: Helena Blavatsky, a Russian occultist, and Henry Olcott, an American colonel, founded the Theosophical Society in New York in 1875 and moved to India in 1879, first to Bombay and from 1882 to Adyar in Madras. They declared the ancient wisdom of India superior to modern materialism at a time when few Europeans said so. Under Annie Besant the Society founded the Central Hindu College at Vārāṇasī in 1898, and many educated Indians credited it with restoring their self-respect.

events.title: Sayājīrāv Gāikvāḍ III
events.description: Sayājīrāv Gāikvāḍ III was chosen as Mahārāja of Baroda in 1875 as a boy and ruled until 1939. He introduced compulsory primary education in the state in 1906, set up libraries and supported Sanskrit scholarship through the Oriental Institute (1927). He gave a scholarship to the young B. R. Ambedkar, who studied at Columbia University from 1913, and he promoted social reforms. Baroda was regarded as one of the best-governed princely states.

events.title: Lahore Ārya Samāj and the Ten Principles
events.description: The Ārya Samāj found its real home in Punjab. At Lahore in 1877 its principles were reduced to ten short statements still used today: God is the source of all true knowledge; the Vedas are the books of true knowledge; one should always be ready to accept truth and give up untruth; the aim of the Samāj is to do good to the whole world, physical, spiritual and social.

events.title: Gajānan Mahārāj of Śegāv
events.description: Gajānan Mahārāj was an ascetic who, according to devotees, first appeared in 1878 at Śegāv in Vidarbha, where a householder saw him eating leftover food outside a house. He lived there as an unconventional saint, said to wear little and to indifferently move through the town, while drawing people for healing and guidance. Devotees regard him as an avadhūta. He took samādhi in 1910, and the Gajānan Mahārāj Saṃsthān at Śegāv is now a major pilgrimage centre in Maharashtra.

events.title: Max Müller's Sacred Books of the East
events.description: Friedrich Max Müller, a German scholar at Oxford who never visited India, spent twenty-five years editing the Ṛgveda with Sāyaṇa's commentary, published in six volumes from 1849 to 1874 at the East India Company's expense. He then organised the Sacred Books of the East, fifty volumes of translations from Sanskrit, Pāli, Chinese, Persian and Arabic. Indians called him Mokṣamūlar; his dating of the Vedas is still debated.

events.title: Birth of Ramaṇa Maharṣi at Tirucuḻi
events.description: Veṅkaṭarāman Ayyar was born on 30 December 1879 at Tirucuḻi in Tamil Nadu, the son of a village lawyer. He was an ordinary schoolboy, good at football and known for sleeping so deeply that friends could carry him about without waking him. Nothing in his childhood suggested a sage, until at sixteen a relative mentioned that he had come from Aruṇācala, and the name struck him with awe.

gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.

events.title: Sanskrit printing presses of Pune, Bombay and Vārāṇasī
events.description: In the late nineteenth century the pandits of Vārāṇasī, Pune and Bombay took to the printing press. The Nirṇaya Sāgara press at Bombay, founded in the late 1860s, set the standard for Sanskrit typography; the Ānandāśrama press at Pune and the Chowkhamba house at Vārāṇasī issued series of philosophical, legal and medical texts with their commentaries. Works that had existed in a few manuscripts could now be bought in any town.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Narendra meets Rāmakṛṣṇa
events.description: In November 1881 Narendranāth, eighteen, was brought to sing for Rāmakṛṣṇa. He asked the question he asked everyone: "Sir, have you seen God?" Rāmakṛṣṇa answered at once that he had, more clearly than he saw the boy in front of him, and that anyone could who wept for God as people weep for wife and money. Narendra argued with him for five years before accepting him.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Rendition of Mysore to the Wodeyars
events.description: After direct British administration from 1831, Mysore was handed back to the Wodeyar dynasty in 1881 under Chāmarāja Wodeyar X, an event known as the Rendition. The state was then run with the help of capable dīwāns, beginning with C. Raṅgācārlu, and was widely seen as a model of modern administration with a strong tradition of Sanskrit and Kannada learning. The Mysore Sanskrit college, founded earlier under the Wodeyars, and the University of Mysore (1916) grew from this setting.

events.title: Baṅkim's Ānandamaṭh and "Vande Mātaram"
events.description: Baṅkimcandra Caṭṭopādhyāya, a deputy magistrate and Bengal's first great novelist, published Ānandamaṭh in 1882. It tells of an order of warrior-monks, during the famine of the 1770s, who worship their country as the Mother. Into it he set a song written earlier, "Vande Mātaram": "I bow to thee, Mother, rich in waters, rich in fruit". It became the anthem of the freedom movement and is India's national song.

events.title: Cow protection movement
events.description: Dayānanda's pamphlet of 1881 argued for protecting cows on economic as well as religious grounds, and the first cow-protection society was formed in Punjab the next year. The movement spread through the north with travelling preachers, village councils and a vast petition, drawing support across castes. It also deepened tension with Muslims: riots over slaughter at the Bakr-Īd festival in 1893 left over a hundred dead.

events.title: Dayānanda dies at Ajmer
events.description: Dayānanda was a guest of the Mahārājā of Jodhpur in 1883 and rebuked him for keeping a dancing girl. Soon after, he was given milk containing powdered glass; his followers have always held that she bribed the cook. He lingered for a month and died at Ajmer on the evening of Dīpāvalī, 30 October, forgiving the cook and, it is said, giving him money to escape.

events.title: Indian National Congress founded in Bombay
events.description: In December 1885 seventy-two lawyers, editors and teachers from every province met in a Sanskrit college in Bombay, at the suggestion of a retired British official, A. O. Hume. They asked politely for more Indians in the civil service and the councils. For twenty years the Congress did little more than pass resolutions. Under Ṭiḷak and then Gāndhī it became the mass movement that won independence.

events.title: Ayodhyā suit of Mahant Raghubar Dās
events.description: In 1885 Mahant Raghubar Dās, head of the Hindu shrine in the outer court at Ayodhyā, asked the court for permission to build a temple over the platform. The judge, a Hindu, refused, fearing bloodshed. On appeal in 1886 the British district judge visited the site and wrote that it was most unfortunate a mosque had been built on land specially held sacred by Hindus, but that it was too late to remedy the grievance.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Edwin Arnold's The Song Celestial
events.description: Edwin Arnold's The Song Celestial, published in 1885, was an English verse rendering of the Bhagavad Gītā that was popular in Britain and the United States. In 1889, in London, a young Mohandas Gāndhī read it for the first time, at the request of two Theosophist brothers who asked him about the Sanskrit original. Gāndhī later said the Gītā became his guide in daily conduct, and Arnold's version is one of the ways it reached him.

events.title: Death of Rāmakṛṣṇa at Kāśīpur
events.description: Rāmakṛṣṇa developed cancer of the throat in 1885 and was moved to a garden house at Kāśīpur, where a dozen young disciples nursed him. He gave them ochre cloths and placed them in Narendra's care. He died on 16 August 1886. The young men rented a ruined house at Barānagar and, on Christmas Eve at Antpur, took monastic vows before a sacred fire. They lived on rice and boiled leaves.

events.title: Dayānanda Anglo-Vedic School founded at Lahore
events.description: Dayānanda's followers honoured him with a school, opened at Lahore on 1 June 1886. Lālā Haṃsrāj, a young graduate, served as its headmaster for twenty-five years without salary. The "Dayānanda Anglo-Vedic" formula joined English and science with Sanskrit and the Vedas. The DAV movement today runs some nine hundred schools and colleges, among the largest non-government education networks in India.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

gitaQuote.verse: ईश्वरः सर्वभूतानां हृद्देशेऽर्जुन तिष्ठति । भ्रामयन्सर्वभूतानि यन्त्रारूढानि मायया ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: īśvaraḥ sarva-bhūtānāṁ hṛd-deśe 'rjuna tiṣṭhati | bhrāmayan sarva-bhūtāni yantrārūḍhāni māyayā ||
gitaQuote.translation: The Supreme Lord abides in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all living creatures to spin as if mounted upon a cosmic machine (yantra) made of nature.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1 correlation

events.title: Śāradā Devī guides the Rāmakṛṣṇa order
events.description: Śāradā Devī (1853–1920), the wife of Rāmakṛṣṇa, is known to followers of the Ramakrishna movement as the Holy Mother. After her husband's death in 1886 she guided his disciples, including Vivekānanda, and gave initiation to many devotees at Kolkata, Jayrāmbāṭī and elsewhere. The Śāradā Maṭh, a monastic order for women founded in 1954, honours her, and a temple dedicated to her stands at Belūr Maṭh.

events.title: Olcott founds the Adyar Library
events.description: In December 1886 Henry Steel Olcott, president of the Theosophical Society, founded the 'Library Olcott' at Adyar, Madras, where the Society had made its headquarters in 1882. It began as a collection of Sanskrit and other Oriental manuscripts and became the Adyar Library and Research Centre. Today it holds roughly 250,000 books and some 20,000 palm-leaf manuscripts, many of them Sanskrit works.¶The library is one of the principal manuscript collections of southern India and a centre of editing and publication of Sanskrit texts, including the Upaniṣads and works on Yoga. It also records how the Theosophists, Western by origin but allied with Hindu and Buddhist reformers, helped to preserve and spread the study of Indian texts in the late nineteenth century.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ | ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||
gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.
gitaQuote.source: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) Critical Edition; Rāmānuja Gītā Bhāṣya

events.title: Trailaṅga Svāmī of Kāśī
events.description: Trailaṅga Svāmī was a yogin said to have been born in Andhra and to have lived in Vārāṇasī for many decades, until about 1887, with some traditions giving him a very long life of nearly three hundred years. He was known for long silences and unusual feats, and drew crowds to the Kāśī ghāṭs. Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṃsa visited him and is reported to have described him as the living Viśvanātha, the "walking Śiva of Vārāṇasī". The dates for his birth and life are uncertain.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Sanātana Dharma Sabhās
events.description: In the late nineteenth century, orthodox Hindus organised themselves in sabhās to respond to the criticism of reformers like the Brāhmo Samāj and Ārya Samāj and of missionaries. The Bhārat Dharma Mahāmaṇḍal, led by Dīn Dayālu Śarmā, was begun in 1887 and reorganised in 1902, with its centre in Kāśī. These groups defended traditional practices, such as image worship and the varṇa order, and supported Sanskrit education. The name "Sanātana Dharma" was popularised in this period as a self-description of traditional Hindus.

events.title: Nārāyaṇa Guru's Aruvippuram consecration
events.description: On Śivarātri night in 1888 a wandering ascetic from the Īḻava community, barred by birth from entering temples, took a stone from the bed of the Neyyār river at Aruvippuram and installed it as a Śiva-liṅga. Consecration was a right reserved to brāhmaṇas.¶When challenged he replied, with dry wit, that he had only installed an Īḻava Śiva. On the wall he wrote that this was a model place where all live as brothers, free of caste division and religious hatred. He went on to found dozens of temples, and finally one with a mirror in place of an image.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Pandita Ramābāī's Śāradā Sadan
events.description: Ramābāī, daughter of a brāhmaṇa who had defied custom to teach her Sanskrit, was given the title Paṇḍitā by the scholars of Calcutta. Widowed young, she wrote on the misery of high-caste widows and in 1889 opened a home and school for them in Bombay. She had become a Christian, which cost her Hindu support. Dhoṇḍo Keśav Karve, who married a widow from her school, founded a Hindu home on the same lines and later a women's university.

events.title: Śrīmad Rājacandra and Gāndhī
events.description: Rāycandbhāī Mehtā, a Jaina jeweller of Bombay who could attend to a hundred things at once, was also a poet indifferent to wealth. Gāndhī met him in 1891 and wrote to him from South Africa when Christian friends pressed him to convert. His replies, patient and learned, persuaded Gāndhī that Hinduism could give him all he sought. Gāndhī named him, with Tolstoy and Ruskin, as one of three who shaped his life.

events.title: Age of Consent Act
events.description: In 1889 Phulmoni, a girl of ten or eleven, died in Calcutta after her adult husband forced himself on her. The government proposed raising the age of consent from ten to twelve. Reformers supported it. Ṭiḷak agreed that the custom was wrong but argued that a foreign government had no business legislating on Hindu marriage, and that reform must come from within. The Act passed in 1891.

events.title: Birth of B. R. Ambedkar at Mhow
events.description: Bhīmrāo Rāmjī Āmbeḍkar was born on 14 April 1891 at Mhow, a military station in central India, the fourteenth child of a Mahār soldier. At school he had to sit on a sack he brought from home and could drink water only if someone of higher caste poured it from above. He went on to earn doctorates from Columbia University and the London School of Economics.

events.title: Dharmapāla's Bodh Gayā campaign begins
events.description: In 1891 the Sri Lankan Buddhist Anagārika Dharmapāla began a campaign to restore Bodh Gayā, the site of the Buddha's enlightenment, to Buddhist care, founding the Mahā Bodhi Society. The temple was in the hands of a Śaiva mahant, whose family had managed it for centuries. The dispute over control went on for decades, involving courts and public debate, and was settled in part by the Bodh Gaya Temple Act of 1949, which set up a joint committee. It remains a sensitive case of shared sacred ground.

events.title: Oriental Research Institute, Mysore
events.description: The Oriental Research Institute at Mysore began in 1891 as the Oriental Library, established under the Wodeyar government to collect and edit Sanskrit manuscripts; it is now part of the University of Mysore. Its librarian R. Śāmaśāstrī acquired the manuscript of Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra there, reportedly from a pandit of Tañjāvūr, and edited the text, published in 1909. The institute continues to hold a large collection of palm-leaf and paper manuscripts and to publish critical editions.

events.title: Vivekānanda at Kanyākumārī
events.description: After two years of walking the length of India as an unknown monk, Vivekānanda reached its southern tip in December 1892. He swam, tradition says, to a rock offshore and sat for three days. He wrote later that he thought there about India's poverty and concluded that religion was not the cause of its fall, and that he must find the means to raise the masses. He decided to go to America.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Vivekānanda at the Parliament of Religions
events.description: On 11 September 1893 an unknown thirty-year-old monk rose at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago and began, "Sisters and Brothers of America". The audience of several thousand stood and applauded for two minutes.¶He spoke for a few minutes on tolerance: India had sheltered the persecuted of every faith, and all religions are paths to one truth. Over the following days he presented Vedānta as a rational, universal philosophy. He stayed in the West nearly four years, and returned to India a national hero who had changed how Hindus saw themselves.

events.title: Ṭiḷak promotes the public Gaṇeśa festival
events.description: Gaṇeśa Caturthī had been a household festival in Maharashtra, and a palace one under the Peśvās. In 1893, after communal riots in Bombay, Bāḷ Gaṅgādhar Ṭiḷak promoted public celebrations in Pune: large images in neighbourhood pavilions, ten days of songs, lectures and plays, and a grand immersion procession. Bhāūsāheb Raṅgārī had set up a public Gaṇeśa the year before.¶The British had restricted political meetings but could hardly ban a religious festival. The pavilions became schools of nationalism and brought castes together around one deity. The model spread across India and is still followed.

events.title: Gāndhī thrown off the train at Pietermaritzburg
events.description: In June 1893 Gāndhī, a young barrister a few weeks into his first job in South Africa, was travelling first class to Pretoria. At Pietermaritzburg a white passenger objected and a constable threw him and his luggage onto the platform. He spent the night shivering in the waiting room, deciding whether to go home. He stayed twenty-one years and worked out there the method of satyāgraha, "holding to truth".

events.title: Aurobindo returns to Baroda
events.description: Aurobindo landed at Bombay in February 1893 and felt, he said, a vast calm descend as he set foot on Indian soil. For thirteen years he served the Mahārājā of Baroda as secretary and professor, and used the time to learn Sanskrit, Bengali and Marathi and to read the epics and Upaniṣads in the original. He began to practise yoga in 1904, at first to gain strength for political work.

events.title: Nāgarī Pracāriṇī Sabhā
events.description: The Nāgarī Pracāriṇī Sabhā was founded at Kāśī in 1893 to promote the Devanāgarī script and Hindi language. It campaigned for official use of Devanāgarī in the courts of the North-Western Provinces, and it carried out a search for Hindi manuscripts in many places. It also compiled the large Hindi dictionary, the Hindī Śabdasāgara. The Sabhā was important in making Hindi a language of education and public life.

events.title: Vīrcand Gāndhī and Dharmapāla at Chicago
events.description: At the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago, Swami Vivekānanda spoke for Hinduism. Vīrcand Gāndhī, a Jaina lawyer from Gujarat, and Anagārika Dharmapāla of Sri Lanka, a Buddhist reformer, also addressed the Parliament, speaking for their own traditions. Together they presented Indian religions to a Western audience, in a setting that was both a landmark of interfaith meeting and an occasion for competing claims about Asia's religions.

events.title: Vedanta Society of New York
events.description: In November 1894, after a year of lecturing across America, Vivekānanda founded the Vedanta Society in New York. It was the first Vedānta centre in the West, and its members were mostly Americans. In 1895 he trained a few students intensively at a cottage at Thousand Island Park on the St Lawrence, and later sent brother monks from India to run centres in New York and California.

events.title: Ṭiḷak launches the Śivājī festival
events.description: Śivājī's tomb on Rāygaḍ had lain neglected for decades. In 1895 Ṭiḷak launched a fund to repair it and began an annual festival on his birthday, with processions, ballads and lectures. Ṭiḷak presented him as a national hero of all Indians who had fought for self-rule. The British watched uneasily, and within two years jailed Ṭiḷak for a speech at one of the festivals.

events.title: Vivekānanda's Rāja Yoga
events.description: Vivekānanda's Rāja Yoga, published in 1896, contained his lectures on the discipline of meditation and a free translation of Patañjali's Yoga Sūtra. With his books on Karma, Bhakti and Jñāna Yoga, it presented Hinduism as four paths suited to four temperaments: work, love, psychic control and philosophy. This scheme is his own arrangement of older ideas, and it strongly shaped how yoga was later presented in the West.

events.title: Ramaṇa's death-experience at Madurai
events.description: In July 1896 a sixteen-year-old schoolboy in Madurai was seized by a sudden fear that he was about to die. He lay down, held his breath, and asked himself what it is that dies. The body would be burned, he saw, but the "I" watching the question was untouched.¶The fear never returned. Six weeks later he left home with three rupees for the hill of Aruṇācala, and stayed there for the remaining fifty-four years of his life. He wrote little and taught mostly in silence. To those who asked he gave one method: trace the thought "I" back to its source.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Ramakrishna Mission founded
events.description: On 1 May 1897 Vivekānanda gathered Rāmakṛṣṇa's monastic and lay disciples in Calcutta and founded an organisation with a new idea for Hindu monasticism: monks would run schools, hospitals and relief camps.¶The principle was his master's remark that one should not speak of compassion for living beings but of service to them as God, "śiva-jñāne jīva-sevā". Its motto is "for one's own liberation and the welfare of the world". Land for the headquarters at Belūr Maṭh on the Gaṅgā was bought in 1898 and the monastery consecrated in 1899, while plague and famine relief began at once.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Cāpekar brothers assassinate Rand at Pune
events.description: Plague reached Pune in 1897. The commissioner, W. C. Rand, sent British soldiers to search houses; they entered kitchens and prayer rooms and examined women in public. On 22 June the three Cāpekar brothers shot Rand and an officer as they left a celebration of Queen Victoria's jubilee. All three were hanged. Ṭiḷak, whose newspaper had denounced the searches, was sentenced to eighteen months for sedition.

events.title: Nārāyaṇa Guru's Ātmopadeśa Śatakam
events.description: Nārāyaṇa Guru, the Kerala saint and reformer, wrote the Ātmopadeśa Śatakam, "a hundred verses of self-instruction," in Malayalam in about 1897. The poem expounds a non-dual vision, in which the self is the same in all and knowledge is the way beyond sorrow, and its tone is simple and lyrical. Nārāyaṇa Guru is known for his social work against untouchability, in particular his consecration of a Śiva liṅga at Aruvippuram in 1888. His teachings, including "one caste, one religion, one God for man," were influential.

events.title: Vivekānanda's Colombo-to-Almora lectures
events.description: After his success in the West, Vivekānanda returned to Colombo in January 1897 and travelled to Madras, Calcutta and later to Almora, receiving a hero's welcome and giving a series of lectures, later published as Lectures from Colombo to Almora. He called on Indians to awaken, drawing on the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, and to serve the poor as God, the idea of Daridra Nārāyaṇa. In May 1897 he founded the Ramakrishna Mission, to put service into practice.

events.title: Sister Niveditā arrives in Calcutta
events.description: Margaret Noble, an Irish schoolteacher, heard Vivekānanda in London and followed him to Calcutta in 1898. He named her Niveditā, "the dedicated". She opened a school for girls in a lane of north Calcutta, nursed plague victims in the slums, and after his death threw herself into the national movement, encouraging scientists, artists and revolutionaries alike. Her epitaph at Darjeeling reads: here reposes Sister Niveditā who gave her all to India.

events.title: Annie Besant founds the Central Hindu College
events.description: In 1898 Annie Besant, the Theosophist, founded the Central Hindu College at Benares with the support of local Hindu leaders. Its aim was to give Hindu students a modern education together with instruction in Hindu religion and ethics, so that they would not have to choose between Western secular schooling and missionary schools. The college prepared its own textbooks of Sanātana Dharma for this purpose.¶When Madan Mohan Malaviya's plan for a Hindu university took shape, the college was handed over to it and became the nucleus of Banaras Hindu University, founded in 1916. It stands at the start of a long effort to combine a Hindu education with modern science, and it shows the part Theosophists played in the Hindu revival of the period.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Birsā Muṇḍā's Ulgulān
events.description: Birsā Muṇḍā, a young man of the Muṇḍā tribe in Choṭānāgpur, preached that his people should worship one God, give up sacrifice and spirits, and recover the land taken by landlords and missions. He was hailed as "Father of the Earth". At Christmas 1899 his followers attacked police stations and churches with bows and axes. He was captured and died in Ranchi jail in June 1900, aged twenty-five.

events.title: Advaita Āśrama, Māyāvatī
events.description: Advaita Āśrama was founded at Māyāvatī, in the Himalayas near Lohāghāṭ in Uttarakhand, in 1899 at Vivekānanda's inspiration, with Captain J. H. Sevier and his wife Charlotte as chief supporters. It was dedicated to the pure Advaita Vedānta teaching and has no images or ritual worship. It is also the home of the journal Prabuddha Bharata and of a publishing house, and it holds the collected works of Vivekānanda.

events.title: Vivekānanda begins Durgā Pūjā at Belūr
events.description: In 1901 Vivekānanda organised the Durgā Pūjā at Belūr Math, the headquarters of the Ramakrishna order near Kolkata, in the traditional manner, with the image of the goddess. Śāradā Devī, the wife of Rāmakṛṣṇa, was present and supported it, and the ritual included Kumārī Pūjā, the worship of a young girl as the goddess. This continues today as an annual observance, and presents the order's approach of merging Vedāntic monasticism with devotion to the Mother.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: P. C. Rāy's History of Hindu Chemistry
events.description: Prafulla Chandra Rāy, a chemist, wrote the two-volume History of Hindu Chemistry (1902 and 1908), which collected material on rasa-śāstra, the Sanskrit tradition of mercury and mineral preparation, and argued for its achievements. It helped recover texts and shaped national pride in Indian science. Jagadīś Candra Bose, the physicist and plant physiologist, was a contemporary in Kolkata who worked on radio waves and plant response, and both men used their science to answer colonial claims about Indian capacity.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Svāmī Rāmatīrtha's mission to Japan and America
events.description: Tīrtha Rām, a brilliant professor of mathematics at Lahore, heard Vivekānanda in 1897 and became a monk as Svāmī Rāmatīrtha. He travelled to Japan in 1902 and spent two years lecturing in America on "practical Vedānta", speaking of himself only as "Rāma" and laughing constantly. He drowned in the Gaṅgā in 1906 at thirty-three. Other teachers followed the same road west in these years.

events.title: Death of Vivekānanda at Belūr Maṭh
events.description: Vivekānanda died at Belūr Maṭh on the evening of 4 July 1902, aged thirty-nine, after a day spent teaching Sanskrit grammar to the novices and walking with a brother monk. He had said he would not live to see forty. In nine years of public life he had given Hindus a new confidence, told them that service of the poor is worship, and told the West that India had something to teach.

events.title: Munśīrām founds Gurukul Kāṅgṛī
events.description: Lālā Munśīrām, a Punjabi lawyer and Ārya Samāj leader, believed the DAV schools were too English. In 1902 he founded a residential school in the forest near Haridvāra on the ancient pattern: boys entered at seven, lived with their teachers for sixteen years, and were taught everything, including science, through Hindi and Sanskrit. He later became a monk as Svāmī Śraddhānanda.

events.title: Śāhū Mahārāj's reservation order
events.description: Chatrapati Śāhū of Kolhāpur, a descendant of Śivājī, issued an order in 1902 reserving half of the vacancies in the state's government posts for backward communities, one of the earliest such measures in British India. He had been in a dispute with orthodox brāhmaṇa priests, who in 1899 refused to perform Vedic (vedokta) rites for him on the ground that he, as a Marāṭhā, was not a kṣatriya. His reforms were supported by the Satyaśodhak movement.

events.title: SNDP Yogam founded for the Īḻavas
events.description: The Śrī Nārāyaṇa Dharma Paripālana Yogam was founded in 1903 with Nārāyaṇa Guru as president, the doctor Palpu as organiser and the poet Kumāran Āśān as secretary. It set out to raise the Īḻavas, a large community treated as untouchable in Kerala, by building their own temples, schools and businesses. The Guru's advice was: gain strength through organisation, gain freedom through education.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Ṭiḷak's Arctic Home and Orion
events.description: Ṭiḷak was a mathematician by training. In Orion (1893) he argued from references to the position of the spring equinox among the stars that parts of the Ṛgveda go back to about 4500 BCE. In The Arctic Home in the Vedas (1903), written partly in jail, he proposed that the ancestors of the Vedic people had lived near the North Pole. Few scholars accept either, but both were serious attempts to date the Veda scientifically.

events.title: British fill Koṇārka's jagamohana with sand
events.description: The Sūrya temple at Koṇārka in Odisha, built in the 13th century, had been in a poor condition by the 19th and early 20th centuries, with its tower fallen and its main hall at risk of collapse. Around 1903 to 1905, the British authorities filled the jagamohana, the hall of the temple, with sand and sealed the openings to stop it from falling in. The sand remained for about a century, and the Archaeological Survey of India has since studied removing it.

events.title: Ancient Monuments Preservation Act
events.description: The Ancient Monuments Preservation Act of 1904 was passed under Viceroy Lord Curzon, with John Marshall as the Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India. It gave the government powers to protect and repair historic buildings, including temples, and to regulate their trade and sale, and it covered monuments in private hands. It laid the foundation for the state's role in conserving temples as heritage, which later laws updated, and it continues to shape their care.

events.title: Partition of Bengal and Svadeśī
events.description: In 1905 the Viceroy, Lord Curzon, divided Bengal into a Hindu-majority west and a Muslim-majority east. On the day it took effect, 16 October, Calcutta fasted and people tied rākhī threads on one another's wrists at Tagore's suggestion. The boycott of British cloth and the Svadeśī movement followed, with "Vande Mātaram" as its cry. Abanīndranāth Tagore painted Bhārat Mātā as a saffron-robed ascetic. The partition was annulled in 1911.

events.title: Servants of India Society
events.description: Gopāl Kṛṣṇa Gokhale, a mathematics professor and the leading moderate in Congress, founded the Servants of India Society at Pune in 1905. Its members took vows of poverty and gave their lives to public work: education, famine relief, the uplift of the depressed classes. He wanted, he said, to spiritualise politics. Gāndhī called Gokhale his political guru.

events.title: Muslim League and Punjab Hindu Sabhā founded
events.description: In December 1906 Muslim landowners and nobles meeting at Dhaka founded the All-India Muslim League to protect Muslim political interests, and soon won separate electorates. In Punjab, where Hindus were a minority, Lālā Lājpat Rāy and others formed a Hindu Sabhā from 1906–09 to speak for them. From this point Indian politics was increasingly organised by religious community.

events.title: First Hindu temple in the USA
events.description: The Vedanta Society of San Francisco built a temple in 1905–06 under Svāmī Trigunātītānanda, a disciple of Rāmakṛṣṇa. Its towers deliberately mix a Bengal temple spire, a Śiva temple dome, a Moorish cupola and a European castle turret, to show that all religions lead to one truth. It survived the earthquake of 1906 and still stands. It is regarded as the first Hindu temple in the Western world.

events.title: Badung Puputan in Bali
events.description: A puputan is a ritual fight to the death. In 1906 the Balinese rulers of Badung, near Denpasar, faced a Dutch military expedition and chose to go out in formal dress to face the guns rather than surrender, followed by their families. A similar event occurred at Klungkung in 1908. Dutch accounts record large numbers of dead. The events ended the independence of southern Bali and are remembered on the island as acts of honour.

events.title: BAPS founded at Bocāsaṇ
events.description: Svāmī Yajñapuruṣdās, known as Śāstrījī Mahārāj, held that Svāminārāyaṇa had named the monk Guṇātītānanda as his ideal devotee, "Akṣara", and that God and this devotee should be worshipped together. The existing leadership rejected the idea. In 1905 he left Vaḍtāl with five monks, and in 1907 consecrated images of both at a new temple in Bocāsaṇ. The organisation takes its name, BAPS, from that village.

events.title: Candraśekharendra Sarasvatī ascends the Kāñcī Pīṭha
events.description: In 1907 a thirteen-year-old schoolboy named Svāmināthan was installed as the sixty-eighth head of the Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi monastery, following the death of his predecessor. As Candraśekharendra Sarasvatī he held the seat for eighty-seven years, until 1994, travelling widely on foot. He is remembered for a life of extreme simplicity and for talks, collected as "The Voice of God", that explain Hindu tradition in plain Tamil.

events.title: Gaṇapati Muni names Ramaṇa
events.description: Kāvyakaṇṭha Gaṇapati Muni was a Sanskrit scholar and tapasvin who met the young sage of Aruṇācala in 1907. Asking for instruction, he was told to watch where the sense of "I" arises. Moved by this, he declared the sage to be "Bhagavān Śrī Ramaṇa Maharṣi", the name by which the sage has since been known. Gaṇapati Muni's Sanskrit work Śrī Ramaṇa Gītā records the teaching, and the name given to Venkaṭarāman marked the start of wide recognition of his teaching.

events.title: Khudīrām Bose hanged
events.description: Khudīrām Bose, a schoolboy from Midnapore, joined a revolutionary group at fifteen. On 30 April 1908 at Muzaffarpur he and a companion threw a bomb at a carriage they believed carried a hated magistrate; it killed two Englishwomen. He was caught the next day and hanged on 11 August, aged eighteen. Witnesses said he walked to the scaffold smiling. Weavers in Bengal made dhotis with his name on the border.

events.title: Sāvarkar's 1857 history and Ḍhīṅgrā's shooting
events.description: Vināyak Dāmodar Sāvarkar, a law student at India House in London, wrote a history of 1857 calling it not a mutiny but the first war of independence; it was banned in India before it was printed. In July 1909 Madanlāl Ḍhīṅgrā, one of his circle, shot a senior India Office official in London. At his trial Ḍhīṅgrā said that an Englishman would do the same if Germans occupied England.

events.title: Gāndhī writes Hind Svarāj on a ship
events.description: In November 1909, on the ship from London to South Africa, Gāndhī wrote Hind Svarāj in ten days, in Gujarati, using both hands when one tired. It is a dialogue with an imagined revolutionary. He argues that India is held down not by the English but by its fascination with their civilisation of machines, lawyers and doctors, and that real self-rule is rule over oneself. The British banned it.

events.title: Shamasastry publishes the Kauṭilīya Arthaśāstra
events.description: In 1905 a pandit from the Tañjāvūr region handed a palm-leaf manuscript to R. Shamasastry, librarian at Mysore. It proved to be the Arthaśāstra, the treatise on statecraft ascribed to Cāṇakya, known for centuries only by name. He published the text in 1909 and a translation in 1915. It showed the world an ancient India of bureaucrats, spies, tax tables and hard-headed foreign policy.

events.title: Śṛṅgeri pontiff restores Śaṅkara's birthplace Kālaḍi
events.description: The thirty-third head of the Śṛṅgeri monastery, Saccidānanda Śivābhinava Nṛsiṃha Bhāratī, went looking for Śaṅkara's birthplace, which had been lost to memory. He identified Kālaḍi on the Periyār in Kerala, acquired the land with the help of the Mahārājā of Travancore, and in 1910 consecrated temples there to Śaṅkara and to Śāradā. Kālaḍi is now a pilgrimage centre, and the Śṛṅgeri tradition accepts his identification, though sources on Śaṅkara's life do not all agree on his birthplace.

events.title: Ṭiḷak writes Gītā Rahasya at Mandalay
events.description: Sentenced in 1908 to six years for sedition, Ṭiḷak was sent to Mandalay in Burma. There, with a few hundred books and pencils, he wrote the Gītā Rahasya in Marathi in about five months.¶Most commentators since Śaṅkara had read the Gītā as teaching renunciation, or devotion. Ṭiḷak argued that its real message is karma yoga: energetic action in the world, done as duty and without selfish attachment, even after wisdom is gained. For a generation fighting foreign rule, this made the Gītā a manual of action. Gāndhī and Aurobindo each answered it with their own readings.

events.title: Aurobindo arrives at Pondicherry
events.description: Aravinda Ghoṣ had been the most radical voice of the freedom movement, the first to demand full independence in print. Jailed for a year in the Alipore bomb case, he reported in his Uttarpārā speech that he had a vision of Kṛṣṇa in every prisoner and jailer.¶Acquitted, and warned of re-arrest, he sailed in 1910 to French-ruled Pondicherry and never left. Over forty years he worked out an "integral yoga" whose aim was not escape from the world but the descent of a higher consciousness to transform it. His partner in the work was Mirra Alfassa, known as the Mother.

events.title: Sāvarkar's leap at Marseilles
events.description: Arrested in London in 1910, Sāvarkar was being shipped to India for trial when the vessel anchored at Marseilles. He squeezed through a porthole, swam ashore and ran, but French police handed him back. A court sentenced him to two life terms, fifty years, in the Cellular Jail of the Andamans. He spent ten years there, yoked to an oil mill, composing poems on the walls of his cell.

events.title: Upāsanī Mahārāj and Meher Bābā's Sāī lineage
events.description: Upāsanī Mahārāj of Sākorī, who lived from 1870 to 1941, was a disciple of Sāī Bābā of Shirdi and a major figure in spreading his tradition. He established the Sākorī āśram near Shirdi, and in 1932 founded the Kanyā Kumārī Sthān, a community for unmarried women ascetics, a rare institution at the time. Meher Bābā, born in Pune, was another who credited Sāī Bābā and Upāsanī as his masters, and later gathered his own following across the world.

events.title: Janakī Mandir built at Janakpur
events.description: The Janakī Mandir at Janakpur (Janakpurdhām) in Nepal's Dhanuṣā district was built in 1910 by Queen Vṛṣabhānu Kuṃvari of Ṭīkamgaṛh, a state linked with Orchhā. The three-storeyed white building of stone and marble, with lattice windows and Maithil wall paintings, stands on the ground that tradition identifies with Sītā's home in Mithilā, the land of King Janaka.¶Janakpur is among the most important Rāma–Sītā pilgrimage places, linked with the Rāmāyaṇa story of Sītā found in the furrow and with her marriage to Rāma. The temple, built by a queen from central India, shows that Vaiṣṇava devotion ties Nepal's Tarai to the Gaṅgā plain, and it draws large crowds at Vivāha Pañcamī.

events.title: Bāmākṣepā, the mad saint of Tārāpīṭh
events.description: Bāmākṣepā, who lived from 1837 to 1911, was a Śākta saint of Tārāpīṭh in Bīrbhūm, Bengal, known as the "mad saint" for his indifference to social rules. He was a devotee of the goddess Tārā and is said to have practised at the cremation ground near the temple, where his samādhi stands. Stories of his eccentric conduct and miracles circulate widely in Bengal and shaped the popular image of Bengali Tantra, though most accounts come from devotional biographies.

gitaQuote.verse: पिताहमस्य जगतो माता धाता पितामहः । वेद्यं पवित्रमोंकार ऋक्साम यजुरेव च ॥ गतिर्भर्ता प्रभुः साक्षी निवासः शरणं सुहृत् । प्रभवः प्रलयः स्थानं निधानं बीजमव्ययम् ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ | vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛk sāma yajur eva ca || gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣī nivāsaḥ śaraṇaṁ suhṛt | prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||
gitaQuote.translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer and the grandsire. I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the sacred syllable OM, and also the Rig, the Sama and the Yajur Vedas. I am the goal, the supporter, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the creation and dissolution, the foundation and the imperishable seed.
gitaQuote.chapter: Bhagavad Gītā 9.17–18 (Rāja Vidyā Rāja Guhya Yoga)

events.title: Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies
events.description: The research department of the Ḍogrā state of Jammu and Kashmir began to print important Sanskrit texts of Kashmiri Śaivism and other traditions in 1911, in a series called the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies. It published works such as the Tantrāloka of Abhinavagupta and other Trika texts, edited by scholars like Mukunda Rāma Śāstrī. Because Kashmiri Śaiva works had been only in manuscripts, this printing made them available to modern readers and began their international study.

events.title: Delhi Durbar of 1911 moves the capital
events.description: In December 1911 George V held a durbar at Delhi, the only British monarch to visit India as emperor. He announced two things: the partition of Bengal was cancelled, and the capital would move from Calcutta to Delhi. A new city designed by Lutyens and Baker was built over the next twenty years and inaugurated in 1931, on a site long associated in tradition with the Pāṇḍavas' Indraprastha.

events.title: Bhāsa's plays rediscovered
events.description: In 1909 the scholar T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī found palm-leaf manuscripts at Manalikkara in the former Travancore state containing thirteen Sanskrit plays, none of which named an author. He edited and published them from Tiruvanantapuram in 1912 and attributed them to Bhāsa, the early dramatist praised by Kālidāsa and long thought lost. They include the Svapnavāsavadatta. Scholars have debated both the authorship and the date, but the find greatly widened knowledge of early Sanskrit drama.

events.title: Candraśekhara Bhāratī III becomes Śṛṅgeri jagadguru
events.description: Candraśekhara Bhāratī III was the jagadguru of the Śṛṅgeri Śāradā Pīṭha from 1912 to 1954, regarded by devotees as a jīvanmukta, one liberated while living. He was known for personal austerity and for deep learning in Advaita. He wrote a well-known commentary on Śaṅkara's Vivekacūḍāmaṇi, which continues to be studied. His life as a monk and teacher is recalled in books by the Śṛṅgeri community, and Paul Brunton wrote of a meeting with him in A Search in Secret India.

events.title: Brahmacaitanya Goṇḍavalekar and Rāma-nāma
events.description: Brahmacaitanya Goṇḍavalekar Mahārāj (1845–1913) was a Marathi saint of Goṇḍavale in Satara district who taught the repetition of Rāma's name. His guru was the saint Tukāmāī, and he taught that constant remembrance of the Name was the simplest path for all. He is reported to have drawn a large following, including people from many communities. His samādhi at Goṇḍavale is a pilgrimage centre, and the Rāma-nāma teaching continues through his institutions.

gitaQuote.verse: सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः । रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥ अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ | rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ || avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavanty ahar-āgame | rātry-āgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-saṁjñake ||
gitaQuote.translation: Those who understand the cosmic day of Brahma extending for a thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion years) and his night ending after a thousand Mahayugas—they indeed know the truth of day and night. At the dawn of Brahma’s day all manifestations stream forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night they dissolve into that very unmanifest.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur Edition; commentary by Ādi Śaṅkarācārya and Śrīdhara Svāmī

events.title: Tagore's Nobel Prize
events.description: Rabindranāth Tagore translated some of his Bengali songs into English prose during an illness in 1912. The poet W. B. Yeats read them in manuscript and wrote that he had to close the book in buses lest strangers see how it moved him. Gītāñjali, "Song Offerings", won the Nobel Prize in 1913, the first to an Asian. Its God is the Upaniṣadic one found in the dust and in the labourer.

events.title: Ghadar Party
events.description: Punjabi farmers who had emigrated to the west coast of America and Canada met racism and exclusion laws there, and concluded that they would have no respect abroad while India was unfree. In 1913 they founded the Ghadar, "Mutiny", party in San Francisco, Sikh, Hindu and Muslim together. When war came in 1914 thousands sailed home to raise a revolt. The plan was betrayed and dozens were hanged.

events.title: Rāmānujan writes to Hardy
events.description: In January 1913 the Madras Port Trust clerk Srinivāsa Rāmānujan sent the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy a letter with pages of formulas and theorems, many without proof. Hardy recognised genius and arranged for him to come to Cambridge in 1914. Rāmānujan was a devotee of the family goddess Nāmagiri of Nāmakkal and said that she inspired his results, which came to him in dreams. He is a rare case of a modern mathematician who openly linked his work with his faith.

events.title: Rājā Hariścandra
events.description: Rājā Hariścandra, made in 1913 by Dhuṇḍirāj Govind Phāḷke, known as Dādāsāheb Phāḷke, is regarded as India's first full-length feature film. It was a silent film telling the story of the truthful king Hariścandra, drawn from the Purāṇas. Phāḷke continued with mythological subjects, including Laṅkā Dahan in 1917 about Hanumān. Epic and Purāṇic stories became the foundation of early Indian cinema, which thus carried Hindu narrative to a mass audience.

events.title: Ṭembe Svāmī (Vāsudevānanda Sarasvatī)
events.description: Vāsudevānanda Sarasvatī, called Ṭembe Svāmī, lived from 1854 to 1914 and was a leading figure of the Datta tradition, a Marāṭhī scholar-ascetic who travelled widely in Maharashtra and Gujarat and settled along the Narmadā. He wrote prolifically in Sanskrit, including a Sanskrit rendering of the Gurucaritra, the Marathi scripture of Datta devotion, called the Dvisāhasrī Gurucaritra. He was also a defender of Vedic orthodoxy, and his works include commentaries and hymns. He is remembered as a major reviver of Datta worship.

events.title: Aurobindo launches the journal Arya
events.description: From 1914 to 1921 Aurobindo published a sixty-four page philosophical monthly, Arya, writing nearly all of it himself. In it his major works appeared in instalments side by side: The Life Divine, on evolution as the unfolding of spirit in matter; The Synthesis of Yoga; Essays on the Gita; and The Secret of the Veda, which reads the Ṛgvedic hymns as a record of inner experience.

events.title: Seal's Positive Sciences of the Ancient Hindus
events.description: Brajendranāth Seal's The Positive Sciences of the Ancient Hindus (1915) surveyed Indian work in mechanics, chemistry, biology and mathematics, drawing on Sanskrit sources, and sought to show a scientific tradition. Bibhūtibhūṣaṇ Datta, a mathematician, studied Indian mathematics, and later with A. N. Singh wrote a History of Hindu Mathematics. events.title: Akhil Bhāratīya Hindū Mahāsabhā
events.description: Provincial Hindu Sabhās had existed for a decade. At the Haridvāra Kumbha in April 1915 they joined to form an all-India body, with Madan Mohan Mālavīya as its guiding figure. In its early years most of its leaders were also Congress members, and it worked on cow protection, Hindi and social reform. Under Sāvarkar from 1937 it became a political party opposed to both the Congress and the Muslim League.

events.title: Gāndhī returns to India
events.description: Gāndhī returned from South Africa in January 1915, aged forty-five, already famous. On Gokhale's advice he spent a year travelling India third class "with his ears open and his mouth shut". He founded an āśram at Ahmedabad, moved in 1917 to the bank of the Sābarmatī, and scandalised his backers by admitting a family of untouchables as full members.

events.title: Prājña Pāṭhaśālā founded at Wāī
events.description: At Wāī in Maharashtra, Kevalānanda Sarasvatī founded the Prājña Pāṭhaśālā in 1916, a school for Vedic and śāstric learning that became a centre of research. Lakṣmaṇaśāstrī Jośī, a scholar linked with the school, later edited the Dharmakośa, a large Sanskrit encyclopaedia of Hindu law and ritual terms drawn from the old texts. The work shows how traditional paṇḍits in the early twentieth century organised their learning in modern scholarly forms.

events.title: Banaras Hindu University founded
events.description: Paṇḍit Madan Mohan Mālavīya spent a decade raising money, village by village and prince by prince, for a university that would teach modern science and engineering alongside Sanskrit learning. The foundation stone was laid on 4 February 1916.¶At the opening Gāndhī, newly back from South Africa, gave a speech scolding the jewelled princes on the platform, and several walked out. BHU became one of Asia's largest residential universities, with faculties from Sanskrit theology to mining and medicine.

events.title: Ṭiḷak founds the Home Rule League
events.description: Released from Mandalay in 1914, Ṭiḷak founded the Home Rule League in 1916 and toured Maharashtra and Karnataka. His sentence, "Svarāj is my birthright and I shall have it", spoken in Marathi, became the best-known line of the freedom movement. The same year at Lucknow he reunited the two wings of Congress and agreed a common platform with the Muslim League.

events.title: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute
events.description: The Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute was founded at Pune in 1917 and named for the Sanskritist R. G. Bhāṇḍārkar. Two years later it took on a task many thought impossible: a critical edition of the Mahābhārata.¶Scholars led by V. S. Sukthankar collated 1,259 manuscripts in a dozen scripts from Kashmir to Kerala and printed the text they share, with every variant below. Passages found in only some regions, including some famous episodes, went to the notes. The nineteen volumes took forty-seven years and were completed in 1966. They are the edition most serious study of the epic now cites.

events.title: Campāraṇ satyāgraha
events.description: In Campāraṇ, in north Bihar, European planters forced tenants to grow indigo on part of their land and sell it at a fixed price. A farmer, Rājkumār Śukla, pestered Gāndhī until he came in April 1917. Ordered to leave the district, Gāndhī refused and pleaded guilty in court; the case was dropped. He recorded the statements of eight thousand peasants, and the system was abolished within a year.

events.title: Indian festivals take root in the Caribbean
events.description: From 1838 to 1917, Indian indentured labourers were brought to Trinidad, Guyana, Suriname and other colonies. They carried the Rāmāyaṇa, Holī (called Phagwah) and Dīvālī with them, and by about 1917 had built mandirs and gathered communities of worship. These festivals became public and national in character: Trinidad made Dīvālī a public holiday in 1966. The communities kept Bhojpurī and Awadhī songs and rites alive for generations, shaping a distinct Caribbean Hindu culture.

events.title: Yogānanda founds Yogoda Satsaṅga
events.description: Kriyā Yoga traces itself to an immortal Himalayan master, Bābājī, who is said in tradition to have taught it in 1861 to Lāhiṛī Mahāśaya, a householder and government accountant living at Vārāṇasī. He taught it quietly to many of any caste or religion. His disciple Śrī Yukteśvar, an astrologer-monk, trained Yogānanda, who founded the Yogoda Satsaṅga Society of India in 1917. Its American counterpart, the Self-Realization Fellowship, followed in 1920.

events.title: Death of Sāī Bābā of Śirḍī
events.description: A fakir of unknown birth arrived as a youth at Śirḍī, a village in Maharashtra, and lived for sixty years in a ruined mosque he called Dvārakāmāī, keeping a sacred fire burning. He quoted the Gītā and the Qur'an, and his constant saying was "the Lord of all is one". Hindus and Muslims both claimed him. He died on 15 October 1918. Śirḍī is now among the most visited shrines in India.

events.title: Kashmir Series begins publishing Abhinavagupta
events.description: The Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies was begun in 1911 under the patronage of the rulers of Jammu and Kashmir and continued until 1947. Its editors, among them Mukunda Rāma Śāstrī and later Madhusūdan Kaul Śāstrī, published major works of Kashmir Śaivism, including the Tantrāloka of Abhinavagupta, issued in volumes from 1918, in editions that made these texts accessible to scholars. Abhinavagupta's Abhinavabhāratī, his commentary on the Nāṭyaśāstra, was edited separately in the Baroda Gaekwad's Oriental Series.

events.title: Yogendra and Kuvalayānanda begin scientific yoga
events.description: Two Indian teachers began studying yoga with laboratory instruments and medical methods, hoping to show its effects on the body in terms modern science could assess. Yogendra founded the Yoga Institute at Mumbai in 1918, and Swāmī Kuvalayānanda opened Kaivalyadhāma at Loṇāvaḷā in 1924, publishing the journal Yoga-Mīmāṃsā. Their work moved āsana and prāṇāyāma from ascetic practice towards health, education and hospital settings. It also set a pattern of presenting yoga through physiology that shaped its spread in India and abroad during the twentieth century.

events.title: Jallianwala Bagh massacre
events.description: On 13 April 1919, the day of the Vaisākhī festival, a crowd of perhaps fifteen thousand gathered in Jallianwala Bagh, a walled garden in Amritsar, in defiance of a ban on meetings few knew about. General Dyer marched in fifty riflemen, blocked the main exit, and without warning fired 1,650 rounds in ten minutes. The official count was 379 dead; Indian estimates exceed a thousand. Tagore returned his knighthood.

events.title: Non-Cooperation begins as Ṭiḷak dies
events.description: Ṭiḷak died in Bombay on 1 August 1920; a crowd of two hundred thousand followed his body, and Gāndhī was among the bearers. That same day Gāndhī launched Non-Cooperation: Indians would give up titles, courts, schools and foreign cloth. He had allied with Muslim leaders angry at the fate of the Turkish Caliphate. For two years it was the largest movement India had seen.

events.title: Yogānanda sails for America
events.description: Mukunda Lāl Ghoṣ, a Bengali disciple of Śrī Yukteśvar, took monastic vows as Yogānanda. In 1920 he sailed to Boston as India's delegate to an international congress of religious liberals and stayed in America for most of the next three decades. He lectured to packed halls, taught the breathing technique called Kriyā Yoga through lessons sent by post, and founded the Self-Realization Fellowship in 1920, establishing its Los Angeles headquarters at Mount Washington in 1925.

events.title: Akālī Gurdwārā Reform Movement
events.description: In the early twentieth century many Sikh shrines were controlled by hereditary mahants, including Udāsī ascetics, whom reformers accused of misusing endowments and of practices at odds with Sikh teaching. The Akālī movement campaigned to bring the gurdwaras under Sikh community management, with protests and some violent episodes, such as the Nankāṇā Sāhib killings in February 1921. The Shiromaṇi Gurdwārā Prabandhak Committee was formed in 1920, and the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925 gave it legal authority over the major shrines.

events.title: Indian indentured labour system abolished
events.description: Indian indentured emigration was suspended in 1917, and the system was officially abolished in 1920. Campaigners had denounced the abuses of the system, which sent about a million people to colonies such as Fiji, Mauritius, the Caribbean and Natal. Mohandas Gāndhī, Madan Mohan Mālavīya and the missionary C. F. Andrews were among those who spoke out against it. Indian nationalists treated the matter as one of national honour. The descendants of indentured workers form many of today's Hindu diaspora communities.

events.title: Death of Śāradā Devī
events.description: Śāradā Devī, the wife and spiritual companion of Rāmakṛṣṇa, whom the order calls the Holy Mother, died in Kolkata in July 1920. After her husband's death she became the guide of the monastic order and of many householders, and she initiated disciples. She is remembered for her warmth and for saying that no one is a stranger and that the whole world is one's own. Her teaching of universal kinship is cited as one of the order's central ideals.

events.title: Harappa excavated
events.description: Bricks from an ancient mound at Harappa in Punjab had been carted away in the 1850s as ballast for a railway. In 1921 Dayā Rām Sāhnī of the Archaeological Survey began to dig what remained and found seals with an unknown script in levels far below anything dated. With Mohenjo-daro the next year, it pushed back the known beginning of Indian civilization by some two thousand years.

events.title: Moplah (Māppiḷa) rebellion
events.description: In August 1921 the Māppiḷas, Muslim tenants of Malabar in Kerala, rose against British authority and their landlords, many of them Hindu, amid the Khilāfat agitation. For some months rebel leaders ruled parts of the district. Hindus were killed or forcibly converted and temples were attacked, as the official reports record. The army suppressed the rising, and about seventy prisoners died in the "wagon tragedy" in November. Historians still debate whether it was chiefly an agrarian, anti-colonial or communal revolt. It strained Hindu–Muslim cooperation in the freedom movement.

events.title: Viśva-Bhāratī founded at Śāntiniketan
events.description: Rabindranāth Tagore, who had opened a school at Śāntiniketan in 1901, inaugurated Viśva-Bhāratī there in 1921 as a place where India could meet the world. The institution emphasised teaching in open surroundings, along with art, music and the study of Asian cultures. It drew scholars from India and abroad, including Sylvain Lévi. It became a central university in 1951.

events.title: Mohenjo-daro discovered
events.description: In 1922 Rākhāl Dās Banerji was excavating a Buddhist stūpa on a mound in Sindh locally called "the mound of the dead" when he found seals like those from Harappa, 600 kilometres away. Sir John Marshall announced the discovery of a new civilization in 1924. Within a week scholars pointed out that identical seals had turned up in Mesopotamia, which gave the date.

events.title: Chaurī Chaurā
events.description: On 4 February 1922 at Chaurī Chaurā, a market town near Gorakhpur, police fired on a Non-Cooperation procession. The crowd chased them into their station and set it alight; twenty-two policemen burned to death. Gāndhī, who had promised the movement would be non-violent, called it off at once across the whole country, to the fury of his colleagues, and fasted for five days. He was jailed weeks later.

events.title: Dasgupta's History of Indian Philosophy
events.description: Surendranāth Dāsgupta, a philosopher at Calcutta and Cambridge, wrote A History of Indian Philosophy in five volumes, published between 1922 and 1955. It surveyed the major darśanas, Hindu, Buddhist and Jaina, drawing on primary manuscripts and commentaries. For decades it was the standard English-language account, and it is still cited, though later scholars have corrected and updated many of its views.

events.title: Gītā Press founded
events.description: Jayadayāl Goyandkā, a Mārvāṛī trader devoted to the Gītā, was annoyed by the misprints in the editions he gave away. In 1923 he started his own press at Gorakhpur. With Hanumān Prasād Poddār as editor it began the monthly Kalyāṇ in 1926. It sells at cost, takes no advertisements and prints no living person's picture. It has published the Gītā in tens of millions of copies, and the Rāmcaritmānas in vast numbers.

events.title: Sāvarkar writes Essentials of Hindutva
events.description: Vināyak Dāmodar Sāvarkar wrote this essay in 1922 while confined at Ratnāgirī, after about ten years in the Andaman cellular jail, and it was published in 1923. It asks who is a Hindu, and answers in terms of nation and culture rather than doctrine: anyone who regards the land from the Indus to the seas as both fatherland (pitṛbhū) and holy land (puṇyabhū).¶By that test Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists are Hindus whatever they believe, and Sāvarkar, himself an atheist, distinguished "Hindutva" sharply from Hinduism as a religion. The book became the founding text of Hindu nationalism and remains one of the most argued-over works of modern India.

events.title: Śraddhānanda's śuddhi campaign among Malkānās
events.description: After the Malabar rising, Svāmī Śraddhānanda took up śuddhi, a purification rite by which converts and their descendants could return to Hinduism. In 1923 it was offered to the Malkānās, Rajput-descended communities near Āgrā who were nominally Muslim but kept many Hindu customs, and tens of thousands are reported to have accepted. Muslim organisations replied with their own missions, and tension grew. On 23 December 1926 a Muslim visitor shot Śraddhānanda dead on his sickbed.

events.title: Ānandamayī Mā recognised at Dhaka
events.description: Nirmalā Sundarī, born in 1896 in a village now in Bangladesh, passed through intense states of absorption as a young wife. Followers in Dhaka in the 1920s began to call her Ānandamayī Mā, "the bliss-filled mother". She said of herself that she had always been the same and claimed no teaching of her own. Her devotees included householders, scholars and political figures, and after 1947 she travelled widely in India. She died in 1982, and her āśrams continue in several cities.

events.title: Vaikom Satyāgraha
events.description: In Travancore, Īḻavas and other "lower" castes were forbidden even to walk on the roads around the Śiva temple at Vaikom. From March 1924 volunteers in groups of three, one from each community, walked up to the barrier each day and were arrested.¶The campaign lasted about twenty months. Nārāyaṇa Guru gave his support, Periyār came from Tamil Nadu and was jailed, upper-caste Hindus marched to the capital in sympathy, and Gāndhī negotiated with the regent. In 1925 three of the four roads were opened. It was one of the first organised mass movements in India for the rights of the excluded castes.

events.title: Bhāratī Kṛṣṇa Tīrtha becomes Purī Śaṅkarācārya
events.description: Bhāratī Kṛṣṇa Tīrtha became the Śaṅkarācārya of the Govardhana Maṭha in Purī in 1925 and held the post until his death in 1960. A scholar of mathematics as well as Sanskrit, he is known as the author of "Vedic Mathematics", published posthumously in 1965, which presents sixteen sūtras said to give quick methods of calculation. Scholars have not found the sūtras in any known Vedic text, and the book's claim to Vedic origin is disputed. He is reported to have travelled to the United States in 1958.

events.title: Rāṣṭrīya Svayaṃsevak Saṅgh founded
events.description: On Vijayādaśamī, 27 September 1925, Dr Keśav Baḷirām Heḍgevār, a physician and former Congress worker, gathered a few young men at his house in Nāgpur. He believed India had been conquered again and again because Hindu society was divided and undisciplined.¶His method was the śākhā: a daily hour of games, drill, songs and discussion in an open ground, building character and comradeship across caste. The RSS stayed out of electoral politics itself but grew into what it describes as the largest voluntary organisation in the world, and inspired a family of affiliates in labour, education, tribal welfare and politics.

events.title: Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act
events.description: The Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act of 1925 created a board to oversee the administration of Hindu temples and religious endowments in the Madras Presidency, a milestone in state regulation of temples in modern India. It followed earlier, weaker measures. Supporters said it curbed abuses by hereditary managers, while critics argued that it gave government control over religious institutions, a debate that continues. Tirupati was later brought under its own separate legislation.

events.title: Aurobindo's Siddhi Day
events.description: On 24 November 1926 Aurobindo told his disciples that a decisive stage of his yoga had been reached, which he described as the descent of Kṛṣṇa, the overmind consciousness, into the physical. He then withdrew to his rooms and for the rest of his life saw disciples only a few times a year, answering their questions by letter, thousands of them. The Mother organised the community into the Śrī Aurobindo Āśram.

events.title: Mahāḍ Satyāgraha
events.description: On 20 March 1927 Dr B. R. Ambedkar led several thousand Dalits to the Cavdār tank at Mahāḍ in Maharashtra and drank its water. The municipality had declared the tank open to all, but caste Hindus still barred "untouchables" from it. A mob attacked the marchers afterwards, and the tank was ritually "purified".¶Ambedkar returned in December and publicly burned the Manusmṛti as the symbol of the system. The courts confirmed the Dalits' right to the water ten years later. The date is observed in India as Social Empowerment Day.

events.title: Death of Nārāyaṇa Guru
events.description: Nārāyaṇa Guru died on 20 September 1928 at his hilltop hermitage of Śivagiri, at Varkala in Kerala. In forty years he had consecrated over forty temples, the later ones holding a lamp, a tablet reading "Truth, Duty, Compassion, Love", and finally a mirror. Tagore, who met him, said he had seen no one spiritually greater. A pilgrimage to Śivagiri in yellow dress is held every New Year.

events.title: Madras Music Academy founded
events.description: The Madras Music Academy, founded in 1928 after a conference held the previous year, gradually standardised the Carnatic concert. It organised annual conferences, set norms for performance, and promoted research into the theory and history of the tradition. Its December season became the central event of the Carnatic calendar, and its decisions on concert format, the place of Tamil songs and the status of performers influenced the music for decades. It shows how an urban institution helped to reshape a temple and court tradition for the modern public.

events.title: Child Marriage Restraint (Sarda) Act
events.description: Marriages of children, with the bride sent to her husband at puberty, were common among all communities. Harbilās Sārdā, an Ārya Samāj member and judge from Ajmer, piloted a bill through the central legislature in 1929 setting the minimum age of marriage at fourteen for girls and eighteen for boys. The fine was small and enforcement weak, but it was an important early social reform law passed by the Indian legislators themselves, and it provoked debate on state interference in custom.

events.title: Lakṣmaṇa Jhūlā bridge built at Ṛṣikeśa
events.description: Ṛṣikeśa, on the Gaṅgā at the foot of the Himalaya, has long been a place for ascetics. The Lakṣmaṇa Jhūlā, an iron suspension bridge completed in 1929 to replace an earlier bridge damaged by floods, spans the river. In the twentieth century institutions such as Parmārth Niketan, founded in 1942, and Gītā Bhavan, built in 1944, were established beside the older Svarg Āśram. They gave pilgrims lodging and teaching, and helped make Ṛṣikeśa known worldwide as a centre of yoga.

events.title: Gāndhī's Anāsakti Yoga
events.description: Gāndhī's Gujarati commentary on the Gītā, Anāsakti Yoga, was prepared around 1929 from talks he gave in 1926 at the Satyāgraha Āśrama in Ahmedabad. He read the Kurukṣetra battlefield as an allegory of the struggle between good and evil inside a person, and taught that the Gītā's central message is selfless action without attachment to results. Because he read it as a call to nonviolence, his view differed from many other interpreters who took the war literally.

events.title: Kālārām temple satyāgraha
events.description: On 2 March 1930 Dr Ambedkar led some fifteen thousand Dalits to the Kālārām temple at Nāsik, a Peśvā-period shrine of Rāma, and found the gates shut. They sat outside in protest. When they tried to join the chariot procession at Rāma Navamī they were stoned. The campaign went on for five years without success, and persuaded Ambedkar that Hindu society would not reform. The temple was opened to all after independence.
