events.title: Salt March
events.description: On 12 March 1930 Gāndhī, sixty years old, set out from his āśram at Sābarmatī with seventy-eight companions to walk 240 miles to the sea. The government taxed salt and forbade anyone to make it. On 6 April at Dāṇḍī he picked up a lump of natural salt from the shore. Across India people began making salt; sixty thousand were jailed. Newsreels carried it round the world.

events.title: 4D Spacetime Relativity, Quantum Mechanics & DNA
events.description: Einstein introduces 4-dimensional curved spacetime (General Relativity G_uv + Lambda g_uv = 8pi G/c^4 T_uv); Planck, Bohr, and Schrödinger formalize quantum wave mechanics (ih dpsi/dt = H psi); Watson, Crick, and Franklin discover the DNA double helix polymer. Humanity penetrates the foundations of macro-cosmic curvature and microscopic genetic reality.
events.eraDesc: Independence, constitutional democracy, technological self-reliance, and cosmic space research.

gitaQuote.verse: अणोरणीयान्महतो महीयान् आत्मास्य जन्तोर्निहितो गुहायाम् । तमक्रतुः पश्यति वीतशोको धातुप्रसादान्महिमानमात्मनः ॥

gitaQuote.translation: Subtler than the subatomic particle, vaster than the vast cosmic spacetime, the Self is seated in the heart of all beings. The serene sage perceives His glory and is freed from sorrow.
gitaQuote.source: Kaṭha Upaniṣad & Bhagavad Gītā commentary on the quantum and cosmic scale

events.title: Dharasāṇā salt raid and women in satyāgraha
events.description: After the Dāṇḍī march of April 1930, in which Gāndhī and followers broke the salt law, the campaign spread. Following Gāndhī's arrest in May, the poet Sarojinī Nāyaḍū led the raid on the Dharasāṇā salt works in Gujarat, where volunteers were beaten by police. Women took part in large numbers: Kamalādevī Chattopādhyāya organised salt-making in Bombay, and Kasturbā Gāndhī picketed shops. It was a turning point for women's role in the freedom movement.

events.title: Svāmī Rāmdās founds Ānandāśram
events.description: Svāmī Rāmdās, called "Papa" by his followers, was a Kerala-born ascetic who lived from 1884 to 1963. After a period of wandering, he came to teach the repetition of "Śrī Rāma Jaya Rāma Jaya Jaya Rāma." He founded Ānandāśram in Kāñhaṅgāḍ, Kerala, in 1931, where the daily chant of Rāma's name continued. His book In Quest of God described his travels, and his teachings have been widely read.

events.title: Bhagat Singh, Rājguru and Sukhdev hanged
events.description: Bhagat Singh, a young Sikh socialist, with Rājguru shot a police officer at Lahore in 1928 to avenge the death of Lālā Lājpat Rāy after a police beating. The next year he threw harmless smoke bombs in the central assembly and let himself be arrested, to use the trial as a platform. He was hanged with Rājguru and Sukhdev on 23 March 1931, aged twenty-three. All India mourned.

events.title: Guruvāyūr Satyāgraha
events.description: In November 1931 K. Kelappan, a Nāyar Congress leader, began a campaign to open the Kṛṣṇa temple at Guruvāyūr in Kerala to all castes, and in 1932 went on a fast which Gāndhī asked him to end. A vote was then taken among the caste Hindus of the surrounding area: 77 per cent favoured entry. The temple's trustee still refused. It was opened in 1947.

events.title: Poona Pact
events.description: In 1932 the British announced separate electorates for the "Depressed Classes", in which only Dalits would vote for Dalit representatives. Dr Ambedkar had asked for this. Gāndhī, in Yeravḍā jail, believed it would divide Hindu society for ever and began a fast to death.¶After six tense days the two sides signed a compromise at Pune: joint electorates, but with 148 seats reserved for Dalits, more than twice the number first offered. It is the origin of reserved constituencies in India. Ambedkar later said he had been coerced; the argument between the two men's visions has never quite ended.

events.title: Vinobā's Gītā talks at Dhuḷe jail
events.description: Vinobā Bhāve gave a series of talks on the Gītā in 1932 while imprisoned at Dhuḷe in Maharashtra, speaking to fellow prisoners; these were written down as Gītā Pravacane. His Gītāī, a Marathi rendering in verse, was composed in the same period. It became very popular among Marathi readers and was translated into many languages, and shaped Vinobā's later Bhūdān movement, which sought voluntary land gifts for the landless.

events.title: Nisargadatta Mahārāj meets his guru
events.description: Nisargadatta Mahārāj, who lived from 1897 to 1981, was a Mumbai shopkeeper who became a teacher of Advaita. In 1933 he met Siddharāmeśvar Mahārāj, who belonged to the Inchegiri branch of the Navnāth Sampradāya, a tradition tracing back to the Nāth yogis. After his guru's death in 1936 he continued his trade and later taught in a small flat in Khetwadi, Mumbai. A book of his conversations, I Am That, edited by Maurice Frydman, introduced his teaching to an international audience in 1973.

events.title: Krishnamacharya's Yogaśālā
events.description: Tirumalai Krishnamacharya, a scholar of the six philosophies who is said to have studied yoga with a master in the Himalaya, was given a hall in the Mysore palace in 1933 by the Mahārājā. There he taught a vigorous, flowing sequence of postures to the boys of the royal family and others. His pupils Pattabhi Jois, his brother-in-law B. K. S. Iyengar, Indra Devi and his son Desikachar founded the main schools of modern yoga.

events.title: Ṛgveda with Sāyaṇa's commentary published at Pune
events.description: The Vaidika Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala, a research institute at Pune, began publishing the Ṛgveda with the commentary of Sāyaṇa in 1933, and the five-volume edition was completed in 1951. It made the fourteenth-century commentary, long the standard traditional interpretation of the hymns, available in a carefully edited printed form. Its scholars, such as Tarkatīrtha Lakṣmaṇaśāstrī Jośī, preserved and edited Vedic texts in ways accessible to both Indian and foreign scholars.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Brunton brings Ramaṇa to the West
events.description: Paul Brunton, an English journalist, described his meeting with Ramaṇa Maharṣi in A Search in Secret India in 1934, and seekers began arriving from Europe and America. Ramaṇa wrote little, so disciples kept records. Talks with Sri Ramana Maharshi, compiled from notes made between 1935 and 1939 and first published in 1955, gives his answers to visitors, almost always turning the question back: find out who it is that asks.

events.title: Yoga Makaranda
events.description: Published in 1934, Yoga Makaranda is a manual by Tirumalai Kṛṣṇamācārya, written while he taught at the Mysore palace under the patronage of the Mahārāja. It describes āsanas, prāṇāyāma and the principles of breath-linked movement, and it argues for yoga as practice suited to health and spiritual growth. Its sequences of movement joined to breath are the root of the vinyāsa approach later taught by his students, among them Paṭṭābhi Jois, B. K. S. Iyengar and T. K. V. Desikachar, whose lineages carried yoga across the world.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Ambedkar's Yeola declaration
events.description: At a conference at Yeola near Nāsik on 13 October 1935, after the failure of the temple-entry campaign, Dr Ambedkar told ten thousand listeners that it had been his misfortune to be born a Hindu untouchable, which was not in his power to prevent, but that he solemnly assured them he would not die a Hindu. Leaders of every religion then approached him. He took twenty-one years to choose.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Ārya Samāj organisations spread overseas
events.description: The Ārya Samāj, founded by Dayānanda Sarasvatī to revive Vedic religion and reject image worship, sent preachers to the Indian diaspora. By the 1930s, Ārya Pratinidhi Sabhas, regional representative bodies, ran schools and temples in Fiji, Mauritius, South Africa and Suriname. They taught Hindi, Vedic ritual and reformist ideas, and offered an alternative to missionary schools. Their work helped overseas Hindus keep language and religion, though they were also in tension with more traditional Sanātanī groups.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Bhārat Mātā Mandir opened at Vārāṇasī
events.description: The Bhārat Mātā temple at Vārāṇasī, built by the nationalist Śivprasād Gupta at the Kāśī Vidyāpīṭh, has no deity image but instead a large marble relief map of undivided India, with mountains and rivers, representing the motherland. The idea dates to the early 20th century, and the temple was inaugurated by Mahātmā Gāndhī in 1936. It reflects the nationalist idea of the land as sacred, expressed in a temple form.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Kalākṣetra founded to revive Bharatanāṭyam
events.description: Kalākṣetra was founded in Chennai in 1936 by Rukmiṇī Devī Aruṇḍale, who studied sadir, the temple and court dance of Tamil Nadu, and recast it as Bharatanāṭyam for the modern concert stage, with a focus on devotional themes and polished presentation. The revival was preceded in the 1920s by a campaign led by E. Krishna Iyer, a lawyer and dancer, to restore the art's respectability. The change came with the decline of the devadāsī system, and the form became a symbol of national culture.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Travancore Temple Entry Proclamation
events.description: On 12 November 1936 the young Mahārājā of Travancore, Citra Tirunāḷ, on the advice of his minister C. P. Rāmasvāmi Ayyar, declared every temple controlled by the state open to all Hindus regardless of birth.¶Kerala had practised some of the harshest caste exclusion in India; some communities could not even walk the roads near temples. The Vaikom and Guruvāyūr agitations and the teaching of Nārāyaṇa Guru had prepared the ground. Gāndhī called the proclamation a miracle of modern times, and other provinces followed over the next decade.

events.title: Divine Life Society
events.description: Svāmī Śivānanda founded the Divine Life Society in 1936 on the bank of the Gaṅgā at Ṛṣikeśa, where he had earlier run a free dispensary. The society grew to run a hospital and a printing press, and it welcomed anyone, of any country or faith, who wished to learn. His "yoga of synthesis" combined service, devotion, meditation and study. The teachers he trained founded yoga organisations on five continents.

events.title: Rāṣṭra Sevikā Samiti
events.description: Lakṣmībāī Keḷkar, a widow of Wardha with children, asked the founder of the RSS why it admitted only men. He advised her to start a parallel body. She founded the Rāṣṭra Sevikā Samiti on Vijayādaśamī 1936, with daily branches where girls trained in drill, self-defence and discussion. It is the oldest of the women's organisations associated with the Saṅgh and describes itself as the largest Hindu women's organisation in India.

events.title: Death of Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī
events.description: Bimalā Prasād Datta, son of the reformer Bhaktivinoda, was a brilliant astronomer who became a monk as Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī. He founded the Gauḍīya Maṭh in 1920, opened sixty-four centres, used the printing press as his "big drum", and insisted that a devotee of any birth could be a brāhmaṇa. He sent preachers to London and Berlin. He died on 1 January 1937. Among his disciples was the future founder of ISKCON.

events.title: Bhāratīya Vidyā Bhavan
events.description: Kanhaiyālāl Munshi, a Gujarati novelist, lawyer and Congress minister, founded the Bhāratīya Vidyā Bhavan in Bombay in 1938 with Gāndhī's blessing. Its purpose was to revive Indian culture through Sanskrit study, publishing and the arts. Its Book University series sold millions of inexpensive volumes, among them Rājājī's retellings of the epics, and it now has over a hundred centres in India and abroad.

events.title: Rāmakṛṣṇa temple consecrated at Belūr Maṭh
events.description: On 14 January 1938, Makara Saṅkrānti, the Rāmakṛṣṇa temple at Belūr Maṭh, on the Hooghly opposite Calcutta, was consecrated. Swami Vijñānānanda, a direct disciple of Rāmakṛṣṇa and a trained engineer, designed it on the basis of Vivekānanda's ideas. The land had been bought in 1897, and Vivekānanda placed relics of Rāmakṛṣṇa at the site on 9 December 1898.¶The temple joins Hindu, Buddhist, Christian and Islamic forms: the ground plan is cruciform, and depending on the angle it can recall a temple, a church or a mosque. This was Vivekānanda's idea of the harmony of religions, which the Rāmakṛṣṇa Order taught, expressed in building. Belūr Maṭh is the headquarters of the Order.

events.title: Birla Mandir, Delhi
events.description: The industrialist Birlā family built a large temple to Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa in New Delhi, in red and cream sandstone, between 1933 and 1939. Gāndhī agreed to open it on the condition that people of every caste, including those called untouchable, be admitted. A plaque at the gate says so. It was among the earliest of some two dozen Birlā temples across India.

events.title: Dalits enter Mīnākṣī temple at Madurai
events.description: On 8 July 1939, A. Vaidyanātha Ayyar, a Congress leader and Brahmin lawyer, led a group of Dalits, as well as Nāḍār leaders, into the Mīnākṣī Sundareśvara temple at Madurai, which had been closed to them. The event was part of the temple entry movement in Tamil Nadu, and it was supported by the Madras government under C. Rājagopālācāri, who had passed the Madras Temple Entry Authorization and Indemnity Act of 1939. It was an important step toward opening Hindu temples to all.

events.title: Golvalkar becomes RSS head
events.description: Dr Heḍgevār died in June 1940, naming as his successor Mādhav Sadāśiv Golvalkar, a thirty-four-year-old zoology lecturer who had been a disciple of a Ramakrishna Order monk. Known as "Guruji", he led the RSS for thirty-three years through the Partition, a ban after Gāndhī's murder, and its expansion across India. His writings on nationhood are both foundational for the organisation and the main target of its critics.

events.title: Lahore Resolution
events.description: On 23 March 1940, at Lahore, the Muslim League under M. A. Jinnah resolved that the Muslims of India were a separate nation and that the Muslim-majority areas of the northwest and east should become independent states. The word Pakistan was not used. Seven years later the demand was conceded. Gāndhī called the idea of two nations an untruth; Ambedkar wrote a book examining it coolly.

events.title: Nityānanda of Gaṇeśpurī
events.description: Bhagavān Nityānanda was an avadhūta, an ascetic outside conventional rules, who settled in the 1930s and 1940s at Gaṇeśpurī, in Thane district near Mumbai, where hot springs flow near the Vajreśvarī temple. His origins are unknown. Devotees came for his blessing and for healing, and he taught mostly through silence and gesture. His disciple Swami Muktānanda later founded the Siddha Yoga movement, which spread in the West from the 1970s. He took samādhi in 1961.

events.title: Brahmānanda Sarasvatī installed at Jyotirmaṭha
events.description: Jyotirmaṭha in the Himalaya is one of the four Advaita maṭhas, traditionally founded by Śaṅkara. According to its tradition the seat was left vacant for many years during the colonial period, a vacancy often given as 165 years. In 1941 Brahmānanda Sarasvatī was installed as Śaṅkarācārya there. Other maṭhas dispute the continuity of the line, and disputes over the succession to this and other seats have continued in later years.
events.eraDesc: Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.

events.title: Quit India
events.description: On 8 August 1942, with Japan at India's border, the Congress at Bombay demanded that the British leave at once. Gāndhī gave the people a mantra: "Do or die". He and every leader were arrested before dawn. Leaderless crowds attacked railways, post offices and police stations for weeks; parallel governments ran some districts. More than a thousand people were shot and sixty thousand jailed.

events.title: Āzād Hind government
events.description: Subhās Candra Bose, twice president of the Congress, escaped house arrest in 1941 and reached Germany, then Japan by submarine. At Singapore in October 1943 he proclaimed a Provisional Government of Free India and took command of the Indian National Army, raised from prisoners of war. It fought alongside the Japanese at Imphal and was defeated. The trial of its officers in 1945 stirred the whole country.

events.title: Rām Rājya film released
events.description: Rām Rājya, directed by Vijay Bhaṭṭ and released in 1943, was a Hindi film on the story of Rāma's rule. It is reported to be the only film Mohandas Gāndhī ever saw. Mythological films were a major genre in the first decades of Indian cinema, and their popularity showed the hold of the epics on the public. Gāndhī himself used the idea of Rām Rājya as an image of just government.

events.title: Oppenheimer recalls the Gītā after Trinity
events.description: Robert Oppenheimer, who led the Los Alamos laboratory, studied Sanskrit and read the Gītā. After the first atomic test, called Trinity, in New Mexico in July 1945, he later recalled a line from the text. He quoted verse 11.32, where Kṛṣṇa reveals himself as Time, the destroyer of worlds, and gave it in English as "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds". The account comes from his later recollections, notably a 1965 television interview.

events.title: Calcutta killings and Noakhali riots
events.description: The Muslim League called 16 August 1946 "Direct Action Day" to press for Pakistan. In Calcutta, under a League ministry, violence broke out and became four days of mutual slaughter in which Hindus and Muslims were killed, with estimates of dead running from about four thousand upward. In October, Hindus in the Noakhali district of east Bengal were attacked: killings, rapes, forced conversions. Gāndhī, aged seventy-seven, walked barefoot from village to village there for about four months.

events.title: Autobiography of a Yogi
events.description: Yogānanda's Autobiography of a Yogi appeared in 1946. It tells of his boyhood search for a teacher, of saints who levitate or live without food, of his guru Śrī Yukteśvar and of the deathless Bābājī, in a warm and humorous voice. It has been translated into over fifty languages and has never been out of print. For many Westerners it was their first Indian book.

events.title: Independence and Partition
events.description: At midnight on 14–15 August 1947 British rule ended and two states came into being. The line between them, drawn in five weeks by a lawyer who had never been to India, was published two days later.¶About fifteen million people crossed the new borders in both directions, the largest migration in history, and between several hundred thousand and a million were killed. West Punjab, Sindh and later East Bengal lost most of their Hindus and Sikhs; ancient centres such as Lahore, Multan, Taxila and the Śāradā temple were now across a frontier.
events.eraDesc: Independence, constitutional democracy, technological self-reliance, and cosmic space research.

events.title: Bombay and Madras Temple Entry Acts
events.description: Before independence, several provinces passed laws to open Hindu temples to all Hindus, including castes then barred from entering. The Madras Temple Entry Authorization Act of 1947 and a Bombay act of the same year are among them, and they followed the earlier Madras measure of 1939. After 1950, Article 17 of the Constitution abolished untouchability, and later laws expanded temple entry rights across the country, although practice at the local level did not always follow.

events.title: Integration of the princely states
events.description: At independence in August 1947, there were roughly 565 princely states, which were free to choose between India and Pakistan or, in principle, stand apart. The States Department, under Sardār Vallabhbhāī Patel with V. P. Menon as secretary, negotiated accession to India, using instruments of accession, assurances and some pressure. Difficult cases included Travancore, Jodhpur, Junāgaḍh and Kashmir, along with Hyderabad. Most states joined peacefully, and in the following years they were merged into larger units.

events.title: Somanātha reconstruction pledged
events.description: Junāgaḍh's Muslim ruler had tried to join Pakistan although his state was mostly Hindu and surrounded by India; his people revolted and he fled. Days later, on 13 November 1947, Sardār Patel visited the ruined shrine of Somanātha on the nearby coast and announced that the temple would be rebuilt. Gāndhī agreed, provided the money came from public donations and not the treasury. K. M. Munshi took charge of the trust.

events.title: Gāndhī assassinated
events.description: On the evening of 30 January 1948, as Gāndhī walked to his daily prayer meeting in Delhi, Nāthūrām Goḍse stepped from the crowd and shot him three times in the chest. Goḍse, a Pune newspaper editor, blamed him for Partition and for pressing India to pay Pakistan its share of funds.¶Gāndhī had spent his last months walking through riot-torn Bengal and fasting in Delhi to stop the killing of Muslims. His death shocked the country into calm. Goḍse was tried and hanged in 1949. The RSS, of which he had once been a member, was banned for eighteen months and then cleared of involvement.

events.title: Karpātrī's Rāmarājya Pariṣad
events.description: Svāmī Karpātrī, a Daśanāmī monk and scholar, founded the Akhil Bhāratīya Rāma Rājya Pariṣad in 1948 as a political party that favoured a state organised around Hindu law, śāstra. It sought to protect the cow and Hindu tradition, and won a few seats in the early elections, but faded by the 1960s. He had earlier founded the Dharma Saṅgh in 1940 and opposed the Hindu Code Bill of the 1950s as an intrusion into religious law.

events.title: Operation Polo ends Hyderabad's independence
events.description: Hyderabad, the largest princely state, had a Muslim ruler, the Nizām, and a population about 85 per cent Hindu. He refused to join India, and a private militia, the Razākārs, terrorised villages to keep it independent. In September 1948 the Indian army entered in a five-day "police action" called Operation Polo. The Nizām surrendered and the state was merged. An official inquiry later recorded that the aftermath also saw serious reprisal killings of Muslims.

events.title: Idols placed in the Babri Masjid at Ayodhyā
events.description: Hindus worshipped on a platform in the outer court of the Babri mosque at Ayodhyā, while Muslim prayers continued inside until mid-December 1949, as the Supreme Court later noted. On the night of 22–23 December 1949, images of the child Rāma were placed beneath the central dome; devotees spoke of a miraculous appearance, and the police report named those who had carried them in. Nehru wanted them removed. The local magistrate, K. K. Nayar, refused, warning of riots. The gates were locked and a priest was allowed in daily. Every later lawsuit begins from this night.

events.title: Cinmayānanda begins study with Tapovanam
events.description: Svāmī Tapovanam, a teacher of Vedānta from Kerala who lived in Uttarkāśī in the Himalaya and wrote Wanderings in the Himalayas, took as his pupil Bālakṛṣṇa Menon, a former journalist who had first met Svāmī Śivānanda at Ṛṣikeśa. Under the name Cinmayānanda he studied Vedānta with Tapovanam for several years. Tapovanam's instruction led him in 1953 to found the Chinmaya Mission, which taught Vedānta widely to the educated public.

events.title: Constitution of India
events.description: India's Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950. It guarantees every person freedom of conscience and the right to practise and spread religion (Articles 25–28), abolishes untouchability (Article 17), and directs the state to work toward protecting cows and a common civil code. The original was written out by hand, and the artist Nandalāl Bose and his students illustrated each part with a scene from India's past: a Vedic hermitage, Rāma returning from Laṅkā, Kṛṣṇa teaching Arjuna, the Buddha, Naṭarāja.

events.title: East Bengal riots and the Nehru–Liaquat Pact
events.description: In February 1950 riots against Hindus spread through East Pakistan, including Dhaka and Barisal; thousands were killed and over a million fled to West Bengal within months. India and Pakistan signed a pact in April promising to protect each other's minorities. Śyāmāprasād Mukherjee, a minister in Nehru's cabinet, called it worthless and resigned. The flow of Hindu refugees from the east continued for decades, and the Hindu share of that region's population fell from about a quarter to under a tenth.

events.title: Ramaṇa Maharṣi's mahānirvāṇa
events.description: Ramaṇa Maharṣi died of cancer at his āśram below Aruṇācala on the evening of 14 April 1950. He had refused to treat the pain as his own, telling grieving devotees, "They say I am dying, but where could I go? I am here." Witnesses, among them the photographer Henri Cartier-Bresson, reported a bright meteor crossing the sky toward the hill at the moment of his death. His teaching of self-enquiry spread worldwide after him.

events.title: Śrī Aurobindo's passing
events.description: Śrī Aurobindo died at Pondicherry on 5 December 1950. For twenty-four years he had lived in a few rooms, writing and practising his yoga, seen by disciples only on four days a year. His last great work was Sāvitrī, an epic poem of almost 24,000 lines in English that turns a short Mahābhārata legend, a wife winning her husband back from Death, into a symbol of the soul's conquest of mortality. The Mother led the āśram for another twenty-three years.

events.title: R. C. Majumdar's History and Culture of the Indian People
events.description: The History and Culture of the Indian People is an eleven-volume series published by the Bhāratīya Vidyā Bhavan in Mumbai between 1951 and 1977, edited by R. C. Majumdar. Written by many scholars, it narrated Indian history from ancient to modern times from an Indian viewpoint, in reaction to colonial accounts. It is still widely used as reference, though critics note that its approach and conclusions reflect the nationalist concerns of its time.

events.title: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act
events.description: The Madras government had supervised temple finances since the 1920s. The 1951 Act went further and let officials appoint managers and take over administration. The head of the Śirūr monastery at Uḍupi challenged it, and in 1954 the Supreme Court ruled that the state may regulate a religious body's secular affairs but not practices "essential" to the religion. Courts have had to decide what is essential ever since. Tens of thousands of temples in southern states remain under government departments, a continuing grievance for many Hindus.

events.title: Bhāratīya Jana Saṅgh founded
events.description: Śyāmāprasād Mukherjee, a former university vice-chancellor and Hindu Mahāsabhā leader, founded the Bhāratīya Jana Saṅgh on 21 October 1951 with organisational help from the RSS. It stood for one nation and one law, and opposed the special status of Kashmir. In 1953 he entered Kashmir without the permit then required, was arrested, and died in custody six weeks later. The party he founded became part of the Janata Party in 1977, and its members formed the BJP in 1980.

events.title: Vanavāsī Kalyāṇ Āśram
events.description: Bāḷāsāheb Deśpāṇḍe, a government officer posted among the tribal communities of Jaśpur in central India, founded the Vanavāsī Kalyāṇ Āśram in 1952 with a hostel for thirteen boys. Christian missions were then the main providers of schools and clinics in such areas. The organisation, linked to the RSS, now runs thousands of schools, hostels and health centres across tribal India, and insists that "forest-dwellers" are part of Hindu society and not a separate people.

events.title: Lothal and Kalibangan found
events.description: After Partition, Mohenjo-daro and Harappa lay in Pakistan, and Indian archaeologists set out to find Harappan sites in India. In 1953 Amalananda Ghosh surveyed the Ghaggar region of Rajasthan and found Kalibangan, later excavated by B. B. Lal and B. K. Thapar. S. R. Rao located Lothal in Gujarat in 1954 and excavated it in 1955–62, finding a large brick basin that he interpreted as a dock. Today the greater number of known Harappan sites are in India. The discoveries rewrote the map of the civilisation.

events.title: Chinmaya Mission
events.description: Bālakṛṣṇa Menon was a sceptical young journalist who went to the Himalaya to expose the holy men and stayed to become a monk, Svāmī Cinmayānanda. He came down to the cities and from 1951 gave long public lecture series on the Upaniṣads and Gītā in English, until then taught only to initiates in Sanskrit. The mission founded in 1953 now has hundreds of centres and schools, and brought the scriptures to India's educated middle class.

events.title: Kumbha Melā stampede at Prayāga
events.description: The Kumbha of 1954 was the first after independence, and politicians and dignitaries came in numbers. On the main bathing day, 3 February, a procession of ascetics met a surging crowd on a narrow embankment made slippery by rain. Several hundred people were trampled or drowned; estimates run from about 350 to 800. The inquiry that followed set the rules still used for managing the fair: separate routes, barriers, and no VIP visits on the principal days.

events.title: Śrī Śāradā Maṭh
events.description: Śrī Śāradā Maṭh was founded in 1954 at Dakṣiṇeśvar in Kolkata, as an independent monastic order for women, parallel to the Ramakrishna Math for men. Its nuns, called pravrājikās, follow the ideals of Śāradā Devī and Vivekānanda and run schools, hospitals and relief work. The order was a new step in the tradition because it gave women formal sannyāsa and independent leadership, a theme that Vivekānanda had hoped for, and it has centres in India and abroad.

events.title: Hindu Code Bills enacted
events.description: Between 1955 and 1956 Parliament passed four laws that replaced the regional mix of scriptural commentary and custom with a single civil code for Hindus, a term defined to include Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists.¶The Marriage Act made monogamy the rule, allowed divorce and permitted marriage across caste. The Succession Act gave daughters and widows a share in property. Dr Ambedkar had drafted an earlier Hindu Code Bill and resigned as Law Minister in 1951 when it stalled against orthodox opposition; the acts as passed carried much of his design.

events.title: Untouchability (Offences) Act
events.description: Article 17 of the Constitution declared untouchability abolished, but a declaration punishes no one. The 1955 Act made it a crime to bar anyone on that ground from temples, shops, wells, roads, schools or hospitals. It was strengthened and renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976, and a tougher Atrocities Act followed in 1989. The laws gave legal force to what the reformers, from Nārāyaṇa Guru to Gāndhī and Ambedkar, had argued on moral grounds.

events.title: Kosambi's Marxist history of ancient India
events.description: D. D. Kosambi, a mathematician and historian, published An Introduction to the Study of Indian History in 1956, applying Marxist methods to ancient India and looking at material conditions and class. The traveller and scholar Rāhul Sāṅkṛtyāyan worked in a similar spirit earlier, notably in Volga se Gaṅgā. Their approach opened new questions on economy and society but was challenged by other scholars, who argued that it neglected the role of religious ideas and traditional sources. The debate over method has remained part of Indian historiography.

events.title: Ambedkar embraces Buddhism
events.description: Twenty-one years after declaring that he would not die a Hindu, and after studying Islam, Christianity and Sikhism, Dr Ambedkar chose the Buddha's path as rational, egalitarian and Indian in origin.¶On 14 October 1956 at Nāgpur he took the refuges and precepts from a Burmese monk, then turned and administered them, with twenty-two vows of his own, to a crowd of several hundred thousand, mostly from his own Mahār community. The vows include rejecting belief in Hindu deities and rites. He died seven weeks later. The movement he began, Navayāna, counts millions of followers.

events.title: Buddha Jayantī 2500 observed in India
events.description: In 1956, two thousand five hundred years after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa by the traditional count, India joined other Buddhist countries in observing Buddha Jayantī, with state-sponsored events and the publication of works on Buddhism. At Bodh Gayā, the site of the Buddha's enlightenment, a law of 1949 placed the Mahābodhi temple under a committee with Hindu and Buddhist members. Its management has long been contested by Buddhists, who seek full control of the site.

events.title: Śaka calendar adopted
events.description: India used several calendars at once. A committee under the astrophysicist Meghnād Sāhā designed a single civil one: the Śaka era, which counts from 78 CE, with months of fixed length beginning at the spring equinox. It took effect on 1 Caitra 1879 Śaka, 22 March 1957, and appears beside the Gregorian date on official documents. Religious festivals, however, still follow the traditional lunar almanacs, which differ from region to region.

events.title: Sanskrit Commission submits its report
events.description: In 1956 the Government of India appointed a Sanskrit Commission, which reported in 1957 with proposals for promoting Sanskrit in education and research. Its recommendations led, in the following years, to the creation of national institutions, notably the Rāṣṭrīya Sanskrit Saṃsthān in 1970, and the founding of Sanskrit universities. These bodies fund study, publish texts and train teachers, and they now form the main institutional support for Sanskrit education in India.

events.title: Maharishi launches Transcendental Meditation
events.description: Maheś Prasād Varmā, a physics graduate, served for thirteen years as secretary to Brahmānanda Sarasvatī, the Śaṅkarācārya of Jyotirmaṭha. After his master's death he began teaching a simple technique: twenty minutes, twice a day, of silently repeating a mantra. He launched it as a world movement at Madras in 1958. Presented as a method anyone could use, and later studied in laboratories, Transcendental Meditation was learned by several million people and made "mantra" an English word.

A new temple was built in stages during the following decades, with the Bhāgavata Bhavan completed in 1982. Legal disputes over the adjacent mosque have continued.

events.title: Rāmāyaṇa critical edition begins
events.description: Following the model of the Mahābhārata project, the Oriental Institute at Baroda compared some two thousand manuscripts of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa from every part of India and published a critical text in seven volumes between 1960 and 1975. It showed that the epic survives in northern and southern recensions which differ in thousands of lines, and it marks the passages that appear in only some of them. It is the standard text for scholars, though recitation everywhere still follows the regional versions.

events.title: Goa liberated
events.description: Portugal had held Goa since 1510 and refused to negotiate after 1947, calling it part of Portugal itself. On 18–19 December 1961 the Indian armed forces took the territory in thirty-six hours with little fighting. Those temples at Ponda and elsewhere are still Goa's chief shrines.

Munshi.¶Their aim was a common platform for all traditions born in India, to defend Hindus abroad, counter conversion and remove untouchability. At Uḍupi in 1969 its assembled ācāryas declared that untouchability has no sanction in scripture. From 1984 it led the movement for the Rāma temple at Ayodhyā.

events.description: The Tulasī Mānas Mandir in Vārāṇasī is a white marble temple dedicated to Rāma, built by the Surekā family and opened in 1964. On its walls are inscribed the verses of the Rāmcaritmānas, the Hindi Rāma epic written by Tulasīdāsa in the 16th century, whom tradition says lived in Vārāṇasī. The temple is located near the Durgā temple and is a popular site for visitors, and its walls make the text a visible part of the building.

events.title: Prabhupāda sails to America
events.description: Abhay Caraṇ De, a Calcutta pharmacist, had been told by his guru in 1922 to teach Caitanya's message in English. He began in earnest only after retiring. In August 1965, aged sixty-nine, with a free ticket on the cargo ship Jaladuta, he crossed the Atlantic and suffered two heart attacks on the way. He landed at Boston on 17 September with about forty rupees and several trunks of his translation of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa. He knew almost no one in America.

events.description: In April 1965 Dīn Dayāl Upādhyāya, a leader of the Bhāratīya Jana Saṅgh, gave four lectures in Mumbai setting out Integral Humanism (Ekātma Mānavavāda). It proposed an Indian alternative to capitalism and socialism, based on the whole person with body, mind, intellect and soul, and on dharma and the four puruṣārthas of dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa. The Jana Saṅgh adopted it as its official philosophy that year, and the BJP later cited it as a guiding doctrine.

events.title: ISKCON incorporated
events.description: A. C. Bhaktivedānta Svāmī arrived in New York in 1965 aged sixty-nine, with a few dollars and trunks of his own translation of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa. He began by chanting under a tree in Tompkins Square Park, where young people of the counterculture gathered round him.¶On 13 July 1966 he registered the International Society for Krishna Consciousness in a rented shopfront on Second Avenue. In the eleven years before his death he circled the globe fourteen times, opened 108 temples, and published some seventy volumes. events.title: Death of V. D. Sāvarkar
events.description: Vinayak Dāmodar Sāvarkar, the revolutionary and Hindutva ideologue, died in Mumbai on 26 February 1966. His life remains debated, with supporters honouring his revolutionary career and critics pointing to his ideas and the controversies over his role in the Gāndhī assassination case, in which he was acquitted.

events.title: Iyengar publishes Light on Yoga

The violinist Yehudi Menuhin became his student and brought him to Europe. Light on Yoga (1966) describes about two hundred postures with six hundred photographs and precise instructions on alignment, and has sold millions of copies. His method uses blocks, belts and chairs so that any body can reach a pose.

events.title: Mahābhārata critical edition completed
events.description: On 22 September 1966 President Rādhākṛṣṇan released the final part of the Mahābhārata's critical edition at Pune. The Bhandarkar Institute had worked on it for forty-seven years, and its first general editor, V. S. Sukthankar, had died in 1943. The result is nineteen volumes of some seventy-five thousand verses, with every variant from 1,259 manuscripts recorded in the notes. It showed for the first time which parts of the epic are shared by all regions and which are later, local growth.

events.title: Anti-cow-slaughter march on Parliament
events.description: Cow protection had been promised as a goal in the Constitution's Directive Principles but left to the states. On 7 November 1966 a crowd estimated in the hundreds of thousands, led by sādhus including Svāmī Karpātrī and the Śaṅkarācārya of Purī, marched to Parliament demanding a national ban on slaughter. Part of the crowd turned violent and the police opened fire. Official figures put the dead in single digits; organisers claimed far more. The Home Minister, Gulzārīlāl Nandā, resigned soon after. Slaughter laws remain a matter for the states, and most have their own.

events.title: M. S. Subbulakshmi at the United Nations

The concert helped bring Indian devotional music to a world audience and is remembered as one of the great moments of her career.

events.description: Prabhupāda's young followers in San Francisco built a cart on a flatbed truck, and on 9 July 1967 pulled small images of Jagannātha, Balabhadra and Subhadrā through the Haight-Ashbury district to the sea. The festival, which in Purī goes back at least eight centuries, is now held every year in more than a hundred cities from London to Durban.

events.description: Amar Chitra Kathā, started in 1967 by Anant Pai, is a series of illustrated comic books on subjects from the epics, Purāṇas, saints' lives and history. Sold in huge numbers in English and many Indian languages, the comics gave several generations their first knowledge of Hindu stories, and they are still widely read.

events.title: Dholavira Harappan city discovered
events.description: Dholavira, on Khadir island in the Rann of Kutch, was reported in 1967–68 by J. P. Joshi of the Archaeological Survey. R. S. Bisht's long excavations from 1990 uncovered a city with a fortified citadel, a middle town and a lower town, laid out by careful planning. Its most striking feature is a water system of reservoirs, channels and stepped wells that captured seasonal runoff in a dry landscape. A gateway had a signboard with ten large Indus signs, still unread. The city flourished in the third millennium BCE and was in use until about 1500 BCE.

events.title: The Beatles at Ṛṣikeśa

events.title: Mauritius becomes independent
events.description: Mauritius became independent from Britain in 1968, with Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam, a Hindu of Indian descent, as its first prime minister, leading a country in which Hindus are the largest religious group. The island has the sacred lake Gaṅgā Talāo, or Grand Bassin, where pilgrims gather at Mahāśivarātri, carrying water from the lake. Its waters are believed to be linked to the Gaṅgā. It shows how indentured descendants created a new sacred geography overseas.

events.title: Auroville inaugurated
events.description: Auroville, "the city of dawn", was founded by the Mother on 28 February 1968 on a barren plateau near Pondicherry. Young people from 124 countries each poured a handful of their own soil into a marble urn. Its charter says the town belongs to no one in particular but to humanity as a whole. UNESCO endorsed it. Some three thousand people from about sixty nations live there now, around the golden sphere of the Mātṛmandir, a hall for silent concentration.

events.title: Bhagavad-gītā As It Is
events.description: A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda, founder of ISKCON, published Bhagavad-gītā As It Is in 1968 (abridged) and in its full form in 1972. It presents the Gītā from the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava viewpoint, with Sanskrit text, transliteration, word meanings, translation and extended purports. ISKCON followers have distributed very large numbers of the book worldwide, in many languages. Its reading of Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Person differs from Advaita interpretations, and academic critics have questioned some of its choices.

events.title: Uḍupi Dharma Saṃsad rejects untouchability
events.description: In December 1969 the VHP held a conference at Uḍupi in Karnataka. Viśveśa Tīrtha, the young head of the Pejāvar monastery and one of the most orthodox seats in the south, moved a resolution, and the assembled heads of monasteries adopted it: all Hindus are brothers, no Hindu is fallen, and untouchability has no basis in the scriptures. The slogan was "hindavaḥ sodarāḥ sarve". It was a notable public statement by religious authorities of that rank.

events.title: Bangladesh genocide
events.description: On 25 March 1971 the Pakistan army began Operation Searchlight to crush the Bengali independence movement in East Pakistan. Hindus, then roughly fifteen per cent of the population, were disproportionately targeted; American consular cables at the time used the word genocide. Estimates of the dead range from three hundred thousand to three million. About ten million refugees, most of them Hindu, crossed into India. On 27 March the army demolished the old Ramnā Kālī temple in Dhaka and killed those sheltering in it. India's intervention in December ended the war.

events.description: Pramukh Svāmī Mahārāj, born Śāntilāl Paṭel, was the fifth guru of the BAPS Swaminarayan Sansthā, the head from 1971 until his death in 2016. Under his leadership BAPS built more than a thousand temples, as well as cultural centres in India and overseas, including the Akṣardhām complexes in Delhi and Gāndhīnagar, and ran relief and education programs. Followers revere him as the successor in the line of Guṇātītānanda Svāmī, and he guided the community's growth in the Gujarati diaspora.

events.title: Privy purses abolished
events.description: After 1947 the Indian princes had been guaranteed annual payments, called privy purses, along with privileges, in return for joining India. An attempt to end these failed in the Rajya Sabha in 1970. In 1971 the 26th Constitutional Amendment, passed by Parliament under Indira Gāndhī, removed the recognition of princes and abolished the purses and privileges. It ended the last formal link with the old order, and many former rulers entered electoral politics, some with success.

events.title: East African Hindus resettle in Britain
events.description: Indians had settled in East Africa under British rule as traders and railway workers. In August 1972 Uganda's ruler Idi Amin gave about sixty thousand Asians ninety days to leave, taking almost nothing. Some twenty-eight thousand, mostly Gujarati Hindus, came to Britain, joining others from Kenya and Tanzania. They rebuilt their businesses within a generation and built the temples of Leicester, Wembley and Neasden, giving Britain one of the most established Hindu communities outside India.

events.title: Chipko movement
events.description: In 1973 the villagers of Maṇḍal in the Garhwal Himalaya stopped a sports-goods company from felling ash trees by threatening to hug them; "chipko" means "cling". The next year, at Reṇī, the men had been called away when the loggers arrived. Gaurā Devī and twenty-seven women stood between the trees and the axes through the night. The movement won a fifteen-year ban on commercial felling in the Himalayan forests of the state and became a model of non-violent environmental protest worldwide.

events.title: Bāḷāsāheb Devras succeeds Golvalkar
events.description: M. S. Golvalkar, head of the RSS for thirty-three years, died on 5 June 1973. His successor, Madhukar Dattātreya "Bāḷāsāheb" Devras, turned the organisation outward toward social service. In a lecture at Pune in 1974 he is reported to have said that if untouchability is not wrong, then nothing in the world is wrong, and that it must go. Under him the RSS started many welfare projects among Dalits and tribal communities. The Emergency of 1975–77 saw the Saṅgh banned and many workers jailed.

events.title: Chhatarpur Kātyāyanī temple founded in Delhi
events.description: The Kātyāyanī temple at Chattarpur in south Delhi was founded in 1974 by Bābā Nāgpāl and has grown into a very large complex with many shrines, among the largest in the city. It draws crowds during Navarātri and is dedicated to the goddess Kātyāyanī, regarded as an aspect of Durgā. Built in a mix of north and south Indian styles, it shows the growth of large modern temple complexes in the capital.

events.title: ISKCON Māyāpur and Vṛndāvana
events.description: ISKCON, founded by A. C. Bhaktivedānta Swāmī Prabhupāda in New York in 1966, opened its Krishna-Balarāma Mandir at Vṛndāvana in 1975, one of its first major temples in India. The movement had acquired land at Māyāpur in West Bengal, said to be Caitanya's birthplace, in the early 1970s, and it later became ISKCON's international headquarters. These centres drew devotees from around the world and made the Gauḍīya tradition a global presence.

events.title: Emergency
events.description: On 25 June 1975, facing a court verdict against her election and mass protests led by Jayaprakāś Nārāyaṇ, Prime Minister Indira Gāndhī had a state of emergency declared. For twenty-one months the press was censored and more than a hundred thousand people were held without trial. The RSS and several other organisations were banned, and its volunteers formed much of the underground resistance. She called an election in 1977 and lost.

events.title: Agnicayana filmed in Kerala
events.description: In 1975 a group of Nambūtiri brāhmaṇas performed the Agnicayana, the building of the fire altar, together with the twelve-day Atirātra soma ritual, at Pāññāḷ in Kerala. The ritual is described in the Vedic texts and was said to be extremely rare. The scholar Frits Staal organised its documentation and made the film Altar of Fire, later followed by a two-volume book, Agni. The record is highly valued as evidence of a living Vedic ritual, though some Nambūtiris questioned the outside attention.

events.title: Jai Santoṣī Mā
events.description: Jai Santoṣī Mā, a modest 1975 Hindi film, tells of a devotee of Santoṣī Mā, a goddess associated with satisfaction, and her fast on Fridays. The film was a surprise commercial hit. It spread the worship of the goddess, who had been little known in the Purāṇic tradition, across northern India, with women observing the Friday vrata. The film is a well-known example of how cinema can create and spread a form of devotion.

events.title: "Secular" added to the Preamble
events.description: The Constitution of 1950 did not use the word "secular"; its authors thought the guarantees of religious freedom made it unnecessary. During the Emergency, with the opposition in jail, the 42nd Amendment added "socialist" and "secular" to the Preamble. Later governments kept the words. In Indian usage secularism has meant the state keeping an equal distance from all religions, though whether it does so in practice, for instance in controlling temples but not mosques or churches, is disputed.

events.title: Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara temple, Pittsburgh
events.description: The first Hindu immigrants to America after 1965 were mostly engineers and doctors, and they wanted temples built properly. At Pittsburgh they raised a temple to Veṅkaṭeśvara with craftsmen and advice from Tirupati, consecrated on 8 June 1977. Weeks later a Gaṇeśa temple opened in Flushing, New York. Both followed the Āgamas for design and ritual. There are now well over a thousand Hindu temples in the United States.

events.title: Prabhupāda's passing
events.description: Prabhupāda died at Vṛndāvana on 14 November 1977, aged eighty-one, dictating his translation of the Bhāgavata almost to the last day. In twelve years he had initiated about five thousand disciples, opened 108 temples, farms and schools, and published more than seventy volumes that were translated into dozens of languages. His society went through a difficult period of scandals and reform after him, and has since grown, especially in India and Eastern Europe.

events.title: Ādi Śaṅkara Kīrti Stambha at Kālaḍi
events.description: The Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi monastery built a multi-storey octagonal tower at Kālaḍi in Kerala, on the bank of the Periyār where Śaṅkara is said to have been born. Opened on 12 May 1978, it has a spiral ramp inside leading past paintings of the events of his life. Kālaḍi had been little known as a pilgrimage place until the early twentieth century, when the Śṛṅgeri monastery also established shrines there.

events.title: Second World Hindu Conference at Prayāga
events.description: In January 1979 the VHP held its second World Hindu Conference at the confluence at Prayāga. Delegates came from India and abroad, and representatives of the main monastic orders, along with Jaina and Sikh representatives, shared one platform. The Dalai Lama inaugurated it. The conference stressed Hindu unity and the rejection of untouchability, and was an early large-scale expression of the VHP's effort to present Hindu traditions as a common front.

events.title: Hinduism Today magazine founded
events.description: Śivāya Subramuniyasvāmī, an American-born teacher of Śaiva Siddhānta, founded a monastery on the island of Kauai, Hawaii, in 1970, and in 1979 started the magazine Hinduism Today. The Himalayan Academy, as his order is known, publishes the magazine and many books on Hindu thought and practice, and it reaches a worldwide readership. The monastery's temple, Kadavul Hindu Temple, was built in the 1970s and 80s. The publication gives Hindus in the diaspora a shared source of news and teaching.

events.description: Svāmī Dayānanda Sarasvatī, who lived from 1930 to 2015, was a Tamil-born teacher who studied Vedānta with Svāmī Cinmayānanda in the 1960s before teaching on his own. He helped convene the Hindu Dharma Ācārya Sabhā in 2003, a gathering of leaders of Hindu traditions. He is not to be confused with Dayānanda Sarasvatī, founder of the Ārya Samāj.

events.title: Mīnākṣīpuram conversions
events.description: In February 1981 some two hundred Dalit families in the village of Mīnākṣīpuram in Tamil Nadu converted to Islam in a public ceremony, saying they were tired of humiliation by the dominant caste. The event caused a national shock. Hindu leaders of every kind, including the Kāñcī Śaṅkarācārya, went to the area, and organisations launched campaigns against untouchability and for temple entry. It also gave a new urgency to the movement for Hindu unity that fed into the Ayodhyā campaign.

events.title: Samskrita Bharati
events.description: Samskrita Bharati, a movement to promote spoken Sanskrit, began in Bengaluru in 1981. It teaches Sanskrit conversation through short camps and courses run by volunteers, aimed at ordinary people who had only studied the language through grammar. Its work has trained many thousands of learners. The village of Mattūr in Karnataka is often called a "Sanskrit village", since many of its residents speak the language, and it is a frequent example of the movement's aims.

events.title: Mātā Amṛtānandamayī Maṭh
events.description: Sudhāmaṇi was born in 1953 to a poor fishing family on the Kerala coast and left school at nine to keep house. From childhood she was found absorbed in devotion to Kṛṣṇa and comforting neighbours in distress. A group of disciples formed around her, and the Mātā Amṛtānandamayī Maṭh was registered in 1981. Known as Amma, "mother", she is famous for embracing each person who comes to her, a number her organisation puts in the tens of millions, and her mission runs hospitals, universities and disaster relief.

events.title: Art of Living founded at Bengaluru
events.description: Ravi Śaṅkar, a young teacher from Tamil Nadu who had worked with Maharṣi Mahesh Yogi, founded the Art of Living in 1981, with Bengaluru as its base, around a rhythmic breathing practice called Sudarśana Kriyā. The foundation says it teaches in more than 150 countries and runs courses, schools and humanitarian projects. It has also drawn criticism, and scholars debate how its techniques relate to older yogic and prāṇāyāma traditions.

events.title: Marine archaeology at Dvārakā
events.description: From 1983 the archaeologist S. R. Rao led underwater surveys off Dvārakā and the island of Bet Dvārakā in Gujarat. Divers recorded stone walls, bastions and many stone anchors on the seabed. Rao dated the remains to about 1500 BCE and identified them with Kṛṣṇa's city; later studies date much of the material to the historical or medieval period. The site has not yet been fully excavated.

events.title: Ekātmatā Yātrā
events.description: In November 1983 the VHP sent three great processions across India: from Kathmandu to Rāmeśvaram, from Gaṅgāsāgar to Somanātha, and from Haridvāra to Kanyākumārī. Each carried a large pot of Gaṅgā water and an image of Bhārat Mātā, Mother India, on a decorated truck. Smaller processions joined from every district, mixing local river water with that of the Gaṅgā. Organisers claimed some sixty million took part. It was a rehearsal for the mass campaigns that followed.

events.title: VHP launches Rāma Janmabhūmi campaign
events.description: In April 1984 the VHP called an assembly of several hundred religious leaders, a Dharma Saṃsad, in Delhi. It resolved to "liberate" three sites where mosques stood on the remains of major temples: Rāma's birthplace at Ayodhyā, Kṛṣṇa's at Mathurā and the Viśvanātha temple at Kāśī. In September a procession set out from Sītāmaṛhī, Sītā's birthplace in Bihar, toward Ayodhyā, demanding that the locks on the building be opened.

events.title: Mahābalipuram and Koṇārka inscribed by UNESCO
events.description: In 1984, UNESCO inscribed the Group of Monuments at Mahābalipuram and the Sun Temple at Koṇārka as World Heritage Sites. Further Hindu sites followed: Hampi and Khajurāho in 1986, and Elephanta Caves, Paṭṭadakal and the Great Living Cōḻa Temples in 1987. The listings recognised the monuments' artistic and historic value, and they also brought attention to conservation, visitor management and tourism at these living places of worship.

events.title: Hindu temples rise in California and Illinois
events.description: In the 1980s Hindu communities in the United States built large temples in the Indian style. The Sri Venkateswara temple at Malibu, California, was consecrated in 1981, and the Shiva-Vishnu temple at Livermore opened in 1986. In the Chicago area, the Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago at Lemont, with a Rāma shrine, was consecrated in 1986. They used craftsmen from India and followed traditional ritual, and became centres of social life for the diaspora.

events.title: Anti-Sikh violence after Indira Gāndhī's assassination
events.description: On 31 October 1984 Prime Minister Indira Gāndhī was shot by two of her Sikh bodyguards, in revenge for the army's assault on the Golden Temple that June. Over the next three days mobs, which inquiries said were in many cases organised by local Congress politicians, hunted Sikhs in Delhi and other cities. About 2,800 were killed in Delhi alone by the official count. Many Hindus sheltered their Sikh neighbours. Justice for the victims took decades and remains incomplete.

events.title: Helensburgh Veṅkaṭeśvara temple, Australia
events.description: The Sri Venkateswara Temple at Helensburgh, south of Sydney, was consecrated in 1985 and is among the earliest large Hindu temples in Australia, built in the South Indian style for the Tamil and Telugu communities. From the 1980s and 1990s more Hindu temples were built across Australia and New Zealand as the communities grew, among them Murugan temples in Sydney and Melbourne. They serve as places of worship and as centres for cultural and language classes.

events.title: Ayodhyā locks opened
events.description: On 1 February 1986 a local lawyer asked the district judge at Faizabad to remove the locks placed on the Ayodhyā building in 1949. The district officials told the court they were not needed for keeping order. The judge ordered them opened, and it was done within the hour, in front of television cameras. Hindus could now enter and worship. Muslim groups formed the Babri Masjid Action Committee in protest, and the dispute became a national one.

events.title: Ekal Vidyālaya founded
events.description: Ekal Vidyālaya began in 1986 as a movement of one-teacher schools in tribal villages of what is now Jharkhand, then part of Bihar. A single local teacher runs a school for a few hours a day, teaching basic literacy, health and values. It has since spread to many thousands of villages across India, and it is supported by donations, including from overseas supporters. It is linked to organisations of the Saṅgh family, and is a much-cited example of low-cost education.

events.title: Hampi inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site
events.description: In 1986, at its tenth session, UNESCO inscribed the Group of Monuments at Hampi on the World Heritage List. Hampi, on the Tuṅgabhadrā, was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire from 1336 to 1565; after the Battle of Tālīkoṭa a coalition of the Deccan sultanates took and ruined the city, and it was never resettled. The ruins include the Virūpākṣa, Viṭṭhala and Hazāra Rāma temples.¶The inscription recognised Hampi as the best surviving evidence of the south Indian Hindu imperial city, with temples, bazaars, royal enclosures, water works and ceremonial structures spread across a boulder-strewn landscape. Virūpākṣa is still a living place of worship, so Hampi is both an archaeological site and a pilgrimage centre. The listing has brought conservation work and also pressure from tourism.
events.eraDesc: Independence, constitutional democracy, technological self-reliance, and cosmic space research.

events.title: Anantnāg riots of 1986
events.description: In February 1986, after the opening of the locks at Ayodhyā and amid local political intrigue, mobs in the Anantnāg district of south Kashmir attacked the Hindu minority. Dozens of temples were damaged or destroyed and many homes and shops were looted and burned. The state government was dismissed soon after. For Kashmiri Paṇḍits it was the first warning of what would come four years later.

events.title: Rāmāyaṇ on Doordarshan
events.description: From 25 January 1987, Rāmānand Sāgar's seventy-eight episode serial went out on the state television channel every Sunday morning. India had one channel and few sets; neighbours crowded into the houses that owned one.¶Streets emptied and trains were held at stations. Viewers bathed first, garlanded the television and lit incense before it. Audiences of eighty million or more are claimed for each week, and it was said to be the most-watched programme in the world at the time. It gave the whole country a single shared image of Rāma just as the Ayodhyā movement was gathering strength.

events.title: Śrīraṅgam's Rājagopuram completed
events.description: The Rājagopuram, the main southern tower of the Raṅganātha temple at Śrīraṅgam, was begun in the 16th century under the Nāyakas and left unfinished for centuries. It was completed in 1987 with the efforts of the 44th head of the Ahobila Maṭha, and stands about 236 feet, or about 72 metres, tall, among the tallest temple towers in Asia. The completion was celebrated with a consecration ceremony, a kumbhābhiṣeka.

events.title: Fiji coups of 1987
events.description: In 1987 military coups in Fiji overthrew a government supported by Indo-Fijians, who are mostly descendants of indentured labourers and are largely Hindu. Later events in 1999–2000 added further turmoil. Indo-Fijians reported discrimination, loss of land leases and insecurity, and many emigrated to Australia, New Zealand, Canada and the United States. The coups changed the community's size and shaped the diaspora, and they remain an important example of the political difficulties faced by Hindus overseas.

events.title: Paṭṭadakal temples inscribed by UNESCO
events.description: In 1987, at its eleventh session, UNESCO placed the Group of Monuments at Paṭṭadakal in Karnataka on the World Heritage List. The site has ten major temples, nine Hindu and one Jain, mostly built by the Early Cālukyas in the seventh and eighth centuries. The largest, the Virūpākṣa temple, was sponsored by Queen Lokamahādevī and is dated to about 740 CE.¶UNESCO described the group as a harmonious blend of northern and southern Indian architectural forms, Nāgara and Drāviḍa side by side. The Virūpākṣa was modelled on the Kailāsanātha at Kāñcī, and the Kailāsa temple at Ellora was in turn modelled on the Virūpākṣa. Paṭṭadakal thus shows how a temple style passed between dynasties in the early medieval Deccan.

events.title: Roop Kanwar and the Satī Prevention Act
events.description: In September 1987 Roop Kanwar, an eighteen-year-old widow, died on her husband's funeral pyre at Deorālā in Rajasthan. The event provoked a national debate. Supporters of the rite called it a voluntary satī and held a large gathering, while critics and women's groups said she was forced or coerced. The central government passed the Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act in 1987, which made aiding, abetting or glorifying satī a crime, and strengthened earlier laws.

events.title: Mahābhārat on Doordarshan
events.description: B. R. Copṛā's Mahābhārat ran for ninety-four Sunday episodes from October 1988. The script was by the Urdu writer Rāhī Māsūm Razā, who answered those surprised that a Muslim was writing it by saying he was a son of the Gaṅgā. Each episode opened with Time itself as narrator. It drew audiences even larger than the Rāmāyaṇ before it, was dubbed for broadcast abroad, and fixed the faces of Kṛṣṇa, Draupadī and Bhīṣma in the Indian imagination.

The first brick was laid by Kāmeśvar Caupāl, a Dalit volunteer from Bihar, chosen deliberately to show that the temple belonged to every Hindu.

events.title: Pālampur resolution
events.description: Until 1989 the Ayodhyā movement was run by the VHP and religious leaders. In June that year the BJP's national executive, meeting at Pālampur in Himachal Pradesh, passed a resolution calling for the site to be handed to Hindus and comparing it to the rebuilding of Somanātha. It was the first time a major political party had adopted the demand. In the election that November the BJP went from two seats to eighty-five.

events.title: Exodus of the Kashmiri Paṇḍits
events.description: As an armed separatist insurgency spread in the Kashmir Valley in late 1989, prominent Paṇḍits were assassinated one after another. On the night of 19 January 1990 mosque loudspeakers and crowds in Śrīnagar raised slogans telling the Hindus to convert, leave or die.¶Over the following weeks almost the whole community, between one and three hundred thousand people by differing estimates, left their homes for camps in Jammu and Delhi. They had lived in the Valley for several thousand years and produced much of its Sanskrit learning. Most have not been able to return.

events.title: Hindu student groups in USA and UK
events.description: The children of Hindu immigrants grew up between two worlds. In 1990 the Hindu Students Council was founded in the United States, and in 1991 the National Hindu Students Forum began in Britain. Campus chapters held festivals, study circles and service projects, and gave young people a way to explain their tradition in their own words. Both groups have been linked to the Vishva Hindu Parishad network, and some critics have questioned their politics.

events.title: Sanskrit texts go online
events.description: From the 1990s, scholars and volunteers began to put Sanskrit texts online. The Muktabodha Indological Research Institute digitised Śaiva and Tantric works, and the Sanskrit Documents project and GRETIL (Göttingen Register of Electronic Texts in Indian Languages, from 2001) provided editions in searchable form. The Digital Library of India scanned books and manuscripts. These resources made the śāstras available worldwide and enabled computer-assisted study of vocabulary and style, although quality varies from one source to another.

events.description: On 25 September 1990 the BJP president L. K. events.title: Kar-sevaks fired upon at Ayodhyā
events.description: Despite a ban and sealed borders, tens of thousands of volunteers reached Ayodhyā on foot for the date set to begin building, 30 October 1990. Some broke through and planted a flag on the domes. The state police opened fire that day and again on 2 November. The official figure was sixteen dead; the VHP claimed far more. Among them were two brothers from Calcutta, Rām and Śarad Koṭhārī. The movement honours the dead as martyrs.

events.title: Places of Worship Act
events.description: With the Ayodhyā dispute at its height, Parliament passed a law in 1991 declaring that every place of worship must keep the religious character it had on 15 August 1947, and barring courts from hearing claims to change it. Ayodhyā, already in court, was exempted. The law was meant to stop similar disputes at Kāśī, Mathurā and elsewhere. Its constitutionality has been challenged, and courts have still allowed surveys to determine what a site's character was.

events.title: Svāmī Lakṣmaṇ Joo's passing
events.description: Svāmī Lakṣmaṇ Joo, a Kashmiri Śaiva master born in 1907 in Śrīnagar, died there in September 1991. He is regarded as the last great teacher in the direct oral lineage of the Trika, the tradition of Abhinavagupta, and taught at the Īśvara Āśrama near Dal Lake. He instructed many scholars and students from India and the West, and his lectures and translations helped introduce Kashmir Śaivism to the wider world.

events.title: Demolition of the Babri Masjid
events.description: On 6 December 1992 a rally of well over a hundred thousand volunteers gathered at Ayodhyā for a symbolic ceremony beside the disputed building. Around midday groups broke through the cordon, climbed the domes, and within about five hours had brought the sixteenth-century structure down with hand tools.¶A makeshift shrine for the image of the child Rāma was put up on the spot. Riots across India in the following weeks killed some two thousand people, and temples were attacked in Pakistan and Bangladesh. The central government dismissed four state governments. The legal dispute over the land ran until 2019.

events.title: Isha Foundation
events.description: Jaggī Vāsudev, known as Sadhguru, founded the Isha Foundation in 1992 in Tamil Nadu, offering yoga programs, and later set up its center at the foot of the Velliangiri hills near Coimbatore. events.title: Akṣardhām, Gāndhīnagar
events.description: BAPS opened its first Akṣardhām at Gāndhīnagar, the capital of Gujarat, on 30 October 1992. The monument is built of six thousand tonnes of pink sandstone from Rajasthan, carved by hand and assembled without steel, and houses a gilded image of Svāminārāyaṇa. Around it are exhibition halls and gardens. It set the pattern for a new kind of Hindu sacred complex that teaches visitors as well as receiving worshippers.

events.title: Parliament of the World's Religions, Chicago
events.description: In 1993, a hundred years after Svāmī Vivekānanda's address of 1893, the Parliament of the World's Religions met again in Chicago, drawing several thousand participants from many faiths, with a large Hindu presence. events.title: Death of the Kāñcī Paramācārya
events.description: Candraśekharendra Sarasvatī became head of the Kāñcī monastery in 1907 at the age of thirteen and led it for eighty-seven years. He walked across India on foot for decades, slept in cowsheds, and revived Vedic schools, temple arts and Tamil hymn-singing that were close to dying out. events.title: Śrī Śiva Subramaṇiya temple consecrated at Nadi
events.description: On 15 July 1994 the new Śrī Śiva Subramaṇiya temple at Nadi, on the island of Viti Levu in Fiji, was consecrated. The Hindu community of Fiji is descended largely from the indentured labourers brought from India from 1879, and the temple, with its Tamil rites and ritual specialists, shows how that diaspora has rebuilt classical temple tradition in the Pacific.

events.description: The Svāminārāyaṇa temple at Neasden in north-west London opened on 20 August 1995. Volunteers did much of the work and raised much of the money, some by collecting aluminium cans.

events.description: Svāmī Rāmdev, a yoga teacher from Haryana, and his associate Ācārya Bālkṛṣṇa founded Divya Yog Mandir in Haridvāra in 1995. From 2003, Rāmdev's yoga camps were broadcast on television, which made him widely known and brought prāṇāyāma into many homes. The Patañjali Yogpīṭh, founded in 2006, and the Patañjali Āyurved company, started in 2006 and later a large consumer goods firm, grew from this base. The movement shows how modern media have shaped the practice of yoga.

events.title: Gaṇeśa "milk miracle"
events.description: Early on 21 September 1995 a worshipper in Delhi offered a spoonful of milk to an image of Gaṇeśa and saw it disappear. By midday the report had spread by telephone across India and to temples in Britain, America and elsewhere; shops ran out of milk and traffic stopped. Scientists explained it as capillary action drawing liquid across the stone surface. By the next day it had mostly ceased. It was one of the first religious events to travel the world in hours.

events.title: "Hindutva is a way of life" judgment
events.description: In December 1995 the Supreme Court heard appeals against election results in Maharashtra where candidates had appealed to "Hindutva". The court held that the word does not by itself mean a narrow religious appeal; following a 1966 judgment, it described Hinduism as a way of life of the people of the subcontinent that cannot be defined by one prophet, book or creed. Whether a particular speech sought votes on religion still depends on what was said. The ruling is much cited and much criticised.

events.title: ISKCON temple consecrated in Bengaluru
events.description: The ISKCON Śrī Rādhā Kṛṣṇa temple on Hare Kṛṣṇa Hill at Rajajinagar, Bengaluru, was consecrated in 1997. It is dedicated to Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa and became the centre of ISKCON's work in the city, which includes the Akṣaya Pātra Foundation, founded in 2000 to serve mid-day meals to schoolchildren. The temple is among the best known and most visited ISKCON centres in India, attracting large crowds at festivals such as Janmāṣṭamī.

events.title: Wandhama massacre
events.description: On the night of 25 January 1998 gunmen dressed as soldiers entered the village of Wandhama in Kashmir, took tea with the few Paṇḍit families who had stayed on after 1990, and then shot twenty-three of them, including women and children. In 2003 twenty-four more Paṇḍits were killed in the same way at Nadimarg. The massacres deepened the community's fear and weakened hopes that those displaced in 1990 could return home.

events.title: Tiruvaḷḷuvar statue at Kanyākumārī
events.description: The 133-foot statue of Tiruvaḷḷuvar, the Tamil poet of the Tirukkuṟaḷ, stands on a rock island near the Vivekānanda Rock Memorial at Kanyākumārī, where the Indian Ocean, the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal meet. It was unveiled on 1 January 2000. Its height, 133 feet, stands for the 133 chapters of the Tirukkuṟaḷ. The statue is a major landmark and a symbol of Tamil culture, and it is open to visitors.

events.title: Sattriya recognised as a classical dance of India
events.description: On 15 November 2000 the Saṅgīt Nāṭak Akādemī recognised Sattriya as a classical dance of India. The form is credited to the sixteenth-century Assamese saint Śaṅkaradeva, who used dance, drama and song to teach devotion to Kṛṣṇa. It grew inside the sattras, the monasteries of the Assamese Vaiṣṇava movement, where it was long performed only by male monks.¶Śaṅkaradeva's art, with its gestures, rhythms and the ritual plays known as aṅkīyā nāṭ, was thus kept alive inside a monastic tradition before it was formally placed among the classical arts. Today it is performed by both men and women, on and off the stage, and the sattras at Mājulī remain its main home.

events.title: Akṣaya Pātra
events.description: The Akṣaya Pātra Foundation, associated with ISKCON, began in 2000 in Bengaluru by serving mid-day meals to a small number of schoolchildren. It uses large centralised kitchens and has expanded to many states, working with government school-meal schemes. It now describes itself as the world's largest NGO-run school meal programme, serving millions of children a day. The name comes from the Akṣaya Pātra, the inexhaustible vessel of food in the Mahābhārata story of the Pāṇḍavas.

events.title: First Hindu prayer in the US House
events.description: In August 2000 about a thousand religious leaders gathered at the United Nations in New York for the Millennium World Peace Summit, in which Hindu leaders took part. On 14 September 2000 Veṅkaṭācalapati Samuldrāla, priest of the Śiva Viṣṇu temple at Parma, Ohio, opened a session of the US House of Representatives with a prayer, the first Hindu to do so. Rajan Zed later gave the first Hindu prayer in the Senate, in 2007.

events.title: Kumbha Melā at Prayāga, 2001
events.description: The Kumbha at Prayāga in January–February 2001 was the first of the new millennium and drew wide coverage in Indian and international media. On the main bathing day, Maunī Amāvasyā, some thirty million people are estimated to have bathed at the confluence, by the authorities' count, and the fair as a whole was among the largest gatherings in human history. A temporary city of tents, roads and hospitals was built on the riverbank for the pilgrims.

events.title: Godhrā train burning
events.description: On the morning of 27 February 2002 the Sābarmatī Express, carrying volunteers home from Ayodhyā, was stopped just outside Godhrā station in Gujarat. A coach was set on fire and fifty-nine people, including women and children, were burned to death. Courts later convicted thirty-one men of conspiracy.¶In the days that followed, mobs attacked Muslim neighbourhoods across Gujarat. Official figures give 790 Muslims and 254 Hindus killed; other estimates are higher. The events remain among the most bitterly contested in recent Indian history.

events.title: Akṣardhām attacked
events.description: On the afternoon of 24 September 2002 two gunmen entered the Akṣardhām complex at Gāndhīnagar and fired on visitors, killing thirty-three people, including a commando and policemen, before they were shot the next morning. Pramukh Svāmī Mahārāj, the head of BAPS, asked his followers and the public to pray for the dead and for peace, and blamed no community. There was no retaliation, and the temple reopened within two weeks.

events.title: ASI excavates at Ayodhyā
events.description: In 2003 the Allahabad High Court ordered the Archaeological Survey to excavate the Ayodhyā site. Over about five months it dug dozens of trenches under the eyes of observers from both sides. Its report described a large structure beneath the mosque, with rows of pillar bases, decorated stonework and a circular shrine, dated around the twelfth century and of north Indian temple type. Some archaeologists disputed the reading. The Supreme Court in 2019 accepted that the mosque had not been built on vacant land.

events.description: The Hindu American Foundation was founded in 2003 as an advocacy group for Hindu Americans. It works on issues such as the portrayal of Hinduism in school textbooks, civil rights, and interfaith relations, and it publishes reports and engages with lawmakers. events.title: National Mission for Manuscripts founded
events.description: The National Mission for Manuscripts was set up by the Government of India's Ministry of Culture in 2003. It estimated that India holds about ten million manuscripts, probably the largest collection in the world, many in private hands, temples, mathas and libraries, in a great variety of languages and scripts. Its task is to survey, catalogue, conserve and digitise them, and its Kritisampada database gives scholars access to records. Damp, insects and neglect threaten the manuscripts, which lay behind the effort.
