events.title: Vedic chanting proclaimed by UNESCO
events.description: In 2003 UNESCO proclaimed the tradition of Vedic chanting a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity; it was placed on the Representative List in 2008. What it recognised is a technology of memory. Students learn each verse in continuous form, then word by word, then in interlaced patterns such as the jaṭā ("braid") and ghana ("dense") recitations, which repeat words forwards and backwards. These methods allowed the texts to be preserved with exceptional fidelity for some three thousand years without writing. Of more than a thousand śākhās once counted, only a handful are still recited.

events.title: Kāñcī Śaṅkarācārya arrested
events.description: Jayendra Sarasvatī, head of the Kāñcī monastery, was arrested on the night of Dīpāvalī 2004 on a charge of ordering the murder of a former temple official. He was held for two months. The case was moved out of Tamil Nadu at his request, and in 2013 the court acquitted him and all other accused, with most witnesses having withdrawn their statements. The arrest of a Śaṅkarācārya shocked many Hindus.

events.title: Akṣardhām, New Delhi
events.description: Opened on 6 November 2005 on the bank of the Yamunā, the Akṣardhām complex was built in five years by some 11,000 artisans and volunteers under Pramukh Svāmī Mahārāj. The central monument uses pink sandstone and white marble and, following the old Śilpa texts, no structural steel.¶Its plinth carries 148 life-size stone elephants, and its walls and pillars some 20,000 carved figures. It is as much a statement as a temple: that the traditional craft of temple building is alive and can work at scale in the modern world.

events.title: Kaṭās Rāj restoration
events.description: Kaṭās Rāj in the Salt Range of Pakistan's Punjab is a complex of ancient temples around a sacred pool, which tradition links with Śiva's tears after the death of Satī. In 2005 the Indian leader L. K. Advani visited and the Pakistani government began a programme of conservation and restoration. Work has continued since then, and the site is visited by Hindu pilgrims from India, though poor maintenance and falling water levels have also drawn criticism.

events.title: Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act
events.description: Under the Mitākṣarā law of the joint family, sons acquired a share in ancestral property at birth, while daughters did not. The Succession Act of 1956 gave daughters a share only in what a father left at death. The 2005 amendment made a daughter a co-owner by birth on exactly the same footing as a son, married or not. In 2020 the Supreme Court confirmed that this applies whether or not the father was alive in 2005.

events.title: Batu Caves Murugaṉ statue
events.description: The Batu Caves, limestone caverns north of Kuala Lumpur, have housed a Murugaṉ temple since 1891. In January 2006 a statue of the god 42.7 metres tall, coated with gold paint, was unveiled at the foot of the 272 steps. Each year at Tai Pūcam about a million people climb them, many carrying kāvaḍi, decorated frames borne in fulfilment of vows. It is the largest Tai Pūcam celebration outside India.

events.title: California textbook controversy
events.description: When California revised its sixth-grade history textbooks in 2005–06, Hindu American groups, including the Vedic Foundation and the Hindu Education Foundation, asked for changes to passages they said presented Hinduism mainly through caste and the oppression of women, unlike the chapters on other faiths. A group of scholars objected that some of the edits distorted history. The state board accepted some changes and rejected others, and a lawsuit followed. The dispute drew wide attention to how Hinduism is taught in American schools.

events.title: Rāma Setu controversy
events.description: A line of shoals runs between Rāmeśvaram and Sri Lanka, known as Rāma Setu, the bridge built by Rāma's army. In 2005 work began on dredging a shipping canal through it. Protests spread, and in September 2007 an affidavit filed in the Supreme Court by the Archaeological Survey said there was no historical evidence that Rāma existed. After an outcry the affidavit was withdrawn within days, and the Court stayed work on the shoals. The canal has not gone ahead through them.

events.title: First Hindu prayer in the US Senate
events.description: On 12 July 2007 Rajan Zed, a Hindu leader from Nevada, delivered the opening prayer in the United States Senate, the first Hindu to do so. The event was disrupted by protesters who shouted from the gallery. Zed's prayer included Sanskrit passages from the Upaniṣads and a call for peace, and it was widely reported. It is seen as a sign of the growing recognition of Hindus in American public life.

events.title: Invading the Sacred challenges Hindu studies
events.description: In 2007 the volume Invading the Sacred, edited by Krishnan Ramaswamy, Antonio de Nicolás and Aditi Banerjee, collected essays by Hindu authors criticising how some American scholars of religion, especially those using psychoanalytic readings, portrayed Hindu deities and traditions. It grew out of earlier disputes over works such as Paul Courtright's book on Gaṇeśa. Scholars of Hindu studies replied that critique should not be confused with disrespect. The controversy raised questions about who has authority to interpret Hindu traditions and how scholarship should treat living faiths.

events.title: HINDRAF rally
events.description: Tamils were brought to Malaya as plantation labour under British rule, and their descendants are about seven per cent of Malaysia's people. After a series of temple demolitions, a coalition called HINDRAF organised a rally in Kuala Lumpur on 25 November 2007. Tens of thousands came despite a ban; police used tear gas and water cannon, and five leaders were jailed without trial. The rally changed Malaysian politics at the next election.

events.title: Nepal ceases to be a Hindu kingdom
events.description: Nepal's kings had ruled as Hindu monarchs since the eighteenth century and were regarded by many as forms of Viṣṇu. After a decade of Maoist insurgency and a popular uprising in 2006, the restored parliament declared the state secular. On 28 May 2008 a newly elected assembly abolished the monarchy. The cow remains the national animal, and a movement to restore a Hindu state persists.

events.title: Amarnāth land agitation
events.description: In May 2008 the Jammu and Kashmir government transferred forty hectares of forest land to the board that manages the pilgrimage to the Amarnāth cave, for temporary shelters. Protests in the Kashmir Valley led it to cancel the transfer. The Jammu region then rose in a two-month agitation with strikes and road blockades. In August the land was made available to the board for the pilgrimage season each year.

events.title: Svāmī Lakṣmaṇānanda killed
events.description: Svāmī Lakṣmaṇānanda Sarasvatī had worked for forty years among the tribal people of Kandhamāl in Odisha, running schools and opposing conversion. On 23 August 2008, as his āśram celebrated Kṛṣṇa's birthday, gunmen killed him and four others. Maoists claimed responsibility, and seven Christian tribals were later convicted. In the weeks that followed, mobs attacked Christian villages; about forty people died and tens of thousands were displaced.

events.title: Allahabad High Court's Ayodhyā verdict
events.description: On 30 September 2010 three judges of the Allahabad High Court, sitting at Lucknow, ruled on the sixty-year-old Ayodhyā title suits. By majority they held that the area under the central dome was the birthplace of Rāma according to Hindu faith, and that the mosque had been built on the site of a demolished structure. They then divided the land into three parts: for the deity, for the Nirmohī order and for the Sunni board. All sides appealed.

events.title: Tañjāvūr Big Temple turns one thousand
events.description: The Bṛhadīśvara temple at Tañjāvūr was built by the Cōḻa king Rājarāja I and consecrated in 1010, so in 2010 it marked a thousand years. Its great vimāna, a tower about 66 metres tall, is crowned by a massive granite capstone, and the temple is known for its inscriptions, frescoes and the large Nandī. The anniversary was marked with celebrations, a commemorative coin and a stamp, and the temple is still an active place of worship.

events.title: Padmanābhasvāmī temple vaults opened
events.description: The rulers of Travancore had for centuries placed offerings in the cellars of the Padmanābhasvāmī temple at Tiruvanantapuram. In 2011, on the Supreme Court's order, five of the six vaults were opened and listed: sacks of gold coins from Roman to Napoleonic times, jewelled crowns, and gold images. Press estimates, not official figures, put the value at about twenty billion dollars or more. The sixth chamber, Vault B, is kept shut; the royal family and many devotees hold that opening it would be a sacrilege.

events.title: Death of Satya Sāī Bābā
events.description: Satyanārāyaṇa Rāju was born in 1926 in the village of Puṭṭaparti in Andhra and at fourteen declared himself the return of the saint Sāī Bābā of Śirḍī. He taught that all religions are one and that service is worship, and his following ran into millions across the world. His trust built free hospitals, colleges and a water system for hundreds of villages. He was also the subject of allegations, which his organisation denied and which never led to a conviction. He died on 24 April 2011.

events.title: Kedāranātha flood
events.description: In mid-June 2013 early monsoon rain and a bursting glacial lake sent a wall of water, mud and boulders down the valley of Kedāranātha at the height of the pilgrim season. The town was buried; over five thousand people died or were never found. The eighth-century temple was hardly damaged. A huge rock had come to rest just behind it and split the flood to either side. It is now worshipped as Bhīma Śilā.

The authorities estimated some 100 million visits over about fifty-five days, and thirty million on the main bathing day, 10 February. A Harvard University team studied the temporary city as a model of urban planning. A crush at Allahabad railway station that day killed thirty-six people.

events.title: International Day of Yoga adopted
events.description: In September 2014 India's Prime Minister proposed at the United Nations that 21 June, the northern summer solstice, be observed as a day of yoga. The resolution was adopted on 11 December without a vote, co-sponsored by 177 countries, the most for any General Assembly resolution of its kind.¶On the first Yoga Day in 2015, nearly thirty-six thousand people practised together on Rājpath in Delhi. The recognition marked how far yoga had travelled, from Himalayan hermitages to gyms worldwide, and it also sharpened a debate about how much of its spiritual root survives the journey.

events.title: Rāṇī kī Vāv inscribed by UNESCO
events.description: On 22 June 2014, at its thirty-eighth session, UNESCO inscribed the Rāṇī kī Vāv at Patan, Gujarat, on the World Heritage List. The stepwell was commissioned, according to the Prabandhacintāmaṇi, in 1063, by Queen Udayamatī in memory of her husband Bhīma I of the Caulukya dynasty; some historians propose an earlier date. Its shaft and steps were buried under silt from floods of the Sarasvatī river, and a major restoration took place in the 1980s.¶The stepwell has more than five hundred principal sculptures and over a thousand minor ones, with Viṣṇu in his avatāras, Śiva and apsarases. It shows a water structure built like an inverted temple, joining water and sacred space, and is among the most elaborate works of Caulukya art.

events.title: Nepal adopts a secular constitution
events.description: Nepal's constitution, promulgated on 20 September 2015, declared the country a federal democratic republic and secular, after the monarchy was abolished in 2008. This wording reflects an effort to balance equal treatment of all faiths with the long Hindu heritage of the country. Debates continue in Nepal over whether the Hindu state should be restored.

events.title: Rakhigarhi ancient DNA published
events.description: In 2019 scientists published the DNA of a woman buried at Rakhigarhi in Haryana about 2500 BCE, the first genome from a Harappan site. Her ancestry combined ancient Iranian-related and South Asian hunter-gatherer lines and had none of the Steppe ancestry found in many Indians today. The authors concluded that Steppe ancestry arrived after the Harappan cities declined. Others stress that one sample cannot settle the origins of Vedic culture.

events.title: Kedāranātha rebuilt after the flood
events.description: Kedāranātha, the Himalayan Śiva shrine in Uttarakhand, was devastated in June 2013 when floods and debris flows swept through the valley, killing thousands of pilgrims and locals and wrecking the town, though the stone temple itself largely stood. Reconstruction followed over several years: new embankments, rebuilt paths, and an improved route up from Gaurikuṇḍa. By 2019 the pilgrim town and the trek were functioning again, and the work, including the redevelopment around the sanctum, was widely publicised as a model of post-disaster rebuilding at altitude.

events.title: National Education Policy 2020 approved
events.description: The National Education Policy 2020 is India's major education reform document of recent decades. It stresses mother-tongue instruction in early years, a larger place for Sanskrit and other classical languages, and the incorporation of Indian knowledge systems, which include mathematics, astronomy, medicine, yoga, arts and philosophy, into curricula. A division for Indian Knowledge Systems was set up at the Ministry of Education. Supporters see this as a recovery of neglected heritage; critics worry about the quality of standards, uneven implementation and the risk of mixing historical research with cultural advocacy.
events.eraDesc: Independence, constitutional democracy, technological self-reliance, and cosmic space research.

events.title: Mob burns Karak temple in Pakistan
events.description: On 30 December 2020 a mob attacked and burned the Paramahaṃsa Jī Mahārāj samādhi temple at Teri in Karak district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, in Pakistan. The Supreme Court of Pakistan ordered the temple to be rebuilt and action taken against those responsible, and it was restored. The attack came months after work on a Kṛṣṇa temple for the small Hindu community of Islamabad, begun in 2020 on land allotted earlier, was halted after objections from some religious leaders and the matter went to the courts.

events.title: Dholavira becomes a UNESCO World Heritage Site
events.description: In July 2021 UNESCO inscribed "Dholavira: A Harappan City" on the World Heritage list, making it the first site of the Indus tradition in India to be listed. Mohenjo-daro in Pakistan was listed in 1980. The inscription cited the city's planning, defences and water management. It was India's fortieth World Heritage Site. The listing came after more than thirty years of excavation and was seen as a recognition of the wider Harappan heritage within India.

events.title: Rāmappa Temple inscribed by UNESCO
events.description: In July 2021 UNESCO inscribed the Rāmappa temple at Pālampet in Telangana on the World Heritage list. Built in 1213 under the Kākatīya ruler Gaṇapati Deva by his general Recarla Rudra, it is a Śiva temple known for its 'floating' lightweight bricks used in the tower, its carved bracket figures of dancers and musicians, and its star-shaped platform. It is the first Kākatīya monument to be listed, and it is still used for worship.

events.title: Attacks on Durgā Pūjā in Bangladesh
events.description: On 13 October 2021, during Durgā Pūjā, a copy of the Qur'an was found placed at a festival pavilion in Cumilla, Bangladesh; the police later arrested a Muslim man for putting it there. Images spread online, and over several days mobs attacked pavilions, temples and Hindu homes in a number of districts, including an ISKCON temple in Noakhali. Several people were killed. The government deployed troops and made hundreds of arrests.

events.title: Kāśī Viśvanātha Corridor
events.description: The Viśvanātha temple stood hemmed in by lanes barely wide enough for two people. The project opened on 13 December 2021 cleared a five-hectare corridor from the temple to the river, with halls and a museum. About three hundred buildings were bought and removed, and more than forty old temples that had been built over and hidden inside them were uncovered and restored. Pilgrims can again carry Gaṅgā water directly to the shrine.

events.title: Durgā Pūjā inscribed by UNESCO
events.description: In December 2021 UNESCO inscribed Durgā Pūjā in Kolkata as intangible heritage. For about five days each autumn, with preparations beginning weeks earlier, the city becomes an open-air gallery: neighbourhood committees put up thousands of temporary pavilions, each with a clay image of the goddess slaying the buffalo demon, made by the image-makers of Kumārṭulī. On the last day the images are carried to the river and immersed.

events.title: Statue of Equality
events.description: For the thousandth anniversary of Rāmānuja's birth, his follower Cinna Jīyar Svāmī built a seated statue of him 216 feet high at Hyderabad, dedicated on 5 February 2022. It is made of five metals and surrounded by replicas of the 108 Viṣṇu shrines praised by the Āḻvārs. It is called the Statue of Equality because Rāmānuja taught that devotion is open to every person whatever their birth.

events.title: Kāśī Tamiḻ Saṅgamam
events.description: Kāśī Tamiḻ Saṅgamam was a month-long cultural festival held in Vārāṇasī in November and December 2022, organised by the Government of India with Indian Institute of Technology Madras and Banaras Hindu University as partners. It celebrated the long relationship between Kāśī and the Tamil country, a bond visible in Tamil pilgrims, the Tamil saints' hymns to Kāśī's Viśvanātha, the Kāśī Maṭha lineages, and Tamil scholars who studied there. Delegations of Tamil students, artists, teachers and craftspeople travelled north, and further editions followed.

events.title: Yādādri temple reopens after rebuilding
events.description: The Government of Telangana, formed in 2014, undertook a large rebuilding of the Lakṣmī Narasiṃha temple at Yādagirigutṭa, renamed Yādādri, from the mid-2010s, using stone in the traditional Kṛṣṇa-śilā style, at a cost of about 1,200 crore rupees by official accounts. The renewed temple reopened with consecration rites in March 2022. The project drew praise for its scale as well as criticism over its cost and the use of public money.

events.title: Gyānvāpī survey
events.description: Five Hindu women petitioned a Vārāṇasī court in 2021 for the right to worship images on the outer wall of the Gyānvāpī mosque, which Hindu parties say stands on the site of the Viśvanātha temple demolished in 1669. In May 2022 a court-appointed team filmed the premises and reported an object in the ablution pond that the petitioners identify as a Śiva-liṅga and the mosque committee as a fountain. The Supreme Court ordered the spot protected. A later ASI survey reported that a large Hindu temple had existed before the mosque; the Muslim side disputes this.

events.title: Flag raised on Pāvāgaḍh Kālikā temple
events.description: The Kālikā Mātā shrine on Pāvāgaḍh hill in Gujarat, near Campāner, is an ancient goddess site and one of the Śākta pīṭhas in local tradition. Its spire was long missing; tradition and local accounts link the loss to the 15th-century conquest of the area by Maḥmūd Begaḍā, who took Pāvāgaḍh in 1484 after a long siege, and a dargāh was built on part of the hill. After a redevelopment project, a new śikhara was completed and a ceremonial flag raised on 18 June 2022, the first in about five hundred years.
events.eraDesc: Independence, constitutional democracy, technological self-reliance, and cosmic space research.

Misinformation on social media, much of it from outside the city, was widely blamed.

events.title: A Hindu Prime Minister in Britain
events.description: On 25 October 2022, during the week of Dīvālī, Rishi Sunak became prime minister of the United Kingdom, the first person of Indian heritage and the first Hindu to hold that office. Born in Southampton to parents of Punjabi descent whose families had come from East Africa, he has spoken of his Hindu faith and took his oath as an MP on the Bhagavad Gītā. Many in the Indian diaspora saw his rise as a symbolic milestone.

events.title: Seṅgol installed in the new Parliament
events.description: A seṅgol is a sceptre given to a Tamil king at his accession as a sign of just rule. The government says that in August 1947 the heads of the Tiruvāvaḍuturai monastery presented a golden one, topped with Nandī, to Nehru as a symbol of the transfer of power; some historians question whether it was understood that way. It lay for decades in a museum in Allahabad. On 28 May 2023 it was installed beside the Speaker's chair when the new Parliament building was opened, with monastery heads from Tamil Nadu present.

events.title: Cār Dhām yātrā sets attendance record
events.description: The Cār Dhām yātrā, the pilgrimage to Yamunotrī, Gaṅgotrī, Kedāranātha and Badarīnātha in Uttarakhand, set attendance records in 2023, with figures reported at more than five million. The Himalayan shrines open only from spring to autumn, and heavy numbers have raised concerns about road safety, landslides, waste and the carrying capacity of fragile valleys. In the same period, pilgrim interest grew in the Ādi Kailāśa and Pārvatī Sarovara region in Pithoragarh, promoted as an Indian alternative to the Kailāśa journey in Tibet.

events.title: "Śiva Śakti" point
events.description: On 23 August 2023 India's Chandrayaan-3 made a soft landing near the south pole of the Moon, the first craft to do so in that region. The Prime Minister announced that the landing point would be called Śiva Śakti: Śiva for the resolve to work for the good of all, and Śakti for the strength to carry it out, with a nod to the women scientists of the mission. The International Astronomical Union approved the name in 2024.

events.title: "Sanātana Dharma" controversy
events.description: In September 2023 Udhayanidhi Stalin, a Tamil Nadu minister and the son of the chief minister, said at a conference that "Sanātana Dharma" should be eradicated, comparing it to diseases such as dengue and malaria, and linking it to caste hierarchy. The remark sparked controversy across India. Many critics took it as an attack on Hindus, while supporters said he meant caste discrimination. It also revived the debate over what the term means, as scholars and religious leaders offered differing definitions.

events.title: G20 Naṭarāja and Hoysaḷa temples inscribed
events.description: For the G20 summit in September 2023 a bronze Naṭarāja twenty-seven feet high was set up at the Bharat Maṇḍapam hall in Delhi. It was cast by the traditional lost-wax method by craftsmen of Svāmimalai in Tamil Nadu, the home of Cōḻa bronze-casting. In the same month UNESCO inscribed the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysaḷas, the temples of Belūr, Haḷebīḍu and Somanāthapura in Karnataka, and Tagore's Śāntiniketan, as World Heritage Sites.

events.title: Statue of Oneness unveiled at Oṃkāreśvara
events.description: On 21 September 2023, a 108-foot bronze-and-alloy statue of Ādi Śaṅkara as a boy was unveiled at Oṃkāreśvara in Madhya Pradesh, on Māndhātā hill above the Narmadā. Named the Statue of Oneness, it forms the centre of the Ekātma Dhām project. Oṃkāreśvara matters in Śaṅkara's biography because tradition says the young ascetic met his teacher Govinda Bhagavatpāda in a cave here. The state government plans an Advaita Vedānta institute and museum nearby.

gitaQuote.translation: The Self is never born nor does it ever die; nor having once been, does it cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval, it is not slain when the body is slain.

events.title: Akṣardhām, Robbinsville
events.description: The BAPS Akṣardhām at Robbinsville, New Jersey, was dedicated on 8 October 2023. Built over about twelve years with the help of some 12,500 volunteers, it uses nearly two million cubic feet of stone carved in India and shipped across the ocean. It is among the largest Hindu temples built in modern times. A 2021 lawsuit by workers from India alleged that they were underpaid during construction; BAPS denied wrongdoing.

events.title: Garbā inscribed by UNESCO
events.description: Garbā is the circle dance of Gujarat performed on the nine nights of Navarātri around a lamp or an image of the Goddess. The name comes from garbha, "womb", for the pierced clay pot holding the lamp. People of every age and class dance together in the open, clapping in time. UNESCO added it to its intangible heritage list in December 2023.

events.title: Rāma Lallā's prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā
events.description: On 22 January 2024, in the sanctum of the new temple at Ayodhyā, a 51-inch image of Rāma as a five-year-old child, carved from dark stone by Aruṇ Yogirāj of Mysore, was consecrated. Prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā, "establishing the breath", is the rite by which an image becomes the living presence of the deity.¶The temple is built of pink sandstone in the northern Nāgara style, without iron or steel, to a design by the Somapurā family of temple architects. For devotees the day closed a struggle they count as five centuries long. Four Śaṅkarācāryas did not attend, some objecting that the temple was not yet complete.

gitaQuote.transliteration: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham || paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām | dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
gitaQuote.translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and for the firm establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.

events.title: Purī Śrīmandira Parikramā and Ratna Bhaṇḍāra
events.description: Purī's Jagannātha temple saw two large developments in 2024. On 17 January the state opened the Śrīmandira Parikramā, a new walkway and surrounding complex that cleared encroachments and created open space around the main shrine. In July, officials opened the Ratna Bhaṇḍāra, the temple's treasury, to inventory its jewels and valuables, the first full entry in forty-six years. The inner chamber had been sealed and reports of missing keys had caused controversy. Priests, archaeologists and officials took part, and the count was meant to precede conservation.

events.title: Pūjā resumes in Gyānvāpī's Vyāsa cellar
events.description: The southern cellar of the Gyānvāpī compound was in the hands of a family of priests, the Vyāsas, who conducted worship there until the state stopped it in 1993. The mosque committee's appeals to the High Court and Supreme Court did not stop it.

events.title: BAPS Hindu Mandir, Abu Dhabi
events.description: The first traditional Hindu stone temple in Abu Dhabi opened on 14 February 2024, on land gifted by the rulers of the United Arab Emirates. Built by BAPS of pink Rajasthan sandstone and Italian marble, it has seven spires for the seven emirates. More than three million Indians live and work in the country. That a Muslim-majority state gave land for it was widely noted as a sign of changing times.

events.title: New Nālandā University campus opens
events.description: In 2010 India's Parliament passed an act, backed by other Asian countries, to found a new international university near the ruins of ancient Nālandā in Bihar, which had taught for some seven hundred years before its decline and destruction around 1200. On 19 June 2024 its permanent campus was opened at Rājgīr, a "net zero" site of brick buildings and water bodies that echo the old monastery's plan, with students from many countries.

events.title: Bhojaśālā survey
events.description: The Bhojaśālā in Dhār, Madhya Pradesh, is a medieval complex that Hindus identify with a Sarasvatī temple and college linked to the Paramāra king Bhoja. It also houses the tomb and mosque of Kamāl Maulā. Under an arrangement made by the Archaeological Survey of India, Hindus worship there on Tuesdays and Muslims pray on Fridays. In 2024 the Madhya Pradesh High Court directed the ASI to survey the site, and the survey proceeded under court monitoring; the case remains disputed and the findings were subject to further legal process.

Hindus, now under eight per cent of the population, held large protests in Dhaka and Chittagong.

events.title: Tirupati laḍḍū controversy
events.description: In September 2024 a laboratory report was cited to allege that ghee used for the laḍḍū prasāda at Tirumala, the Veṅkaṭeśvara temple in Andhra Pradesh, contained animal fat and other adulterants. The charge became a sharp political dispute between the state's ruling party and the former government, which denied it, and the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthānams said the supplier had been blacklisted. The Supreme Court asked for an independent investigation, and a special team under central supervision took up the matter. The episode revived demands for temple management free of state control.

events.title: Mahā Kumbha at Prayāgrāj
events.description: From 13 January to 26 February 2025 the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā hosted a Kumbha billed as falling once in 144 years. A temporary city of 4,000 hectares was built on the riverbed with pontoon bridges, hospitals and 150,000 toilets.¶The state government counted more than 600 million visits over forty-five days, a figure based on camera and ticketing estimates. On the main bathing night, 29 January, a crowd crush killed at least thirty people by the official count. The thirteen ākhāṛās of ascetics led the royal baths as they have for centuries.

events.title: Waqf (Amendment) Act
events.description: The Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025, was passed by Parliament in early April 2025 and received presidential assent soon after. It changed the rules governing waqf properties, which are charitable endowments under Islamic law, including their management boards, the registration of properties and the process for deciding disputed claims. Supporters said it would improve transparency and reduce encroachment; opponents, including many Muslim organisations and opposition parties, said it interfered with religious endowments. Petitions challenging it were taken up by the Supreme Court.

events.title: Gītā and Nāṭyaśāstra in UNESCO's Memory of the World
events.description: In April 2025 UNESCO added manuscripts of the Bhagavad Gītā and of Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra to its Memory of the World register, which lists documents of universal value. The Nāṭyaśāstra is the founding treatise on drama, dance, music and the theory of rasa. The listed manuscripts are kept at the Bhandarkar Institute in Pune. India now has fourteen entries on the register, among them the Ṛgveda.

events.title: Pahalgām attack
events.description: On 22 April 2025 gunmen attacked tourists in the Baisaran meadow above Pahalgām in Kashmir, killing twenty-six men. Survivors said the attackers asked people their religion and shot Hindus; a Christian visitor and a local Muslim pony-man who resisted also died. India blamed Pakistan-based groups and on 7 May struck sites across the border in an operation named Sindūr, after the vermilion worn by married Hindu women. Four days of fighting ended in a ceasefire.

events.title: Maratha Military Landscapes inscribed by UNESCO
events.description: In July 2025 UNESCO inscribed twelve forts as "Maratha Military Landscapes of India": eleven in Maharashtra, including Rāygaḍ, Rājgaḍ, Pratāpgaḍ, Śivnerī, Panhāḷā and the sea forts Sindhudurg and Vijayadurg, and Jiñjī in Tamil Nadu. events.title: Kailāsa–Mānasarovara yātrā resumes
events.description: The Kailāsa–Mānasarovara yātrā, the pilgrimage to Mount Kailāśa and Lake Mānasarovara in Tibet, sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jainas and Bön followers, was suspended in 2020 because of the Covid-19 pandemic and later tensions on the border. events.title: Dhvajārohaṇa at the Rāma Mandir
events.description: On 25 November 2025, the day that marks the wedding of Rāma and Sītā, a saffron flag about twenty feet long was raised on the 161-foot spire of the Rāma temple at Ayodhyā. It bears the Sun, the syllable Om and the kovidāra tree, the emblem of Rāma's dynasty in the Rāmāyaṇa. In temple tradition, raising the flag declares a temple complete; the trust announced that the main building and its surrounding shrines were finished.

events.title: Dīpāvalī inscribed by UNESCO
events.description: On 10 December 2025, at a session held at the Red Fort in Delhi, UNESCO inscribed Dīpāvalī on its list of the intangible heritage of humanity, the sixteenth entry from India. The festival of lamps marks, among other things, Rāma's return to Ayodhyā and the worship of Lakṣmī, and is also kept by Jainas and Sikhs for their own reasons. It is a public holiday in more than a dozen countries.

events.title: Somanātha Amṛt Parv

events.title: Siṃhastha Kumbha begins at Nāsik–Tryambakeśvara
events.description: On 31 October 2026 the flag was raised at Nāsik and Tryambakeśvara to open the Siṃhastha, the Kumbha held when Jupiter enters Leo, about once in twelve years. Śaiva ascetics bathe at Tryambakeśvara and Vaiṣṇava ascetics at Nāsik, an arrangement fixed by the Peśvā after a deadly clash between ascetic orders in the late eighteenth century. The main bathing days fall in 2027.

events.title: You are here

New discoveries change old dates, and the entries for this decade are still being written.

events.title: Ten thousand years of devotion in Kali
events.description: The Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa (Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa, chapters 90 and 128) says that for ten thousand years of Kali Yuga Kṛṣṇa's worship will remain on earth, with Gaṅgā and the tīrthas present for half that period before they depart. Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas and others have read this as a golden age of devotion within Kali. Some count the ten thousand years from the start of Kali, which gives a date near 7000 CE, as placed here; others count from Caitanya's appearance around 1486. This is scriptural prophecy, not history, and interpretations vary.

events.description: As Kali deepens, the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (12.2) says, kings will be no better than thieves, taking people's property and wives. events.title: Kalki is born at Śambhala
events.description: The Purāṇas say that at the very end of Kali Yuga, when rulers have become robbers and the Veda is forgotten, Viṣṇu will be born as Kalki in the village of Śambhala, in the house of a brāhmaṇa named Viṣṇuyaśas.¶He is the tenth and last avatāra of the present cycle. The Bhāgavata (12.2.18) and Viṣṇu Purāṇa (4.24) give only this outline; the details of his life come from the Kalki Purāṇa, a much later minor work. By traditional reckoning the event lies more than 426,000 years ahead. Claims that any living person is Kalki have no basis in these texts.

events.title: Paraśurāma instructs Kalki
events.description: The detailed life of Kalki comes from the Kalki Purāṇa, a late minor Purāṇa probably composed in Bengal in the last few centuries. In it the immortal warrior-sage Paraśurāma, the sixth avatāra, teaches the young Kalki the Vedas and the science of arms on the Mahendra mountain, and Śiva grants him a white horse, a sword and a wise parrot. The major Purāṇas give none of these details. Scriptural prophecy, not history.

This is scriptural reckoning, not history.
