The end is the beginning; the ultimate Type IX civilization is revealed to be the Supreme Divinity from whom creation originally arose.
events.eraDesc: Humanity reaches planetary transition; theoretical Kardashev evolution and the return to Vishnu in Yoganidra.

gitaQuote.verse: सर्वभूतानि कौन्तेय प्रकृतिं यान्ति मामिकाम् । कल्पक्ॣये पुनस्तानि कल्पादौ विसृजाम्यहम् ॥ प्रकृतिं स्वामवष्टभ्य विसृजामि पुनः पुनः । भूतग्राममिमं कृत्स्नमवशं प्रकृतेर्वशात् ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: sarva-bhūtāni kaunteya prakṛtiṃ yānti māmikām | kalpa-kṣaye punas tāni kalpādau visṛjāmy aham || prakṛtiṃ svām avaṣṭabhya visṛjāmi punaḥ punaḥ | bhūta-grāmam imaṃ kṛtsnam avaśaṃ prakṛter vaśāt ||
gitaQuote.translation: All created beings, O son of Kunti, enter into My material nature at the end of the cosmic Kalpa. Again, at the beginning of the next Kalpa, I project them forth. Presiding over My own material energy, I send forth again and again this entire multitude of beings, which is helpless under the sway of cosmic law.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur; Śaṅkara Bhāṣya & Śrīdhara Svāmī Subodhinī

events.trustedSource: Bhagavad Gītā 9.7-8, Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.4, & Frank Tipler's Omega Point Physics

events.title: The Rebirth of Satya Yuga & The Eternal Wheel Closes
events.description: From the navel of Sri Vishnu reposing in Yoganidrā upon the cosmic ocean of Mahāpralaya blooms the golden lotus of Brahmā (Hiraṇyagarbha). Primordial cosmological re-inflation ignites: Satya Yuga begins anew with Dharma upright on all four pillars (Satya, Dayā, Śauca, Tapas). The wheel of time returns to Event 0: Śveta-Vārāha Kalpa, closing the eternal Kalachakra cycle without beginning or end.
events.eraDesc: Humanity reaches planetary transition; theoretical Kardashev evolution and the return to Vishnu in Yoganidra.

gitaQuote.verse: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन्नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
gitaQuote.transliteration: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ | ajo nityaḥ śāśvato 'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||
gitaQuote.translation: It is neither born nor does it ever die; nor, having once existed, does it ever cease to be. Unborn, eternal, ever-existing, and primeval, it is not slain when the body dissolves.
gitaQuote.source: Gita Press Gorakhpur; The eternal, indissoluble nature of Atman and Cosmic Time

events.trustedSource: Bhagavad Gītā 9.7-8, Mahābhārata Vana Parva 149.11-13, Manusmṛti 1.81-82

eras: Yugas of tradition
The Purāṇas measure time in vast cycles: four yugas make a mahāyuga of 4.32 million years, and a thousand of those make one day of Brahmā.
Neolithic beginnings
Farming villages appear from Balochistan to the Gaṅgā plain. Barley, wheat, rice, and zebu cattle are domesticated.
Indus–Sarasvatī age
One of the world’s first urban civilizations spreads over a million square kilometres, with planned cities and standard weights.
Vedic age
The cities fade and the Vedas are composed and preserved by ear with astonishing phonetic exactness.
Mahājanapadas & Śramaṇas
Sixteen great states, coinage and walled cities rise on the Gaṅgā plain.
Maurya age
Candragupta and Aśoka unite most of the subcontinent for the first time.
Classical formation
Śuṅgas, Sātavāhanas, Kuṣāṇas and Tamil kings rule a patchwork of states open to global trade.
Gupta age
Often called the classical golden age: Kālidāsa writes, Āryabhaṭa computes, and stone temples flourish.
Temples & ācāryas
Regional kingdoms compete in building monolithic temples; Ādi Śaṅkara synthesizes Advaita Vedānta.
Cōḻa–Rajput age
The Cōḻas build an empire of temples and maritime trade in the south while Rajput houses hold the north.
Sultanate, Vijayanagara, Bhakti
Vijayanagara rises as a southern shield, and saint-poets like Jñāneśvara, Kabīr and Caitanya lead the Bhakti renaissance.
Mughal age, Bhakti zenith
Tulasīdāsa, Tukārāma and the Vṛndāvana Gosvāmīs compose devotional classics; Śivājī establishes Svarājya.
Maratha Svarājya & Peśvās
From Śivājī’s coronation to the Peśvās, the Marathas become the paramount power across India.
Company, Crown, Renaissance
Hindu renaissance: Rāmmohan Roy, Dayānanda Sarasvatī, Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṁsa and Swami Vivekānanda.
Republic of India
Independence, constitutional democracy, technological self-reliance, and cosmic space research.
The Future & The Foretold
Humanity reaches planetary transition; theoretical Kardashev evolution and the return to Vishnu in Yoganidra.

1857.name: The uprising of 1857
1857.desc: A revolt of Indian soldiers that became a wide war against Company rule across north India. Its failure ended the Company and brought direct rule by the British Crown.

kashi.name: Kāśī (Vārāṇasī)
kashi.desc: The city of Śiva on the Gaṅgā, continuously lived in for nearly three thousand years. It has been India's foremost seat of Sanskrit learning and the place where Hindus hope to die, because death here is believed to give liberation.

unesco.name: UNESCO recognition
unesco.desc: The United Nations body lists World Heritage Sites and "intangible heritage" such as festivals and chant. Listing brings no control over worship, but it does bring conservation funds and worldwide attention.

advaita.name: Advaita Vedānta
advaita.desc: The "non-dual" school associated with Śaṅkara. It teaches that the individual self (ātman) and ultimate reality (Brahman) are one, and that the world of separate things is an appearance (māyā) seen through ignorance.

rigveda.name: The Ṛgveda
rigveda.desc: The oldest of the four Vedas: 1,028 hymns to deities such as Agni, Indra and Soma, arranged in ten books. It was composed in the Punjab region and passed on orally for some three thousand years.

upanishad.name: The Upaniṣads
upanishad.desc: The closing layer of the Vedas, where teachers and students inquire into the Self, Brahman, karma and liberation. All schools of Vedānta rest their case on these dialogues.

yoga.name: Yoga
yoga.desc: Disciplines for stilling and mastering the mind. Patañjali's eight-limbed system is the classical statement; haṭha yoga later added postures and breath work, and the Gītā speaks of yogas of action, knowledge and devotion.

chola.name: The Cōḻas
chola.desc: A Tamil dynasty of the Kāverī delta. At their height (c. 985–1070) they ruled south India, Sri Lanka and sent fleets to Southeast Asia, and they built the great temples of Tañjāvūr and their famous bronzes.

women.name: Women in the tradition
women.desc: Seers, queens, poets and reformers appear in every age of this timeline, from the Ṛgvedic ṛṣikās to modern leaders. The tag gathers them so their thread can be followed across eras.

shiva.name: Śiva
shiva.desc: The "auspicious one": ascetic and householder, destroyer and healer, worshipped most often as the liṅga. For Śaivas he is the supreme reality; his Vedic forerunner is the fierce god Rudra.

krishna.name: Kṛṣṇa
krishna.desc: The eighth avatāra of Viṣṇu and for many traditions God himself: the child of Vṛndāvana, the king of Dvārakā and the teacher of the Bhagavad Gītā.

tamil.name: Tamil tradition
tamil.desc: Tamil has an unbroken literature of over two thousand years. Its Śaiva Nāyaṉmārs and Vaiṣṇava Āḻvārs created bhakti poetry in the mother tongue centuries before the north.

temple.name: The Hindu temple
temple.desc: A temple is the house of a consecrated image in which the deity is held to be present. From small Gupta shrines it grew into two great styles, the curved-tower Nāgara of the north and the pyramidal Drāviḍa of the south.

bengal.name: Bengal
bengal.desc: The eastern delta, home of the Pāla and Sena kingdoms, Caitanya's devotion, the worship of Durgā and Kālī, and the nineteenth-century "Bengal Renaissance".

kashmir.name: Kashmir
kashmir.desc: For a thousand years a leading centre of Sanskrit learning, aesthetics and Śaiva philosophy, called Śāradā-deśa, the land of the goddess of learning.

vedanta.name: Vedānta
vedanta.desc: "The end of the Veda": philosophy built on the Upaniṣads, the Brahma Sūtra and the Gītā. Its schools, Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita and others, differ on how the soul, the world and God are related.

ayurveda.name: Āyurveda
ayurveda.desc: India's classical medicine, the "knowledge of long life". It explains health as a balance of three doṣas and is preserved in the compendia of Caraka, Suśruta and Vāgbhaṭa.

shivaji.name: Chatrapati Śivājī
shivaji.desc: Founder of the Maratha kingdom (1630–1680). Starting with a handful of hill forts he defied Bijapur and the Mughals, built a navy, and was crowned a sovereign Hindu king in 1674.

maratha.name: The Marathas
maratha.desc: The Marathi-speaking power founded by Śivājī. Under the Peśvās in the eighteenth century it became a confederacy that reached from Tamil Nadu to the Indus before falling to the British in 1818.

diaspora.name: The Hindu diaspora
diaspora.desc: Communities outside India, from nineteenth-century indentured labourers in Mauritius, Fiji and the Caribbean to modern professionals in Britain, North America and the Gulf.

mahabharata.name: The Mahābhārata
mahabharata.desc: The great epic of the war between the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas, about 100,000 verses in its full form and containing the Bhagavad Gītā. Tradition ascribes it to Vyāsa; scholars see it growing between c. 400 BCE and 400 CE.

templedestruction.name: Temple destruction
templedestruction.desc: Many temples were plundered or demolished during raids and under some sultans and emperors, often recorded by the conquerors' own chroniclers. Several were later rebuilt, sometimes more than once.

ayodhya.name: Ayodhyā
ayodhya.desc: The city on the Sarayū revered as Rāma's birthplace and capital. A dispute over the Janmabhūmi site ran from the nineteenth century until the Supreme Court's 2019 verdict.

jaina.name: Jainism
jaina.desc: An ancient śramaṇa religion of strict non-violence, taught by twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras ending with Mahāvīra. It does not accept Vedic authority, yet shared kings, cities and scholars with Hindu traditions throughout history.

gupta.name: The Guptas
gupta.desc: The dynasty (c. 320–550 CE) under which Sanskrit literature, science, temple building and the Purāṇas flourished. Later ages looked back on it as a classical standard.

vijayanagara.name: Vijayanagara
vijayanagara.desc: The "City of Victory" at Hampi and the empire named after it (1336–1646). It protected temple culture across south India; visitors compared the city to Rome.

ramayana.name: The Rāmāyaṇa
ramayana.desc: Vālmīki's epic of Rāma, Sītā and the war with Rāvaṇa, in about 24,000 verses. It has been retold in nearly every Indian and Southeast Asian language.

shaiva.name: Śaivism
shaiva.desc: The traditions that worship Śiva as supreme. They include the ascetic Pāśupatas, temple-centred Śaiva Siddhānta, the non-dual Śaivism of Kashmir and the Vīraśaivas of Karnataka.

gaudiya.name: Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism
gaudiya.desc: The Bengali school of Kṛṣṇa devotion begun by Caitanya (1486–1533). It centres on chanting the divine names and the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa; ISKCON is its best-known modern branch.

bhagavata.name: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa
bhagavata.desc: The most beloved Purāṇa, 18,000 verses telling Viṣṇu's descents and above all Kṛṣṇa's life. It is the root scripture of most Kṛṣṇa-bhakti schools.

mathematics.name: Indian mathematics
mathematics.desc: From altar geometry to the decimal place-value system with zero, algebra, trigonometry and, in Kerala, infinite series. Much of it was written in Sanskrit verse inside works on astronomy.

shankara.name: Ādi Śaṅkara
shankara.desc: The teacher who gave Advaita Vedānta its classical form through commentaries on the Upaniṣads, Gītā and Brahma Sūtra. Tradition dates him 788–820 CE and credits him with four monasteries; many scholars place him about a century earlier.

law.name: Law and courts
law.desc: Hindu personal law moved from the Dharmaśāstras and their commentaries, through colonial "Anglo-Hindu law", to acts of Parliament and rulings of India's courts.

southeastasia.name: Greater India in Southeast Asia
southeastasia.desc: From about the first century CE, kingdoms from Burma to Vietnam and Indonesia adopted Sanskrit, Indian scripts, the epics and the worship of Śiva and Viṣṇu, by trade and invitation, not conquest.

mewar.name: Mewar
mewar.desc: The Rajput kingdom of the Guhila and Sisodiyā house, ruled from Chittor and later Udaipur. It is remembered for refusing to submit, from Rāṇā Kumbha to Mahārāṇā Pratāp.

peshwa.name: The Peśvās
peshwa.desc: Hereditary prime ministers of the Maratha kingdom from 1713, ruling from Pune. Men like Bājīrāv I made them the real heads of the Maratha confederacy until 1818.

dharmashastra.name: Dharmaśāstra
dharmashastra.desc: The body of texts on dharma: duty, ritual, law and kingship. It runs from early Dharma Sūtras through verse smṛtis like Manu and Yājñavalkya to medieval commentaries and digests.

puri.name: Purī
puri.desc: The seaside city of Jagannātha in Odisha, one of the four dhāmas. Its annual Ratha-yātrā draws the three wooden deities through the streets on giant chariots.

ramjanmabhoomi.name: Rāma Janmabhūmi
ramjanmabhoomi.desc: The site in Ayodhyā held to be Rāma's birthplace, where a mosque stood from 1528 to 1992. After a long legal and political struggle the Rāma Mandir was consecrated there in 2024.

kumbh.name: The Kumbha Melā
kumbh.desc: A bathing pilgrimage held in rotation at Prayāga, Haridvāra, Ujjain and Nāsik when Jupiter enters particular signs. It is the largest peaceful gathering of people on earth.

ganga.name: The Gaṅgā
ganga.desc: The holiest river, worshipped as a goddess who descended from heaven through Śiva's hair. Bathing in her, and having one's ashes placed in her, is held to purify.

aurangzeb.name: Aurangzeb
aurangzeb.desc: Mughal emperor from 1658 to 1707. He reimposed the jizya tax, ordered leading temples demolished and spent his last twenty-six years fighting the Marathas in the Deccan.

vrindavan.name: Vṛndāvana
vrindavan.desc: The town in Braj on the Yamunā where Kṛṣṇa is said to have spent his childhood. Rediscovered by Caitanya's followers in the 1500s, it became a city of temples.

bhagavadgita.name: The Bhagavad Gītā
bhagavadgita.desc: Kṛṣṇa's 700-verse teaching to Arjuna on the battlefield, set within the Mahābhārata. It joins action without attachment, knowledge and devotion, and every major school has commented on it.

shakta.name: Śāktism
shakta.desc: The traditions that worship the Goddess (Devī, Śakti) as the supreme power, as Durgā, Kālī, Lalitā and many others. Its key scripture is the Devī Māhātmya.

shaivasiddhanta.name: Śaiva Siddhānta
shaivasiddhanta.desc: A Śaiva theology of three eternal realities: the Lord (pati), souls (paśu) and bonds (pāśa). Born in Sanskrit Āgamas, it became the dominant temple tradition of Tamil Nadu.

chalukya.name: The Cālukyas
chalukya.desc: Deccan dynasties ruling from Bādāmi (6th–8th century) and later Kalyāṇī (10th–12th). Their temples at Aihoḷe and Paṭṭadakal are the workshop where Indian temple styles were worked out.

vishnu.name: Viṣṇu
vishnu.desc: The preserver, who descends as avatāras such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa whenever dharma declines. For Vaiṣṇavas he is the supreme Lord.

astronomy.name: Jyotiṣa: astronomy
astronomy.desc: Indian astronomers computed planetary positions, eclipses and calendars in works called siddhāntas. Ujjain served as their prime meridian.

sanskrit.name: Sanskrit
sanskrit.desc: The "perfected" language of the Vedas, epics, sciences and philosophy, fixed by Pāṇini's grammar. For two thousand years it linked scholars from Kashmir to Java.

vaishnava.name: Vaiṣṇavism
vaishnava.desc: The traditions that worship Viṣṇu or his avatāras as supreme. They are traditionally grouped into four sampradāyas, those of Rāmānuja, Madhva, Nimbārka and Viṣṇusvāmī/Vallabha.

pallava.name: The Pallavas
pallava.desc: Rulers of Kāñcīpuram (c. 275–897). They pioneered stone temple architecture in the south, including the monuments of Māmallapuram.

kashmirshaivism.name: Kashmir Śaivism
kashmirshaivism.desc: The non-dual Śaiva philosophy of Vasugupta, Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta. It holds that all reality is the free, conscious play of Śiva, and that liberation is recognising oneself as that.

jyotirlinga.name: The twelve Jyotirliṅgas
jyotirlinga.desc: Twelve shrines where Śiva is said to have appeared as a pillar of light, from Somanātha in Gujarat to Rāmeśvaram in the south and Kedāranātha in the Himalaya.

delhi.name: Delhi
delhi.desc: Capital of Tomaras and Cauhāns, then of the Sultanate and Mughals, of the British from 1911, and of the Republic.

gandhi.name: Mahātmā Gāndhī
gandhi.desc: Leader of India's freedom struggle (1869–1948). He turned truth and non-violence (satyāgraha, ahiṃsā) into mass politics, and read the Gītā as his guide to selfless action.

debate.name: Śāstrārtha: formal debate
debate.desc: Public disputation under agreed rules was how Indian schools tested ideas. The loser, in the stories, often became the winner's disciple.

bhakti.name: Bhakti
bhakti.desc: Loving devotion to a personal God, open to all regardless of caste, sex or learning. From Tamil beginnings it swept the whole subcontinent between the 7th and 17th centuries.

grammar.name: Vyākaraṇa: grammar
grammar.desc: Regarded as the gateway to all learning. Pāṇini's rule-system for Sanskrit, with its commentaries, is one of the great intellectual achievements of the ancient world.

tantra.name: Tantra
tantra.desc: Ritual and yogic systems using mantra, maṇḍala, initiation and the body's subtle energies. They are found in Śaiva, Śākta, Vaiṣṇava and Buddhist forms and underlie most temple worship.

nepal.name: Nepal
nepal.desc: The Himalayan kingdom whose Kathmandu valley preserved Hindu and Buddhist traditions side by side. It was the world's only Hindu kingdom until 2008.

sant.name: The Sants
sant.desc: Poet-saints of north and west India, many from artisan and "low" castes, who sang of a God beyond ritual and image. Kabīr, Ravidāsa and Nāmadeva are the best known.

sikh.name: The Sikh tradition
sikh.desc: Founded by Guru Nānak (1469–1539) in Punjab and shaped by ten Gurus. It appears on this timeline where its history meets that of Hindus, especially in resistance to Mughal persecution.

vivekananda.name: Svāmī Vivekānanda
vivekananda.desc: Rāmakṛṣṇa's chief disciple (1863–1902). His 1893 Chicago address introduced Vedānta to the West, and he founded the Ramakrishna Mission to join spirituality with service.

dashavatara.name: The ten avatāras
dashavatara.desc: Viṣṇu's ten descents: Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, the Buddha (or Balarāma) and Kalki, who is yet to come.

rama.name: Rāma
rama.desc: Prince of Ayodhyā, seventh avatāra of Viṣṇu and the model of righteous conduct. His reign, Rāma-rājya, is the Indian image of ideal government.

mathura.name: Mathurā
mathura.desc: Kṛṣṇa's birthplace on the Yamunā. In the early centuries CE its workshops carved the first images of many Hindu, Jaina and Buddhist deities.

ujjain.name: Ujjayinī (Ujjain)
ujjain.desc: City of the Mahākāla jyotirliṅga on the Śiprā, capital of Avanti, home of Kālidāsa in tradition and the zero meridian of Indian astronomy.

pandya.name: The Pāṇḍyas
pandya.desc: The Tamil dynasty of Madurai, known from the Sangam age to the fourteenth century, patrons of Tamil poetry and the Mīnākṣī temple.

kanchi.name: Kāñcīpuram
kanchi.desc: "City of a thousand temples", Pallava capital and a seat of Sanskrit and Tamil learning for Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Buddhists and Jainas alike.

jagannath.name: Jagannātha
jagannath.desc: "Lord of the Universe", the form of Kṛṣṇa-Viṣṇu worshipped at Purī with his brother Balabhadra and sister Subhadrā as large wooden images, periodically renewed.

dvaita.name: Dvaita Vedānta
dvaita.desc: Madhva's school, which holds that God, souls and matter are eternally distinct and that liberation comes through devotion to Viṣṇu and his grace.

varkari.name: The Vārakarīs
varkari.desc: Maharashtra's devotional movement centred on Viṭhobā of Paṇḍharpūr. Its saints, from Jñāneśvara to Tukārāma, came from every caste, and its followers still walk to Paṇḍharpūr each year.

prophecy.name: Scriptural prophecy
prophecy.desc: Descriptions of the future found in the Purāṇas and the Mahābhārata. They are presented here as what the texts say, not as events.

music.name: Music
music.desc: Indian classical music traces itself to the chanting of the Sāmaveda. Its two living systems, Hindustani and Carnatic, are both steeped in devotional poetry.

purana.name: The Purāṇas
purana.desc: "Ancient lore": eighteen major and many minor compilations of cosmology, genealogy, myth, pilgrimage and worship, put together over a thousand years from about the 3rd century CE.

mimamsa.name: Mīmāṃsā
mimamsa.desc: The school of Vedic interpretation founded on Jaimini's sūtras. It worked out rules for reading scripture and defended ritual duty as the heart of dharma.

nyaya.name: Nyāya
nyaya.desc: The school of logic and epistemology. It defined valid means of knowledge, the structure of inference and the rules of debate, and argued for the existence of God.

madurai.name: Madurai
madurai.desc: The Pāṇḍya capital on the Vaigai, legendary seat of the Tamil Sangam and city of the goddess Mīnākṣī.

shrivaishnava.name: Śrīvaiṣṇavism
shrivaishnava.desc: The south Indian Vaiṣṇava tradition that reveres both the Sanskrit Veda and the Tamil hymns of the Āḻvārs. Rāmānuja is its great teacher.

hoysala.name: The Hoysaḷas
hoysala.desc: Kings of southern Karnataka (c. 1000–1343), famed for star-shaped soapstone temples at Belūr, Haḷebīḍu and Somanāthapura with exceptionally fine carving.

akbar.name: Akbar
akbar.desc: Mughal emperor 1556–1605. He abolished the pilgrim tax and jizya, married into Rajput houses, employed Hindu generals and ministers and had Sanskrit classics translated into Persian.

veda.name: The Vedas
veda.desc: The four collections, Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma and Atharva, held to be revealed (śruti) and without human author. Each has hymns, ritual prose (Brāhmaṇas) and Upaniṣads.

surya.name: Sūrya worship
surya.desc: The Sun was once the centre of a major sect, the Sauras, with great temples at Multan, Mārtaṇḍa, Modhera and Koṇārka.

samkhya.name: Sāṃkhya
samkhya.desc: One of the oldest systems. It explains the world as the interplay of pure consciousness (puruṣa) and matter (prakṛti), unfolding in twenty-five principles; Yoga adopts its framework.

darshana.name: The darśanas
darshana.desc: "Ways of seeing": the philosophical systems. Six accept the Veda (Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Mīmāṃsā, Vedānta); the Cārvāka, Jaina and Buddhist schools do not.

ashoka.name: Aśoka
ashoka.desc: Maurya emperor (r. c. 268–232 BCE). After the bloody conquest of Kaliṅga he promoted dhamma, tolerance and welfare through edicts carved on rocks and pillars across his empire.

pratihara.name: The Gurjara-Pratihāras
pratihara.desc: North Indian emperors (8th–10th century) ruling from Kanauj. They are credited with holding back Arab expansion from Sindh for three centuries.

iskcon.name: ISKCON
iskcon.desc: The International Society for Krishna Consciousness, founded in New York in 1966 by A. C. Bhaktivedānta Svāmī Prabhupāda, which carried Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism around the world.

pashupata.name: The Pāśupatas
pashupata.desc: The earliest organised Śaiva ascetics, followers of Lakulīśa. They smeared themselves with ash and courted public scorn as a spiritual discipline.

mughal.name: The Mughals
mughal.desc: The dynasty founded by Bābur in 1526, which ruled most of India at its height under Akbar, Jahāngīr, Shāh Jahān and Aurangzeb and declined rapidly after 1707.

ramanuja.name: Rāmānuja
ramanuja.desc: The Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya (trad. 1017–1137) who taught Viśiṣṭādvaita: souls and matter are real and form the body of a personal God, reached through devotion and surrender.

swaminarayan.name: The Svāminārāyaṇa tradition
swaminarayan.desc: A Vaiṣṇava movement founded in Gujarat by Sahajānanda Svāmī (1781–1830), stressing moral discipline and devotion. BAPS, known for the Akṣardhām temples, is its largest branch.

maurya.name: The Mauryas
maurya.desc: India's first great empire (c. 322–185 BCE), founded by Candragupta with the minister Cāṇakya and ruled from Pāṭaliputra.

somnath.name: Somanātha
somnath.desc: The first jyotirliṅga, on the Gujarat coast. Destroyed and rebuilt repeatedly from 1026 onward, its reconstruction in 1951 became a symbol of national recovery.

hathayoga.name: Haṭha Yoga
hathayoga.desc: The yoga of postures, breath control, locks and seals, developed by Nātha yogīs from about the 11th century. It is the ancestor of modern postural yoga.

tilak.name: Lokamānya Ṭiḷak
tilak.desc: Bāḷ Gaṅgādhar Ṭiḷak (1856–1920), nationalist leader, scholar of the Vedas and author of the Gītā Rahasya, who turned the Gaṇeśa and Śivājī festivals into public movements.

ambedkar.name: Dr B. R. Ambedkar
ambedkar.desc: Jurist, chief draftsman of India's Constitution and leader of the Dalit movement (1891–1956). He fought untouchability within Hindu society and finally embraced Buddhism.

baps.name: BAPS
baps.desc: Bocāsaṇvāsī Akṣar Puruṣottam Svāminārāyaṇ Saṃsthā, founded in 1907. It has built more than a thousand temples, including Akṣardhām in Delhi and New Jersey.

nastika.name: Āstika and nāstika
nastika.desc: In Indian philosophy an āstika school accepts the authority of the Veda and a nāstika school does not. The terms are about scripture, not about belief in God.

astika.name: Āstika and nāstika
astika.desc: In Indian philosophy an āstika school accepts the authority of the Veda and a nāstika school does not. The terms are about scripture, not about belief in God.

murugan.name: Murugaṉ (Skanda)
murugan.desc: The youthful warrior god, son of Śiva, known in the north as Kārttikeya. He is the favourite deity of the Tamils, worshipped at six hill shrines.

nayanmar.name: The Nāyaṉmārs
nayanmar.desc: Sixty-three Tamil Śaiva saints of the 6th–9th centuries. The hymns of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar form the Tēvāram, sung daily in Tamil temples.

alvar.name: The Āḻvārs
alvar.desc: Twelve Tamil Vaiṣṇava poet-saints "immersed" in God. Their 4,000 verses, the Divya Prabandham, are revered as the Tamil Veda.

trika.name: Trika
trika.desc: The "triad" Śaivism of Kashmir, named for its three goddesses and its three levels of reality. Abhinavagupta's Tantrāloka is its summa.

vishishtadvaita.name: Viśiṣṭādvaita
vishishtadvaita.desc: "Qualified non-dualism", Rāmānuja's Vedānta: there is one reality, God, but souls and the world are real parts of him, as a body is of its soul.

sampradaya.name: Sampradāya
sampradaya.desc: A lineage of teaching passed from guru to disciple, with its own scriptures, practices and marks. Belonging to one is how most Hindus have inherited their tradition.

datta.name: The Dattātreya tradition
datta.desc: Devotion to Dattātreya, the three-headed guru who unites Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva, strong in Maharashtra and Karnataka through saints regarded as his incarnations.

tirumala.name: Tirumala (Tirupati)
tirumala.desc: The hill temple of Veṅkaṭeśvara in Andhra, among the most visited and wealthiest shrines in the world.

chaitanya.name: Caitanya Mahāprabhu
chaitanya.desc: The Bengali saint (1486–1533) revered by his followers as Kṛṣṇa himself in the mood of Rādhā. He made congregational chanting of the holy names the centre of religious life.

carnatic.name: Carnatic music
carnatic.desc: The classical music of south India, almost entirely devotional. Its "Trinity", Tyāgarāja, Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar and Śyāmā Śāstrī, composed around 1800.

krishnadevaraya.name: Kṛṣṇadevarāya
krishnadevaraya.desc: Vijayanagara's greatest emperor (r. 1509–1529), a soldier, temple builder and Telugu poet.

rajput.name: The Rajputs
rajput.desc: Warrior clans who ruled much of north and west India from about the 8th century, with a code that prized honour and death before surrender.

aryasamaj.name: The Ārya Samāj
aryasamaj.desc: A reform movement founded by Dayānanda Sarasvatī in 1875. It called Hindus "back to the Vedas", rejected image worship and caste by birth, and founded schools across north India.

templeentry.name: Temple entry
templeentry.desc: Campaigns in the 1920s–40s to open temples and their roads to castes then barred from them, ending in proclamations and laws that made exclusion illegal.

sangam.name: Sangam literature
sangam.desc: The earliest Tamil poetry (c. 300 BCE–300 CE), on love and war, said to have been judged by an academy (saṅgam) of poets at Madurai.

pancharatra.name: Pāñcarātra
pancharatra.desc: The Vaiṣṇava Āgama tradition, whose texts govern worship in most Viṣṇu temples and teach God's fourfold emanation (vyūha).

zero.name: Zero and place value
zero.desc: The decimal system with a symbol for zero, developed in India by about the 5th century, passed through the Arab world to Europe and made modern arithmetic possible.

ganapatya.name: The Gāṇapatyas
ganapatya.desc: Those who worship Gaṇeśa as the supreme being, not only as remover of obstacles. The tradition is strongest in Maharashtra.

ganesha.name: Gaṇeśa
ganesha.desc: The elephant-headed son of Śiva and Pārvatī, lord of beginnings and remover of obstacles, invoked first in nearly every Hindu rite.

lingayat.name: The Liṅgāyatas (Vīraśaivas)
lingayat.desc: Followers of the twelfth-century movement of Basava in Karnataka. They wear a small liṅga on the body, reject caste distinctions and express their faith in short Kannada prose-poems called vacanas.

sringeri.name: Śṛṅgeri
sringeri.desc: The southern of the four monasteries attributed to Śaṅkara, in the Karnataka hills, with an unbroken line of Jagadgurus.

kedarnath.name: Kedāranātha
kedarnath.desc: A jyotirliṅga temple at 3,580 metres in the Garhwal Himalaya, open only in summer, where tradition says Śaṅkara ended his life.

udupi.name: Uḍupi
udupi.desc: The coastal Karnataka town where Madhva installed an image of Kṛṣṇa, worshipped in turn by the heads of eight monasteries.

hampi.name: Hampi
hampi.desc: The ruined capital of Vijayanagara on the Tuṅgabhadrā, a vast field of temples, markets and palaces, and a World Heritage Site.

haridwar.name: Haridvāra
haridwar.desc: "Gateway of Hari", where the Gaṅgā leaves the Himalaya for the plains, one of the seven sacred cities and a Kumbha site.

pushtimarg.name: The Puṣṭi Mārga
pushtimarg.desc: Vallabhācārya's "path of grace", devoted to the child Kṛṣṇa as Śrīnāthajī and expressed through loving service (sevā), music and food offerings.

kashivishvanath.name: Kāśī Viśvanātha
kashivishvanath.desc: The chief Śiva temple of Vārāṇasī and a jyotirliṅga. Demolished several times, most recently in 1669, the present temple was built by Ahilyābāī Holkar in 1780.

eastindiacompany.name: The East India Company
eastindiacompany.desc: The English trading company chartered in 1600 that, after 1757, conquered and governed India until the Crown took over in 1858.

raigad.name: Rāygaḍ
raigad.desc: The hill fort in the Sahyādris that Śivājī made his capital, where he was crowned in 1674 and died in 1680.

indology.name: Indology
indology.desc: The modern academic study of Indian texts and history, begun by scholars such as William Jones and Max Müller. Its findings and its biases are both part of this story.

ramakrishna.name: Śrī Rāmakṛṣṇa
ramakrishna.desc: The Bengali mystic (1836–1886), priest of the Kālī temple at Dakṣiṇeśvara, who practised many paths and taught that all lead to the same God.

rss.name: The RSS
rss.desc: The Rāṣṭrīya Svayaṃsevak Saṅgh, a volunteer organisation founded in 1925 to build Hindu unity and character. Many later bodies, such as the VHP and BJP, grew from its network.

sati.name: Satī
sati.desc: The burning of a widow on her husband's pyre. Never universal and condemned by many Hindu authors, it was outlawed in British India in 1829.

godavari.name: The Godāvarī
godavari.desc: The longest river of peninsular India, called the Gaṅgā of the south, rising at Tryambakeśvara near Nāsik.

taxila.name: Takṣaśilā (Taxila)
taxila.desc: An ancient city and centre of learning in Gandhāra, now in Pakistan, where Pāṇini, Cāṇakya and the physician Jīvaka are said to have studied.

sushruta.name: Suśruta
sushruta.desc: The surgeon to whom the Suśruta Saṃhitā is ascribed. It describes over 300 operations, including reconstruction of the nose and removal of cataracts.

patanjali.name: Patañjali
patanjali.desc: Name of the author of the Yoga Sūtra and of the grammarian who wrote the Mahābhāṣya. Tradition treats them as one sage; scholars usually see two people centuries apart.

kushana.name: The Kuṣāṇas
kushana.desc: Central Asian rulers of north India in the first three centuries CE. Their coins show Śiva and many other gods, and their workshops at Mathurā and Gandhāra made the first great sacred images.

jyotisha.name: Jyotiṣa
jyotisha.desc: The "science of lights": astronomy, calendar-making and astrology together. It began as a Vedic aid for timing rituals.

arunachala.name: Aruṇācala
arunachala.desc: The red hill at Tiruvaṇṇāmalai in Tamil Nadu, worshipped as Śiva in the form of fire, and the home of Ramaṇa Maharṣi.

kamakhya.name: Kāmākhyā
kamakhya.desc: The hilltop temple at Guwahati in Assam, the most important seat of the Goddess in Tantric tradition.

kali.name: Kālī
kali.desc: The dark Goddess of time and transformation, fierce in form and motherly to devotees, especially beloved in Bengal.

khajuraho.name: Khajurāho
khajuraho.desc: The Candella capital in central India, whose tenth- and eleventh-century temples are among the summits of north Indian architecture and sculpture.

mahmud.name: Mahmūd of Ghazni
mahmud.desc: The Turkic sultan who raided north India seventeen times between 1000 and 1027, plundering temple cities such as Mathurā, Kanauj and Somanātha.

bhoja.name: Rājā Bhoja
bhoja.desc: Paramāra king of Mālwā (r. c. 1010–1055), a legendary patron of learning and author of works on everything from architecture to yoga.

chardham.name: The Cār Dhām
chardham.desc: Four abodes at the corners of India: Badarīnātha, Dvārakā, Purī and Rāmeśvaram. A smaller Himalayan circuit of four shrines bears the same name.

radha.name: Rādhā
radha.desc: Kṛṣṇa's beloved among the cowherd women. In later Vaiṣṇava theology she is his own power of bliss, and her love is the highest devotion.

chittor.name: Chittor
chittor.desc: The great hill fort of Mewar, three times besieged and three times the scene of jauhar, in 1303, 1535 and 1568.

jauhar.name: Jauhar
jauhar.desc: The mass self-immolation of Rajput women when a fort was about to fall, while the men rode out to die fighting.

vidyaranya.name: Vidyāraṇya
vidyaranya.desc: Fourteenth-century Advaita teacher and head of Śṛṅgeri, linked by tradition with the founding of Vijayanagara.

navyanyaya.name: Navya-Nyāya
navyanyaya.desc: The "new logic" founded by Gaṅgeśa in Mithilā around 1325, with a precise technical language that all later Sanskrit philosophy borrowed.

goa.name: Goa
goa.desc: A Konkan coastal territory ruled by Portugal from 1510 to 1961, where Hindu worship was long restricted under the Inquisition.

sambhaji.name: Chatrapati Sambhājī
sambhaji.desc: Śivājī's elder son and successor (r. 1681–1689), captured and executed by Aurangzeb after refusing to convert.

ahilyabai.name: Ahilyābāī Holkar
ahilyabai.desc: Queen of Indore (r. 1767–1795), remembered as a model ruler. She rebuilt temples, ghāṭs and rest-houses at pilgrim sites all over India.

durgapuja.name: Durgā Pūjā
durgapuja.desc: Bengal's autumn festival of the Goddess's victory over the buffalo demon, celebrated with elaborate temporary shrines.

ramana.name: Ramaṇa Maharṣi
ramana.desc: The sage of Aruṇācala (1879–1950), who taught self-enquiry through the single question "Who am I?".

narayanaguru.name: Śrī Nārāyaṇa Guru
narayanaguru.desc: Kerala's sage and reformer (1856–1928). Born in a community barred from temples, he consecrated his own and taught "one caste, one religion, one God for man".

kriyayoga.name: Kriyā Yoga
kriyayoga.desc: A breath-based meditation lineage made known by Lāhiṛī Mahāśaya and carried West by Paramahaṃsa Yogānanda.

vhp.name: The VHP
vhp.desc: The Viśva Hindū Pariṣad, founded in 1964 to unite Hindu sects and serve Hindus worldwide; it led the Rāma Janmabhūmi movement.

shaktipitha.name: The Śakti Pīṭhas
shaktipitha.desc: Shrines of the Goddess said to mark where parts of Satī's body fell to earth, traditionally fifty-one, spread from Balochistan to Assam.

harappan.name: The Harappan civilization
harappan.desc: The Bronze Age culture of the Indus and Sarasvatī basins (c. 2600–1900 BCE), named after Harappa, the first site excavated.

prayag.name: Prayāga
prayag.desc: The confluence of the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā and the unseen Sarasvatī, called the king of tīrthas, and site of the largest Kumbha Melā.

sannyasa.name: Saṃnyāsa
sannyasa.desc: Renunciation: giving up home, property and social identity to seek liberation. Orders of renouncers have been the teachers of most Hindu traditions.

vakataka.name: The Vākāṭakas
vakataka.desc: A Deccan dynasty (c. 250–500) allied with the Guptas, patrons of the Ajaṇṭā caves.

siddha.name: The Siddhas
siddha.desc: "Perfected ones": yogins and alchemists, especially of Tamil and Nātha traditions, who sought to transform body and mind and often mocked empty ritual.

ramanandi.name: The Rāmānandīs
ramanandi.desc: North India's largest ascetic order, devoted to Rāma and Sītā and founded by Rāmānanda, who accepted disciples of every caste.

travancore.name: Travancore
travancore.desc: The princely state of southern Kerala whose rulers governed as servants of the deity Padmanābha.

aurobindo.name: Śrī Aurobindo
aurobindo.desc: Revolutionary turned yogin and philosopher (1872–1950), who taught at Pondicherry an "integral yoga" aimed at transforming life on earth.

manu.name: Manu
manu.desc: The progenitor of humankind in each cosmic age, and the name attached to the most influential Dharmaśāstra, the Manusmṛti.

yuga.name: The four yugas
yuga.desc: Satya, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali: ages of declining virtue lasting 1,728,000, 1,296,000, 864,000 and 432,000 years. The cycle then begins again.

kaliyuga.name: Kali Yuga
kaliyuga.desc: The present age of strife, reckoned from 3102 BCE and due to last 432,000 years.

sarasvati.name: The Sarasvatī
sarasvati.desc: The river most praised in the Ṛgveda, widely identified with the now-seasonal Ghaggar-Hakra. She is also the goddess of speech and learning.

brahmana.name: The Brāhmaṇas
brahmana.desc: Prose texts attached to each Veda that explain the meaning and performance of the sacrifices, full of early myth and speculation.

agama.name: The Āgamas
agama.desc: Scriptures of the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava and Śākta traditions that lay down temple building, image-making, initiation and daily worship.

naga.name: The Nāgā ascetics
naga.desc: Naked, weapon-bearing renouncers organised in regiments called ākhāṛās. They defended monasteries and pilgrims and still lead the bathing processions at the Kumbha.

ashvamedha.name: The Aśvamedha
ashvamedha.desc: The horse sacrifice by which a king claimed overlordship: a consecrated horse roamed for a year, and any ruler who stopped it had to fight.

calendar.name: Calendars and eras
calendar.desc: India counts years in several eras, chiefly Vikrama (from 57 BCE), Śaka (from 78 CE) and Kali (from 3102 BCE), with lunar months adjusted to the solar year.

kumbha.name: Rāṇā Kumbha
kumbha.desc: Ruler of Mewar (r. 1433–1468), a soldier, builder of Kumbhalgaṛh and the Victory Tower, and writer on music.

maharanapratap.name: Mahārāṇā Pratāp
maharanapratap.desc: The Mewar king (r. 1572–1597) who refused to submit to Akbar and fought on from the hills after Haldīghāṭī.

bajirao.name: Bājīrāv I
bajirao.desc: Peśvā from 1720 to 1740, a cavalry general said never to have lost a battle, who carried Maratha power into north India.

nanasaheb.name: Nānāsāheb
nanasaheb.desc: The name of two figures: Peśvā Bāḷājī Bājīrāv (r. 1740–1761), and the last Peśvā's adopted son who led the 1857 revolt at Kānpur.

abdali.name: Ahmad Shāh Abdālī
abdali.desc: The Afghan king who invaded India repeatedly between 1748 and 1767 and defeated the Marathas at Pānīpat in 1761.

vallabha.name: Vallabhācārya
vallabha.desc: Founder (1479–1531) of the Puṣṭi Mārga and of Śuddhādvaita, "pure non-dualism", in which the world is a real expression of Kṛṣṇa.

madhva.name: Madhvācārya
madhva.desc: Founder of Dvaita Vedānta (trad. 1238–1317), born near Uḍupi, who taught the eternal difference between God and the soul.

nimbarka.name: Nimbārka
nimbarka.desc: Founder of a Vaiṣṇava school teaching Dvaitādvaita, "difference and non-difference", and devotion to Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa together.

gajapati.name: The Gajapatis
gajapati.desc: "Lords of elephants", kings of Odisha (1434–1541) who ruled as deputies of Lord Jagannātha.

keralaschool.name: The Kerala school
keralaschool.desc: Astronomer-mathematicians from Mādhava (c. 1340–1425) onward who found infinite series for π and the trigonometric functions long before European calculus.

ramcharitmanas.name: The Rāmcaritmānas
ramcharitmanas.desc: Tulasīdāsa's retelling of the Rāma story in Avadhī (begun 1574), the most widely read scripture of north India.

savarkar.name: V. D. Sāvarkar
savarkar.desc: Revolutionary, long-term prisoner in the Andamans and author of "Hindutva" (1923), which defined Hindu identity in national and cultural terms.

malaviya.name: Madan Mohan Mālavīya
malaviya.desc: Educationist and nationalist (1861–1946), founder of Banaras Hindu University and a leader of the Hindu Mahāsabhā.

prabhupada.name: Śrīla Prabhupāda
prabhupada.desc: A. C. Bhaktivedānta Svāmī (1896–1977), who sailed to America at sixty-nine and founded ISKCON.

akshardham.name: Akṣardhām
akshardham.desc: Large temple-monuments built by BAPS in Gāndhīnagar, New Delhi and New Jersey, carved by hand in stone without structural steel.

rammohanroy.name: Rājā Rāmmohan Roy
rammohanroy.desc: Bengali reformer (1772–1833), founder of the Brāhmo Samāj, campaigner against satī and translator of the Upaniṣads.

dayananda.name: Svāmī Dayānanda Sarasvatī
dayananda.desc: Founder of the Ārya Samāj (1824–1883), who held the Vedas alone to be authoritative and attacked idolatry, child marriage and untouchability.

kashmiripandit.name: The Kashmiri Paṇḍits
kashmiripandit.desc: The Hindu community of the Kashmir Valley, heirs to its Sanskrit and Śaiva learning, most of whom were driven out in 1990.

jat.name: The Jāṭs
jat.desc: A farming community of the region around Delhi, Mathurā and Bharatpur that rose against the Mughals and founded its own kingdom.

bundela.name: The Bundelās
bundela.desc: Rajput rulers of Bundelkhand in central India, with capitals at Orchā and Pannā.

holkar.name: The Holkars
holkar.desc: The Maratha house that ruled Indore; Malhārrāv, Ahilyābāī and Yaśvantrāv are its famous names.

mahadjishinde.name: Mahādjī Śinde
mahadjishinde.desc: Maratha ruler of Gwalior (d. 1794) who restored Maratha power in north India after Pānīpat and became regent of the Mughal empire.

rishikesh.name: Ṛṣikeśa
rishikesh.desc: A town of āśrams on the Gaṅgā above Haridvāra, known today as a world centre for yoga.

mayapur.name: Māyāpur
mayapur.desc: The site in Bengal identified as Caitanya's birthplace, now the world headquarters of ISKCON.

golwalkar.name: M. S. Golvalkar
golwalkar.desc: "Guruji", second head of the RSS from 1940 to 1973.

patel.name: Sardār Patel
patel.desc: Vallabhbhāī Patel (1875–1950), India's first Home Minister, who integrated the princely states and initiated the rebuilding of Somanātha.

bhedabheda.name: Bhedābheda
bhedabheda.desc: "Difference and non-difference": a family of Vedānta views in which the soul is both distinct from and one with Brahman, as a wave is with the sea.

lakshmi.name: Lakṣmī (Śrī)
lakshmi.desc: Goddess of fortune and beauty and consort of Viṣṇu, worshipped especially at Dīpāvalī.

hanuman.name: Hanumān
hanuman.desc: The monkey hero of the Rāmāyaṇa, model of strength joined to selfless devotion.

vyasa.name: Vyāsa
vyasa.desc: The sage credited with arranging the Vedas and composing the Mahābhārata, the Purāṇas and the Brahma Sūtra. Guru Pūrṇimā is celebrated in his honour.

aryabhata.name: Āryabhaṭa
aryabhata.desc: The mathematician-astronomer (b. 476 CE) whose Āryabhaṭīya gave a value of π, a sine table and the idea that the Earth turns on its axis.

chanakya.name: Cāṇakya (Kauṭilya)
chanakya.desc: The minister who, in tradition, engineered Candragupta Maurya's rise, and the author to whom the Arthaśāstra on statecraft is ascribed.

brahmasutra.name: The Brahma Sūtra
brahmasutra.desc: Bādarāyaṇa's 555 terse aphorisms summarising the Upaniṣads. A school of Vedānta is established by writing a commentary on it.

linga.name: The liṅga
linga.desc: The aniconic "mark" of Śiva, the commonest form in which he is worshipped.

huna.name: The Hūṇas
huna.desc: Central Asian invaders, related to the Huns, who broke Gupta power in north India around 500 CE before being defeated.

harsha.name: Harṣavardhana
harsha.desc: King of Kanauj (r. 606–647) who ruled most of north India; a playwright, and host of the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang.

pala.name: The Pālas
pala.desc: Buddhist kings of Bengal and Bihar (c. 750–1160), patrons of Nālandā and Vikramaśīlā, under whom Hindu temple art also flourished.

chidambaram.name: Cidambaram
chidambaram.desc: The Tamil temple where Śiva is worshipped as Naṭarāja, lord of the cosmic dance, and as empty space.

harihara.name: Harihara
harihara.desc: A single image that is half Viṣṇu (Hari) and half Śiva (Hara), expressing the unity of the two great gods.

konark.name: Koṇārka
konark.desc: The thirteenth-century Sun temple on the Odisha coast, built as a colossal stone chariot with twenty-four carved wheels.

pandharpur.name: Paṇḍharpūr
pandharpur.desc: The town on the Bhīmā in Maharashtra where Viṭhobā, a form of Kṛṣṇa, stands on a brick; the goal of the Vārakarī pilgrimage.

nirguna.name: Nirguṇa bhakti
nirguna.desc: Devotion to a God "without attributes", beyond image and form, as taught by Kabīr and the Sants.

orchha.name: Orchā
orchha.desc: The Bundelā capital on the Betwā, where Rāma is worshipped as the reigning king.

conversion.name: Conversion
conversion.desc: Changes of religion, voluntary or forced, have been a charged subject throughout this history, as have movements to bring converts back (śuddhi).

panchayatana.name: Pañcāyatana worship
panchayatana.desc: The Smārta practice of worshipping five deities together, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Devī, Sūrya and Gaṇeśa, as forms of one reality.

vastu.name: Vāstu and Śilpa
vastu.desc: The traditional sciences of architecture and image-making, laid out in manuals that prescribe plans, proportions and rites.

dharma.name: Dharma
dharma.desc: A word with no single English equivalent: the order that upholds the world, and so duty, law, virtue and right conduct.

rivers.name: Sacred rivers
rivers.desc: Rivers are goddesses in Hindu thought, and most great tīrthas stand on their banks or at their meetings.

brahmi.name: Brāhmī
brahmi.desc: The script of Aśoka's edicts, ancestor of nearly every writing system of South and Southeast Asia.

smriti.name: Śruti and smṛti
smriti.desc: Śruti, "what is heard", is the revealed Veda. Smṛti, "what is remembered", covers the epics, Purāṇas and law books, authoritative because they rest on the Veda.

itihasa.name: Itihāsa
itihasa.desc: "Thus indeed it was": the two epics, Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata, regarded as sacred history.

yajna.name: Yajña
yajna.desc: The Vedic sacrifice, an offering into fire accompanied by mantras, from the daily household Agnihotra to great royal rites.

vaisheshika.name: Vaiśeṣika
vaisheshika.desc: The school of Kaṇāda, which analyses reality into categories such as substance, quality and motion, and holds that matter is made of eternal atoms.

kalinga.name: Kaliṅga
kalinga.desc: Ancient coastal Odisha, whose conquest changed Aśoka and whose later kings built Bhubaneśvara, Purī and Koṇārka.

satavahana.name: The Sātavāhanas
satavahana.desc: Rulers of the Deccan (c. 1st century BCE–3rd century CE) who performed Vedic sacrifices and controlled trade between north and south.

rashtrakuta.name: The Rāṣṭrakūṭas
rashtrakuta.desc: Deccan emperors (753–973) whose armies reached both Kanauj and Rāmeśvaram, and who cut the Kailāsa temple at Ellora from a single rock.

paramara.name: The Paramāras
paramara.desc: Rajput kings of Mālwā (9th–14th century), ruling from Dhārā; Bhoja was the most famous.

khalji.name: The Khaljīs
khalji.desc: Delhi sultans (1290–1320). Alauddin Khaljī conquered Gujarat and Rajasthan and sent raids to the far south.

rathore.name: The Rāṭhoṛs
rathore.desc: The Rajput clan of Mārwāṛ (Jodhpur) and Bikaner.

nizam.name: The Nizām
nizam.desc: Title of the rulers of Hyderabad, the largest of the Mughal successor states, from 1724 to 1948.

mysore.name: Mysore
mysore.desc: The southern kingdom of the Wodeyar dynasty, famed for its Dasarā festival and its patronage of Sanskrit, music and yoga.

kannauj.name: Kanauj (Kānyakubja)
kannauj.desc: The imperial city of north India from Harṣa's time to the twelfth century, fought over by Pratihāras, Pālas and Rāṣṭrakūṭas.

thanjavur.name: Tañjāvūr
thanjavur.desc: Cōḻa capital in the Kāverī delta, later ruled by Nāyakas and Marathas, a home of temple architecture, bronze casting, music and dance.

solanki.name: The Solaṅkīs (Caulukyas)
solanki.desc: Kings of Gujarat (c. 940–1244), builders of the Modhera Sun temple and the Rāṇī-kī-Vāv stepwell.

chandela.name: The Candellas
chandela.desc: Rajput kings of Bundelkhand (9th–13th century), builders of Khajurāho.

kakatiya.name: The Kākatīyas
kakatiya.desc: Telugu kings of Warangal (c. 1163–1323), builders of the Rāmappa temple.

ahom.name: The Ahoms
ahom.desc: A dynasty of Tai origin that ruled Assam for six hundred years (1228–1826), adopted Hinduism and defeated repeated Mughal invasions.

yadava.name: The Yādavas
yadava.desc: Kṛṣṇa's clan in the epics; also the medieval dynasty of Devagiri in Maharashtra (1187–1317) under which Marathi literature began.

magadha.name: Magadha
magadha.desc: The kingdom in southern Bihar from which the Nandas, Mauryas and Guptas built their empires.

mithila.name: Mithilā
mithila.desc: The land of King Janaka and Sītā in north Bihar, a stronghold of logic and Vedic learning for two thousand years.

dwarka.name: Dvārakā
dwarka.desc: Kṛṣṇa's city on the western sea, one of the four dhāmas and seven sacred cities.

assam.name: Assam
assam.desc: The Brahmaputra valley, ancient Kāmarūpa, home of the Kāmākhyā temple, the Ahom kingdom and Śaṅkaradeva's Vaiṣṇava movement.

pune.name: Pune
pune.desc: Seat of the Peśvās in the eighteenth century and afterwards a centre of education, reform and nationalism.

kerala.name: Kerala
kerala.desc: The south-western coast, with its own temple arts, Vedic ritual traditions and schools of astronomy and medicine.

odisha.name: Odisha
odisha.desc: The eastern coastal land of Jagannātha, with a distinctive school of temple architecture at Bhubaneśvara, Purī and Koṇārka.

punjab.name: Punjab
punjab.desc: The land of five rivers, heart of the Ṛgvedic world, later the gateway for every invasion from the northwest and the home of the Sikhs.

gujarat.name: Gujarat
gujarat.desc: The western coastal region of Dvārakā and Somanātha, long enriched by sea trade.

bauddha.name: Buddhism
bauddha.desc: The path taught by the Buddha in the 5th century BCE. It does not accept the Veda, and its long debate with Hindu schools sharpened both.

decline.name: Decline of a power
decline.desc: Dynasties here usually fall by a mix of succession disputes, overstretch and rivals' rise; the tag marks those turning points.

inscription.name: Inscriptions
inscription.desc: Records cut in stone or copper are the firmest evidence for early Indian history, since most carry dates, names and places.

kavya.name: Kāvya
kavya.desc: Ornate Sanskrit court poetry and drama, prized for suggestion, sound and emotional flavour (rasa).

painting.name: Painting
painting.desc: From the murals of Ajaṇṭā to Rajput and Pahāṛī miniatures, Indian painting has mostly illustrated sacred story and poetry.

java.name: Java
java.desc: The Indonesian island whose kings built Prambanan and wrote their own Rāmāyaṇa in Old Javanese.

bali.name: Bali
bali.desc: The Indonesian island where Hindu Dharma has continued unbroken to the present.

heritage.name: Heritage listing
heritage.desc: Formal recognition, national or international, of a monument or practice as worth protecting.

asi.name: The Archaeological Survey of India
asi.desc: The government body, founded in 1861, that excavates and conserves India's ancient sites and monuments.

trade.name: Trade
trade.desc: Merchants carried Indian goods, scripts and gods along the sea lanes to Rome, Arabia and Southeast Asia.

medicine.name: Medicine
medicine.desc: See Āyurveda: India's classical medical tradition and its later regional forms such as Tamil Siddha medicine.

archaeology.name: Archaeology
archaeology.desc: What is known of the ages before texts comes from excavation, and new digs still revise the picture.

education.name: Learning and teaching
education.desc: From forest hermitages and temple schools to universities ancient and modern.

reform.name: Reform
reform.desc: Movements from within Hindu society against practices such as untouchability, child marriage and the bar on widow remarriage.

nationalism.name: Nationalism
nationalism.desc: The modern movement for Indian self-rule drew heavily on Hindu symbols, texts and festivals.

revolutionary.name: The revolutionaries
revolutionary.desc: Those who took up arms against British rule; many drew courage from the Gītā.

sculpture.name: Sculpture
sculpture.desc: Images of the gods were carved to strict rules of proportion and gesture so that they could serve as bodies for the divine.

coins.name: Coins
coins.desc: Ancient coins often show deities and royal titles, and so date both kings and cults.

cave.name: Rock-cut architecture
cave.desc: Temples and monasteries excavated from living rock, at their height between the 5th and 9th centuries.

drama.name: Sanskrit drama
drama.desc: Plays mixing prose and verse, Sanskrit and Prakrit, governed by the Nāṭyaśāstra's theory of rasa.

logic.name: Logic
logic.desc: Indian logic studied how inference works and what counts as proof, in debate between Hindu, Buddhist and Jaina thinkers.

pilgrimage.name: Tīrtha-yātrā: pilgrimage
pilgrimage.desc: Travel to sacred "crossings", rivers, mountains and temples, open to everyone and praised as equal to great sacrifices.

commentary.name: Commentary
commentary.desc: Most Indian thinking was done by commenting on earlier texts; an original idea usually arrives as an explanation of an old line.

translation.name: Translation
translation.desc: The passage of Sanskrit works into Persian, Arabic, European and Indian languages changed how the world, and Indians, saw them.

printing.name: Printing
printing.desc: From the nineteenth century, presses put scriptures once kept by a few into the hands of anyone who could read.

mission.name: Christian missions
mission.desc: Missionary preaching and criticism under colonial rule provoked both reform and self-defence among Hindus.

british.name: British rule
british.desc: From the Company's rise after 1757 to independence in 1947.

portuguese.name: The Portuguese
portuguese.desc: The first European power in India, from 1498, ruling Goa and coastal enclaves.

navy.name: Sea power
navy.desc: Indian rulers such as the Cōḻas and Marathas built fleets; the tag follows that maritime thread.

invasion.name: Invasion
invasion.desc: Armies entering the subcontinent, usually through the northwestern passes.

caste.name: Caste
caste.desc: The division of society into birth groups. Its scriptural basis, its injustices and its reform are debated throughout this timeline.

seva.name: Sevā: service
seva.desc: Service of others as service of God, the motive behind much modern Hindu charity.

ecology.name: Reverence for nature
ecology.desc: Hymns to Earth and rivers, and communities that died defending trees, show an old ethic of protection.

nayaka.name: The Nāyakas
nayaka.desc: Former Vijayanagara governors who ruled Madurai, Tañjāvūr and other southern states in the 16th–18th centuries.

anglomaratha.name: The Anglo-Maratha wars
anglomaratha.desc: Three wars (1775–82, 1803–05, 1817–18) by which the East India Company broke the Maratha confederacy.

simhastha.name: Siṃhastha
simhastha.desc: The Kumbha Melā held when Jupiter is in Leo (siṃha), at Ujjain and at Nāsik–Tryambakeśvara.

tughlaq.name: The Tughlaqs
tughlaq.desc: Delhi sultans (1320–1414) whose armies destroyed the southern kingdoms; revolt against them gave rise to Vijayanagara.

ghazni.name: Ghazni
ghazni.desc: The Afghan city from which Mahmūd raided India in the early eleventh century.

hindushahi.name: The Hindu Śāhis
hindushahi.desc: Kings of Kabul and Gandhāra (c. 843–1026) who for two centuries bore the brunt of invasions from the west.

arab.name: The Arabs in Sindh
arab.desc: Arab armies conquered Sindh in 712 but were stopped from advancing further by Indian kingdoms.

martyr.name: Martyrdom
martyr.desc: Those remembered for choosing death over giving up their faith or cause.

revolt.name: Revolt
revolt.desc: Uprisings against imperial or colonial power.

kangra.name: Kāṅgṛā
kangra.desc: A Himalayan hill kingdom with the old goddess shrines of Vajreśvarī and Jvālāmukhī, later famous for its painting.

gwalior.name: Gwalior
gwalior.desc: A fortress city of central India with temples from the 8th to 11th centuries and a great tradition of music.

bhubaneswar.name: Bhubaneśvara
bhubaneswar.desc: Odisha's "city of temples", where the Kaliṅga style can be followed from the 7th to the 13th century.

khmer.name: The Khmer empire
khmer.desc: The Cambodian empire of Angkor (9th–15th century), whose kings built vast temples to Śiva and Viṣṇu.

champa.name: Champa
champa.desc: The Hindu kingdoms of the Cham people on the coast of Vietnam, devoted chiefly to Śiva.

badami.name: Bādāmi
badami.desc: The early Cālukya capital in Karnataka, with four cave temples cut into a sandstone cliff.

aihole.name: Aihoḷe
aihole.desc: A village in Karnataka with over a hundred early temples, an open-air laboratory of temple design.

ajmer.name: Ajmer
ajmer.desc: The Cauhān capital in Rajasthan, close to the sacred lake of Puṣkara.

jaipur.name: Jaipur
jaipur.desc: The planned capital of the Kacchavāha Rajputs, founded in 1727.

kolkata.name: Kolkata (Calcutta)
kolkata.desc: Capital of British India until 1911 and the stage of the Bengal Renaissance.

nashik.name: Nāsik
nashik.desc: The city on the Godāvarī linked with Rāma's exile at Pañcavaṭī, and a Kumbha site.

kurukshetra.name: Kurukṣetra
kurukshetra.desc: The plain north of Delhi revered as the "field of dharma", site of the Mahābhārata war and the Gītā.

indus.name: The Indus (Sindhu)
indus.desc: The great river of the northwest. Its Persian name, Hindu, eventually became the name of a people and a land.

mohenjodaro.name: Mohenjo-daro
mohenjodaro.desc: The largest excavated city of the Indus civilization, in Sindh.

harappa.name: Harappa
harappa.desc: The Punjab site whose excavation in 1921 revealed the Indus civilization.

dholavira.name: Dholavira
dholavira.desc: A Harappan city in Kutch, remarkable for its reservoirs and stone architecture.
